R1529.decision_summary: The x-axis can be UTC time (Qt QDateTimeAxis, d3 scaleUtc). pinion-chart had two axis kinds and neither is the axis a monitoring chart actually has: a timestamp reaching either was a plain number. The time axis is AFFINE, so unlike the log axis it reuses LinearScale untouched and adds no arithmetic at all - which is the finding, because everything that makes it a distinct kind lives in its ticks and its labels. Both were wrong: the nice-number step is a DECIMAL quantiser and time above a second is mixed-radix, so a one-hour domain got gridlines at 00:06:40; and the label compacted by magnitude, which at the giga scale has 27-hour resolution, so every tick of a sub-day axis rendered as the same string. An axis kind is therefore more than its arithmetic - the two-layer split of R1528 is what let a third kind land without touching the affine core.
changes_bullets: civil.rs (new): Hinnant's days_from_civil / civil_from_days, the proleptic-Gregorian pair C++20 <chrono> is specified against, plus the field breakdown and month/year arithmetic they compose into. Hand-rolled with the citation rather than pulled from a date crate: pinion-chart depends on pinion-core and nothing else, and what a time axis needs from a calendar is two total functions over an integer day count, not a parser, a formatter and a tzdb.

ticks.rs: time_ticks over d3's tickIntervals ladder (1s..3mo, with a whole-year stride above it), nice_time_domain, format_time_tick (multi-resolution: the finest calendar field that is not already zero) and format_time_stamp (the unambiguous readout form).

The nice-number ladder is a DECIMAL quantiser. Its 1/2/5x10^n step assumes the quantity subdivides by powers of ten, which held for every axis the crate had, so the assumption was never visible. Above a second time is mixed-radix, so the step is not coarser but wrong. Note the ladder is bracketed by nice_step at BOTH ends - below a second and above a year the decimal quantiser is still right - so the mixed-radix region is exactly second-to-year.

scale.rs: ValueScale::Time(LinearScale) and AxisKind{Linear,Log,Time}. Time is affine, so it reuses the arithmetic core untouched; what makes it a kind is entirely its ticks and labels. AxisKind replaces the is_log bool and the Option<f64> base, which is what a boolean discriminator always is: an encoding that fits exactly two arms.

TickFormat::readout, for a value that stands ALONE. A tick label is relative - it names only what distinguishes it from its neighbours - so out of its row it is ambiguous. The distinction reached this round already spelled differently in the timeline and the line chart, and a rule with two spellings is two rules.
timeline.rs: Timeline::time_axis, the machinery's second consumer. Its ruler was the crate's most literally time-shaped view and could only be a number line.
examples/hello-time-chart (new, 6 tests) + tools/demos/r1529_time_axis.py (40 assertion sites): four hours of incident latency straddling midnight, one click between numeric and time.
verification_bullets: The defect was measured before it was fixed, and it is two defects. On a one-hour epoch-millisecond domain the decimal step is 16m40s, putting gridlines at 00:06:40 and 00:23:20; and format_si compacts an epoch millisecond to 1772.4G, which at one decimal has 27-hour resolution, so all six gridlines print the same string. Both are pinned as counterfactuals in the unit tests, and both on screen in the example: nine gridlines, one distinct label.

Every expected tick set was derived from an INDEPENDENT oracle (Python datetime) before being written into a Rust assertion, so the tests could not be read off the implementation. All matched on the first run.

Because that agreement is itself suspicious, the assertions were mutation-tested one change at a time: geometric rung nearness -> arithmetic, Monday week alignment -> epoch weekday, calendar months -> a fixed 30-day stride, and the label cascade -> a single HH:MM format. Each mutation is caught by the test that names the property, and the geometric-nearness case needed a NEW test - the spans in hand all landed on a rung exactly, where the two comparisons agree and neither is under test.

Reference dates were checked against date -u. One assertion failed on the first run and the algorithm was right: the hardcoded expectation was wrong (1772582400000 is 2026-03-04, not 03-02). The exhaustive inverse over 1583..2400 - every leap rule, including 1700/1800/1900 common and 1600/2000 leap - passed throughout.

The example test found a real defect in this round's own work: the line chart's scrub header was still using the axis tick format, so a time axis reported 23:50 with no day. Fixed at the crate level by TickFormat::readout rather than per chart, which also collapsed the duplicate spelling in the timeline.

The demo's discriminator is the LABELS, not the spacing: gridlines are evenly spaced on both axes, and that is asserted on both, so a spacing-only check would prove nothing. The y-axis labels are captured on both kinds and required identical, so a change that timed both axes would fail rather than look like a success.

Local gates: pinion-chart 274 tests + 2 doc-tests and hello-time-chart 6 tests pass, 22 of them new r1529 units; clippy -D pedantic clean; every pre-existing pinion-chart test passes unchanged, which is what makes this a generalisation rather than a rewrite.

Consumer regression: demos r1406_crosshair, r1528_log_axis, r1377_scatter_scrub, r1389_frame_timeline and r1413_transport pass unchanged - the scrub-header and timeline-ruler paths this round rewired.
carry_forward_bullets: The axis is UTC only. A local-time axis needs a timezone database, and - the reason it is not merely deferred - it would make every axis test read the host's configuration, which is the R1500 failure class. d3 draws the same line with scaleUtc beside scaleTime; this crate has the UTC half.

Month and day names are the C-locale abbreviations, matching the decimal separator and SI suffixes the crate already emits. Locale-aware formatting is a crate-wide concern that would need the same treatment in every readout, so it is recorded rather than decided inside the tick formatter.

A time axis contributes no minor gridlines. A log axis NEEDS them - without the subdivisions its evenly-spaced decade lines read as a linear axis with odd labels - whereas a time axis's labels name the calendar directly. Legibility requirement versus decoration, so the silence is deliberate; hour subdivisions inside a day axis are a real future slice.

The bar chart and the sparkline still use LinearScale directly rather than ValueScale, so neither can take a time axis. For the bar that is right (its x is a categorical slot, not a number); for the sparkline it is simply not wired.

Two-day ticks stride uniformly from the epoch rather than resetting each month as d3's timeDay.every(2) does. Uniform has no month-end anomaly, and any offset choice is arbitrary; recorded because it is a visible divergence from the cited reference.

The Steps duplication between line.rs and scatter.rs, carried from R1528, is untouched and now has a third field-type change behind it. The crate's own two-consumer rule still defers the split; a third numeric-x chart settles it.

R1530.decision_summary: The data grid asks for the header sections it paints (Qt headerData). R1523 windowed which header cells reach the tree and R1524 made the cell contract per-cell, but the labels were never asked for at all: they arrived as a slice of every column, because VirtualTableData read its column count off that slice's length. The extent was welded to the labels, so a 200-column grid could not learn its own width without being handed all 200 names - and built them twice a frame, once for the paint and once for the a11y pass. Qt separates the two (columnCount is a number, headerData is an accessor) and so does this: column_count beside item_count, header beside cell in a GridModel. The row axis never had the defect, which is the tell - one axis had been given the contract and the other had not, and 786 rounds of grid work went past the asymmetry because no grid in the tree was wide enough for it to cost anything.
changes_bullets: VirtualTableData::headers (&[&str], every column) becomes column_count: usize. The row axis has always carried item_count, a number beside a windowed accessor; the column axis carried a slice and read its extent off that slice's length. That weld is the whole defect: a grid could only learn how many columns it had by being handed every one of their names, so a 200-column binding materialized 200 String a frame to paint five - and again for the a11y pass.

GridModel { cell, header } replaces the bare cell argument. Qt answers both from one QAbstractItemModel (data(index) / headerData(section, orientation)) and they are the same kind of thing: an accessor invoked once per painted unit. Bundling them also keeps view_virtual_table at seven arguments, which is what forced the question of whether they belong together.

header_texts + GridRender::header_band: the three panes that paint a header band (unsplit, and the frozen split's pinned + scrolling) share one path, so none can ask for a section it will not paint. The span is DERIVED from the pane's ColumnLayout rather than passed beside it - every pane's sections are exactly col_base..col_base + widths.len(), so a second statement of it could only disagree.

header_from_slice: the accessor for a grid whose labels are a fixed const array, which eleven bindings have. Mechanical wiring with no per-binding opinion, so obligation 3b lifts it rather than leaving eleven copies. It does not reintroduce the defect: a &'static array is already there and costs nothing per frame; a computed 200-column axis passes a closure.

pinion-a11y windowed_grid_nodes_wide takes the WINDOWED labels plus an explicit column_count, and GridColumns::windowed becomes ::window. R1523's clamp existed because the labels and the window arrived separately and a bad slice would panic the walker; there is no slice left to get wrong, so the failure is unrepresentable rather than handled.

hello-virtual-columns publishes a second readout (vcol_hstatus) counting header requests, separate from R1524's cell counter. The two axes cost differently - cells scale with both windows, sections with one - and a single total would let a regression on either hide inside the other.
verification_bullets: Set EQUALITY in both directions, not a threshold, on both the paint and the a11y path: the sections asked for and the sections painted are the same set. A <= bound would pass a grid that asks for too few and paints blanks under real columns.

Measured, not recalled: the same fixture at a wide viewport asks for 200 sections and at the 560px one asks for 5 (40x), and hello-virtual-columns' readout shows 7 of 200 at boot. The pre-R1530 number is what the wide viewport produces, because a whole-table slice was viewport-independent by construction.

Counts alone cannot see a pane asking with a pane-relative index - it would ask for exactly as many sections as it paints. So every painted header is held against the label of the ABSOLUTE column it is tagged with, at four offset/frozen combinations in the unit tests and six in the demo.

Six counterfactuals, injected one at a time (R1439): ask for the whole table then slice; the scrolling pane asks with rel instead of abs; the extent stops at the first blank label; the frozen pane asks twice; the a11y pass builds all 200; and the whole-table shape run against the demo end to end. Each is caught, and each by a different assertion - the absolute-address test and the split test both catch the rel/abs one, which is the pair that would otherwise be redundant.

The a11y counterfactual is the one a paint-only counter would have missed: access_node built all 200 labels too, so the defect lived twice and the round would have half-closed it while reporting success.

tools/demos/r1530_headers_asked_for.py: 276 assertions executed (measured with trace --count, not estimated), PASS. It also asserts axis independence - scrolling ROWS changes the cell count and leaves the section count identical - which is why there are two readouts rather than one sum.

Local gates: 1066 tests across the 14 changed packages (pinion-widget-paint, pinion-a11y, 12 example bindings) and clippy -D pedantic clean on all of them. Twenty demos covering those examples pass against freshly rebuilt binaries.

r786_grid_resize_drag fails locally and was confirmed pre-existing by stashing this round's work and rebuilding: it needs native pointer injection through a visible window, the CI-only class the SEED lists. NOT verified green by this round.
carry_forward_bullets: The eager view_table still takes headers: &[&str]. That is right for it - it builds every row anyway - but it means the tree now has two header contracts, and a reader of TableData will not find the per-section one next to it.

GridModel::header returns a String and has no role dimension. Qt's headerData takes Qt::DisplayRole / EditRole / DecorationRole / ToolTipRole, and so does data(); the cell accessor has the same gap. This is now the largest remaining Model/View gap and it is one gap, not two.

The a11y builders other than windowed_grid_nodes_wide still take every label. Correct today - their consumers hold const arrays of at most ten - but the column-window contract exists in only one of the six, so a second wide consumer will have to widen the family rather than use it.

The header row's a11y bounds and the paint band are still assembled from two separate reads of the same window in the binding. R1530 gave them one label source; the window itself is still stated twice.

The tally reports DECLARED AHEAD for this round until the commit lands, and may then demand a re-judgment of the Model/View axis as R1527-R1529 were demanded. That re-judgment is structurally a follow-up commit, not part of this one.

R1558.decision_summary: R1558 §5.16 §5.18 §5.34 — a profile is rooted where you ask. R1557 attributes a frame per subtree and does it for the whole window every time; its only narrowing knob, depth, trims the REPLY after a full window has been re-encoded, so 'profile this panel' was a question you asked by profiling everything and reading one row. path is the other axis: it names a subtree by the same address every profile row already publishes and scopes the MEASUREMENT — only that subtree is re-encoded, only its nodes are attributed, and nodes_total itself shrinks, which is how the two axes are told apart from outside. That makes the profiler a bisection tool, each drill-down costing less than the last. It rests on one property of the ENCODER, asserted rather than assumed: a subtree's draw work is independent of the context it is drawn in — an inherited transform moves coordinates and changes no count (R1520 already relies on this), an ancestor's clip is an input to damage reporting rather than a cull, and a Scroll's clip layer is charged to the scroll's own row. Qt has no floor here at all: QSG_RENDERER_DEBUG dumps every batch to stderr unscoped, and Qt Quick's batch renderer MERGES geometry across items, so per-item cost is not even compositional there. Reaching for the address found a real defect underneath: the address vocabulary was bound to the wrong window registry. path::resolve validates a prefix against the SCE topology while the windows a host actually has open are the shell's WindowSpec slots — sets that differ whenever a binding opens a second window without a second AppState — so R1557 published /window[inspector]/… rows that no path-taking method could read back. Split into split_window_prefix (syntax) plus a registry judgment, this method now judges against the live slots, and a request naming two different windows is refused rather than silently resolved.
changes_bullets: `pinion-rpc` `path`: `split_window_prefix` (new) answers the PREFIX SYNTAX
question with no registry consulted; `resolve` is now that plus the SCE
lookup. `segments` lifted here when `draw_profile` became the third site to
split a scene tail (`split_at_external`, `locate::parse_segments`), and
`preview::kinds::scene_segments` — a fourth, hand-rolled copy under a doc
conceding it mirrored `resolve` — now routes through both.
`pinion-rpc` `resolve`: `lookup_addressed_chain` (new) answers the node AND
the chain that addresses it; `lookup_addressed` is it, projected. The two
differ under the root alias, where the query is one segment and the chain
is empty.
`pinion-runtime` `draw_profile`: `DrawProfile::scope` records the chain the
walk was rooted at; `DrawProfiler::finish` takes it, so no order of calls
forgets it.
`pinion-shell` `ShellCore::draw_profile_for_window` takes a scope, resolves
it against the painted scene and re-encodes ONLY that subtree; an address
that reaches no node is an `Err` carried to the wire, not a `None` the
dispatcher would report as "no profile". `AppShell` parses the params once
and judges an addressed window against its LIVE slots.
`pinion-rpc` `draw_profile`: `path` param + `ProfileScope`; `nodes_total`
now states what was MEASURED; the reply echoes `path`; `DrawProfileParams::
window` is the ONE window rule both the embedder and the projection call;
new `UnknownPath` / `UnknownWindow` / `WindowMismatch` / `Path` errors. The
row projection is seeded from the profile's own scope.
`pinion-rpc` `wire_census`: `DrawProfileOutcome.path`, string|null.
`tools/demos/r1558_profile_is_rooted_where_you_ask.py`;
`r1557_...py` outcome key set gains `path`; `docs/phase-b-rounds.tsv` 1558.
verification_bullets: `cargo test` on every changed crate: `pinion-rpc` 1101 + wire-census 4,
`pinion-runtime` (vello) 657, `pinion-shell` all suites. `cargo clippy` on
the three, `cargo fmt --all --check`, and `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps
--document-private-items` all clean.
`r1558_profile_is_rooted_where_you_ask.py` PASS. Neighbours re-run and
PASS: r1557 (its key-set assertion updated), r1484 (the preview address
path whose segment splitter was lifted).
Compositionality asserted against a REAL encode, not a fixture: a subtree
profiled alone equals the whole profile's row for it, node for node, in all
six units — and again with that subtree nested under a scrolled, offset,
clipping ancestor, which is the case that breaks first if an inherited
transform or an ancestor clip changed a count.
Counterfactuals, one at a time, 8 run, 8 caught. CF1 (producer ignores the
scope) was FIRST RUN INVALID: the mutation left a variable unused, `-D
warnings` failed the release build, and the demo harness — which builds
before launch — reported a build refusal that read as a behavioural catch.
Re-run in a compiling form it is caught by the demo's node-for-node subtree
comparison. Every revert is verified by SHA-256 against a pristine copy.
CF3 (the resolver echoes the query instead of the chain) is caught by the
unit test ONLY: the root alias needs a tagged scene root, and the paint
root is the shell's composition root, which four probed bindings show
carries no tag. Recorded rather than overclaimed.
Measured: on `hello-scene-scale` the scopes PARTITION the frame — each root
child profiled separately plus the root's own `own` reproduces the frame's
census field for field; `path` shrinks `nodes_total` where `depth` does
not; a 1e2 -> 1e6 model leaves a scoped profile byte-identical while the
eager arm's grows 5x. On `hello-multi-window` an address selects the window
on its own, and naming two different windows at once is refused.
carry_forward_bullets: The other five `path::resolve` callers still judge a path's window against
the SCE topology rather than the live slots — `locate::bbox`, `screenshot`,
`snapshot`, `resolve_external_path`, `layout_query`. Not mechanical: every
one of them parses the window and then DISCARDS it, so the fix is deciding
what a path's window MEANS to a method that ignores it (select the dispatch
window, the unfinished R16 slice, or require agreement with `{window: …}`).
A semantic change across five shipped methods; recorded at `path::resolve`.
No general reader for a profile row's address still. This method is now one
reader of it, and `scene/layout`'s `path` filter is still accepted and
ignored (R47.7.x).
Per-node replay status is still absent — the profile re-encodes into a cold
cache by design, so it cannot say which subtrees the LIVE frame replayed.
The root alias is unreachable from a paint-scene-rooted profile today
(the paint root carries no tag), so `DrawProfile::scope` is exercised on
the wire only in its identity form.
`scene/locate` answers `OutOfBounds` at every point of `hello-scene-scale`
(pre-existing, R1557): the hit-test root has zero area, so the spatial half
of "point at it, then profile it" does not close on that binding.

R1559.decision_summary: R1559 §5.36 §5.40 §5.12 — an item is numbered by its place among its siblings. Everything else a list has can be written by hand: the indent is a margin, the bullet is a glyph. The NUMBER cannot, because it is not a property of the item — it is a property of the item's position among its siblings, so inserting one item renumbers every item after it, and nesting one restarts the inner sequence while the outer one carries on underneath. R1551 named `QTextList` first among what was left of the document model, and this is it: a `ListSpec` declares MEMBERSHIP (a format, a depth) and never a number, `number_blocks` derives the numbering by the grouping rule HTML and CommonMark already use, and `view_document` rebuilds the derived runs into real container nodes — so a list is an object with a box, and a nested list is inset by its PARENT's gutter with no level arithmetic anywhere. Five things past Qt 6.11, all read over the wire. (1) The counter styles have RANGES and fall back: Roman numerals have no standard form past 3999 — a fact about the notation, not about any toolkit — and Qt's `itemText()` answers "?" there, losing the value; CSS Counter Styles Level 3 renders through the fallback style, so item 4000 reads `4000.` and `rendered_as` / `fell_back` name the notation that wrote it, which is what keeps it distinguishable from a list that declared `decimal`. (2) A BULLET IS TEXT. Qt's `QTextDocumentLayout` draws `ListDisc` / `ListCircle` / `ListSquare` as an ellipse or a rectangle, so no Qt API can say what an unordered marker looks like and it is not in the text at all; here every style renders to a string, which is the whole reason one painter draws every marker, the cell backend needed no list code, and a marker has a tag and a published box. (3) The list structure is ENUMERABLE: `scene/text_lists` answers what lists are on screen, in what order, numbered how, where each marker landed — Qt has no such accessor, so finding a `QTextDocument`'s lists means walking every block, calling `textList()` and de-duplicating pointers, in-process. (4) It reaches ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY: `list` / `listitem` with `aria-posinset` / `aria-setsize` / `aria-level`, where `QAccessibleTextInterface` — the interface a `QTextEdit` implements — has no method that reports block structure at all, so a Qt document's lists stop at its layout, and its bullets are not even characters an AT could read. (5) A suffix's default belongs to the STYLE: Qt hides "unset" in a null `QString`, a distinction no serialization carries; here `number_suffix` is an `Option` and the wire publishes both the resolved string and whether it came from the style. The numbering rides the painted node, so the marker on screen, the `aria-posinset` an AT hears and the census an agent reads are one computation with no second source. Reaching for it also retired `attach_block_headings`'s private scene walk onto `Scene::for_each_text_leaf` — the same traversal, whose load-bearing `Scroll` arm R1536 measured the cost of getting wrong.
changes_bullets: `pinion-core` `text_list` (new): `ListStyle` (Qt's eight `QTextListFormat`
arms = CSS's eight predefined counter styles), each with the RANGE its
notation has and a `fallback` outside it; `ListFormat` (Qt
`QTextListFormat`) with `number_suffix: Option`, so "the style's default"
is a state the type shows; `ListSpec` (authored membership),
`ListPlacement` (derived place), `ListRun` / `ListNumbering`.
`number_blocks` is the derivation: a flat block sequence plus depths ->
one marker per item, one run per list, by the grouping rule HTML and
CommonMark already use.
`pinion-core` `TextNode::list` + `with_list_placement`; `DocumentTag::list`
/ `item` / `marker`.
`pinion-widget-paint` `document`: `TextBlock::in_list`; `view_document`
numbers once and rebuilds the runs into real container nodes, so a list
has a box and a nested list is inset by its PARENT's gutter. A marker is
an ordinary `TextNode`, end-aligned in a gutter of the declared width.
`pinion-a11y` `list` (new): `attach_block_lists` emits `list` /
`listitem` with `aria-posinset` / `aria-setsize` / `aria-level`, wired
into `build_access_tree` after the heading pass. `heading`'s private
recursive walk retired onto `Scene::for_each_text_leaf`.
`pinion-rpc` `text_lists` (new): `scene/text_lists` — one row per list,
its items in order, each marker's text, ordinal and PAINTED box;
`fell_back` names a CSS range fallback. `scene/snapshot`'s text node
carries the placement. `wire_census` gains the three types;
`snapshot_node_to_json`'s text arm lifted to its own function.
`examples/hello-richtext-list`;
`tools/demos/r1559_list_numbering.py`; `docs/phase-b-rounds.tsv` 1559.
verification_bullets: `cargo test` on every changed crate: `pinion-core` 2998, `pinion-rpc`
1109 + wire-census 4, `pinion-a11y` 270, `pinion-widget-paint` 800,
`pinion-shell`, `pinion-tui`, both example crates. 32 suites, 0 failures.
`cargo clippy` on all eight, `cargo fmt --all --check`, and `cargo doc
--workspace --no-deps --document-private-items` all clean.
`r1559_list_numbering.py` PASS, 83 assertions. Neighbour re-run and
PASS: `r1551_block_format.py` (same composition, same a11y assembler,
and `scene/snapshot`'s text node gained a key).
Counterfactuals, one at a time, 8 run, 8 caught, every revert verified by
md5 against a pristine copy and rebuilt before the next. CF1 constant
position, CF2 a deeper item closes its parent, CF3 Qt's "?" instead of
the CSS fallback, CF4 the a11y pass unwired, CF5 no painted marker node,
CF6 a list's count is the document's, CF7 a style-blind suffix default,
CF8 every paragraph an item.
The renumbering is asserted through PAINTED markers addressed by their
paragraph's TEXT, not by block index: inserting a step shifts every later
index, so a test keyed on indices would assert against its own subject.
The §2 #6 claim is the consumer's: the same laid-out scene painted
through the cell backend contains `1.` `2.` `3.` the bullet
`MMMCMXCIX.` and `4000.`, with no list code in `pinion-tui` at all.
carry_forward_bullets: `QTextTable` and `setMarkdown` / `toHtml` are still absent, and with
`QTextList` closed they are what is left of the document model. Neither
has a scene primitive.
`QTextListFormat::marker` (the CSS `::marker` content override) is not
taken: it belongs with the list-item half of `QTextBlockFormat` and would
be a second way to say what `number_prefix` / `number_suffix` say.
`list-style-position: inside` is not expressible. It would prepend the
marker to the paragraph's own text, which shifts every `StyleRun` byte
range in that paragraph — a run-remap design, not an omission. Qt has no
equivalent either, so this is at parity.
A list's `count` and `format` are restated on every one of its items
because a `TextNode` is the only carrier the scene has. One derivation
writes all of them so they cannot disagree, and the census folds them
back into one row, but the redundancy is real and is what a scene-level
group node would remove.
`scene/text_blocks` does not report a paragraph's list placement.
Deliberate — a list's defining facts are not any one paragraph's — but it
means an agent joining "where did this line land" to "which item is it"
makes two calls.

R1569.decision_summary: R1569 §5.39 §5.20 §5.15 §2 #6 — THE FOCUSED WIDGET CAN SHADOW THE WINDOW'S ACCELERATOR LAYERS. A window's accelerators fire from anywhere in it regardless of focus, which is what an accelerator IS and is wrong for the widget being typed into. pinion has two such layers — R1543's mnemonic map and the binding's `WidgetCore::keybinding` character map — and both ran ahead of the focused widget with no way to say otherwise. Qt HAS the hatch (`QEvent::ShortcutOverride`, which `QLineEdit` accepts for any unmodified printable key: if it would be text, it is mine), so this is one of the places the tree sat BELOW the floor rather than above it — and the consequence was SHIPPED, not theoretical. Measured over the wire before anything changed: in `hello-textfield`, which binds `d` to Disable, typing `d` into the FOCUSED field disabled the field and the character never arrived. Four bindings carried it. R1543's own doc had recorded the escape as "the absence of a declaration — a widget that wants Alt+F for itself simply does not publish a mnemonic on it", and that escape is available only to a widget that OWNS the colliding declaration; a text field does not own the binding's `keybinding("d")` and a key-sequence editor does not own the File menu's Alt+F. THE SHAPE IS A QUESTION THE ROUTER ASKS, not an event a widget must accept, and the difference is not stylistic: Qt's override must be accepted on EVERY press, so a widget that forgets the `event()` arm loses exactly the presses that collide with a shortcut — invisible until someone adds the colliding shortcut, in another file, possibly years later. And a question can be evaluated WITHOUT a keystroke, which is what makes `scene/accelerators` possible: what each declared accelerator would do right now, which are shadowed, and BY WHOM. Qt can answer none of it — `QShortcutMap` is private and the override is transient and anonymous. THE DECLARATION IS PER CHORD because the right answer differs by chord for the same widget, and the round's two consumers prove it: a text field claims a bare `d` (it is text) but NOT Alt+F (a mnemonic still works while typing, as in Qt), while `KeySequenceEdit` — Qt's `QKeySequenceEdit`, the widget whose entire job is to record a chord that already means something — claims everything while recording. PAST QT ON THE WIDGET, four things: recording is a state the user CHOSE (`record` / `cancel` are events, where Qt starts on focus-in and stops only on a private 1-second timer, so a Qt keymap editor cannot stop grabbing while focused); a modifier-only press is a PUBLISHED PREFIX rather than a silent early return; overflow is a NAMED refusal carrying the chord that did not fit, where `setKeySequence` truncates silently; and a chord's collision is answerable BEFORE it is recorded, where `QKeySequenceEdit` records it and the collision surfaces later at dispatch as `isAmbiguous()`. TWO COUNTERFACTUALS CAME BACK AS PASSES AND BOTH WERE FINDINGS: the gate inside `dispatch_mnemonic_for_window` had zero coverage (both substrates ask first, so no wire assertion can reach it) and the TUI gate had none at all (the demo is GUI-only). Both closed — the first by the direct-call test that is the only shape reaching it, the second by a fixture both backends drive — and both re-verified. The end-of-round census then found a third: `RecordOutcome::Full` was unreachable by construction and is removed, a variant that cannot occur being a false statement in the type.
changes_bullets: `pinion-core` `accelerator`: `Chord` — a W3C `KeyboardEvent.key` string paired with the modifiers it arrived with, and the unit both accelerator layers are asked about. `portable()` renders Qt's `PortableText` vocabulary and `parse()` reads it back; the round trip is a GUARANTEE here and is not one in Qt, whose `QKeySequence::fromString` maps an unrecognised name to `Qt::Key_unknown` and reports nothing, so a typo becomes a shortcut that silently never fires.

`is_text_bearing` IS Qt's own rule, from `QWidgetLineControl::processShortcutOverrideEvent`: an unmodified (or Shift-only) printable key is text. Alt is excluded deliberately — Alt+char is R1543's mnemonic vocabulary, and treating it as text would make a focused field swallow every accelerator in the window.

`modifier_bit` is the ONE name-to-field mapping, reached `&mut` in both directions. Clippy's complex-type warning on the previous reader table pointed at the real defect rather than at an allow: a separate reader and writer are two tables, and the failure they permit — `"Alt"` setting one bit and reading another — is silent.
`AcceleratorLayer` — which of a window's two layers claims a chord. A property of the WINDOW, not of any widget, which is why it is not a slot on the key-sequence editor.

`KeySequence` + `SequenceFull` — Qt's `QKeySequence` with the bound carried by the value. `push` REFUSES past the maximum and names the chord that did not fit, where `setKeySequence` truncates silently and a caller cannot tell a sequence that fit from one that was cut down.

`pinion-core` `External::shadows_accelerator` — the axis. Qt spells it `QEvent::ShortcutOverride`, an event the focus widget must `accept()`; here it is a QUESTION the router asks, for two reasons. Qt's override must be accepted on EVERY press, so a widget that handles a key in `keyPressEvent` and forgets the `event()` arm loses exactly the presses that collide with a shortcut — invisible until someone adds the colliding shortcut, in another file. And a question can be evaluated WITHOUT a keystroke, which is what makes `scene/accelerators` possible at all.
Per CHORD, deliberately: the right answer differs by chord for the same widget, and the two consumers in this round give different answers.

`pinion-core` `TextFieldExternal::shadows_accelerator` — the BELOW-QT defect, closed. `hello-textfield` binds `d` to Disable through `WidgetCore::keybinding`, which runs ahead of the focused widget, so typing `d` into the focused field DISABLED THE FIELD and the character never arrived. Measured over the wire before anything changed. Four bindings in the tree carried it; one widget-level declaration fixes all four with no per-binding change.
A DISABLED field claims nothing, for Qt's own `isReadOnly()` reason: a widget that will not act on the key must not stop the accelerator that would have.

`pinion-core` `widgets/key_sequence`: `KeySequenceEdit` + `KeySequenceEditExternal` (Qt `QKeySequenceEdit`) — the widget a keymap-preferences pane is built from, and the extreme consumer of the axis: while recording it claims EVERY chord.

`widgets/key_sequence.scxml` — idle / recording / disabled. `record` and `cancel` are EVENTS where Qt has neither: Qt starts on focus-in and stops only on focus-out or a 1-second release timer, so a Qt keymap editor cannot stop grabbing while it still has focus and a user who tabs in and presses Save silently overwrites the binding they were reading.
A modifier-only press is a PUBLISHED PREFIX (`pending`), where Qt's `keyPressEvent` returns early on modifier keys and the fact is lost.

The fill-commit is driven through the emitter rather than raised behind it, so a run that fills emits exactly the intent an explicit commit emits — a second path that silently fired nothing would be the defect.

`KeySequenceDisplay` + `use_key_sequence_display` — the spelling shared with the view fn. A `WidgetCore::State` is `Copy` and a chord run is `String`-shaped, so this is the case `use_text_edit_state` already exists for rather than a gap.

`pinion-runtime` `CoreShell::accelerator_shadow` — the ONE derivation both backends read, so a window and a terminal cannot disagree about whether a keystroke was an accelerator. Only the focused widget is asked, which is what bounds the mechanism.

`CoreShell::accelerator_map_for_window` / `accelerator_for_chord` + `AcceleratorRow` — the RESOLUTION layer over R1543's DECLARATION layer. The `keybinding` half is PROBED, not enumerated, because `WidgetCore::keybinding` is a function; the probed domain is published (`ASCII_PROBE_RANGE`) rather than left implicit.
`dispatch_mnemonic_for_window` now takes a `Chord` and gates INSIDE, so the mnemonic layer cannot be entered without the question having been asked.

`pinion-rpc` `scene/accelerators` — what each declared accelerator would do right now, which of them the focused widget has taken, and BY WHOM. Qt keeps its shortcut state in the private `QShortcutMap` and its override in a transient event, so no Qt application can ask either. `params.chord` answers what a chord would COLLIDE with before it is recorded.

`ChordVerdict::resolve` lifted at its second consumer: the construction is the wire type's own field mapping, and a second copy permits a GUI reporting `shadowed` from one fact and a TUI from another — the §2 #6 divergence this method exists to make visible.
`pinion-core` `test_fixtures::ShadowingFixture` — one binding both backends drive, so the GUI and the TUI assert the same precedence through the same `WidgetCore` body.

`examples/hello-key-sequence` — a keymap pane built to be HOSTILE to its own editor: a `&File` / `&Save` menubar and a `keybinding` map claiming `r` / `c` / `d` / `e`, so there is no chord the editor can record that the window does not already want.
verification_bullets: THE ABSENCE WAS PROVEN BY RUNNING IT, not by reading the dispatch order. `hello-textfield`, focused, typed `a` `b` `c` `d` `e`: text stayed `"abc"` and the field went Disabled then Idle. That is a shipped defect in four bindings, and Qt does not have it.

`tools/demos/r1569_focus_shadows_the_accelerators.py` (new) — 14 phases, PASS, 52 checks. Phase (N) re-runs the defect on the binding that shipped it and gets `"abcde"`, with the unfocused accelerator asserted FIRST as the control.
NEGATIVE CONTROLS throughout: unfocused, `r` still starts the recording and `d` still disables the field, so no later assertion can pass by the accelerator layers simply being broken.
Alt+d reaches the accelerator layer even while a field is focused — Qt's behaviour, and the reason the declaration is per CHORD rather than a bool on the widget.
New unit tests: 10 on `Chord` / `KeySequence`, 12 on the widget, 8 in the binding, 1 on the mnemonic gate, 1 on the terminal.
COUNTERFACTUALS, eight, each applied alone, each reverted by file copy with md5 verification.
TWO CAME BACK AS PASSES, and both were FINDINGS rather than results.

CF4: removing the gate inside `dispatch_mnemonic_for_window` changed nothing observable, because both substrates ask first and no wire assertion can reach it. That gate is defence for a third backend and had zero coverage. Closed by a DIRECT-CALL test, which is the only shape that reaches it; re-run, the counterfactual is caught.
CF8: removing the TUI gate left every GUI assertion green. Closed by `ShadowingFixture` plus a `pinion-tui` integration test; re-run, caught.

The remaining six discriminate: the GUI gate, a field claiming everything, an editor claiming regardless of state, `is_text_bearing` including Alt, the shared handle not being published, and the revision not bumping.

END-OF-ROUND CENSUS, with POSITIVE CONTROLS covering five call forms — free fn, turbofish, method, associated fn, const. The control caught its own pattern TWICE before the census ran: once a `grep -F` that read `\.` literally, once a pattern blind to `name::<T>(`. A census whose controls do not see a known caller has its clean verdict discarded.

ONE FINDING SURVIVED: `RecordOutcome::Full` was UNREACHABLE by construction, because a run that fills commits first. Removed — a variant that cannot occur is a false statement in the type and a branch no test can cover.

Clippy pointed at two real designs, not two allows: the modifier reader/writer duplication, and a `pub fn` whose `expect` was reachable through the public inner type (now crate-private, where the External maintains the invariant).

Pre-existing, measured this round with a control, and not this round's to fix; the contract is held by a unit test that drains the emitter directly.

R1569.1.decision_summary: R1569.1 §5.12 §2 #6 — THE PRE-RESOLVE IS ONE PLACE, AND ITS GATE IS TESTED. R1569's end-of-round duplication census found what the round itself had not recorded: the two embedders carried logically identical copies of ' chord pre-resolve — the method gate, the parameter read, the malformed-spelling tolerance, and the verdict construction — differing only in a variable name. R1569 had already lifted the verdict's field mapping () one paragraph earlier for exactly the §2 #6 reason, and stopped one layer short. R1570.decision_summary: R1570 §5.16 §5.12 — A DECLARED `#[widget]` FORWARD MUST REACH A REAL BODY, AND THE COMPILER IS WHAT SAYS SO. Stop-the-line: CI was red on R1569 and R1569.1 with 37 demos failing, four of them deterministically in both runs. `#[widget(keybinding)]` generates `fn keybinding(key) { <TheView>::keybinding(key) }` INSIDE the trait impl that defines `keybinding`. When the view declares an inherent function of that name it wins and the line is a bridge; when it does not, the call resolves back to the trait method it is standing inside and the forward calls itself. Release-mode tail-call optimisation turns that into a bare jump — 100% CPU, no stack growth, no syscall, no return, process alive and answering nothing. FOUR SHIPPED BINDINGS WERE IN THAT STATE (`hello-richtext-background` / `-blocks` / `-list` / `-cells`), each a copy of `hello-richtext`'s attribute without its three method bodies, so `keybinding`, `event_name` AND `apply_key` were each an infinite self-call. THE DEFECT IS NOT R1569's, and the control build is what settled it rather than reading the diff: at R1568.2 the same four hang on one character key, while `hello-richtext` answers in 0.3 ms. R1569 only gave `WidgetCore::keybinding` a caller on the RPC read path, which turned a trap nothing had stepped on into one every request steps on. THE TOOLCHAIN DOES NOT CATCH THIS: `#[deny(unconditional_recursion)]` on the generated body compiles silently, because the lint does not fire for a trait-qualified associated-function path. So the fix is a mechanism, not four edits. Each forward now brings `pinion_core::widget_forward`'s guard for THAT ONE NAME into scope for the length of its own body: a blanket-implemented trait carrying a method of the same name, which an inherent function shadows outright and a missing one does not, so the absent case becomes E0034 at the `#[widget(...)]` attribute and the present case compiles unchanged and pays nothing. The guards' signatures are nullary and unrelated to the forwarded ones, because ambiguity is decided by NAME before any signature is checked — which is what lets one guard cover every binding without knowing its `State` or `Event`. ALL NINE FORWARDING SITES ARE GUARDED, not just the one that bit: the defect is a property of the shape. RUSTC THEN RAN THE CENSUS, and it was wider than the symptom — the four bindings were each missing THREE functions, and every other binding in the tree is clean. A COUNTERFACTUAL FOUND THE HOLE IN THE CENSUS ITSELF: it pairs forwards to guards by TRAIT name and cannot see whether the trait declares a method of the promised name, so a misspelled guard method would leave the gate dead with every test green — closed by a correspondence test that names both sides from a place that can see both. CLIPPY'S LENGTH LIMIT, hit twice by the guards, pointed at two real seams rather than two allows: the three always-emitted `WidgetCore` bodies are now one group, and the a11y impl's two arms — one deriving a node from declarations, one forwarding — are now two functions.
changes_bullets: `pinion-core` `widget_forward` — one guard trait per name the `#[widget]` macro forwards, blanket-implemented for every type. The mechanism is Rust's own resolution order: an inherent associated function shadows every trait candidate, so a binding that HAS the function compiles unchanged and pays nothing, while one that does not now has two applicable candidates and rustc rejects it as E0034 naming the guard. Nine guards, one per forwarding site.

The guards' signatures are nullary and unrelated to the forwarded ones, deliberately: ambiguity is decided by NAME before any signature is checked, so a guard does not need to know the view's `State` or `Event` types. That is what lets one guard cover every binding.

One trait per name rather than one trait carrying nine, because ambiguity is per name: bundling would bring every guarded name into scope at every forward, widening the blast radius of a mechanism whose whole value is that it is narrow.

`pinion-derive` `guarded_forward` — wraps each `<TheView>::name(..)` body in a block that imports that name's guard anonymously (`as _`) and nothing else. Scoped to the generated body, so the guard is a resolution candidate and never a name the binding's own code can see.

All nine forwarding sites now go through it: `read_state`, `event_name`, `view`, `initial_size_strategy`, `apply_key`, `keybinding`, `fmt_state_log`, `update`, `access_node`. The defect was found in `keybinding` and is a property of the SHAPE, so guarding only the one that bit would leave eight loaded.

`pinion-derive` `CoreMethodBodies` + `emit_core_method_bodies` — the three always-emitted `WidgetCore` bodies lifted out of `expand`, which the guards pushed past the length limit. They share one decision (derive, or forward to an inherent fn), and that decision is now the thing worth reading in one place.

`pinion-derive` `emit_a11y_forwarding_impl` — the no-`role` arm of `emit_a11y_impl`, lifted for the same reason. The two arms have nothing in common but the trait they implement: one derives a node from declarations, the other forwards. The limit was pointing at the right seam.

`examples/hello-richtext-background` / `-blocks` / `-list` / `-cells` — the three functions each has declared since the round that wrote it and never had. Copied from `hello-richtext`, whose `#[widget(...)]` attribute these four were copied from without its method bodies.

`event_name` is answered by the macro's `event_name_derive` flag rather than written out, because the body would be character-for-character what that flag emits. Hand-rolling a substrate that already exists is the shape this round is about, so the repair does not add four more copies of it. The census behind that choice: 30 bindings in the tree hand-write exactly this body against 14 that declare the flag, which is a pre-existing class this round records rather than sweeps.
`keybinding` maps `d` / `e` as the sibling binding does — binding policy, not mechanical wiring, so it is written out.

`apply_key` is ARIA activation on a `role = Switch`, which such a widget owes its user regardless of this defect; it was not merely absent here, it was a hang. Written out because the macro has no declarative form for it, which 26 identical hand-rolled copies across the tree say it should have.
verification_bullets: STOP-THE-LINE ENTRY. CI was red on R1569 and R1569.1: 37 demos failed in the sweep, and the two runs shared exactly four failures — `r1546` / `r1551` / `r1559` / `r1560` — while their other failures differed. The four are deterministic, the rest are the wake left by four orphaned processes the sweep could not kill.

REPRODUCED LOCALLY FIRST, then bisected by measurement rather than by reading. The process was ALIVE and answering nothing; a first CPU reading said it was idle and blocked, and that reading was WRONG because no request was pending. With one in flight it is 100 ticks/second, flat, for 340 seconds — a runaway, not a deadlock.
`strace` located it exactly: the reader thread reads the request and posts the waker, the main thread reads the waker, and then makes NO further syscall. Userspace, spinning.
OWNERSHIP DECIDED BY A CONTROL BUILD, not by reading the diff: a `git worktree` at R1568.2 answered in 0.3 ms. That said R1569, and it was WRONG about the defect — see below.
Bisected inside `accelerator_map_for_window` by instrumenting it: `scene_mnemonics` returned 0 rows, and the next line printed `keybinding(" ")?` and never printed again.

THE DEFECT IS NOT R1569's. Driving one character key into the CONTROL build — `scene/key` with `"q"` at R1568.2 — hangs identically. The recursion had been in those four bindings since the rounds that wrote them; R1569 only gave `WidgetCore::keybinding` a caller on the RPC read path, which turned a latent trap into an unconditional one. `hello-richtext`, which has the inherent function, answers in 0.3 ms in the same control build — the negative control that makes the discrimination exact.

`#[deny(unconditional_recursion)]` on the generated body was tried and COMPILES SILENTLY. The lint does not fire for a trait-qualified associated-function path, which is why nothing in the toolchain had objected for the ~24 rounds these bindings shipped.

THE CENSUS WAS RUN BY RUSTC, not by grep: `cargo check --workspace --all-targets --keep-going` with the guards in place. Exactly four bindings, and each was missing THREE inherent functions, not one — `apply_key` and `event_name` were the same infinite self-call as `keybinding`. Every other binding in the tree is clean.
FOUR COUNTERFACTUALS, each applied alone, each reverted by file copy with md5 verification.
CF-A: delete one binding's inherent `keybinding`. Exactly one E0034, at the `#[widget(...)]` attribute. Re-run after the two extractions, still caught.

CF-B: delete the guard from the macro as well, so the defect compiles again. The demo FAILS on the repaired binding and PASSES on the control, exit code 2 — so the demo discriminates independently of the compiler, which a compile-only gate could never show.
CF-C: remove the guard from the macro with the bindings intact. `every_unqualified_forward_is_guarded` fails and names the missing guard exactly.

CF-D: misspell a guard's method name. The correspondence test stops compiling AND the gate goes dead — 0 E0034 with the inherent function removed. That is what the correspondence test defends, and it was a real hole in the census, which pairs by trait name and cannot see the method name.

`tools/demos/r1570_declared_forward_reaches_its_body.py` (new) — 55 assertions across five bindings, PASS. The same body drives the control and the four repaired ones, so a half-fix cannot look like a passing control.

The read ANSWERING AT ALL is asserted first and with no wall-clock threshold: `scene/accelerators` answers by CALLING `keybinding`, so a row for a character proves the forward reached the binding's own function and returned.

`d` reaching the statechart traverses TWO forwards in one keystroke (`keybinding` names the event, `event_name` spells it), `e` proves it was a transition and not an absorbing state, an unmapped key proves `apply_key` ran and returned, and a mapped key after it proves the widget is not merely inert.
New unit tests: 5 macro census tests in `pinion-derive`, 2 correspondence tests, 3 on the guards themselves.
The four CI-red demos re-run and PASS: `r1546` 1.58s, `r1551` 3.14s, `r1559` 1.59s, `r1560` 1.62s.
CLIPPY POINTED AT TWO REAL SEAMS, not two allows: `expand` and `emit_a11y_impl` both crossed the length limit, and both extractions are decompositions the functions wanted anyway.

`cargo test --workspace`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D pedantic`, `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --document-private-items`. All clean. The workspace scope is correct here rather than generous: this round changes generated code for all 215 bindings.
`tools/phase_b_tally.py --selftest` PASS; no UNDECLARED / UNCLASSIFIED / STALE.
carry_forward_bullets: `apply_key`'s ARIA half is not driven over the wire in any of the five bindings, because `main_toggle` is not a focus stop in any of them — `focus/set` refuses it as `tag_not_focusable`, and `apply_aria_activate` gates on the focused tag. Pre-existing, on the axis `debt-a11y-focus-stop-absent-from-tree` already tracks, and this round does not widen its scope to five bindings' focus declarations. The forward itself is exercised and proven by the unmapped-key path.

The guard makes a MISSING inherent function a compile error; it does not make a WRONG one one. A binding whose inherent `keybinding` returned the wrong events would still compile and still be silent. That is a different class from the one this round closes and the demo is what covers it, per binding.

The E0034 diagnostic names the guard trait and points at the `#[widget(...)]` attribute, which is the right place, but rustc offers no way to attach a sentence to it. The guard names carry the explanation instead (`KeybindingNeedsInherentFn`), and their doc comments carry the fix. A `#[diagnostic::on_unimplemented]` cannot help, because the blanket impl always applies.

`WidgetCore::keybinding` is still a FUNCTION rather than a table, so `scene/accelerators` probes it over printable ASCII. Carried unchanged from R1569; closing it is a trait change every binding pays for.

TWO PRE-EXISTING DUPLICATION CLASSES, censused by this round and NOT swept by it: 26 bindings hand-write a byte-identical `apply_key` that is only `apply_aria_activate(scene, focused, key, Self::tag())`, and 30 hand-write an `event_name` that is only `WidgetEventName::as_name(&event)` while 14 declare the flag that emits it. The second has a substrate already and the repair adopted it; the first has none, and a declarative `apply_key = aria_activate` is the shape 26 consumers are asking for. Both predate this round, which added no instance of either. Sequenced after the CI fix deliberately: a stop-the-line round should not carry a 50-file sweep, and the sweep is compiler-verified whenever it is taken.

R1570.1.decision_summary: R1570.1 §5.39 §5.16 — A DECLARED INTERACTIVE ROLE IS A KEYBOARD FOCUS STOP. R1570's end-of-round census left three debts; this closes the one it said to take first, and the order mattered. `#[widget(role = Button | CheckBox | Switch | RadioButton | Listbox)]` announces an operable control to assistive technology, and WAI-ARIA requires such a control to be focusable — HTML's native `<button>` / `<input type=checkbox>` are focusable with no `tabindex`, Qt's `QAbstractButton` / `QCheckBox` / `QRadioButton` are `Qt::StrongFocus`. pinion's focus enumeration is scene-derived (R1020 §5.39, which retired the trait-level `focusable_tags()` precisely so there is ONE source), and that is right — but it is an OPT-IN, and the opt-in was missing in **17 of 23** such bindings. Measured over the wire before anything changed: `focus/set` refused the tag and `focus/next` answered `None`, so those windows had NO keyboard focus stop at all. THE SECOND-ORDER CONSEQUENCE is what makes this more than an a11y gap: `apply_aria_activate` gates on `focused == Some(my_tag)`, so in a binding whose control can never hold focus that body CAN NEVER RETURN TRUE — **13 of the 25 byte-identical `apply_key` bodies** R1570 censused were unreachable code, under doc comments describing a Space/Enter behaviour that could not happen. That is why R1570 recorded "look at this BEFORE lifting the 25": a declarative lift of mostly-dead code would have inherited its zero coverage, the R1567 lesson. WHY THE TREE DID NOT ALREADY KNOW is the round's other finding, and it is about a gate rather than about a widget: R1518's focus sweep DOES assert that every binding it walks has a stop, but its population is a **hand-written list of 14** composites. A curated population cannot find an absence — a binding with zero focus stops is simply never walked. So the gate this round adds DERIVES its population from the source declarations and prints it, which is the R1526 move (git enumerates the rounds, not the ledger) applied to bindings. THE FIX IS SPLIT THE WAY OWNERSHIP IS: where a paint helper owns the tagged node, the helper declares it (`CheckboxStyle::focusable`, defaulting `true`, mirroring what `ButtonStyle` has had since R1030 — which is exactly why the six FOCUSABLE controls were focusable); where the binding hand-paints its own control, the binding declares it. THE WIRE CAUGHT A REAL SLIP: `hello-gradient` got the declaration on `hue_strip`, a decorative gradient `Scene::Box`, because a source scan read a tag out of a doc comment. The probe reported the wrong tag focusable and the right one not, the declaration moved, and the negative control that now guards it is that same decorative node. A pixel demo then found a consequence nothing else would have: a click now FOCUSES a checkbox, so the focus ring paints around the tagged Container and merges box and label into one ink band. The ring is real and the behaviour is correct; `r1511` puts the focus state back before measuring rather than teaching its finder to ignore ink.
changes_bullets: `pinion-widget-paint` `CheckboxStyle::focusable` + `with_focusable` — the tagged Container declares its focus stop, defaulting `true`. Mirrors `ButtonStyle::focusable` (R1030), whose fail-safe default is the reason every `view_button` consumer was already reachable while `hello-checkbox` was not.

Sixteen bindings that hand-paint their own control declare `.with_focusable(true)` on the tagged node: `hello-command-palette` `hello-commands` `hello-elevation` `hello-gradient` `hello-image` `hello-path` `hello-pdf-export` `hello-popover` `hello-radio` `hello-richtext` `hello-richtext-background` `hello-richtext-blocks` `hello-richtext-cells` `hello-richtext-list` `hello-theme` `hello-toggle`.

The split is by OWNERSHIP, not by convenience: a painter that owns the tagged node owns the declaration, so its future consumers inherit it; a binding that paints its own control declares it there, because there is nowhere else it could live. Ten of the sixteen paint a switch track by hand, which is the absent `switch` painter showing up as duplication — recorded, not built here.

`tools/demos/r1570_1_interactive_role_is_a_focus_stop.py` — the gate, with a population DERIVED from `#[widget(role = ..., tag = "...")]` across `examples/*/src/main.rs` rather than listed. Prints both the interactive set and the set excluded by role, so the judgment is visible and a scan that matched nothing reads as zero rather than as a pass.

Its regexes are ANCHORED to line starts. Unanchored, they read `tag = "..."` out of a module's own doc comments, which is exactly how this round put a focus stop on a decorative gradient before the wire caught it.

`tools/demos/r1511_container_border.py` — puts focus back before its ink captures. A click now focuses the checkbox, so the focus ring surrounds the tagged Container (`[box] [label]`) and the leftmost-ink-band finder returns the whole row. The state is restored rather than the finder weakened.
verification_bullets: MEASURED BEFORE AND AFTER, over the wire, on release binaries: 23 interactive-role bindings, `focus/set {tag}` + `focus/next`. Before: 6 FOCUSABLE, **17 with no focus stop at all**. After: **23 of 23**.
The before-measurement had a working CONTROL — the 6 that passed — so it was never "the probe is broken and everything looks red".

THE PROBE CAUGHT MY OWN SLIP. `hello-gradient` reported the decorative `hue_strip` focusable and `main_toggle` not, because a source scan had read a tag out of a doc comment. Reading the diff would not have found it; the wire did. The declaration moved, the census regexes were anchored, and that same decorative node is now the demo's negative control.
`tools/demos/r1570_1_interactive_role_is_a_focus_stop.py` (new) — 77 assertions, PASS. Population derived, printed, and asserted non-empty before anything depends on it.

Three facts per binding, not one: `focus/set` accepts the declared tag, `focus/get` then reports exactly that tag, and `focus/next` from cold reaches a stop. "The tag is focusable" and "the tag is in the Tab order" are different claims and the tree failed both.
CONSEQUENCE asserted, not assumed: on the Switch family, `Enter` with focus on the control now flips the value bit through `apply_key` — the path that was unreachable code.
COUNTERFACTUALS, two, each applied alone, each reverted by file copy with md5 verification.
CF-E1: remove one binding's `.with_focusable(true)`. The demo fails, exit 2.

CF-E2: stamp the decorative `hue_strip` focusable again. The demo fails on the NEGATIVE CONTROL with its own message — so the sweep cannot pass by `focusable` being stamped on everything, which is the failure mode a sweep of this shape invites.

THE 39 DEMOS naming any changed binding were re-run: 38 PASS and 1 real regression, `r1511_container_border`, which is the fix working — a click now focuses, the ring paints around the row, and the pixel finder saw one band where it expected the box. Fixed by restoring the focus state before the capture; PASS.
CI-only pixel guards were checked for the same exposure by name and none touches the 23.
`cargo test --workspace`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D pedantic`, `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --document-private-items`. All clean.
carry_forward_bullets: A POINTER CLICK PAINTS THE FOCUS RING. There is no `:focus-visible` distinction: the ring is a function of being focused, not of how focus arrived. The web suppresses it for mouse focus; Qt's common styles do not, so this is not below the Qt floor and is a design axis rather than a defect — but it is now visible on 17 more controls than it was, and `r1511` had to hold the focus state constant because of it. Registered rather than decided here.

TEN OF THE SIXTEEN hand-paint a switch track, because `pinion-widget-paint` has no `switch` painter. That is why the declaration had to be repeated ten times instead of once. Building one is a widget-catalog round, not this one.

`debt-r1570-widget-macro-hand-rolled-bodies` is now unblocked and unchanged otherwise: the 25 identical `apply_key` bodies are all LIVE, so the declarative `apply_key = aria_activate` lift no longer risks lifting dead code. The `event_name` half never depended on this.
`debt-demo-harness-leaks-hung-process` is untouched and is the next one.

R1518's own sweep still walks a CURATED list of 14. This round did not change it; it added a second sweep whose population is derived. Merging them is worth doing and is a gate round, not a widget round.

R1570.2.decision_summary: R1570.2 §5.16 — THE `#[widget]` ATTRIBUTE CAN DERIVE AN `apply_key` BODY, AND THE TWO DUPLICATION CLASSES R1570's CENSUS FOUND ARE GONE FROM EVERY BINDING THE MACRO CAN REACH. R1570 registered two: 25 bindings hand-writing a byte-identical `apply_key` that is only `apply_aria_activate(scene, focused, key, Self::tag())`, and bindings hand-writing an `event_name` that is only `WidgetEventName::as_name(&event)` while the macro already has an `event_name_derive` flag that emits exactly it. THE FIRST THING THIS ROUND DID WAS CORRECT ITS OWN REGISTERED FIGURES, because the debt file said to run an exact-body census before touching anything and the census disagreed with the registration: the `event_name` class is **10**, not 30 — the number came from a loose grep that counted files already declaring the flag and files whose body differs (`"__internal__"`, or a real mapping). And BOTH classes are smaller than they look once you ask what the macro can reach: `apply_key` is 25 but only **18** are macro bindings, `event_name` is 10 but only **7** are; the rest hand-write `impl WidgetCore` and are outside the attribute entirely. That is a stated limit, not a deferral — bringing them in is a different job. THE SHAPE IS `apply_key = <strategy>`, NOT A SECOND BARE FLAG, and the reason is already in the tree: `widget_core.rs` documents `menu_apply_key` (R772.1) as the canonical body for the command-menu family, so there is a SECOND strategy coming and a pair of bare flags (`apply_key_aria` / `apply_key_menu`) would say nothing about being alternatives. The parser refuses an unknown strategy by naming the accepted set, and refuses declaring both forms at once — they are alternatives, and accepting both would make the emitted method depend on which one the reader noticed. The derived body carries NO `widget_forward` guard, deliberately and asserted: R1570's guard exists to catch a forward that resolves to itself, and a derived body is not a forward — guarding it would demand the very inherent fn the strategy exists to remove. It reaches `tag()` through the qualified `<View as WidgetCore>::tag()` so the emitted code does not depend on which trait `Self` resolves through at the expansion site. THE COUNTERFACTUAL SEQUENCE IS THE ROUND'S OTHER LESSON, three attempts to break the derived body: the first FAILED TO APPLY (the pattern occurred three times and the driver's own uniqueness assert refused the edit) and the gate then reported PASS — a vacuous one, exactly the trap the notes record; the second compiled-error'd, which is discrimination zero because the compiler caught it rather than any assertion; only the third compiled AND was wrong, and the R1570.1 gate caught it precisely on "Enter reached apply_key's ARIA activation". Deleting the inherent fns then made `WidgetCore` unused at module scope in 17 bindings and STILL used inside their `#[cfg(test)]` modules and their doc links — all three consequences were enumerated by rustc rather than guessed, which is the same move R1570 made when it let the compiler run the census.
changes_bullets: `pinion-derive` `apply_key = <strategy>` — a keyed form beside the bare `apply_key` flag. The flag forwards to an inherent fn; the keyed form names a body the macro DERIVES. `APPLY_KEY_STRATEGIES` publishes the vocabulary and the parser refuses anything else by naming it.

`= <strategy>` rather than a second bare flag because a second strategy is already implied by the tree: `menu_apply_key` (R772.1), the command-menu family's canonical body. Two bare flags would not say they are alternatives.
Declaring both forms at once is refused at parse time. They ARE alternatives, and accepting both would make the emitted method depend on which one the reader noticed.

`emit_derived_apply_key` — the body, emitted as the whole trait method and carrying NO `widget_forward` guard. R1570's guard catches a forward that resolves to itself; a derived body is not a forward, and guarding it would demand the inherent fn the strategy exists to remove. Asserted both ways rather than left to reading.

18 macro bindings adopt `apply_key = aria_activate` and delete their hand-written body. The other 7 of the censused 25 hand-write `impl WidgetCore` with no `#[widget]` attribute, so the attribute cannot reach them — stated, not deferred.
7 macro bindings adopt `event_name_derive` and delete their hand-written `event_name`. The class is 10, of which 3 are hand-written impls.

The deletions made `WidgetCore` unused at module scope in 17 bindings while it stayed used inside their `#[cfg(test)]` modules and their doc links. Both were fixed where they belong: the import moved INTO the test module, and the doc links became qualified paths. rustc enumerated every site.
verification_bullets: THE REGISTERED FIGURES WERE WRONG AND THE EXACT-BODY CENSUS CORRECTED THEM, which is why the debt file said to run it first. `event_name` is 10, not the 30 a loose grep reported: that count included bindings already declaring the derive flag and bindings whose body is something else entirely.

AND BOTH CLASSES ARE SMALLER THAN THEY LOOK once the question is what the macro can reach: `apply_key` 25 -> 18 macro bindings, `event_name` 10 -> 7. The remainder hand-write `impl WidgetCore` and are outside the attribute.
AFTER: 0 macro bindings hand-roll either body; 18 declare the strategy. Measured by the same exact-body scan that found them.

New macro tests, 5: the strategy emits the body and NO guard, the bare flag still forwards UNDER its guard (the negative control — without it, deleting the forwarding arm would satisfy every other assertion), both forms at once is refused, an unknown strategy names the accepted set, and no `apply_key` at all emits neither.
COUNTERFACTUALS, three attempts on the derived body, and the first two are findings about counterfactual DISCIPLINE rather than about the code.

CF-F FAILED TO APPLY: the target text occurs three times (the derived body plus two in the a11y derive) and the driver's uniqueness assert refused the edit. The gate then reported PASS — a VACUOUS pass, and it looked exactly like a real one. The assert is what made it visible.
CF-F2 applied but did not compile. Discrimination zero: the compiler caught it, not any assertion.

CF-F3 compiles and is wrong (the derived body activates a tag that is not the widget's). The R1570.1 gate fails precisely on "Enter reached apply_key's ARIA activation" — so this migration is verified BEHAVIOURALLY, not merely by the workspace still building.
The 37 demos naming any migrated binding: 37 PASS, 0 FAIL.
`r1570_1_interactive_role_is_a_focus_stop` 77 assertions PASS after the migration — the ARIA path the 18 derived bodies now serve.
`cargo test --workspace`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D pedantic`, `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --document-private-items`. All clean.
Clippy pointed at one more by-value token stream in the new tests; taken as a signature fix rather than an allow.
carry_forward_bullets: SEVEN bindings hand-write `impl WidgetCore` with no `#[widget]` attribute and so keep their own `apply_key` (`hello-button-tui` `hello-commands-tui` `hello-multi-window` `hello-paged-stream` `hello-streaming-log` `hello-toggle-tui` `hello-window-focus-multi`), and three keep their own `event_name` (`hello-code-fold` `hello-key-sequence` `hello-textarea`). The attribute cannot reach them; converting them is a per-binding job with its own risk, and for a hand-written impl `WidgetEventName::as_name` IS the canonical body with nothing better available.

`APPLY_KEY_STRATEGIES` has ONE entry. The second is named and not built: `menu_apply_key` (R772.1), whose consumers are the MenuBar / Toolbar / ContextMenu family. Building it is the round that has those bindings in front of it, not this one.
Ten of the bindings R1570.1 touched still hand-paint a switch track because `pinion-widget-paint` has no `switch` painter. Unchanged by this round and unchanged in reason.
`debt-demo-harness-leaks-hung-process` is untouched and is the last of R1570's three.

AND BOTH CLASSES ARE SMALLER THAN THEY LOOK once the question is what the macro can reach: `apply_key` 25 -> 18 macro bindings, `event_name` 10 -> 7. The remainder hand-write `impl WidgetCore` and are outside the attribute.

R1570.3.decision_summary: R1570.3 §5.12 — A DEMO THAT LEAVES A PROCESS BEHIND FAILS, AND THE HARNESS THAT DRIVES EVERY DEMO NOW HAS TESTS. Last of the three debts R1570's end-of-round census registered, and the one that turned R1570's own defect into a much larger CI failure than it was. `RpcSubprocess.shutdown` did `SIGTERM; wait(2); kill(); wait(1)`, and the second `wait`'s `TimeoutExpired` escaped **out of the demo while leaving the process running**. Measured, in the R1570 CI run: four binaries left spinning became four orphans that outlived the demos which launched them, and the 33 demos that ran afterwards on the same machine failed in a set that DIFFERED between the two runs. Four deterministic failures were reported as thirty-seven non-deterministic ones, and the root cause was reachable only by intersecting the two runs' failure sets — the log itself said "several axes broke at once". TWO THINGS WERE WRONG AND BOTH ARE FIXED. Signals reached only the direct child, so a binary that spawns a helper leaked the helper whatever the timeouts were; the launch now asks for a fresh session and teardown signals the process GROUP, which is the half `Popen.kill` cannot do at any timeout. And a survivor is now a RETURN VALUE rather than an exception, so `__exit__` decides: a leak fails the demo that caused it, unless an assertion failure is already in flight, in which case that is the more useful verdict and the leak is its consequence. A GATE WHOSE ONLY ENFORCEMENT LIVES INSIDE THE THING BEING GATED IS THE SHAPE R1495 ALREADY PAID FOR, so the sweep checks independently: it baselines the residual pinion processes before it starts (a developer box may legitimately have one running), attributes any NEW survivor to the demo that had just finished, kills it, and fails the sweep — reported for a PASSING demo too, because a demo that passes and leaks is the dangerous one, since the poisoning then looks like it came from somewhere else. THE LARGER FINDING IS THAT THE HARNESS HAD NO TESTS AT ALL. `tools/rpc_verify.py` drives every demo in this repo and nothing verified any of it — the identical gap R1495 closed for the hook libraries after the identical cost. `tools/test_rpc_verify.py` is the mirror of `tools/test_hooks.sh`: eleven assertions over the teardown path, using synthesised subjects rather than tree binaries because the interesting cases are ones a demo binary is not — a process that ignores `SIGTERM`, and one that leaves a child behind. It runs in under a second with no cargo and no display, and it is wired into pre-push AND into CI, so a `--no-verify` push cannot skip it. THE COUNTERFACTUAL IS THE GRANDCHILD CASE, and it is the only one that can tell the fix from the defect: reverting the group signal to `Popen.kill` leaves every other assertion green and fails exactly "the HELPER is reaped too". A second counterfactual drove a deliberately-leaking demo through the sweep — it PASSED its own assertions and the sweep failed it by name — against a negative control of 56 real demos, which reported no leak and exited 0.
changes_bullets: `tools/rpc_verify.py` `terminate_process_tree` — the one function teardown goes through, lifted out of `shutdown` so it can be tested without launching a pinion binary. SIGTERM then SIGKILL, each to the process GROUP, each with its own grace; returns `None` when reaped or a sentence naming the pid and what was tried.
The launch asks for `start_new_session=True`, which is what makes the group exactly this binary and its children. Without it the group is the sweep's own, and signalling it would kill the sweep.
A survivor is REPORTED, not raised. `__exit__` raises `LeakedProcess` only when the demo body otherwise succeeded — an assertion failure is the more useful verdict and the leak is downstream of it.
`shutdown` returns the leak instead of swallowing it, and takes the process out of the field before signalling, so a second call cannot double-signal a pid that has since been reused.

`tools/test_rpc_verify.py` (new) — eleven assertions over the teardown path: a cooperative child, one that ignores `SIGTERM`, one that leaves a GRANDCHILD behind, an already-exited child, a survivor being named rather than swallowed, and teardown not raising when the signal itself fails.

Subjects are synthesised python processes, not tree binaries: the cases that matter are ones a demo binary is not, and the suite has to run with no cargo and no display to be worth putting in front of a push.

`tools/sweep_headless.sh` — an independent residual-process backstop. Baselines the pinion processes present before the sweep, attributes any new survivor to the demo that just finished, kills it, names it, and fails the sweep at the end. Reported for passing demos too.
`.githooks/pre-push` + `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — the harness tests run at both gates, beside the hook-library tests they are modelled on.
verification_bullets: `tools/test_rpc_verify.py` — 11 passed, 0 failed, under a second.

COUNTERFACTUAL CF-G: revert the group signal to `Popen.kill` (the pre-R1570.3 reach). Ten assertions stay green and exactly one fails — "the HELPER is reaped too". That is the only case that can distinguish the fix from the defect, and it is the case the CI failure was made of.

COUNTERFACTUAL CF-H: a fixture demo that PASSES its own assertions and leaks a binary under `target/`. The sweep reports `LEAK: pid N still running after zz_cf_leaky.py`, kills it, and exits 1. The passing-and-leaking case is the one worth catching, because its damage is attributed to whatever runs next.

NEGATIVE CONTROL for the backstop, two ways: 56 real demos through the sweep — 56 PASS, 0 LEAK, exit 0 — and 8 demos that FAILED for an unrelated reason (no wgpu adapter under Xvfb on this box, VELLO-002) also reported 0 leaks. A failing demo is when teardown matters most, so that arm is the stronger one.
`start_new_session=True` changes how EVERY demo is launched, so the 56-demo sample was chosen to cover the families rather than the round's own bindings: no behaviour change anywhere.

The sweep's runner body is a single-quoted shell string, and the first draft of the comment inside it contained an apostrophe, which closed the quote and broke the runner. Caught by running it, not by reading it; the comment is now apostrophe-free and `bash -n` passes.
`tools/test_hooks.sh` 78 passed (unchanged), and the adjacent demos re-run clean.
carry_forward_bullets: The residual check's predicate is "a process whose command line names this workspace's `target/`". It cannot see a leaked process that re-execs into something else, and it would attribute a CONCURRENT build's test binary to whatever demo happened to be running. The baseline handles the pre-existing case; a genuinely concurrent sweep on one machine is out of scope and is what the CI job's isolation gives for free.

`LeakedProcess` fires only when the demo body succeeded. A demo that fails AND leaks reports its assertion failure, and the leak is visible only in the sweep's backstop. That is the intended precedence and it means the two gates are not redundant.

The harness has tests for its process LIFECYCLE and for nothing else. `request` / `wait_until` / the snapshot helpers — the parts every demo calls on every line — are still unverified, and the same argument that justified this suite applies to them.
R1518's focus sweep still walks a CURATED list of 14 bindings; R1570.1 added a second sweep with a derived population rather than merging them. Unchanged here, and still worth doing.
