R1592.decision_summary: R1592 §5.32 §5.38 §2 #2 — A SHAPE SELECTS IN THE CALLER'S OWN COORDINATES. R1591 gave the framework a region primitive and left it with one consumer, which is a thing that drifts; hello-node-editor had held its own marquee hit test as four inequalities since R880. Migrating it is this round, and the migration found a real defect in R1591's own design: Region was welded to Rect, an unsigned WINDOW-pixel type, while a node editor's marquee selects in GRAPH units that pan into negative coordinates. A shape predicate has no business knowing what its numbers mean, so Region is signed throughout now and Region::covers_span is its one Rect-free entry point, with Region::rect kept as the surface spelling and Region::span as the world one. That is [[abstraction-needs-second-consumer]] working exactly as it is meant to — the second consumer revealed the type was over-fitted to the first, and it revealed it in the round that added the consumer rather than a year later. What the migration then makes possible is the point: select_lasso and select_circle in hello-node-editor are the SAME call the pointer marquee makes, one Region value handed to one selection policy, where Blender needs an operator and an implementation each. It also CORRECTS R1591's own debt note, which named pinion-chart's brush as the second consumer — measured, that brush is a 1-D RangeSliderExternal x-window with no shape, no rect and no hit test, so the note was wrong about half of what it listed, one round after this project recorded that a debt note's diagnosis is itself an audit target. And it closes a coverage hole three counterfactuals surfaced between them: the marquee's "touching counts" rule — stated in prose since R880, and shared with Qt's rubber band — had no test that could fail, because a pointer-driven sweep in screen pixels cannot land on an exact graph-unit edge. The rule now has a name, card_span, and a test at the unit where it is decidable.
changes_bullets: Region is signed throughout: Region::span for world coordinates, Region::rect for the surface, covers_span as the one predicate
hello-node-editor's apply_marquee becomes apply_region over that predicate; the four inequalities are gone
select_lasso / select_circle: two Blender operators as one Region value, in graph units, refused by name when degenerate
card_span names the "touching counts" rule the marquee has stated since R880 and nothing asserted
CORRECTION: R1591's debt note named pinion-chart's brush as a consumer; it is a 1-D range slider, not a region select
verification_bullets: 8 counterfactuals, each reverted with hash verification. THREE did not do what they were named for and each is a finding. CF-4 narrowed a card's extent by one unit on each far side and PASSED r880_node_marquee_select.py — the demo drives the marquee through a pointer drag in screen pixels, which cannot land on an exact graph-unit edge, so the rule that demo exists to check was unasserted. It is now a unit test on card_span, which can fail. CF-6 was INVALID twice before it compiled (unreachable_code, an unstable attribute position) and then caught. CF-1 through CF-3 and CF-5 were caught first time.

pinion-core: 3132 tests (2 new for the space-agnostic predicate, asserting selection in negative graph coordinates that Rect cannot hold at all). hello-node-editor: 265 (1 new). pinion-rpc: 1150 plus its four wire-census gates. Every existing test passed unchanged, which is the claim that the migration preserved behaviour.

Demo: tools/demos/r1592_a_shape_selects_in_graph_units.py, 6 phases, and not one pixel is read: the shapes are stated in the graph's own units and the node positions come from the model through detail.x / detail.y. A triangular lasso is shown to take STRICTLY fewer nodes than its own bounding rectangle, with the cut placed in the WIDEST gap between two consecutive node sums — the first draft used the midpoint of the whole range and landed on the near side of every node, which is a fixture that would have passed by luck.
r880_node_marquee_select.py and r838_node_editor.py both pass unchanged after a release rebuild, which is the regression proof for the migration.
Gates: cargo fmt --check, clippy -D pedantic on four packages, cargo doc --document-private-items, validate-workspace, and all six node-editor / node-graph demos.
carry_forward_bullets: The lasso and the circle are reachable over RPC and not from the pointer: a lasso GESTURE needs the pointer path captured across a drag, which is a different axis from this one (the region value). The marquee gesture is unchanged and still the only pointer-driven area select.

R1592.publishable_decision_summary: R1592 §5.32 §5.38 §2 #2 — A SHAPE SELECTS IN THE CALLER'S OWN COORDINATES. R1591 gave the framework a region primitive and left it with one consumer, which is a thing that drifts; hello-node-editor had held its own marquee hit test as four inequalities since R880. Migrating it is this round, and the migration found a real defect in R1591's own design: Region was welded to Rect, an unsigned WINDOW-pixel type, while a node editor's marquee selects in GRAPH units that pan into negative coordinates. A shape predicate has no business knowing what its numbers mean, so Region is signed throughout now and Region::covers_span is its one Rect-free entry point, with Region::rect kept as the surface spelling and Region::span as the world one. That is [[abstraction-needs-second-consumer]] working exactly as it is meant to — the second consumer revealed the type was over-fitted to the first, and it revealed it in the round that added the consumer rather than a year later. What the migration then makes possible is the point: select_lasso and select_circle in hello-node-editor are the SAME call the pointer marquee makes, one Region value handed to one selection policy, where Blender needs an operator and an implementation each. It also CORRECTS R1591's own debt note, which named pinion-chart's brush as the second consumer — measured, that brush is a 1-D RangeSliderExternal x-window with no shape, no rect and no hit test, so the note was wrong about half of what it listed, one round after this project recorded that a debt note's diagnosis is itself an audit target. And it closes a coverage hole three counterfactuals surfaced between them: the marquee's "touching counts" rule — stated in prose since R880, and shared with Qt's rubber band — had no test that could fail, because a pointer-driven sweep in screen pixels cannot land on an exact graph-unit edge. The rule now has a name, card_span, and a test at the unit where it is decidable.

R1593.decision_summary: R1593 §5.38 §5.52 §2 #7 — A LINK MAY CONVERT. A node system's type relation is DIRECTED: a scalar feeds a colour by broadcasting, and a colour never narrows back into a scalar. pinion-node-graph decided a wire with source.ty != sink.ty, and != is symmetric — so the crate's own NodeKind doc, which told a coercing taxonomy to "model that by making the coercion part of equality", was asking for something no equality relation can be, and its flagship consumer is the counter-example: hello-node-editor's PortType lattice was INEXPRESSIBLE on this crate, which is the first structural reason debt-two-node-graph-models could not be closed. NodeKind::conversion declares the relation once, AS THE CONVERSION ITSELF, and that single declaration decides the four things the crate had spelled as == in four separate places: whether connect accepts a wire, what arrives along it, which input a bypassed node routes to which output, and whether a document from a file still type-checks. Blender keeps THREE independent answers to that one question — validate_link, DataTypeConversions and get_internal_link_type_priority — and its shader validate_link returns true for pairs its conversion table has no entry for at all.
changes_bullets: Conversion<V> (Refused / Direct / Converted(fn)) plus NodeKind::conversion, whose provided default IS equality
Document::conversion and link_conversion: what would happen to a value, askable before the wire exists
The four == sites become one relation: connect, passthrough eligibility, fragment re-attach, validate
The bypass rule gains its first clause since R1586: it changes a value only when it has to, and Route::converts says which
hello-node-groups declares the lattice (amount broadcasts to grey, colour never narrows) and paints a converting wire DOTTED
verification_bullets: All 151 pre-existing crate tests passed UNCHANGED under the new relation, which is the backwards-compat proof: the default conversion is equality, so a taxonomy that declares nothing behaves exactly as before. 160 crate tests after (9 new over a second test taxonomy with an asymmetric lattice, kept apart from the first because every assertion above it reads its meaning from equality). hello-node-groups 12.

7 crate counterfactuals, each reverted with hash verification, each caught by a distinct test: symmetric connect gate (6 tests), evaluator skipping the conversion (3), routing preferring the output's own index over a direct crossing (2), bypass eligibility back to equality (1), validate back to equality (1), fragment re-attach back to equality (1), and conversion() defaulted to allow-everything (5).

CF-2 found a discrimination hole in a NEIGHBOURING test and that is the round's process finding: every_accepted_wire_can_carry_a_value asserted only that a value arrived, so a wire that carried the value across UNCONVERTED passed it — the very failure the property exists to exclude. It now asserts the arriving value has the DESTINATION's type, and the counterfactual was re-run against the strengthened form.

5 demo counterfactuals. D-CF-4 PASSED on the first run, which is a finding of the same class one level up: the section asserting the routing preference was written against Fade, whose own-index input is already the direct one, so both the rule and its counterfactual give the same answer — zero discriminating power. A shape where the preference is falsifiable (Glaze: Amount, Colour -> Colour) was added and the counterfactual then failed on it.

carry_forward_bullets: NAME COLLISION FOUND AND AVOIDED: the type was first written as Crossing, and pinion_graph::group::Crossing already means a value crossing a GROUP boundary — the same one-word-two-meanings hazard R1586 spent a round untangling in Blender's vocabulary. Renamed to Conversion before the round closed; the wire vocabulary follows it (conversion, link_conversions).

A conversion cannot be declared per PORT, only per type pair. Blender has no per-port override either, so this is a stated limit rather than a divergence; the forcing case would be a port that wants a different broadcast from every other port of its type.

Conversion::Converted carries fn(V) -> Option<V>, so a conversion that is DECLARED for a pair can still decline a particular value. Nothing in the tree exercises that arm's None leg through a link yet — the lattice conversions here are total on their own type.

The evaluator re-derives the conversion per link read rather than caching it. Free today (the relation is a pure function of two types and both are already in hand), and it is where a cost would show up if a taxonomy made conversion() expensive.

R1594.decision_summary: R1594 §5.38 §5.52 §2 #7 — A SOCKET'S VALUE IS AUTHORED ON THE NODE. A port's TYPE and NAME come from the kind, so every node of a kind shares them; its VALUE does not — two Swatch nodes are two colours, and the number typed into an unwired input belongs to that input and to no other node's. pinion-node-graph had nowhere to put that, because Port::default is derived from the kind, so the crate's own flagship consumer had to carry each source's constant as a payload inside its taxonomy (Swatch([i64;3])) where nothing could ever edit it. Blender keeps exactly what was missing, as bNodeSocket::default_value, per socket per node. Node::values is that, and the rule the evaluator applies is ONE SENTENCE COVERING BOTH SIDES: an authored value is what a port carries when nothing else supplies one — for an input that means no link, for an output it means the kind computed nothing there, which is what makes a source node's constant this same mechanism instead of a second one. Found by mapping every model operation hello-node-editor performs against the crate: this and R1593's directed type relation are the only two the crate could not express, and they are the whole of what blocked debt-two-node-graph-models.
changes_bullets: Node::values plus PortRef / Side: a sparse map of values authored on a node's own ports
The fallback is symmetric and three deep on both sides: supplied, then the node's, then the kind's
Document::set_port_value refuses a port the SIGNATURE lacks, and a value NodeKind::value_type says is the wrong type
Violation::StrayPortValue for a value that outlived its port, which a shrinking interface can produce
hello-node-groups' Swatch and Level become UNIT variants: the taxonomy got SMALLER and the constant became editable
verification_bullets: All 161 pre-existing crate tests passed UNCHANGED, which is the compatibility proof: a node with nothing authored behaves exactly as before. 173 crate tests after (12 new), hello-node-groups 16 (4 new).

7 crate counterfactuals, each reverted with hash verification: input ignoring the node's value (1 test), output fallback removed (2), output fallback also applied when bypassed (1), adopt_from dropping the values (1), set_port_value not checking the signature (1), the wrong-type gate removed (1), and the stray-value check never firing (1).

TWO of those seven had ZERO discriminating power on their first draft and each failed differently: CF-5 did not compile, and CF-7 was caught by the dead_code lint rather than by any assertion — the R1558 class. Both were rewritten until an assertion caught them.

2 demo counterfactuals. D-CF-2 PASSED TWICE for two different reasons and both are findings. The first time the demo asserted the CARRIED value after a clear, which is 0 whether the value was removed or the kind's default was written over it — zero discrimination, and the distinguishing fact is whether anything is still AUTHORED. The second time the counterfactual's own anchor did not match after rustfmt had reindented the target, so the edit applied NOTHING and the run reported PASS: a counterfactual that does not apply is indistinguishable from one that was caught. The driver now asserts the anchor matched.

Demo: tools/demos/r1594_a_value_is_authored_on_the_node.py, 59 assertions over 8 phases, driving the three-step fallback in order and back again, both refusal gates, a duplicate, a group collapse, an interface that shrinks under an instance, and a bypass.
Blast radius: all eight demos over hello-node-groups and pinion-node-graph re-run green after a release rebuild.
Gates: cargo fmt --all --check, clippy -D pedantic on both packages, cargo doc --document-private-items, phase_b_tally --selftest.
carry_forward_bullets: Port::default's doc said "None on outputs". That was a consequence of nothing reading it there rather than a rule, and this round makes the output side read it — so a source KIND can declare its resting value and a source NODE can override it. The doc is corrected rather than left to be discovered.

A bypassed node does NOT consult its authored outputs. R1586 NAMES the outputs no input can feed, and filling one in from an authored value would make dropped_outputs a lie. Asserted rather than assumed, and it is the one place the two rules had to be ordered.

NodeKind::value_type is a second provided-default trait method in as many rounds. A taxonomy that cannot classify its values is not asked to, and pays by having set_port_value accept anything — which is what Port::with_default has always done, so nothing regressed; but the crate now has two extension points whose default is "say nothing", and a third would be worth resisting.

The values travel unremapped through adopt_from because a PortRef indexes the node's OWN signature. That is only true while a copy keeps its body; a future set_kind (the census's swap_node) is exactly the operation that would invalidate them, and it does not exist yet.

R1595.decision_summary: R1595 §5.38 §5.52 — A FRAME HAS A HEIGHT, and the migration is MEASURED rather than estimated. Appearance::height is the last of the three crate gaps that made debt-two-node-graph-models a capability problem rather than a scope one. R1589 recorded both the absence and its reason: an ordinary node's height is a FUNCTION of how many ports it draws, so authoring one would be a second statement free to disagree with the first — while a NodeBody::Frame has no ports at all, so its height is a fact about the canvas that nothing derives. Option<u32> is what says exactly that, and it is why the field is an Option rather than absent. Blender carries bNode::width and bNode::height on every node with no such distinction, and its NODE_OT_resize is horizontal-only for ordinary nodes by convention rather than by anything in its model. The second half of the round is the measurement the next session needs: parsing main.rs's function bodies by brace depth rather than grepping, 147 of 344 functions (43%) touch the model, across 9,186 lines plus a 9,094-line test file written against its own types.
changes_bullets: Appearance::height, with the Option stating why an ordinary node has none
The migration is measured by parsing, not estimated: 147 of 344 functions, 43%
An eight-step execution plan recorded in the debt file, in dependency order
The one POLICY decision named: the example queries cycles after the fact, the crate refuses before
verification_bullets: 173 crate tests, all green, and the one Appearance struct literal in the suite was enumerated by the compiler rather than found by hand — which is the property adding a field to a public struct is supposed to have.

The measurement is a parse, not a grep: function bodies are cut by brace depth from each `fn`, so a model identifier inside one function is not attributed to its neighbour. A substring census over the file would have counted 350 occurrences and said nothing about how many call sites must change.
Gates: cargo fmt --all --check, clippy -D pedantic, cargo doc --document-private-items, phase_b_tally --selftest.
carry_forward_bullets: THE MIGRATION ITSELF IS NOT DONE, and this round says so with a number rather than a feeling. A half-migration cannot exist — a model cannot be half-replaced — so it is one dedicated session, and the honest thing was to scope it precisely rather than start it with too little room and leave a broken tree. Nothing here is committed that is not green.
The three blockers are all gone: R1593 (a directed type relation), R1594 (a value authored on a node's port), R1595 (a frame's height). What remains is scope.

Appearance still has no `shrink` (Blender's NODE_FRAME_SHRINK, a frame that auto-fits its contents). It is derivable by the application from its members' bounds, which R1589 already placed on the application side, so it is a stated limit rather than a gap — and the flagship example's frames are explicitly sized, so nothing forces it.

R1596.decision_summary: R1596 §5.38 §5.52 — A CYCLE NAMES THE NODES ON IT. Document::cycle_nodes is the localisation Violation::Cycle carried no room for, and it was surfaced by starting the debt-two-node-graph-models migration rather than by reasoning about the crate: hello-node-editor publishes eval.cycle_nodes, and the crate could say only THAT a tree had a cycle, so the flagship consumer would have lost a read on the way in. A node is on a cycle exactly when it is reachable from itself, which is its strongly-connected component having two members or a self-loop of one; validate now derives both halves from that one walk, so "is there a cycle" and "who is on it" cannot disagree. Past Blender 6.x at 8cf50599, which answers the tree-level question with a BOOL (bNodeTreeRuntime::has_available_link_cycle) and localises to LINKS by a heuristic that is not a property of the cycle at all: update_link_validation clears NODE_LINK_VALID wherever from_node.toposort_left_to_right_index exceeds to_node's, and update_toposort restarts, for a tree with no acyclic start node, "at this node which is somewhere in the middle of a loop" in nodes_by_id order — so the wire Blender blames moves when only the CREATION ORDER does. That rule is held here as a test helper and the divergence is asserted rather than described. The walk is iterative Tarjan and not recursion, for the same reason the evaluator has a depth cap: validate runs on documents that arrived from a file or a peer, so a 4,001-node ring has to be a test rather than a stack overflow in the process doing the validating.

Blender's own localisation rule is implemented as a test helper (blender_blamed_links) and the divergence is ASSERTED: the same cyclic graph with its two loop members created in the other order makes Blender blame a different wire, while cycle_nodes answers the same two nodes. R1619.decision_summary:
R1619 — the pointer wire says which buttons are held.

A `PointerEnter` delivered while the primary button is down is a different fact from one delivered with nothing held: the first is the inner step of a drag-select, the second is a hover. They were BYTE-IDENTICAL on the send wire, so no consumer could tell them apart and every drag-select in the framework was blocked at the substrate — not deferred for want of a consumer, but unbuildable. `debt-pointer-wire-omits-held-button-state` measured that at R1562 and re-recorded it at R1563 as the Model/View axis's named blocked item.

THE DEBT FILE'S DIAGNOSIS WAS HALF WRONG, AND IT COST 188 LINES BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE WAS WRITTEN. It said the wire had no counterpart to the W3C `PointerEvent.buttons` state. The TYPE existed from R1418 — `PointerButtons`, `lmr` wire codec, encode/decode SSOT. What was missing was the CHANNEL: the held set rode `RawPointerButton` only, which an `External` reaches by opting into `wants_raw_pointer_buttons`, and a drag-select is BY DEFINITION a press that leaves the pressed widget, so that path could not reach it. A duplicate type was written, then found by the `lib.rs` re-export, then reverted. A debt that records an absence must record the AXIS of the absence, or the round that opens it rebuilds what is already there.

WHAT THE ROUND ACTUALLY BUILT. The held set is now the router's own per-pointer state, written only by `InputRouter::note_button_edge`, and stamped onto EVERY dispatched pointer event — Enter, Down, Up, Leave, Cancel, DoubleClick — as the send payload's fourth segment. Against the reference: the toolkit carries `buttons()` on `QSinglePointEvent`, so its mouse, hover and enter events answer it, but its LEAVE is not a pointing event at all — `virtual void leaveEvent(QEvent *)` takes a plain `QEvent`, with no position, no modifiers and no buttons — so "did the pointer leave me mid-drag" is answerable there only by consulting global state at an unrelated moment. Here every arm is stamped, and the state is on the introspection wire too (`scene/input_state.held_pointer_buttons`), which the reference has no analogue of at all.

THE PROMOTION FIXED A PRE-EXISTING DEFECT. `RawGrab` kept its OWN copy of the set, seeded EMPTY at the grab's first press, so a raw sink grabbed while another button was already down was told that button was up. The copy is gone and the grab's lifetime is read from the pointer's set — one writer, one answer, and the doc comment that already claimed the toolkit implicit-grab discipline is now true.

THE RELEASE IS ITSELF AN EVENT REPORTING THE BUTTON UP. This is the round's sharpest finding and it was a live bug for an hour. The coordinator's rule "if the primary button is not held, close the gesture" sat at the top of the handler, so the release tripped it BEFORE the sweep could be consumed, and every drag collapsed back to one row on mouse-up. The end verdict is now taken and carried down the handler rather than tested later. A rule about "the button is no longer held" cannot be evaluated ahead of the event that says so.

THE SECOND DEFECT THE DEBT NAMED CLOSED WITHOUT BEING WORKED ON. A non-capture release routes to the tag under the cursor, so releasing outside the window delivered no `PointerUp` to the presser and a coordinator's re-derived "am I pressed" flag latched forever. There is no flag now. The state travels with the event, so whatever arrives next — even much later, on a pointer that wandered back in — reports an empty set and closes the gesture. The fix for the first defect WAS the fix for the second.

THE WRITER IS IDEMPOTENT ON PURPOSE. It assigns a bit rather than counting, so every entry point that represents a button edge notes its own without coordinating: the routed left channel, the pan channel, the raw channel, and the shell's one button seam, which sits AHEAD of a routing switch that is per-button and asymmetric (a right release has no GUI arm at all, and a raw sink consumes the edge and returns early). The alternative was a census of which of those overlap on a given press. A list goes stale; the property does not.

THE 3-TUPLE BECAME A NAMED `SendPayload` OVER 79 SITES. The wire has grown a segment three times — R51.42 `key:Event`, R781 `:mods`, R1619 `:buttons` — and each growth re-broke every consumer's destructuring, not because the consumer was wrong but because an anonymous tuple has no way to say a fourth fact exists and may be ignored. The modifier segment may now be empty while the button segment is present, so the two context axes are independent and trailing-empty elision keeps exactly one spelling of every state; compose and split are proved inverses over the whole grid.

AN ADJACENT GAP HAD TO CLOSE TOO, AND ONLY THE DEMO FOUND IT. R781 put modifiers on the RELEASE only. That held for 838 rounds because every chord-aware widget acted on the activation edge, and it stops holding the moment a gesture BEGINS at a press: a Ctrl-anchored sweep is a function of the chord held when the finger went down, and there was no way to read it. The unit test passed because it fed the payload directly; the wire could not produce that payload. The router now caches the shell's absolute modifier state — the funnel `AppSubstrate::set_modifiers` already owned — and stamps both context axes on every arm.

HAND-ROLLED GRAMMAR IS NOT EXEMPT FROM THE SSOT ARGUMENT. Two `split_once(':')` decoders broke when the fourth segment appeared: a test fixture, and `hello-scene-scale` — and the latter had ALREADY been silently inert on any Shift-click since R781. A fixture that re-derives the grammar is exactly what the shared codec exists to prevent, and being a fixture is not an exemption.

THE CONSUMER. `VirtualSelectExternal` drag-select over three axes (row, section, cell) and three chords, through the SAME `press_axis` resolution and the SAME chord product a click travels, so a sweep cannot mean something a click does not. `RangeWrite::{Replace, Add}` names the one difference a chord makes to a range write, which is what lets a Ctrl sweep ADD its span instead of restarting the selection — the six near-identical extend functions that would otherwise have been needed could each have drifted while all still compiling.

THE COUNTERFACTUAL DRIVER ITSELF HAD TO BE FIXED FIRST. A killed first run left one file mutated — the R1617 lesson, hit again — and the next run therefore started RED. Every case then reported CAUGHT, because the gate was already failing, and the summary read `8/12 caught` while all eight verdicts were void. That is the only failure mode this driver had that LOOKS like success; the other four announce themselves. `tools/counterfactual.py` now runs the gate once unmutated and refuses a red baseline, with its own test asserting the refusal reports no verdict and mutates nothing.

TWO COUNTERFACTUALS THEN PASSED AND BOTH WERE REAL FINDINGS. Nothing in the Rust suite caught the press losing its chord — the demo did, over the real wire, which is the R1618 lesson recurring: a demo is not the gate a round is judged by. And nothing caught the RPC read publishing a constant, because the producer that joins the router state to the serialized reply sat BETWEEN the two suites that could have covered it and was reached by neither. Both now have tests, and the final run is 12 of 12 caught from a green baseline.

WHAT THE ROUND ACTUALLY BUILT. The held set is now the router's own per-pointer state, written only by `InputRouter::note_button_edge`, and stamped onto EVERY dispatched pointer event — Enter, Down, Up, Leave, Cancel, DoubleClick — as the send payload's fourth segment. Against the reference: the toolkit carries `buttons()` on `QSinglePointEvent`, so its mouse, hover and enter events answer it, but its LEAVE is not a pointing event at all — `virtual void leaveEvent(QEvent *)` takes a plain `QEvent`, with no position, no modifiers and no buttons — so "did the pointer leave me mid-drag" is answerable there only by consulting global state at an unrelated moment. Here every arm is stamped, and the state is on the introspection wire too (`scene/input_state.held_pointer_buttons`), which the reference has no analogue of at all.

THE PROMOTION FIXED A PRE-EXISTING DEFECT. `RawGrab` kept its OWN copy of the set, seeded EMPTY at the grab's first press, so a raw sink grabbed while another button was already down was told that button was up. The copy is gone and the grab's lifetime is read from the pointer's set — one writer, one answer, and the doc comment that already claimed the toolkit implicit-grab discipline is now true.

THE RELEASE IS ITSELF AN EVENT REPORTING THE BUTTON UP. This is the round's sharpest finding and it was a live bug for an hour. The coordinator's rule "if the primary button is not held, close the gesture" sat at the top of the handler, so the release tripped it BEFORE the sweep could be consumed, and every drag collapsed back to one row on mouse-up. The end verdict is now taken and carried down the handler rather than tested later. A rule about "the button is no longer held" cannot be evaluated ahead of the event that says so.

THE SECOND DEFECT THE DEBT NAMED CLOSED WITHOUT BEING WORKED ON. A non-capture release routes to the tag under the cursor, so releasing outside the window delivered no `PointerUp` to the presser and a coordinator's re-derived "am I pressed" flag latched forever. There is no flag now. The state travels with the event, so whatever arrives next — even much later, on a pointer that wandered back in — reports an empty set and closes the gesture. The fix for the first defect WAS the fix for the second.

THE WRITER IS IDEMPOTENT ON PURPOSE. It assigns a bit rather than counting, so every entry point that represents a button edge notes its own without coordinating: the routed left channel, the pan channel, the raw channel, and the shell's one button seam, which sits AHEAD of a routing switch that is per-button and asymmetric (a right release has no GUI arm at all, and a raw sink consumes the edge and returns early). The alternative was a census of which of those overlap on a given press. A list goes stale; the property does not.

THE 3-TUPLE BECAME A NAMED `SendPayload` OVER 79 SITES. The wire has grown a segment three times — R51.42 `key:Event`, R781 `:mods`, R1619 `:buttons` — and each growth re-broke every consumer's destructuring, not because the consumer was wrong but because an anonymous tuple has no way to say a fourth fact exists and may be ignored. The modifier segment may now be empty while the button segment is present, so the two context axes are independent and trailing-empty elision keeps exactly one spelling of every state; compose and split are proved inverses over the whole grid.

AN ADJACENT GAP HAD TO CLOSE TOO, AND ONLY THE DEMO FOUND IT. R781 put modifiers on the RELEASE only. That held for 838 rounds because every chord-aware widget acted on the activation edge, and it stops holding the moment a gesture BEGINS at a press: a Ctrl-anchored sweep is a function of the chord held when the finger went down, and there was no way to read it. The unit test passed because it fed the payload directly; the wire could not produce that payload. The router now caches the shell's absolute modifier state — the funnel `AppSubstrate::set_modifiers` already owned — and stamps both context axes on every arm.

HAND-ROLLED GRAMMAR IS NOT EXEMPT FROM THE SSOT ARGUMENT. Two `split_once(':')` decoders broke when the fourth segment appeared: a test fixture, and `hello-scene-scale` — and the latter had ALREADY been silently inert on any Shift-click since R781. A fixture that re-derives the grammar is exactly what the shared codec exists to prevent, and being a fixture is not an exemption.

THE CONSUMER. `VirtualSelectExternal` drag-select over three axes (row, section, cell) and three chords, through the SAME `press_axis` resolution and the SAME chord product a click travels, so a sweep cannot mean something a click does not. `RangeWrite::{Replace, Add}` names the one difference a chord makes to a range write, which is what lets a Ctrl sweep ADD its span instead of restarting the selection — the six near-identical extend functions that would otherwise have been needed could each have drifted while all still compiling.

THE COUNTERFACTUAL DRIVER ITSELF HAD TO BE FIXED FIRST. A killed first run left one file mutated — the R1617 lesson, hit again — and the next run therefore started RED. Every case then reported CAUGHT, because the gate was already failing, and the summary read `8/12 caught` while all eight verdicts were void. That is the only failure mode this driver had that LOOKS like success; the other four announce themselves. `tools/counterfactual.py` now runs the gate once unmutated and refuses a red baseline, with its own test asserting the refusal reports no verdict and mutates nothing.

TWO COUNTERFACTUALS THEN PASSED AND BOTH WERE REAL FINDINGS. Nothing in the Rust suite caught the press losing its chord — the demo did, over the real wire, which is the R1618 lesson recurring: a demo is not the gate a round is judged by. And nothing caught the RPC read publishing a constant, because the producer that joins the router state to the serialized reply sat BETWEEN the two suites that could have covered it and was reached by neither. Both now have tests, and the final run is 12 of 12 caught from a green baseline.

R1620.decision_summary:
R1620 — a drag reaches past the edge.

R1619 made drag-select expressible; it could still only select what was on screen. A row that is not painted is never entered, so a sweep stopped at the last visible line — and every virtualized view in this tree is windowed, so that is most of the model. Auto-scroll is the other half, and the reference names it on its abstract item view: an auto-scroll property, an edge-margin property, and a start entry point. No view without it can select past its own bottom edge.

THE DEBT NOTE THIS ROUND OPENED WITH WAS WRONG, AND A TEST SAID SO IN FIVE MINUTES. R1619 wrote it, one round earlier, and it claimed the hard part was re-resolving hover when content moves under a stationary cursor — that the router had no trigger for it and that building the timer without that would leave the view scrolling while the selection stood still. Measured: the trigger exists. `refresh_hover_for_all_active_pointers` runs on every repaint and skips only pointers a gesture has PINNED, which a plain drag-select is not, so scrolling the content mid-sweep already extended the selection (`[[0,1]]` -> `[[0,2]]` -> `[[0,3]]`, cursor untouched). That is two rounds running where a debt note's diagnosis was false — R1619 on an inherited note, R1620 on its own, one round old. A note written at round-end without a test is a guess, and the cost lands on the next round as the time to disprove it.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY MISSING was the ramp and the frame tick, and the design parts from the reference on the axis that matters. Read from its source rather than assumed: a counter starts at zero when auto-scroll begins and increments once per timer tick, capped at the page step, and THAT counter is the per-tick distance. So the speed is a function of elapsed time alone, and the pointer's depth into the margin is read as a boolean — in, or out. A user who wants to go faster cannot; one who overshoots waits for the ramp to restart. Here the band IS the ramp: zero at its inner edge, the declared maximum at the viewport boundary, linear between, saturating outside so a pointer dragged far past the window asks for max speed and not for an unbounded jump. Measured over ten identical frames through the wire: 61 px shallow against 231 px deep. It also removes a state — there is no ramp counter to reset, because speed is a pure function of position. And it integrates a velocity against the frame's own `dt`, where the reference scrolls a fixed step per 50 or 150 ms timer tick, hard-coded, with a source comment wishing it were a style hint.

NOTHING IS FABRICATED. Scrolling moves content under a stationary cursor, so the address under the pointer changes with no input at all. The reference handles that by SYNTHESISING a mouse-move and posting it to the viewport, flagged as framework-synthesised — an event the application receives and, at the widget, cannot tell from the user's. Here the new hover target is a derivation of the new picture. That is why the probe mattered before anything was built: the round leans on that path, so it proved it first rather than assuming it.

THE PIN IS THE GESTURE. The scroll region is captured at the press — weakly, so a panel torn down mid-drag ends the gesture rather than being kept alive by it, and with its viewport rect AND its declared policy beside it. All three are read at the moment the pointer is OUTSIDE the region, where a hit-test finds nothing, and that is not an edge case: it is where auto-scroll does its work. Pinning also makes the gesture belong to ONE region, the way its selection already does. The policy is snapshotted for a reason a counterfactual proved: a default-valued fallback switched a region that had declared auto-scroll OFF back on at exactly the moment the pin starts being used.

A COUNTERFACTUAL MADE THE ROUND DELETE CODE, which is the best outcome one can have. The tick was gated both on `held_buttons(id).is_empty()` and on the pin's presence, and nothing could catch removing the first — because a pin exists exactly while a button is held, so the two could never disagree. Two readers of one fact. The fix was to delete a check rather than to write a test for it.

ANOTHER MOVED THE COMPOSITION. `tick_auto_repeat(..) || tick_auto_scroll(..)` short-circuits, so a press that is both repeating a step and holding an edge loses half of itself the moment the first says yes — a bug invisible in either mechanism's own tests. The composition sat in the shell, where no fixture could drive both at once, so it moved onto the router next to the R1549 auto-repeat fixtures and got the test it could not otherwise have had. The per-frame shell seam is renamed `tick_pointer_hold_for_window` to match: a second continuation arriving under a name that promises only the first is how three backends end up with two seams that drift.

A THIRD found that `off()` zeroes both the band and the speed, so no test could say which half of `is_enabled` was load-bearing; a zero-width band beside a live speed now has one. Nine counterfactuals, nine caught, after one was retired as mis-written — its edit was inert because the real gate sits a level below where it cut, and the property it named is covered by the pin case. R1619's own baseline gate on the driver paid for itself here: every run started from a verified-green tree.

R1621.decision_summary:
R1621 — a display says how much of it is usable, and how sure it is.

The last BUILDABLE analyzer-tool plane-C gap. A dashboard that tears a widget off into its own window could say where to put it — R1087 position, R1576 display-relative placement, R1617 `display_home` — but not where it was ALLOWED to go, so a torn-off window opens under the panel.

THE REFERENCE'S OWN SOURCE IS THE FINDING, and it was read rather than assumed. Its X11 plugin carries an internal comment saying that deriving a per-monitor work area from the desktop-wide atom is unreliable, that window managers disagree about what the atom means with several monitors attached, and that the window-manager specification has no atom for the per-monitor answer at all. Its conclusion is the part that matters: its screen accessor RETURNS THE FULL BOUNDS for every display as soon as more than one is attached, unless an environment variable overrides. So on any two-monitor desk the reference answers "all of it is available", and the caller cannot tell that from a measurement. Two different facts arriving as one value with the difference discarded at the boundary — R1617's shape, one field over.

SO THE ANSWER CARRIES ITS PROVENANCE. Four arms rather than `Option<Rect>`: `Reported` (a measurement), `DesktopWide` (a work area exists, but this desk has several displays and the clip cannot be attributed to one), `Unpublished` (the platform has none — Wayland, where the protocol does not tell a client where the shell's panels are), `Unprobed` (nobody asked). `rect()` answers on every arm, so a client placing a window never has to match; `is_measured()` is true only for the first. An `Option` would have fused "this desk has no panels", "the platform cannot say" and "nobody looked" into one absence, and those are three different things to a client deciding where to open something.

AND THE DERIVATION RECOVERS DISPLAYS THE REFERENCE GIVES UP ON. If the desktop-wide work area takes NOTHING from a display, that display's whole bounds are usable and that is a real answer, however many displays the desk has. A dock down the left monitor therefore leaves the right monitor with a measurement, where the reference loses both. Only the displays the atom actually clips are unattributable, and they say so. A display the work area misses entirely reports its bounds rather than an empty rectangle, because "none of this display can be used" is the one answer that is certainly wrong.

THE PROBE IS REAL AND IT RAN. `x11rb` was already in the tree transitively through winit's own X11 backend, so the dependency is a direct edge at the same version rather than a second copy, and it is target-scoped. Measured on this desk through the wire: `usable 2494x1568+66+32, reported` — a 66-pixel left dock and a 32-pixel top bar, read off the live root window. A Wayland session is refused BEFORE connecting, because under XWayland the atom describes the X root window rather than the compositor's panels, and answering would be a confident guess about the wrong desk. Every failure inside the probe collapses to `None` deliberately: a work area is an optimisation on window placement, and a shell that refused to start because a property was missing would trade a cosmetic answer for the whole application.

THREE COUNTERFACTUALS PASSED FIRST AND ALL THREE WERE REAL. Nothing caught "probed and told there is nothing" collapsing into "never probed" — which is the distinction the type exists for. Nothing caught the wire publishing a constant provenance. And nothing caught the schema's closed value set being hand-written rather than derived from the arms, which is the second-copy failure this project keeps paying for. The demo could catch none of them, because a real desk produces one arm out of four. All three now have tests, and the schema test asserts that the DECLARED set equals the set the conversion can actually emit — the R1616 published-equals-accepted property, applied to a set this round introduced.

The wire type is declared in `pinion-rpc` rather than in core, following `DisplayHomeWire`: the census that keeps `rpc/schema` honest reads only that crate. The closed value set is R1616's `values` slot, fed from `UsableRegion::WIRE_NAMES` — a `const` computed from the arms, so it cannot go stale against the type it describes.

R1622.decision_summary:
R1622 — the crate stacks.

The chart residue's plainest item, and the one the standing directive names most directly: `pinion-chart` drew several areas over one another and left the ACCUMULATION to the application. A binding wanting a stacked area chart had to hand in a series whose `y` was already a running sum — so the chart's tooltips, its legend and its value axis all reported the TOTAL where the reader sees a band, and the original measurement was gone before anything could ask for it. The deliverable is a crate that composes, not an example that pre-computes.

THE AUDIT CAME FIRST, BECAUSE THE DEBT FILE DEMANDED IT, AND IT MOVED THE LIST. That file's own "How to apply" says every item is an R1568 judgment to re-check against the code, since its #1–#7 all went stale exactly that way. Measured: the CATEGORY AXIS IS PRESENT (`TickFormat::Category(Categories)` in `ticks.rs`) — that entry was stale. LABEL THINNING exists in some form (a whole-decade stride). LOCAL TIME is absent BY STATED DESIGN, `civil.rs` saying it needs a timezone database, which makes it an external dependency rather than a gap. And the per-mark a11y item is MIS-FRAMED: it names box / candle / polar as lacking what others have, but the whole crate has no `AccessNode` at all, so that is one axis-wide question and not three widget ones. Genuinely absent and correctly framed: OHLC, spline, stacked area, violin, and SVG `d` / Arc-Quad — the last of which the file itself says is a `Scene::Path` vocabulary axis rather than dataviz.

STACKING IS TWO CURVES, NOT ONE, which is exactly why `area_path` could not express it: it closes onto a SCALAR baseline. `area_between` walks the upper curve forwards and the lower backwards, so the ring closes without a bow tie wherever a negative series makes the two cross. And a band keeps both facts — `Series::points` is what was measured, `upper` / `lower` is where it is drawn — so nothing downstream has to reconstruct one from the other.

IT REFUSES TO GUESS. Stacking is only defined when the series share an x grid: adding a value sampled at 10:00 to one sampled at 10:07 requires deciding what the second was doing at 10:00, and every answer to that is an interpolation the chart would be inventing. A series whose grid disagrees is drawn UNSTACKED on the baseline rather than resampled, because a picture whose totals are not the data's totals is the one failure a stacked chart must not have. The f64 grid comparison is exact on purpose and says so in an `expect` reason: these are the same numbers the caller put in, not computed ones, so a tolerance would only admit a genuinely different grid. Negatives stack DOWNWARD from the running total rather than being clamped away. A hidden series contributes nothing and draws no band, while the ones above it keep their palette index — `Series::visible`'s existing rule, extended to the stack, so a legend toggle re-stacks without re-colouring.

THE AXIS DEFECT IS THE ONE A CALLER MEETS FIRST. Three series each peaking at 40 reach 120, and a plot scaled to the per-series maximum clips two thirds of the picture. `stacked_value_bounds` is its own function for that reason, and `resolved_y_domain` was EXTRACTED out of `build_body` because a counterfactual proved the choice untestable while it lived inline: a test can compare two pictures, but it cannot say which domain produced either. That extraction is the round's second finding-driven structural change, after the four clippy signals — a four-bool struct, a 114-line function, and two deliberate exact float comparisons — were each answered with a reason rather than a silence.

Eight counterfactuals, eight caught, every run from a verified-green baseline. Two had to be rewritten after `cargo fmt` moved their anchors and one after it did not compile — the standing three, met again.

R1629.decision_summary:
A chart says what it derived, and the wire carries it. A picture is made from two sources -- the data it was given and the request that said how to draw it -- and neither survives into the pixels. Every chart in this crate already knew what it had done to them: LineChart::overshoot names where a spline left the data, Density knows the kernel and bandwidth that decide a violin's whole outline, BoxPlotChart::without_density names the categories that cannot become one, five charts report off-scale data. ALL OF IT WAS IN-PROCESS RUST, so under §2 #2 the primary client -- which holds a Scene and no chart -- was the one reader that could not ask. pinion_core::derivation is the channel, pinion_chart::derivations is the vocabulary, and scene/derivations {tag, kind?} is the wire.

THE FOUR KINDS ARE A CLOSED 2x2, NOT A LIST. A derivation is a disagreement between the picture and one of its two sources, and a disagreement has a direction: {data, request} x {the picture has more, the source has more} = invented / omitted / chosen / discarded, complete by construction. That is why DerivationKind is a PLAIN enum where the round's other new type is not -- a fifth kind would have to name a third source or a third direction and there is not one, so a client's exhaustive match stays exhaustive. Evidence, whose arms are SHAPES of answer rather than cells of a table, is non_exhaustive for the opposite reason. Each arm is also a different ACTION, which is the test of whether a taxonomy earns its arms: invented asks the reader to be warned, omitted asks for a different scale, chosen asks for the control, discarded says the caller's code is wrong.

THE CARRIER WAS DECIDED BY STRUCTURE, NOT BY TASTE. The debt asked whether this should be a general channel or a method per report; the RPC server holds a Scene and the chart object is gone by then, so a per-report method is not merely worse, it is impossible. The fact has to be ON the node. It rides on ContainerNode because a derivation is a statement about a COMPOSITION -- attributing a bandwidth to the one path carrying the outline would publish one fact once per stroke -- and SceneNodeKind::derives_channel is exhaustive with four arms so a kind added later must decide rather than inherit an absence.

TWO RULES KEEP THE REPORT HONEST. A Chosen entry is ALWAYS published: a control that only appears once it has misbehaved is not a control, and a defaulted bandwidth is still a decision the reader did not make. An Invented, Omitted or Discarded entry exists EXACTLY when there is something to report: publishing spill = 0 would make "did this chart invent anything" answer yes for every violin ever drawn. And one entry per (name, subject), never per datum -- a scatter with 10,000 off-scale points publishes one count per series, because a report that grows with the data is a report nobody can read.

THE DEAD CAPS CONTROL IS CLOSED BY REPORTING RATHER THAN DRAWING. with_caps(true) under the OHLC mark added no node and said nothing, so the option reproduced as "it does not work". The bar's own open and close ticks already play the caps' role, so there is no counterpart to draw; the answer is a Discarded entry whose evidence NAMES the mark that made the setting meaningless. And the same defect class was found one step away: without_density is keyed off the DATA, so it fires under a box mark where no violin was ever asked for. The derivation is keyed off the REQUEST, and a counterfactual proves the difference.

THE WRITER REMOVES THE CENSUS. Every chart reaches the scene through derivations::chart_root, which TAKES the derivation set rather than defaulting it, so a chart added later cannot compile without deciding what its drawing derived -- the alternative was a hand-written list of chart types in a test, the shape that goes stale in silence (R1619's general form). The five charts with nothing to report pass an EMPTY set, which is Published-with-no-entries and a different answer from Silent: "I ran my reports and the picture hides nothing" against "this composition does not answer".

THE CHANNEL TEST DERIVES EVERY EXPECTATION FROM AN INDEPENDENT OBSERVABLE, never from the declaration -- how many of two offered children a kind's own constructor accepts (a list is a composition, one is a viewport), whether an opaque-handle walk resolves it, whether the kind has a tag field at all. That is the trap the marks sibling recorded: its first draft compared the declaration to the declaration and a counterfactual retagging a kind passed. A new fixture, scene_of_kind_holding, states the arity because ContainerNode::new takes a Vec and ScrollNode::new takes one Scene.

TWO COUNTERFACTUALS PASSED AND BOTH WERE REAL. The order test for per-subject tallies used slot.10 before slot.2, and "slot.10" sorts BEFORE "slot.2", so the fixture could not tell first-seen order from map order -- it proved nothing and the map iteration passed it. And nothing at all held the published excursion to being the WORST one: inverting the max to a min left the whole suite green, because "beyond > 0.0" is true of the smallest excursion too. One entry per series is only defensible if the entry is the one a reader must be warned about. 13 counterfactuals, 13 caught after those two repairs, from a verified-green baseline.

THREE EXISTING GATES CAUGHT THE ROUND. rpc/errors' published-vocabulary test refused UnknownDerivationKind reaching the wire unpublished; the method catalog refused an unsorted entry; the wire census refused four undescribed Serialize types, and its optional-vs-nullable distinction refused a first draft that claimed the absent fields arrive as null. The filter's accepted set is DERIVED from DerivationKind::ALL in all three places it appears -- the refusal message, the census, and the answers -- because a second copy of a closed set goes stale in silence, and here it would make the exhaustive-match claim wrong at exactly the moment a fifth kind arrived.

OBLIGATION 3b LIFTED THE THIRD COPY. params.from's paint/state resolution was written out in scene/locate_region and scene/marks and would have been a third time here; resolve_scene_basis takes the DEFAULT as an argument, which is the only thing that differed (a geometry question defaults to state, a question about what was DRAWN defaults to paint). It returns an owning enum because a produced frame has to live somewhere -- the three hand-written `let painted;` declarations were doing that by hand. One consequence reached the wire: the refusal now has one wording where it had two orderings of the same two words, and r1615's demo asserted the old one.

Dataviz re-judged 95 -> 96, demanded by the tool (round-axis 9 -> 12 across R1626, R1628 and this round). Small on purpose and the size is the finding: R1626 closed the violin, one of six buildable items; R1628 repaid debts THIS SERIES created, which restores credit rather than adding capability; and this round's new surface is not on any gap list the axis has ever kept, which by R1528's rule is worth a point rather than several. The audit found drag pan / rubber-band zoom NO LONGER BLOCKED -- four judgments called it unbuildable pending a pointer wire that could not report a held button, and R1619 and R1620 built both halves -- and it found a gap the axis had never named: only five of the ten chart builders have anything to derive, and a treemap's tiling and a timeline's lane packing are layout decisions a reader cannot recover that are modelled as choices nowhere.

R1630.decision_summary:
A vocabulary counts its own arms. This tree carries the same shape eighteen times: an enum that publishes a vocabulary writes a hand-maintained `pub const ALL: [Self; N]` beside itself, and every consumer that must "cover the vocabulary" iterates it. Nothing connects that list to the enum's definition -- add a variant, forget the const, and every such consumer silently covers one fewer case while the code compiles and every test passes. It is the `#[non_exhaustive]` wildcard moved one line down. `#[derive(VariantCensus)]` closes it, and the two debts that were waiting on exactly this closed with it.

THE LIST CANNOT BE REPLACED, SO THE DEFINITION IS PUBLISHED INSTEAD. A variant carrying a payload cannot appear in a value list at all, so no derive can generate `ALL`. What only the definition knows is its SIZE, so the derive emits `ARMS` and `ARM_NAMES`, and `#[variant_census(all)]` adds a `const` assertion that the hand-written list is the same length. A `const` block rather than a test, because a check somebody has to run is the shape this replaces: a stale list is now a BUILD failure carrying the derive's own sentence. Applied to all eighteen sites across three crates, which cost pinion-chart and pinion-rpc a `pinion-derive` dependency. NONE OF THE EIGHTEEN WAS STALE -- the honest result, and the point: this is a ratchet, not a bug hunt.

THE PATH DEBT CLOSED BY A CARDINALITY ARGUMENT, not by a census the language cannot express. R1623 left one hole it called unclosable: an arm added to `PathCommand` could REUSE an existing `PathCommandKind`, giving two commands the same `type` on the wire, and its own debt note said `non_exhaustive` arms cannot be enumerated from outside so a census cannot close it -- offering "state the limit and close" as a legitimate ending. It was not needed. `kind()` is TOTAL by the compiler (exhaustive inside pinion-core); the fixture test already proved it SURJECTIVE (every kind has a command that answers with it); and a total surjective map between finite sets of EQUAL SIZE is injective. So the only missing fact was the size, and the derive reads it off the definition. What was absent was never the method -- it was a tool that reads the definition, which is R1619's shape again ("the type was there; the channel was not").

THE EVIDENCE DEBT CLOSED BY R1623'S OWN RECIPE, and that debt's stated reason for deferring was wrong. `Evidence::describe` projects onto `EvidenceForm`, a closed type obtainable no other way, so the serializer one crate over matches exhaustively and its `_ => {}` is DELETED rather than extended; `EVIDENCE_WIRE_NAMES` is derived from `EvidenceForm::ALL` instead of hand-listed. The debt file said the value representation would have to be closed "a second time" and that doing so was a guess without a fifth arm to look at. There was nothing to close: the four shapes already exist, and a fifth `Evidence` arm must either map onto one (a duration is a real) or add a form -- and adding a form breaks every consumer LOUDLY, which is the outcome worth having. A round-end note written without a test is a guess, one day later this time.

THE TWO DEBTS LOOKED LIKE ONE CLASS AND WANTED OPPOSITE PROPERTIES. Both are "a projection from an enum's arms onto a wire vocabulary", but `PathCommandKind` must be INJECTIVE -- the kind is the command's identity on the wire and two commands sharing one is a defect -- while the evidence map must NOT be, because a form is the SHAPE of a value and two evidences sharing one is correct. That asymmetry is now a test of its own, because a reader will otherwise assume it away.

THE DEMO CHECKS THE END A BUILD GATE CANNOT REACH. `rpc/schema` publishes the accepted set for four fields, and the demo reads those sets OFF THE WIRE -- a hard-coded copy in the demo would be a fifth copy of the closed set, which is the defect the round removes -- then asserts BOTH directions: every observed value is promised (soundness), and every promised value is produced by a real surface in the run (reachability). Neither alone is worth anything: soundness passes trivially against an over-long list and reachability against an under-long one. All four channel arms are reached from real surfaces, `opaque` through the STATE scene because that is where an External lives and a view-fn binding's view emits a container. And every evidence object on the wire is checked to carry a payload, which is the exact signature of the fallthrough this round removed: an object with one key.

THE HARNESS CANNOT SCORE A BUILD GATE, AND THAT IS THE ROUND'S OTHER FINDING. `counterfactual.py`'s oracle is the test suite, and its property 3 declares a compile error a FAILURE rather than a catch -- correct for a case that breaks accidentally, exactly backwards for a gate whose mechanism IS breaking the build. Three cases came back BROKEN because a `const` assertion fired before any test could run, so the eighteen strongest defences this round added scored zero. Worse in the other direction: a case that DELETES the assertion compiles and passes, and is reported PASSED. The incentive runs backwards -- adding compile-time gates makes a round's `n/m caught` worse. Registered with the fix (a declared per-case expectation, which would also remove any need for a separate compile-fail harness).

ONE COUNTERFACTUAL PASSED AND IT WAS REAL: the derive's own doc claims an unknown `variant_census` option is "refused by name rather than ignored", and nothing held it to that -- making the `else` arm return `Ok(())` left the whole suite green. A misspelled opt-in that silently does nothing is the worst outcome available here, because the author then believes a build gate exists where there is none. Closed by unit-testing the parser function directly, since the refusal itself is a compile error this tree cannot assert.

AND THE ROUND'S OWN FIXTURE REPRODUCED R1629's FINDING ONE DAY LATER. The derive test's declaration-order assertion used First / Second / Third, which sort into their own declaration order, so it could not fail whatever the derive did. Renamed to Zebra / Apple / Mango. That is the second consecutive round in which a fixture could not distinguish the two orders it was written to distinguish.

Declared `none` on the Phase B ledger: a soundness gate and two debt closures move no capability, and crediting an axis for being made sound is the inflation R1606, R1613, R1614, R1618 and R1623 each refused.

R1630.publishable_decision_summary:
A vocabulary counts its own arms. This tree carries the same shape eighteen times: an enum that publishes a vocabulary writes a hand-maintained `pub const ALL: [Self; N]` beside itself, and every consumer that must "cover the vocabulary" iterates it. Nothing connects that list to the enum's definition -- add a variant, forget the const, and every such consumer silently covers one fewer case while the code compiles and every test passes. It is the `#[non_exhaustive]` wildcard moved one line down. `#[derive(VariantCensus)]` closes it, and the two debts that were waiting on exactly this closed with it.

THE LIST CANNOT BE REPLACED, SO THE DEFINITION IS PUBLISHED INSTEAD. A variant carrying a payload cannot appear in a value list at all, so no derive can generate `ALL`. What only the definition knows is its SIZE, so the derive emits `ARMS` and `ARM_NAMES`, and `#[variant_census(all)]` adds a `const` assertion that the hand-written list is the same length. A `const` block rather than a test, because a check somebody has to run is the shape this replaces: a stale list is now a BUILD failure carrying the derive's own sentence. Applied to all eighteen sites across three crates, which cost pinion-chart and pinion-rpc a `pinion-derive` dependency. NONE OF THE EIGHTEEN WAS STALE -- the honest result, and the point: this is a ratchet, not a bug hunt.

THE PATH DEBT CLOSED BY A CARDINALITY ARGUMENT, not by a census the language cannot express. R1623 left one hole it called unclosable: an arm added to `PathCommand` could REUSE an existing `PathCommandKind`, giving two commands the same `type` on the wire, and its own debt note said `non_exhaustive` arms cannot be enumerated from outside so a census cannot close it -- offering "state the limit and close" as a legitimate ending. It was not needed. `kind()` is TOTAL by the compiler (exhaustive inside pinion-core); the fixture test already proved it SURJECTIVE (every kind has a command that answers with it); and a total surjective map between finite sets of EQUAL SIZE is injective. So the only missing fact was the size, and the derive reads it off the definition. What was absent was never the method -- it was a tool that reads the definition, which is R1619's shape again ("the type was there; the channel was not").

THE EVIDENCE DEBT CLOSED BY R1623'S OWN RECIPE, and that debt's stated reason for deferring was wrong. `Evidence::describe` projects onto `EvidenceForm`, a closed type obtainable no other way, so the serializer one crate over matches exhaustively and its `_ => {}` is DELETED rather than extended; `EVIDENCE_WIRE_NAMES` is derived from `EvidenceForm::ALL` instead of hand-listed. The debt file said the value representation would have to be closed "a second time" and that doing so was a guess without a fifth arm to look at. There was nothing to close: the four shapes already exist, and a fifth `Evidence` arm must either map onto one (a duration is a real) or add a form -- and adding a form breaks every consumer LOUDLY, which is the outcome worth having. A round-end note written without a test is a guess, one day later this time.

THE TWO DEBTS LOOKED LIKE ONE CLASS AND WANTED OPPOSITE PROPERTIES. Both are "a projection from an enum's arms onto a wire vocabulary", but `PathCommandKind` must be INJECTIVE -- the kind is the command's identity on the wire and two commands sharing one is a defect -- while the evidence map must NOT be, because a form is the SHAPE of a value and two evidences sharing one is correct. That asymmetry is now a test of its own, because a reader will otherwise assume it away.

THE DEMO CHECKS THE END A BUILD GATE CANNOT REACH. `rpc/schema` publishes the accepted set for four fields, and the demo reads those sets OFF THE WIRE -- a hard-coded copy in the demo would be a fifth copy of the closed set, which is the defect the round removes -- then asserts BOTH directions: every observed value is promised (soundness), and every promised value is produced by a real surface in the run (reachability). Neither alone is worth anything: soundness passes trivially against an over-long list and reachability against an under-long one. All four channel arms are reached from real surfaces, `opaque` through the STATE scene because that is where an External lives and a view-fn binding's view emits a container. And every evidence object on the wire is checked to carry a payload, which is the exact signature of the fallthrough this round removed: an object with one key.

THE HARNESS CANNOT SCORE A BUILD GATE, AND THAT IS THE ROUND'S OTHER FINDING. `counterfactual.py`'s oracle is the test suite, and its property 3 declares a compile error a FAILURE rather than a catch -- correct for a case that breaks accidentally, exactly backwards for a gate whose mechanism IS breaking the build. Three cases came back BROKEN because a `const` assertion fired before any test could run, so the eighteen strongest defences this round added scored zero. Worse in the other direction: a case that DELETES the assertion compiles and passes, and is reported PASSED. The incentive runs backwards -- adding compile-time gates makes a round's `n/m caught` worse. Registered with the fix (a declared per-case expectation, which would also remove any need for a separate compile-fail harness).

ONE COUNTERFACTUAL PASSED AND IT WAS REAL: the derive's own doc claims an unknown `variant_census` option is "refused by name rather than ignored", and nothing held it to that -- making the `else` arm return `Ok(())` left the whole suite green. A misspelled opt-in that silently does nothing is the worst outcome available here, because the author then believes a build gate exists where there is none. Closed by unit-testing the parser function directly, since the refusal itself is a compile error this tree cannot assert.

AND THE ROUND'S OWN FIXTURE REPRODUCED R1629's FINDING ONE DAY LATER. The derive test's declaration-order assertion used First / Second / Third, which sort into their own declaration order, so it could not fail whatever the derive did. Renamed to Zebra / Apple / Mango. That is the second consecutive round in which a fixture could not distinguish the two orders it was written to distinguish.

Declared `none` on the Phase B ledger: a soundness gate and two debt closures move no capability, and crediting an axis for being made sound is the inflation R1606, R1613, R1614, R1618 and R1623 each refused.

R1631.decision_summary: eleven commands are three parameters: pinion_node_graph::arrange (Align / Distribute / Stack / Straighten over Axis x Edge) closes the ALIGNMENT cluster, the largest single block the node-graph campaign had open and the one its entry file named as the next round's first candidate. Declared `dcc`: the node graph is one of that axis's three named families and this is a capability it did not have. THE REFERENCE SPELLS ITS ARGUMENTS INTO ELEVEN NAMES -- AlignNodesLeft, AlignNodesTop, DistributeNodesHorizontally -- so the set cannot be enumerated, stored, or offered by a generic control, and every consumer writes the eleven-way match again. Here they are an axis (2), an edge (3) and a gap: six aligns, two distributes, two stacks and a straighten. TWELVE, not eleven -- ours takes the axis on Straighten too, so a top-to-bottom editor gets the command the reference's one-way graphs never needed. THREE PLACES PAST THE REFERENCE. (1) The result is a VALUE: every pass answers the same `Placement` the Sugiyama and organic passes answer, so an arrangement can be previewed, diffed or refused before anything moves, where the reference's commands write straight into the graph. (2) The stack's padding is a PARAMETER; the reference compiles a constant into the editor, so an application whose cards are twice as tall cannot ask for a proportionate gap -- the demo drives three gaps through one command and reads the clear space back off the painted scene. (3) STRAIGHTEN SAYS WHAT IT COULD NOT STRAIGHTEN: a fan-in cannot be made straight (two producers both want the consumer's free-axis coordinate) and the reference moves what it can, silently. `Straightened::bent` names every leftover link, which is the difference between 'this is as straight as it goes' and 'this tool is unreliable' -- and it is a fact about the GRAPH, so a caller can split the selection instead of pressing again. A PLACEMENT COULD NOT BE APPLIED, which the round found by needing to: the signature example wrote the write-back loop twice and this crate's own tests were about to write a third, so `Document::apply` is the rule-of-three lift. It counts only the nodes that actually moved, which is what lets an undo stack skip an empty entry -- and that count is what the wire verb answers. THE CENSUS PIN MOVED WITH PROOFS: eleven engine verdicts go absent -> have, each naming the test that exercises it through the public API (R1602's standing rule), taking GraphEditor 20/51 -> 31/51 and the engine tree 40% -> 45%. AND THE DEMO'S OWN DISTRIBUTE FIXTURE COULD NOT DISCRIMINATE at first: packing to a constant gap and then distributing reproduces the same gaps whatever the pass does, so the check would have passed against a no-op. Made uneven first, with a guard asserting it IS uneven -- the third consecutive round in which a fixture failed to distinguish the thing it was written to distinguish. 33-assertion demo reading positions off the painted scene rather than the model.

R1632.decision_summary: a port count is a property of the NODE, not of its kind: NodeKind::variadic declares that one run of a kind's ports repeats, Node::items carries that node's, and Document::insert_item / remove_item / move_item edit them -- which is the reference's FOURTEEN variadic-pin commands as two operations and a position. The engine's AddExecutionPin, InsertExecutionPinBefore, InsertExecutionPinAfter, RemoveExecutionPin, AddOptionPin, RemoveOptionPin, SoundCueGraph::AddInput, SoundCueGraph::DeleteInput, AnimGraph::AddBlendListPin, AnimGraph::RemoveBlendListPin, node::RemovePinAt, node::CreateUniquePinName and MaterialEditor::DeletePin, plus the DCC's socket_items add / remove-by-index / remove-active / move. Declared `dcc`: the node graph is one of that axis's three named families, and this was the campaign entry file's largest remaining engine block. THE WHOLE DIFFICULTY IS RE-INDEXING, AND THE REFERENCE SHIPS IT UNFIXED: UAnimGraphNode_BlendListByInt::RemovePinFromBlendList carries "//@TODO: ANIMREFACTOR: Need to handle moving pins below up correctly" at 5.8.1. A Socket addresses a port BY INDEX, so removing one item moves every link and every authored value after it -- including the FIXED ports past the run, which have no visual cue on the node at all -- and getting it wrong does not fail loudly, it re-points wires at the wrong sockets. So the three operations state only what they are (an insert, a removal, a permutation) as a correspondence over ITEM ORDINALS, one derivation turns that into the port map, and that ONE map drives the links and the authored values together, because a link kept while the value on the same port is dropped is silent corruption. That pairing is why remap_ports is lifted out of set_kind -- not a count of copies but a single source for an invariant, the same argument Document::signature's own doc already makes about the four node bodies. FOUR PLACES PAST THE REFERENCES. (1) A removal NAMES the wires it cut and hands back the values it dropped; the engine's RemoveExecutionPin answers void after UEdGraphPin::DestroyImpl has called BreakAllPinLinks, so what it disconnected is simply gone, and the census proof re-makes the link from the report to show the report is enough for an undo. (2) One Variadic declaration fixes the run's place, its template, its floor and its ceiling, so "may I remove one" and "what happens when I do" cannot disagree; the engine spreads the same facts over IK2Node_AddPinInterface::CanAddPin, a per-class CanRemoveExecutionPin, a per-class GetPinNameGivenIndex and a RemoveInputPin WHOSE INTERFACE DEFAULT IS AN EMPTY BODY, so a node type that implements the interface and forgets the remover silently does nothing. (3) The ordinal is applied to the template's name when the SIGNATURE RESOLVES, so a name can never be stale -- the engine re-runs a renaming loop after every insert and every remove -- and there is no arity ceiling: GetMaxInputPinsNum returns 'Z' - 'A' precisely because its pins are NAMED for the letters, a limit that is a consequence of a naming scheme. (4) An Item may carry its OWN name and socket type, which is what all but one of the DCC's socket-item accessors declare (has_type / has_name at 8cf50599, IndexSwitchItemsAccessor the sole exception) and what the engine cannot express at all; the proof shows a wire refused against the template's type accepted against the item's, so connect really consults the resolved signature. TWO PASSING COUNTERFACTUALS WERE FINDINGS, and both were fixture gaps rather than code faults: dropping the untouched side's identity map severed nothing observable because no fixture wired the node's OUTPUT at all, and disabling the swap-time item clamp broke nothing because the fixture never exceeded the target kind's ceiling and a stale list on a non-variadic kind is invisible until the node becomes variadic again. Both fixtures were widened until the counterfactual failed. THE CENSUS PIN MOVED WITH PROOFS: 17 verdicts absent -> have, 13 owning a test named after the operator and 4 citing another's, taking GraphEditor 31/51 -> 37/51, SoundCueGraph 1/3 -> 3/3, the engine tree 45% -> 51% and the DCC tree 71% -> 76%. The redundancy this model does carry is stated rather than hidden: an empty item list and one holding the declared minimum resolve to the same signature, which is the Node::label precedent, and a test asserts the two are one signature.
