re-derives where every tagged mark is painted — deliberately, because an
independent derivation is what makes a focus-ring assertion a comparison rather
than a tautology (R705.1). It folded each `Scroll`'s OFFSET and not its CLIP.
`NodeVisit::absolute_rect`'s own doc argues at length that reported and visible
have to be ONE fact, because a caller that forgets the second call "asserts
against a rectangle nothing was drawn in" — and this was that caller, for as
long as both existed. It also let a LATER duplicate tag overwrite an earlier one
where the framework keeps the first. Nothing had ever checked that the second
implementation agreed with the first.

THE FLOOR MAKES THE SAME SPLIT, measured offscreen against the mature
retained-mode toolkit at 6.11 rather than argued from documentation. Its item
view, scrolled horizontally to the maximum, answers `x=-232 w=99` for the
leading column against a `0..368` viewport — an intersection of nothing. Its own
point-to-item lookup then AGREES with that rectangle: asked what is at the
centre of a rect lying entirely left of the viewport, it names the cell rather
than refusing, so the two-step is not merely inconvenient, it has an
affirmative wrong answer in it. The honest visible-region call it does have is a
widget member, and an item-view cell is not a widget. There is no enumeration in
either direction.

SO THE ENUMERATION IS THE NEW CAPABILITY. `scene/tag_rects` answers, for every
§5.20 intent tag in the painted tree, its own rectangle and the part of it a
pointer reaches — one round trip, `window: null` when a mark is painted but
wholly clipped away. Carried rather than dropped, because "there is no such
mark" and "it is out of sight" take different repairs and `scene/scroll_reach`
is the method that tells those apart; an enumeration that erased the second
would hand a caller the first. The walk is the one `bbox_of_tag` and
`Scene::absolute_rects_by_tag` already use, so the single lookup and the
enumeration cannot disagree, and the test asserts exactly that over every row.

AND THE TWO QUESTIONS GET TWO NAMES. Restoring the clip to the mirror broke
twenty-six demos, and the sweep is what said so: nearly all of them ask what the
VIEW BUILT — which rows a virtualized grid windowed, which cells it asked the
model for, that the newest transcript entry is painted BELOW the fold — and a
node the renderer then clips away is still one the view built. That is a
different question from "where can a person press", and it had one name.
`unclipped_rects_of` is the second name, both readers come out of one walk so
they cannot disagree about the offsets they share, and `r1445` now uses BOTH:
the visible reader for "pinned means the entry can be seen", the placement
reader for "the newest entry is off the bottom".

THE GATE IS THE PART THAT KEEPS IT TRUE. `_gate_tag_rects_agree` runs at every
demo's boot, compares the harness's whole map against the framework's whole
enumeration, and fails on any disagreement. Full coverage in one round trip, so
it is not a sample.

ONE ASSERTION GOT STRONGER RATHER THAN MOVED. `r1004` claimed "first match
revealed at the top" and asserted that source row 0 was in the band — a claim
about the overdraw, not about what a reader can see. Measured after the jump:
rows 0-2 are painted at y=-20, 16 and 52 above a viewport that starts at 88. The
match IS the topmost visible row, so the assertion now says that.

THE FOURTH RED WAS A FLAKE BY CONSTRUCTION AND ITS CAUSE IS REMOVABLE. R1664
measured that the software rasteriser disagrees with itself by one bit of
coverage and made pixel assertions tolerate it, with the tolerance measured from
a control pair in the same run. Measured here: ten captures of one unchanged
screen, 45 pairs — 3 of 45 byte-identical by default, and 45 of 45 with the tile
count pinned to one. So it is thread interleaving, and it goes away. That
matters twice: a control pair agreeing by luck reports a floor of 0 and then
fails a tested pair that noised by 1, which is exactly what put `r1527` red on
CI and green here; and with a tolerance of 1 a stale fragment differing by one
bit is invisible, so removing the noise gives the assertion its strength back.
The pin is set where the binary is LAUNCHED, not in the CI job, because a repro
on a developer machine has to have the property CI has.

TWO MORE REDS BELONGED TO THE ROUND BEFORE THIS ONE. R1674 added `chrome` to
`BoxFacet` and to the wire and did not move the two demos that restate the key
set independently — which is what those restatements are FOR, and they fired.
The second demand was the sharper one: a facet no binding anywhere can be seen
declaring is a key whose presence on the wire is untested, and neither binding
declared a chrome band, so the demo gained a third one that does.
publishable_changes_bullets: `pinion_rpc::locate::tag_rects_of` — every §5.20 intent tag in one pass, each with its own rectangle and the part of it a pointer reaches, first-tag-wins by the same walk `bbox_of_tag` uses.
`scene/tag_rects` publishes it, reading the PAINT tree by default because a view-fn binding's state scene would enumerate a tree of zero rects.
`abs_rects_of` in the demo harness folds each `Scroll`'s clip as well as its offset, and keeps the FIRST match for a duplicate tag — the two ways it had disagreed with the framework.
`unclipped_rects_of` is the second reader: where a mark would be if nothing clipped it, for the callers whose claim is about what the view BUILT.
`_gate_tag_rects_agree` compares the harness's whole map against the framework's whole enumeration at every demo's boot.

`RpcSubprocess` pins the software rasteriser to one tile thread, so a picture is a function of the scene rather than of how the scheduler interleaved the tiles; the `--ignored` GPU pixel job takes the same setting in CI.
Twenty-four demos whose claim is about emission move to `unclipped_rects_of`; `r1445` uses both readers, one per assertion.
`r1004` asserts that the first match is the topmost VISIBLE row, which is what its own sentence always claimed.
`r1514` / `r1516` restate the facet census with `chrome`, and `r1514` gains a third binding that actually declares a chrome band.
publishable_verification_bullets: Full local demo sweep, 575 demos: 29 failures before, and every one accounted for — 26 from the mirror's corrected semantics, 2 from R1674's facet addition, 1 environmental (the silent test card is not loaded on this host).
The four CI reds are green: r914 / r915 / r932 pass with the corrected press point, r1527 passes under software Vulkan three runs in a row with a measured self-disagreement of 0.
Rasteriser determinism measured, not assumed: ten captures of one unchanged screen, 45 pairs — 3 byte-identical by default, 45 with one tile thread.

The floor was measured by a probe linked against 6.11 and run offscreen, not read: unclipped per-item rects, a point-to-item lookup that answers for points outside its own viewport, a visible-region call that exists only for widgets, and no enumeration.

Counterfactuals 4/4 CAUGHT — the mirror dropping the clip, a later duplicate tag winning, the enumeration reporting a rectangle where nothing is shown, and the enumeration reading the state tree by default.
`cargo test -p pinion-rpc` green, `cargo clippy -p pinion-rpc --all-targets --features pinion-runtime/vello` green under -D pedantic.
The one demo still failing locally, `r806`, was measured to fail IDENTICALLY at HEAD with none of this round's changes applied: it is the known local x11grab class and passes on CI.
publishable_carry_forward_bullets: `r806_focus_ring_corner` fails on this host and passed at HEAD identically, so it is not this round's — it is the documented local x11grab class (a live-pixel demo needing a mapped window) and it is green on CI. Stated rather than silently excluded.
`hello-audio-device` needs a silent test card this host does not have loaded; environmental, and the demo refuses loudly rather than opening an audible default, which is the designed behaviour.

The two facet mirrors are independent restatements on purpose, and nothing tells an author who adds a `BoxFacet` that two demos must move with it. They fired as designed and cost one CI run; the mechanism that would make it cheaper — a tripwire at the enum — would have to not destroy the independence that makes the restatements worth having.

R1677.decision_summary:
The screen's specification says what it HAS. It now says what it can be asked
to DO, and a gate drives every declared way of asking.

WHY A CENSUS OF THE PAINT COULD NOT FIND THIS. `spec.rs` describes panes, roles,
cards, fields and a hint strip; `painted.rs` compares the painted scene against
all of it in both directions, and that comparison has caught several rounds of
drift. It cannot catch a missing OPERATION, and the reason is structural: an
operation the screen does not answer paints nothing, so there is no tag to look
for and no run to measure. The blind spot was measured — the reference prototype
publishes its own operation list and measures its own coverage against it, so
the population is ITS declaration and not anyone's reading, and against those
thirty this screen answered seven outright and sixteen not at all while every
check here was green.

TWO COLUMNS OF CAUSE, BECAUSE THAT IS WHERE THE DEFECTS LIVE. Every failure a
person reported while using this screen had one shape: the screen advertises an
operation, an agent driving the wire gets it, and the pointer does not — a wheel
that zooms through an action and not through the wheel hook, a form row whose
press resolves to a named target and falls through an unhandled arm, a frame
that drags without selecting. A single column hides all of them, because the
column that works is the one a test naturally drives. So an operation declares
the action an agent invokes AND whether a person has a way in, and the gate
drives both — the second through this screen's own pointer handlers and aimed at
rectangles read out of the painted scene, never by writing the state, because a
state a test invents can be one no mouse can reach.

ABSENT IS A ROW, NOT A GAP. An operation this screen cannot do is written down
with no verb and no gesture, which is what lets it be counted, ratcheted, and —
the direction that matters more — falsified: a row claimed absent that turns out
to work fails as loudly as one claimed present that does not.

WHAT THE GATE'S FIRST RUN FOUND, and none of it was visible to anything already
running. Six of eighteen declared ways caused nothing, and the six split three
ways.

★ THREE WERE A SILENCE ON THE WIRE. Moving a node, moving a frame and
re-parenting a node between frames each had a gesture and NO OBSERVABLE RESULT:
the canvas positions lived only inside the document and reached the wire
nowhere, and frame membership was witnessed by a toast sentence. An agent
driving any of those three could not observe its own drag. A gesture whose
effect cannot be read is indistinguishable from a gesture that did nothing,
which is precisely how "the frame drags but does not select" survived. `layout`
and `frames` are published reads now, in canvas coordinates because that is the
question a caller placing or comparing nodes is asking — `scene/tag_rects`
answers the window question for the same cards, and the two are different reads
on purpose.

★ ONE WAS THE DECLARATION GATE DOING ITS JOB. Both new reads answered
`UnknownIntrospectPath` on their first drive, because since R1637 the schema
declaration is a PRECONDITION of dispatch rather than a description of it. The
arm exists and the slot has to be declared.

★ TWO WERE MY OWN TABLE BEING OPTIMISTIC, and both corrections are measurements.
The integer stepper cannot cause an edit on the opening screen: the field it
steps is already at its ceiling, so a driver aimed there clamps and causes
nothing. And `validate` has NO pointer path at all — the verdict is derived from
the form, causing it means making a value cross a bound, the stepper correctly
refuses to and the text rows have no pointer path. An agent can close the launch
gate and a person cannot. That is now written down as `gesture: false` rather
than assumed away.

THE COUNT IS EIGHTEEN AND THE READING THAT MOTIVATED THIS SAID SIXTEEN. Kept
visible rather than quietly reconciled: that reading was three-way — answered,
partly, absent — and "partly" is a judgement, while this is binary and
mechanical. Two rows it called partly answered have neither way in: the
configuration export says how many keys there are without exporting them, and
the launch script does not exist. The gate disagreeing with the reading that
motivated it is the gate doing its job.
changes_bullets: `spec::OPERATIONS` — the reference's thirty operations, each with the action an agent invokes, whether a person has a gesture, and the slot that must differ once it has run. Published on the wire beside the rest of the specification, with `absent` derived rather than stored.

`r1677_every_declared_way_of_causing_an_operation_causes_it` — the two tables must name the same operations, every declared way must move its witness, and the absent count is a ratchet the gate refuses to let drift in either direction.
`OPERATION_GESTURES` — eleven drivers, each aimed at a rectangle read out of the painted scene and acting through this screen's own pointer handlers.
`layout` and `frames` are published reads: where each card sits in canvas coordinates, and which host it starts on. Three operations had a gesture and no observable result before them.
`reset_lab_state` (test-only) — the gate's rows have to be independent, and the swept states next door are cumulative on purpose.
`validate` is declared as having no pointer path, measured: the stepper respects its field's bound and the text rows have none.
verification_bullets: `cargo test -p hello-node-lab` 36 passed / 0 failed, including the new gate.

The gate's first run found six of eighteen declared ways causing nothing; all six were diagnosed to a cause and none was waved away — three were an unpublished result, one was the declaration gate, two were my own table being optimistic.
Counterfactuals 4/4 CAUGHT: a declared gesture with no driver, a press that never presses, a witness pointed at a slot its verb cannot move, and a ratchet number that drifted from the table.

Driven over the wire from the running binary: thirty operations published, six with a verb, ten with a gesture, eighteen absent — the same numbers the in-process gate asserts. `layout` answers eight cards with canvas positions, `frames` answers eight memberships.
`r1651_the_node_lab_matches_the_reference.py` green, so the specification's existing forward and backward sweeps still hold with the table extended.
carry_forward_bullets: Eighteen operations remain absent and the gate now names every one of them at each run. The three clusters are the entry plan and they are not random: there is no reset of any kind (five operations — nodes, layout, fields, links, view), half of a link's life is missing (delete, rewire, choose an endpoint, adopt an observed one, reset), and the rest are single features (rename, collapse, disable, add a field by typing, fit to view, export, launch script, go to the first problem).

The reset family is the cheapest of the three and the most clearly one thing: every scope can be rebuilt from `spec`, which is where the opening state already comes from, so the repair is derived rather than authored.

`toggle discovery` has no entry in the action column because it is written through `scene/intervene` — a published slot with a value, where an action would be a second path to one fact. The column models actions only, and that limit is stated in the table rather than papered over.

The gesture drivers live in the test module and the specification carries a bool, because a gesture is a sequence and not a value a table can hold. The pair is asserted in both directions, so neither can drift, but a third form of cause (a key chord, say) would need the table to gain a vocabulary rather than another bool.

R1678.decision_summary:
The screen says what has changed since it opened, and puts it back — and the
same fact decides whether the affordance to do so exists at all.

THE SHAPE IS MEASURED, NOT REMEMBERED. The reference prototype's own operation
list names five resets — which cards exist, where they sit, what the forms hold,
which links are authored, where the view is looking — and this screen answered
none of them. Extracting its markup rather than recalling it settles two things
a guess would have got wrong: four of the five affordances are wrapped in a
CONDITIONAL on a per-scope "has this changed" predicate, so a reset with nothing
to put back is not disabled, it is ABSENT; and the fifth, the view, sits
unconditionally beside the zoom controls. That asymmetry is a judgement worth
keeping — pan and zoom always have a home to go to, while a graph reset
appearing out of nowhere over an untouched screen is an invitation to destroy
work.

★★★ THE REFERENCE CAN DO THIS IN ONE LINE PER RESET BECAUSE OF A STRUCTURAL
CHOICE, AND SEEING IT IS THE ROUND'S REAL CONTENT. It keeps every edit as an
OVERLAY on the opening state, so each reset is one `clear` and each "is there
anything to put back" is one `is_empty`. This tree mutates its document in
place, so both facts have to be derived by comparing against the SPECIFICATION —
which is where the opening state comes from in the first place, so there is no
snapshot that could fall out of step with anything. The two halves are one type
(`ResetScope::changed` / `ResetScope::apply`) because a screen deciding for
itself when to show a "put it back" affordance would be a second author of the
rule, and that failure is silent in both directions: a button over an unchanged
screen does nothing when pressed, and a missing one strands the change.

★★ THE SUBSTRATE HAD THE ASYMMETRY WRITTEN INTO IT AND NOBODY HAD NAMED IT.
`ConfigField::settle` has existed since R1651 — accept the current value as the
one this form opened with — and there was no way back. `revert` is its mirror,
and `ConfigForm::edited` is the question it answers, both in the crate so every
consumer of the settings form gets them rather than the one screen that needed
them today.

The membership half is not decoration, and a value-only baseline is exactly what
this type had: a row ADDED after the form opened is NOT edited — its value is
its original — and a row REMOVED is not in the form to be asked. Both are
changes. `opened_with` carries the keys, not a copy of the rows, because `add`
and `remove` only ever MOVE a field between the held set and the offered set, so
the union is invariant and the keys are enough to put the membership back. The
ORDER is restored too, which a set-based repair would lose, and the order is
what a reader navigates a settings form by. `settle` now accepts the shape as
well as the values, because a launch means "what is running now IS what the
screen shows" and a form reporting its added rows as changes after one would
contradict that in the one place a person looks to check it.

★★ THE GATE LEARNED A REAL PROPERTY OF THE TOOL RATHER THAN A CONVENIENCE.
R1677's operation gate drives every declared way of causing an operation from a
FRESH screen — and a reset cannot be caused from a fresh screen at all, because
there is nothing to put back and its affordance is not painted. That is not an
awkwardness to work around; it is why the reference gates those four buttons. So
`OperationSpec` gained `needs`, naming the operation that has to have run first,
and the gate reaches it the way a person would — by doing the earlier thing,
preferring its GESTURE where it has one. A setup that wrote the state directly
would let a reset be proven against a state no session can produce, which is the
rule the swept states already state. A `needs` naming an operation the table
does not hold is a failure, and one whose target has no way in at all is a
failure too — an unreachable precondition would silently stop exercising the
operation that declared it.

★ THE ONE PLACE THE BACKWARD CHECK HAD TO GROW A NEW IDEA. The four conditional
affordances are tags that are legitimately absent, and the specification names
precisely the buttons that must exist at any given moment rather than declaring
a family that may or may not be there — `declared_tags` reads the same changed
list the painter does. That makes the in-process check unable to see a
`changed_scopes` that always answered yes, since the paint and the specification
would move together; the DEMO is what catches it, because it asserts from
outside that a gated affordance is absent on the opening screen. Measured: the
counterfactual that makes every affordance unconditional is caught there and
nowhere else.

WHAT DID NOT COME ACROSS, AND WHY. The reference's predicate counts an edit that
was made and then undone as a change, because its overlay still holds the key. A
comparison says the screen is back where it started and hides the button. The
button's job is to put something back; if it is already back, the affordance
would do nothing, so the derived answer is the one kept — stated here rather
than left for a reader to discover by diffing behaviour. And its view reset goes
to 100%, while this one goes to the zoom the SCREEN opens at, which the screen
specification fixes at a different number: "reset" means "back to how it opened"
in both, and the two files disagree about what that is.
changes_bullets: `ConfigField::revert` and `ConfigForm::revert` — the mirror `settle` never had; `ConfigForm::edited` is the question they answer, covering values AND the rows added or taken away.
`ConfigForm::settle` accepts the current shape as well as the current values, so a launch leaves nothing reported as changed.
`ResetScope` — five scopes, each carrying both `changed` and `apply`, both derived from `crate::spec` rather than from a snapshot.
`reset` is one action with a declared scope vocabulary (`ArgDomain::OneOf`, built from the census so the words and the arms cannot come apart), not five verbs.
The gate panel grows a row of affordances — one per scope with something to put back — and the view reset sits unconditionally in the zoom cluster, which is where the reference keeps it.
`changed` is a published read: the affordances are derived from it, so a driver and a person are reading one fact.
`seed_links` is lifted out of `opening`, because a reset re-authors those links and the accept-pin run arithmetic must not exist twice.
`spec::OperationSpec::needs` names the operation that has to have run first; the five resets declare theirs and `ABSENT_OPERATIONS` falls 18 to 13.
`tools/demos/r1678_a_screen_puts_itself_back.py` drives the whole journey per scope over the wire and through the router.
verification_bullets: `cargo test -p hello-node-lab` 36 passed / 0 failed, including the operation gate now driving five more operations by both verb and gesture, each from its declared precondition.
`cargo test -p pinion-core -p pinion-widget-paint` green; `cargo clippy -p pinion-core -p hello-node-lab --all-targets` green under -D pedantic.

The new demo passes end to end: per scope, change it, see `changed` report it, see the affordance appear, press it — through the ROUTER for two of them — see the scope go back and the affordance go with it.
The screen's own spec demo is green with the reset family added to both directions of its tag check, the ungated one demanded and the gated four permitted.

The three form-difference kinds are asserted separately in the substrate — an edited value, an added row, a removed row — because a value-only baseline answers the first and silently misses the other two, which is the state the type was in.

Counterfactuals 4/4 CAUGHT: a value-only changed-predicate, a revert that loses the opening order, an affordance painted whether or not there is anything to put back, and a view reset that lands somewhere other than where the screen opened. ★ The third is caught by the DEMO alone — the paint and the specification both derive from one list, so nothing in-process can see it.

which links are authored, where the view is looking — and this screen answered
none of them. Extracting its markup rather than recalling it settles two things

to put back is not disabled, it is ABSENT; and the fifth, the view, sits

snapshot that could fall out of step with anything. The two halves are one type

itself when to show a "put it back" affordance would be a second author of the

screen does nothing when pressed, and a missing one strands the change.

one this form opened with — and there was no way back. `revert` is its mirror,

them today.

R1679.decision_summary:
Every debt this session opened is paid, and paying two of them found defects
neither debt note knew about.

WHAT WAS OWED. Four notes, all written by the rounds that caused them: two from
R1676 (nothing says which of the two rect readers a demo should ask; a new
`BoxFacet` arm moves two demo mirrors by hand and nothing says so) and two from
R1678 (the layout predicate is blind to cards the palette added; only a demo can
see the affordance predicate lie).

★★★ THE AFFORDANCE GATE FOUND A REAL DEFECT ON ITS FIRST RUN, WHICH IS WHY IT
HAD TO STOP ASKING THE PREDICATE. R1678's own counterfactual showed that making
`changed_scopes` always answer yes left all thirty-six in-process checks green —
the paint and the specification both derive from that one function, so they move
together and agree. The repair is not a second copy of the predicate; it is to
judge by RESULT: in every swept state, for every gated scope, take the witness,
apply the reset, take it again, and assert the button was painted **iff** the
value moved. Nothing in that test knows what the predicate answers.

Its first run reported the link reset as changing the screen in all eight states
INCLUDING the opening one, where the affordance was correctly absent. The cause
is real and was invisible before: the reset cleared every link and re-authored
the set, and the model assigns a fresh identifier to each new link, so putting
an UNTOUCHED graph back renumbered all seven of them. The reference's reset is
idempotent because it drops an overlay that is already empty; this one now earns
that by DIFFING — removing only what the specification does not have and adding
only what it is missing, so a link nobody touched keeps its identity. It
deliberately does not consult `changed`, because an `apply` that early-returned
on "nothing differs" would make the new gate compare the predicate with itself.

★★ THE LAYOUT REPAIR WAS UNPROVABLE UNTIL A COUNTERFACTUAL SAID SO, AND THE
REASON WAS A SILENT NO-OP. The predicate's population was the specification's
node list, so a card the palette added could be dragged anywhere and the screen
reported its layout unchanged. It now compares every card against where it came
into being — recorded at creation, from the specification for the opening cards
and from the placement arithmetic for an added one, because a card the
specification does not describe has no other source.

The swept states had no state where an added card is dragged, which the debt
note itself had said. Adding one was not enough: the first draft aimed the drag
with `card_rect`, which answers in the WORLD SURFACE's coordinates while
`move_cursor` takes the window's, so the press went nowhere, the state was a
no-op, and the counterfactual for the very defect it was written for PASSED. The
aim comes from the painted tag now.

★ AND THAT STATE EXPOSED A STRUCTURAL FACT ABOUT THE SWEPT STATES: they have two
consumers with opposite assumptions. The painted sweeps apply them cumulatively
— state n is state n-1 plus one edit — while the operation gate and this new one
reset the screen before each, because their rows must be independent. A state
that leaned on an earlier one for the card it drags passed three tests and
panicked in the fourth. It is self-contained now, and the reason is written
where the next author will be standing.

THE OTHER TWO ARE TRIPWIRES, EACH PUT WHERE THE COST BELONGS. The facet census
gains a test beside itself that reads both demos' hand-written restatements and
fails when they drift — the restatements stay hand-written ON PURPOSE, since
their job is to fail when the projection and the type drift TOGETHER, and a list
derived from the wire would agree with the wire by construction. Only the moment
of discovery moves, from a CI run to the commit that caused it.

And the two rect readers: measured first — twenty-five demos read the placement
reader and NONE of them aims a press with it — then held there by an AST taint
check in the harness's own test suite, which pre-push runs. Aiming a press with
the placement reader re-creates exactly what R1676 paid off: a rectangle that may
be entirely off screen, a press silently dropped, and the failure surfacing sixty
lines later as a value that did not change. What the check can and cannot see is
stated in it rather than left to be discovered by getting away with it.
changes_bullets: `r1679_a_reset_affordance_is_painted_exactly_when_it_would_do_something` — judges by RESULT: painted iff applying the reset moves the witness, in every swept state, consulting no predicate.
`ResetScope::Links::apply` diffs instead of rebuilding, so putting an untouched graph back keeps every link's identity and changes nothing.
The layout scope compares every card against a recorded `Placement` — where it came into being — instead of against the specification's node list, which could not see a card the palette added.
A swept state where an added card is dragged, self-contained so it holds under both the cumulative sweeps and the per-state-reset gates.
`r1679_the_demo_restatements_of_this_census_are_told_when_it_moves` reads both demos' hand-written facet lists and fails, beside `BoxFacet::ALL`, when they drift from it.
`test_no_demo_aims_a_press_with_the_placement_reader` — AST taint over the demo tree, in the harness suite pre-push already runs.
verification_bullets: `cargo test -p pinion-core -p pinion-widget-paint -p hello-node-lab` green (37 in the screen's suite); `cargo clippy` on both changed crates green under -D pedantic.
`python3 tools/test_rpc_verify.py` 31 cases / 82 checks green, including the new press-point taint check.
The two analyzer demos green, including R1678's, which drives the whole reset journey per scope over the wire and through the router.
The added-card gap was re-measured with the same probe that found it: dragging an added card now flips `changed.layout` to true where it stayed false before.

Counterfactuals 5/5 CAUGHT: the affordance predicate always saying yes; the layout predicate back on the specification's node list; the link reset rebuilding instead of diffing; a demo's facet restatement drifting; a demo aiming a press with the placement reader.

★ Two of those were PASSED or BROKEN on the first attempt and both told me something — the layout one because the new swept state was silently a no-op (world coordinates handed to a window-coordinate call), the link one because the mutation did not compile and so tested nothing.
carry_forward_bullets: The press-point taint check does not follow a rectangle through a function parameter or a container, and it cannot know which reader a helper used inside itself. Those need real dataflow; what it catches is the shape every demo actually writes, and the limit is stated in the check.

The swept states now have two consumers with opposite assumptions — cumulative for the painted sweeps, reset-per-row for the operation and affordance gates — and nothing enforces that a new state is self-contained. It is written down at the one state that needs it; a state that quietly depends on an earlier one would fail loudly in the gates rather than silently, which is why this is a note and not a mechanism.
`ConfigForm::revert` and `edited` have one consumer. They are in the crate because that is where the asymmetry was, not because a second consumer asked.

The push was refused, and the red it refused over was not the one this session
had paid off.

STOP-THE-LINE DID ITS JOB AND SO DID THE LESSON THIS SESSION WROTE. R1676 paid
off five CI reds, all of them in the demo sweep, and the push gate still refused
— the last completed run failed. The tempting read is "that is the red I fixed,
override and go", and this session's own entry says why not: **"still failing"
is not "still failing for the same reason"**. Reading the run took one call. The
failing job is `workspace tests`, not the sweep, and the failing test is one
R1674 ADDED.

WHAT FAILED, AND THE DEBT THAT PREDICTED IT.

    toolbar focused=false at 180x120: 1 painted mark(s) left the box that owns
    them — [(Some("Undo"), "toolbar#3", Overhang { left: 1 }, [Outside])]

R1674 built `frame_gate` — every painter in the crate that strokes a border is
asked whether it keeps its own contents inside it — and R1674.1's close audit
found that the zero-flake claim written into its doc was only half true: it said
the font moves a box and its ink TOGETHER, which holds for a content-sized box
and not for a fixed one, and measured ten of fifteen painters pinning a fixed
box with no overflow policy. That is
[[debt-ten-painters-pin-a-box-and-state-no-overflow-policy]], registered one
round earlier, and the very next CI run turned the exposure into a red.

Reproduced rather than reasoned about: with this host's fonts the gate is green,
and with `FONTCONFIG_FILE` pointing at a DejaVu-only config — what the runner
has — "Undo" overhangs by 2 left and 1 right and "Redo" by 1 each side. Same
instrument R1660 built for the ink ratchet, one layer down.

★★★ THE CAUSE IS A POLICY APPLIED TO THE WRONG BOX, AND THAT IS THE GENERAL
FORM. `TextOverflow::Ellipsis` shortens a run to fit ITS OWN rect. Taffy gives a
flex child its content width and `JustifyContent::Center` centres it, so a
child wider than its parent still has a rect it fits exactly — the policy never
fires and the ink spills out both sides. R1674 released the CONTROL's automatic
minimum size so a crowded bar could shrink it, and left the LABEL at its own,
so the control got narrower and the text box did not.

The repair is the same release one level down: the label may shrink below its
content, taffy then clamps the text box to the control, and the elide policy
finally has the right rectangle to shorten against. One line, and the comment
beside it says which round gave the control the same thing and why the label was
missed.

THE CLASS IS NOT CLOSED AND IS REGISTERED RATHER THAN CLAIMED
([[debt-an-overflow-policy-applies-to-the-runs-own-rect]]). Nobody has counted
how many painters centre a text child without releasing its minimum size; the
toolbar is simply the one CI found. The entry plan starts with a parser census
rather than a grep, and names the deeper repair — letting `TextOverflow` see the
parent's content box, so "which box is this policy about" becomes the
framework's answer instead of each painter's.

AND THE GATE THAT FOUND IT CANNOT FIND THE REST HERE. `frame_gate` measures with
the HOST's fonts, so this whole class stays green locally and turns red
elsewhere. The reproduction path exists and is written down; wiring it into a
run somebody actually performs is part of that debt, not a claim made here.

verification_bullets: Reproduced before repairing: `FONTCONFIG_FILE` at a DejaVu-only config turns `r1674_a_toolbar_keeps_its_controls_inside_their_outlines` red on this host with the same overhang CI reported, and the host's own fonts leave it green.

`cargo test -p pinion-widget-paint --lib` green under BOTH font sets after the repair — 873 passed, 0 failed each way, which is the point: the box now moves with the ink instead of only sometimes agreeing with it.

`cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` under that font set, because cargo's default stops at the first failing test binary and CI therefore never ran the packages after `pinion-widget-paint` — a second font-dependent failure would have been invisible behind this one.

WHAT FAILED, AND THE DEBT THAT PREDICTED IT.

    toolbar focused=false at 180x120: 1 painted mark(s) left the box that owns
    them — [(Some("Undo"), "toolbar#3", Overhang { left: 1 }, [Outside])]

R1674 built `frame_gate` — every painter in the crate that strokes a border is
asked whether it keeps its own contents inside it — and R1674.1's close audit
found that the zero-flake claim written into its doc was only half true: it said
the font moves a box and its ink TOGETHER, which holds for a content-sized box
and not for a fixed one, and measured ten of fifteen painters pinning a fixed
box with no overflow policy. That is
[[debt-ten-painters-pin-a-box-and-state-no-overflow-policy]], registered one
round earlier, and the very next CI run turned the exposure into a red.

Reproduced rather than reasoned about: with this host's fonts the gate is green,
and with `FONTCONFIG_FILE` pointing at a DejaVu-only config — what the runner

fires and the ink spills out both sides. R1674 released the CONTROL's automatic
minimum size so a crowded bar could shrink it, and left the LABEL at its own,
so the control got narrower and the text box did not.

content, taffy then clamps the text box to the control, and the elide policy
finally has the right rectangle to shorten against. One line, and the comment
beside it says which round gave the control the same thing and why the label was
missed.

([[debt-an-overflow-policy-applies-to-the-runs-own-rect]]). Nobody has counted
how many painters centre a text child without releasing its minimum size; the
toolbar is simply the one CI found. The entry plan starts with a parser census
rather than a grep, and names the deeper repair — letting `TextOverflow` see the
parent's content box, so "which box is this policy about" becomes the
framework's answer instead of each painter's.

elsewhere. The reproduction path exists and is written down; wiring it into a

R1681.decision_summary:
A link keeps its identity while one of its ends moves — and the screen that
draws links gains the rest of a link's life.

The node-graph screen could MAKE a link and could do nothing else to one. Of the
reference's own thirty operations, five concerned a link and this screen
answered one. The four it did not are one group and they arrive together:
delete, re-aim at another node, choose which of a listening target's addresses
the wire dials, and take a link a source REPORTED into the drawing.

★★★ THE VERB IS NOT DISCONNECT-THEN-CONNECT, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE ROUND.
`Document::connect` mints a `LinkId`. A link taken out and put back is therefore
a NEW link, and everything holding the old name — a selection, a breakpoint, an
undo entry, a renderer's cache — is holding a dangling one. This session watched
exactly that from the other side one round earlier: a reset that rebuilt its
links silently changed a screen that should not have moved, because the rebuild
re-minted every id.

So `Document::relink` takes the link OUT, vets the graph WITHOUT it, and puts it
back under its own id, its own mute and its own place in the tree's order. A
refusal puts it back exactly as it was and returns the authoring refusal whole,
so a move refused for a type mismatch and one refused for a cycle are still the
different findings they are. Three properties, and each has a counterfactual:
minting a new id is caught by six tests, dropping the restore is caught by two,
and skipping the lift is caught by four.

★★ THE FLOOR WAS PROBED RATHER THAN RECALLED. Measured offscreen against the
reference toolkit's 6.11.1 build, whose relocation verb answers the same
question over a different shape: a persistent handle SURVIVES an in-place
relocation and is INVALIDATED by remove-plus-insert — which is precisely why
that verb exists — but it is offered only over a FLAT sequence. The STRUCTURAL
model, the arbitrary-shape one and the closest analogue to a graph document,
inherits the base class's `false` and implements none. And a refusal carries one
bit: the signature is `bool`, so the only thing a caller can learn is that
something failed. A graph is neither a list nor a tree, and "no" is not a
reason.

★★ AN ENDPOINT BELONGS TO THE LINK, NOT THE NODE. That is the reference's own
first sentence about it, and it is a real property of the subject: a target
listening in two places can be dialled in two ways, and which one a wire took is
a fact about the wire. Here that fact is the accept run's ITEM — one slot per
arriving link, LABELLED with the address it dials and TYPED by that address's
own transport. So choosing an endpoint is the same `relink` over a different
socket rather than a second mechanism, and dialling an address this link cannot
speak is refused by the model with both transports named. The reference sets an
index on the wire and checks nothing.

The reference's other rule falls out of the same place: a second wire between
the same two nodes must dial a different address, because that is what a second
transport connection IS, while two different peers may of course dial the same
one. It is one derivation over the item labels, used by the canvas and by the
opening graph's own seeding, because two copies of that arithmetic would agree
while the graph was empty and disagree the moment a reset ran over an edited one
— which is exactly when nobody is looking.

★ A COUNTERFACTUAL PASSED, AND THE HEADER WAS CORRECTED RATHER THAN THE CODE.
Taking the link out before the VET rather than merely before the placement is
NOT observable today: a counterfactual that moved the lift down between the two
left the whole suite green. The four vetting rules are provably blind to the
link being moved in an acyclic graph — a path closing a cycle through it would
have to reach that link's producing node before arriving at its consuming one,
which is a cycle the document already refused. It is the PLACEMENT that can see
it, and that is what the failing counterfactual pins. The lift stays where it is
for the scope it names — every read of the graph happens without the link, so a
check added later cannot inherit the bug silently — and that this is defence
rather than repair is written down instead of implied by a comment nothing can
falsify.

★★ THE SCREEN'S OWN INVARIANT BIT, AND THE ANSWER IS A DERIVATION. This screen
holds that a press ANYWHERE on a card reaches that card, and a floating
affordance is the one thing that can break it: measured, at the zoomed-out sweep
the `delete` seat covered nine sampled points of one card, its centre and its
accept pin among them. Structural rather than a bad constant — a card shrinks
with the zoom while a column whose parts are derived from a type size with a
legibility floor under it does not. So the column is placed where it fits, and
kept inside what the canvas is showing, because the first draft of that nudge
pushed both endpoint seats out of the visible world entirely and traded one
unreachable affordance for another.

★ A REPORTED LINK IS NOT IN THE GRAPH, AND THE SELECTION NOW SAYS SO. It carries
no `LinkId` because it is not a link, so what the canvas picks out is one of two
things and the type says which; the affordance it offers is the opposite one,
since a drawn link can be deleted and a reported one can only be taken into the
drawing. `Document::adopt` runs the AUTHORING rules on it, so a link the world
has and this model cannot express is NAMED rather than dropped — which is the
finding the whole two-layer idea exists to produce. On the wire a reported link
is named by the pair it runs between, because that is the only identity an
observation has.

★ THE DRIVERS PRESS WHAT A PERSON PRESSES. A wire is a PATH and a path's painted
rectangle is its bounding box, whose centre is nowhere near the stroke, so the
aim is read from the two things that DO have rectangles: the pins the wire runs
between. And a link is named to the wire by its ENDS rather than by an id,
because an id is minted in seeding order and a declared argument of `3` would be
asserting something about the order this screen happened to author its opening
graph in.

end of an existing link, keeping its `LinkId`, its mute and its position in

R1681.2.decision_summary:
A reported link is drawn in a rhythm a drawn one is not — and the round before
this one invented the limit that stopped it.

★★★ THE CORRECTION IS THE ENTRY. R1681's carry recorded, as a stated limit
rather than a debt: "a reported link is drawn in the warning colour rather than
dashed: the wire primitive carries no dash pattern." **That is false.** `Stroke`
has carried `dash: Option<Dash>` since R1575, `Dash::DOTTED` and `Dash::DASHED`
are named rhythms on it, and the SIBLING screen that draws these same two layers
— the one R1575 was written for — already spells a reported link `Dash::DOTTED`
and a drawn-but-unreported one `Dash::DASHED`.

So this is not a capability the framework lacks. It is a capability the screen
did not reach for, written down as though the framework were the one at fault.
That direction of error is the worse one: a debt says "somebody should do this",
and a stated limit says "nobody can", and only the second one stops the next
reader from looking.

★ HOW IT SURVIVED, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. Nothing on this screen could
tell. The wires are painted, the colour differs, every gate is green, and no
check anywhere asked whether the two layers are distinguishable by anything
other than a colour — which is exactly the shape of the "declared and not done"
group this screen keeps producing. The claim was made in prose and prose is not
a gate.

What tells now is a check over the painted scene: every `lab.link.*` stroke is
solid, every `lab.observed.*` stroke carries a rhythm. Its counterfactual — the
reported link drawn solid again — fails it, which is what makes it a measurement
rather than a restatement.

★ AND THE REASON COLOUR ALONE IS NOT ENOUGH is the sibling's own: the two layers
mean different things, and a reader who cannot tell a claim about the world from
a decision somebody made is reading the wrong diagram. Colour carries a
severity; the rhythm carries the layer.

R1681.3.decision_summary:
The picked link's affordances go back where the reference draws them — on the
wire — and the screen stops showing one thing while answering another.

★★★ FOUND BY LOOKING AT THE RUNNING APP. Every gate was green. Three defects
were on the screen, and the first one is why the other two existed.

**One.** R1681 moved the picked link's column clear of every card, to satisfy
this screen's invariant that a press ANYWHERE on a card reaches that card.
Measured on the running app: the label and the `delete` seat for the link
`P-01 -> R-01` ended up **240 pixels below the wire they belong to**, past two
other cards, because up and down were both blocked at every step until they were
not. An annotation that far from what it annotates is not an annotation, and the
reference puts it at the wire's middle.

So the INVARIANT is the thing that gives, and precisely: a press covered by the
picked link's own chrome is not an unexplained hole in a card — it is an
affordance the person summoned by picking that link, drawn where the reference
draws it. The card sweeps take that exception from the function that PAINTS the
chrome rather than from a list beside them, so a chrome that wandered somewhere
absurd is still caught covering cards it has no business covering.

★★ AND AN EXCEPTION MUST NOT SWALLOW WHAT IT IS EXCHANGED FOR. The first draft
excused every probe the chrome covered — which includes the chrome — so making
the `delete` seat unpressable left the sweep green. The seats are now declared
controls that must answer at their own centres, and the exception explicitly
does not apply to them. A counterfactual is what said so.

**Two.** With the column back on the wire, the label rendered as `…0.7447`: the
seat width estimated three fifths of the type size per character and the run
elided, losing the SCHEME, which is the half that carries the transport. Both
bounds either side were measured on the running screen — a whole em per
character made a sixteen-character address a seat wider than the card it belongs
to — and seven tenths fits.

**Three, and the one that matters.** The label was still half-hidden, and the
reason was not width. The chrome was painted WITH THE WIRES, before the cards,
while `Hit::at` resolves it FIRST — so a card was drawn over it and a press on
that card answered `link:act`. **The paint and the hit test disagreed about
which thing is on top.** That is this example's oldest defect class, the one
R1656 exists for, and R1681 re-created it the moment it made the chrome
pressable: before that the chrome was a label nobody could press, so there was
no order to disagree about.

The chrome paints last now, and the check is an ORDER over the painted tags
rather than a pixel sample — "later wins" is the rule the renderer follows, and
a sample only reaches the overlaps that happen to exist today.

R1682.decision_summary:
A node keeps its identity while its NAME changes — and the screen that draws
nodes gains the rest of a node's life.

The node-graph screen could PLACE a node and could do nothing else to one. Of
the reference's own thirty operations, eight concern a node itself and this
screen answered four. The four it did not are one group and they arrive
together: delete it, rename it, draw it small, switch it off. That is the same
shape a link's second half had one round ago, in the other half of the model.

★★★ A RENAME IS NOT A RE-CREATION, AND THE COST OF PRETENDING OTHERWISE IS
MEASURED. The behaviour reference has no rename at all: it copies the node under
the new name, covers the old one with a deletion overlay, and then hand-moves
TEN separate side tables to compensate — the placement, the containment, the
edits, the extra fields, the hidden fields, the collapse, the mute, the wire
list, the selection and the draft. Every one of those is a chance to forget one.

`Document::relabel` moves one string. The node keeps its `NodeId`, so its links,
its position, its containment, its authored port values and every table a caller
keys by identity are untouched — and the assertion is that emptiness rather than
a claim about it: the form, the placement, the frame, the degree and the whole
list of link ids are compared across the rename, on both sides of the wire.

★★ THE FLOOR WAS PROBED RATHER THAN RECALLED. Measured offscreen against the
reference toolkit's 6.11.1 build, over its own naming surface. An object's
identity DOES survive a rename there — the handle stays valid, nothing is
destroyed. Three things do not:

  * naming a second sibling what the first is already called is ACCEPTED. Both
    then hold the name, the enumerating lookup answers TWO, and the singular
    by-name lookup answers an arbitrary one of them and says nothing. Its item
    model behaves the same way with a duplicate display string.
  * the rename notification carries exactly ONE argument, and it is the NEW
    name. A listener holding a table keyed by the old one is told that something
    changed and not what to un-key.
  * the rename returns `void`, so nothing can be refused and nothing is
    reported.

So two properties here are strictly better and both are cheap. A name another
node in the tree answers to is REFUSED, with the holder named, which makes
"authored names are unique within a tree, and therefore address exactly one
node" an invariant this crate maintains instead of one every caller re-checks.
And the edit ANSWERS the old name, which costs nothing because the edit already
had it in hand. Where the invariant is broken from OUTSIDE the verb — the field
is public and a caller can still write a duplicate — the singular lookup
declines to guess and a plural one says which of the two failures it was, since
"nothing answers to this" and "several things do" are different problems with
different repairs.

★★ SWITCHING A NODE OFF IS NOT BYPASSING IT, and the difference is what reaches
the nodes downstream. A bypassed node stops computing and its inputs travel
straight through it, so the graph below carries on unaffected; a disabled one
produces nothing, so everything that depended on it reads nothing. An editor
needs both — "route around this" and "switch this off" are different intentions
— and a model with only the first makes the second unsayable, which is how it
ends up in application state where no derivation can see it. `Document::
set_disabled` is a second field beside `bypassed` because it is a second fact
about the graph's MEANING, not a bit in the node's looks.

Driven through the evaluator rather than read off the flags, including the one
path it could still have leaked through: every other exit from that walk falls
back to what was authored on the output port, and a disabled SOURCE — whose
authored value is the only thing it has — must not reach that fallback either.

It deliberately does NOT cascade through containment, the way the reference
toolkit's enabled-ness cascades through its widget tree. That tree is the
interaction tree and a child of a disabled widget genuinely cannot be reached; a
frame in a graph is a grouping on a canvas. The relation along which "this is
not running" actually travels here is the FLOW, and that cascade is DERIVED — a
node fed only by disabled ones reads nothing without anybody having marked it.
Copying the containment cascade would author a fact the flow already answers,
and the two would be free to disagree.

★★ THE SCREEN'S SECOND NAME FOR A CARD WAS LIFTED AWAY, AND RENAMING IS WHAT
MADE IT LOAD-BEARING. The screen kept its own name-to-node map beside the
document's own label: two records of one fact, and a rename that updated either
one alone leaves the canvas and the wire calling a single card two different
things. The model owns names now — it is the thing that can refuse one — so
there is one record and no way to update half of it.

★★★ AND THE RENAME FORCED A DEFECT OUT OF A RESET THAT HAD NOTHING TO DO WITH
IT. The node reset told an opening card from a palette-added one by asking
whether its NAME appears in the specification — which is exactly the thing a
rename changes. A renamed opening card therefore read as a stray, and the reset
whose whole job is to PUT ITS NAME BACK would have deleted the node instead. A
card is a stray when nothing recorded it opening; the record already existed
(R1679 added it so the layout predicate could see a card the palette added) and
now carries the name the card came into being as.

Two more derivations keyed off the current name in the same way and were
silently wrong after a rename: a card's digest lines and its width. A renamed
card stopped matching any specification row, fell through to the
palette-added path, redrew its digest from the first three form fields and
snapped to the default width. Nothing was broken loudly enough to fail, which is
how it would have stayed.

★ A COLLAPSE IS THE SAME REQUEST THE ZOOM ALREADY MAKES. The card already drops
its rows below the zoom at which their face would be illegible; a collapse is

R1682.publishable_decision_summary:
A node keeps its identity while its NAME changes — and the screen that draws
nodes gains the rest of a node's life.

The node-graph screen could PLACE a node and could do nothing else to one. Of
the reference's own thirty operations, eight concern a node itself and this
screen answered four. The four it did not are one group and they arrive
together: delete it, rename it, draw it small, switch it off. That is the same
shape a link's second half had one round ago, in the other half of the model.

★★★ A RENAME IS NOT A RE-CREATION, AND THE COST OF PRETENDING OTHERWISE IS
MEASURED. The behaviour reference has no rename at all: it copies the node under
the new name, covers the old one with a deletion overlay, and then hand-moves
TEN separate side tables to compensate — the placement, the containment, the
edits, the extra fields, the hidden fields, the collapse, the mute, the wire
list, the selection and the draft. Every one of those is a chance to forget one.

`Document::relabel` moves one string. The node keeps its `NodeId`, so its links,
its position, its containment, its authored port values and every table a caller
keys by identity are untouched — and the assertion is that emptiness rather than
a claim about it: the form, the placement, the frame, the degree and the whole
list of link ids are compared across the rename, on both sides of the wire.

★★ THE FLOOR WAS PROBED RATHER THAN RECALLED. Measured offscreen against the
reference toolkit's 6.11.1 build, over its own naming surface. An object's
identity DOES survive a rename there — the handle stays valid, nothing is
destroyed. Three things do not:

  * naming a second sibling what the first is already called is ACCEPTED. Both
    then hold the name, the enumerating lookup answers TWO, and the singular
    by-name lookup answers an arbitrary one of them and says nothing. Its item
    model behaves the same way with a duplicate display string.
  * the rename notification carries exactly ONE argument, and it is the NEW
    name. A listener holding a table keyed by the old one is told that something
    changed and not what to un-key.
  * the rename returns `void`, so nothing can be refused and nothing is
    reported.

So two properties here are strictly better and both are cheap. A name another
node in the tree answers to is REFUSED, with the holder named, which makes
"authored names are unique within a tree, and therefore address exactly one
node" an invariant this crate maintains instead of one every caller re-checks.
And the edit ANSWERS the old name, which costs nothing because the edit already
had it in hand. Where the invariant is broken from OUTSIDE the verb — the field
is public and a caller can still write a duplicate — the singular lookup
declines to guess and a plural one says which of the two failures it was, since
"nothing answers to this" and "several things do" are different problems with
different repairs.

★★ SWITCHING A NODE OFF IS NOT BYPASSING IT, and the difference is what reaches
the nodes downstream. A bypassed node stops computing and its inputs travel
straight through it, so the graph below carries on unaffected; a disabled one
produces nothing, so everything that depended on it reads nothing. An editor
needs both — "route around this" and "switch this off" are different intentions
— and a model with only the first makes the second unsayable, which is how it
ends up in application state where no derivation can see it. `Document::
set_disabled` is a second field beside `bypassed` because it is a second fact
about the graph's MEANING, not a bit in the node's looks.

Driven through the evaluator rather than read off the flags, including the one
path it could still have leaked through: every other exit from that walk falls
back to what was authored on the output port, and a disabled SOURCE — whose
authored value is the only thing it has — must not reach that fallback either.

It deliberately does NOT cascade through containment, the way the reference
toolkit's enabled-ness cascades through its widget tree. That tree is the
interaction tree and a child of a disabled widget genuinely cannot be reached; a
frame in a graph is a grouping on a canvas. The relation along which "this is
not running" actually travels here is the FLOW, and that cascade is DERIVED — a
node fed only by disabled ones reads nothing without anybody having marked it.
Copying the containment cascade would author a fact the flow already answers,
and the two would be free to disagree.

★★ THE SCREEN'S SECOND NAME FOR A CARD WAS LIFTED AWAY, AND RENAMING IS WHAT
MADE IT LOAD-BEARING. The screen kept its own name-to-node map beside the
document's own label: two records of one fact, and a rename that updated either
one alone leaves the canvas and the wire calling a single card two different
things. The model owns names now — it is the thing that can refuse one — so
there is one record and no way to update half of it.

★★★ AND THE RENAME FORCED A DEFECT OUT OF A RESET THAT HAD NOTHING TO DO WITH
IT. The node reset told an opening card from a palette-added one by asking
whether its NAME appears in the specification — which is exactly the thing a
rename changes. A renamed opening card therefore read as a stray, and the reset
whose whole job is to PUT ITS NAME BACK would have deleted the node instead. A
card is a stray when nothing recorded it opening; the record already existed
(R1679 added it so the layout predicate could see a card the palette added) and
now carries the name the card came into being as.

Two more derivations keyed off the current name in the same way and were
silently wrong after a rename: a card's digest lines and its width. A renamed
card stopped matching any specification row, fell through to the
palette-added path, redrew its digest from the first three form fields and
snapped to the default width. Nothing was broken loudly enough to fail, which is
how it would have stayed.

R1682.1.decision_summary:
A red already on main, paid off as its own round: one check did not know an
exception the screen's other checks have taken since the round before it.

`r1656_a_mark_says_the_box_it_left` fails on the tip commit — pressing where
`T-01`'s identity line is painted, on a grown window, answers `Q-01`. Checked
by stashing this session's work and running it again rather than assumed either
way, because "still failing" is not "failing for the same reason" and this
session has already been caught by that once.

★★ WHAT IT ACTUALLY MEETS, MEASURED RATHER THAN REASONED ABOUT. Driving the
screen to the demo's own phase-3 state and asking `point` at that pixel answers
`link:endpoint:0`. Phase 3 grows the picked link's TARGET to seven listen
addresses, so the picked link's endpoint seats — one per address, laid in a row
on the wire — span far enough to cover a card two columns away. The press lands
on the overlay, the selection does not move, and the assertion reads it as the
card being unreachable.

★★ AND THE OVERLAY IS RIGHT TO BE THERE. R1681.3 narrowed the chrome's
placement to "inside what the canvas is showing" and made the card sweeps take
an exception for whatever it covers, on the stated grounds that a summoned
overlay covering part of a card is what the reference does. That judgement is
now CHECKED rather than trusted: the behaviour reference lays its endpoint seats
as a flex row positioned on the wire's midpoint, `z-index` above the graph, with
no avoidance of anything at all. So this is agreement with the reference, and
the seats being a row rather than a stack is agreement too — the row simply gets
wide when a target listens in seven places.

So the repair is in the check, and it is the same exception, taken the same way:
the seats carry their own tags, so "is this aim point under the chrome" is
derived from the PAINT rather than restated beside it, and cannot drift from
where the chrome actually is.

★ THE EXCEPTION IS BOUNDED, AND THE BOUND IS THE PART WORTH HAVING. A check that
merely skips whatever an overlay covers passes just as happily when the overlay
covers the whole canvas — which is how this sort of excuse goes wrong. The
number of identity lines the chrome covers is asserted (at most one of eight,
measured exactly one), so an overlay that grew would fail here rather than
quietly widening its own excuse.

R1683.decision_summary:
The screen learns to be typed into, and what arrived is an AXIS rather than a
box.

The debt this round pays says it plainly: the analyser's node screen had no text
entry ANYWHERE, so every operation needing a value TYPED was pointer-unreachable
together. The rename had a verb and no gesture. "Add a field by typing its key"
had neither. The settings form's text rows resolve a press to a named target and
drop it. The launch gate can be closed by an agent and not by a person. Four
rows of one table, one absence.

★★★ SO ONE FIELD, THE FRAMEWORK'S OWN, WITH A TARGET. `TextEditState` behind the
shared text-field painter, and the lifted `edit_field_keymap` as its FOURTH call
site after the data grid, the property grid and the sibling node editor. The
same box renames a card and adds a configuration path, which is what makes this
a substrate arriving rather than a widget appearing — and the reason a rename
box would have been the wrong answer even though the rename is what asked.

★★ THE QUESTION THE DEBT SAID TO ANSWER BY TEST, ANSWERED BY TEST.
`use_text_edit_state` panics outside an owner scope, and this screen's pointer
handlers and its wire both run outside one — the same fact R1662 met with the
scroll offsets. The shell keeps a ROOT owner that lives as long as the
application, so the hook returns one object for the application's life; the
screen takes its reference at construction, which is inside an owner, and uses
it from the paths that have none. `r1683_the_screen_and_the_painter_hold_one_buffer`
compares the two with `Rc::ptr_eq` across three frames, and the counterfactual
that makes the screen build its own buffer fails it.

★★ THE FIELD'S EXTERNAL IS THE SHELL'S TO MOUNT, AND FINDING THAT OUT COST A
MEASUREMENT. `view_field` paints a container; the thing that holds focus, takes
a keystroke and answers what it is doing is a separate external addressed by the
same tag, mounted through `create_extra_externals`. Without it the field
painted, the screen's `editing` slot said it was open, and every keystroke was
refused. The consequence is a real limit on the in-process sweep and it is
written into the driver rather than glossed: that harness builds a scene by
calling the view directly, so it has no external to forward to. What is the
SCREEN's is driven there with the pointer; the keystroke path is the
framework's, and it is driven end to end in the demo where a real shell exists.

★★ THE CATALOGUE IS NOT THE BOUNDARY, AND THE FORM DID NOT KNOW THAT.
`ConfigForm::add` moves a key out of the offered set — exactly right for a chip
somebody pressed, and exactly wrong for a path they typed, because a settings
form that can only hold what somebody thought to offer cannot claim to edit a
configuration. `add_typed` takes the whole `ConfigField`, because what a typed
path IS — its type, its shape, whether it applies hot — is the application's
knowledge and not the widget's. A key already held is refused rather than
upserted: "add" and "replace" are different requests.

★ THE SEAT THAT LOOKS LIKE SOMEWHERE TO TYPE IS SOMEWHERE TO TYPE. The shut box
opens the field, because a box that looks like a field and ignores a press is
the class this screen keeps producing.

★ AND THE HEAD HAD GROWN TOO TALL, WHICH THE DEMOS CAUGHT: two rounds added two
rows to the inspector's head and the settings form's add-a-key chips fell below
the pane's fold on the opening screen. Nothing was unreachable — the pane
scrolls — but a person should not have to scroll to reach an affordance the
screen opens with. The rows are 20 tall now, measured back to fitting.
changes_bullets: `pinion-core` — the settings form learns a key nobody offered:
* `ConfigForm::add_typed(ConfigField)` — put a row in that was never in the
offered set, refusing a key already held (`FormError::AlreadyHeld`). The
caller supplies the descriptor because the type of a typed path is the
application's knowledge.
`hello-node-lab` — one text field, two targets:
* `Editing` (`Name` / `Key`) — what the field is for, with the keystroke gate
derived from it.
* the field itself: `use_text_edit_state` taken at construction,
`tf_paint::view_field` in the inspector head, and
`create_extra_externals` mounting `blur_committing_field_extra` so a click
away commits.
* `WidgetCore::State` is now `(TextFieldState, u32)` — the field's posture and
caret, read out of the painted scene by the shell and handed to the view.
* `WidgetCore::apply_key` routes to `edit_field_keymap` while the field owns
focus: Enter commits through the same verb the wire calls, Escape closes.
* three seats and a box: the shut box and "rename" open/apply the name,
"+ key" opens on a path. All three declared in `must_answer`.
* actions `edit` / `type` / `apply` (the box's three) and `add_key` (the
one-shot, beside `rename`); `editing` is a published read carrying the
target and the text.
* the inspector head's rows trimmed to 20px so the form's chips stay above
the fold on the opening screen.
Gates:
* `spec::OPERATIONS` — "rename a node" gains its gesture, "add a field by
typing its key" gains both. `ABSENT_OPERATIONS` 5 -> 4.
* `r1683_the_screen_and_the_painter_hold_one_buffer` — the owner question.
* `tools/demos/r1683_a_name_is_typed.py` (>= 30 assertions) drives real
keystrokes through a real shell.
* `r1651`'s inspector family pin 11 -> 14; `r1682`'s rename-has-no-gesture
assertion retired, because it no longer does.

the rest pass, 0 fail. Run on the build machine rather than here: this host

* the screen was LOOKED at, and the look was corrected by measurement: the

R1684.decision_summary:
A form row is where its value is typed, and the specification is driven in a
real window.

The analyzer node screen's settings rows had resolved a press to `field:<key>`
since R1651 — the hit test named it and the wire answered that word — while the
release handler ended in `_ => {}`. A person reported it as "the text box does
nothing", which is exactly what it was: a declared arm with no implementation is
worse than no arm, because the declaration stops the next reader looking.

The rule adopted is the behaviour reference's own, stated beside its inspector:
THE TYPE DECIDES THE CONTROL. A switch flips from anywhere in its control, and
every other shape opens the screen's one text field ON the row that was pressed
— which is what R1683's target parameter was built for. The field MOVES; a form
has as many rows as the document has keys, and a live box per row would be a
focus owner, a keymap and a commit path per key.

Three things followed rather than being aimed at:

* the launch gate gained its gesture. The verdict is derived from the form, so
  closing it means putting a value out of range, and the integer stepper clamps
  at the field's ceiling — correctly. An agent could close that gate and a
  person could not.
* a list ELEMENT became a target of its own, because the affordance that grows
  a list writes a placeholder, and a screen that can add one and never say what
  it is only ever grows invented values.
* the option rows became typable, because a bordered box with dead space
  between its chips is a control that lies — and because typing is the only way
  a person can put an unknown word on an option row and see it reported.

The specification is now driven end to end in a real window: a demo reads the
published operation table and causes all forty-five declared ways from fresh
processes, aims read out of the painted scene, keystrokes through the shell's
own key path. That closes the half of the operation gate the in-process sweep
cannot reach, and it is what caught the two counterfactuals nothing local can.
changes_bullets: `Editing::Value { node, key, element }` — the one field's third target, and
the first that is a PLACE rather than a thing. `edit_box` answers the row's
control, or a list element's own row, from the geometry the form painter
published; the field is painted last so it stands over what it is editing.
`Hit::Field(key)` gains its release arm (`press_row`): a switch flips, every
other shape opens the field. `act_on_part` gains the numbered `item.<key>.<n>`
arm (`press_element`), which had fallen through a dispatcher that handled only
`add`.
`set_value` — ONE function for the wire's `set_field`, for the affordances
inside a control (`set_and_sync` now delegates) and for a value typed. Before
this there were two, and only one of them said what it had done.
`set_element` splices one element of a list row, leaving its neighbours alone;
emptying it removes it, which is what the form's own splitter already means.
`select_card` — one function for the four sites that moved the selection, so
a box opened over the inspected card's row cannot survive a change of card.
`begin_edit` returns a `Result` and COMMITS an open edit on a different target
before moving. A refused commit refuses the move.
`body_origin` — the inspector's one signed pane-origin. `in_body` clamps it
per rectangle and `inspector_geometry` translates by it, so the form's window
geometry is no longer a second arithmetic that was short by `PANEL_FRAME`.
`NodeLabView::position_caret_for_point` / `select_drag_to_point` +
`field_byte_at` + `edit_field_style` — click-to-caret and drag-select, which
the screen never had; the paint and the hit test now shape through one style.
The wire: `edit` takes `value:<key>` and `value:<key>[<n>]` (`row_target`
parses the spelling `editing.target` reads back) and refuses a row the form
does not hold, an element the row does not have, a number that is not one and
a bracket that never shuts.
`spec::OPERATIONS`: `validate` moves to `gesture: true`, with a driver.
Six gates in `painted.rs`: the centre of every control does something; the
field stands on the seat that was under the cursor, holding what that seat
holds, and applying puts it there; leaving the field applies it and a refusal
refuses the move; picking another card shuts it; a control answers at its
CORNERS; a click resolves to the byte whose caret is painted under it; and the
wire's target grammar with its four refusals.
`tools/demos/r1684_the_specification_is_driven_in_a_window.py` — the whole
published operation table caused in a real shell, both columns, fresh process
per operation, recipes cross-checked against the declaration in both
directions.
verification_bullets: Local gates, on the crate this round touched:
`cargo test -p hello-node-lab --features pinion-runtime/vello` — 56 passed.
`cargo clippy -p hello-node-lab --all-targets --features pinion-runtime/vello`
— clean under the workspace pedantic baseline.
`cargo fmt --all --check`.
Every demo that drives this screen, run locally against a release build:
The new demo's own measurement: 30 operations, 20 by action and 25 by gesture,
45 declared ways, every one of them caused something an agent can observe. Four
operations remain absent by declaration (fit the graph to the view, export the
configuration, produce the launch script, go to the first problem).
The gate that opened this round MEASURED the defect before it was fixed: 24 of
45 painted controls did nothing when pressed in the middle, in eight swept
states, and the two causes were both different from the prediction that
motivated the round.
Sixteen counterfactuals, all caught:
Fourteen by the local suite: the dropped `Field` arm; the numbered list-item
arm; the field left in the head of the pane; the field on the row instead of
the element; the element seeded with the whole row; applying an element
writing the whole row; the two coordinate transforms drifting apart again;
an option row going back to dead-in-the-middle; the selection moving with the
field left open; the wire accepting an element a row does not have; leaving
the field throwing typing away; a refused commit letting the field move; the
hit test shaped differently from the paint; and a `gesture: true` with no
driver.
Two only by the demo, which is stated rather than hidden: the screen ceasing
to stand aside inside the open box, and a click that does not move the caret.
Neither can be asked in process — that harness calls the view directly, so
there is no field external and no shell input router.
Three of the sixteen PASSED on a first attempt and each was a finding: the
element-press break was invisible because the placement check derived the
expected seat from the field's own answer (it now also asserts the seat was
under the cursor); the selection break and the refused-commit break had no gate
at all until this round wrote one.
carry_forward_bullets: Nothing is carried that this round could have closed. What is left is stated:
**Four operations remain absent by declaration** — fit the graph to the view,
export the configuration, produce the launch script, go to the first problem.
They are rows of the published table with neither a verb nor a gesture, which
is what makes them countable and what the ratchet holds at four.
**"remove a field" still has a verb and no gesture.** The behaviour reference
draws a delete affordance on every non-derived row; ours has none, so the wire
can take a row out and a person cannot. It is a row of the operation table
rather than a note here, which is the register that gets read.
**The in-process sweep cannot mount the screen's extra externals** — the
standing limit ([[debt-the-in-process-sweep-cannot-mount-a-screens-extra-externals]]),
and this round measured what it costs: two of sixteen counterfactuals are
catchable only by a demo, so those two claims are CI-gated rather than
commit-gated. The demo now exists and catches them; making the local gate able
to ask is the framework-side work that debt names.
**A press inside the open box is answered by the SCREEN, not the field.** That
is now written where it is relied on, and it is why the caret hooks had to be
