R1689.decision_summary:
A graph survives being closed: the analyser screen learns to save, open and
clear its work, and the read half of that moves into `pinion-node-graph` as
`Archive` — because what was missing was never the writing.

`Document` has derived serde since R1577, so writing one out is a call. The
measurement is what the two node canvases in this tree did with the OTHER
direction. `hello-node-editor` wrapped the document in `{schema_version, graph}`
of its own and answered a failed load with `false` for four different reasons —
the text was not JSON, the version did not match, the graph broke an invariant,
or nothing was stored — so neither a person with a file from last year nor an
agent with a truncated download could tell which had happened, and neither could
act. `hello-node-lab` had no save at all. Neither is those screens' fault: there
was nothing to reach for.

The reference toolkit's own state restore is the same shape, and is the floor
this is measured against: its window-state restore takes an opaque byte blob
and a version number, and answers a **bool**;
a version mismatch returns false with the window untouched and nothing said; an
item in the blob whose widget is no longer present becomes a placeholder
announced only through a logging category that is off by default. It also runs
its parse TWICE — once in a private "testing" mode, to find out whether the blob
is usable before touching anything — and that answer is not available to the
caller at all.

`Archive::read` does that check pass and hands it back, as `Opening`:

* `Unreadable` names which of four things stopped it — nothing saved, not the
  envelope, a different format revision (carrying both numbers), or a document
  this build's taxonomy cannot hold.
* `Opening::violations` is `Document::validate`'s own verdict, so a structurally
  broken document is refused for STATED reasons — a dangling link, a containment
  cycle, a value on a port that is not there. Thirteen kinds, where the editor
  hand-rolled four.
* `Opening::dropped` names what would not survive with the document intact: a
  saved selection pointing at a node that is gone (the case the reference turns
  into a logged placeholder), a camera whose zoom or pan would blank the canvas
  permanently, and the application's own extras when they are the part that
  cannot be read.
* `Opening::reason` is the one sentence a screen puts in front of a person and a
  wire answers with. That is the value the `bool` was standing in for.

The companion is parsed INDEPENDENTLY of the document, and that asymmetry is the
decision rather than an implementation detail. A stream read front to back
cannot do it: one bad field and everything after it is gone, which is why the
reference's restore is all-or-nothing. Here they are two parses over one
envelope, so an application whose own saved state changed shape still gets its
graph back and is told what was left behind. The direction is deliberate — the
document is this crate's and can be checked, the companion is the application's
and cannot, and refusing a graph because a screen's saved zoom was written by a
newer build would be this crate making a decision it has no standing to make.

There is no migration hook. A chain written before a second revision exists is a
guess at what the change will be; naming the mismatch is the half the reference
does not do, and an application that versions its OWN state does so inside its
companion, where it knows what changed. The node editor now does exactly that:
eleven of its twelve schema bumps are changes to its taxonomy, which the
substrate cannot know about, so that list stays with it and is checked there.

On the screen, the cluster this closes is one a self-census cannot see. The
reference publishes its own list of this screen's operations and measures its
coverage of it; `spec::OPERATIONS` mirrors those thirty one-for-one and R1688
brought the absences to zero. Saving is not on that list — and is nonetheless in
the reference, together with a FOURTH self-meter asking whether every piece of
state is either carried or declared volatile. A census taken over a declared
list is complete against that list and blind to whatever the list leaves out,
which is R1688's own finding one level up.

So `spec::KEPT` is that partition, over every slot the operations can move, and
the gate asks the stronger question the reference's meter cannot: drive the
operation, save, open the save on a screen that has just started, and a `Saved`
slot must read what it read AFTER the operation while a `Volatile` one must read
the opening value. A key can be classified as carried and still not come back;
classifying everything as volatile would pass a meter that only checks
classification. The discriminating set is checked too — five of the thirty put
their scope back to how it opened, so their two readings are equal to begin with
and prove nothing about a round trip, and every classified slot must therefore
have at least one operation that genuinely moves it away from the opening
reading.

The three affordances are the reference's own, in the reference's own place: a
pill of `save` / `open` / `clear` between the launch-script button and the run
button. That costs width, and the cost is stated rather than absorbed —
`TOOLBAR_RIGHT_CLUSTER` 431 to 609 and `MIN_W` 1447 to 1625, so a 1600-wide
display no longer holds this screen. What would take it back is a toolbar
overflow affordance, which is a round of its own.
changes_bullets: SUBSTRATE — `crates/pinion-node-graph/src/archive.rs` (new, ~560 lines with its
header) exporting `Archive`, `Opening`, `Unreadable`, `Dropped`, `Unwritable`
and `REVISION`. Nine crate tests.
* `Archive<K, C>` carries the document, the camera, the selection and the
application's own companion. The REVISION is not a field on it: a value in
hand is always this build's, so carrying the number would be carrying a fact
that cannot be false. It is a property of the TEXT, which is where it can
differ, and that is where `Unreadable::Revision` reports it.
* `Archive::read` is a PLAN. Nothing is installed; everything decidable before a
change is decided — the envelope parses, the revision matches, the document
parses, its own invariants hold, the selection points at nodes that are there,
the camera is a usable number, the companion is readable.
* `Opening::take` gives the archive only when it opens;
`take_despite_violations` is the separate, named override for a tool whose job
is to look at a broken document. A caller cannot reach it without saying so.
* Named `Opening` and not `Reading` because the compiler refused the first
draft: `Reading` is already what a watch answers in this crate's debugger.
* The envelope is JSON and says so — the document and the companion are parsed
in two independent steps, which a format-agnostic `Serializer` cannot express,
and a saved graph an agent can read without the process that wrote it is §2 #7.
No `serde_json` type appears in the public API.
SUBSTRATE — `Camera` gains `Serialize`/`Deserialize`: where a canvas is pointed
is part of what somebody left behind.
SUBSTRATE — `Violation` gains `Display`. It was the one error-shaped type in
that crate without a sentence, and the one most likely to be put in front of a
person — the documents that break invariants are the ones that came from a file
— so a consumer reporting one reached for `{:?}` and printed Rust syntax. One
sentence per variant, all thirteen, asserted distinct.
CONSUMER — `hello-node-editor` drops its hand-rolled `SerializedGraph` envelope
for `Archive`, and `graph_invariants_hold` becomes test-only: the gate moved to
where the blob is read. `load_json` keeps its `bool` and delegates to a new
`open_json -> Result<(), String>`, which is what `set_graph` now refuses with —
the arm used to answer one fixed sentence for four different failures.
`PERSISTED_SCHEMA_VERSION` 11 -> 12 and stays in the editor, inside the
companion, because eleven of its twelve bumps are changes to the editor's own
taxonomy and no substrate can know about those. A companion this build cannot
read is REPORTED by the crate and REFUSED by the editor, which is the split
working: two different decisions, made by whoever is entitled to make them.
CONSUMER — `hello-node-lab` gains `src/persist.rs`: `Kept` (the screen's
companion — each card's form, the host names, the opening placements, the
discovery switch and the selection by NAME), `save`, `open`, `clear`, `stored`.
* `open` takes an argument that may be EMPTY, meaning "the saved one", which is
the reference's own shape (its box loads the saved copy when left blank).
* Opening a graph clears the produced artifacts. That is `spec::KEPT`'s own
reasoning acted on: an exported configuration belongs to the moment it was
taken, and leaving one beside a graph that has just been replaced puts a
document on screen that describes something no longer there — worse than none,
because it looks current.
SCREEN — three toolbar seats (`lab.toolbar.save` / `.open` / `.clear`) as one
pill between the launch-script button and the run button, which is where the
reference puts them. The `open` seat's accessible name says whether there is
anything to open, which is the fact a person cannot see from the button.
SCREEN — every right-anchored toolbar inset is now DERIVED from the seat to its
right. Three constants (`120`, `196`, `268`) encoded the GAPS between five
seats, so inserting a sixth meant re-deriving all of them by hand. R1687 paid
for this once on `TOOLBAR_RIGHT_CLUSTER`; this is the same fact one level down.
SCREEN — `TOOLBAR_RIGHT_CLUSTER` 431 -> 609, `MIN_W` 1447 -> 1625. The number is
the GATE's: the first draft said 594 by hand and
`r1687_the_toolbars_declared_width_covers_what_it_paints` answered 609 from the
rectangles, with two other gates failing beside it because a floor that small
paints the left cluster into the right one.
WIRE — `save_graph`, `open_graph` (optional argument), `clear_graph` as actions;
`archive` and `stored` as reads. Two reads and not one because they are two
questions: `archive` is what a save WOULD write and `stored` is what is on disk,
and a single slot would make "has this been saved" unanswerable. `archive` and
not `graph`, because `graph` is already this screen's read for the graph's NAME
— the compiler said so, as an unreachable arm.
SPEC — `spec::KEPT`: every slot an operation can move, partitioned into `Saved`
and `Volatile`, each with WHERE it lives or why it is left behind. Published on
the wire beside the operations, for the reason everything else there is: it is a
claim about the tool that a reader cannot get any other way.
SPEC — `spec::OPERATIONS` is UNCHANGED at thirty. Saving is not on the
reference's own operation list, so adding rows would have broken the one-for-one
this table's whole claim rests on. What the round adds is the second table and
the finding that goes with it.
GATE — `r1689_what_a_save_carries_is_declared_and_comes_back` (in `painted.rs`,
so it drives the screen's own pointer paths): the partition covers exactly the
witnesses in both directions; every operation is round-tripped; and every
classified slot must have at least one operation that moves it away from the
opening reading, or the round trip is comparing two equal readings.
GATE — `r1689_the_screen_says_which_of_four_things_stopped_a_load`: the
substrate's four refusals arrive on the screen as four different sentences, and
each leaves the graph alone. A screen that caught them all and said "could not
open" would have the `bool` back with extra steps.
GATE — `hello-node-editor`'s persisted-shape digest is now taken over THE TEXT
THAT IS WRITTEN rather than over a proxy struct serialized by a different call.
Until this round the gate hashed a `SerializedGraph` while the file came out of
`serialized_json`, so a change to how the blob is composed — exactly what this
round did — could have moved the file without moving the digest.
TESTS — `app_storage()` returns an in-memory backend under `cfg(test)`, stated
once rather than injected at each fixture. This screen has seventy tests and two
of them are about saving; the one that forgot would have written into the
developer's real data directory and the next run would open with somebody else's
graph. The file backend is what the demo exercises, under an isolated directory,
across two launches — which is the only place it CAN be proven, since a unit
test in one process cannot show that a graph survived the process.
DEMO — `tools/demos/r1689_a_graph_survives_being_closed.py`, two launches
against a real file under an isolated storage directory.
verification_bullets: COUNTERFACTUALS — 12 run, 11 caught outright, 1 PASSED and is the round's own
finding.
Caught, substrate: the revision check removed; a companion that will not parse
made fatal instead of reported; a stale selection dropped without being named;
`opens` ignoring the violations; the camera's usability check removed; two
`Violation` variants sharing one sentence.
Caught, screen: `install` skipping the saved forms (five rows red at once,
including the DERIVED `verdict`, which is what says the derivation travels with
what it is derived from); `KEPT` marking `produced` as carried; a `KEPT` row
deleted (the partition census, both directions); `open_graph` collapsing the
substrate's reason into one fixed sentence.
One is caught by the TYPE system rather than a test, as R1688 established: a
file seat taken out of `toolbar_seats` makes its `Hit` arm dead code and the
build fails, because the roster is the only constructor of the toolbar's hits.
★★★★★ PASSED, AND IT IS THE FINDING: **deleting the line that clears the
produced artifacts on a load changed nothing.** The volatile half of the
partition was being asked on a screen that had just started — where the slot is
at its opening value because nothing ever set it — so "the load did not bring it
back" was true whatever the load did. The check could not fail. That is the
shape R1644.1 and R1681.1 both wrote down, arriving here in a gate written in
the same round that quotes them.
The repair is that the two halves are asked on DIFFERENT screens, which is what
the two claims actually are: a SAVED slot is proven by opening the archive on a
screen that has just started (it must read what the operation left), and a
VOLATILE slot by opening it on the screen that HAS the value (it must go back to
the opening reading rather than keep a stale one). Re-run with the repair, the
counterfactual fails as it should.
The `discriminating` assertion was already there and did not save it: it
guarantees a slot has an operation that moves it away from the opening value,
which makes the SAVED arm non-vacuous and says nothing about the other one.
LOCAL GATES
* `cargo test -p pinion-node-graph` — 326 + 145 + 2 green, nine of them new.
* `cargo test -p hello-node-lab` — 72 green (70 before this round).
* `cargo test -p hello-node-editor` — 256 green.
* `cargo clippy -p pinion-node-graph -p hello-node-lab -p hello-node-editor
--all-targets --features pinion-runtime/vello` — green.
* Eleven node-lab demos green: r1651, r1656, r1662, r1678, r1682, r1683, r1684,
r1685, r1686, r1687, r1688 — the whole set, because the toolbar's geometry
moved and every one of them reads it.
* Six node-editor demos green: r852, r1135, r1227, r1258, r1260, r1261, r1542,
r1598 — chosen by which of them read the serialised blob or the viewport.
* The new demo, `r1689_a_graph_survives_being_closed.py`: two launches against a
real file under an isolated storage directory, 50 assertion sites.
DEMOS THIS ROUND HAD TO CHANGE, and why each is a fact rather than a fix
* `r1651` — the toolbar family pin 12 -> 15. Three seats arrived and none left;
the pin moving by exactly three is what says the group landed whole.
* `r1662` — `WIN` was `(1500, 900)`, written down. R1687 read the FLOOR from the
screen for exactly this reason and left `WIN` — the same fact, in the same
file — as a constant, so raising the floor past 1500 fired that demo's own
guard on a demo that was not wrong about anything. It is derived from the floor
now: a constant that has to stay in a RELATION with a moving number is not one.
* `r1227` / `r1258` — three string patterns assumed COMPACT JSON and the archive
writes indented text. Each failed loudly rather than silently, because both
demos guard their string surgery with "the edit changed the blob" — which is
the pattern that makes a mismatched replacement a red instead of a test of the
unmodified blob.
LOOKED AT — on a private Xvfb display, never the user's.
carry_forward_bullets: DELIBERATE DIVERGENCES FROM THE BEHAVIOUR REFERENCE — registered, and the
owner's to rule on. Both are cheap to reverse and the round-trip gate checks
BOTH directions, so whichever is chosen is proven the moment it is chosen.
* The screen does NOT restore itself when it opens; the reference does, from
browser storage. Auto-restoring would make every gate in this example a
function of whatever is on the machine that runs it, which the zero-flake rule
refuses and which the sibling node editor refused for the same reason in R852
("launch 2 boot: fresh seed — no surprise auto-load", asserted in its demo).
Following the reference here needs a harness rule that every demo runs under
an isolated storage directory; today a demo opts in.
* The view IS carried; the reference's own volatile list names the pan and the
zoom. The reference is a page that gets reloaded and this writes a file
somebody opens later, and a document that comes back looking nothing like it
was left is one you have to find your place in again — which is what the
reference toolkit's `saveGeometry`/`restoreGeometry` exists for. Reversing it
is two rows of `spec::KEPT` and the camera line in `persist::install`.
STATED, not carried:
* `MIN_W` is 1625. A 1600-wide display no longer holds this screen, and the
reference's own toolbar is what put the three buttons there. What takes it
back is a toolbar overflow affordance — the reference toolkit raises an
extension button and moves the overflowing actions into a popup, keeping every
label whole — which this tree does not have and which is a round of its own
([[debt-a-toolbar-has-no-overflow-affordance]], registered R1674).
* There is no migration hook on `Archive`. With one revision in existence, a
chain is a guess at what the second change will be; naming the mismatch is
already the half the reference toolkit does not do. An application that
versions its own state does so in its companion, which the node editor now
demonstrates.
* The reference publishes FOUR self-censuses and this tree now mirrors two. The
remaining two are a configuration-schema reach meter (how much of the tool's
option surface the palette can actually author) and a string-leaf
classification meter (every string path is an enum, a format, or free text, and
whatever is none of those is reported). Both are measurements this screen could
make and does not; they are named here so the next round does not have to
rediscover the list.
* `Kept` carries the screen's selection by NAME while the archive carries its own
by `NodeId`. Two records of one fact, deliberately: the crate's is checked
against the document it came with, which is right and is what makes a stale
selection reportable, and the screen addresses a card the way a person reads it
everywhere else. A reader that is not this screen still finds a selection where
it expects one.

The companion is parsed INDEPENDENTLY of the document, and that asymmetry is the
decision rather than an implementation detail. A stream read front to back
cannot do it: one bad field and everything after it is gone, which is why the
reference's restore is all-or-nothing. Here they are two parses over one
envelope, so an application whose own saved state changed shape still gets its
graph back and is told what was left behind. The direction is deliberate — the
document is this crate's and can be checked, the companion is the application's
and cannot, and refusing a graph because a screen's saved zoom was written by a
newer build would be this crate making a decision it has no standing to make.

guess at what the change will be; naming the mismatch is the half the reference
does not do, and an application that versions its OWN state does so inside its
companion, where it knows what changed. The node editor now does exactly that:
eleven of its twelve schema bumps are changes to its taxonomy, which the
substrate cannot know about, so that list stays with it and is checked there.

R1690.decision_summary:
The palette says how much of the option surface it can author, and every
string on that surface either has a shape or is named as having none.

The behaviour reference this screen reproduces publishes **four** self-censuses.
Two of them this tree already mirrors — its operation table (R1677) and its save
partition (R1689) — and this round is the other two. Neither is a screen detail:
they are the two questions a person picking a configuration tool asks first, and
neither could be answered here because nothing declared what the thing being
configured accepts.

`pinion_core::widgets::config_schema` is that declaration. A `ConfigSchema` is
the set of leaf paths with the shape each one holds, built once and validated at
the point of declaration — a path cannot be declared twice, and cannot be a value
and a section at the same time, because no document can hold both and a schema
that admitted it would make the form's own `document()` pick one silently.

Over it, two meters:

* `reached_by` — how much of the surface a palette can author, as **two**
  numbers. Two because one hides the other: a tool can touch every section of a
  configuration and reach a small fraction of its leaves, and reporting the
  first alone reads as finished at the moment it is least true. Measured on this
  screen: sections 11/19, leaves 11/36.
* `strings` — the string half of the surface partitioned into the three kinds a
  string can be: one of a fixed set of words, a string that has to parse, and
  free text. Exclusive and total **by construction**, because the class is read
  off the declared shape rather than kept in three lists beside it. What stays
  measurable is the third: a string nobody has pinned down. Measured: 11 of 21
  pinned.

Neither number is written anywhere. Both are computed from the palette against
the schema every time they are asked, which is the only version of a coverage
meter worth painting — drop a field and the figure falls with nobody editing it.

## The half the reference does not have is the half that found the defects

A reach count answers "is the key offered" and stops. It is therefore blind to
two ways a key can be present and useless, and this screen had **both**.

**A key offered at a shape the target refuses.** The chip is there, the row is
there, the value a person types is accepted, and the node does not come up —
every count says that key is covered. This screen's node identifier is read by a
parser and was typed as **free text** for its whole life. `Reach::mistyped` is
that column, and the repair is not the row: a row's shape now comes FROM the
option surface, so the palette cannot offer a key the target would refuse.

**A key that names a SECTION rather than a leaf.** Three of this screen's six
chips did. A form field holds a scalar — `FieldType` has no arm for an object —
so such a row composes a **string where the configuration wants a subtree**, and
the schema refuses to declare a path as both, which is the same fact from the
other side. The first draft of this meter counted such a key as reaching every
leaf beneath it, which is what a coverage figure over two path lists usually
means and is exactly wrong here: it inflates the number using keys that can
author nothing. A leaf is reached only when a catalogue key **equals** it, and
the rest are reported as `Reach::unauthorable` — a palette author who meant one
of the leaves under it and has not said which. `Reach::unknown` stays for a key
on no line of the surface at all; the two take different repairs.

And the sections figure is a **fold of the leaves figure** rather than a second
count, because two independently counted numbers over one catalogue can tell
different stories — "every section reached, almost no leaves" is a sentence a
reader would have to reconcile.

## The arm the middle class needed, and the three states it answers with

A string that has to parse had no spelling in the form's type set, which is why
every such field was free text. `FieldType::Formatted { of: TextFormat }` is
that spelling, and `TextFormat` is a small declarative grammar — characters with
a class and a length, a bounded number, a word from a set, a `head sep tail`
split, a repeated part, an alternation — with no domain in any arm. An address
of the `<scheme>/<host>:<port>` kind is a composition of three of them; the next
domain needs no new arm.

`judge` answers **three** states, and past what a caret-level validator in a
mature toolkit answers, it says two things that kind of validator does not:

* `Unfinished` is not a softer refusal — it is "some continuation of this text
  would be right", which is what lets a value be *typed*. The gate over it is a
  property rather than an example: **every prefix of every acceptable text is
  never refused**, walked over a corpus, because typing is a walk through
  prefixes.
* every refusal carries the shape as a **sentence**, derived from the
  declaration so it cannot drift from what is checked, and the **byte offset**
  the text first went wrong at, so a caller can point at the character rather
  than colour the field. A validator that answers only a state leaves both the
  person and the agent to guess.

And because the grammar is data — serialisable, comparable, walkable — an agent
can read what a field will accept before writing to it, and a saved document
carries the grammar it was checked against. A closure would do the checking and
none of that.

## What enforcing a declared shape found on the screen's own seed data

Three of the opening graph's eight node identifiers were values the target would
refuse: they were written as role initials and two of those initials are outside
the hexadecimal alphabet the identifier is read with. The launch gate reported
them on the first drive after the shape came from the surface. The fallback was
worse than the seed — every card the palette added opened holding the same
unparseable value, so the defect was being *produced*, once per added node. It
is derived now, in the format's own alphabet.

Three extra problem lines were then enough to reach a second defect nothing had
been able to produce before: the launch gate's panel sized itself from **how
many problems there are**, which is unbounded, so it was placed above the top of
the canvas and the pane-local conversion underflowed. It is bounded by the canvas
now and **counts** what it has no room for, because the verdict is derived from
all of the problems and a silent truncation would leave a gate closed for
reasons the screen is not showing.

## Two names chosen by looking at the running screen

The meter's label says `sections`, not the word the reference uses for its
top-level keys, because on a panel sitting directly above a form made of *field
rows* that word reads as a count of those rows — and on the first screen it was
painted on, that count and the section count happened to be the same number.
A label whose two plausible readings agree by coincidence is the worst kind.

R1690.publishable_decision_summary:
The palette says how much of the option surface it can author, and every
string on that surface either has a shape or is named as having none.

The behaviour reference this screen reproduces publishes **four** self-censuses.
Two of them this tree already mirrors — its operation table (R1677) and its save
partition (R1689) — and this round is the other two. Neither is a screen detail:
they are the two questions a person picking a configuration tool asks first, and
neither could be answered here because nothing declared what the thing being
configured accepts.

`pinion_core::widgets::config_schema` is that declaration. A `ConfigSchema` is
the set of leaf paths with the shape each one holds, built once and validated at
the point of declaration — a path cannot be declared twice, and cannot be a value
and a section at the same time, because no document can hold both and a schema
that admitted it would make the form's own `document()` pick one silently.

Over it, two meters:

* `reached_by` — how much of the surface a palette can author, as **two**
  numbers. Two because one hides the other: a tool can touch every section of a
  configuration and reach a small fraction of its leaves, and reporting the
  first alone reads as finished at the moment it is least true. Measured on this
  screen: sections 11/19, leaves 11/36.
* `strings` — the string half of the surface partitioned into the three kinds a
  string can be: one of a fixed set of words, a string that has to parse, and
  free text. Exclusive and total **by construction**, because the class is read
  off the declared shape rather than kept in three lists beside it. What stays
  measurable is the third: a string nobody has pinned down. Measured: 11 of 21
  pinned.

Neither number is written anywhere. Both are computed from the palette against
the schema every time they are asked, which is the only version of a coverage
meter worth painting — drop a field and the figure falls with nobody editing it.

## The half the reference does not have is the half that found the defects

A reach count answers "is the key offered" and stops. It is therefore blind to
two ways a key can be present and useless, and this screen had **both**.

**A key offered at a shape the target refuses.** The chip is there, the row is
there, the value a person types is accepted, and the node does not come up —
every count says that key is covered. This screen's node identifier is read by a
parser and was typed as **free text** for its whole life. `Reach::mistyped` is
that column, and the repair is not the row: a row's shape now comes FROM the
option surface, so the palette cannot offer a key the target would refuse.

**A key that names a SECTION rather than a leaf.** Three of this screen's six
chips did. A form field holds a scalar — `FieldType` has no arm for an object —
so such a row composes a **string where the configuration wants a subtree**, and
the schema refuses to declare a path as both, which is the same fact from the
other side. The first draft of this meter counted such a key as reaching every
leaf beneath it, which is what a coverage figure over two path lists usually
means and is exactly wrong here: it inflates the number using keys that can
author nothing. A leaf is reached only when a catalogue key **equals** it, and
the rest are reported as `Reach::unauthorable` — a palette author who meant one
of the leaves under it and has not said which. `Reach::unknown` stays for a key
on no line of the surface at all; the two take different repairs.

And the sections figure is a **fold of the leaves figure** rather than a second
count, because two independently counted numbers over one catalogue can tell
different stories — "every section reached, almost no leaves" is a sentence a
reader would have to reconcile.

## The arm the middle class needed, and the three states it answers with

A string that has to parse had no spelling in the form's type set, which is why
every such field was free text. `FieldType::Formatted { of: TextFormat }` is
that spelling, and `TextFormat` is a small declarative grammar — characters with
a class and a length, a bounded number, a word from a set, a `head sep tail`
split, a repeated part, an alternation — with no domain in any arm. An address
of the `<scheme>/<host>:<port>` kind is a composition of three of them; the next
domain needs no new arm.

`judge` answers **three** states, and past what a caret-level validator in a
mature toolkit answers, it says two things that kind of validator does not:

* `Unfinished` is not a softer refusal — it is "some continuation of this text
  would be right", which is what lets a value be *typed*. The gate over it is a
  property rather than an example: **every prefix of every acceptable text is
  never refused**, walked over a corpus, because typing is a walk through
  prefixes.
* every refusal carries the shape as a **sentence**, derived from the
  declaration so it cannot drift from what is checked, and the **byte offset**
  the text first went wrong at, so a caller can point at the character rather
  than colour the field. A validator that answers only a state leaves both the
  person and the agent to guess.

And because the grammar is data — serialisable, comparable, walkable — an agent
can read what a field will accept before writing to it, and a saved document
carries the grammar it was checked against. A closure would do the checking and
none of that.

## What enforcing a declared shape found on the screen's own seed data

Three of the opening graph's eight node identifiers were values the target would
refuse: they were written as role initials and two of those initials are outside
the hexadecimal alphabet the identifier is read with. The launch gate reported
them on the first drive after the shape came from the surface. The fallback was
worse than the seed — every card the palette added opened holding the same
unparseable value, so the defect was being *produced*, once per added node. It
is derived now, in the format's own alphabet.

Three extra problem lines were then enough to reach a second defect nothing had
been able to produce before: the launch gate's panel sized itself from **how
many problems there are**, which is unbounded, so it was placed above the top of
the canvas and the pane-local conversion underflowed. It is bounded by the canvas
now and **counts** what it has no room for, because the verdict is derived from
all of the problems and a silent truncation would leave a gate closed for
reasons the screen is not showing.

The meter's label says `sections`, not the word the reference uses for its
top-level keys, because on a panel sitting directly above a form made of *field
rows* that word reads as a count of those rows — and on the first screen it was
painted on, that count and the section count happened to be the same number.
A label whose two plausible readings agree by coincidence is the worst kind.

R1691.decision_summary:
The screen says all of itself: every addressable region either has a voice in
the accessibility tree or declares why it has none.

A screen paints regions and publishes an accessibility tree, and the two are
built by different code. Nothing in either said whether they AGREE — and a
region nobody gave a node to is not an error anywhere. It paints perfectly, it
takes presses, every question about its rectangle is answered, and a reader is
simply never told it exists.

Measured on the analysis tool's first screen the day this was written: **166
addressable regions painted, 30 of them announced** — the accessibility tree had
35 nodes and five of those are virtual description regions the form points at,
which is itself a distinction nothing had ever drawn. **136 were
unclassified.** The palette, the icon rail, the
canvas's frames and wires and pins, the launch gate, the gesture hint and the
inspector's own chrome had no voice at all. The three clusters that DID have one
each had a round that asked for it — the cards at R1651, the toolbar at R1687 —
and nothing had ever asked about the rest. Accessibility existed on that screen
exactly where somebody had once looked.

## Against the reference toolkit at 6.11 — built and RUN, not read

Its accessibility layer builds an interface for every widget automatically,
which sounds like the stronger position and is precisely why the question cannot
be asked there. A probe built against 6.11.1 and run:

* A window of six children answered **7 nodes, 4 of them with an empty
  accessible name**: a button whose name the author forgot, a decorative rule, a
  custom painted region, and the window. **The forgotten button and the
  decorative rule are the same answer** — a role and no name. One is a defect
  and one is correct, and nothing separates them.
* Clearing every author-settable accessibility slot on the rule (its widget has
  exactly three: a name, a description, an identifier) left the tree at 7 nodes.
  **A region cannot be declared deliberately silent.**
* Hiding it left the tree at 7 nodes too, with one state bit flipped — so the
  only act that quiets a region takes its ink with it, and does not even remove
  the node. Silence and invisibility are one act there.
* A label bound to a field announced its text **twice**, once as the label's own
  name and once as the field's. The duplicate is produced by construction and
  nothing suppresses it.

So the floor has an accessibility tree and no census of it.

## The substrate: `pinion_core::voice`

A declaration carries a `Silence` — a `kind` from a closed vocabulary and one
`detail` the kind gives meaning to, the same shape `Unavailable` has and for the
same reason: the arms exist because each leaves a reader somewhere different,
and that difference is derived ONCE as a `Relay` rather than restated per site.
`Decorative` relays nowhere, `Layout` to the children, `NameOf` to a named peer,
`PartOf` to a named node that announces the whole. No two share a relay, which
is what makes the vocabulary four things rather than a bool with extra words.

It lives on `LayoutStyle` beside `unavailable`, reaches the descendants exactly
when the kind `covers_subtree` — every kind but the layout box, which has said
nothing about what it merely placed — and is **independent of the ink**, which
is the conflation the floor cannot escape.

`voice_census` then classifies every addressable region of a produced paint
scene against the tree built beside it, and answers with one of five arms. Two
are correct outcomes and **three are three different defects**, each with a
different repair:

* `unvoiced` — painted, addressable, no node and no reason. Nobody decided.
* `ghost` — a name announced for a tag nothing paints and nobody refers to. A
  reader can be sent somewhere that is not there. (A node another node POINTS
  at — a description region, a composite child, a name source — is deliberately
  virtual and is not this; the reference is what makes it reachable.)
* `dangling` — quiet because another node says its name, where that node does
  not speak either. It reads as handled and is a hole.

That last arm is the one no set difference could produce, and it is what caught
this round's own largest defect: a draft that dropped the cards from the tree
showed up as 8 unvoiced cards AND 16 dangling redirects from their captions.

## Published: `scene/voice`

Joins the last painted scene with the **same** access-tree producer
`scene/access` runs — deliberately, because a census that built its own idea of
what is announced would be a second opinion able to disagree with the very fact
it exists to check. `total` and `counts` are derived on every call: a coverage
figure that is written down is one that stops falling when the thing it measures
does.

`scene/access` also grew the column R1668 gave the framework and this serializer
never published: **why** a node is inert. An agent reading it saw `disabled` and
nothing else, which is exactly the one bit the floor carries — measured on a rail
whose two locked seats are booked for named requirements, where a reader was told
they refuse and never told they will stop refusing.

## The consumer, and why totality alone would have been worthless

The screen closed all 136. Panes announce as named groups, the rail through the
framework's own navigation landmark (its fourth consumer, extended this round to
carry the reason a destination is inert), the palette's roles as buttons, its
determinism control as a SWITCH, the canvas's cards and frames and wires and
pins each with what a drag on them would do, the launch gate as a list a reader
walks one finding at a time, and the gesture strip — this screen's only statement
of what a pointer can do, which was inaudible.

But a total census is satisfiable by declaring everything silent. So the split is
the specification's: `VOICES` and `SILENCES` name what owes a voice and what owes
a declared silence, by POPULATION rather than by tag — the table a family expands
from — so a ninth role or a sixth field is demanded without anybody editing a
list. Both are published on the wire and driven in both directions.

## The form painter, where the defect had a name already

`row_access_nodes` announced every control as a **text box**. A boolean row is a
toggle and was telling a reader to type into it; an integer row is a stepper, a
single-choice set is a radio group and a subset is not. The role is the shape's
now, and every affordance inside a control — the stepper's two seats, the
checkbox, each option chip, each list element and the seat that appends — has a
voice, derived from the parts list the painter and the hit test already share.
This is the substrate, so the property grid gets it in the same act.

R1691.publishable_decision_summary:
The screen says all of itself: every addressable region either has a voice in
the accessibility tree or declares why it has none.

A screen paints regions and publishes an accessibility tree, and the two are
built by different code. Nothing in either said whether they AGREE — and a
region nobody gave a node to is not an error anywhere. It paints perfectly, it
takes presses, every question about its rectangle is answered, and a reader is
simply never told it exists.

Measured on the analysis tool's first screen the day this was written: **166
addressable regions painted, 30 of them announced** — the accessibility tree had
35 nodes and five of those are virtual description regions the form points at,
which is itself a distinction nothing had ever drawn. **136 were
unclassified.** The palette, the icon rail, the
canvas's frames and wires and pins, the launch gate, the gesture hint and the
inspector's own chrome had no voice at all. The three clusters that DID have one
each had a round that asked for it — the cards at R1651, the toolbar at R1687 —
and nothing had ever asked about the rest. Accessibility existed on that screen
exactly where somebody had once looked.

## Against the reference toolkit at 6.11 — built and RUN, not read

Its accessibility layer builds an interface for every widget automatically,
which sounds like the stronger position and is precisely why the question cannot
be asked there. A probe built against 6.11.1 and run:

* A window of six children answered **7 nodes, 4 of them with an empty
  accessible name**: a button whose name the author forgot, a decorative rule, a
  custom painted region, and the window. **The forgotten button and the
  decorative rule are the same answer** — a role and no name. One is a defect
  and one is correct, and nothing separates them.
* Clearing every author-settable accessibility slot on the rule (its widget has
  exactly three: a name, a description, an identifier) left the tree at 7 nodes.
  **A region cannot be declared deliberately silent.**
* Hiding it left the tree at 7 nodes too, with one state bit flipped — so the
  only act that quiets a region takes its ink with it, and does not even remove
  the node. Silence and invisibility are one act there.
* A label bound to a field announced its text **twice**, once as the label's own
  name and once as the field's. The duplicate is produced by construction and
  nothing suppresses it.

So the floor has an accessibility tree and no census of it.

## The substrate: `pinion_core::voice`

A declaration carries a `Silence` — a `kind` from a closed vocabulary and one
`detail` the kind gives meaning to, the same shape `Unavailable` has and for the
same reason: the arms exist because each leaves a reader somewhere different,
and that difference is derived ONCE as a `Relay` rather than restated per site.
`Decorative` relays nowhere, `Layout` to the children, `NameOf` to a named peer,
`PartOf` to a named node that announces the whole. No two share a relay, which
is what makes the vocabulary four things rather than a bool with extra words.

It lives on `LayoutStyle` beside `unavailable`, reaches the descendants exactly
when the kind `covers_subtree` — every kind but the layout box, which has said
nothing about what it merely placed — and is **independent of the ink**, which
is the conflation the floor cannot escape.

`voice_census` then classifies every addressable region of a produced paint
scene against the tree built beside it, and answers with one of five arms. Two
are correct outcomes and **three are three different defects**, each with a
different repair:

* `unvoiced` — painted, addressable, no node and no reason. Nobody decided.
* `ghost` — a name announced for a tag nothing paints and nobody refers to. A
  reader can be sent somewhere that is not there. (A node another node POINTS
  at — a description region, a composite child, a name source — is deliberately
  virtual and is not this; the reference is what makes it reachable.)
* `dangling` — quiet because another node says its name, where that node does
  not speak either. It reads as handled and is a hole.

That last arm is the one no set difference could produce, and it is what caught
this round's own largest defect: a draft that dropped the cards from the tree
showed up as 8 unvoiced cards AND 16 dangling redirects from their captions.

## Published: `scene/voice`

Joins the last painted scene with the **same** access-tree producer
`scene/access` runs — deliberately, because a census that built its own idea of
what is announced would be a second opinion able to disagree with the very fact
it exists to check. `total` and `counts` are derived on every call: a coverage
figure that is written down is one that stops falling when the thing it measures
does.

`scene/access` also grew the column R1668 gave the framework and this serializer
never published: **why** a node is inert. An agent reading it saw `disabled` and
nothing else, which is exactly the one bit the floor carries — measured on a rail
whose two locked seats are booked for named requirements, where a reader was told
they refuse and never told they will stop refusing.

## The consumer, and why totality alone would have been worthless

The screen closed all 136. Panes announce as named groups, the rail through the
framework's own navigation landmark (its fourth consumer, extended this round to

pins each with what a drag on them would do, the launch gate as a list a reader
walks one finding at a time, and the gesture strip — this screen's only statement

`row_access_nodes` announced every control as a **text box**. A boolean row is a
toggle and was telling a reader to type into it; an integer row is a stepper, a

now, and every affordance inside a control — the stepper's two seats, the
checkbox, each option chip, each list element and the seat that appends — has a
voice, derived from the parts list the painter and the hit test already share.
This is the substrate, so the property grid gets it in the same act.

R1692.decision_summary:
A voice is judged, not only counted: a node in the accessibility tree is not a
voice, and the census stops accepting one as an answer.

R1691 made every addressable region of a screen **classified** — announced, or
declared silent with a stated reason. It could not ask the next question. An
accessibility node carrying `role = Button, name = ""` counted as `announced`,
and so did one named `×`, and so did one named after its own paint tag. The
census counted nodes and called them voices, which is the same mistake the floor
makes, one level up.

Measured across this tree the day this was written, through the running
applications rather than the source: **216 of 225 surfaces answer, 5,427
addressable regions, 2,645 announced** — and the first run of the rules flagged
**42 rows across 24 surfaces that were all green**.

**Thirty of those were defects, and twelve were the rules being wrong.** That
split is the finding, not a caveat on it: a census that has never run has never
been shown to be about anything, and the twelve are what the first run taught it.

The thirty: eight scrub sliders and a switch announced their role and no name. A
code editor announced `▾`, the fold chevron in its gutter — the first text
under its tag. Five document table rows and seven list items announced nothing at
all. Two grid corners and a tree container had no name, a tab panel announced its
own identifier, and four names had no region behind them.

The twelve: **ten grid cells whose emptiness is the data** (the empty half of an
optional column — a screen reader says "blank" and there is nothing to repair),
and **two live regions**, which are announced when they change rather than
navigated to and therefore owe no rectangle at all. Each produced a rule rather
than an exception: `AriaRole::name_required` and `Announcement::live`.

## Against the reference toolkit at 6.11 — built and RUN, not read

A probe compiled against 6.11.1 and executed offscreen, six regions in a window:
a properly named button, a button whose text is a glyph, a button whose name the
author forgot, a decorative rule, a label whose accessible name was set to its
own object name, and a box holding two ornamental children.

It answered **9 nodes, 8 of which fail one of the three rules this round adds**.
Five had an empty name — of which **exactly one is a defect** and four are
ornament, a layout box and the window itself. One announced its own identifier.
And one announced `×`, which the framework had **derived from the button's
visible text by construction**, with no test that the text is a word.

That is the finding, and it is not that the rules are wrong: it is that the
rules are **noise without the rest of the surface**. Eight flags to find one
defect, because nothing there separates a region that owes a reader a voice from
one that does not — a distinction that cannot be expressed, since R1691 measured
that clearing every author-settable accessibility slot on the ornament changes
the tree by nothing. Here the R1691 silences supply exactly that separation, so
the same three rules run only where a voice is owed and a flag is a defect. The
name judgment is the second half of a mechanism whose first half had to exist.

## The vocabulary

`NameFault` — three rules with no taste in them, each decidable from the tag and
the name alone and each a real defect on this tree:

* `absent` — nothing is said. The floor's default for any control without
  visible text, and there indistinguishable from ornament.
* `address` — the name is this node's own tag, and the tag is structured rather
  than a word. A tag is how a program addresses a region, not how a person is
  told what it is. The structure test is load-bearing: three tags on this tree
  (`notch`, `violin`, `caps`) equal their names and are **right**, because those
  screens paint that word as the control's visible label and a name matching the
  visible label is WAI-ARIA's own rule.
* `wordless` — no letter or digit anywhere: `×`, `…`, `☐`, `⠿`.

`Voice::Mumbled` carries it, and is deliberately not `Unvoiced`: an unvoiced
region needs a **decision** (does it owe a reader anything?), while a mumbled one
was already decided and came out empty.

## The promise that could only be checked from below

`Silence::Layout` says "the children speak". Every other reachable relay names a
node, and R1691 already refused a redirect to a node that does not speak
(`dangling`). The children relay names a **subtree**, and nothing asked. A box
over a subtree where nothing is announced leaves that whole region inaudible
while every per-node check passes — each descendant is correctly quiet on its
own terms.

`Voice::Hollow` is that arm, and it is expressed as a property of the relay
rather than of the kind: `Relay::unkept` maps every relay to what a broken
promise makes it, and the invariant a fifth `SilenceKind` must answer for is that
a relay is reachable exactly when its unkept form is a defect. `Nowhere` promises
nothing, so there is nothing to break.

## The exemption that was one-directional

`ghost` (a name with no region) exempted a node **something points at**. The
mirror was missing: a node that points at something painted. A composite
container — a legend, a transcript, a radio group, a print dialog — is announced
for a tag the scene need not paint, because what it stands for is what it holds,
and a reader landing on it descends to ink. Measured: **eight of this tree's nine
ghosts were exactly that shape and none was a defect**. A third anchor is a live
region, which owes no rectangle for a different reason — it is announced when it
changes rather than reached by navigating.

The ninth ghost was real, and so were the five the two new anchors did not save.

## What the census could not see for itself

Two facts belong to the role, which `pinion-core` cannot name: whether an empty
name is a defect, and whether the node is a live region. `AriaRole::name_required`
answers the first, and is deliberately **stricter than WAI-ARIA's own
"Accessible Name Required" table** — that table excuses `group`, `list`,
`toolbar`, `navigation`, `status`; this excuses only `cell`, `gridcell` and
`generic`, the roles where emptiness is the data rather than an omission. Ten
cells of one grid are the empty half of an optional column, and a name there
would be an invention, not a repair.

## The second consumer

`scene/voice` answered every binding since R1691 and exactly one screen ever
asked it. The other 196 surfaces' numbers were not unmeasured — they were
**unrequested**, which is the failure this whole family of boot gates exists to
end. `_gate_voice_census` now runs on every demo, prints unconditionally, and
refuses the four arms that need **no per-screen judgment**: `mumbled`, `hollow`,
`dangling`, `ghost`. `unvoiced` is reported and not judged, because refusing it
needs a screen-by-screen answer to "which regions owe a reader anything" — a
round of work per screen, and 2,695 of the 5,427 regions are waiting for it.

verification_bullets: ## The measurement this round is answering, taken over the whole tree
Read off 216 running applications over the wire (9 of 225 do not answer: three
terminal bindings, an audio device, two cross-repo consumers, a code-generator
demo and one that times out — infrastructure absence, not defect).
**5,427 addressable regions. 2,645 announced. 51 declared quiet. 2,695
unvoiced.** The first run of the rules flagged **42 rows across 24 surfaces**,
and the split is the measurement: **30 defects and 12 rule corrections**.
By kind, exactly as the census reported them: 10 `absent` on `gridcell` (the
empty half of an optional column — a rule correction, `name_required`), 8 on
`slider`, 7 on `listitem`, 5 on `row`, 2 on `columnheader`, 1 each on `switch`
and `tree`; 1 `wordless` on `textbox`; 1 `address` on `tabpanel`; 3 `ghost`
groups, 1 `ghost` list, and 2 `ghost` statuses (live regions — the second rule
correction). Re-measured after: **0**, and the boot gate holds every surface
there.
Only **57 of 216 surfaces are fully classified**, which is the shape of the debt
this round hands on rather than pays: the worst two are the analysis tool's own
screen B (183 of 186 unvoiced) and screen C (123 of 128).
## The floor, built and run
A probe compiled against the reference toolkit at 6.11.1 and executed offscreen,
six regions in a window. It answers **9 nodes, 8 of which fail one of the three
rules added here**: five with an empty name (of which exactly ONE is a defect —
the other four are ornament, a layout box and the window), one announcing its own
object name, and one announcing `×`, which the framework derived from the
button's visible text by construction (`derivedFromText=1`, printed). Clearing
the ornament's accessible name leaves it in the tree, named nothing, exactly as
before. Those numbers are what the "rules are noise without owedness" claim rests
on, and none of them was read out of a header.
## Counterfactuals — 18 run, and FIVE passed
Every one of the five that passed had the same shape: **the round's own new
function had no test**. Repaired in place, then re-run and CAUGHT.
* `AriaRole::name_required` returning `false` for every role — which switches the
`absent` rule off across 216 surfaces — compiled and passed everything. It had
no test at all. Now: an exhaustive match (a forty-third role cannot inherit an
answer nobody chose) plus a test pinning the three exemptions and 23 required
roles. Re-run with a fourth role quietly excused: CAUGHT.
* Naming a table row from **no cells** left every crate green; only a demo two
crates away went red. Now tested in the crate that does it, including that an
authored name survives and an empty cell contributes nothing. CAUGHT.
* `announcements` reporting **no node as a live region** — which turns every
off-screen status back into a ghost — passed everything. Now a field-by-field
test of what the census reads out of a node. CAUGHT.
* The macro accepting `access_name` and **emitting nothing** passed everything:
the declared-and-dropped shape this tree has been bitten by before. Now the
consumer asserts the name, and that the name clears the three rules. CAUGHT.
* Deleting `enrich_names_from_scene` from the screen's own gate changed nothing —
because that screen names every node itself, so the call fills zero. The repair
is **not** deleting it: it keeps the gate on production's path, and its being a
no-op is now asserted (`filled == 0`), so the day the screen starts relying on
the paint derivation the gate says so.

arm, the address rule inverted (fires on `notch`, which is correct on this tree),
the children relay's broken promise made not-a-defect, a mumbling child no longer
keeping its box's promise, the composes anchor removed, the live anchor removed,
`name_required` defaulting to false, a tagged text node made unreachable by the
enrichment again, a text node shadowing the container that carries its tag, the
grid corner unnamed, `announcements` forgetting what a node composes, and the
wire dropping the fault column.
## Local gates
`cargo test -p pinion-core -p pinion-a11y -p pinion-widget-paint -p pinion-rpc
-p pinion-derive -p hello-node-lab -p hello-image` — green.
`cargo check --workspace --all-targets` and `cargo clippy --workspace
--all-targets --features pinion-runtime/vello` — green.
## The demo sweep
**328 demo runs**, every one of them paying the new boot gate. Nothing failed
for a reason this round is responsible for.
Four failures, each attributed:
* `hello_audio_device` — the silent test card is not loaded on this host
(`modprobe snd-dummy`), which the demo itself says.
* `r1518_at_focus_one_answer` and `r1521_shape_cache_working_set` — the sweep's
180-second per-demo budget, on a machine where the first is measured at ~17
minutes. Both are known-slow and neither is an assertion.
* `r1005_paged_stream` — fails **deterministically here and passes in CI**, and
it is not this round's: proved by stashing the whole round, rebuilding the
example from the pristine tree, and getting the identical message. Registered
as debt — its docstring claims "no wall-clock race" beside an 8-second
`wait_until`, and only a full local sweep could ever have found that.

my error, not a finding. Both pass on a clean re-run, which is how they are
counted above.
carry_forward_bullets: ## Registered as debt rather than carried
**`unvoiced` is reported and not judged.** 2,695 of 5,427 regions, and only 57 of
216 surfaces are fully classified. Refusing it needs a per-screen answer to
"which regions owe a reader anything", which R1691 spent a whole round giving to
ONE screen. The two worst are the analysis tool's own screen B (183/186) and
screen C (123/128), which is where the next a11y round goes.
**Name-from-contents is applied to roles whose contents are their VALUE.** The
`wordless` rule caught the loudest instance — a code editor announcing its
gutter chevron — and the class is untouched: without that chevron the editor
would have announced the first line of its buffer, which is a wrong name that no
rule here can see. The narrow repair is to exempt `textbox` / `combobox` /
`spinbutton` from the derivation, and it must be measured first, because the same
derivation is doing genuinely useful work for `group` and `list`.

announced node exempted from `ghost` (referenced, composing ink, or live) never
becomes a row at all, so its name is unseen. Some of that is correct — a `row`
and a `cell` are named by contents — and some is not: one chart's accessibility
table announces its rows with empty names. Closing it means redefining the
population (rows = painted ∪ announced, with a `painted` flag and a `virtual`
count), which also removes the arm-specific "ghost is the one excluded" rule that
this round already had to work around.
## Deliberately not built
**A helper for the eight scrub sliders.** Seven surfaces made the same omission
in the same shape, which is normally the lift signal. What is shared is the
*omission*, not a value: each slider names a different thing, and a helper that
supplied one name would be wrong at the ninth. The gate is the lift.
**`Decorative` cannot be checked** — the one silence whose relay promises
nothing, so there is nothing to catch it breaking. A per-screen ratio ratchet is
the only shape anybody has proposed and no screen has needed it yet.

**`_gate_voice_census`** runs on every demo, prints unconditionally, and refuses

publishes rather than from a list of arm names, which is why R1691's own demo
did not silently go on summing four arms out of seven.

named, having announced its gutter chevron; a tree container named; two grid
corners named; five document rows and seven list items reached by the derivation

its own children cover. That gate was right and this one had no opinion —
which is the argument for a screen paying every gate rather than the one its

and `Announcement::live` (two live regions, one of which R873's own comment

**`unvoiced` is reported and not judged.** 2,695 of 5,427 regions, and only 57 of

"which regions owe a reader anything", which R1691 spent a whole round giving to

rule here can see. The narrow repair is to exempt `textbox` / `combobox` /

derivation is doing genuinely useful work for `group` and `list`.
**A virtual node's name is never judged.** The census judges painted regions; an
announced node exempted from `ghost` (referenced, composing ink, or live) never

and a `cell` are named by contents — and some is not: one chart's accessibility

population (rows = painted ∪ announced, with a `painted` flag and a `virtual`
count), which also removes the arm-specific "ghost is the one excluded" rule that

## Deliberately not built
**A helper for the eight scrub sliders.** Seven surfaces made the same omission
in the same shape, which is normally the lift signal. What is shared is the
*omission*, not a value: each slider names a different thing, and a helper that
supplied one name would be wrong at the ninth. The gate is the lift.
**`Decorative` cannot be checked** — the one silence whose relay promises

R1693.decision_summary:
A screen is a tree a reader can walk: an announced role that promises members
and holds none is a lie no per-node check can see, and the census stops
accepting it.

R1691 asked whether every painted region has a voice. R1692 asked whether that
voice says anything usable. Both are questions about one node at a time, and
neither can see the failure this round is for: a node that is **perfect on its
own terms and structurally a lie**.

A pane announces `role = table`. It has a name a reader can hear and a rectangle
they can land on. Every check passes. It holds no row. An assistive technology
says "table" and there is nothing to move into — the sixteen messages painted
inside it are not in the tree at all.

Measured across the 216 surfaces that answer, the day this was written:
**12 carry a violation — 13 collections owning nothing and 44 members outside
the collection their role requires.** Small enough to close in the round that
found it, which is what lets the new gate refuse at a budget of **zero** instead
of becoming another ratchet.

Two of the twelve were the reference analysis tool's **screen B**, which is
where the round started: it painted **186** addressable regions and announced
**three** nodes — a `table` with no row, a `tree` with no item, and a group.

## Against the reference toolkit at 6.11 — built and RUN, not read

Two probes compiled against 6.11.1 and executed offscreen. Its item views derive
the whole accessibility tree from their model, which is the **stronger** position
for a populated view and the reason the question cannot be asked there:

* a 16x7 item view answered **137 nodes**, a table interface reporting sixteen
  rows and seven columns, and a cell lookup by row and column naming the cell and
  reporting its own row, column and column header. That is why screen B's grid is
  now built cell by cell: tagging only its rows would have been strictly *less*
  navigable than the thing it is meant to beat.
* the same view with its **model emptied** answered the table role, a row count
  of zero, and **no diagnostic**. A tree with no items answered the same way.
  Nothing there separates a collection that is empty from one nobody filled.
* a **two-column tree** — exactly screen B's decode pane — announced a row as
  **two sibling items**: the field and its value are peers, the value reports
  itself expandable like the field it belongs to, leaf rows report themselves
  expanded while reporting they cannot expand, and the hierarchy is gone
  entirely: every item is a direct child of the tree whatever its depth.
* a **custom-painted 72-cell pane** answered **one** node, empty-named, with no
  children. Everything painted rather than modelled is simply absent — which is
  what a byte pane is.

So the floor gives a complete tree for the shapes it owns, nothing at all for the
shapes it does not, and in neither case a verdict about the tree's **form**.

## Emptiness is declared, not inferred

A collection with no members is a real state — a filter that matched nothing, a
capture with no messages — and a rule that refused it would make that state
unrepresentable. So the rule is the one R1691 applied to silence: **an empty
collection is well-formed when it says it is empty.** ARIA already has the
vocabulary, so nothing is invented: `aria-rowcount` / `aria-colcount` /
`aria-setsize` of zero.

That is the distinction the floor cannot draw, and it is the whole reason the
gate can be budget zero: "it is legitimately empty" is not an exception a screen
pleads, it is a declaration the screen makes and the census checks.

**And there is a third answer**, which the round found late and from outside its
own sweep: a collection that has *asked* for its members and not received them is
neither full nor empty. WAI-ARIA calls it `aria-busy`, AccessKit already carried
it, and nothing here had ever exposed it. Declaring zero would have been a lie in
the other direction — the list has forty assets, it just has not got them yet.
The gate accepts a busy collection for exactly the reason an assistive technology
should be told to wait rather than told the list is empty.

## The vocabulary

`AriaRole::required_owned` / `required_context` — WAI-ARIA 1.2's own two
columns, as exhaustive matches so a forty-second role cannot inherit an answer
nobody chose. The relation is genuinely **asymmetric** where the spec is: a
`radiogroup` requires radios and a lone radio is well-formed, and copying one
column into the other would have invented a rule.

`StructureFault` — two arms because the relation has two directions and the
repairs differ. `Empty` wants members; `Stray` wants a parent. Folding them into
one "malformed" would report both and say neither.

`structure_census` reads the a11y tree alone — ownership there is
`AccessNode::children`, which is exactly what the shell lowers, so the census
measures the tree an assistive technology will receive rather than a second model
of it.

`scene/conform` publishes it beside `scene/access` and `scene/voice`, running the
**same** producer all three run, and `judged` is published as the denominator: a
structural census over a tree with no collections is green, and "well formed"
must not read like "nothing to check".

## What the twelve turned out to be

Three classes, and only one of them is what the round expected:

* **The role was wrong.** Three panels announced `list` and had never built a
  `listitem` — they paint prose in a column. A `list` promises members a reader
  moves through. Each had a perfectly good *name* the whole time, which is why a
  good name is not evidence of a right role.
* **The tree stopped short.** A movable column-header strip announced a `row`
  owning none of its five `columnheader`s, and sat inside nothing — the
  requirement chain is ARIA saying the tree ended two levels early. A calendar
  owned its seven headers and thirty-one days **directly**, with no weeks in it,
  so the shape a sighted reader sees was not the shape a reader was given. A
  grouped grid's header row owned no cell. A command palette announced a
  `listbox` and never announced one option.
* **The collection was empty and did not say so.** Three lists open with nothing
  in them. The repair is one declaration each — and the *lift* is that the
  framework's own builders now state their extent, so the fourth consumer gets
  it by construction rather than by being repaired.

## Screen B

The forcing consumer, and the one this round was chartered for. Its grid is now
sixteen rows of seven addressable cells under a header row; its decode is a tree
of items that carry **their own values** and their depth; its bytes are nine rows
of eight cells, each row headed by its offset. **291 addressable regions, 266
announced, 25 declared quiet, 0 unclassified, 0 defects, 0 structural faults** —
from 186 regions and 3 nodes.

`spec::VOICES` / `spec::SILENCES` pin the split, because a total census is
satisfied by declaring everything silent.

### The population question, settled by measurement

`debt-a-voice-family-can-only-expand-from-a-table-the-spec-has` asked whether a
screen's `Population` has to be a closed enum, and said the second consumer was
the only evidence that could answer it. Screen B is that consumer, and the answer
is **no new machinery**: it declares two families of shapes screen A has none of
— `Cells` is a **product** of two tables and `Bytes` a **range** derived from a
scalar — plus four **conditional** families expanded by a predicate over a table
(the messages that carry an annotation, the fields the decoder computed). What
has to generalise is the *expander*, which was already a function; the arm list
stays per-screen and closed on purpose, so a screen naming a family it does not
have fails to compile.

## The defect the round found by accident, and the one that found it

Tagging screen B's cells made the forward-paint gate fail at the declared floor:
message 6's resource name was painted at **zero width** and simply was not there.
Its annotations (`Last 3/3` + `reassembled 3,144 B`) are wider than the whole
name column, and the column's floor was a number somebody picked. It is the same
defect the comment one level up already recorded — a floor somebody picks can be
wrong about the thing it is a floor FOR — and the same repair: the floor is now
derived at compile time from the widest annotation load the capture holds.

A sighted reader had been losing that message's name, and no check had ever asked
whether the cell was painted, because until this round the cell had no tag to ask
about.

a11y builders, which by the standing rule makes a full 388-demo sweep the
justified verification. What ran is **112 demos**: every demo driving an example
whose accessibility tree this round changed, plus every consumer of
`grid_table_nodes`, `listbox_option_nodes` and `grouped_grid_access_nodes`.
The argument for narrowing: the new gate's *subject* was already measured
tree-wide — all 216 answering surfaces, which is what found the 12 violations and
justified a budget of zero. What a full sweep adds over that is demos whose
assertions break from the builder changes, and those demos are exactly the 112.
What it leaves unrun: a demo that asserts on `scene/access` for an example this
round did not touch, through a builder it does not use. The residue is real and
this is where it is written down.
## The `ALL` roster is not self-proving
Registered as `debt-a-hand-written-arm-roster-is-not-self-proving` rather than

## External
`AriaRole::ALL` is a hand-written roster and no non-macro construction makes it
self-proving. The three exhaustive matches stop a forty-second role compiling,
and `every_role_the_relation_names_is_in_the_roster` closes the half that
