R1693.publishable_decision_summary:
A screen is a tree a reader can walk: an announced role that promises members
and holds none is a lie no per-node check can see, and the census stops
accepting it.

R1691 asked whether every painted region has a voice. R1692 asked whether that
voice says anything usable. Both are questions about one node at a time, and
neither can see the failure this round is for: a node that is **perfect on its
own terms and structurally a lie**.

A pane announces `role = table`. It has a name a reader can hear and a rectangle
they can land on. Every check passes. It holds no row. An assistive technology
says "table" and there is nothing to move into — the sixteen messages painted
inside it are not in the tree at all.

Measured across the 216 surfaces that answer, the day this was written:
**12 carry a violation — 13 collections owning nothing and 44 members outside
the collection their role requires.** Small enough to close in the round that
found it, which is what lets the new gate refuse at a budget of **zero** instead
of becoming another ratchet.

Two of the twelve were the reference analysis tool's **screen B**, which is
where the round started: it painted **186** addressable regions and announced
**three** nodes — a `table` with no row, a `tree` with no item, and a group.

## Against the reference toolkit at 6.11 — built and RUN, not read

Two probes compiled against 6.11.1 and executed offscreen. Its item views derive
the whole accessibility tree from their model, which is the **stronger** position
for a populated view and the reason the question cannot be asked there:

* a 16x7 item view answered **137 nodes**, a table interface reporting sixteen
  rows and seven columns, and a cell lookup by row and column naming the cell and
  reporting its own row, column and column header. That is why screen B's grid is
  now built cell by cell: tagging only its rows would have been strictly *less*
  navigable than the thing it is meant to beat.
* the same view with its **model emptied** answered the table role, a row count
  of zero, and **no diagnostic**. A tree with no items answered the same way.
  Nothing there separates a collection that is empty from one nobody filled.
* a **two-column tree** — exactly screen B's decode pane — announced a row as
  **two sibling items**: the field and its value are peers, the value reports
  itself expandable like the field it belongs to, leaf rows report themselves
  expanded while reporting they cannot expand, and the hierarchy is gone
  entirely: every item is a direct child of the tree whatever its depth.
* a **custom-painted 72-cell pane** answered **one** node, empty-named, with no
  children. Everything painted rather than modelled is simply absent — which is
  what a byte pane is.

So the floor gives a complete tree for the shapes it owns, nothing at all for the
shapes it does not, and in neither case a verdict about the tree's **form**.

## Emptiness is declared, not inferred

A collection with no members is a real state — a filter that matched nothing, a
capture with no messages — and a rule that refused it would make that state
unrepresentable. So the rule is the one R1691 applied to silence: **an empty
collection is well-formed when it says it is empty.** ARIA already has the
vocabulary, so nothing is invented: `aria-rowcount` / `aria-colcount` /
`aria-setsize` of zero.

That is the distinction the floor cannot draw, and it is the whole reason the
gate can be budget zero: "it is legitimately empty" is not an exception a screen
pleads, it is a declaration the screen makes and the census checks.

**And there is a third answer**, which the round found late and from outside its
own sweep: a collection that has *asked* for its members and not received them is
neither full nor empty. WAI-ARIA calls it `aria-busy`, AccessKit already carried
it, and nothing here had ever exposed it. Declaring zero would have been a lie in
the other direction — the list has forty assets, it just has not got them yet.
The gate accepts a busy collection for exactly the reason an assistive technology
should be told to wait rather than told the list is empty.

## The vocabulary

`AriaRole::required_owned` / `required_context` — WAI-ARIA 1.2's own two
columns, as exhaustive matches so a forty-second role cannot inherit an answer
nobody chose. The relation is genuinely **asymmetric** where the spec is: a
`radiogroup` requires radios and a lone radio is well-formed, and copying one
column into the other would have invented a rule.

`StructureFault` — two arms because the relation has two directions and the
repairs differ. `Empty` wants members; `Stray` wants a parent. Folding them into
one "malformed" would report both and say neither.

`structure_census` reads the a11y tree alone — ownership there is
`AccessNode::children`, which is exactly what the shell lowers, so the census
measures the tree an assistive technology will receive rather than a second model
of it.

`scene/conform` publishes it beside `scene/access` and `scene/voice`, running the
**same** producer all three run, and `judged` is published as the denominator: a
structural census over a tree with no collections is green, and "well formed"
must not read like "nothing to check".

## What the twelve turned out to be

Three classes, and only one of them is what the round expected:

* **The role was wrong.** Three panels announced `list` and had never built a
  `listitem` — they paint prose in a column. A `list` promises members a reader
  moves through. Each had a perfectly good *name* the whole time, which is why a
  good name is not evidence of a right role.
* **The tree stopped short.** A movable column-header strip announced a `row`
  owning none of its five `columnheader`s, and sat inside nothing — the
  requirement chain is ARIA saying the tree ended two levels early. A calendar
  owned its seven headers and thirty-one days **directly**, with no weeks in it,
  so the shape a sighted reader sees was not the shape a reader was given. A
  grouped grid's header row owned no cell. A command palette announced a
  `listbox` and never announced one option.
* **The collection was empty and did not say so.** Three lists open with nothing
  in them. The repair is one declaration each — and the *lift* is that the
  framework's own builders now state their extent, so the fourth consumer gets
  it by construction rather than by being repaired.

## Screen B

The forcing consumer, and the one this round was chartered for. Its grid is now
sixteen rows of seven addressable cells under a header row; its decode is a tree
of items that carry **their own values** and their depth; its bytes are nine rows
of eight cells, each row headed by its offset. **291 addressable regions, 266
announced, 25 declared quiet, 0 unclassified, 0 defects, 0 structural faults** —
from 186 regions and 3 nodes.

`spec::VOICES` / `spec::SILENCES` pin the split, because a total census is
satisfied by declaring everything silent.

### The population question, settled by measurement

`debt-a-voice-family-can-only-expand-from-a-table-the-spec-has` asked whether a
screen's `Population` has to be a closed enum, and said the second consumer was
the only evidence that could answer it. Screen B is that consumer, and the answer
is **no new machinery**: it declares two families of shapes screen A has none of
— `Cells` is a **product** of two tables and `Bytes` a **range** derived from a
scalar — plus four **conditional** families expanded by a predicate over a table
(the messages that carry an annotation, the fields the decoder computed). What
has to generalise is the *expander*, which was already a function; the arm list
stays per-screen and closed on purpose, so a screen naming a family it does not
have fails to compile.

## The defect the round found by accident, and the one that found it

Tagging screen B's cells made the forward-paint gate fail at the declared floor:
message 6's resource name was painted at **zero width** and simply was not there.
Its annotations (`Last 3/3` + `reassembled 3,144 B`) are wider than the whole
name column, and the column's floor was a number somebody picked. It is the same
defect the comment one level up already recorded — a floor somebody picks can be
wrong about the thing it is a floor FOR — and the same repair: the floor is now
derived at compile time from the widest annotation load the capture holds.

A sighted reader had been losing that message's name, and no check had ever asked
whether the cell was painted, because until this round the cell had no tag to ask
about.

R1694.decision_summary:
A locked seat nobody can hear is not a locked seat.

The reference analysis tool's **screen C** is the dashboard, and its subject is
what the release does **not** have yet: four widgets the first release places and
**nine it reserves**, each shown rather than hidden, each naming the requirement
it is booked under — *"a second-release item is not a missing thing, it is a
locked seat"*. Two rail destinations are locked the same way.

The framework has computed that reason since R1668. `Unavailable` carries a kind,
a detail, and a recourse derived from the kind; the disabled cascade resolves it
down the subtree; `scene/disabled` publishes it. Measured the day this was
written, all **eleven** locked regions published a complete reason — and **not
one of them was in the accessibility tree at all**. The reason was computed,
published, painted as faded ink, and inaudible.

That is the whole screen underneath it: **128** addressable regions painted,
**five** announced (a group for the window and one per card, each holding
nothing), **123** undecided. `scene/conform` judged **zero** nodes — not "zero
faults": zero *judged*, because no announced role on this screen carried a
structural requirement at all. The rail, both bars, two tables, the decode tree,
seventy-two bytes and the whole thirteen-entry palette reached a reader as four
names and a summary sentence.

## Against the reference toolkit at 6.11.1 — built and RUN, not read

The same shape assembled there and its accessibility tree read back: a rail of
seven seats with two locked, a thirteen-entry palette in three sections with nine
locked, a tab bar with a locked tab, a locked plain widget as a control.

* the locked **palette entries** answer `focusable, selectable` and carry **no
  unavailable state at all**. Both spellings were built — the convenience item
  and a model whose `flags()` drops the enabled bit — and both lose it.
* the locked **tab** answers `focusable, selectable` too, and is not marked
  current. So a reader there is invited to activate exactly the seats the screen
  has closed.
* the locked **plain widget** does carry the bit, which is how the probe is known
  to be sound: the loss belongs to **collections**, which is what a palette and a
  navigation rail are.
* the palette's three **section headings** come back as list items
  indistinguishable in role from the entries — sixteen flat items, no grouping,
  and no way to derive "thirteen entries, nine reserved" from what is announced.
* the one slot that could carry a reason is a free-form description that nothing
  classifies and nothing links to the lock. On a toolbar action it is worse than
  empty: measured directly, every **unlocked** seat comes back with its
  description equal to its name, because the slot defaults to the action's own
  label.

## What this round did

**Screen C closes at 193 addressable regions — 190 announced, 3 declared quiet,
0 undecided, 0 voice defects — with `scene/conform` judging 159 nodes, 0 empty
and 0 stray.** Every locked seat is announced, named, marked unavailable, keeps
its place in the set of thirteen, and carries the kind, the detail and the
recourse the bit cannot hold. The reason is **not restated** by the screen: it is
declared once on the row's layout style, and the accessibility assembler relays
what the cascade resolved.

**The `stated-reason` gate gained the half its own failure text had always
named.** R1669 counted the regions that state a reason; nothing asked whether the
reason reached the audience it was built for. It did not. Measured over the
**215** surfaces that answer: **13 stated reasons, 11 of them unheard, every one
on this screen.** Small enough to close in the round that found it, which is what
lets the gate refuse at a budget of **zero** with an empty exception list.

★★★★★ **And the round found a rule that had been living in prose.** Both this
screen and the sibling capture screen hand-rolled a header-row grid, and the two
**disagreed about where the header row sits**. WAI-ARIA counts it in
`aria-rowcount`, so it has to be counted in `aria-rowindex` too — and the shared
builder `grid_table_nodes` stated a grid's *extent* and gave **no row or cell its
coordinates at all**. So a reader could be told a grid has seventeen rows and
seven columns and could not learn which row or column anything was in — below the
floor on the one dimension the floor is strongest on, whose cell query answers
the cell's name, its row, its column and its column header. The capture screen's
copy had counted the header in the count and numbered its data rows from one,
leaving its header unplaced and its last row unreachable. The rule now lives once,
in the builder, together with the row's WAI-ARIA name-from-contents, and **both
screens were converted onto the builder** rather than corrected in place.
changes_bullets: ## The framework
* **`pinion_a11y::grid::grid_table_nodes` gives every row and cell its
coordinates.** The header row is `aria-rowindex` **1** — WAI-ARIA's own
reading, and the one `aria-rowcount` already took by counting the header — so
a data row is `n + 2` and the last data row **is** the row count. Column
headers and cells carry `aria-colindex`. Held by two tests: one asserts the
whole numbering including "the last data row is the row count, so no row is
unreachable", the other that a cell carries its own coordinates rather than
only its row's.
* **A row is named from the cells it holds.** WAI-ARIA gives `row`
name-from-contents, and a row is usually painted as an empty band with its
cells as siblings, so nothing under the row's own tag can be read. One screen
computed it and the other did not; it is computed once now.
* **`RpcSubprocess._gate_stated_reasons` gained its heard half**
(`_unheard_reasons`). Every region the disabled cascade states a reason for
must have an accessibility node carrying that reason. Two failure shapes,
because the repairs differ: *no node at all* (announce it) and *announced,
reason dropped* (look at the assembler). Budget **zero**, no exception list.
A row whose reason is `unstated` is deliberately outside this population — it
is already the other half of the same gate, and one region reported under two
arms makes one repair look like two.
* Three cases in `tools/test_rpc_verify.py` drive the new half directly: a
stated reason with no node fails **by name**, the same region announced and

R1694.publishable_decision_summary:
A locked seat nobody can hear is not a locked seat.

The reference analysis tool's **screen C** is the dashboard, and its subject is
what the release does **not** have yet: four widgets the first release places and
**nine it reserves**, each shown rather than hidden, each naming the requirement
it is booked under — *"a second-release item is not a missing thing, it is a
locked seat"*. Two rail destinations are locked the same way.

The framework has computed that reason since R1668. `Unavailable` carries a kind,
a detail, and a recourse derived from the kind; the disabled cascade resolves it
down the subtree; `scene/disabled` publishes it. Measured the day this was
written, all **eleven** locked regions published a complete reason — and **not
one of them was in the accessibility tree at all**. The reason was computed,
published, painted as faded ink, and inaudible.

That is the whole screen underneath it: **128** addressable regions painted,
**five** announced (a group for the window and one per card, each holding
nothing), **123** undecided. `scene/conform` judged **zero** nodes — not "zero
faults": zero *judged*, because no announced role on this screen carried a
structural requirement at all. The rail, both bars, two tables, the decode tree,
seventy-two bytes and the whole thirteen-entry palette reached a reader as four
names and a summary sentence.

## Against the reference toolkit at 6.11.1 — built and RUN, not read

The same shape assembled there and its accessibility tree read back: a rail of
seven seats with two locked, a thirteen-entry palette in three sections with nine
locked, a tab bar with a locked tab, a locked plain widget as a control.

* the locked **palette entries** answer `focusable, selectable` and carry **no
  unavailable state at all**. Both spellings were built — the convenience item
  and a model whose `flags()` drops the enabled bit — and both lose it.
* the locked **tab** answers `focusable, selectable` too, and is not marked
  current. So a reader there is invited to activate exactly the seats the screen
  has closed.
* the locked **plain widget** does carry the bit, which is how the probe is known
  to be sound: the loss belongs to **collections**, which is what a palette and a
  navigation rail are.
* the palette's three **section headings** come back as list items
  indistinguishable in role from the entries — sixteen flat items, no grouping,
  and no way to derive "thirteen entries, nine reserved" from what is announced.
* the one slot that could carry a reason is a free-form description that nothing
  classifies and nothing links to the lock. On a toolbar action it is worse than
  empty: measured directly, every **unlocked** seat comes back with its
  description equal to its name, because the slot defaults to the action's own
  label.

its place in the set of thirteen, and carries the kind, the detail and the
recourse the bit cannot hold. The reason is **not restated** by the screen: it is
declared once on the row's layout style, and the accessibility assembler relays

named.** R1669 counted the regions that state a reason; nothing asked whether the
reason reached the audience it was built for. It did not. Measured over the
**215** surfaces that answer: **13 stated reasons, 11 of them unheard, every one

★★★★★ **And the round found a rule that had been living in prose.** Both this
screen and the sibling capture screen hand-rolled a header-row grid, and the two
**disagreed about where the header row sits**. WAI-ARIA counts it in
`aria-rowcount`, so it has to be counted in `aria-rowindex` too — and the shared

leaving its header unplaced and its last row unreachable. The rule now lives once,
in the builder, together with the row's WAI-ARIA name-from-contents, and **both
screens were converted onto the builder** rather than corrected in place.

* **`pinion_a11y::grid::grid_table_nodes` gives every row and cell its
coordinates.** The header row is `aria-rowindex` **1** — WAI-ARIA's own
reading, and the one `aria-rowcount` already took by counting the header — so

whole numbering including "the last data row is the row count, so no row is
unreachable", the other that a cell carries its own coordinates rather than
only its row's.

name-from-contents, and a row is usually painted as an empty band with its
cells as siblings, so nothing under the row's own tag can be read. One screen
computed it and the other did not; it is computed once now.

(`_unheard_reasons`). Every region the disabled cascade states a reason for
must have an accessibility node carrying that reason. Two failure shapes,
because the repairs differ: *no node at all* (announce it) and *announced,
reason dropped* (look at the assembler). Budget **zero**, no exception list.

arms makes one repair look like two.

not visit.** The backlog debt is explicit that the judgment is one round per
screen — "does this region owe a reader something" is a decision about a
screen, not a rule — and this round closed the second of the two screens the
reproduction directive names. The worst remaining surfaces are the chart
family, and the count for them is a measurement the next a11y round takes
before it chooses a budget, exactly as this one did.

every row and cell its index, so a grid built by the builder can be checked
against what it announces. What is still unchecked is the WINDOWED case, where
a container legitimately declares an extent larger than the tree it holds: the
repair shape the debt names is to make *windowing itself a declaration*, so
only a container that says it is windowed may over-declare, and every member it
does announce must carry its index within the declared extent. This round did
not force that — nothing on either screen is windowed — and building a rule

announces. Stated rather than silently absent.

host, because a paint-source snapshot blocks a full second waiting for a frame
from an idle window, and the fetch it waits on resolves after about eight. It
passes here with the budget widened (79.7s) and passes in CI unwidened. The

change whose blast radius is every demo, so it is its own round.

R1695.decision_summary:
Round 1695 — arriving is not highlighting: a destination is a place you arrive
at, and a navigation rail that moves a string is not a rail.

DECISION. The framework gains a paged container — `pinion_core::widgets::
destination` (a keyed roster, a standing per destination, and a navigation that
returns why it refused) and `pinion_widget_paint::pages` (the region, which
builds exactly the destination the journey is at). The analysis tool's dashboard
adopts it, and its rail stops lying.

WHY NOW, AND WHY IT IS A DEFECT RATHER THAN A GAP. Driven through the §5.35
router against the running application before anything was changed: the
dashboard's rail offers seven destinations, and pressing four of them — Stream,
Decode, Catalog, Settings — moved `nav`, the string the rail highlights ITSELF
from and which nothing else read, while the painted scene stayed at 193 tagged
regions before and 193 after, nothing added and nothing removed. The screen said
Stream and showed the dashboard. The sibling screen answered every seat with "X
is not this screen", including the seat that screen already was and the two
declared unavailable with a stated reason. And the two screens' rosters share two
keys out of seven: one tool, two lists of what the tool contains.

WHY EVERY GATE WAS GREEN. The check this tree had is `assert_router_press_moves`,
which asserts a press MOVED THE STATE — which is exactly what a screen that
highlights a seat and shows nothing new does. Moved is not arrived, and the
difference is a rectangle. So the rail's own consequence had to become a fact
about the window rather than about a variable, and that is what the region's tag
is for.

THE FLOOR, BUILT AND RUN AT 6.11.1 rather than read about. Its paged container
addresses a page by ORDINAL; `setCurrentIndex` returns void, so an out-of-range
ordinal is a silent no-op; a DISABLED PAGE IS ARRIVED AT ANYWAY; a destination
that has no page yet cannot be expressed at all; a non-current page stays live
and, sent a press, a key and a wheel directly, counted all three; and the
container's accessible value is EMPTY, so no client can ask which page is
showing, while a locked rail seat answers focusable, selectable with no
unavailable state at all. Seven rows, seven answers here: a key, a typed refusal
carrying the reason, a roster entry for a destination with no page, a page that
is never constructed when it is not current (so input scoping is structural
rather than a guard the author repeats — which is what the behaviour reference
itself does, opening its wheel handler by testing the active section), and a
named `region` landmark that publishes which destination arrived.

THE REASON IS THE FRAMEWORK'S EXISTING VALUE, WITH ONE ARM ADDED. A closed
destination carries `Unavailable` rather than a second vocabulary, so the seat's
paint, its refusal, `scene/disabled` and the accessibility tree are one fact.
`UnavailableKind::Elsewhere` is the new arm and it earns its place by that
module's own rule — the reader's next action is its own, so it derives its own
`Recourse::OpenElsewhere`. A product with more than one surface has to be able to
say BUILT, SHIPPING AND NOT HERE: `reserved` would send a reader to wait for
something that already exists and `unsupported` would tell them to give up on a
feature one window away.

A SECOND PAGE, BECAUSE A PAGED REGION WITH ONE PAGE PROVES NOTHING ABOUT PAGING.
The behaviour reference's own Settings section is reproduced: four switch rows in
two groups with its alternating opening values, two affordances booked for a
later release, and a two-way appearance segment. Both new control shapes are
catalogue widgets rather than hand-drawn.

in both directions. That is half of the "the voice gate judges only the opening
screen" debt, and the half that had been called unclosable because nothing
enumerated the screens an application has — the rail's roster is that
enumeration.

quiet, 0 undecided, 0 voice defects, 4 structurally judged, 0 empty, 0 stray. The
dashboard is unchanged at 193 / 190 / 3 / 159.
carry_forward_bullets: NEW DEBT, from this round's own findings.
1. A DECLARED TEXT ALIGNMENT DOES NOTHING ON AN ABSOLUTELY-PLACED RUN. Measured
by ink span, three times on one page: with `TextStyle::with_align(Center)` the
glyphs sat at the node's left edge in every case. The property is published,
accepted, round-tripped on `scene/snapshot` and mapped in the text cache, and
a pixel rig elsewhere in the tree proves it works on some other node shape —
so what is unknown is WHICH shape, not whether the property exists. Not chased
here because the catalogue's own button centres with flex and that is the
idiom, but a property a consumer can set and cannot rely on is the class this
tree has paid for repeatedly.
2. THE OTHER HALF OF THE ROSTER DIVERGENCE IS UNCLOSED, and it is the one this
round could not close from one screen. The two analyzer screens declare
rosters sharing two keys out of seven, and neither matches the behaviour
reference's eight sections. A single roster is only possible in a single
application, and the tool is three binaries here. This round made each
screen's own roster honest and checkable; making them ONE is a campaign, and
the shape is stated rather than started: the three screens become library
crates hosting their views, one binary owns the roster, and each screen's
painted gates move to a region-local frame.
3. THE SIBLING SCREEN'S RAIL IS STILL PROSE. `hello-node-lab` answers every seat
with "X is not this screen", including the seat it is and including two seats
whose declaration states a different reason. The substrate to fix it exists
now and the fix is small; it is not in this round because the screen was not
this round's consumer and converting it moves its painted gates.
CARRIED, EXTERNAL, UNCHANGED.
* The full demo sweep cannot return a verdict on this host — 379 of 589 fail as
harness RPC timeouts, because a paint-source read blocks for exactly one second
here against a five-second per-request bound. Blast radius was counted instead:
the crate changes are additive arms and a new module, the only screens that
declare a destination roster are this one, and the analyzer demos were run
directly.

R1696.decision_summary:
Round 1696 — the screen has a keyboard: a stop-the-line repayment, and the
gate that should have caught it locally did not exist.

WHAT WAS RED. R1694's push failed CI on the demo sweep — two demos, one cause:
`hello-analyzer-shell` presents an interactive ARIA role and `focus/next` from
cold answered nothing at all. It announces a navigation landmark of links, two
toolbars, a list of items, four tabs, a textbox and thirty-nine buttons, and a
keyboard reached none of them. Announced as operable, unreachable.

WHY THAT ROUND CAUSED IT AND COULD NOT SEE IT. R1694 gave the screen its
accessibility tree — 128 announced regions became 190 — and an interactive role
is what puts a binding into `r1570.1`'s population. The population is derived
from what a screen DECLARES, so the screen joined the gate the moment it started
declaring, and both gates that walk it are python demos that run only in CI. The
sibling screen learned the identical lesson at R1693 from the identical pair.

THE REPAIR IS THE WAI-ARIA COMPOSITE PATTERN, which is what the sibling screen
already holds: one stop per composite — the application bar, the rail, the
layout bar, the board, the palette — rather than one per control, plus the
Settings page's switches and its appearance segment, which are not inside a
composite and declare their own stop through the catalogue widgets.

THE RING IS A DECLARATION, NOT FIVE DECISIONS. `spec::FOCUS_RING` is the table
and the paint reads it, so a stop added to the specification appears on screen
and one removed disappears. Each row also says WHAT the stop holds, which is the
part a tag cannot carry: an agent reading `focus_ring` off the wire learns that
landing on the rail puts it among the tool's destinations rather than on one.

THE ORDER IS THE PAINT ORDER, AND THAT IS RATIFIED. §5.39's alternatives reject
a manual tab index — imitating HTML's `tabindex` violates the declarative spirit
of a view function, and automatic traversal is canonical — so the ring starts at
the page, because the page must be painted UNDER the chrome. Measured against
the floor by building a probe and running it, that is a dimension where this
project is below: `setTabOrder` there reorders the chain while the geometry
stays put. It is not worked around here. Changing it is a spec round, and the
argument that round has to weigh is recorded rather than acted on: "tree order
is canonical" is a claim about an order the author CHOSE, and z-order takes that
choice away from a screen whose chrome is painted over its page.

THE LIFT. R1693 wrote a four-line free function to turn a painted region into a
Tab stop; this round needed the same thing on the second screen, which is the
trigger `Scene::silenced` was lifted on in that same round. It is
`Scene::with_focusable` now, and the free function is gone.

on the same evidence and at the same trigger: a verbatim second copy of a

question rather than implying a missing builder. `hello-packet-view` adopts it
and deletes its local helper.

what it holds. `keyboard_stop` is the only place the paint consults it, applied
to the page region, the application bar, the rail, the layout bar and the

enumerates IS the declared one *in order* (the order is not derived from the
table, so this half is not self-comparison); no stop exists that the

the paint reads the table and R1669's rule says a check against its own source

keyboard_stop` on `hello-packet-view`, derived from its own pane table plus its
saved filters. R1693 added that screen's ring and left it verified only by the
tree-wide python demos; a counterfactual here proved the gap by reverting the
framework builder and watching every test in that example stay green while the

order" and explicitly rejected a manual tab index, and this round obeyed that
rather than working around it. The case the rejection did not address is now

all — giving chrome a layer of its own so child order stops carrying z-order.

R1697.decision_summary:
A torn-off panel can be moved, and the dashboard declares its operations.

A person opened the analysis tool, tore a card off the board into a floating
panel, tried to drag it, and asked whether it being nailed in place was
intended. It was not. The press arm that would have started the gesture read
`Hit::Float(_) | Hit::Nothing => {}` — a detached panel folded in with hitting
nothing at all — and nothing anywhere opened a drag for one.

Every gate on that screen was green, and each was right about its own question:
the panel is painted, hit-testable, inside its own rectangle, named, and
announced to a screen reader with its reason for being inert when it is. None
of them asks whether GRABBING IT MOVES IT, and none of them could, because the
screen had no table saying it should.

The sibling screen has had such a table since R1677 and it has caught this exact
class three times there. So the decision is not "add a drag handler": it is that
the dashboard declares what it can be asked to DO, that the shape of that
declaration moves into the framework so a third screen cannot invent a third
copy of it, and that a gate drives every row through both of its cause columns
and asserts the introspection slot each row names actually moves.

The behaviour reproduced is the reference's own, read out of its source rather
than inferred from a picture: a panel opens 520x380 with a stacking number from
a monotonic counter; grabbing it RAISES IT FIRST and then moves it by the
pointer's delta; its corner sizes it and clamps at 320x220. The three are one
gesture — the drag calls the raise — so building one alone leaves the other two
in the wrong place.

Two structures follow from the pixel plane being a different plane from the
board's cells. A card is dragged between cells and PREVIEWS where it would land,
because the board reflows and a preview that lied would be worse than none; a
panel is dragged in pixels and moves as the pointer moves, because it lands
where it is put. So the gesture in flight is its own type rather than an arm
added to the card drag, whose fields are a cell coordinate and a snap target and
cannot carry a pixel origin. And stacking becomes an explicit `z` from a
monotonic counter rather than the roster's order read backwards: the roster's
order is the same answer only while nothing reorders the panels, and a raise is
exactly a reorder.
changes_bullets: `pinion_core::operation` — the operations-table shape, lifted out of the node
laboratory's `spec.rs` at its second consumer: `Operation` (name / verb /
gesture / witness / needs) plus the checks a reader of the table alone can
run. `faults` reports a precondition naming nothing, a name declared twice, a
row with no witness, a row naming itself, and an unreachable row that still
carries a precondition; `in_order` derives the order the preconditions impose
and reports a cycle rather than ordering it — which stops a driver encoding a
second and silently different order. `absent` is the ratchet's population.
10 unit tests.
Screen A adopts it by re-export (`pub use ... as OperationSpec`) with no edit
to any of its thirty rows.
The dashboard's `spec::OPERATIONS` — twelve rows scoped to direct
manipulation of the board and its panels, each measured against the screen
rather than wished for. The rail, the settings switches and the transport are
deliberately outside it, because they are driven by WRITING a slot and a
`verb` column meaning "invoke" for some rows and "intervene" for others would
be a column with two meanings.
`Float` gains `w`, `h` and `z`; `float_rect` reads them, and `float_grip_rect`
is the corner both the paint and the hit test take from one function.
`FloatGrab` — a panel being moved or sized, in flight. Its own type rather
than an arm on the card drag: a card is dragged between cells and PREVIEWS,
a panel is dragged in pixels and moves, and the card drag's fields are a cell
coordinate and a snap target.
`ShellState::raise_float` / `floats_front_to_back` / `set_float` / `float` —
the stacking order becomes state, and the paint walks the reverse of what the
hit test walks, so "drawn on top" and "reached first" are one decision.
`ShellOracle::open_float_grab` raises then grabs (the reference's order, and
load-bearing: a panel grabbed from under another must come out from under
before the pointer starts moving it); `carry_float_grab` applies a signed
delta from the grab's origin rather than accumulating, and clamps a resize at
`Hit::FloatResize` — the corner is its own hit target, tested before the body
it sits inside, and painted last for the same reason.
The card header's maximise control TOGGLES, and paints a restore mark when it
will. The two wire verbs stay separate: `maximize` still refuses on an
already-maximised card and `restore` is its own action.
`floats` and `float_grab` reads: each panel's x/y/w/h/z front to back, and
what the pointer is doing to one right now. `spec.operations` publishes the
table so an agent reads the operations rather than discovering them by trying.
`r1697_every_declared_way_of_causing_an_operation_causes_it` drives all
nineteen declared ways and asserts each moves the slot its row names, read
through the introspection surface. Two more gates came from counterfactuals
that PASSED: a point both panels cover reaches the raised one after a raise,
and a press that moved nothing does not announce a move.
`tools/demos/r1697_a_torn_off_panel_can_be_moved.py` — the integration test,
driven through a real window.
verification_bullets: `cargo test -p pinion-core -p hello-analyzer-shell -p hello-node-lab` green:
core 3522, the dashboard 57, the node laboratory 83. `cargo clippy` on the
same three with `--all-targets --features pinion-runtime/vello` green.
The operations gate drives NINETEEN declared ways of causing an operation —
twelve rows, seven of which carry both a wire verb and a pointer gesture —
and asserts each one moves the introspection slot its row names. It went red
on its first run, on a row nobody had written this round: "restore a
maximised card" by gesture. That is how the second defect was found.
Five demos green against release binaries: the new integration test, plus
`r1649`, `r1694`, `r1695` on the same screen and `r1690` on the sibling
whose specification module this round edited.
The new demo drives the canon's behaviour end to end through a real window:
the table is on the wire and every row's witness is a slot the screen
answers; a torn-off panel opens at 520x380; a drag moves it by EXACTLY the
pointer's delta and the painted rectangle follows; a click moves nothing; the
corner grows it by the delta and clamps at 320x220; two panels stack, and
pressing the covered one brings it forward on the wire; re-dock and close
empty the roster and leave no geometry behind; the maximise control toggles
while the wire verb still refuses. 39 assertions and 46 narrated checks.
10 of 10 counterfactuals CAUGHT. The first run was 3 CAUGHT / 2 PASSED / 3
BROKEN and both halves were findings: the three BROKEN did not compile, so
they tested nothing, because removing a helper's only call site makes it dead
code under `-D warnings` — each was recast as a WRONG answer rather than an
absent one. The two that PASSED became the two gates named above.
Looked at, in a real window on a private display: eight photographs of the
panel being detached, moved, sized larger, sized past its floor, stacked with
a second, raised, and of the maximise control wearing its restore face. The
size grip is visible in the corner at both sizes.
The floor was BUILT AND RUN at 6.11.1 for the composite-cursor questions this
round's substrate work raises, and its results are recorded there rather than
here; the panel behaviour was taken from the behaviour reference's own source
by extracting its inline script, not from the mockup.

R1697.publishable_decision_summary:
A torn-off panel can be moved, and the dashboard declares its operations.

A person opened the analysis tool, tore a card off the board into a floating
panel, tried to drag it, and asked whether it being nailed in place was
intended. It was not. The press arm that would have started the gesture read
`Hit::Float(_) | Hit::Nothing => {}` — a detached panel folded in with hitting
nothing at all — and nothing anywhere opened a drag for one.

Every gate on that screen was green, and each was right about its own question:
the panel is painted, hit-testable, inside its own rectangle, named, and
announced to a screen reader with its reason for being inert when it is. None
of them asks whether GRABBING IT MOVES IT, and none of them could, because the
screen had no table saying it should.

The sibling screen has had such a table since R1677 and it has caught this exact
class three times there. So the decision is not "add a drag handler": it is that
the dashboard declares what it can be asked to DO, that the shape of that
declaration moves into the framework so a third screen cannot invent a third
copy of it, and that a gate drives every row through both of its cause columns
and asserts the introspection slot each row names actually moves.

The behaviour reproduced is the reference's own, read out of its source rather
than inferred from a picture: a panel opens 520x380 with a stacking number from
a monotonic counter; grabbing it RAISES IT FIRST and then moves it by the
pointer's delta; its corner sizes it and clamps at 320x220. The three are one
gesture — the drag calls the raise — so building one alone leaves the other two
in the wrong place.

Two structures follow from the pixel plane being a different plane from the
board's cells. A card is dragged between cells and PREVIEWS where it would land,
because the board reflows and a preview that lied would be worse than none; a
panel is dragged in pixels and moves as the pointer moves, because it lands
where it is put. So the gesture in flight is its own type rather than an arm
added to the card drag, whose fields are a cell coordinate and a snap target and
cannot carry a pixel origin. And stacking becomes an explicit `z` from a
monotonic counter rather than the roster's order read backwards: the roster's
order is the same answer only while nothing reorders the panels, and a raise is
exactly a reorder.

row with no witness, a row naming itself, and an unreachable row that still
carries a precondition; `in_order` derives the order the preconditions impose
and reports a cycle rather than ordering it — which stops a driver encoding a
second and silently different order. `absent` is the ratchet's population.
10 unit tests.
Screen A adopts it by re-export (`pub use ... as OperationSpec`) with no edit
to any of its thirty rows.

manipulation of the board and its panels, each measured against the screen
rather than wished for. The rail, the settings switches and the transport are
deliberately outside it, because they are driven by WRITING a slot and a

R1698.decision_summary:
A composite has a cursor inside it — and the dashboard's keyboard reaches it
from a keyboard at all.

WAI-ARIA's composite widget pattern is two halves. R1693 and R1696 gave the two
analysis screens the first: one Tab stop per composite, so a keyboard reaches a
toolbar in one press rather than in as many presses as it has controls. Nobody
built the second — INSIDE the composite an arrow moves a cursor between the
members, and the composite publishes where that cursor rests. Measured by
driving both running applications the day this round opened: eleven Tab stops,
four arrow keys each, FORTY-FOUR PRESSES THAT MOVED NOTHING, and an active
descendant that was `None` at every one.

Measuring it found something worse underneath. The dashboard's keymap of twelve
chords was reachable only through the wire: `invoke("key", "ArrowRight")` moved
the board's selection and a REAL key press moved nothing, because the screen
implemented no `apply_key` hook at all. Across 225 examples, 172 bindings
implement that hook and 135 of them read its `focused` argument; this screen
implemented it zero times. Every test that drove its keyboard passed for exactly
the reason R1693's did on the sibling screen — the test and the defect were the
same mistake, because every test used the channel that worked.

And the sibling, whose keys did arrive, dropped `focused`: at all six of its
stops — the three filter chips, the decode tree and the byte grid included —
`ArrowDown` moved the MESSAGE LIST. So an arrow meant one thing no matter where
anybody was standing, on both screens, for opposite reasons.

The decision is that the keyboard behaviour of a composite becomes a
DECLARATION rather than whatever its key handler happens to do. `RovingSpec`
names three things a real application answers differently per composite — which
arrows move the cursor, what happens at the ends, and whether arriving also
chooses — and a fourth is settled once for everybody: the cursor rests on a
member that refuses, because a screen whose subject is that its locked seats are
heard cannot use a cursor that hides them.

The roster a composite's arrows walk is published as its own fact, NOT as its
accessibility children. Those are not the same list and the measurement is what
settles it: this project's palette has three section groups and two status
readouts as children while its cursor walks thirteen catalogue entries, and at
the floor a tab bar of three tabs reports five accessible children. A client
reading `children` to learn what the arrows reach is told things that are not
members.

The floor was built and run rather than read about, and it is below this on
every axis the declaration names: a toolbar there is not a keyboard destination
at all (its buttons and the bar take no focus, so no arrow reaches them), making
its buttons focusable turns one stop into five while the arrows walk straight
out of the bar, its tab list implements neither `Home` nor `End`, its selection
always follows its cursor with no property to say otherwise, and it skips
disabled members so a locked one is undiscoverable from the keyboard.
changes_bullets: `pinion_core::widgets::roving` — the cursor and the policy, with no paint and
no tag: `Axis` (which arrows, and the `aria-orientation` it implies, with
`Both` lowering to no attribute because that is what ARIA's absence means),
`Ends`, `Activation`, `Member`, `Step` (including `Home` / `End`), `Landing`,
and `Roving`. Its key mapping is DERIVED from `Axis::keys`, so a composite
cannot publish one set of keys and answer another. 14 unit tests.
`Roving::seat` keeps the cursor on the MEMBER rather than the index, so a
roster that grows at the front does not move the cursor without a key press;
a member that is gone takes the nearest survivor. `point_at` is what a
pointer press calls, so the mouse and the keyboard never disagree.
`pinion_a11y::Orientation` + `AccessNode::orientation` — WAI-ARIA
`aria-orientation`, lowered to AccessKit and published on `scene/access`.
`AccessNode::with_axis` / `with_navigation` set it FROM the roving
declaration, so the attribute and the arrows are one call.
`AccessNode::navigation` — the roster the arrows reach, in cursor order, with
each member's enabled bit, beside `children` rather than instead of it.
`scene/access` publishes it with the axis, the ends, the activation, the keys
and the cursor, so an agent reads the composite instead of pressing every key
to find out.
The dashboard implements `apply_key` — the hook it never had — and threads
`focused` through it, so the composite that owns the focus is asked before the
screen. Its ring rows declare a cursor each: the application bar, the rail and
the layout bar wrap; the palette stops at its ends; the board declares none
because its cursor is spatial, and publishes the card it is on instead.
The board's arrows now require the board to have focus (or nothing to) — an
arrow a composite declines used to move a card on a board the reader had left.
The capture viewer reads `focused` in `apply_key` and projects the cursor each
pane ALREADY has into a `Roving` rather than growing a second one: the message
list's cursor is `row`, the decode tree's is `field`. Both declare `Follows`,
which is where that arm's real consumer lives.
The byte grid gains `byte` — its own cursor. Found by trying to derive it from
the selected field's extent, which cannot move within a field: every arrow
snapped back. Selection and cursor are two facts in every grid that has both,
and a press writes the cursor too.
Four in-process gates on the dashboard and three on the capture viewer, plus
`tools/demos/r1698_a_composite_has_a_cursor_inside_it.py` driving both screens
through real windows.
verification_bullets: Measured BEFORE anything changed, by driving both running applications: five
Tab stops on the dashboard and six on the capture viewer, four arrow keys at
each, and an active descendant that was `None` at every one — forty-four
presses that moved nothing. On the dashboard, a real `scene/key` press moved
nothing at all while the wire's `invoke("key", …)` moved the board; on the
capture viewer, `ArrowDown` moved the message list from all six stops
including the decode tree and the byte grid.
Measured AFTER, the same way: every declared composite's cursor moves on its
axis, holds on the other, reaches its ends with `Home` / `End`, and is
published as `aria-activedescendant` beside `aria-orientation` and the roster.
On the capture viewer the three panes move their own cursors and the three
filter chips move nothing.
The floor was BUILT AND RUN at 6.11.1 offscreen rather than read about. A
toolbar there is not a keyboard destination at all — its buttons and the bar
itself take no focus, so the window's Tab chain contains its scroll buttons
and none of its actions, and arrow keys reach nothing. Making the buttons
focusable turns one stop into FIVE (the chain went from 5 entries to 11) and
the arrows then walk straight OUT of the bar into the next widget, so the
choice on offer is no keyboard access or N stops with no containment. Its tab
list does have a cursor: it skips a disabled tab, does not wrap, changes the
current tab on every press with no property to say otherwise, and implements
neither `Home` nor `End` — both keys left the current tab where it was. And
its accessible child count for three tabs is FIVE.
`cargo test` green: core 3536, the dashboard 61, the capture viewer 38, a11y
317, rpc 1240. `cargo clippy --all-targets --features pinion-runtime/vello`
green on all five.
The integration test drives both screens through real windows: 46 narrated
checks plus assertions, including the negative controls — an off-axis arrow
moves neither the cursor nor the board, a plain button publishes no roster and
claims no arrow, and the wire's own channel still reaches the list with
nothing focused.
★★★★★ Counterfactuals: the FIRST run was 6 of 10 caught, and all four that
PASSED were this round's own headline defects — deleting the dashboard's
`apply_key` hook entirely (the exact state it was in before the round),
dropping `focused` from it, dropping `focused` from the capture viewer's, and
replacing the composite focus target with an atomic one. Every in-process gate
stayed green through all four, and the reason is one sentence: the gates drove
`key_at`, which is the layer BELOW the door a person's key comes in by. So the
gates were rewritten to press through `WidgetCore::apply_key` with a real
scene, and a fifth was added that reads `access_focus_target` — the hook the
framework lowers to `aria-activedescendant` and frames the focus ring from.
This is the fourth recorded occurrence of a gate testing the layer beneath the
defect, and the first where the counterfactual named all four at once.
Each break is written as a WRONG answer rather than an absent one, because a
break that does not compile tests nothing.
The derived-population gates (`r1518`, `r1570.1`) were run directly rather
than left to CI, which is the standing rule for a round that changes what the
focus surface publishes.
carry_forward_bullets: **The two screens still disagree about how a stop is declared.** The dashboard
reads a `spec::FOCUS_RING` table that now carries each stop's cursor policy;
the capture viewer marks four painters `.with_focusable(true)` by hand and
derives its cursors from the panes it happens to have. Both work and both are
tested, but a third screen would have two shapes to copy — the class
`debt-a-shape-two-screens-hand-roll-is-a-substrate-hole-nobody-censuses`
names. NOT lifted here because the right shape is not yet obvious: the
dashboard's ring is a static table and the capture viewer's cursors are
projections of state it already holds, and a lift that flattened the second
into the first would make it grow a second copy of every cursor.
**Roving inside a nested composite is not built.** The application bar reaches
its two view tabs as ONE member, which is WAI-ARIA's nesting and correct as
far as it goes; what is missing is that landing on that member and pressing an
arrow should move between the two tabs rather than past them. Both screens are
equally without it, so it is one shared axis rather than a divergence — the
same shape this round's own subject had.
**`Activation::Follows` has one consumer and it is on one screen.** The
capture viewer's three panes take it and every dashboard stop declares
`Explicit`, with a unit test asserting that so the bit cannot quietly become
one nobody reads. If a dashboard stop is ever declared `Follows`, that test
fails and the arm has to be written.
**A painted character the face lacks is still a box** — registered at R1697,
untouched here, and the repair is a font fallback stack rather than a
character swap.

R1699 — a keyboard can do what a pointer can: a cursor that can ACT, and a composite that can be ENTERED.

WAI-ARIA's composite widget pattern has three parts and this project had built
two of them. R1696 gave the two analysis screens one Tab stop per composite.
R1698 gave each composite a cursor its arrows move. Driving the result is what
found the third missing: a cursor a reader can walk and never act on.

MEASURED BEFORE ANYTHING WAS CHANGED, by driving both running applications.
Eleven Tab stops across the two screens, Enter and Space at every one of them,
twenty-two presses that changed nothing painted. Four of those stops declare
Activation::Explicit, whose documented meaning is "arriving only moves the
cursor; Enter or Space chooses" -- and nothing anywhere implemented the second
half. The navigation rail's cursor could walk to a destination and pressing
Enter would not go there, while a mouse click would. Three more stops announce
role=button and a keyboard could not press them at all, which is below the
floor rather than above it: a push button at 6.11.1 activates on both keys,
always.

And the one nested composite each screen has was reachable with no way in. The
dashboard's application bar passes over its tab list in a single step, which is
WAI-ARIA's nesting and correct, and no key descended into it -- so from a
keyboard the two views could not be switched. The capture viewer announces its
message list as a `grid` whose sixteen rows each report seven cells, and
ArrowRight standing on a row moved nothing: the columns existed for a reader
and were unreachable by one.

DECISION 1 -- the nesting is modelled RECURSIVELY, in the substrate.

A `Member` may CONTAIN a `Roving`. The alternative considered and rejected was
a boolean "this member is a composite" plus a lookup the screen performs in its
own cursor map: that keeps the type flat and pushes the walk to every consumer,
and the walk is the whole difficulty. With containment, `active_descendant()`
answers the innermost tag in one recursion -- which is exactly what ARIA's
attribute addresses, any descendant of the element owning the Tab stop, not
only a child -- and the depth is unbounded rather than fixed at one, tested to
three levels. `tag_path()` is the same walk for a screen that has to act on
what a nested cursor rests on.

`entered` is state of the ENCLOSING composite rather than of the member,
because exactly one member can be entered at a time and hanging the flag off
the member would let two of them claim it.

DECISION 2 -- both new key families are DERIVED, not declared.

`Axis::entry_keys` is the perpendicular ADVANCING arrow plus Enter, and
`Axis::Both` therefore offers only Enter: an axis that navigates by all four
arrows has no free one left, and a key that both moved the cursor and descended
would answer two questions at once. `Activation::choose_keys` is Enter+Space
for Explicit and EMPTY for Follows, because arriving already chose and a second
way to do what the arrow just did is not a feature. A unit test asserts, for
every axis arm, that the entry keys are disjoint from the navigating keys --
that property is what makes derivation sound rather than convenient.

DECISION 3 -- `Landing` gains four arms because each has a different repair.

Chosen and Refused are distinct so a screen cannot silently do nothing at a
member that refuses; that silence is the defect R1694 named from the other
side, on the screen whose whole subject is that its locked seats are heard. A
refusal still CONSUMES the key, because a refusal is an answer and letting it
fall through would act somewhere else. Entered and Exited are distinct from
Moved because the cursor did not move along this composite's axis at all.

DECISION 4 -- a keyboard activation is SEMANTIC, so it needs a second address
space, so it needs a gate before it needs a function.

Synthesising a pointer press at the centre of the member's rectangle was
rejected twice over: a member scrolled out of a pane has a rectangle and is
clipped, and a member that paints nothing (the tab list, anchored by the tabs
it composes) has no rectangle at all. `Hit::of_tag` is the inverse of the
existing tag naming, and two address spaces drift -- so the gate was written
first. For every member of every composite, nested rosters included, the
round-trip must hold AND the answer must equal what a press at the centre of
that tag's PAINTED rectangle produces. Two derivations of one fact with the
paint as arbiter, which is what keeps it a check rather than a table compared
with itself.

DECISION 5 -- the account chip stops announcing an action it does not have.

The gate above found it before it ran: the rail's account seat was announced
role=button and seated in the rail's cursor, and no press path reached it from
either channel. The reference mockup's own source settles the direction -- the
avatar is a plain styled element with no handler, no link and no menu -- so it
becomes a `group` that says whose session this is and leaves the cursor.
Removing two false claims rather than inventing a product decision.

WHAT WAS NOT DONE, AND WHY. A pointer still cannot place the CELL cursor on a
particular column, which the floor's item view does. The screen has no
behaviour canon for cell selection -- screen B comes from a static mockup and
the behaviour prototype is a different screen -- and giving a click a column
would make a click imply a descent, which is a decision the canon has to make
rather than this round. Registered with the measurement and with the shape the
repair has to take.

plus the painted-rectangle arbiter); choosing any member does something a
reader can tell (repaint OR sentence, with both halves asserted non-empty);

* 11 Tab stops, `Enter` and `Space` at each, 22 presses, zero painted change;
* 4 composites declaring Explicit; 12 Enter/Space presses across their cursor
positions moved no destination and changed no toast;
* nested composites: 1 on the dashboard (a tablist of 2), 16 on the capture
viewer (rows of 7 cells); all four candidate entry keys moved the active
descendant nowhere at every one of them.

DERIVED-POPULATION GATES RUN DIRECTLY rather than left to CI, because both
screens change their accessibility trees and a screen that changes its tree

`r1518_at_focus_one_answer` 529 assertions over 96 focus stops in 96 bindings,
and `r1570_1_interactive_role_is_a_focus_stop` 151 assertions. Both PASS.
DEMOS: eight analyzer demos green (r1649, r1691, r1692, r1693, r1694, r1695,
r1697, r1698) plus the new integration test, 41 assertion sites and 13 narrated
checks over two real windows.
COUNTERFACTUALS: 14 of 14 CAUGHT on the second run. The first was 11 CAUGHT, 1
PASSED, 2 BROKEN.

report: four call sites rendered a refusal to a person with `Debug`, so the
palette announced a Rust struct literal with escaped quotes to somebody who had
asked to place a widget. The photographs confirm the ring frames the TAB inside
the list, the CELL inside the row, and the booked palette entry whose refusal

MNEMOSYNE: validate-workspace clean before and after — T1 orphan total 0, new
carry_forward_bullets: REGISTERED AS A DEBT FILE, not left as prose (R1696's lesson: a statement with
no file is a statement nobody reads again).

* debt-a-screens-tab-order-is-its-z-order — needs a SPEC ROUND; not worked

* debt-a-painted-character-the-face-lacks-becomes-a-box — untouched.
* debt-two-screens-declare-a-keyboard-stop-differently — untouched, and this
round did not make it worse: both screens took the nesting through the same

WHAT THIS ROUND DECLINED TO INVENT. The account chip could have been made a
control (an account menu is universal in this class of tool) and the canon has

menu is already the announcement WAI-ARIA specifies, so the GATE was fixed

canon which one is wrong.

bar reported under its current tab's name, plus an unnamed child;

cell cursor, and its accessibility interface names the focused cell (role 29)
— parity we had to reach rather than exceed. What it still cannot express is
a row as a unit with an inside, and measured, Tab INSIDE the view moves
between cells rather than leaving the widget.

* 11 Tab stops, `Enter` and `Space` at each, 22 presses, zero painted change;
* 4 composites declaring Explicit; 12 Enter/Space presses across their cursor
positions moved no destination and changed no toast;

viewer (rows of 7 cells); all four candidate entry keys moved the active
descendant nowhere at every one of them.

hello-packet-view 42, hello-node-lab 83. `cargo fmt --all` and clippy

DERIVED-POPULATION GATES RUN DIRECTLY rather than left to CI, because both
screens change their accessibility trees and a screen that changes its tree
joins those gates the moment it declares:
`r1518_at_focus_one_answer` 529 assertions over 96 focus stops in 96 bindings,
and `r1570_1_interactive_role_is_a_focus_stop` 151 assertions. Both PASS.

r1697, r1698) plus the new integration test, 41 assertion sites and 13 narrated
checks over two real windows.
COUNTERFACTUALS: 14 of 14 CAUGHT on the second run. The first was 11 CAUGHT, 1
PASSED, 2 BROKEN.

R1700.decision_summary:
what is drawn is what is pressed — the framework's pointer guarantee reaches
inside a self-hit-testing surface, and the three analysis screens answer one
question about how big they are instead of three.

THE DEFECT WAS REPORTED BY A PERSON, TWICE, AND MEASURED BEFORE ANYTHING WAS
CHANGED. "R-01 will not press." "The row under the timestamping field does not
respond." Both reports were about a maximised window; both times every gate was
green. Driving the capture viewer through a real shell at 2494x1011 and asking
it, at the centre of each rectangle it had just painted, what is here: of the
166 painted rectangles that moved under the resize, 166 answered NOTHING. Zero
agreed. The paint reflowed to the live window and the hit test went on resolving
against the size the screen was designed at.

WHY NO GATE COULD SEE IT, IN TWO SENTENCES THAT ARE BOTH STRUCTURAL. The
in-process sweeps paint and hit-test inside ONE owner scope, where both halves
resolve the size hook and therefore cannot disagree — the size axis is void by
construction there. And the framework's own pointer guarantee, scene/pointer_reach,
covers the REGISTERED widgets: §2 #7 makes a pinion screen one External so an
agent can query it, so on that screen the framework vouched for 1 of 291 painted
rectangles and the other 290 were on the screen's honour.

THREE SCREENS SPELLED ONE QUESTION THREE WAYS AND ONE OF THEM WAS WRONG. Asked
off a view scope, the node lab read the framework's record (correct, R1684.4),
the shell read a Signal it kept on its own state through a weak handle (correct,
R1671), and the capture viewer read the design constant. So the POLICY moved
into the framework as pinion_core::external::layout_size — take the tracked
viewport read inside a view, the recorded surface rectangle outside one, honour
the caller's layout floor, and fall back to the design size only for a surface
nothing has painted yet. A policy re-derived per consumer has as many versions
as consumers; this one had three versions and one defect.

THE REPAYMENT DID NOT HAVE TO BE ARGUED, IT STOPPED COMPILING. The shell's
scope-free weak handle existed for exactly one reason, and with layout_size
answering in both places -D dead-code named it on the first build. It is gone,
and so is the size copy on that screen's state that it reached.

THE SUBSTRATE IS THE MISSING QUESTION, ASKED TWICE. External::target_at says what
a press at a point addresses; External::target_of_tag says what the thing painted
under a tag addresses; both answer in the surface's own vocabulary, the one its
wire already uses. scene/pointer_target asks both for every painted rectangle and
holds the pair against the paint, which is the arbiter. Two questions rather than
one because a single "what tag is here" would need a hand-written inverse from
the vocabulary back to the tags, and an inverse written by hand drifts from what
it inverts — R1699 met exactly that and wrote its gate before its function.
PointerTarget has three arms and Unanswered is not Nothing: a surface that does
not resolve presses is not one that resolved every press to nothing, and
collapsing them would let a screen nobody checked read as a screen that checked
out.

THE VERDICTS ARE POINTER_REACH'S VOCABULARY ONE LEVEL DOWN — deliverable, handle,
covering, inert, unreachable — and only unreachable fails, because only it has no
benign reading. A caption over a row is covering and correct.

THE FIRST DRAFT'S RULE WAS REFUTED BY ITS OWN FIRST RUN. It asked whether a
rectangle's CENTRE addresses it, and reported the node lab's two host frames as
defects. They are not: a group paints one rectangle around its members and is
gripped by its tab strip, deliberately, because a group that took presses over
its own members would make a card undraggable the moment it joined one. So the
question became "somewhere inside", probed at nine points — the centre first,
then four edge midpoints and four inset corners, which is what reaches a strip a
proportional grid would step over — and a rectangle addressable at none of the
nine is the failure.

WHAT THE FLOOR DOES AND DOES NOT DO, BUILT AND RUN OFFSCREEN AT 6.11.1 RATHER
THAN READ ABOUT. A widget's own size answers live inside a press handler there
(1200x700 after a resize), which is the property layout_size had to match and
did. None of the rest exists: a self-painting widget's eight painted marks are
invisible to the framework's point lookup, which answers null; the scene-graph
point lookup trusts an item's DECLARED shape and finds nothing where a paint drew
outside it; and no member enumerates what a widget painted, because the only
framework-held record of a paint there is pixels, which carry no identity.
Introspection-from-paint is what makes the comparison possible at all.
changes_bullets: pinion-core (§5.15):
`external::layout_size(tag, floor, design)` — the one spelling of "how big is
this surface", answering the same in and out of a view scope. The tracked
viewport read inside a view (the window is the live fact there and the
surface's own rectangle is not, because it comes out of the layout the view is
feeding); the recorded surface rectangle outside one (available, and the very
rectangle a pointer fraction is a fraction of); the caller's floor honoured in
both; the design size only for a surface nothing has painted. The stated limit
is written down: a surface that does not fill its window gets the window from
the in-view branch, and nothing can do better during its own view.
`external::PointerTarget` — `Unanswered` / `Nothing` / `Word(String)`, with
`answered()` keeping the first two apart as a census partition.
`External::target_at(x, y)` and `External::target_of_tag(tag)`, both defaulting
to `Unanswered`. §5.15's contract gains the inverse of `pointer_press`.
pinion-rpc (§5.35 §2 #7):
`pointer_target` module + `scene/pointer_target`, registered in the method
catalogue. Per surface: `painted_size`, `announced`, `answers`, and the counts
`deliverable` / `handle` / `covering` / `inert` / `unreachable`, plus a row per
painted rectangle carrying both answers, the point the verdict is about and the
verdict. `defects` is published rather than left to each consumer to derive.
`probes(rect)` — nine points, centre first, then the four edge midpoints and
four inset corners, every one `saturating_sub`-safe because this runs in a
dispatcher over every painted rectangle in the tree.
Four unit tests over the classification and the probe set, including the
gripped-group case that refuted the first draft.
examples/hello-packet-view — THE DEFECT:
`window_size` reads `layout_size` instead of the design constant.
`Hit::word` lifted out of the inline `query("hit.<x>.<y>")` arm, so the wire's
word and the census's word are one function.
`target_at` / `target_of_tag` over `Hit::at` and R1699's `Hit::of_tag`.
examples/hello-node-lab:
`window_size` reads `layout_size`; the R1684.4 case analysis moves out.
`Hit::of_tag` — the by-name half, reading the tables the painter reads
(`toolbar_seats` pairs each seat's tag with its hit already) and parsing only
the parametric families, each checked against the state that names them.
`Hit::target` + the two trait methods.
FOUND BY LOOKING AT A MAXIMISED WINDOW: the gesture strip was a flat 470px and
read "… drag a pin = author a li…" with sixteen hundred pixels of empty canvas
beside it. It is now the size of its own sentence (`seat_w`, which the toast
in the same file already used), bounded by `gate_panel_x()` — a third caller
for the launch panel's left edge, which was a repeated `canvas.w - 262`.
examples/hello-analyzer-shell:
`window_size` reads `layout_size`; `word_or_nothing` + the two trait methods
over R1699's `Hit::of_tag` and the existing `hit_word`.
DELETED, because the compiler named them: the `SHELL` thread-local weak handle
and `shell_state_handle()`, whose only purpose was answering the size question
off a view scope, and `ShellState::surface`, which nothing then read.
`painted.rs` publishes the sweep's size through the FRAMEWORK's channel
(`record_surface_size`) instead of through a signal only that screen's own
sweep could drive.
tools/rpc_verify.py:
`_gate_pointer_targets` — a boot gate on every demo, fatal on `unreachable`,
reporting the rest and naming any surface told a size it was not painted at.
`assert_targets_survive_resize(tf, sizes)` — resize, settle, and require at
every size that nothing disagrees, that something is addressable, and that the
framework told the surface the size it painted it at.
tools/test_rpc_verify.py — three cases, 103 assertions total: the gate fails only
the verdict with no benign reading, `unanswered` never reads as covered, and the
helper refuses a screen that goes unreachable, goes silent, or is misannounced.
tools/demos/r1700_what_is_drawn_is_what_is_pressed.py — the integration test,
three screens x four window sizes, each screen's design size ASKED FOR rather
than written down.
verification_bullets: MEASURED BEFORE ANYTHING WAS CHANGED, through a real shell, on the capture
viewer: at 1440x900 every one of 166 painted rectangles resolved to itself; at
2494x1011, after the same rectangles moved, 166 of 166 resolved to nothing.
Agreement 0. The node lab (8 of 8 cards) and the shell (7 of 7 rail seats) held
at both sizes, which is what identified the divergence as three spellings of one
question rather than one framework fault.
MEASURED AFTER, at four window sizes on all three screens — each screen's own
design size, the two a person actually reported (2494x1011 and 2494x1531) and one
below every screen's design width: `unreachable` 0 everywhere. What the framework
can now vouch for, against the 1 that `scene/pointer_reach` alone vouched for on
each: capture viewer 224 of 290 painted rectangles addressable and pressable
where drawn, node lab 61 plus 2 gripped of 157, shell 28 of 192 with 152 honest
`covering` — that last number is the under-coverage this leaves, reported rather
than hidden.
10 OF 10 COUNTERFACTUALS, over two plans with two different gates.
Five through `cargo test -p pinion-rpc --lib` (the classification): invert the
grip test; make `Unanswered` read as `Nothing`; probe two pixels outside the
rectangle; probe the centre second; inset the probes proportionally so a tab
strip is stepped over. Five through the integration test itself: each of the
three screens reading a surface nothing has painted, the framework recording a
height that is not the painted one, and a by-name answer that names a
NEIGHBOURING tag.
TWO OF THEM PASSED FIRST AND BOTH ARE FINDINGS.
Falsifying the RECORDED surface height changed nothing anywhere, because none
of these three screens has an addressable rectangle positioned by the window's
height — the vertical axis of the size question had no consumer to disagree
through. `announce_external_sizes` states that invariant in its own comment and
nothing read it. The report now publishes `painted_size` beside `announced` and
the helper asserts they agree.
Making the by-name answer name a neighbouring tag also passed, and the reason
is the census's own tolerance: a rectangle that stops being answered for by
name becomes `covering`, which is a LEGITIMATE verdict (a label over the row it
labels). The collapse was published as a number and nothing read the number. A
committed coverage floor per screen now fails a screen that quietly stops
vouching for two thirds of itself.
THE GATE'S FIRST RUN REFUTED THE GATE. Probing only the centre reported the node
lab's two host frames as defects; a group is gripped by its tab strip and holds
its members everywhere else, so the rule became "somewhere inside" with the point
that worked reported.
THE FIRST DRAFT OF THE INTEGRATION TEST WAS WRONG TWICE MORE, both times by
assuming instead of asking. It allowed a pane below the layout floor to be
painted narrower "because the window clips" — measured, a painted rectangle is
the LAYOUT's and is cut only by the scroll viewports above it, so the allowance
would have accepted a pane that had genuinely shrunk. And it wrote 1440x900 down
as the design size; the node lab opens at 1625x900, so the constant was resizing
that screen below its own floor and reporting it vouching for 54 rectangles where
it vouches for 61.
CRATES: 5 green — pinion-core 3548, pinion-rpc 1246 (4 new), node lab 83, capture
viewer 42, shell 66. Harness suite 36 cases / 103 assertions.
DEMOS: the new integration test, 33 named checks over 3 screens x 4 sizes, plus
the eight per-boot gates each screen pays.
BLAST RADIUS OF A NEW BOOT GATE IS EVERY DEMO, and a full sweep is not
judgeable on this host (measured R1694: 379 of 589 failures are harness RPC
timeouts). So 25 further screens were booted under it directly — grids, docks,
charts, canvases, a rich-text surface, a multi-window shell, and three that
register no external at all: 25 of 25 boot, every surface `unanswered`, defects 0.
LOOKED AT: nine photographs on an offscreen display of my own, three screens at
their design size and at 2494x1011 before and after a real press aimed at the
rectangle furthest from the origin. That is what found the elided gesture strip,
and the strip's repair is what the text-smear gate then refused on its next boot
until it was bounded by the launch panel it had started painting over.
carry_forward_bullets: WHAT THIS LEAVES, STATED AS NUMBERS RATHER THAN AS "DONE".
1. The shell answers by name for 28 of its 192 painted rectangles and leaves 152
`covering`. That is honest — most of them are labels and rules inside cards,
and a card's sub-parts have no by-name resolution — but it means the
framework's new guarantee covers a seventh of that screen. The number is
published on every boot and floored in the integration test, so a drop fails
and a rise is visible; raising it is a round of its own.
Registered: debt-a-surface-vouches-for-a-seventh-of-what-it-paints.
2. The boot gate is fatal on `unreachable` for every demo in the tree, and only
28 of the ~225 screens were actually booted under it here (the three analysis
screens plus a 25-screen sample). The remaining population is untested against
it in this session, and a full sweep is not judgeable on this host. CI is the
reader of that verdict.
3. `assert_targets_survive_resize` asserts that a surface is told the size it was
painted at; the boot gate only REPORTS it. The reason is stated in both
places: the helper runs where the agreement has been measured and the boot
gate runs on a population that has not been. Promoting it is a measurement,
not a design question.
Registered: debt-a-surface-size-agreement-is-gated-on-three-screens-of-many.
4. Nothing forces a screen that resolves presses to resolve ALL of them. A
`Nothing` by name for something addressable reads as `covering` and passes;
the committed floor catches a collapse, not a single omission. Closing it
would need a screen to declare which of its painted rectangles it takes
responsibility for, which is a declaration this round did not want to invent
for three consumers.
5. The gesture strip's repair used `seat_w`, which estimates a run's width from
its character count rather than measuring it. That is the file's existing
helper and the toast beside it has the same estimate; a face whose advance
widths differ from the estimate makes both boxes wrong in the same direction.
Not introduced here and not repaired here.
EXTERNAL / NOT OURS: none this round.

at both sizes, which is what identified the divergence as three spellings of one
question rather than one framework fault.

design size, the two a person actually reported (2494x1011 and 2494x1531) and one
below every screen's design width: `unreachable` 0 everywhere. What the framework
can now vouch for, against the 1 that `scene/pointer_reach` alone vouched for on
each: capture viewer 224 of 290 painted rectangles addressable and pressable
where drawn, node lab 61 plus 2 gripped of 157, shell 28 of 192 with 152 honest

than hidden.

grip test; make `Unanswered` read as `Nothing`; probe two pixels outside the
rectangle; probe the centre second; inset the probes proportionally so a tab
strip is stepped over. Five through the integration test itself: each of the
three screens reading a surface nothing has painted, the framework recording a
height that is not the painted one, and a by-name answer that names a
NEIGHBOURING tag.

of these three screens has an addressable rectangle positioned by the window's
height — the vertical axis of the size question had no consumer to disagree
through. `announce_external_sizes` states that invariant in its own comment and

the helper asserts they agree.

is the census's own tolerance: a rectangle that stops being answered for by
name becomes `covering`, which is a LEGITIMATE verdict (a label over the row it
labels). The collapse was published as a number and nothing read the number. A
committed coverage floor per screen now fails a screen that quietly stops
vouching for two thirds of itself.
