R1701.decision_summary:
a title bar takes two clicks — the desktop convention a person asked for,
built where the framework owns the chrome and where the application owns a card.

THE ASK WAS A QUESTION AND THE ANSWER WAS MEASURED. "Shouldn't double-clicking a
window toggle minimise and maximise?" It should — maximise and restore, which is
what the convention actually is — and nothing here did it. Driven through a real
shell with a working positive control: pressing the dashboard card's maximize
CONTROL took `maximized` from `''` to `'decode#1'` and back, so the witness
moves; double-clicking the same card's header left it at `''`.

★THE FIRST MEASUREMENT MEASURED NOTHING, and saying so is the point. It watched
the window chrome's painted GLYPHS, which are paths rather than text runs, so the
witness came back empty at rest and after every gesture — "nothing happened" read
off a list that could not have said anything else. That is the same defect class
this session had already recorded twice, met a third time in the act of
investigating it.

THE CANON CANNOT SETTLE THIS AND SAYS SO. The behaviour reference is a browser
prototype with no window chrome at all: zero double-click handlers in 194,828
bytes of application script, measured by extracting it. That absence is an
artifact of the medium, not a design decision, so the debt's own rule applies —
the floor justifies the gesture, and this is filed as floor parity.

THE FLOOR, BUILT AND RUN OFFSCREEN AT 6.11.1 RATHER THAN READ ABOUT. An
in-application sub-window's title-bar double-click takes it from 300x200 to its
parent's full 900x600 (maximised 0 -> 1); a docking panel's takes it from docked
to floating; and a frameless top-level is left ENTIRELY to its application, with
no framework member that maps the gesture. A client-side chrome is exactly that
last case, which is why the framework is where the application lives here.

TWO PLACES NEEDED IT AND ONLY ONE OF THEM WAS THE SCREEN'S FAULT.

The screen's half: the router has synthesised a `DoubleClick` send event since
R664 and the dashboard REFUSED it as "not a pointer event". It decodes it now,
through the same `act` entry the header button's press takes — refusal and all,
so a card whose header does not offer maximise refuses the gesture by name.

The framework's half: a press on client-side chrome is consumed by the shell and
returns before the widget router runs, deliberately, because a title bar is not a
widget — so the router's double-click detector never sees one and a title bar
could not tell a second click from a first. `chrome_press_intent(tag, count)`
answers it in pinion-overlay, beside the tag SSOT, with the count as an argument
rather than a second function so the shell cannot grow a private rule.

AND THE RULE BECAME A TYPE, BECAUSE THERE ARE TWO DETECTORS NOW.
`RawPointerButton::click_count`'s doc promised since R1422 that the raw stream
and the send wire "share the framework double-click time + distance window so the
two rules cannot drift" — a guarantee resting on a comment and two literals in one
file, which held while there was one detector. `DoubleClickWindow` is that
promise as a value: the router keeps one per pointer, the chrome keeps one per
window, and the thresholds have one definition.

★★DRIVING IT FOUND A SECOND DEFECT THE DEBT FILE HAD PREDICTED. A grip press
OPENS A BOARD DRAG, so a double-click is press/release/press/release over a card
that maximises in the middle of it — and the trailing release committed a move
aimed at the board that existed before the card grew. Measured: "Decode Inspector
moved, displacing Message Stream, Identifier Map, Search & Filter", and a second
double-click never came back to the arrangement the screen opened with. A
double-click SUPERSEDES the gesture its second press opened, so the drag and the
latch are dropped before the toggle runs.

★★★AND A THIRD, PRE-EXISTING, WHICH IS R1697's OWN RULE ON THE ARM BESIDE THE
ONE IT FIXED. R1697 wrote "nothing checked that a press which moved nothing does
not announce a move" and built the guard for a detached panel. A card on the
board told the same lie — a single click on a header reported "Decode Inspector
moved" with the layout byte-identical — and worse, `move_to` is a real edit, so a
click that carried nothing could still reflow the board. The board arm has the
guard now, comparing against where the tile IS rather than a remembered origin,
because a maximise between the press and the release moves it without the drag
having carried it.

AND THE ROUND WAS LOOKED AT, TWICE, WHICH IS WHERE THE LAST TWO REPAIRS CAME
FROM. The gesture strip did not name the new gesture — a capability built and not
announced, the mirror of one announced and not built, and this screen has been on
both sides of that. Adding it pushed the strip past the band it is painted in, so
the band is derived from the panel beside it now rather than being a flat 470;
measured, the room at the design width IS 470, so the derivation reproduced the
constant and the SENTENCE had to give. `Enter max` is what left, by the same rule
that let the new item in: a double-click has no affordance, and `Enter` duplicates
a button that is on screen and a keymap panel that names it in full. Measured
after: ink 468 -> 427 in a 470 band.
changes_bullets: `input::DoubleClickWindow` — the W3C `dblclick` window as a value: `TIME_MS`,
`DIST_PX`, `press(now, x, y, tag) -> u8` answering the consecutive ordinal and
clearing on 2, and `forget()` for a press that has become something else. Four
unit tests, including the three ways a second press fails to pair and the
reset that keeps a triple-click from reading as two doubles.
pinion-runtime:
the router's per-pointer `last_press` IS that type now; the two threshold
constants are aliases of its associated ones, so the file's three readers cite
one definition; the drag-stray path calls `forget` rather than removing the
entry.

`chrome_press_intent(tag, click_count)` — the ordinal-aware sibling of
`chrome_tag_semantic`, in the crate that owns the tags. The grip's second press
asks for `WindowControl::Maximize`; every other region means the same thing
however often it is pressed. Two tests, one of them the negative control over
the whole tag vocabulary.
pinion-shell (§5.16):
`AppShell::chrome_click_window` — one `DoubleClickWindow` per window, because
`try_chrome_press` consumes a chrome press before the router can count it.
`try_chrome_press` resolves through `chrome_press_intent` with that ordinal,
measured against the cursor position the hit test resolved with.
`chrome_action_for_semantic` split out of `chrome_action_for_tag`, so the
ordinal-aware path and the ordinal-free one share one winit conversion and the
exhaustive match still fails to compile on a ninth chrome region.
`ShellCore::cursor_position_for_window` — the position leg of the existing tag
leg, which the chrome's detector needs.

a positive control, the toggle, the layout equality that proves nothing else was

verification_bullets: MEASURED BEFORE, with a positive control that moves: the card header's maximize
button took `maximized` from `''` to `'decode#1'` and back; double-clicking the
same card's header left it at `''`. MEASURED AFTER: `''` -> `'decode#1'` ->

7 OF 7 COUNTERFACTUALS, and the one that had to be rewritten is the class this

second press; widening the pairing distance by a thousand; leaving the window

NOTHING — recast as a WRONG answer rather than an absent one, which is the

CRATES: 5 green — pinion-core 3551 (+3), pinion-overlay, pinion-runtime,
pinion-shell, and the dashboard 68 (+2 in-process, driven through `invoke`).
★STOP-THE-LINE, ATTRIBUTED AND REGISTERED RATHER THAN RERUN. One `pinion-shell`
test went red on the build host on the last run of the round —
`shell_threads_engine_into_measure_and_excludes_caret_bearing`, on its own
self-validating control, `74 != 74`. Attribution, not a rerun: it PASSED on the
same host fifteen minutes earlier with that crate's inputs unchanged (this
round's edits there are one accessor, unrelated to text measurement) and it
passes on this host. So the tree did not move and the host did not either — what
moved is which face the system font enumeration resolved, which is an INPUT to
that test's control: it asserts "our fixture measures differently from the
host's sans-serif" to prove itself non-vacuous. The test's own comment predicted
exactly this failure and forbids weakening it, and the honest repair — pin the
off-path fontconfig so "the host's sans-serif" is a known face — cannot be
verified from here because it does not reproduce here. Registered with the
measurement: debt-a-discriminating-control-depends-on-the-hosts-fonts.
DEMO: a new one in a real window — a positive control, the toggle both ways, the
layout equality, the sentence the screen says, two negative controls (a card's
body and the navigation rail), and every one of the four card headers.
THE FLOOR: built and run offscreen at 6.11.1. An in-application sub-window's

floats it; a frameless top-level has no framework member for the gesture at all.
WHAT COULD NOT BE MEASURED HERE, STATED RATHER THAN GLOSSED: the OS window's

changes nothing measurable either, which makes the positive control void and any

LOOKED AT: three photographs on an offscreen display of my own — the board as it
opens, the card maximised by two clicks on its header, and the board restored by
two more. That is what found the strip that did not name the new gesture, and
then the strip that could not fit it.
carry_forward_bullets: WHAT THIS LEAVES.
1. EXTERNAL — the chrome half is unverified end to end. This host has no window

Registered on the debt this round closes, which stays as the record of it.
2. Two more title-bar-shaped surfaces did NOT get the gesture, and both are
named rather than forgotten:
a detached panel (`float.{id}`), whose peer gesture by the floor's reading
is redock rather than maximise — the floor's docking panel toggles

the dock widget's panel header (`{panel}#header` in pinion-widget-paint),
where the floor's answer IS float/dock and where our press opens a

which this round answered once and did not generalise.
Registered: debt-two-more-title-bars-take-no-second-click.

carries one `gesture: bool` per operation and so cannot say "two ways in".

second driver for it. Whether the table should hold the set of gestures
rather than a bool is a question for the round that meets a third one.
4. `ink_h: 15` in a `h: 14` box makes the gesture strip report `overflows: true`
on its vertical axis. Pre-existing, unrelated to this round, and inside the
surface's budget; the horizontal axis is what this round measured and moved

R1703.decision_summary:
A wheel is the one pointer gesture whose meaning is entirely local policy: the
same motion over the same pixel scrolls a page, steps a value, flips a tab or
zooms a canvas, and the event says nothing about which. Every toolkit resolves
that the same way — the widget under the cursor overrides a wheel handler — and
the cost is that the behaviour is discoverable only by trying it. So R1703 makes
"what a wheel at this point does" a DECLARATION, and makes that declaration the
precondition of dispatch rather than a description beside it.

WHAT FORCED IT was a consumer defect a person reported and nothing could see.
The analysis tool's node canvas prints `wheel = zoom` on its hint strip, where a
person reads it, and no wheel answered — measured again at the start of this
round, eight wheel events and two modified ones over the canvas left the zoom at
84 and the pan at 0,0. Every gate was green, and the reason is structural: the
screen's operation table has a `zoom` row and that row is satisfied by the zoom
BUTTONS, which work. A hint strip is a different population — it enumerates
GESTURES — so a join over operations is blind to it by construction. Anything a
screen prints for a person to read is a population, and a population with no
gate is where "declared and not built" lives.

THE FLOOR WAS MEASURED BY BUILDING A PROBE AND RUNNING IT OFFSCREEN, not by
reading documentation. Across the four widget classes that answer a wheel on the
reference toolkit at 6.11.1, 309 introspectable properties and 172 introspectable
methods name the wheel ZERO times. The same probe measured what that silence
costs: a CLOSED, UNFOCUSED combo box sitting in a form steps its value on a wheel
aimed at the form, and nothing in that widget's interface lets the form find out
beforehand, ask it to stop, or learn afterwards which control ate the scroll. One
leg of that probe was VOID on its first run and had to be repaired before it
could be quoted — the graphics view's cursor anchor reads the GLOBAL cursor,
which offscreen is (0,0), so the measurement said the floor drifts by 74 units
when in fact the probe had placed no cursor. With a positive control (place the
cursor, read it back) the floor holds a point to 0.21 units, and that is the
number this round is held against.

THE DESIGN, in one sentence: a widget answers `wheel_intent(at)`, the router
offers `External::wheel` only where that answers `Some`, and `scene/wheel_intent`
publishes the value the router routed by. A wrong answer is therefore not
expressible — removing the declaration removes the behaviour — which is a
stronger property than a documented convention, and it is what lets a form ask
which of its controls will take a scroll away from the page.

TWO CHOICES INSIDE THAT ARE WORTH RECORDING. The intent enum carries only the
meanings a widget can take AWAY from the scroll chain (`Step`, `Zoom`);
"it scrolls" is what happens when nobody declares anything, and an arm nobody
returns is a declaration the compiler cannot tell from a mistake. And the gesture
phase reuses `GesturePhase` rather than adding a wheel-shaped copy of its four
arms: the bracket is the gesture-agnostic half, winit reports it for a wheel with
the same type it reports for a pinch, and two enums with the same arms is how two
producers come to disagree about what "cancelled" means.

THE PHASE HAD BEEN DISCARDED AT THE WINIT BOUNDARY (`MouseWheel { delta, .. }`)
for the whole life of this shell, which is why the one rule it exists for had
nowhere to live: a stepped widget must drop its banked sub-notch remainder when
the gesture ENDS, or a trackpad flick leaves a fraction of a notch for the next
gesture — minutes later, possibly aimed at something else — to spend.

THE MECHANISM CAUGHT THIS ROUND'S OWN DESIGN ERROR, which is the strongest thing
that can be said for it. A list was given a wheel that walked its cursor,
because the floor's COMBO BOX does that; the tree's own `hello-listbox` demo went
red, and re-measuring the floor showed the two widgets are opposites there — its
list scrolls and leaves the choice alone (`currentRow 5 -> 5`,
`scrollbar 0 -> 3`), while what steps is the closed, unfocused combo box's value.
So the list declares nothing, scrolling stays what declining already gave it for
free, and the recorded lesson is not to generalise a measurement of one widget to
another that merely resembles it.

THE CONSUMER'S ARITHMETIC IS THE CANON'S AND THE SUBSTRATE'S, not this screen's:
one event is one step whichever way the platform sizes a notch (the direction is
read, the magnitude is not — reading it is what makes a zoom leap on one mouse
and crawl on another), the step is multiplicative so out and back is the
identity, and the anchor is `Camera::zoomed_at`. The seats zoom about the middle
and the wheel about the cursor, which are the same operation with a different
point, so they share one function; `point_canvas_at` had the middle written into
it twice and would otherwise have turned a cursor-anchored zoom silently into a
centred one.
changes_bullets: FRAMEWORK — `pinion_core::widgets::wheel` is new: `WheelReading` (the cursor
normalised over the same basis a drag uses, the pixel delta on the W3C sign, the
gesture phase, the held modifiers), `WheelIntent` (`Step(StepUnit)` / `Zoom`),
`WheelDirection` (`Away` / `Toward`, named from the person because "up" is
already taken twice over by the content's motion and the delta's sign, with
`scaled(k)` giving the multiplicative step), and `WheelSteps` — the whole-notch
accumulator plus the one rule the phase exists for. `GesturePhase` gains
`settles()`, where the rule reads, rather than a second four-arm enum.
`External::wheel` now takes one `&WheelReading` instead of five positional
parameters, and `External::wheel_intent(at)` is new. The trait's own doc states
that `wheel` is only reached where `wheel_intent` answers `Some`.
ROUTER — the phase is carried through `WheelDispatchArgs` and forwarded to the
widget; `offer_wheel_to_external` asks `wheel_intent` at the normalised point
before offering; `pinion_runtime::wheel_intent_at` answers "what a wheel at this
window point would do" through the identical resolution (`resolve_pointer_tag`
then the widget's own `CaptureNormalize` basis), so the wire reads the router's
answer rather than forming a second one.
SHELL / TUI — the winit `MouseWheel` arm stops discarding `phase` and maps it
with the same `winit_gesture_phase_to_pinion` the pinch and rotation arms use;
`AppShell::wheel_phase_for_window` and `ShellCoreTui::wheel_phase` carry it, and
the phase-less wrappers state that they mean a notched mouse wheel.
WIRE — `scene/wheel_intent` is new (`at` / `path` optional; with neither it is a
census over painted surfaces, each row naming the point it was asked at and who
answered there), and `scene/wheel` accepts an optional `phase`, without which it
means a notch. Three response types are declared in `WIRE_TYPES`, which is the
census that caught them missing.
CATALOG — a radio group declares itself a tab STRIP (`with_wheel`) and walks
under a wheel, clamping at the ends and DECLINING there so the wheel it cannot
spend reaches whatever scrolls behind; it defaults OFF because a form's mutually
exclusive answers must not change when a person scrolls past them, and one type
serves both roles. `hello-tabs` declares its strip. `External::wheel`
implementors in the widget catalogue: 2 -> 3, the first movement since R1554.
★ A LIST DECLARES NO WHEEL, and that is a measurement rather than an omission.
This round gave it one — a cursor walking by notches, on the reasoning that a
combo box does that on the floor — and `hello-listbox`'s own wheel demo went red
because a scrolling list stopped scrolling. The floor was then measured rather
than argued (40 rows, current row 5, one notch): `currentRow 5 -> 5`,
`scrollbar 0 -> 3`. A wheel over a list SCROLLS it, which this tree already did
for free, because declining is how a widget hands the event to the scroll chain.
What steps there is the CLOSED, UNFOCUSED combo box's value, which is the hazard
refused on purpose — and the demo asserts that refusal shut and open.
SCREEN A — `External::wheel` zooms, anchored under the cursor, only over the
canvas; `wheel_intent` answers per point for the same reason. `zoom_to_at` is the
one anchored-zoom path the seats and the wheel share, `point_canvas_at` takes the
anchor from its caller instead of writing the middle into itself twice, and
`WHEEL_ZOOM_STEP` is the canon's 1.12 applied by direction only.
GATES — `r1703_every_gesture_the_hint_strip_advertises_is_answered` drives all
four advertised gestures through the screen's own pointer and wheel entry points
and requires the printed list and the driver list to be equal as SETS;
`r1703_every_catalog_wheel_declares_what_it_says_it_declares` is a table over the
six catalog wheels, four declaring and two declining;
`tools/demos/r1703_the_wheel_says_what_it_does.py` is the integration UI test (38
assertion points, six binaries) covering the strip, the answer-versus-behaviour
agreement in BOTH directions on a screen and on the catalog, the canon's
arithmetic including the cursor anchor measured on the paint, and the ended
flick.
verification_bullets: SEVENTEEN COUNTERFACTUALS, ALL CAUGHT — and the two that did not catch on their
first run are the round's two most valuable findings.
* Core (7/7, gate `cargo test -p pinion-core --lib`): the gesture's end drops
the banked remainder; direction is read from the W3C sign; a multiplicative
step is what makes out-and-back the identity; a strip clamps rather than
wrapping; A LIST DECLARES NO WHEEL; a form's radio set declares none by
default; and a declared step names the right unit.
* Screen and wire (gate `cargo test -p hello-node-lab -p pinion-runtime --lib`

R1703.publishable_decision_summary:
A wheel is the one pointer gesture whose meaning is entirely local policy: the
same motion over the same pixel scrolls a page, steps a value, flips a tab or
zooms a canvas, and the event says nothing about which. Every toolkit resolves
that the same way — the widget under the cursor overrides a wheel handler — and
the cost is that the behaviour is discoverable only by trying it. So R1703 makes
"what a wheel at this point does" a DECLARATION, and makes that declaration the
precondition of dispatch rather than a description beside it.

WHAT FORCED IT was a consumer defect a person reported and nothing could see.
The analysis tool's node canvas prints `wheel = zoom` on its hint strip, where a
person reads it, and no wheel answered — measured again at the start of this
round, eight wheel events and two modified ones over the canvas left the zoom at
84 and the pan at 0,0. Every gate was green, and the reason is structural: the
screen's operation table has a `zoom` row and that row is satisfied by the zoom
BUTTONS, which work. A hint strip is a different population — it enumerates
GESTURES — so a join over operations is blind to it by construction. Anything a
screen prints for a person to read is a population, and a population with no
gate is where "declared and not built" lives.

THE FLOOR WAS MEASURED BY BUILDING A PROBE AND RUNNING IT OFFSCREEN, not by
reading documentation. Across the four widget classes that answer a wheel on the
reference toolkit at 6.11.1, 309 introspectable properties and 172 introspectable
methods name the wheel ZERO times. The same probe measured what that silence
costs: a CLOSED, UNFOCUSED combo box sitting in a form steps its value on a wheel
aimed at the form, and nothing in that widget's interface lets the form find out
beforehand, ask it to stop, or learn afterwards which control ate the scroll. One
leg of that probe was VOID on its first run and had to be repaired before it
could be quoted — the graphics view's cursor anchor reads the GLOBAL cursor,
which offscreen is (0,0), so the measurement said the floor drifts by 74 units
when in fact the probe had placed no cursor. With a positive control (place the
cursor, read it back) the floor holds a point to 0.21 units, and that is the
number this round is held against.

THE DESIGN, in one sentence: a widget answers `wheel_intent(at)`, the router
offers `External::wheel` only where that answers `Some`, and `scene/wheel_intent`
publishes the value the router routed by. A wrong answer is therefore not
expressible — removing the declaration removes the behaviour — which is a
stronger property than a documented convention, and it is what lets a form ask
which of its controls will take a scroll away from the page.

TWO CHOICES INSIDE THAT ARE WORTH RECORDING. The intent enum carries only the
meanings a widget can take AWAY from the scroll chain (`Step`, `Zoom`);
"it scrolls" is what happens when nobody declares anything, and an arm nobody
returns is a declaration the compiler cannot tell from a mistake. And the gesture
phase reuses `GesturePhase` rather than adding a wheel-shaped copy of its four
arms: the bracket is the gesture-agnostic half, winit reports it for a wheel with
the same type it reports for a pinch, and two enums with the same arms is how two
producers come to disagree about what "cancelled" means.

THE PHASE HAD BEEN DISCARDED AT THE WINIT BOUNDARY (`MouseWheel { delta, .. }`)
for the whole life of this shell, which is why the one rule it exists for had
nowhere to live: a stepped widget must drop its banked sub-notch remainder when
the gesture ENDS, or a trackpad flick leaves a fraction of a notch for the next
gesture — minutes later, possibly aimed at something else — to spend.

THE MECHANISM CAUGHT THIS ROUND'S OWN DESIGN ERROR, which is the strongest thing
that can be said for it. A list was given a wheel that walked its cursor,
because the floor's COMBO BOX does that; the tree's own `hello-listbox` demo went
red, and re-measuring the floor showed the two widgets are opposites there — its
list scrolls and leaves the choice alone (`currentRow 5 -> 5`,
`scrollbar 0 -> 3`), while what steps is the closed, unfocused combo box's value.
So the list declares nothing, scrolling stays what declining already gave it for
free, and the recorded lesson is not to generalise a measurement of one widget to
another that merely resembles it.

THE CONSUMER'S ARITHMETIC IS THE CANON'S AND THE SUBSTRATE'S, not this screen's:
one event is one step whichever way the platform sizes a notch (the direction is
read, the magnitude is not — reading it is what makes a zoom leap on one mouse
and crawl on another), the step is multiplicative so out and back is the
identity, and the anchor is `Camera::zoomed_at`. The seats zoom about the middle
and the wheel about the cursor, which are the same operation with a different
point, so they share one function; `point_canvas_at` had the middle written into
it twice and would otherwise have turned a cursor-anchored zoom silently into a
centred one.

R1704.decision_summary:
A person driving the running application reported that the picked link's caption
and its `delete` chip follow the canvas as it is panned. They do, and the second
half of what they do is worse than the first: measured before the fix, panning
left until neither endpoint of the link was painted at all, the chip held station
at x=316 across pans of -949, -1898, -2847 and -3796 — and **pressing it deleted
the link**, seven links to six, with nothing on screen to say which one had gone.
An affordance for a thing nobody can see, which still acts.

WHERE IT CAME FROM, and it is not a careless line. R1681 gave the picked link a
column that is nudged clear of the cards it would otherwise cover, because a
floating `delete` seat had been measured covering nine sampled points of one card
including its centre and its accept pin. That vertical search needed a bound —
R1681's own entry records that its first draft "pushed both endpoint seats out of
the visible world entirely and traded one unreachable affordance for another" —
so the column was also clamped into what the canvas is showing.

THE CLAMP IS RIGHT AND ITS DOMAIN WAS UNBOUNDED. It exists to stop a column being
pushed out of sight BY ITS OWN AVOIDANCE SEARCH. It was never meant to fetch a
column back that the PAN had carried away, and nothing said so, so once the link
had left the view the horizontal clamp went on pinning its chrome to the edge
for ever.

THE BEHAVIOUR CANON SETTLES THE SHAPE rather than this being a judgement call.
Extracted from the prototype: the caption is placed at the wire's own midpoint
(`abs(mx, my - 24)`), with no clamp of any kind, and the viewport clips. So the
correct bound is the simplest one — a column whose natural place has left the
visible world is left there, and R1653's canvas clipping takes it away with the
link it belongs to. One guard, expressed as what it means: if no part of the
column intersects what the canvas is showing, do not move it.

WHY NO GATE SAW IT, and this is the reusable half: every check panned ONCE. At a
single pan the column tracks the graph to the pixel — verified again while
diagnosing this, at four window sizes, the column's delta matching a card's
exactly — because the clamp only engages after the column's natural place has
crossed the edge. A gate that drives a gesture a little cannot see a rule that
only fires when the gesture is driven a lot.
changes_bullets: `hello-node-lab`'s `placement` gains one guard: when no part of the picked link's
column intersects the rectangle the canvas is showing, the nudge answers `(0, 0)`
and leaves the column where the wire put it, so the canvas clipping carries it
away with the link. `any` rather than `all` — a column with one part still
showing is the case the nudge exists for, and only a column entirely gone is the
case it must keep its hands off.
TWO GATES, and they divide the two halves of the report.
`r1704_a_link_that_has_left_the_canvas_takes_its_affordances_with_it` picks the
link on the wire the way a person does, pans until neither of its cards is
painted, and asserts the caption and the chip are gone — then presses where the
chip used to be and asserts the link count did not move, because a chip that is
merely invisible and still pressable is the worse of the two states.
`r1704_the_picked_links_column_is_never_half_out_of_the_canvas` sweeps the pan
and holds the invariant across it: at every step the column is wholly absent or
wholly present AT ITS FULL SIZE. Two things about that test are the round's own
findings rather than decoration — see the verification.
verification_bullets: MEASURED BEFORE THE FIX, driving the wire: pan -949, -1898, -2847, -3796, the
link's own cards `GONE` from the paint at all four, and `lab.link.act` painted at
x=316 throughout. Pressing its centre took the graph from seven links to six.
MEASURED AFTER: the chip is absent from the paint at the same pans, the
diagnostic that pressed it now stops with "the chip is gone, so there is nothing
to press", and a screenshot of the panned canvas shows a clean empty grid where
the stranded caption and chip used to sit against the edge.
★ AND THE MEASUREMENT WAS BRIEFLY WRONG IN THE OTHER DIRECTION: the first
after-fix run still reported the ghost, because it ran under `PINION_ASSUME_BUILT`
against a binary the counterfactual driver had left behind. Re-run with the
rebuild on, it was gone. The tree's own recorded trap, walked into once more.
TWO COUNTERFACTUALS, both CAUGHT — after the second one twice PASSED and each
pass was a finding:
* CF-18, the reported state itself (a guard written so it can never fire) —
caught from the first.
* CF-19, `all` in place of `any`, which switches the nudge off as soon as ONE
part of the column crosses the edge — the case R1681 built it for. It passed
twice.
First because the assertion could not fail: "every part lies inside the
canvas" is trivially true of a CLIPPED part, since clipping trims the
reported rectangle to the edge. The observable is the part's SIZE — a nudged
column keeps 108x19 and 45x19, a clipped one is narrower.
Then because the sweep's STRIDE was wrong for the geometry it samples. The
two spellings differ only while the canvas edge falls between two parts of
the column, and the parts are clustered: the caption spans 108 px and the
chip sits inside that span 32 px in and 45 px wide, so the window is about
26 px wide and a 90 px stride steps straight over it. Eight pixels a step,
stopping two steps after the column disappears.

R1704.publishable_decision_summary:
A person driving the running application reported that the picked link's caption
and its `delete` chip follow the canvas as it is panned. They do, and the second
half of what they do is worse than the first: measured before the fix, panning
left until neither endpoint of the link was painted at all, the chip held station
at x=316 across pans of -949, -1898, -2847 and -3796 — and **pressing it deleted
the link**, seven links to six, with nothing on screen to say which one had gone.
An affordance for a thing nobody can see, which still acts.

WHERE IT CAME FROM, and it is not a careless line. R1681 gave the picked link a
column that is nudged clear of the cards it would otherwise cover, because a
floating `delete` seat had been measured covering nine sampled points of one card
including its centre and its accept pin. That vertical search needed a bound —
R1681's own entry records that its first draft "pushed both endpoint seats out of
the visible world entirely and traded one unreachable affordance for another" —
so the column was also clamped into what the canvas is showing.

THE CLAMP IS RIGHT AND ITS DOMAIN WAS UNBOUNDED. It exists to stop a column being
pushed out of sight BY ITS OWN AVOIDANCE SEARCH. It was never meant to fetch a
column back that the PAN had carried away, and nothing said so, so once the link
had left the view the horizontal clamp went on pinning its chrome to the edge
for ever.

THE BEHAVIOUR CANON SETTLES THE SHAPE rather than this being a judgement call.
Extracted from the prototype: the caption is placed at the wire's own midpoint
(`abs(mx, my - 24)`), with no clamp of any kind, and the viewport clips. So the
correct bound is the simplest one — a column whose natural place has left the
visible world is left there, and R1653's canvas clipping takes it away with the
link it belongs to. One guard, expressed as what it means: if no part of the
column intersects what the canvas is showing, do not move it.

WHY NO GATE SAW IT, and this is the reusable half: every check panned ONCE. At a
single pan the column tracks the graph to the pixel — verified again while
diagnosing this, at four window sizes, the column's delta matching a card's
exactly — because the clamp only engages after the column's natural place has
crossed the edge. A gate that drives a gesture a little cannot see a rule that
only fires when the gesture is driven a lot.
publishable_changes_bullets: `hello-node-lab`'s `placement` gains one guard: when no part of the picked link's
column intersects the rectangle the canvas is showing, the nudge answers `(0, 0)`
and leaves the column where the wire put it, so the canvas clipping carries it
away with the link. `any` rather than `all` — a column with one part still
showing is the case the nudge exists for, and only a column entirely gone is the
case it must keep its hands off.
TWO GATES, and they divide the two halves of the report.
`r1704_a_link_that_has_left_the_canvas_takes_its_affordances_with_it` picks the
link on the wire the way a person does, pans until neither of its cards is
painted, and asserts the caption and the chip are gone — then presses where the
chip used to be and asserts the link count did not move, because a chip that is
merely invisible and still pressable is the worse of the two states.
`r1704_the_picked_links_column_is_never_half_out_of_the_canvas` sweeps the pan
and holds the invariant across it: at every step the column is wholly absent or
wholly present AT ITS FULL SIZE. Two things about that test are the round's own
findings rather than decoration — see the verification.
publishable_verification_bullets: MEASURED BEFORE THE FIX, driving the wire: pan -949, -1898, -2847, -3796, the
link's own cards `GONE` from the paint at all four, and `lab.link.act` painted at
x=316 throughout. Pressing its centre took the graph from seven links to six.
MEASURED AFTER: the chip is absent from the paint at the same pans, the
diagnostic that pressed it now stops with "the chip is gone, so there is nothing
to press", and a screenshot of the panned canvas shows a clean empty grid where
the stranded caption and chip used to sit against the edge.
★ AND THE MEASUREMENT WAS BRIEFLY WRONG IN THE OTHER DIRECTION: the first
after-fix run still reported the ghost, because it ran under `PINION_ASSUME_BUILT`
against a binary the counterfactual driver had left behind. Re-run with the
rebuild on, it was gone. The tree's own recorded trap, walked into once more.
TWO COUNTERFACTUALS, both CAUGHT — after the second one twice PASSED and each
pass was a finding:
* CF-18, the reported state itself (a guard written so it can never fire) —
caught from the first.
* CF-19, `all` in place of `any`, which switches the nudge off as soon as ONE
part of the column crosses the edge — the case R1681 built it for. It passed
twice.
First because the assertion could not fail: "every part lies inside the
canvas" is trivially true of a CLIPPED part, since clipping trims the
reported rectangle to the edge. The observable is the part's SIZE — a nudged
column keeps 108x19 and 45x19, a clipped one is narrower.
Then because the sweep's STRIDE was wrong for the geometry it samples. The
two spellings differ only while the canvas edge falls between two parts of
the column, and the parts are clustered: the caption spans 108 px and the
chip sits inside that span 32 px in and 45 px wide, so the window is about
26 px wide and a 90 px stride steps straight over it. Eight pixels a step,
stopping two steps after the column disappears.

R1705.decision_summary:
A person driving the node canvas reported two things and they were one fact:

    "the dots only go so far, so it doesn't feel infinite"
    "and zooming out is slow — is this the floor's quality?"

The answer to the second is no, and the reason is the framework's rather than
the screen's. pinion had no repeating fill, so a consumer wanting a canvas grid
had to build it out of the only fill there was — a box per pip — and inherited
both problems from that. Measured on the running application before this round:
zooming out took the painted scene from 12,879 nodes to 95,131 and a zoom step
from 23 ms to 155 ms, with every one of those nodes laid out, hit-tested, cached
and published for a 1 px dot; and because an enumerated lattice has to stop
somewhere, it was cut to a 6,400-unit world surface, so panning past that edge
left the canvas blank.

THE FLOOR WAS MEASURED, not recalled: a probe built at 6.11.1 and run offscreen
over a scene one million units square. A tiled background brush costs 0.6-0.8 ms
a frame and DOES NOT MOVE as the zoom falls; the hand-drawn variant stays under
2 ms while drawing 27,448 pips, because it paints into the exposed rectangle
rather than materialising anything. Neither idiom enumerates the scene, so
neither can run out. That is the shape to match.

`BoxStyle::lattice` is that primitive: pitch, dot size, phase and colour, on the
style where `gradient` already sits. Three things follow from it being a
DECLARATION rather than a callback, and the third is the one worth arguing:

* the dots are emitted at paint time, so nothing about them is laid out,
  hit-tested or cached;
* the walk is bounded by the box, so a lattice can no more run off its surface
  than a fill can;
* and §2 #1's ban on opaque paint callbacks is honoured rather than dodged. This
  is the opposite of a callback — it is four numbers and a colour that
  `scene/snapshot` reads. A client used to receive 23,000 anonymous 1x1 boxes
  carrying no tag and no name; it now receives "a 1 px dot every 22 px, phased
  at (-60, -40)" and can place every dot from it. The wire got MORE knowable,
  not less, which is why the primitive belongs in the style rather than in a
  consumer's paint hook.

WHERE THE LATTICE GOES WAS THE ROUND'S REAL DECISION. On the world surface it
would be bounded by the world exactly as the pips were, and a far pan would
blank the canvas again; on the VIEWPORT it is always full and the phase carries
the pan, so the surface still reads as a thing being moved rather than a window
sliding over a static picture. The behaviour canon settles it — it puts its
background on the viewport element and parameterises it by zoom and pan, which
is this lattice's pitch and phase exactly.
changes_bullets: `pinion_core::style::DotLattice` is new — pitch, dot, phase, colour, with `new`
clamping both sizes to at least one pixel (a caller derives the pitch from a
zoom, so zero arrives by arithmetic, and a zero pitch is the one value that makes
the painter's walk never end) and `first` taking the phase with `rem_euclid` so a
negative pan lands inside the lattice rather than before it.
`BoxStyle::lattice` carries it, and because `BoxFacet` is the census the owning
crate publishes, adding it was a compile error in five places, each of which had
to answer: `BoxStyle::facets`'s destructure, the disabled cascade (a lattice is
ink and fades with the rest), the RPC wire projection, the three-renderer parity
matrix, and two demos that restate the census BY HAND on purpose.
The vello adapter paints it in `fill_box_bg`, after the fill rather than instead
of it — a grid is dots on a ground and both are wanted — clipped to the box on
the far edges so a straddling dot is trimmed like every other mark.
The parity matrix's three verdicts are stated rather than assumed: vello
`Observes`; the TUI `Ignores` it, because the declaration is a one-PIXEL dot and
a terminal's smallest ink is a whole cell, so rounding it into cells would be a
different picture at a different weight rather than a coarser rendering of this
one; the PDF projector is a `Gap`, because PDF has Type 1 tiling patterns and
can equally emit filled rectangles — the medium carries this comfortably and the
projector simply does not read it yet. `declaration` was split into
`verdicts_for` + `fixture_for` when the seventh facet took it past the 100-line
ceiling: an extract, never an `#[allow]`.
`hello-node-lab` declares one lattice on its canvas box and deletes the pip
loop. The world surface's fill becomes transparent — see the verification for
why that line is the round's own defect made visible.
verification_bullets: MEASURED, before and after, on the running application:
painted nodes, opening zoom   12,879  ->  2,025
painted nodes, zoomed out     95,131  ->  1,713
a zoom step                23-155 ms  ->  ~10 ms, flat
grid at pan -3,435             blank  ->  full
The node count now FALLS slightly as the zoom drops (fewer cards on screen)
instead of growing sevenfold, which is the floor's shape: constant in the grid.
★★★★★ AND THE FIRST DRAFT DREW NOTHING AT ALL, which is the finding this round
would most like remembered. The scene was right, the declaration was published
correctly, the node count had fallen exactly as intended, every test passed —
and comparing the before and after SCREENSHOTS BY EYE, they looked the same, so
the round was one step from being committed. A pixel scan said otherwise:
before:  1,731 grid-coloured pixels across the canvas
after:       0
The world surface carried an opaque `ink.bg` — invisible while it was the only
ground, and a lid over every dot the moment the canvas grew a lattice. Fixed by
making the surface transparent (it is a coordinate space, not a colour), and the
demo now asserts the pixels rather than the intent: 36 of 36 probed lattice
points carry the grid colour, and the gap between two dots does NOT, or the
first check would pass against a canvas painted entirely grid-colour.
SIX COUNTERFACTUALS, ALL CAUGHT — the renderer handed a degenerate rectangle;
`%` in place of `rem_euclid`; the lattice moved to the world surface; the world
surface opaque again; the pitch not following the zoom; the phase not carrying
the pan.
★ CF-22 TOOK THREE ATTEMPTS AND ALL THREE FAULTS WERE MINE, not the gate's:
BROKEN first (deleting the only call site made `canvas_lattice` dead code — the
sixth instance of that class), then PASSED twice, once because the edit ADDED
the lattice to the world while leaving it on the viewport (not the move it was
named for) and once because the `find` range stopped short of the canvas's own
`with_style`, leaving two of them with the later winning. Reproducing the
mutation BY HAND settled it: the demo fails with "the canvas declares no lattice
at all". A passed counterfactual is a finding OR a broken counterfactual, and
only re-doing it by hand tells you which.
★ WRITING CF-25 FOUND A HOLE BEFORE IT RAN: nothing asserted that the phase
carries the pan, which is the whole reason a phase exists. The demo now checks
it, and the case is caught.
FIVE GATES FIRED ON THE NEW FACET, each naming its own repair: the `facets`
destructure, the wire projection's match, the parity matrix's match, and two
demos whose census lists are hand-written ON PURPOSE — their own message says so
("the repair is to edit it, not to derive it"), because deriving them is exactly
how the wire and the type drift together in silence. `r1514` goes further and
requires every facet to be witnessed by a PRODUCTION binding, so `hello-node-lab`
joins as the fourth: a key that reaches the wire with nobody declaring it is the
state that gate exists to refuse.
★ THE COUNTERFACTUAL DRIVER REFUSED ITS FIRST RUN — "the gate is ALREADY RED
before any case ran, so every case would report CAUGHT for the wrong reason" —
which is R1619's protection working. The red was the second hand-written census,
`r1516`, named precisely by the failing assertion.

Blast radius driven rather than assumed: the two facet-census demos and the

* THE PDF PROJECTOR DOES NOT READ THE LATTICE, and the parity matrix says so in

* `bx` REFUSED EVERY REMOTE RUN OF THIS ROUND with "the remote working tree

R1706.decision_summary:
The analysis tool's node canvas has one gesture that acts on many cards at once:
grab a host frame by its tab and it selects everything that host holds, then
carries it. Both halves are one act — the behaviour canon's frame-drag handler
calls its select-the-frame function on its first line and moves the members
after.

This screen had only the second half, and the reason it could not have the first
was a TYPE rather than a missing line. Its selection was `Option<NodeId>` — a
leader with no set — so "select these six" had nowhere to land. Measured before
the round on the built binary through the wire: pressing either host's tab left
`selected` exactly where it was, six cards visibly moving under the cursor while
the inspector went on showing whichever card had been picked minutes earlier.

THE SAME HOLE IS IN THIS TREE TWICE, and the other copy is the mirror image.
Measured the same way: the material node editor holds a `BTreeSet` with no
leader, so selecting two of its nodes makes `query selected` answer NOTHING —
its details panel empties, rename refuses, and the whole `detail.*` read/write
path goes dead — in exactly the case a set exists for.

THE FLOOR WAS MEASURED, not recalled: a probe built at 6.11.1 and run offscreen,
enumerating the meta-object system and then running the classes.

* The free-form canvas family — the shape a node canvas actually IS — publishes
  11 properties and 21 methods, of which exactly TWO name selection (a changed
  signal and a clear) and ZERO name a current, a primary, a lead or an anchor.
  Selecting three of its items leaves its focus item null, so nothing there
  answers "which of the three".
* That changed signal carries NO ARGUMENTS AT ALL, so a listener re-derives the
  delta from a fresh read.
* The item-model family DOES carry a current index — and its whole vocabulary is
  a model index, so it cannot address an item on a canvas. The family that has
  the fact and the family that has the shape are not the same family.
* Zero anchor accessors on the selection model AND on the view.
* Across all three selection-bearing classes exactly ONE member names a reason,
  and it is about focus.
* Selecting a group item reports one selected item to the scene while each child
  reports itself selected: two answers to "what is selected".

So the value lives in the framework, once, generic over whatever a surface calls
a thing. `pinion_core::selection::Selection<T>` holds the members in arrival
order and the leader AS AN INDEX INTO THEM, which is what makes "the inspector
follows something that is not selected" unrepresentable rather than merely
avoided. The free-floating cursor a keyboard walks WITHOUT selecting is a
different fact and already has a home (`widgets::roving`); conflating the two is
what leaves a surface unable to say which of them moved. Every mutation returns a

R1707.decision_summary:
A filter says what it keeps, and why it dropped the rest.

The analysis tool's capture viewer painted a filter and did not filter.
Measured on the built binary before this round, through the wire: the bar
drew a three-clause query, three saved-filter chips and a
`12,418 / 184,392` matched count, and the message list held its sixteen
rows whatever any of them said. There was no `filter` verb; there was no
text entry anywhere on the screen; pressing a saved chip flipped a
boolean, announced "applied units only", and moved nothing. Every check
in that example was green throughout, because nothing had ever asked what
the filter DID -- the same structural blind spot the sibling screen's
operation table was built to remove, in the same shape.

The framework answer is a layer, not a screen fix. `GridFilter` was
already the predicate -- a conjunction of facets, each naming a column by
ORDINAL and an operand by string -- which is the right shape to evaluate
and the wrong shape to type, to show, or to save.
`pinion_core::widgets::row_query::RowQuery` is the layer between: the
query as a person writes it, parsed against a roster of column NAMES,
keeping each clause's own source text, compiling to the `GridFilter` that
does the work. Two operators join `FilterOp` because the domain needs
them and the floor has neither: `Glob` (segment-aware `?` / `*` / `**`)
and `In` (set membership). And `GridFilter::admit` answers WHICH facet
dropped a row, with `matches` defined in terms of it so the boolean and
the attributed answer cannot drift apart.

The floor was measured by building a probe against 6.11.1 and running it
offscreen, not by reading headers. Its row-filtering proxy filters on ONE
column at a time -- `filterKeyColumn` is a single int, and setting a
second predicate replaces the first (measured 3 rows then 2, where a
conjunction gives 1) -- addresses that column by ORDINAL, offers three
operator setters with no set membership or inequality among them,
publishes 12 properties and 101 methods of which NONE names a reason a
row was dropped, and loses the query the person typed:
`setFilterWildcard("sensors/unit/*")` reads back as
`(?s:sensors/unit/[^/]*)`.

Two judgments the screen forced. The screen opens UNFILTERED even though
the reference mockup shows a query in its bar, because that example's own
row table states why it holds the rows it does -- a fragment run, a
dropped piece, a declaration, an out-of-band payload, an unknown
extension -- and a screen opening with thirteen of them hidden could not
show what it exists to show; the reference's exact query is preserved as
the first saved filter instead. And the query text is held as the text
FIELD'S OWN BUFFER rather than a `Signal<String>` beside it, so the list
filters live as the reference's does and "what the bar shows" and "what
the list runs" are one read rather than two copies.
changes_bullets: Framework (`pinion-core`):
`widgets::grid_sort::FilterOp` gains `Glob` (wire `~=`) and `In` (wire
`:`), with `FilterOp::ALL` so a caller enumerating the vocabulary
cannot enumerate a stale subset. `glob_matches` is iterative with a
backtrack point (`?` = one non-separator character, `*` = a run within
one `/` segment, `**` = a run across them), so a pattern off the wire
cannot blow the stack. `members_of` is the shared reading of an `In`
operand.
`ColumnFacet::any_of` is the only constructor for a set facet, and it
REFUSES a member containing the comma the operand is joined by --
turning a limit that would otherwise be documented into one that is
checked.
`GridFilter::admit` returns `Admission::{Admitted, Rejected{facet}}`,
naming the FIRST facet that refused; `matches` is now defined in terms
of it rather than beside it.
`CellValue::matches_facet` gains both arms, each following the policy
of the op it refines: `Glob` is textual over the display label like
`Contains`, `In` reuses the TYPE-AWARE `matches_filter` member by
member so `sn in (024, 25)` matches an `Int(24)` exactly as `sn = 024`
already does.
New `widgets::row_query`: `RowQuery::parse(text, columns)` with
`Clause{column, col, op, operand, text}`, `QueryError` with six arms
each naming the offending text, `filter()` compiling to a `GridFilter`
whose facet index IS the clause index, `admit` / `rejecting_clause`
for attribution, and `to_text` normal form that re-parses to the same
predicate. 12 tests, including one asserting every `FilterOp` is
writable.
`Rect::contains_point` lifted out of the node lab, which was about to
be copied into the capture viewer for the same click-to-caret reason.
Screen B (`hello-packet-view`):
`spec::QUERY_COLUMNS` (9 names, wider than the 7 columns on purpose --
`note` and `fragment` are facts a row carries and shows inside itself),
`spec::QUERY_PLACEHOLDER`, `spec::EXAMPLE_QUERY` (the reference's own,
in this screen's vocabulary), `spec::GESTURES` (this screen's first),
and `SAVED_FILTERS` becomes `&[SavedFilter{name, query}]`.
`RowSpec::attributes` is the roster-ordered read a query does.
The bar is a real text field: `QUERY_TAG` mounted as an extra External
through `blur_committing_field_extra`, `WidgetCore::State` moves from
`()` to `(TextFieldState, u32)`, `apply_key` routes to
`edit_field_keymap` while the box has focus, and `WidgetView`'s two
caret hooks make it clickable. The query is the FIELD'S buffer, so the
filter is live as it is typed.
`ViewState::{query, kept, why_hidden, cursor_row, query_fault}` are the
one derivation the painter, the hit test, the roving roster, the
accessibility tree and the wire all read.
Wire: `filter` verb (refusing a malformed query with the reason);
`query`, `query_clauses`, `query_fault`, `kept_rows`, `why_hidden`
reads; `spec` publishes gestures, roster, placeholder, example and the
saved filters' queries.
The count line derives when filtered and keeps the capture's scale when
not; the fault is PAINTED, not only wired.
Framework (`pinion-widget-paint`): `text_field::view_field` declares its
own text run `part_of` the field. The run has carried a tag since R1615
and no declaration, so it was an unclassified region in every voice
census in the tree; the second screen to grow a field is what surfaced
that the first was carrying one.
Gates: `r1707_every_gesture_this_screen_advertises_is_answered` (with a
non-empty-population assertion, because an empty one reads as a kept
promise), `r1707_a_query_narrows_the_paint_the_press_the_cursor_and_the_count`
(four channels together, plus a swept press over the whole list pane and
per-row attribution), `r1707_a_saved_filter_chip_runs_the_query_it_names`,
`r1707_a_press_in_the_query_box_lands_on_a_byte_of_the_query`. The Tab
ring gate gains the query box, the row/cell populations of the forward
and voice gates become the kept set, and the voice total NAMES the
unclassified regions instead of only counting them — which is what found
the one this round added, in a minute.
Deleted, on a counterfactual's evidence: the stand-aside arm in
`Hit::at` and the nine-point test guarding it. On this screen nothing is
painted under the query box, so `Hit::None` was the answer with or
without the arm — the arm did nothing and the test could not fail.
verification_bullets: Baseline, taken BEFORE the round on the built binary through the wire,
not read out of the source:
`hello-packet-view` answered `row_count` = 16 with every saved filter
toggled and every value the bar painted; `filter` did not exist
(`UnknownInvokePath`); `operations` and `gestures` did not exist
(`UnknownIntrospectPath`); the painted filter bar held

`toggle_saved` moved `saved` and nothing else.

its row-filtering proxy publishes 12 properties and 101 methods; 6 and

a hidden row's `mapFromSource` is an invalid index, the same answer for

A filter says what it keeps, and why it dropped the rest.

The analysis tool's capture viewer painted a filter and did not filter.
Measured on the built binary before this round, through the wire: the bar
drew a three-clause query, three saved-filter chips and a
`12,418 / 184,392` matched count, and the message list held its sixteen
rows whatever any of them said. There was no `filter` verb; there was no
text entry anywhere on the screen; pressing a saved chip flipped a
boolean, announced "applied units only", and moved nothing. Every check
in that example was green throughout, because nothing had ever asked what
the filter DID -- the same structural blind spot the sibling screen's
operation table was built to remove, in the same shape.

The framework answer is a layer, not a screen fix. `GridFilter` was
already the predicate -- a conjunction of facets, each naming a column by
ORDINAL and an operand by string -- which is the right shape to evaluate
and the wrong shape to type, to show, or to save.
`pinion_core::widgets::row_query::RowQuery` is the layer between: the
query as a person writes it, parsed against a roster of column NAMES,
keeping each clause's own source text, compiling to the `GridFilter` that
does the work. Two operators join `FilterOp` because the domain needs
them and the floor has neither: `Glob` (segment-aware `?` / `*` / `**`)
and `In` (set membership). And `GridFilter::admit` answers WHICH facet
dropped a row, with `matches` defined in terms of it so the boolean and
the attributed answer cannot drift apart.

The floor was measured by building a probe against 6.11.1 and running it
offscreen, not by reading headers. Its row-filtering proxy filters on ONE
column at a time -- `filterKeyColumn` is a single int, and setting a
second predicate replaces the first (measured 3 rows then 2, where a
conjunction gives 1) -- addresses that column by ORDINAL, offers three
operator setters with no set membership or inequality among them,
publishes 12 properties and 101 methods of which NONE names a reason a
row was dropped, and loses the query the person typed:
`setFilterWildcard("sensors/unit/*")` reads back as
`(?s:sensors/unit/[^/]*)`.

the reference mockup shows a query in its bar, because that example's own
row table states why it holds the rows it does -- a fragment run, a
dropped piece, a declaration, an out-of-band payload, an unknown
extension -- and a screen opening with thirteen of them hidden could not
show what it exists to show; the reference's exact query is preserved as
the first saved filter instead. And the query text is held as the text
FIELD'S OWN BUFFER rather than a `Signal<String>` beside it, so the list
filters live as the reference's does and "what the bar shows" and "what
the list runs" are one read rather than two copies.

R1709.decision_summary:
R1709 — a resize is followed by pixels, and a window that is dark says why.

A recovery that never verifies it recovered is not a recovery. Until this round
pinion's whole answer to a swapchain that would not hand over an image was one
line — reconfigure the surface, skip the frame — repeated on every failed frame
for ever, under a comment asserting that it "re-establishes the swapchain so the
NEXT frame acquires a fresh texture". Nothing had ever checked whether the next
frame did, and on one real window it does not: measured, a never-mapped X11
window on this host's driver goes dark after a single resize and stays dark, and
scene/screenshot answers RenderBackendUnavailable for the rest of the process.

Three things are decided here.

FIRST, the response to a failed present is a LADDER whose rung is chosen by how
many attempts in a row have failed since the last frame reached the screen
(pinion_gpu::{Missed, Rung, SurfaceHealth}). That makes "did the previous
response work?" structural rather than assumed: if a rung worked, the next frame
presents, the count resets, and the ladder is never climbed — so the ordinary
case (a resized, mapped window) still costs exactly one reconfigure. Reconfigure,
then remake the surface, then repeat the cheap rung while publishing that
everything known has been tried. Repeated deliberately does not give up, because
a surface reachable only through a reconfigure would be dead for ever if it did.

Two counters, not one, because they answer different questions: a frame missed
because the surface BROKE and a frame missed because the window is WAITING
(occluded, timed out) are both frames a viewer did not see, but only the first is
evidence that recovery is needed. Collapsing them would send a window that sat
occluded five frames straight past the cheap rung to the exhausted one having
tried nothing.

SECOND, the ladder runs in the frame that just reconfigured the surface for the
size the window actually has — the emitted renderer's own acquire, which retries
in-frame — and NOT in the capture path, which takes one rung and reports. Both
halves of that split were forced by measurement after the first design got them
backwards, and both are recorded below.

THIRD, presentability is PUBLISHED. scene/render_fidelity carries how many
frames in a row missed the screen, how many of those were breakages, why the last
one missed, which rung it earned, and how many times this window's surface has
had to be remade over its whole life. present_ok is one frame's outcome and
cannot distinguish a dropped frame from a window dark since a resize forty frames
ago; that inability is why a permanently unpresentable surface went unnoticed for
the life of the tree.

The floor was built and run rather than read. The reference toolkit's
rendering-hardware-interface names four outcomes for a frame that missed the
screen and publishes a per-window presentable fact, and gives the consumer
nothing to remember it with: no consecutive-failure count, no frames-since-last-
present, no record that a recovery was attempted or whether it worked, no
distinction between resizing a swapchain and remaking a surface, no reason for
the last failure. Each of those five was proven ABSENT BY COMPILE FAILURE
against a 6.11.1 build, which is a test rather than a reading. So the ladder is
entirely the consumer's to run there, and entirely the consumer's to remember;
here it is the framework's, and it is on the wire.
changes_bullets: MEASURED FIRST, AND THE DEBT FILE WAS WRONG TWICE. Its hypothesis was that the
surface was configured for a size the X drawable never took. Instrumented, all
three parties agreed — xwininfo said 1100x700, winit's inner_size() said
1100x700, the swapchain config was 1100x700 — and the window was still dead.
Isolated in a 200-line reproducer with no framework in it: a frame drawn after
the window resized WITHOUT touching the surface presents fine; configure() to
the new size makes every acquire outdated for ever; dropping the surface and
making another one for the same window presents again. The reconfigure is the
poison, and it is exactly what this tree ran. And "unmapped" names one cell of
four — real Xorg x hidden is dead, real Xorg x mapped is fine, a bare offscreen
server is fine either way, same adapter — so R1708 had changed two variables at
once and named the wrong one.
pinion-gpu: new `health` module. `Missed` (five arms, one per non-presentable
acquisition status, with `is_invalidation` telling a breakage from a wait and
`of` mapping wgpu's status once for both paths that present); `Rung`
(Reconfigured / Rebuilt / Repeated); `SurfaceHealth` holding the two counters,
the last reason, the last rung and the cumulative rebuild count. The decision is
separated from the action so the ladder is unit-testable with no GPU.
`GpuContext::recover` replaces `configure_surface`, which had no other consumer
once both paths went through the ladder. `GpuContext::new` now takes a
`W: Clone + 'static` and keeps a closure that can make the surface AGAIN — the
one place the target type is named, and what makes the heavy rung reachable at
all. `GpuSurface::rebuild`'s three lines are the whole method: the replacement is
created while the old surface lives, the ASSIGNMENT drops the old one, and only
then is the new one configured. Configuring a second surface for one window
while the first is alive fails outright (`Invalid surface`), which the first
draft did — and getting the order right is what let the field stay a plain
`Surface` instead of an `Option`.
pinion-forge: the emitted renderer's five-arm status match becomes one call into
the ladder, and the acquire RETRIES IN-FRAME while a new rung is earned. Its
`render` settles the ladder on a presented frame, and it publishes
`surface_health()`. The template's own comment, which asserted the false claim
above, now records what was measured instead.
pinion-shell: `VelloRenderer::surface_health` (no default — the rule
`last_acquire_us` and `capture_rgba8` already state); the capture path runs the
same ladder through the same call; `RenderFidelity` carries the health; and the
shell projects it at the one point that holds a renderer.
pinion-runtime / pinion-rpc: `PresentHealth` and `PresentHealthView`, published
under `scene/render_fidelity`.`health`, with the vocabulary's spellings coming
from pinion_gpu rather than being written a second time.
THREE COUNTERFACTUALS PASSED AND CHANGED THE DESIGN. Under the demo's first
order — resize, settle, screenshot — three of four repairs could each be deleted
with everything still green, because a capture IS a present and healed whatever
was broken before anything looked. A new section that only READS then falsified
two of them outright. The "a frame that missed asks for another one" repair NEVER
FIRED: paint_seq stuck at 3 for 3.2 seconds with a rung recorded and no frame
following, so every earlier "recovers on the next frame" observation had been the
capture healing it. It is deleted rather than documented. And the capture path's
in-frame climb was spending the HEAVY rung on a window merely mid-resize — a
capture cannot tell that from a broken surface, because persistence is a fact
about successive frames. So the climb moved to `render`, which runs every frame
and knows the size it just configured for, and the capture takes one rung and
reports.
A demo section was DELETED for the same reason and the deletion is commented:
"an agent that resizes and immediately asks for a picture gets one" is a premise
the measurement refuted, and the only way to satisfy it was to let one request
rebuild a surface that was about to be fine.
Harness: `screen_spec`, `declared_panes`, `design_size`, `names_in_spec`,
`declared_and_painted` and `assert_declared_panes_on_screen` lifted out of
r1708's demo on their second consumer, before a third derived them differently.
r1708's demo, repaired where this round's blast radius found it environment-
dependent rather than wrong: it located the window by NAME among root's children
and under a window manager that is the DECORATION FRAME, which carries the
application's title (measured under mutter: frame 1653x966, application window
1625x900), so it had been resizing the frame. It now finds the window by its own
class, asks the X server what size was actually GRANTED instead of predicting it,
and when a reparenting manager refuses the resize outright it says so loudly and
reports how many screens the real-path section really ran on. Confirmed
pre-existing by stashing this round's work and reproducing the identical failure.
verification_bullets: THE DEFECT, BEFORE AND AFTER, ON THE HOST THAT HAS IT. Before: one resize of a
hidden window took present_ok from true to false and it never came back — eight
consecutive dead frames across two resizes, with scene/screenshot answering
RenderBackendUnavailable on all eight. After: the window presents again within
the same frame, and scene/screenshot answers at every size on all three analyser
screens. The wire says why it needed to: `rebuilds` reads 1, 2, 3 across three
resizes on the affected display and 0 on an unaffected one, from the same binary
running the same assertions, with identical ink counts.
THE GATE THAT WAS MISSING — tools/demos/r1709_a_resize_is_followed_by_pixels.py,
156 assertions over three screens, in HIDDEN mode, which is the mode every demo
and every CI job runs and the one cell of four where the defect occurs. It asks
the question no file in this tree had asked: after a resize, is there anything on
the screen. Of the sixteen demos that take screenshots, none also resized, and
scene/snapshot from=paint reads the encoded scene — built before the swapchain is
ever asked for an image — so every introspection surface answers healthy about a
window nobody can see. Green on both displays.
COUNTERFACTUALS: 8/8 at unit level (the ladder never climbs; a presented frame
does not reset it; a wait counts as a breakage; the heavy rung is counted every
failure; an outdated swapchain classified as a wait; a rung renamed on the wire;
a dark window published as presenting; the reason dropped on the way to the
wire). Integration: 1/4 on the first pass and 3/4 after the redesign those three
findings forced — and the fourth is registered rather than papered over
(debt-a-captured-frame-settles-a-ladder-nothing-can-observe: the capture path's
ladder settle can only be the ONLY settle for an application driven purely by
captures with no event-loop frames, and this tree has no such consumer, so the
line stays and the gate's absence is written down).
THE FLOOR, BY TEST RATHER THAN BY READING. A probe built against the reference
toolkit at 6.11.1 and run offscreen drives beginFrame and reads its four named
outcomes, and confirms the per-window presentable fact. Five further queries were
each proven ABSENT BY COMPILE FAILURE: consecutive failures, frames since last
present, whether a recovery was attempted or worked, resize-versus-remake, and a
reason for the last failure. Five for five.
CRATES: pinion-gpu, pinion-forge, pinion-runtime, pinion-rpc, pinion-shell —
tests and clippy green, plus workspace clippy over every example's generated
renderer (the template changed, so the whole tree recompiles it).

R1709.publishable_decision_summary:
R1709 — a resize is followed by pixels, and a window that is dark says why.

A recovery that never verifies it recovered is not a recovery. Until this round
pinion's whole answer to a swapchain that would not hand over an image was one
line — reconfigure the surface, skip the frame — repeated on every failed frame
for ever, under a comment asserting that it "re-establishes the swapchain so the
NEXT frame acquires a fresh texture". Nothing had ever checked whether the next
frame did, and on one real window it does not: measured, a never-mapped X11
window on this host's driver goes dark after a single resize and stays dark, and
scene/screenshot answers RenderBackendUnavailable for the rest of the process.

Three things are decided here.

FIRST, the response to a failed present is a LADDER whose rung is chosen by how
many attempts in a row have failed since the last frame reached the screen
(pinion_gpu::{Missed, Rung, SurfaceHealth}). That makes "did the previous
response work?" structural rather than assumed: if a rung worked, the next frame
presents, the count resets, and the ladder is never climbed — so the ordinary
case (a resized, mapped window) still costs exactly one reconfigure. Reconfigure,
then remake the surface, then repeat the cheap rung while publishing that
everything known has been tried. Repeated deliberately does not give up, because
a surface reachable only through a reconfigure would be dead for ever if it did.

Two counters, not one, because they answer different questions: a frame missed
because the surface BROKE and a frame missed because the window is WAITING
(occluded, timed out) are both frames a viewer did not see, but only the first is
evidence that recovery is needed. Collapsing them would send a window that sat
occluded five frames straight past the cheap rung to the exhausted one having
tried nothing.

SECOND, the ladder runs in the frame that just reconfigured the surface for the
size the window actually has — the emitted renderer's own acquire, which retries
in-frame — and NOT in the capture path, which takes one rung and reports. Both
halves of that split were forced by measurement after the first design got them
backwards, and both are recorded below.

THIRD, presentability is PUBLISHED. scene/render_fidelity carries how many
frames in a row missed the screen, how many of those were breakages, why the last
one missed, which rung it earned, and how many times this window's surface has
had to be remade over its whole life. present_ok is one frame's outcome and
cannot distinguish a dropped frame from a window dark since a resize forty frames
ago; that inability is why a permanently unpresentable surface went unnoticed for
the life of the tree.

The floor was built and run rather than read. The reference toolkit's
rendering-hardware-interface names four outcomes for a frame that missed the
screen and publishes a per-window presentable fact, and gives the consumer
nothing to remember it with: no consecutive-failure count, no frames-since-last-
present, no record that a recovery was attempted or whether it worked, no
distinction between resizing a swapchain and remaking a surface, no reason for
the last failure. Each of those five was proven ABSENT BY COMPILE FAILURE
against a 6.11.1 build, which is a test rather than a reading. So the ladder is
entirely the consumer's to run there, and entirely the consumer's to remember;
here it is the framework's, and it is on the wire.
