R1710.decision_summary:
A resize says what it GRANTED, and which declared bound moved it.

A window declares a floor for its own inner size. Before this round nothing in
the framework resolved a resize request against that declaration, and the
response echoed the request back with a constant `requested: true`. Measured on
this host, driving the analysis-tool dashboard (floor 1440x900) through
`scene/resize` with a 1560x880 ask: on the bare offscreen server every gate in
this tree runs on, the window really became 880 tall, because the declared floor
was enforced by NOTHING; on a real desktop the window manager enforced it and
the window sat at 900 while the wire still answered 880. Two defects hiding each
other — one that no test could ever fail, and one that makes the §2 #2 path an
AI agent drives answer with a number the window does not have.

The decision: the framework owns the resolution. `pinion_core::size_grant`
carries the bounds a surface declares (`SizeBounds`), which bound decided each
axis (`Bound`), and the resolution of one ask (`Grant`). The shell projects its
`SizeStrategy::min_inner_floor` — the same floor it declares to the window
system at create — into those bounds, the dispatcher resolves the ask against
them, and the closure forwards the GRANTED size, so the answer no longer depends
on which window system is running. `scene/resize` publishes the resolution:
granted size, the ask, per-axis bound with the declared extent that moved it,
`as_asked`, and `applied`. A `dry_run` param answers the same resolution without
touching the window (§2 #3), which is also how a client reads a window's floor
in one call.

`Grant` does not store the granted size — it derives it from the bound, so a
grant that names a floor cannot also report the asked number. `SizeBounds::new`
refuses a floor above its ceiling, which is what leaves `resolve` with no
precedence rule to learn. `applied` replaces `requested`, whose documented
`false` state was unreachable, and it means dry-run and only dry-run: an
unreachable closure stays an `Err`, so one value never answers two reasons.

Against the reference at 6.11.1, measured by building a probe rather than
reading headers: its widget layer resolves an ask against the declared bounds
client-side (880 -> 900, 1340 -> 1440) and its window layer does not — which is
exactly where this tree was. That half is parity and this round takes it. Five
things it does not have were each proven absent by a compile error naming the
member: a return value from `resize()`, a reason for a refusal, a per-axis
"which bound moved me", a signal carrying asked and granted, and any way to ask
without acting. Its window class publishes 18 properties and 52 methods, of
which zero name a reason and zero name a grant.

Deliberately NOT done: no ceiling is declared to the window system, so none is
enforced. Capping only the RPC path would give one question two answers
depending on which path asked it — the shape of defect this round removes.
changes_bullets: NEW `pinion_core::size_grant` — `SizeBounds` (declared floor/ceiling, with a
constructor that refuses a contradictory pair), `Bound` (`AsAsked` /
`Floor{at}` / `Ceiling{at}`, publishing `KINDS` for the wire census), and
`Grant` (the ask plus the two bounds; the granted size is DERIVED). 10 tests,
including an exhaustive grid proving the resolution is order-independent.
`pinion_shell::SizeStrategy::window_bounds()` — the bounds a programmatic
resize resolves against, derived from `min_inner_floor` so the enforcement and
the declaration to the window system are one fact.
`pinion_shell::SizeStrategy::content_bounds(min, max)` — one home for a
declared pair that THREE sites clamped by hand (the live intrinsic walk, the
headless screenshot walk, and the new resolution). A contradictory
declaration now resolves in favour of the floor instead of reaching
`u32::clamp`, whose assertion panicked the render pass.
`ShellCore::primary_window_bounds()` + a method-gated stamp onto
`DispatchContext::window_bounds` (new field + `with_window_bounds`), read by
the `scene/resize` arm; absent resolves to `UNBOUNDED`, so every surface that
declares nothing is byte-unchanged.
`pinion_rpc::resize` — `resize()` takes the bounds, forwards the granted size,
and answers a `ResizeOutcome` of {granted width/height, `asked`,
`width_bound`, `height_bound`, `as_asked`, `applied`}. `requested` is gone
(constant-true; its documented `false` was unreachable). `ResizeParams` gains
`dry_run` (absent = false).
`wire_census`: `ResizeOutcome` and `ResizeParams` rewritten, new `SizeBound`
type whose `kind` vocabulary is `accepting(Bound::KINDS)` — sourced from the
type that owns it.
Harness `resize_and_settle` waits for the size the response says was GRANTED,
not the size asked, and prints the divergence when they differ.
NEW demo `tools/demos/r1710_a_resize_says_what_it_granted.py` — three screens,
the floor MEASURED per screen rather than written down, five asks each checked
against the painted frame, per-axis reasons in both directions, the dry run,
the zero refusal, the specification surviving a clamped resize, a pixel scan,
and a second-channel section reading the declared minimum back out of
`WM_NORMAL_HINTS`.
`pinion-shell` gains three unit tests over the two bound projections, because
the only gate above `content_bounds` could not see it being wrong.
verification_bullets: Counterfactuals 15/15 caught, in three plans and two re-runs. Eight at the
unit gate (`cargo test -p pinion-core -p pinion-rpc --lib`): the granted
extent derived from the bound, the floor-exact ask, the contradictory-pair
refusal on either axis, `Bound::at`, forwarding the granted size, the dry
run's `applied`, the dry run not reaching the window, and the zero refusal.
Three PASSED on the first pass and every one was a finding — see below; all
three are caught after the repairs.
★ CF-12 PASSED and changed the demo's design. The gate measures each screen's
floor rather than writing it down, which is right (one of the three screens
declares a floor its design size is taller than) and which also made every
later section self-consistent with a WRONG floor: replacing
`min_inner_floor` with `initial_logical_size` in the shell left the whole
demo green. Repaired by reading a second, independent channel — the minimum
the shell declared to the window system, back out of `WM_NORMAL_HINTS`
through a libX11 probe, which answers even for the unmapped windows the
harness runs by default. Re-run: CAUGHT, and the message is the diagnosis
★ CF-13 / CF-14 PASSED and moved a gate's layer. The only gate above
`SizeStrategy::content_bounds` was the one binding that declares a ceiling,
and that binding's content bbox reaches NEITHER bound: quadrupling the
declared ceiling and dropping the declared floor to 1x1 both left its demo
green. Repaired with three `pinion-shell` unit tests on the pure function;
re-run at that gate: 3/3 CAUGHT (a fifteenth case covering the
contradictory-declaration fallback was added there and is caught too).
Unit: `pinion-core` + `pinion-rpc` 4,878 green; `pinion-shell` 252 green.
Clippy green on all three changed crates (`--all-targets`, pedantic).
Integration UI test `r1710_a_resize_says_what_it_granted.py`: 3 screens,
134+ assertions — the floor measured per screen, five asks each checked
against the PAINTED frame, per-axis bounds asserted in both directions, the
dry run changing nothing and answering what the real call then answers, the
zero refusal by name, the analyser's declared specification surviving a
clamped resize, a pixel scan at the clamped size, and the second-channel
section. Green on BOTH displays this host has — the bare offscreen server and
the real desktop with a window manager — which is the property the round
exists for.
Blast radius: 22 demos driving `scene/resize` / `resize_and_settle`, all
green. FOUR were red first, all of one cause, and it is the round's most
valuable finding: they resized windows BELOW the floor their own bindings
declare, and passed only because the bare display enforces no minimum. Two
bindings were wrong and now declare `OpenResizable { min: None }` (both are
screens whose whole subject is shrinking); one gate was wrong and now drives
the smallest LEGAL size, read out of the screen's own declaration.
★ Driving that floor immediately found more: at its own declared minimum the
node lab stops painting five regions its specification names. Pinned in the
gate BY NAME (so the set failing in either direction is a failure) and filed
rather than smoothed over.
R1708's demo now passes on the managed display, with its real window-system
section running on 3 of 3 screens where it had run on none.
carry_forward_bullets: No window CEILING is declared to the window system: the shell never calls
`with_max_inner_size`, so `IntrinsicAfterFirstPaint`'s `max` bounds the
content walk only. Measured: exactly one binding declares a real ceiling, and
its content bbox does not reach it — two counterfactuals (quadruple the
ceiling, drop the floor to 1x1) left that binding's own demo green. Filed;
the repair is to declare it on BOTH paths or not at all, and which of those
the `max` means is a consumer's judgment, not this round's.
`Bound::Ceiling` therefore has one production producer (the content walk) and
no integration consumer that exercises it. Kept rather than trimmed: the
reference has a maximum on both its layers, and cutting the arm would make the
next binding that declares a ceiling reinvent it.
One unexplained observation, registered rather than forgotten: under a window
manager, a below-floor width ask once landed at 1495 — neither the ask (1340)
nor the declared floor (1440). An isolated re-measurement (four asks, eight
samples each over 3.2 s) always landed at exactly the floor. Not reproduced,
not explained, and not claimed fixed. It now surfaces as a `resize_and_settle`
timeout rather than as a silent pass, which is the safety this round bought.
`scene/windows` does not publish a window's bounds. Stated, not filed: the
dry run answers the floor in ONE call, through the same resolution the real
path runs, which is stronger than the reference's two readable properties plus
a clamp rule the caller has to know.
The demo's real-path refusal report (R1709) is kept although nothing hit it
this round: today every request form was granted under the manager, but the
R1709 observation of a refusal was never reproduced either, and a
measurement-based skip cannot turn into a false green.

the window sat at 900 while the wire still answered 880. Two defects hiding each
other — one that no test could ever fail, and one that makes the §2 #2 path an
AI agent drives answer with a number the window does not have.

The decision: the framework owns the resolution. `pinion_core::size_grant`
carries the bounds a surface declares (`SizeBounds`), which bound decided each
axis (`Bound`), and the resolution of one ask (`Grant`). The shell projects its
`SizeStrategy::min_inner_floor` — the same floor it declares to the window
system at create — into those bounds, the dispatcher resolves the ask against
them, and the closure forwards the GRANTED size, so the answer no longer depends
on which window system is running. `scene/resize` publishes the resolution:
granted size, the ask, per-axis bound with the declared extent that moved it,
`as_asked`, and `applied`. A `dry_run` param answers the same resolution without
touching the window (§2 #3), which is also how a client reads a window's floor
in one call.

`Grant` does not store the granted size — it derives it from the bound, so a
grant that names a floor cannot also report the asked number. `SizeBounds::new`
refuses a floor above its ceiling, which is what leaves `resolve` with no
precedence rule to learn. `applied` replaces `requested`, whose documented
`false` state was unreachable, and it means dry-run and only dry-run: an
unreachable closure stays an `Err`, so one value never answers two reasons.

Against the reference at 6.11.1, measured by building a probe rather than
reading headers: its widget layer resolves an ask against the declared bounds
client-side (880 -> 900, 1340 -> 1440) and its window layer does not — which is
exactly where this tree was. That half is parity and this round takes it. Five
things it does not have were each proven absent by a compile error naming the
member: a return value from `resize()`, a reason for a refusal, a per-axis
"which bound moved me", a signal carrying asked and granted, and any way to ask
without acting. Its window class publishes 18 properties and 52 methods, of
which zero name a reason and zero name a grant.

Deliberately NOT done: no ceiling is declared to the window system, so none is
enforced. Capping only the RPC path would give one question two answers
depending on which path asked it — the shape of defect this round removes.

R1711.decision_summary:
A screen says how small it can get, and what stops it going smaller.

Every binding in this tree declares a floor for its own window — 225 of them —
and since R1710 the framework enforces it. Not one of those numbers had ever
been driven against the screen it is about. R1710 tried, with the predicate a
reader reaches for first — *is every declared region still painted?* — and
recorded five regions of the analysis tool's node lab as lost at its own floor,
filed as a defect of the screen. Re-measured through `scene/scroll_reach`: all
five are `scrollable`, each carrying the offset that shows it, and the screen's
`lost` count at that size is zero. The screen was fine; the question was wrong.
Content a reader can scroll to is not content the window is too small for.

The opposite error was measured in the same session. At 1506 pixels wide the
node lab reports nothing out of sight — because one pixel of a 100-pixel status
chip is still on screen and its 312-pixel inspector pane still starts at 1313.
A floor derived from that answer is a floor at which the inspector is sliced and
the chip is a line. "Some of it is visible" is the right answer to *what is the
reader not looking at* and the wrong answer to *how small can this get*.

So the decision is two derivations rather than one. `pinion_core::reach::cut`
answers what a size can never show WHOLE, judged against the viewport's
reachable box instead of its shown one — which makes the answer independent of
where the reader happens to have scrolled, and makes scrolling not a defect.
`pinion_core::size_floor` searches with it: a bisection whose answer is a
boundary it EVALUATED (this extent fits, one less does not, and here is what one
less loses) rather than a minimum it inferred, refusing rather than answering
when the ceiling itself does not fit or when nothing is ever lost. `Measured`
cannot be built without its evidence, so the number and the reason for it are
one fact.

`scene/size_floor` publishes the search beside the declaration and says in one
word which case a screen is in: `short` (a reader can shrink this window past
what it can show — a defect), `exact`, `roomier` (the window refuses sizes it
could take — a decision, and this is how anyone can tell it was made), or
`undeclared`. Each axis carries the marks that go out of reach one pixel below
it. The reference's `minimumSizeHint()` is a bare size whose cause is
unobtainable from outside the widget.

The pair of the two axis answers is a THIRD question and the round asked it
because it answered no. Each axis is measured with the other at the ceiling —
which is what a window minimum is — and the pair lost nine marks on the node lab
and twelve on the capture viewer. The cause was `external::layout_size` falling
back to the design size when EITHER axis was under its floor, so narrowing a
window un-shortened its layout and pushed content out of the bottom. That clamp
is per-axis now, and the pair fits on all three screens.

What the instrument then found, on its first run: the capture viewer declared
`SizeStrategy::Fixed` — a window a reader cannot shrink at all — while telling
its own layout it lays out down to `MIN_W x MIN_H`. Those two numbers are
exactly the measured floor, 1425x346, and the window would not go 554 pixels
shorter than a size the screen works at. It is `OpenResizable` now.

Measured at the reference 6.11.1 by building a probe and running it offscreen:
it DOES derive a floor from its content and DOES enforce it client-side, and
content reachable by scrolling correctly does not force it. Three parities, and
the third is this round's predicate. What it cannot do, each proven by a compile
error naming the member (5/5): say which child forced the floor (on the widget
or on the layout), ask about a size the window is not at, enumerate what would
be out of reach there, or announce that the derived floor moved. Across its
widget, layout and scroll-area classes: 139 properties, 73 methods, zero reason
names.

answers are a size in their own right. Generic over what the probe reports, so
the module is tested against synthetic predicates including the pathological
ones. 11 tests.
NEW `pinion_core::reach::cut` — every mark a size can never show whole, at any

`out_of_sight`, lifted this round on its second caller, so the two derivations

including the case that made it a separate function and the one that pins its
independence from the scroll offset.
`pinion_core::external::layout_size` clamps PER AXIS. It fell back to the design
size when either axis was under its floor, which threw away the live extent of

`scene/size_floor` — new routed read, method catalogue and `WIRE_TYPES` entries

`scene/scroll_reach` gains `at: {width, height}` (§2 #3): reach judged at a size

scanned: the capture viewer at 1425x346 shows app bar, filter, context strip,
four message rows across three panes and the reassembly strip — a size that

carry_forward_bullets: The node lab's measured floor EQUALS its layout clamp by construction: below
`MIN_W` the screen stops reflowing and clips, so the search finds the clamp
rather than an independent fact about the ink. That is a true answer about the
binding and a weak one about the screen — the honest reading is "with the layout
this binding produces today". The capture viewer and the dashboard do not have
that circularity (their layouts reflow below their declared window floors), and
the round did not try to break it, because separating a layout clamp from a
window floor is a decision each screen makes.
`scene/size_floor` costs 26 probes, each a full mirror view and layout (~20 ms
per screen here). It is published as `probes` rather than hidden, and it is a
read a caller chooses to make; nothing calls it per frame.
The two remaining `Fixed` screens of the tool were left alone: the dashboard's
declaration is exactly its measured floor (`exact` without anyone deciding), and
the 178 other `Fixed` bindings in the tree are unmeasured. The instrument for
that census now exists — see
[[debt-a-windows-floor-is-a-default-nobody-decided]].
`cut` reports a mark that is partly visible AND partly unreachable, which is
what a floor needs, but it says nothing about a mark that is fully reachable and
merely OVERLAPPED by a sibling. That is `pointer_reach`'s question and it stays
there.
`PairFit::Loses` has no production consumer now that all three screens fit —
kept because it is the field that stops the answer's likeliest misreading, and
because the two screens that failed it did so until this round's own clamp
repair.
No CEILING is measured. A screen too small is a defect a reader meets; a screen
too large is not, and inventing a maximum nobody declares would be a number with
nothing behind it. R1710's carry about the unenforced window ceiling is
unchanged.

R1711.1.decision_summary:
R1711.1 — the closing audit, and both of its findings were in this round's own
work.

The question was "is every new debt registered", and the standing rule is that
it can only be answered by RUNNING the audit. Running it found two things that
were not debts to file but defects to fix, so they are fixed here.

FIRST: the gate's negative direction was vacuous. Section B claims "one pixel
less and the named marks are cut", and what it asserted was
`scroll_reach(at=short)["marks"] > 0` — the number of painted marks, which is
positive on any screen that paints anything. The cause is structural rather than
careless: `scene/scroll_reach` answers the WEAK predicate (a mark entirely off
screen), and measured at every one of these six boundary sizes it answers
`lost: 0`, because a mark with one pixel showing is not out of sight. The
sharp predicate had no way to be asked at an arbitrary size.

It does have one, and this round already built it: `scene/size_floor {at: S}`
runs the search with its ceiling AT `S`, so a size the screen does not fit in
comes back as `refused: ceiling_is_short` carrying exactly what is cut there.
Measured across three screens and both axes, that refusal's marks are the SAME
SET as the axis's own `forced_by` (6 of 6). The gate asks that now, and a
counterfactual that moves the published extent one pixel off its measurement is
caught — which the old assertion could not have been, since shifting a boundary
does not change how many marks a screen paints.

SECOND: `Refused::CeilingIsShort` carried an axis that could be confidently
wrong. Measured on the node lab: a ceiling of 1625x359 — short by one pixel of
HEIGHT — was refused with `axis: width`, because width is the axis the search
walks first. The field's doc said "which axis was being measured", which is true
and is not what a reader takes from it.

"Does this size fit" is one question about a size, not two about its axes. The
ceiling probe moved out of the per-axis loop to `measure`, where it is asked
once for both axes, and the field is GONE rather than corrected: the evidence is
what says which way a size is short, and it can be short in both. The other
refusal keeps its axis, because that one is genuinely a property of one search.
The wire's `axis` is nullable to match, and the shared probe makes the search
one probe cheaper.
changes_bullets: `pinion_core::size_floor::measure` probes the ceiling ONCE, before either axis,
and `Refused::CeilingIsShort` carries no axis. `Refused::axis()` answers
`Option<Axis>` — `None` for a size that does not fit, `Some` for the per-axis
arm. Two tests pin it in both directions, including the exact 1625x359 case
that was reported as `width`.
`Floor::probes` accounts for the shared ceiling probe; the search costs one
probe fewer (26 -> 25 on these screens) and the per-axis counts no longer double
count it. The probe-order test asserts the ceiling is asked about FIRST and the
pair LAST, so the shape is checked rather than described.
`pinion_rpc::size_floor::RefusedReport::axis` is `Option<&str>`, censused
nullable beside its closed vocabulary.
`tools/demos/r1711_a_screen_says_how_small_it_can_get.py` — section B's boundary
now drives `scene/size_floor {at}` in both directions: the named extent answers
a floor, one pixel less answers `ceiling_is_short`, that refusal names no axis,
and the marks it names ARE the evidence the axis carried. A new `floor_at`
helper spells the "does this screen fit here" idiom once.
verification_bullets: Counterfactuals 3/3 caught at the demo gate, and the first is the one this
sub-round exists for: publishing an extent one pixel off what was measured is
CAUGHT now and could not have been before — shifting a boundary does not change
how many marks a screen paints, which is all the old assertion read. The other
two: a refusal that names an axis again, and a refusal that reports only part of
what is cut.
Unit: `pinion-core` + `pinion-rpc` green, `--all-targets` (which is what runs
the wire-census integration test — the gap this round filed as
[[debt-the-local-gate-is-a-command-somebody-types]]).
The integration UI test is green on all three screens, 81 assertions, and its
section B now fails on a wrong boundary in either direction.

Measured, and it is why the repair took this shape: at all six boundary sizes
across the three screens, `scene/scroll_reach {at}` answers `lost: 0` while
`scene/size_floor {at}` refuses and names the cut marks — the same set the axis

carry_forward_bullets: Asking "what is cut at size S" is spelled as "run the floor search with its
ceiling at S and read the refusal". That is a real idiom rather than a
workaround — the refusal carries exactly the marks, and the search is the thing

R1712.decision_summary:
A window says what it gives up to get smaller.

A screen has two minimums and they are not the same fact: the size below which
its LAYOUT stops reflowing (below it the window clips instead of rearranging),
and the size below which the WINDOW refuses to shrink. Measured before this
round, all three screens of the analysis tool passed one constant to both. That
is not tidiness — one number cannot express the decision "let the reader make
this window smaller than the size it lays out at, and here is what that costs",
so the decision could not be made. R1689 had already written the price down:
raising the node lab's toolbar floor to 1625 meant "a 1600-wide display no
longer holds this screen. That is a real loss." It stayed a loss for 23 rounds,
because lowering the number would have moved the layout with it.

The debt filed at R1711 said this was a property of ONE of the three screens and
to count before generalising. Counted: it is all three — and one of them became
so at R1711 itself, which changed the capture viewer's window floor to its
layout minimum while filing the debt about exactly that shape. `layout_size` has
exactly three consumers, so the census is complete.

`pinion_core::shrink::ShrinkPolicy` holds both numbers and the names of what the
band between them clips, and it is the only place either number is written: the
layout clamp reads `comfortable`, the window floor reads `floor`. A contradictory
declaration is refused, and because the constructor is `const` — which is where
a binding declares its policy — refusing means it FAILS TO COMPILE. A band that
names nothing it gives up is refused too: if the reader loses nothing between
the two sizes, the layout minimum was the lower number all along. So is a list
of names with no band to give them up in, which is what a screen leaves behind
when its floor is raised back.

`shrink::audit` is the other half, and it reads TWO predicates because a floor
promises two things. What the size cannot show WHOLE is what a concession is
allowed to cost, and it is checked by name against what the binding declared:
clipped-but-undeclared reads `surprised` (a defect), declared-but-not-clipped
reads `stale`. What the size puts OUT OF REACH altogether is what no concession
can excuse, and it reads `unreachable`, which outranks both. Clipping is a
decision a screen may make; losing is not.

The two floors turn out to be the two predicates R1711 already built. `cut`
(what a size can never show whole) is where the layout should stop; `lost` (what
no scroll reaches) is where the window should stop. Nothing new had to be
invented to say where a screen's floor belongs — only the language to say that
there are two of them.

The reference floor was measured by building a probe at 6.11.1 and running it
offscreen on the analysis tool's own shape. It HAS the two numbers and enforces
them client-side, and a caller can put the window floor below the layout minimum
— the window really goes there while the layout keeps reporting the higher
number. That capability is parity, and it is the direction this tree was short
in, which is unusual. What the reference has nothing of is everything about the
band being a claim: no accessor counts or names what is clipped (the sliced pane
reports itself visible), no way to ask about a size the window is not at, no
announcement when the boundary is crossed, no refusal of a contradictory pair
(a floor of 889 and a ceiling of 800 are both held and both reported), and zero
of the 139 properties and 73 methods on its widget, layout and scroll-area
classes carry the idea in their name.

The node lab now concedes 119 pixels of width: its window floor is 1506 where
its layout stops at 1625, and it declares that the app bar's right end and the
inspector are clipped in between. A 1600-pixel display holds the screen again.
The floor is measured rather than chosen — at 1506 the reader can still reach
everything, at 1505 the app bar's state chip goes off the window with no scroll
that brings it back — and the integration test drives both directions. The
height axis was measured too and left rigid on purpose: a 27-pixel concession
clips every full-height pane at once, so its honest declaration is "every pane
on the screen", which buys a reader nothing and costs the list its meaning. The
other two screens declare `rigid`, which is a decision that the window stops
where the layout does, and is deliberately not the same wire answer as a binding
that has never been asked the question.
changes_bullets: `pinion_core::shrink::ShrinkPolicy` — a screen's two floors and the regions the band between them clips, in ONE declaration: the layout clamp reads `comfortable`, the window floor reads `floor`, and there is nowhere to write a second number.

The rule that refuses a bad declaration has one home (`const fn fault`) and two doors: `conceding` panics — a compile error in the `const` context a binding declares in — and `checked` returns the `Fault` for a caller that needs to handle one.

Three refusals, each a statement a screen cannot mean rather than a value out of range: a floor above the layout minimum (per axis, naming the axis), a band that names nothing it gives up, and names with no band to give them up in.

`shrink::audit` checks the declaration against the screen at its own floor and reports three lists, none derivable from the others: `unreachable` (the floor is broken), `unnamed` (the screen gives up more than it admits), `stale` (the declaration outlived its screen). The verdict word is derived from them, never stored.

`ShrinkPolicy::covers` judges by ancestry, so a screen concedes REGIONS and not the runs inside them — measured, two names cover four clipped marks on the node lab — and the audit publishes how many marks each declaration accounted for so the coarser spelling cannot hide its own reach.

`scene/size_floor` grew a `concession` object (censused, eleven fields, its own four-word vocabulary) and a fifth verdict word, `conceded`: the same arithmetic that reads `short` reads `conceded` once a policy accounts for it and the screen honours it.

`SizeStrategy::shrinking(policy, size)` and `WidgetView::shrink_policy()` — the shell's two readers of one declaration, with `declaration_split` on the wire for a binding that reached around the type and spelled its minimum twice.

The node lab concedes 119 pixels of width (floor 1506, layout minimum 1625, giving up `lab.appbar` and `lab.inspector`) so a 1600-pixel display holds it again; the capture viewer and the dashboard declare `rigid`, which is a decision rather than the absence of one.
`crate::ink_of` lifted in pinion-rpc when a third reach walk wanted it — every reach question this crate answers has to measure the same ink the same way.

R1712.1 — the fixture-font test at the §5.37 measure seam now CHOOSES its fixture by measurement instead of naming one: a build host whose resolved sans-serif is the fixture made the discriminating step refuse, exactly as its comment predicted, and swapping by hand would only move the collision to the next host.
verification_bullets: Integration UI test `tools/demos/r1712_a_window_says_what_it_gives_up.py` — three screens, eight sections: the policy is declared and says which kind it is; the audit at the floor is honoured with all three lists empty; the floor is a boundary DRIVEN one pixel below in the predicate its policy binds that axis on; the window really goes there; what is given up is still painted and still pressable; a rigid floor cuts nothing; the two readers read one declaration; and the pixels at the conceded floor are scanned in both halves.

The C section was written wrong first and the capture viewer failed it correctly: a rigid floor is a boundary in the CUT predicate and a conceded one in the REACH predicate, so each axis is now driven in the predicate that binds it.

R1711's own integration test flagged this change as a regression, and it was right to: "what the screen needs is what its binding declares" is a statement about a screen with one minimum. Rewritten to the new truth — needed equals `comfortable`, the declared floor equals `floor`, and the verdict says which of the two cases the screen is in. 84 assertions, all three screens green.

The reference floor was BUILT and RUN, not read: a probe against 6.11.1 in the analysis tool's own shape, offscreen, answering eight questions with numbers (layout minimum 1008x120, enforced; the window floor really reaching 889 below it; a floor of 889 and a ceiling of 800 both held; the sliced pane reporting itself visible; 0 of 139 properties + 73 methods).
Counterfactuals: 13 against the pure layers (`cargo test -p pinion-core -p pinion-rpc`) and 5 against the wire through the integration test itself, each a wrong answer rather than an absent one.

★★★★★ One of them PASSED and it was a finding: inverting `declaration_split` inside `audit_at` left the entire pure-layer suite green, because `audit_at` — the function that assembles the whole concession report — had no test at that layer at all. The report tests build a `ConcessionReport` by hand and check the verdict rule on it; the assembly was only ever exercised through the integration demo, which is the gate living a layer above the defect that R1710 recorded and this round repeated. Repaired with four tests over a scene fixture shaped like the screen itself, and the counterfactual then CAUGHT.

And the fixture cost two wrong answers before it was right: a tagged root does not appear on its children's paths, so ancestry covered nothing; and an app bar as wide as the layout is itself clipped, which the real screen's measurement had said all along.
`pinion-core` 3,673 + `pinion-rpc` 1,269 + `pinion-shell` 252 green, the three screens' own suites green, workspace clippy green, and the 34 demos that drive the analysis tool green.

A build host reported a red that was NOT this round's: the same test fails at HEAD on that host, because its resolved sans-serif is the fixture font. Attributed by stashing and re-measuring on the same host — the rule that an intermittent or host-shaped failure needs two trees measured under one condition.
carry_forward_bullets: 176 bindings still declare no policy at all, and this round is what made that countable: `shrink_policy()` returning `None` (nobody was asked) is deliberately not the same as `rigid` (somebody decided), and `scene/size_floor` omits `concession` entirely for the first. The census is now "boot it and look for the object".

A concession covers by REGION, so a mark that starts being clipped INSIDE a declared region reads honoured. The round chose that granularity knowingly — the alternative enumerates anonymous child indices that move with paint order — and published `covered` so the coarser spelling cannot hide its reach, but publishing is a report and not a gate.

Two of the three screens have a measured band they left unmade: the capture viewer 195x37, the dashboard 49x29. Both are real, both were left rigid because their honest declaration is most of the screen, and both are now one constant away should a display width ever ask for them.

`ShrinkPolicy::checked` has no production caller and is kept on purpose: it is the only way to TEST the refusal, because the `const` door's refusal is a compile error. Every other member the close audit found without a consumer was deleted.

The height axis of the node lab is rigid by decision, not by omission: a 27-pixel concession clips every full-height pane at once. Recorded so a later round does not read the asymmetry as an oversight.

R1713.decision_summary:
Whether a reader can see a mark is a question about the whole clip chain.

FIRST, the correction this entry owes. The R1712 entry records the node lab's
window floor as 1506 with a 119-pixel band. R1712.1 measured 1595 and a band of
30 before the round was pushed, and the ledger takes whole rounds only, so it
could not be amended there. Both numbers are wrong, and this round found out
why: 1506 came from a predicate that could not see the marks the window had
removed, and 1595 came from the scan built to work around that predicate, which
is keyed by tag and therefore blind to the glyph INSIDE a button. The measured
floor is 1601, the band is 24 pixels, and the payoff R1689 asked for — a
1600-pixel display that holds the screen — is missed by one pixel.

`reach::out_of_sight` judged every mark against its NEAREST clipping ancestor.
So when the window sliced a pane, the marks inside that pane were measured
against the pane, which they fit, and the window's cut was invisible to the
read. Measured on the node lab at 1506 wide: `lost` was zero while nine tagged
marks sat entirely outside the window, every one of them an action — five row
remove buttons, two spin steppers, `+ key` and `delete` — in a pane whose
horizontal range is zero, so no gesture anywhere reaches them.

Reachability composes: each level of the chain can only ever show what the level
above it can bring into view. `Viewport` therefore carries two boxes now — the
APERTURE the chain leaves (`origin`/`size`, which is what every predicate here
judges against) and the `declared` box the node itself asked for, so the
narrowing is a subtraction a reader can do rather than a fact only one of the
two numbers knows. Each level is intersected with the level above's
`reachable()` and not with what it happens to be showing, so a pane scrolled out
of an outer pane still offers its children every row the outer range covers; and
a level the chain leaves NOTHING of seals, so the marks below it are not judged
at all. That seal is what keeps the module's oldest promise true rather than
merely claimed: a pane sitting wholly off the window is one report on the pane,
never one per row. Before it, the rows inside came back `Scrollable` with an
offset that moves a pane no pixel of which is on screen — a false reachable, the
exact answer this module was written to end.

The second half is that "is it on screen right now" is now asked of the walk
itself (`NodeVisit::absolute_rect_of`), which is the fold the tag index and
every demo's press points already use. R1676 argued that reported and visible
have to be one fact; this module was the caller that had its own copy.

Then the repair found something underneath it. `shrink::audit` reads this to
decide whether a window's declared concession is honest, and its rule is that a
concession may CLIP and may never LOSE. Its own doc states the split it needs —
"cut says what the reader cannot see at once, lost says what the reader cannot
see at all" — and `Reach::Lost` did not mean that. It meant NOT FULLY
CONTAINABLE, so a form row 310 pixels wide inside a 282-pixel aperture came back
`lost` with 28 pixels of overhang, and a safety rule written to fail on content
nobody can reach failed on content nearly all of which is reachable. Measured at
1595x360: 19 `lost`, of which 6 were marks no pixel of which can ever be seen
and 13 were wide rows. So `Reach` has three arms, and the middle one is named
`Clipped` for the word the rule is written in, so the rule reads off the type.
`cut()` still reports the marks of both arms, because the question it asks — can
this be shown whole — is answered no by each.

The reference floor was measured by building a probe at 6.11.1 and running it
offscreen on this round's exact shape: a 282-wide holder clipping a 310-wide
scrolling pane whose content carries a full-width row and an 8-pixel glyph at
x=286. Its per-widget visible-region answer folds the WHOLE chain, reporting the
scrolled-in row as 281x20 rather than its own 310 — the capability is parity and
this tree was the short one, which is the second round running that has come out
that way. What it has nothing of, each proven by a compile error naming the
member rather than by a search that found nothing (6/6): a reason, a way to ask
about an offset it is not at, the offset that would show something, an
enumeration of what nothing reaches, any answer at all for a mark that is not a
widget, and a success answer from its own "show me this" call — which, measured,
left the offsets untouched and the glyph invisible and said so nowhere.

The node lab's floor is now the boundary this predicate evaluates rather than a
number typed by anyone: 1601 is the width at which nothing is lost, and at 1600
five marks are — the row `×` glyphs, whose ink starts 286 pixels into a pane
that is offered 286 there. The integration test bisects that boundary itself and
requires the conceded floor to EQUAL it, so a floor lowered by hand fails. What
the last pixel would cost is now a registered debt rather than a shrug: below
its comfortable size this layout stops reflowing, so what the window cuts is
simply gone, and the fix that buys the pixel — and hundreds more — is a window
that PANS below that size instead of clipping.

`pinion_core::reach` folds the clip chain: each level is offered only what the level above can EVER bring into view, so a mark inside a pane the window slices is judged against the slice.

`Viewport` carries the aperture (`origin`/`size`) and the box the node asked for (`declared`) side by side, so what the chain took away is a subtraction a reader can do; `max` stays derived from the DECLARED box, because the runtime clamps offsets against the node's own window and a range read off a narrowed aperture would name offsets the scene refuses.

A level the chain leaves nothing of SEALS: the marks below it are not judged, so a pane wholly off the window is one report on the pane. Before this the rows inside came back `Scrollable` with an offset that moves a pane no pixel of which is on screen.

`Reach` has a third arm. `Clipped` is reachable in part and never whole, `Lost` is not reachable at all, and `shrink::audit`'s rule — a concession may clip and may never lose — finally reads what its own doc always said it read.
"Is it on screen right now" is asked of `NodeVisit::absolute_rect_of`, the same clip fold `absolute_rects_by_tag` publishes, so this module and every demo's press points answer one question.

`Rect::intersect` — the other half of `Rect::union`, `None` rather than a zero-area rect, because folding a clip chain is a chain of these and one empty link means nothing below can be seen.

`walk_marks` lost a whole prepass: it built a map of window-absolute rectangles whose only reader took `w`/`h` off it, which a comment claimed folded in "an outer clip narrowing it" and which only ever translated.
`scene/scroll_reach` publishes a third count (`clipped`) and each viewport's `declared` box; both are in the wire census. `scene/size_floor` carries them through the same rows.
The node lab's window floor is 1601 (band 24), measured as the boundary at which nothing is lost, with the five row `×` glyphs lost one pixel below it.
The boot gate that reads this per demo now reports the middle answer as well, and its doc says why the number it budgets became a sharper thing.
verification_bullets: Integration UI test `tools/demos/r1713_reach_composes_down_the_clip_chain.py` — three screens, seven sections: the wire publishes the aperture beside the box it was cut from and no aperture exceeds it; the marks the window removes are reported by name with their pane's range at zero; the three counts partition the list and each arm carries only its own payload; the floor is BISECTED here and the conceding screen's declaration must equal it; a pane the window removes is named once and nothing inside it separately; and the predicate is compared against the paint and a photograph in the live window at a size it will really take.

Two sizes in that file are SEARCHED rather than written down — the width at which the window first cuts into a pane, and the width at which a given pane vanishes altogether — because each screen puts its clipping panes somewhere else. The first draft asserted the conceded floor was the first of those and the screen refused it: a floor is where something is LOST, and a pane starts being narrowed long before anything is.

R1712's own integration test was rewritten where it had worked around the defect: its boundary check reads `scene/scroll_reach` again instead of scanning the paint, and its `viewport` argument is gone because that parameter is ignored once a frame exists. It now also compares the two channels mark by mark at the floor, both directions, with a non-vacuity assertion on each. 65 assertions, three screens, green.

★★★★★ The blast radius was measured across the WHOLE tree rather than argued about: every demo's boot gate compares this predicate's `lost` against a per-example ratchet, so all 225 examples were re-measured through `tools/measure_ink_budgets.py --dry-run`. The result is byte-identical to the committed `docs/scroll-reach-budget.tsv`, including the nine surfaces this host cannot boot and their reasons. Nothing in the tree moved.

The reference floor was BUILT and RUN, not read: a probe at 6.11.1, offscreen, on this round's exact shape. Its per-widget visible-region answer folds the whole chain (`281x20` for a 310-wide row inside a 282 clip) — parity, and the direction this tree was short in. Six absences proven by compile errors naming the member, and one measured behaviour: asking it to show an unreachable widget left the offsets untouched, the widget invisible, and said so nowhere.

Counterfactuals: 10 against the pure layers (`cargo test -p pinion-core -p pinion-rpc --lib`), each a wrong answer rather than an absent one — the fold, the seal, the window in the on-screen test, the clipped/lost split, the range coming off the declared box, the offset solved in the aperture's coordinates, the wire's middle count, the concession rule's filter, the walk placing a caller's rectangle, and the half-open intersection.

★ The counterfactual driver refused the first run because the baseline was red: a test written for this round asserted an offset computed from the box the view PROMISED, and the implementation had used the ink the run actually paints. The implementation was right, the test was wrong, and the fixture now asserts the ink so the next reader cannot repeat it.

Counterfactual 7 PASSED on the first pass and was a finding: the wire's three counts were asserted on a fixture with ONE row per arm, so a counter reading the wrong arm still answered 1. The fixture now has four, two and one, and the case CAUGHT. Final 10/10.

Two example suites would not have compiled and `cargo build --release` does not say so, because both matches live in `#[cfg(test)]` modules: the exhaustive `Reach` matches in the node lab's and the dashboard's own tests. Caught by running those suites rather than by the release build that had already gone green — the local gate this tree keeps re-learning.

Looked at the screens: photographed at 1625, 1601x900, 1601x360, and both rigid screens at their floors, and scanned. The rigid screens cut nothing; at the conceded floor the inspector's action column is a sliver, which is what `clipped` means and what the declaration bought.
`pinion-core` 3,663 + `pinion-rpc` 1,275 + `pinion-shell` 252 green; the three screens' own suites 86 / 68 / 46 green; workspace clippy over ALL targets (629 crates) and `cargo doc` green.
carry_forward_bullets: The offset in `Reach::Scrollable` names ONE viewport's move. On a clip chain deeper than one level an ancestor may have to move too, and the answer does not say which. Measured: every clip chain on all three analysis-tool screens is one level deep, so no reader can meet it today — and the behaviour is pinned by a test rather than left as prose, because a stated limit is one nobody re-reads.

`scene/snapshot {from: "paint", viewport}` prefers the displayed frame and IGNORES the size asked about once a frame exists. Measured: five different asks on two screens, the same live root every time. R1712.1's floor scan believed it was measuring a hypothetical size and was measuring the live one — which is the same geometry on the node lab, whose layout is clamped at its design width, and is NOT on the capture viewer. This round removed the one consumer that leaned on it and registered the rest: the honest repair (produce a mirror when the ask differs) has ~880 call sites in its blast radius and needs a full sweep this host cannot adjudicate.

Photographed at 1625 and at the floor and scanned side by side: at 1601 the inspector's action column is a SLIVER — the row `×` glyphs are one pixel of ink inside the window, which is `clipped` and not `lost` by construction, and is exactly what the declaration says the band costs. A band of 24 pixels that slices the action column is worth little to a reader until it can be panned to; that is the next item and not a defect in this one.

The last pixel of R1689's payoff is not buyable by moving a glyph. Below its comfortable size this layout stops reflowing, so what the window cuts is gone; the repair that buys it — and hundreds of pixels more — is a window that PANS below that size, which changes what a concession MEANS and wants its own round.
`clipped` is reported per boot and not budgeted. A budget with no producer-derived baseline is a number nobody chose, and the producer would have to measure every surface to make one.

The three screens' `cut` counts at their floors are published and unasserted beyond being non-empty on the conceding one: what a band clips is a decision, and the round has no reference point for how much clipping is too much.

Counterfactuals: 10 against the pure layers (`cargo test -p pinion-core -p pinion-rpc --lib`), each a wrong answer rather than an absent one — the fold, the seal, the window in the on-screen test, the clipped/lost split, the range coming off the declared box, the offset solved in the aperture's coordinates, the wire's middle count, the concession rule's filter, the walk placing a caller's rectangle, and the half-open intersection.

★ The counterfactual driver refused the first run because the baseline was red: a test written for this round asserted an offset computed from the box the view PROMISED, and the implementation had used the ink the run actually paints. The implementation was right, the test was wrong, and the fixture now asserts the ink so the next reader cannot repeat it.

Counterfactual 7 PASSED on the first pass and was a finding: the wire's three counts were asserted on a fixture with ONE row per arm, so a counter reading the wrong arm still answered 1. The fixture now has four, two and one, and the case CAUGHT. Final 10/10.

Two example suites would not have compiled and `cargo build --release` does not say so, because both matches live in `#[cfg(test)]` modules: the exhaustive `Reach` matches in the node lab's and the dashboard's own tests. Caught by running those suites rather than by the release build that had already gone green — the local gate this tree keeps re-learning.

Looked at the screens: photographed at 1625, 1601x900, 1601x360, and both rigid screens at their floors, and scanned. The rigid screens cut nothing; at the conceded floor the inspector's action column is a sliver, which is what `clipped` means and what the declaration bought.
`pinion-core` 3,663 + `pinion-rpc` 1,275 + `pinion-shell` 252 green; the three screens' own suites 86 / 68 / 46 green; workspace clippy over ALL targets (629 crates) and `cargo doc` green.
publishable_carry_forward_bullets: The offset in `Reach::Scrollable` names ONE viewport's move. On a clip chain deeper than one level an ancestor may have to move too, and the answer does not say which. Measured: every clip chain on all three analysis-tool screens is one level deep, so no reader can meet it today — and the behaviour is pinned by a test rather than left as prose, because a stated limit is one nobody re-reads.

`scene/snapshot {from: "paint", viewport}` prefers the displayed frame and IGNORES the size asked about once a frame exists. Measured: five different asks on two screens, the same live root every time. R1712.1's floor scan believed it was measuring a hypothetical size and was measuring the live one — which is the same geometry on the node lab, whose layout is clamped at its design width, and is NOT on the capture viewer. This round removed the one consumer that leaned on it and registered the rest: the honest repair (produce a mirror when the ask differs) has ~880 call sites in its blast radius and needs a full sweep this host cannot adjudicate.

Photographed at 1625 and at the floor and scanned side by side: at 1601 the inspector's action column is a SLIVER — the row `×` glyphs are one pixel of ink inside the window, which is `clipped` and not `lost` by construction, and is exactly what the declaration says the band costs. R1714.decision_summary:
A window smaller than its layout moves over it instead of cutting into it.

FIRST, the correction this entry owes. The R1713 entry records the round's
demo count and calls its analysis-tool sweep green; two follow-up commits landed
after it was written — R1713.1 converged three private rectangle intersections
on `Rect::intersect`, and R1713.2 repaid a red that a 35-demo sweep found AFTER
the push, where a check asked "can a reader reach this" with the single word
`scrollable` and a third arm had just been added. The ledger takes whole rounds
only, so neither could be amended there.

R1712 gave a screen two floors and a list of what the space between them costs.
What it could not express is HOW that space is served, and there are two answers.
Until this round every screen here had the first by construction rather than by
decision: `external::layout_size` clamps the layout at the comfortable size and
the window clips whatever sticks out, with no range anywhere to move it. R1713
measured the ceiling that puts on the whole idea — the node lab's band bottomed
out 24 pixels down, at 1601, because one pixel lower five glyphs stop being
reachable by anything, and 1601 misses by one pixel the 1600-wide display R1689
wrote a real loss against. The last pixel could not be bought: below the
comfortable size the layout stops reflowing, so what the window cuts is gone.

`ShrinkPolicy` now carries a `Recourse`. `Clip` is what every screen had — the
window cuts and the declaration names what goes. `Pan` is the other answer: the
window becomes a viewport onto the layout, everything stays one gesture away,
and what the band costs is seeing two things at once rather than any content at
all. A pan therefore names NOTHING, and a policy that declares one beside a list
of losses fails to compile, as does a pan with no band to pan in — the same
argument `BandNamesNothing` already makes about a band that costs nothing.

The declaration is what produces the behaviour. `shrink::pan` is a pure function
the shell applies in `window_view`, the one place all three paint-scene producers
already start from, so a screen cannot declare a pan and ship a clip — the
direction this tree keeps finding rotted the other way round, most recently in
R1699 where `Activation::Explicit` declared a keyboard nothing implemented and
every gate read the declaration. A binding that declares no pan gets the very
same `Scene` back, so the round's blast radius is the screens that opted in; and
the pan exists only where there is range to have, because a pan with no range is
not a pan.

The node lab declares one. Its floor goes 1601 to 748 — derived from the
specification rather than written down, as the width of the four things the
screen is for side by side (rail, palette, one whole node card, inspector) —
and nothing is out of reach at any width down to 400, measured. R1689's payoff
is taken with 852 pixels to spare. `scene/size_floor` publishes the recourse and
a sixth verdict, `panned`: the same arithmetic as `conceded` and a different
fact, because telling a caller that a screen it can reach every corner of has
given something up is the one misreading this round exists to prevent.

The second half of the round is what the pan did to a question R1713 had already
answered. `Reach::Scrollable` carried ONE offset — the row's own viewport's —
and R1713 pinned the gap with a test and a measurement: every clip chain on the
three analysis-tool screens is one level deep, so no reader could meet it. A
window that is a viewport onto its own layout makes every one of those chains
two deep, and the single offset stopped being incomplete and started being
WRONG: measured, the five glyphs the node lab puts outside the window at 1600
came back `scrollable to (0, 0)`, an offset their pane is already at, which moves
nothing. The arm carries `moves` now — every viewport that has to move and where
to, outermost first, and only those whose offset must CHANGE, so a non-empty
list is the invariant. Each step is solved in its own frame: the level takes
`least_move`'s answer, the mark is carried up into the frame above AS THAT
OFFSET LEAVES IT, and the next level solves again. That last clause is the whole
correctness of it, and a counterfactual is what asked for the test that holds it.

Three things were wrong first and execution is what said so, not reading.
`external::layout_point` gives the framework the pointer expression three
screens were writing by hand — and with only that, `scene/pointer_target` fell
to one addressable rectangle of 57 with 26 unreachable, because `target_at` is
handed PIXELS and not a fraction: a widget has more than one door onto its own
basis and fixing one leaves the rest quietly wrong, so `into_layout` is the
second door. Making `cut` mean "no single offset shows this whole" — which its
own doc claimed — was tried and refused by the screens: a scrolling canvas's
content node is 5376 pixels square by design, and the stronger reading made the
node lab's floor unmeasurable and its canvas a permanent defect; a scroller
exists FOR content larger than its window, so the doc was corrected instead. And
a hand-computed expectation in the chain test said the outer pane moves to 150
where the implementation answers 58: `least_move` moves as little as possible,
R1713 had written 150 in that test's prose, and nobody had ever computed it.

The round's own close audit then found the round's own defect, of the round's
own class. A pan with no range is a pan AT ZERO, and only the first half of that
was said: the node is not built once the window can show the whole layout, so
nothing paints at an offset — and `window_pan` went on answering the offset the
reader had left it at, which `into_layout` then added to every press. Measured
on the node lab: pan it, grow the window back to its comfortable size, and
`scene/pointer_target` answers ONE addressable rectangle of 61, with 61
unreachable. The repair is the rule the runtime already applies to every real
scroll node — the layout pass publishes the range and the offset is clamped into
it — reaching the one viewport the layout pass never sees. Two more
counterfactuals, both caught, and the integration test now pans a screen and
grows it back rather than only panning it.

The same audit finished the lift. The capture viewer and the dashboard were
still writing the clamp-and-multiply out by hand, so both now go through
`layout_point`, and with that their hand-held surface sizes joined the node
lab's in having no reader at all — three `on_resize` implementations and three
fields deleted. The pan term is the identity for a screen that does not pan,
which is why adopting it there is free and why it stays right if either screen
ever declares one.

What this round cost, stated rather than left: no screen now drives the fold's
headline case end to end. The node lab was the screen whose window sliced a pane,
and it pans; the capture viewer's losses are all judged against the window
itself. The property is pinned in `pinion_core::reach`'s own suite, which is a
layer below where the defect lived, and it is registered as a debt.
changes_bullets: `pinion_core::shrink`: `Recourse{Clip, Pan}` with a wire word and `pans()`;
`ShrinkPolicy` carries one and publishes it; `panning(comfortable, floor)`
beside `conceding`, both through one `declared` door so a fault is spelled
once; two further refusals, `PanNamesWhatItKeeps` and `PanWithoutBand`, which
are compile errors where a binding writes its policy; `checked` takes the
recourse. `audit` reads the cut half only under `Clip` — a pan gives nothing
up, so the list it would be judged against does not exist, and the half that
stays (`lost`) is the one that can still fail.
`pinion_core::shrink::pan`: the wrap itself, plus the pan's state
(`pan_state`, `window_pan`, `forget_pan`, `PAN_TAG = "window.pan"`) held
outside every owner for the reason `surface_size` is — the hit test that reads
the offset runs in no scope. Identity for a policy that clips, for a window at
or above the comfortable size, and for a window of no extent.
`pinion_shell`: `window_view` applies it, inside the owner wrap and before the
chrome inset, so all three paint-scene producers get the same scene.
`pinion_core::reach`: `Reach::Scrollable { moves: Vec<Move> }` replaces the
single offset; `Move { viewport, to }`; `Reach::moves()`. `clip_chain` returns
the whole chain (`Chain` splits the innermost out so it cannot be empty) with
a `Level::lift` that carries a rectangle into the frame above as the offset
just chosen leaves it; `chain_moves` walks inner to outer and reverses. `Reach`
loses `Copy` and its readers take `&self`.
`pinion_core::external`: `layout_point` (a pointer fraction) and `into_layout`
(a window pixel) both answer in the frame the screen's layout is stated in,
pan included.
`pinion_core::shrink::pan` also CLAMPS an existing pan to zero on the path
where it builds none, because a pan with no range holds no offset; it does not
create one there, which would leave a pan state behind for every binding in
the tree on every frame.
`pinion_rpc`: `MoveReport` and `OutOfSightReport::moves` replace `to_x`/`to_y`;
`ConcessionReport::recourse`; `verdict` answers `panned` for an honoured pan,
read before the arithmetic because a pan's `needed` bottoms out and the
arithmetic alone would say `roomier`. The wire census carries all three — the
new type, the new field with its two-word vocabulary, and the sixth verdict.
`hello-packet-view` and `hello-analyzer-shell` adopt `layout_point`, and with
the multiplication gone their hand-held surface sizes had no reader either:
three `on_resize` implementations and three fields deleted across the three
screens.
`hello-node-lab`: `SHRINK` is `panning((MIN_W, MIN_H), (FLOOR_W, MIN_H))` with
`FLOOR_W` derived from the specification (rail + palette + widest card +
inspector = 748); `pointer_move`, `wheel`, `wheel_intent` and `target_at` go
through the framework's expression; `LabOracle`'s hand-held surface and its
`on_resize` are deleted (no reader left); `pane_scroll` resolves the window's
own pan; the in-process suite paints through `shrink::pan`, so it measures the
scene the shell paints.
Demos: `r1714_a_window_pans_over_its_own_layout` (34 assertions, three
`rpc_verify::assert_declared_panes_on_screen` learn that a declared region is
painted OR one gesture away, and that a recipe is a chain to be performed
whole and from the offsets it was solved against.
verification_bullets: Integration UI test `r1714_a_window_pans_over_its_own_layout`: 34 assertions
across the three analysis-tool screens. The band is swept at every eighth
pixel plus both ends and nothing is `lost` or `clipped` at any of them; the
pan's range is asserted to equal the shortfall at every one of those widths,
directly, rather than waited for as a loss at the far edge. The recipe for a
mark the previous round's floor lost is read off the wire and then PERFORMED
through `scene/scroll`, and the mark is on screen afterwards. `pointer_target`
is taken at the floor and again after panning half the range — 0 unreachable
both times, and the paint is asserted to have actually moved between them, so
the second reading is not the first one twice. Two photographs at the floor,
one panned to the far end, asserted to differ.
The close audit's own case is driven where it can press: the integration test
pans the screen, grows the window back past its layout, and asks the surface
again — 61 addressable rectangles and none unreachable, where before the
repair it was one and 61.
Counterfactuals: 18, 12 caught on the first pass. All four that PASSED were
the same finding — a fixture that cannot tell two answers apart. Neither
`layout_point` nor `into_layout` had a unit test at all (the R1712 shape: the
function that assembles the answer untested, only its readers); the chain
fixture moved the inner pane on y and the outer on x, so ignoring the inner
offset when carrying the mark up changed nothing; and every wire fixture had
exactly one move in it, so reversing the list on the way out was invisible.
Four tests added — a non-square surface with an asymmetric pan, a chain whose
two ranges are on the SAME axis, and a two-element recipe — and the four cases
re-run 4/4 CAUGHT. The last two are the close audit's, 2/2 caught: an offset
that outlives its range, and an identity path that leaves a pan behind for
every binding.
`pinion-core` 3,674 and `pinion-rpc` 1,278 green; `hello-node-lab` 86,
`hello-packet-view` 46, `hello-analyzer-shell` 68 green; workspace clippy
`--all-targets --features pinion-runtime/vello` green. ★ The wire census is a
`--test` and not a `--lib`, so a `--lib` run reported green with a new
serialized type missing from it — the R1711 shape, and the reason the package
suites are run whole here.
Blast radius driven, not reasoned about: all 36 demos in the tree that boot
one of the three analysis-tool screens, 36/36 green. Seven were red at the
first sweep and each is repaired at the level it was wrong: five read the
offset field the chain replaced, and two asserted that a declared region is
PAINTED at a size below the layout — which a window that pans makes false in
the honest direction, since the region is now one gesture away instead of a
rectangle nobody could see being counted as drawn.
Reference floor, built as a 6.11.1 probe and run offscreen rather than read.
The layout minimum is enforced (748 asked, 996 given); wrapping the same
screen in a scrolling area really does take the window to 748 with a range of
250, so the PAN is capability parity. The chain is not: asked to show a widget
two areas deep, it moves ONE area — the inner if asked of the inner, the outer
if asked of the outer — and in both cases the widget is still off screen
afterwards, measured at (325, 686) in a 400x300 window. The ask returns `void`,
so nothing reports the failure, and 0 of 316 members across its scroll-area,
scrollbar and widget classes carry the idea in a name. Five absences proven by
compile failure, one per translation unit.
Looked at: five screenshots of the node lab — as it opens, at 1600x900 (the
display R1689 wrote its loss against, which now holds the screen), at the
floor, panned to the middle and panned to the far end. The five `×` row
actions R1713 declared unreachable at 1600 are visible in a 748-wide window.
carry_forward_bullets: NEW, and it is what this round cost: no screen drives the clip fold's headline
case any more. The node lab was the screen whose window sliced a pane with
marks inside it, and it pans now; the capture viewer's losses are all judged
against the window itself, at every width a ladder reaches. The property is
pinned in `pinion_core::reach`'s own suite, which is a layer below where the
defect lived. What would close it is a screen with a pane clipped by something
that is not the window — a nested scroll — and the canon is what should decide
whether this tool has one, rather than an invention.
Stated, not carried: the node lab's HEIGHT axis still concedes nothing. That
is a decision with its reason in the code — `MIN_H` is 360, below every
display this screen opens on, so a height band buys a reader nothing
measurable, where the width was the axis a real loss was written against.
Stated: a binding with more than one window that declares a pan would share
one pan across them, because the pan is keyed by the surface's tag. That is
the key `surface_size` already uses and the limit it already has, so it is not
a new one; no binding is in that position.
`debt-an-external-reads-a-fraction-without-its-basis` stays open and its
repayment got cheaper: the framework now holds the whole expression, so the
remaining work is moving 27 `pointer_move` consumers onto it rather than
threading a new type through six callbacks. It is still a rule and not a
shape — a consumer that does not move can still multiply by a constant.
`ShrinkPolicy::checked` still has no production caller, kept for the reason
R1712.1 recorded: the `const` door's refusal is a compile error, so this is
the only way the rule can be tested at all, and this round added two arms to
that rule.

R1715.decision_summary:
The focus a dispatch leaves behind is resolved to a fixed point, on every path
out of the seam.

A consumer report (sprag PINION-PR89) opened this: a terminal pane whose child
program had enabled xterm mouse reporting could not be given the keyboard by
clicking it. The pane owns the raw multi-button pointer stream, and owning it is
exactly what suppresses the GUI default for that widget — `click_to_focus`
included — so the focus mailbox is the only channel such a widget has left to
say "the click that reached my child also gave me the keyboard". It was writing
that request. Nothing applied it.

THE REPORTED DEFECT IS A HALF-RIGHT INFERENCE. `ShellCore::pointer_button_for_window`
offers every button edge to a raw sink first; a consumed edge bumped the
revision, requested a redraw, and returned. That early return skipped
`handle_tail`, whose last line was the product's ONLY call to
`drain_focus_mailboxes`. The reasoning behind the return was half right: a raw
edge really has no `DispatchTail`. But `handle_tail` carries two
responsibilities — drain the tail, and resolve the frame's focus — and "there is
no tail" retires only the first. So the request waited for whatever dispatch
came next: focus one input late, and that input swallowed. The symptom reads as
"nothing happened"; those two are not distinguishable by eye, which is why it
survived ~30 rounds.

NOTHING SAW IT BECAUSE IT LIVED BETWEEN TWO LAYERS. Every raw-sink fixture in
the tree sits at `pinion-runtime`'s router, where there is no focus drain to
skip; the layer that OWNS the drain had no test that drove it with a raw sink in
the scene at all. The gates added here drive the public shell seam and read
`focus()`, and deliberately never call `drain_focus_mailboxes` themselves — a
gate that calls what the product does not call is green about nothing.

THE ONE-LINE FIX WAS NOT THE DESIGN, AND STOPPING THERE WOULD HAVE LEFT THE SAME
BUG ONE LAYER IN. Two places inside a single resolution pass run USER code:
`notify_focus_change` fires `External::on_focus_change` observers, and
`apply_focus_request`'s R1020 retry re-runs `V::view`. Either can write a
mailbox the pass has already emptied, and a single-pass resolution deferred that
write to the next dispatch — the reported defect exactly, inside the method
built to abolish it.

So the resolution SETTLES. `drain_focus_mailboxes` repeats its pass until both
mailboxes are empty, bounded at `FOCUS_SETTLE_PASSES = 8`, and a frame that
cannot converge is reported and CLEARED. Clearing rather than leaving is the
point: a request left pending lands on the next unrelated input, which is the
same bug wearing a different hat. Loud in two registers — a `debug_assert` so
the build's own tests fail, an ERROR log so a release build does not die inside
a user's event loop over a binding-side cycle.

Three things follow, and the third is why this is a design entry rather than a
one-line repair.

A CAPABILITY. "I was told I have focus; the real target is my child" is how a
container hands focus on — the reference toolkit's focus proxy, the web's
`delegatesFocus` — and it is written by requesting from `on_focus_change`. One
pass landed that request one input late and ate the input; a fixed point lands
it in the same frame.

IDEMPOTENCE. The mailboxes are empty on return, so calling the resolution twice
in a row is a no-op by construction.

THEREFORE STRUCTURE. Both seams (`pointer_button_for_window` and its terminal
twin) now resolve on EVERY path out instead of on the paths somebody remembered.
The early return that created this defect is gone as a shape, not just as an
instance: a future arm added to that `match` inherits the resolution. And the
acceptance criterion "the six non-raw arms are unchanged" became true BY
CONSTRUCTION rather than by judgement, because an idempotent no-op cannot change
what they do.

R1456 is untouched. Its case — a modal pop's automatic restore and an explicit
request in one frame — puts both requests in the mailbox at the same time, so
they resolve inside a single pass and the intermediate owner is still never
announced. A later pass exists only where user code REACTED to being focused,
and there the intermediate is not a transient the frame is hiding: it is the
widget that chose to hand on.

THE COUNTERFACTUALS FOUND TWO GAPS, BOTH THE ROUND'S OWN, AND BOTH THE SAME
CLASS — a negative or bounded claim is only a check when the observable exists.
Deleting the raw arm's `return`, so an edge is delivered raw AND runs the GUI
arc (the double dispatch a raw sink exists to prevent), left every suite green:
fall-through lands focus on the same tag either way, and the fixture's widgets
had no `introspect_mut`, so the legacy send wire had nowhere to arrive. The sink
carries that wire now. Raising the settle bound from 8 to 200 also left
everything green, because a bound whose only job is to terminate is satisfied by
any finite number; the fixture counts focus-gained calls and both backends'
gates read that count against a literal, so the number is a decision someone has
to take twice and a per-backend bound is caught too.

The harness produced the same shape twice more, before any product code was
touched. A fixture whose hand-written rects the paint pass overwrote gave an
EMPTY raw-edge log under red focus assertions — which reads exactly like the
defect under test, and was caught only because the fixture reports delivery
separately from focus. And the harness's own self-check press left an undrained
request that rode into the next dispatch and overrode it: the reported bug in
miniature, inside the gate built to catch it.
changes_bullets: `ShellCore::drain_focus_mailboxes` and its terminal twin settle to a FIXED POINT: one pass is split out as `drain_focus_mailboxes_once`, and the caller repeats until both mailboxes are empty, so a request written by user code running inside the resolution lands this frame instead of the next dispatch

`FOCUS_SETTLE_PASSES = 8` bounds that loop on both backends, and `report_unsettled_focus` reports a non-converging frame and CLEARS it -- a `debug_assert` for the build's own tests, an ERROR log (tracing on the window, the terminal's own log sink) for a release binary

`pointer_button_for_window` and `ShellCoreTui::pointer_button` have ONE exit: the raw arm's early `return` is gone as a shape, so every path -- raw and the six per-button arms -- resolves, and a future arm inherits it rather than remembering it

`pinion_core::test_fixtures::RawSinkFocusFixture` is the shared forcing consumer: a raw sink that asks for the keyboard from `raw_pointer_button`, a plain control beside it, both painted as declared flex geometry so a real hit-test reaches them

The sink carries a legacy `send` wire and a focus-gained counter, and the control can hand its focus on from `on_focus_change` -- three observables that exist because the round's counterfactuals proved the claims above were unfalsifiable without them
Two integration gates (`pinion-shell`, `pinion-tui`) drive the public seam and read `focus()`, never `drain_focus_mailboxes` -- a gate calling what the product does not call is green about nothing

The doc on `CoreShell::raw_pointer_button_for_window` and `External::wants_raw_pointer_buttons` names what "no DispatchTail" does NOT retire, and that the suppression list covers this widget's GUI defaults rather than the dispatch's own post-processing
verification_bullets: Counterfactuals 11/11 CAUGHT, after runs of 5/6 and 4/5 whose two passes were both findings and both repaid: the raw arm's suppression (no observable until the sink carried a legacy `send` wire) and the settle bound's VALUE (8 -> 200 terminates and reports just the same, until a gate reads how many times user code re-ran)

The defect was proven by execution before any fix: the raw edge WAS delivered (`["left:down"]`) while `focus().focused()` stayed `None` -- the delivery observable is what separated the defect from a broken harness, and it earned that twice

Both backends' gates: 6 shared assertions (headline, all six (button,edge) pairs, delivery in order, GUI-default suppression, modal confinement, non-raw arm unchanged) plus 3 for the redesign (nothing left in the mailbox after any dispatch, a hand-on lands in the same frame, a cycle is reported AND leaves the mailbox clean)

The cycle gate catches the unwind rather than declaring `#[should_panic]`, because the clearing happens on the way to the panic: a should_panic test would have checked the loud half and never the clean half
Changed-crate suites green -- pinion-core, pinion-runtime, pinion-a11y, pinion-shell, pinion-tui, pinion-rpc, 37 test binaries, 0 failed

Blast radius computed rather than remembered (`tools/blast_radius.py --mode staged`); the one demo with a raw sink plus two focus-adjacent ones re-run after the redesign: r1416_raw_pointer, r1462_modal_refocus, r1419_window_focus, 3/3 PASS
Workspace clippy --all-targets (vello) and `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps`: 0 warnings, re-run after the redesign rather than trusted from before it
Measured before designing: 0 of the tree's 9 `on_focus_change` bodies write a mailbox, so the settle loop regresses nothing and needed a deliberate exerciser to be driven at all
carry_forward_bullets: A declared focus proxy is still absent. Handing focus on now WORKS from `on_focus_change`, but it announces the intermediate owner before the final one; the reference toolkit's focus proxy and the web's `delegatesFocus` resolve the redirect BEFORE the commit, so exactly one transition is announced. Measure that at 6.11.1 and prove the absence by compile error before building it

`on_focus_change` writing a mailbox is now a supported shape on both backends, so `mailbox-side-effect-from-reducer-not-effect`'s rule is "written from a dispatch, drained by that same dispatch" -- not "from a reducer or invoke only". Nothing in the tree relies on it yet (0 of 9 bodies), which means the next binding that does is the one that will find whatever this round missed

The settle bound is asserted as a literal in two test files and declared as a constant in two crates -- four places, deliberately, so moving it is a decision taken more than once. If a fifth reader appears, that is the moment to publish the constant instead
