R1716.decision_summary:
R1716 — a settings row says where its value came from, and a row nobody wrote
is nobody's to write.

The node inspector could hold one kind of row: a value somebody typed. The
behaviour canon shows three more — the session mode a node's ROLE implies, the
host a card runs on, and the addresses its drawn LINKS dial — and draws them
with no control, no delete seat, and the source written on the badge. This tree
had no way to say any of that, so those rows were absent; and one of them was
worse than absent. Measured through the wire before the change: the router card
showed `connect.endpoints = tcp/10.0.0.21:7449`, one address at a host nothing
in the graph listens on, while the canvas drew THREE links out of it — and the
exported configuration shipped the typed value, dialling somewhere it was not
drawn to reach and missing one it was. A second measurement, found while
repairing the first: the exported plan put all eight nodes on one host called
`unplaced` while the screen's own `frames` read said six were on `host-a` and
two on `host-b`, because the launch plan asked a map keyed by FRAME about a
CARD. Two derivations of one fact, and the one nobody read was wrong.

So `ConfigField` gains two axes, and they are separate because they cross:
`Source::{Authored, Derived(name)}` says where the value came from, and
`Goes::{Document, Aside(word)}` says where it goes. The name is not decoration
— "this is derived" answers nothing a person can act on and "this comes from
the role" tells them where to go. The consequences are the TYPE's, not a
screen's discipline: the row refuses `set` and the form refuses `remove`, both
naming the source; the painter draws a read-out with no affordances and a seat
that offers the other act (`Seat::{Remove, TakeOver}`, which R1686 predicted as
an `Option` and is stronger as an enum); the a11y node says `read_only` and the
description says what it was worked out from; and `compose` gains a third
bucket, `aside`, so "did not fit" and "does not belong" stay different news.

`ConfigForm::author` is the act the floor performs silently: measured at 6.11.1,
writing into a bound value drops the binding with one ordinary value-changed
notification and leaves the displaced derivation unreachable. Here it is named,
it reports what it displaced and what value it kept, and the row is removable
afterwards — which is the way back.

The screen composes the derived rows at READ time and stores only the authored
half; every amendment goes through one seam that answers from what the screen
SHOWS and keeps what somebody wrote, so a take-over materialises in the same
act. Taking the wire's row over means the wires stop writing it, which is a
deliberate divergence from the canon's merge — and the cost is paid where it
can be read: the launch gate warns, per card, which drawn address the card no
longer dials, without blocking, because dialling outside the drawing is a
legitimate thing to want.
changes_bullets: `pinion_core::widgets::config_form` — `Source::{Authored, Derived(name)}` and
`Goes::{Document, Aside(word)}` on `ConfigField`, with `derived_from` /
`goes_aside` builders. `ConfigField::set` returns `Result` and refuses a
derived row naming its source (`FormError::Derived`); `ConfigForm::remove`
refuses the same; `ConfigForm::author` / `ConfigField::author` take a row over
and answer `Takeover { key, was, seeded }`; `ConfigForm::derived()` is the
rollup. `compose()` gains `Composed::aside: Vec<Aside>` and never puts an
aside row in the document; `defects()` does not raise an unknown-key warning
about a row that is not a configuration path; `adopt()` reports

is nobody's to write.

The node inspector could hold one kind of row: a value somebody typed. The
behaviour canon shows three more — the session mode a node's ROLE implies, the
host a card runs on, and the addresses its drawn LINKS dial — and draws them
with no control, no delete seat, and the source written on the badge. This tree
had no way to say any of that, so those rows were absent; and one of them was
worse than absent. Measured through the wire before the change: the router card
showed `connect.endpoints = tcp/10.0.0.21:7449`, one address at a host nothing

exported configuration shipped the typed value, dialling somewhere it was not
drawn to reach and missing one it was. A second measurement, found while
repairing the first: the exported plan put all eight nodes on one host called
`unplaced` while the screen's own `frames` read said six were on `host-a` and
two on `host-b`, because the launch plan asked a map keyed by FRAME about a

So `ConfigField` gains two axes, and they are separate because they cross:
`Source::{Authored, Derived(name)}` says where the value came from, and
`Goes::{Document, Aside(word)}` says where it goes. The name is not decoration
— "this is derived" answers nothing a person can act on and "this comes from
the role" tells them where to go. The consequences are the TYPE's, not a

description says what it was worked out from; and `compose` gains a third
bucket, `aside`, so "did not fit" and "does not belong" stay different news.

writing into a bound value drops the binding with one ordinary value-changed
notification and leaves the displaced derivation unreachable. Here it is named,
it reports what it displaced and what value it kept, and the row is removable

act. Taking the wire's row over means the wires stop writing it, which is a
deliberate divergence from the canon's merge — and the cost is paid where it
can be read: the launch gate warns, per card, which drawn address the card no
longer dials, without blocking, because dialling outside the drawing is a
legitimate thing to want.

R1717.decision_summary:
R1717 — a configuration row can have TWO contributors, and says which half is whose.

CORRECTION FIRST (R1716's ledger): the R1716 entry's carry clause names four new
debts. There were FIVE — the fifth,
`debt-a-visible-window-demo-lands-on-whatever-display-it-inherits`, was
registered from a user report after the entry was appended, so it appears only
in that entry's verification clause. The ledger is append-only, so the count is
corrected here: R1716 opened 5 debts and closed 1.

R1716 gave a settings row a provenance with two answers — somebody wrote it, or
the screen worked it out — and the behaviour canon's own screen needs three. A
node may be told to dial an already-running peer this canvas does not draw AND
be wired to the peers it does draw. Those are not competing answers to one
question; they are two contributions to one list. R1716 could not say that, so a
written value took the whole row and the drawn links stopped reaching the
configuration; it paid for the loss with a gate warning naming each drawn
address the card no longer dialled. This round removes the thing that warning
was compensating for.

THE SHAPE IS THE TYPE'S, AND IT IS TWO HALVES INSTEAD OF ONE VALUE.
`ConfigField` holds `written` (the half somebody wrote, `None` when nobody has)
and `worked_out` (a `Derivation`: what it was worked out from, and to). The
shown value is COMPUTED from them, so it cannot be a third place the same fact
lives; `Source` is computed too, which is why a form can no longer be read back
claiming to be authored while holding a derivation. `Source` gains
`Shared(name)` beside `Authored` and `Derived(name)`, and `Source::authored()`
— a bool eight consumers were asking the wrong question with — is replaced by
`writable()`, which forced every one of them to re-decide.

THE COMPOSITION RULE IS THE SHAPE'S. `FieldType::merges()` is true for a
sequence and false for a single value: two addresses compose, two modes
contradict. `with_derived` refuses on a single-valued shape rather than picking
a winner, so a screen cannot quietly compose something that has no composition.
The order is written-first, de-duplicated, which is the canon's, and it buys a
second thing: element provenance is then DERIVABLE — the elements before the
written half's count are somebody's and the rest are the derivation's.

`edited()` MOVED TO THE WRITTEN HALF. That was the question R1716 could not
answer and the real reason it did not compose: a row whose shown value moved
because the canvas moved was not edited by anybody, and a form that said it was
would offer a "put it back" that puts nothing back.

THREE ACTS ON ONE RECTANGLE. `Seat::GiveBack` joins `Remove` and `TakeOver`:
removing a shared row takes the written half out and LEAVES the row, because the
derivation is still true and a removed row would be back one render later. The
seat's tag word is now one function both the painter and the accessibility tree
read, which is a duplication this round created and then removed.

PROVENANCE REACHES THE ELEMENT, BECAUSE EDITING DOES. That is this round's
lesson stated once: a gate that fails on a new state is asking the OLD
granularity's question, and the answer is to move the fact rather than to exempt
the gate. Driven the first time the
state existed, an edit over an element the canvas contributed wrote the canvas's
whole contribution into the person's half and moved its neighbours. So
`element_source(at)` answers per line, the painter draws a contributed line with
the read-out's skin, the accessibility node says read-only and what worked it
out, and the box refuses to open over one. The seed and the commit are about the
half being edited, never about the composition.

THE SCREEN. The node-graph lab's `connect.endpoints` row is composed on every
read from the stored half and the drawn wires; the store keeps only the written
half; and the launch gate's warning is now the canon's own — an address somebody
wrote that nothing on this canvas listens on, which suspends nothing and blocks
nothing but says the drawing is no longer the whole picture. R1716's mirror-image
warning is unreachable by construction and is gone.

AND THE GATE'S VOCABULARY BECAME A TYPE, BECAUSE A PHOTOGRAPH SAID SO. The
screen's three graph warnings had no type of their own: each was smuggled inside
a `ConfigDefect::UnknownKey` whose key was really a sentence, and the panel
recovered the wording by sniffing that key's suffix. Two had an arm; the third
fell through to the framework's own wording and read "R-01 · R-01 ·
connect.endpoints · … is outside this graph is not a key the target knows; it
starts and ignores it" — the card named twice, and a sentence about unknown keys
glued to a fact that is not about one. R1716 shipped it and every gate was
green, because every check asked whether the ADDRESS was named and none asked
whether the SENTENCE read. `Finding::{Value, NothingListening, DiscoveryOn,
DialsOutside}` is the repair: the wording comes from the arm and there is no
string left to sniff.

THE FLOOR, MEASURED BY BUILDING A PROBE AND RUNNING IT (6.11.1, offscreen). It
DOES compose two contributors — a settings store falls back to a second store, a
key only the second holds still answers, and taking the written half away brings
the other back — so the capability is parity, not a gap. Four measured absences:
the composition is whole-key, never element-wise (a written one-element list
beside a worked-out three-element list answered ONE element); no reader can ask
which store answered (the file name is the written store's whatever answered,
the scope is the asking object's, and the only discriminator needs a second
object and answers about the KEY); the binding half ends on a contribution
(hasBinding true -> false, and the value never follows its source again); and a
cell holding a composed value answers 2 of 256 standard roles, none of which is
how much of it is not the reader's. Six capabilities this round ships are
compile errors there.
changes_bullets: FRAMEWORK — `pinion_core::widgets::config_form`
* `ConfigField` holds `written: Option<String>` (the half somebody wrote) and
`worked_out: Option<Derivation>` (what the screen worked out, and from what).
`value()` is COMPUTED from them and answers `Cow` — borrowed in both ordinary
cases, allocating only for a row that genuinely has two contributors. The
return-type change is what forced every consumer that reads the composed value
to be re-decided; the eight that were asking whether a value was authored were
forced by the removal of that predicate.
* `Source` gains `Shared(name)`. It is DERIVED from the two halves rather than
stored beside them, so a form cannot be read back saying it is authored while
holding a derivation. `authored()` is replaced by `writable()`; `wire()` and
`WORDS` publish the three-word vocabulary.
* `Derivation { from, value }` — carrying the value is what makes the
composition re-runnable when the written half changes.
* `FieldType::merges()` — a sequence can hold two contributions, a single value
cannot. `FieldType::compose()` — written first, then what the derivation says
and they had not already named, de-duplicated.
* `ConfigField::with_derived()` builds a shared row and refuses
(`FormError::Unmergeable`) on a single-valued shape. A written half that
contributes no elements leaves the row wholly derived, by one private
normaliser every act that can empty it calls.
* `element_source(at)` — provenance per line, derivable because the composition
is written-first. `derived_elements()` — how many lines are the derivation's.
* `edited()` compares the WRITTEN halves. `settle`/`revert` follow.
* `set` writes the written half and gives the row back when it is emptied.
`disown()` is that act by name; `written_row()` is what a caller stores;
`author()` adopts the whole composition and announces it.
* `ConfigForm::remove` on a shared row disowns in place and LEAVES the row;
`shared()` is the rollup beside `derived()`.
PAINTER — `pinion_widget_paint::config_form`
* `Seat::GiveBack` is the third act, with `Seat::act()` as the one place the
seat's tag word lives — the painter and the accessibility tree both read it.

in that entry's verification clause. The ledger is append-only, so the count is
corrected here: R1716 opened 5 debts and closed 1.

R1716 gave a settings row a provenance with two answers — somebody wrote it, or
the screen worked it out — and the behaviour canon's own screen needs three. A
node may be told to dial an already-running peer this canvas does not draw AND
be wired to the peers it does draw. Those are not competing answers to one
question; they are two contributions to one list. R1716 could not say that, so a
written value took the whole row and the drawn links stopped reaching the
configuration; it paid for the loss with a gate warning naming each drawn
address the card no longer dialled. This round removes the thing that warning
was compensating for.

THE SHAPE IS THE TYPE'S, AND IT IS TWO HALVES INSTEAD OF ONE VALUE.
`ConfigField` holds `written` (the half somebody wrote, `None` when nobody has)
and `worked_out` (a `Derivation`: what it was worked out from, and to). The
shown value is COMPUTED from them, so it cannot be a third place the same fact
lives; `Source` is computed too, which is why a form can no longer be read back
claiming to be authored while holding a derivation. `Source` gains
`Shared(name)` beside `Authored` and `Derived(name)`, and `Source::authored()`
— a bool eight consumers were asking the wrong question with — is replaced by
`writable()`, which forced every one of them to re-decide.

THE COMPOSITION RULE IS THE SHAPE'S. `FieldType::merges()` is true for a
sequence and false for a single value: two addresses compose, two modes
contradict. `with_derived` refuses on a single-valued shape rather than picking
a winner, so a screen cannot quietly compose something that has no composition.
The order is written-first, de-duplicated, which is the canon's, and it buys a
second thing: element provenance is then DERIVABLE — the elements before the
written half's count are somebody's and the rest are the derivation's.

`edited()` MOVED TO THE WRITTEN HALF. That was the question R1716 could not
answer and the real reason it did not compose: a row whose shown value moved
because the canvas moved was not edited by anybody, and a form that said it was
would offer a "put it back" that puts nothing back.

THREE ACTS ON ONE RECTANGLE. `Seat::GiveBack` joins `Remove` and `TakeOver`:
removing a shared row takes the written half out and LEAVES the row, because the
derivation is still true and a removed row would be back one render later. The
seat's tag word is now one function both the painter and the accessibility tree
read, which is a duplication this round created and then removed.

PROVENANCE REACHES THE ELEMENT, BECAUSE EDITING DOES. That is this round's
lesson stated once: a gate that fails on a new state is asking the OLD
granularity's question, and the answer is to move the fact rather than to exempt
the gate. Driven the first time the
state existed, an edit over an element the canvas contributed wrote the canvas's
whole contribution into the person's half and moved its neighbours. So
`element_source(at)` answers per line, the painter draws a contributed line with
the read-out's skin, the accessibility node says read-only and what worked it
out, and the box refuses to open over one. The seed and the commit are about the
half being edited, never about the composition.

read from the stored half and the drawn wires; the store keeps only the written
half; and the launch gate's warning is now the canon's own — an address somebody
wrote that nothing on this canvas listens on, which suspends nothing and blocks

R1718.decision_summary:
R1718 — a type that speaks to a person says every sentence it can say, and a
reader can tell them apart.

R1717 closed the defect and left the class open:
`debt-a-gate-vocabulary-was-a-string-with-a-suffix` says the repair was made and
what remains is the audit — is this shape elsewhere, and can anything in this
tree check that a sentence a person reads is a sentence at all? Both were
measured before anything was built.

THE FIRST PREMISE HELD, AND SMALLER THAN FEARED. Of 310 places that recover
something by matching a string prefix or suffix, 49 do it on a key or a tag, and
all but a handful are a census reading a naming scheme its own painter composed
— which is the legitimate direction. The production instances of the R1716 shape
proper, where a fact with no type is stuffed into a string and pattern-matched
back out, are a property grid encoding a row's KIND in a key prefix and two
screens recovering a seat's role the same way. Real, screen-local, and not what
this round is worth spending on.

THE SECOND PREMISE HELD MUCH HARDER, AND IS THE ROUND. Of the wordings this
workspace can put in front of a person, **11 of 39 matched any search at all**,
and most of those eleven were short fragments a search matched for other
reasons. Among the unread: the launch verdict a screen paints and puts in two
toasts, the take-over toast R1716 built precisely so a person would be told what
was displaced, two of three configuration defects, and every reason a shut
affordance gives a screen reader. Nothing anywhere asked whether a sentence
reads; the checks that exist are substring probes over fragments, which is
exactly what let a garbled sentence ship for a round with every gate green.

THE SHAPE. `pinion_core::test_fixtures::speech` is the gate, and it asserts four
properties, each earned by a defect this workspace actually had: every arm is
DRIVEN (the third situation never was); silence is DECLARED (see below); all
sentences are DISTINCT (the third arm read as the first arm's wording); and a
clause OMITS the subject its caller prefixes (the card was named twice). The arm
count is the type's own — `Self::ARMS` from the variant census — so passing
`said.len()` is the one way to hold it wrong, and the doc says so because
nothing can check it.

★★★ THE SILENCE SPLIT IS THE ROUND'S OWN CORRECTION, MADE BY THE FIRST TWO TYPES
THE GATE WAS POINTED AT. A launch verdict's good case says "nothing to fix —
launch is open"; a text judgement's good case returns the empty string. Both are
defensible and they cannot both be the default, so neither is: an arm that says
nothing is named in a `silent` list, and a name in that list whose arm speaks is
a dead declaration and fails too. That is the same split the analysis-tool
screens already draw between the regions that owe a reader a voice and the ones
that declare a silence, and the reason is the same — a census with nothing on
one side is satisfiable by putting everything on the other.

AND THE CENSUS IS THE SOURCE, NOT A ROSTER. A gate nobody points at a new type
is a gate that shrinks, which is how the fourth situation was added unworded. So
an integration test reads the crate's own source twice — for the types that CAN
speak, and for the names the gate is actually driven with — and asserts set
equality in both directions. There is no list to keep in step, a new speaking
type fails until somebody drives it, and a drive naming a type that cannot speak
fails as a check that cannot fail.

★★★★★ AND THE ROUND WALKED INTO ITS OWN CLASS TWICE, WHICH IS THE THING WORTH
RECORDING. First, the counterfactual driver refused to start: it runs its gate
LOCALLY and the baseline was red, because `cargo test -p pinion-core` alone
cannot compile an integration test that reaches `test_fixtures` — every earlier
run had a sibling crate alongside whose dev-dependency turned the feature on.
A gate that is only there when another crate happens to be in the same
invocation is not a gate. Second, three of the eight counterfactuals PASSED:

★ First, a correction the previous round's entry owes. R1718's closing audit
found TWO defects of one class ("a gate I ran" is not "every gate there is"),
and its ledger entry recorded only the first. The second: `cargo doc` cannot
resolve an intra-doc link into a **feature-gated** module, because the doc
build runs without that feature and the module is not there. The commit
failed at rc=1 after clippy was already green, and the background
notification for both said "exit code 0" while the `.rc` file said 1. The
standing rule this yields: a doc link into a feature-gated module is
forbidden — write the capability as a sentence instead.

## The defect, measured by driving the three screens rather than reading them

Each of the analysis tool's three screens keeps "the last thing I said" and
each kept it as a `String`. 117 call sites (58 / 11 / 48) handed one to a
one-line setter, and the wire typed all three as `string`. Nothing downstream
could ask what KIND of thing had been said, so nothing did:

* a **refusal was announced with the same urgency as a confirmation**, because
  the urgency was a per-screen constant. Driven: selecting a card on the node
  lab says `selected R-01` and its live region read `assertive` — a screen
  reader interrupted for something the person did on purpose — while the other
  two screens were `polite`, so on those a refusal waited for a pause a person
  working the tool does not leave. One constant, right for half of what each
  screen says, and wrong in opposite directions on different screens;
* an **act that changed nothing said nothing**, and the previous message stood.
  Driven: renaming a card to the name it already had left an earlier refusal on
  the toast, so a person read a sentence about a different act;
* the toast's bullet was one colour for everything (`ink.accent`,
  unconditional), so a refusal and a confirmation were one picture;
* and the fact that a refusal WAS a refusal travelled in a string prefix,
  spelled three ways: `format!("refused: {sentence}")` five times on one
  screen, a `refusal_sentence` helper on another, `format!("query refused:
  {why}")` on the third. That is R1717's defect — a fact smuggled into wording
  and recovered by whoever remembers to sniff for it — one level above where
  R1718 closed it.

## The floor, measured by building a probe and running it

Against the mature toolkit at 6.11.1, offscreen:

* its status channel **carries no kind at all** — 62 properties and 37 methods,
  and none of them names one; the accessor answers the text;
* its dialogs **do** have a kind (five arms) and **the kind does not change what
  a reader hears**: the accessible role of the critical dialog and of the
  informational one are the same number;
* its announcement event carries an urgency and **the caller passes it, derived
  from nothing**, defaulting to the polite one;
* nothing refuses a malformed message: `refused: refused: refused: ` and the
  empty string are both accepted verbatim.

Six capabilities this round ships are compile errors there: asking the channel
what kind the last message was, saying something *as* a refusal, deriving the
urgency from the kind, refusing a doubly-framed message, reading the producer's
own clause without the frame, and saying "it was already so".

## What was built, and why it is the shape it is

`pinion_core::utterance` — an `Utterance` is a `Tone` and a **clause**, where
the clause is the producer's own sentence stored with no frame on it.
`sentence()` composes the two for a person; `clause()` gives the producer's half
back untouched. So the frame is never in the stored text and no later reader has
to take it off — and the same value answers both channels, the person's framed
and the agent's not, which is what the two `format!`s could not do without
drifting.

The rule about what may be said lives in one place (`Utterance::fault`) behind
two doors, the pattern `shrink` established: `checked` returns the fault and is
what tests drive, and the named constructors panic with the fault's own
sentence, because a screen composing a malformed announcement is a programming
error and there is no rendering of it that helps the person in front of it.
Three faults, each a defect this tree shipped: an empty clause, a clause that
already carries this tone's frame, and **a Rust `Debug` spelling**. That last
one is R1699's: `Rejected(RefusalReason("..."))` reached a person eight times,
and R1699 fixed it with a per-screen helper whose own note said that a screen
which has to remember not to use `Debug` is a screen that will use `Debug`. The
remembering is the constructor's now, and the helper is deleted.

`Tone::urgency` is **derived**, and `pinion_a11y::AccessLive::for_urgency`
lowers it, so a screen cannot choose how urgently it is heard. `Off` is
unreachable from an utterance on purpose: it belongs to a declared region opting
out of a live ancestor, and an utterance is a thing a screen chose to say.

audit has to run BEFORE the ledger closes.** Run after, its answer becomes the
next round's correction.

## The defect, measured by driving the three screens rather than reading them

§2 #2 makes RPC the AI's primary path, so "an agent drives and a person
watches" is the ORDINARY state of these screens rather than an exception.
Driving every action slot the three screens publish, with an argument each verb
must refuse:

| screen | actions that refuse | reached the person |
|---|--:|--:|
| A node lab | 26 | **2** |
| B capture viewer | 9 | **0** |
| C dashboard | 20 | **0** |

Fifty-five refusals; two arrive. And the two that do are the two sites where
somebody wrote the coupling out by hand — `let said = …; state.say(said.clone());
Err(InvokeError::rejected(said.into_clause()))` — so the property held exactly
where it had been remembered, which is the shape every fact this workspace has
since moved into a type used to have.

In the other fifty-three the agent was told, the screen did not move, and the
sentence standing on it was about some earlier act. That is the stale-message
defect `Tone::Unchanged` was built for one round ago, arriving through the other
channel — and nothing anywhere could tell the two situations apart.

The same measurement found the drift that hand-written pairing invites. On the
node lab's link authoring one refusal said `R-01 has no accept pin` to the
person and `R-01 does not listen, so nothing can dial it` to the agent: two
wordings for one fact, three sites away from the round that made them one value.

## The floor, measured by building a probe and running it

Against the mature toolkit at 6.11.1, offscreen:

* refusing a programmatic call emits **0** accessibility events — both for a
  verb nobody declared and for a declared verb that answers "no";
* the caller's whole answer is a **boolean**. A reason for the first exists and
  goes to the process's diagnostic stream, a global sink that no caller and no
  person reads; the second produces no diagnostic line at all;
* its own status channel emits **0** accessibility events, takes no kind, and
  nothing routes a refusal into it: a caller that wants the person told calls
  it, with words it composes itself;
* **nothing anywhere reports whether the person was told**, so a caller that
  wants to avoid saying it twice cannot find out.

Six capabilities this round ships are compile errors there: asking a refusal for
the sentence a person reads, having the framework put it in front of them,
asking a surface where its speech goes, declaring that a surface has nowhere,
learning from a refusal whether the person heard it, and driving every published
action into refusal to check that they all do.

## What was built, and why it is the shape it is

The seam is `invoke_declared` and `intervene_from` — the one place each mutation
channel reaches a surface. A refusal there is turned into an `Utterance` and
handed back to the same surface through a new
`ExternalIntrospect::announce`, which answers what it did about it. There is no
site where a producer can supply one channel and forget the other, because
there is no site at all.

**`InvokeError::said` / `InterveneError::said`** give every arm a sentence. The
wire already had a word for each — and a word is what an agent matches on:
`UnknownInvokePath` is not a thing to put in front of somebody. So the two
renderings come off one value and are held to OPPOSITE rules, which is the
distinction this round's own test got wrong on its first pass. A refusal the
SURFACE authored travels as the producer's sentence, so the agent's copy and the
person's copy must be the same string. A refusal the FRAMEWORK authored travels
as a tag, so they must differ and the person's must be a sentence.

**`Announced` has three arms.** `At` names the live region, so the claim is
readable back rather than believed — the harness goes and reads the sentence
there, and a surface cannot satisfy the gate by answering `At` and doing
nothing. `Nowhere` carries a reason, because a silent list can be grown by
adding a name. And `Undeclared` is its own arm rather than folded into
`Nowhere`, on R1718's finding: if "nothing here speaks" were also the answer of
a surface that never considered the question, a census could be satisfied by
never considering it.

**The refusal's wire record gained its third fact.** R1487 said which surface
refused, R1564 said what it refused about, and `announced` says whether anyone
at the screen heard. That is what answers the question the registered debt left
open — whether the node lab's announcing was right or double-speaking. It is
neither a per-screen decision nor a guess any more: the agent is TOLD, and can
decide.

**Reads are deliberately outside it.** A refused `query` changed nothing and
left nothing stale, so there is nothing the person is missing; announcing every
failed read would fill the one channel a person watches with an agent's probing.
The two mutation channels both route through the seam and the read channel does
not, stated once in the trait's own doc instead of decided three times.

## What the round's own gate found on its first run

Two defects, both of a class that only exists once every refusal reaches a
person.

**A Rust value's `Debug` spelling in a refusal.** Driving the node lab's
`add_key` with a number answered `Int(-987654) is not text`, which the
announcement rule correctly refuses as `Fault::DebugSpelling` — so the person
got the framework's fallback and the agent got Rust syntax. R1699 fixed exactly
this on the person's channel and it was still here on the agent's, because
until this round nothing on that channel had a rule. Two screens carried the
line. The repair is a substrate word: `IntrospectValue::kind` names the KIND and
never the value, in the vocabulary `SchemaField`'s `type` already publishes, so
a refusal about a kind and the declaration of that kind read alike.

**The two-wording drift above**, now impossible: the framework announces the
refusal it hands back, so a second wording at the producer would not merely be
untidy — it would be overwritten a moment later by the one the agent got, and
the person would read whichever the path happened to choose.

R1718's speech census matches `fn sentence(` / `fn message(`. A type that
answers an `Utterance` speaks just as surely — the sentence is one accessor
further away — so both of this round's speakers were invisible to it, and the
crate's census was green while eleven arms of each could have said nothing. It
reads `fn said(` now. This is the third widening of that census in three rounds
(R1719 taught it `self` as well as `&self`), and the lesson is the same each
time: **a census keyed on the accessor's NAME rather than on the fact lets every
future speaker in through whichever spelling it happens to pick.**

never the value, in the vocabulary `SchemaField`'s `type` already publishes, so

refusal it hands back, so a second wording at the producer would not merely be
untidy — it would be overwritten a moment later by the one the agent got, and
the person would read whichever the path happened to choose.

(R1719 taught it `self` as well as `&self`), and the lesson is the same each
time: **a census keyed on the accessor's NAME rather than on the fact lets every
future speaker in through whichever spelling it happens to pick.**

R1721.decision_summary:
R1721 — a row of chips declares how many of its members may be on, and its
roles, its keyboard and its refusal are all derived from that one word.

## The defect, measured by driving the screens rather than reading them

Three screens of the analysis tool paint the same shape — a line of labelled
pills, each on or off — and until this round each of them decided, by hand and
separately, what that shape *is*. Driven 2026-08-19:

| screen | the row | what it DECLARED | what it DID |
|---|---|--:|---|
| B capture viewer | 3 saved filters | 3 independent `button`s, **3** Tab stops | **at most one**: choosing the second cleared the first, choosing the chosen one cleared it |
| C dashboard | 5 saved filters | 5 independent `button`s, **0** Tab stops | **nothing at all** — clicked all five, every `checked` stayed where it was |
| the chip gallery | 4 filters | 4 independent `button`s, 4 Tab stops | any subset |

Two of the three announced a rule they did not obey. The capture viewer told a
screen reader "toggle button, not pressed" three times over a set where only one
member can ever be on, and its own test file was named "the switches are
independent". The dashboard's five were announced as operable controls, were
inert to a pointer, and no keyboard reached any of them — the whole board's
interior was pointer-only.

The registered debt this round closes described the defect as "the same shape
written two ways", and the measurement was worse than the file in two places:
the dashboard row it named is a toolbar rather than a chip group (the real
counterpart is the filter card's five chips, at zero stops and no behaviour), and
the capture viewer's behaviour already WAS at-most-one. So the honest diagnosis
is not "two screens spelled it differently" but **"two screens were publishing a
rule they do not keep"**, which no amount of reading the file would have found.

## The floor, measured by building a probe and running it

Against the mature toolkit at 6.11.1, offscreen — a row of three checkable
buttons joined by the one type it has for expressing a selection rule over a set
of buttons:

* the rule does not reach the accessibility tree: an exclusive set and an
  independent set report the **same** member role, and it is the push-button role
  in both, so a screen reader is never told the members are alternatives;
* the object carrying the rule is not a widget and has **no accessibility node at
  all** — nothing stands for the set, and its members are loose children of
  whatever encloses them;
* **"at most one" is not expressible**: clicking the chosen member of an
  exclusive set leaves it chosen, and the set cannot be emptied;
* the group publishes exactly two properties, one of which is its name — the rule
  is a bare boolean with no roster, cursor or key list readable off it;
* ★ joining the set **costs the keyboard**: three loose checkable buttons are
  three Tab stops, and the moment they join a group — *even a non-exclusive one*
  — two of them accept neither `Tab` nor an arrow and are reachable only by
  pointer. Measured both ways round, with the walk validated against the ungrouped
  row that does move;
* and `Home` / `End` move nothing inside the set.

The last two are defects rather than absences, and everything this round derives
is a compile error there.

## The decision

`Choice { Any, AtMostOne, ExactlyOne }` is the whole declaration a chip row
makes, and six things are derived from it with nowhere for a screen to state any
of them separately: the group's role, each chip's role, the attribute that
carries a chip's on-ness, how many Tab stops the row costs, what the arrows do,
and what happens when the chip that is on is chosen again.

The three arms answer those six differently enough that changing only the word
moves several of them, which is what makes the derivation observable rather than
decorative — and the round's gate asserts the pairwise inequality rather than
trusting the table that states it.

Two consequences are worth naming as decisions rather than mechanics:

* **The three accessibility families were already here.** `chip_group_nodes` adds
  no topology: it *chooses* between `toggle_button_group_nodes`,
  `listbox_option_nodes` and `radiogroup_radio_nodes`, which this crate has built
  since R733, R51.96 and R758. The finding is not that the shapes were missing —
  it is that nothing related them to the rule a row obeys, so three screens each
  picked one by hand and two picked wrongly. The `match` has no wildcard arm, so a
  fourth rule fails to compile here rather than falling through to whichever shape
  was written first.
* **`focusable` stops being a parameter.** `option_chip`'s documentation argued
  that it *must* stay one, because "a radio group is ONE tab stop while
  independent toggles are each a stop" and baking either in would be wrong for
  half its callers. That argument was right about the fact and wrong about where
  the fact lives: `ChipGroup::is_a_stop(tag)` answers it for the row and for its
  chips with ONE derivation, so a screen cannot make both a stop.

## What the round refused to widen into

The rule is one-way on the wire. `Choice::wire` names the rule for a diagnostic;
there is no `from_wire`, because a rule is declared in source by the screen that
owns the row and nothing outside it is entitled to change how many of its chips
may be on — a parser for a message that cannot arrive is the `Fault::wire` shape
R1719.1 deleted. The rule still reaches an agent in a vocabulary it already
knows: a non-multiselect `listbox` is at most one, a `radiogroup` is exactly one,
a `group` of `button[aria-pressed]` is any.
changes_bullets: **`pinion_core::widgets::chip_group`** (new, §5.38 §5.39): `Choice` (the rule,
with `ALL` and a one-way `wire`), `ChipPosture` (one value rather than a posture
plus an `enabled` flag, so a chip cannot be locked and choosable at once),
`Chip`, and `ChipGroup`. From the rule it derives `is_composite`, `cursor()` as a
`RovingSpec` (`Axis::Both` + `Ends::Wrap` + an activation that differs per arm),
`stops()`, `is_a_stop(tag)` — the one read a painter and a focus ring share —
and `choose(index) -> Utterance`. Paint-free and accessibility-free.
**`Choice::apply`** is the only place the rule is applied: an `Outcome` that is
either the whole next on-set or a `Refusal`, so a screen cannot clear the vector
itself and then announce something that disagrees. Three refusals — no such
member, the locked chip, and the `ExactlyOne` row asked to empty itself — and
each clause names the chip and the row rather than an index.
**`pinion_a11y::chip_group`** (new, §5.40): the only place the roles are spelled.
`chip_group_nodes(row, focused)` dispatches on `Choice` to the three families
this crate already had — `toggle_button_group_nodes` / `listbox_option_nodes` /
`radiogroup_radio_nodes` — with no wildcard arm, publishes the row's cursor
through `with_navigation` when the rule makes it a composite, and resolves focus
through `ChipFocus` rather than taking it as a claim. `group_role` / `member_role`
are published so a screen's own accessibility census reads the role from the same
place the tree builds it, and a test binds them to what the builders actually
emit.
**`pinion_widget_paint::chip::chip_row`** (new): the pill per chip, carrying the
focusability the rule derives. `option_chip`'s `focusable` parameter keeps its
place for the chart bindings that paint one chip outside any row, and its
documentation now names where the derivation lives.
**Four bindings adopted it and all three arms have a live consumer.**
`hello-packet-view` and `hello-analyzer-shell` declare `AtMostOne` in their own
`spec` modules; `hello-filter-chip` declares `Any`; `hello-segmented-button`
declares `ExactlyOne`. The two analysis screens keep their own palette — the
reference's tones, not Material's — and ask `is_a_stop` for the one thing a chip
cannot work out by looking at itself.
**The capture viewer's saved-filter bar is now one widget**: a group container at
the chips' own union (pointer-transparent, so the bar cannot swallow a press
nothing resolves), its subtree built by `chip_group_nodes`, its cursor answered
by the row rather than projected by hand, and `toggle_saved` reduced to storing
what the rule decided. Its Tab ring went 7 -> 5 and gained arrows, `Home`, `End`
and `Enter` inside the bar; both of the screen's ring censuses now read `stops()`
instead of listing the chips.
**The dashboard's filter chips became operable at all**: `Hit::FilterChip`, a
`filter_chip_rects` geometry the paint and the hit test share, and
`ShellOracle::choose_filter`. The bar is this screen's first keyboard stop
*inside a card*, declared in `FOCUS_RING` with its cursor read from
`FILTER_ROW.cursor()`. The card's chosen filter is an `Option<usize>` rather than
five booleans, because five booleans would let the screen hold a state the rule
it announces forbids.
**`ShellState` threads rather than fetches.** The first draft called
`use_shell_state()` inside the body painter and the running screen refused it:
the shell's press path has no `Owner` scope, so a click on a chip panicked in
`use_transport_clock`. `card_scene` / `body_scene` / `ready_body` / `filter_body`
and `filter_nodes` now take the state. No unit test could have found this —
every one of them runs inside an `Owner`.
**Two censuses corrected by measuring.** `capture.t1.8` moves gap -> have with a
proof (both halves are here: the language and the chips, and a saved chip runs
the query it names), so the framework owes 8 of 68 rather than 9.
`dashboard.t2.3` keeps its `gap` and loses a false sentence: it said "there is no
legend widget to click" and there are two (`LineChart` R1380, `ScatterChart`
R1392) — what is short is breadth and the absence of any declaration of which
chart kinds support the gesture.

R1721.publishable_decision_summary:
R1721 — a row of chips declares how many of its members may be on, and its
roles, its keyboard and its refusal are all derived from that one word.

## The defect, measured by driving the screens rather than reading them

Three screens of the analysis tool paint the same shape — a line of labelled
pills, each on or off — and until this round each of them decided, by hand and
separately, what that shape *is*. Driven 2026-08-19:

| screen | the row | what it DECLARED | what it DID |
|---|---|--:|---|
| B capture viewer | 3 saved filters | 3 independent `button`s, **3** Tab stops | **at most one**: choosing the second cleared the first, choosing the chosen one cleared it |
| C dashboard | 5 saved filters | 5 independent `button`s, **0** Tab stops | **nothing at all** — clicked all five, every `checked` stayed where it was |
| the chip gallery | 4 filters | 4 independent `button`s, 4 Tab stops | any subset |

Two of the three announced a rule they did not obey. The capture viewer told a
screen reader "toggle button, not pressed" three times over a set where only one
member can ever be on, and its own test file was named "the switches are
independent". The dashboard's five were announced as operable controls, were
inert to a pointer, and no keyboard reached any of them — the whole board's
interior was pointer-only.

The registered debt this round closes described the defect as "the same shape
written two ways", and the measurement was worse than the file in two places:
the dashboard row it named is a toolbar rather than a chip group (the real
counterpart is the filter card's five chips, at zero stops and no behaviour), and
the capture viewer's behaviour already WAS at-most-one. So the honest diagnosis
is not "two screens spelled it differently" but **"two screens were publishing a
rule they do not keep"**, which no amount of reading the file would have found.

## The floor, measured by building a probe and running it

Against the mature toolkit at 6.11.1, offscreen — a row of three checkable
buttons joined by the one type it has for expressing a selection rule over a set
of buttons:

* the rule does not reach the accessibility tree: an exclusive set and an
  independent set report the **same** member role, and it is the push-button role
  in both, so a screen reader is never told the members are alternatives;
* the object carrying the rule is not a widget and has **no accessibility node at
  all** — nothing stands for the set, and its members are loose children of
  whatever encloses them;
* **"at most one" is not expressible**: clicking the chosen member of an
  exclusive set leaves it chosen, and the set cannot be emptied;
* the group publishes exactly two properties, one of which is its name — the rule
  is a bare boolean with no roster, cursor or key list readable off it;
* ★ joining the set **costs the keyboard**: three loose checkable buttons are
  three Tab stops, and the moment they join a group — *even a non-exclusive one*
  — two of them accept neither `Tab` nor an arrow and are reachable only by
  pointer. Measured both ways round, with the walk validated against the ungrouped
  row that does move;
* and `Home` / `End` move nothing inside the set.

The last two are defects rather than absences, and everything this round derives
is a compile error there.

## The decision

`Choice { Any, AtMostOne, ExactlyOne }` is the whole declaration a chip row
makes, and six things are derived from it with nowhere for a screen to state any
of them separately: the group's role, each chip's role, the attribute that
carries a chip's on-ness, how many Tab stops the row costs, what the arrows do,
and what happens when the chip that is on is chosen again.

The three arms answer those six differently enough that changing only the word
moves several of them, which is what makes the derivation observable rather than
decorative — and the round's gate asserts the pairwise inequality rather than
trusting the table that states it.

Two consequences are worth naming as decisions rather than mechanics:

* **The three accessibility families were already here.** `chip_group_nodes` adds
  no topology: it *chooses* between `toggle_button_group_nodes`,
  `listbox_option_nodes` and `radiogroup_radio_nodes`, which this crate has built
  since R733, R51.96 and R758. The finding is not that the shapes were missing —
  it is that nothing related them to the rule a row obeys, so three screens each
  picked one by hand and two picked wrongly. The `match` has no wildcard arm, so a
  fourth rule fails to compile here rather than falling through to whichever shape
  was written first.
* **`focusable` stops being a parameter.** `option_chip`'s documentation argued
  that it *must* stay one, because "a radio group is ONE tab stop while
  independent toggles are each a stop" and baking either in would be wrong for
  half its callers. That argument was right about the fact and wrong about where
  the fact lives: `ChipGroup::is_a_stop(tag)` answers it for the row and for its
  chips with ONE derivation, so a screen cannot make both a stop.

## What the round refused to widen into

The rule is one-way on the wire. `Choice::wire` names the rule for a diagnostic;
there is no `from_wire`, because a rule is declared in source by the screen that
owns the row and nothing outside it is entitled to change how many of its chips
may be on — a parser for a message that cannot arrive is the `Fault::wire` shape
R1719.1 deleted. The rule still reaches an agent in a vocabulary it already
knows: a non-multiselect `listbox` is at most one, a `radiogroup` is exactly one,
a `group` of `button[aria-pressed]` is any.

plus an `enabled` flag, so a chip cannot be locked and choosable at once),

`RovingSpec` (`Axis::Both` + `Ends::Wrap` + an activation that differs per arm),

either the whole next on-set or a `Refusal`, so a screen cannot clear the vector

R1722.decision_summary:
R1722 — a chart's legend is a declared chip row over its own named parts, and
one word gives its shape, its roles, its Tab stops, its keyboard and its refusal.

## The defect, measured against the compiled surface rather than by reading paint

The analysis-tool census (`tools/analyzer_census.py`) said the framework owed 8
of 68 capabilities, and `dashboard.t2.3` — "toggling a series from the legend" —
carried R1721's own correction: two of this crate's chart kinds offered the
gesture, five did not, **and nothing anywhere said which was which**.

Measured 2026-08-19 against the public API:

| chart | named parts | legend before | could a caller toggle a part |
|---|---|---|---|
| line, scatter | series | a static row, or an interactive one on opt-in | yes |
| polar, donut | series / slices | a static row only | **no** |
| bar, box plot, candlestick | one set over categories | none | **no** |

The breadth number was the smaller half. The larger half is **askability**: a
board assembling several charts holds them as different types, so seven inherent
methods could only ever be called by code that already knew which chart it had —
which is precisely the position a dashboard is *not* in. A board therefore either
knew by having read this crate, or offered an affordance that did nothing.

And the two kinds that did offer it each *chose*, per paint: a chart held an
`Option<Vec<String>>` of caller-supplied tags and branched on it, so

* the interactive row and the paint row were two painters a chart picked between,
  with nothing relating the pick to anything a caller could read;
* the tags were zipped against the series, so a caller passing too few silently
  truncated its own legend;
* and the entries were derived **six** times over four files, each copy spelling
  `color.unwrap_or_else(|| palette.color(i))` again.

## The floor, measured rather than read

The mature toolkit at 6.11.1 carries two chart modules. Its charting module is
not among the ones built on this machine, so this is a measurement of its source
and the new module's doc says so — this crate's own claims are asserted by tests
instead.

It is **ahead on breadth**: six legend-marker kinds, one per series family, so
every chart type there has legend entries. That is the one axis on which it led,
and it is why this round's breadth exists rather than only its declaration. On
every other axis it is a floor:

* a marker emits a *clicked* notification and **nothing more** — hiding the
  series is left to whoever wired the signal, so "toggling a series from the
  legend" is application work there and no two applications need agree;
* a marker is **not focusable**: the item that draws it handles a hover event and
  no key event at all, so the row is reachable only by pointer;
* ★ **neither of its two chart modules contains a single accessibility call.**
  Measured across both trees, the count is zero — a legend there is invisible to
  a screen reader except as loose text;
* nothing declares whether a part *may* be hidden, so a caller cannot ask before
  offering the gesture;
* and its successor module went further back: a series publishes a list of
  `{colour, border colour, label}` carrying no identity, no state and no signal,
  so its legend is paint an application redraws.

## What is derived, and from what

`LegendInteraction` is the whole declaration, and a legend has nowhere to state
any of the following separately:

| | `Paint` | `Toggle` |
|---|---|---|
| what the row is | swatches and labels | a chip row where any subset may be on |
| the row's accessibility node | none | a `group` |
| an entry's accessibility node | none | `button` carrying its on-state |
| Tab stops | none | one per drawn entry |
| what a press does | refused, with the reason | turns that part off or on |
| an off entry | (nothing is off) | grey swatch, dimmed label, slot kept |

The guarantee is structural rather than conventional: `Legend::scene` is the
**only** painter, the two row painters moved into the module and are **private**,
so a chart painting an interaction it did not declare is a compile error. This is
R1721's shape one layer down — there a screen announced a rule it did not obey,
and the repair was to derive the announcement and the behaviour from one word.

The rule is any-subset and is not a policy chosen here: a legend over which no
part, some parts or every part may be hidden *is* that rule, and the two
composite rules would each be a claim this crate has no grounds to make about a
caller's data.

## Three decisions worth stating

**The roster a keyboard walks is the roster the row drew.** A too-narrow row
collapses its tail into a `+N` marker; the chip row is built from the same
seating, so a control announced for a part that was never painted is
unrepresentable. A press over the **wire** still reaches such a part, which is
stated on the method and asserted — the pane's width bounds the pointer and the
keyboard, and the marker is what reports that.

**The three single-set chart kinds answer with an empty roster.** A bar chart
here holds ONE set of labelled bars over a category axis, so there is no second
named thing for a legend to distinguish; the reference gives its bar chart legend
markers because a bar chart there holds several bar *sets*, which is a difference
in the data model rather than in the legend. Answering — rather than having no
method to call — is what lets a board ask instead of discovering that nothing was
drawn.

**Where the pointer is comes back from the consumer.** A chart is a value
projected from application state and cannot know hover or press, so `LegendPostures`
takes them back, **indexed** rather than as a parallel list — the same hazard the
derived tags removed, closed the same way.
changes_bullets: **New — `crates/pinion-chart/src/legend.rs`.** `LegendEntry` (a part's swatch,
name and on-ness, derived from the chart's own data), `LegendInteraction`
(`Paint` / `Toggle` — the one word), `Legend` (the roster plus that word),
`LegendSeating` (how many entries a width seats and how many the `+N` stands
for), `LegendSeat` (where a chart puts its row), `LegendPostures` (where the
pointer is, which a chart cannot know), and `StaticLegend` (the refusal, carrying
the sentence a person is shown).
`Legend::group(avail, postures)` derives R1721's `ChipGroup` with the any-subset
rule, so `Legend::access_nodes` is `pinion_a11y::chip_group::chip_group_nodes`
rather than anything new — the legend is that widget's **fourth** consumer and
its first inside a framework crate. `Legend::press` answers with the on-set that
would follow, or refuses because the legend declared itself paint.
**New — the `ChartLegend` trait, implemented by all seven chart kinds.** Two
required methods (`legend`, and `legend_seat` with a top-band default) and two
provided ones (`legend_scene`, `legend_access_nodes`), so a consumer gets the
paint and the accessibility tree seated identically from one call and cannot
reconstruct the width wrongly.
**Moved and made private.** `legend_row`, `interactive_legend_row` and
`legend_overflow_marker` left `draw.rs` for `legend.rs`, where they are private
functions. That is the compile-time gate: a chart can no longer reach a legend

**Breadth.** `PolarChart` and `DonutChart` gain `with_legend`, so a radar's
profiles and a ring's parts can be turned off — neither could before.
`Slice::visible` is new, and a hidden slice **re-normalises** the ring, which is

**Fixed, reachable only once a slice could be hidden.** The donut tagged its
sectors by DRAW order, so hiding one renamed every later part; a sector now

**Removed.** `LineChart::interactive_legend` / `ScatterChart::interactive_legend`

whose captions are *the charts' own answers*: three say how many parts they have,

older screens (`hello-legend-toggle`, `hello-linked-legend`,
`hello-rescale-toggle`) moved to the derived tags and now ask their chart for
their accessibility tree instead of hand-building a toggle group.

Thirteen against `pinion-chart` (gate: the crate's whole lib suite): the declared

R1722.publishable_decision_summary:
R1722 — a chart's legend is a declared chip row over its own named parts, and
one word gives its shape, its roles, its Tab stops, its keyboard and its refusal.

## The defect, measured against the compiled surface rather than by reading paint

The analysis-tool census (`tools/analyzer_census.py`) said the framework owed 8
of 68 capabilities, and `dashboard.t2.3` — "toggling a series from the legend" —
carried R1721's own correction: two of this crate's chart kinds offered the
gesture, five did not, **and nothing anywhere said which was which**.

Measured 2026-08-19 against the public API:

| chart | named parts | legend before | could a caller toggle a part |
|---|---|---|---|
| line, scatter | series | a static row, or an interactive one on opt-in | yes |
| polar, donut | series / slices | a static row only | **no** |
| bar, box plot, candlestick | one set over categories | none | **no** |

The breadth number was the smaller half. The larger half is **askability**: a
board assembling several charts holds them as different types, so seven inherent
methods could only ever be called by code that already knew which chart it had —
which is precisely the position a dashboard is *not* in. A board therefore either
knew by having read this crate, or offered an affordance that did nothing.

And the two kinds that did offer it each *chose*, per paint: a chart held an
`Option<Vec<String>>` of caller-supplied tags and branched on it, so

* the interactive row and the paint row were two painters a chart picked between,
  with nothing relating the pick to anything a caller could read;
* the tags were zipped against the series, so a caller passing too few silently
  truncated its own legend;
* and the entries were derived **six** times over four files, each copy spelling
  `color.unwrap_or_else(|| palette.color(i))` again.

## The floor, measured rather than read

The mature toolkit at 6.11.1 carries two chart modules. Its charting module is
not among the ones built on this machine, so this is a measurement of its source
and the new module's doc says so — this crate's own claims are asserted by tests
instead.

It is **ahead on breadth**: six legend-marker kinds, one per series family, so
every chart type there has legend entries. That is the one axis on which it led,
and it is why this round's breadth exists rather than only its declaration. On
every other axis it is a floor:

* a marker emits a *clicked* notification and **nothing more** — hiding the
  series is left to whoever wired the signal, so "toggling a series from the
  legend" is application work there and no two applications need agree;
* a marker is **not focusable**: the item that draws it handles a hover event and
  no key event at all, so the row is reachable only by pointer;
* ★ **neither of its two chart modules contains a single accessibility call.**
  Measured across both trees, the count is zero — a legend there is invisible to
  a screen reader except as loose text;
* nothing declares whether a part *may* be hidden, so a caller cannot ask before
  offering the gesture;
* and its successor module went further back: a series publishes a list of
  `{colour, border colour, label}` carrying no identity, no state and no signal,
  so its legend is paint an application redraws.

## What is derived, and from what

`LegendInteraction` is the whole declaration, and a legend has nowhere to state
any of the following separately:

| | `Paint` | `Toggle` |
|---|---|---|
| what the row is | swatches and labels | a chip row where any subset may be on |
| the row's accessibility node | none | a `group` |
| an entry's accessibility node | none | `button` carrying its on-state |
| Tab stops | none | one per drawn entry |
| what a press does | refused, with the reason | turns that part off or on |
| an off entry | (nothing is off) | grey swatch, dimmed label, slot kept |

The guarantee is structural rather than conventional: `Legend::scene` is the
**only** painter, the two row painters moved into the module and are **private**,
so a chart painting an interaction it did not declare is a compile error. This is
R1721's shape one layer down — there a screen announced a rule it did not obey,
and the repair was to derive the announcement and the behaviour from one word.

The rule is any-subset and is not a policy chosen here: a legend over which no
part, some parts or every part may be hidden *is* that rule, and the two
composite rules would each be a claim this crate has no grounds to make about a
caller's data.

## Three decisions worth stating

**The roster a keyboard walks is the roster the row drew.** A too-narrow row
collapses its tail into a `+N` marker; the chip row is built from the same
seating, so a control announced for a part that was never painted is
unrepresentable. A press over the **wire** still reaches such a part, which is
stated on the method and asserted — the pane's width bounds the pointer and the
keyboard, and the marker is what reports that.

**The three single-set chart kinds answer with an empty roster.** A bar chart
here holds ONE set of labelled bars over a category axis, so there is no second
named thing for a legend to distinguish; the reference gives its bar chart legend
markers because a bar chart there holds several bar *sets*, which is a difference
in the data model rather than in the legend. Answering — rather than having no
method to call — is what lets a board ask instead of discovering that nothing was
drawn.

**Where the pointer is comes back from the consumer.** A chart is a value
projected from application state and cannot know hover or press, so `LegendPostures`
takes them back, **indexed** rather than as a parallel list — the same hazard the
derived tags removed, closed the same way.

R1723.decision_summary:
R1723 — a drag stops asking the display server where every window is.

## The defect, reported by a consumer and found by following the call path

Dragging a terminal window between docks was, in the consumer's words, "개느리다".

`AppShell::stamp_live_window_origins` runs on **every `CursorMoved` of a drag**
and asked **every live window** where it is. On X11 that question is
`XTranslateCoordinates` — a **synchronous round trip to the display server**,
taken inside the pointer handler — plus a `String` allocation per window and a
fresh `Vec` per event.

So the cost of dragging was `windows × pointer events` blocking round trips, and
it is **linear in how many windows are open**: a single-window app never notices,
and a terminal multiplexer with a board of panes drags through treacle.

It was found by reading the call path back from the gesture, not by profiling.
The query is three frames below the event, behind a gate whose own doc says it
exists so that "idle hovers + single-window apps skip the `inner_position()`
queries" — **the author saw the cost and gated the case that is cheap to gate,
leaving the expensive one running once per event.**

The purpose of the query is right and is kept: a cross-window redock has to
hit-test against where windows *actually* are, because a window-manager-placed
window declares no position and sits at a real offset. What was wrong is where
the cost was paid.

## What was ruled out first, and how

The round began as "did recent work cause this?", and the honest answer needed
call paths rather than suspicion. Every recent change to a crate the consumer
depends on was eliminated:

| round | why it cannot be it |
|---|---|
| a screen says how small it can get; reach composes down the clip chain | reachable only from RPC handlers |
| a window says what it gives up to get smaller; a window pans over its layout | the extra scene is RPC-only, and the pan returns immediately unless the binding declares a shrink policy — the consumer declares none |
| one rect intersection, three callers | the same arithmetic, given a name |
| focus settles to a fixed point | two drains and an emptiness check, then `false` |
| a chip row declares how many may be on | **not in the running binary** — it was built before that commit |
| a chart declares what its legend can do | the consumer does not depend on that crate at all |

★ Two of this session's own measurements were wrong before that table was
trustworthy: the first looked only at *this session's* commits, and the second
globbed **one of sixteen** manifests when asking what the consumer depends on.
Both were corrected by re-measuring after the owner pushed back twice.

## What was built

`OriginFreshness` — a generation counter that holds **no coordinates at all**.

The coordinates are the core's (`set_live_window_origins`) and are already there.
What was missing is the answer to *"is what you hold still true?"*, and that is a
question about **events**, not geometry: a window's desktop origin changes only
when the window system moves it, and winit says so. A cache of positions here
would be a second copy of a fact the core owns, and two copies can disagree; a
generation cannot disagree with anything.

Per-move round trips go from one-per-window to **zero**. A window move, a scale
change (the origins are logical pixels), or a change to the set of windows makes
them stale again.

The residue, stated: this is only as correct as the events it is told about. An
origin that changed with no winit event would go unnoticed — which is true of
every `Moved`-driven state in this shell, and is why the invalidation is called
from the coarsest set of events that can possibly move one, not the narrowest.

## ★★ The round's own first cut reintroduced the defect, and nothing caught it

The invalidation was first placed **before** the tracked-window lookup. The
shell-private **drag preview window** is moved by `set_outer_position` on every
pointer event of a drag and is deliberately kept out of the tracked set — so it
invalidated the cache once per event, **during the very gesture the cache exists
for**. The fix would have measured green and done nothing.

A counterfactual that restored that ordering was **caught by nothing**: a unit
test of the pure type cannot see a window that does not exist there.

⇒ **An ordering is not a gate.** The tracked test moved *inside* the pure type
(`note_window_moved(tracked: bool)`), where flipping it breaks a test. This is
R1721's lesson recurring — a defect outside the premise every test shares is one
no test can see — and the repair is the same shape: make the premise a value.
changes_bullets: **New — `OriginFreshness` in `pinion-shell/src/app.rs`.** A generation counter
and the generation the core's origins were last collected at. Two methods:
`note_changed` (something can have moved a window, or changed which windows
there are) and `take_restamp` (whether they must be collected again — answering
and recording in one call, because a caller that asked and then did not collect
would leave the core holding origins the generation claims are fresh; there is
no way to spell that mistake).
**`stamp_live_window_origins` asks it first.** The drag gate above it was never
enough: inside a drag that function runs on every pointer event, and collecting
is one display-server round trip per window.
**`stamp_all_window_origins` records that it collected.** It is the RPC path's
unconditional stamp; marking fresh there keeps the next pointer event of an
RPC-opened drag from collecting a second time for the same answer.
**Invalidation, from the coarsest events that can move an origin**: a window
move, a scale-factor change (the origins are logical pixels), and the four sites
that add or remove a tracked window.
**★ `note_window_moved(tracked: bool)` carries the tracked test itself.** Not the
call site. The shell-private drag preview window moves on every pointer event of
a drag and is deliberately outside the tracked set, so an invalidation that fires
for it restores the whole defect. The first cut guarded that by line order and a
counterfactual proved the ordering was defended by nothing; the condition now
lives where a test can reach it.
**Three functions became `&mut self`** — `stamp_live_window_origins`,
`stamp_all_window_origins`, `stamp_desktop_facts` — which is the compiler
recording that they now carry state across calls.
**Four tests**, all counting rather than timing: a settled drag collects once
over 240 events; a move makes the origins stale again and then settles; a burst
of moves between two asks is one staleness rather than one per event; and 240
moves of an untracked window change nothing while one tracked move still does.
verification_bullets: **Counterfactuals — 4 of 4 caught**, gate `cargo test -p pinion-shell --lib`:
a settled drag stops collecting; a move makes the origins stale again; asking
records the collect; and an untracked window's move changes nothing.
★ The fourth was **PASSED on its first run — a real finding, and the round's own
defect**. The invalidation had been placed before the tracked-window lookup, so
the drag preview window (moved by `set_outer_position` on every pointer event,
deliberately outside the tracked set) invalidated the cache once per event and
the fix did nothing. Nothing caught it, because a unit test of the pure type
cannot see a window that does not exist there. Repaired by moving the condition
into the pure type; caught after.
**The unit is a COUNT, not a clock.** "240 pointer events collect once" is what
the defect actually was — one round trip per window per event — and a wall-clock
assertion over a display-server round trip is a flake generator
([[zero-flake-policy]]). An honest latency figure would need an in-process
benchmark against a real display connection with a controlled window count,

R1723.publishable_decision_summary:
R1723 — a drag stops asking the display server where every window is.

## The defect, reported by a consumer and found by following the call path

Dragging a terminal window between docks was, in the consumer's words, "개느리다".

`AppShell::stamp_live_window_origins` runs on **every `CursorMoved` of a drag**
and asked **every live window** where it is. On X11 that question is
`XTranslateCoordinates` — a **synchronous round trip to the display server**,
taken inside the pointer handler — plus a `String` allocation per window and a
fresh `Vec` per event.

So the cost of dragging was `windows × pointer events` blocking round trips, and
it is **linear in how many windows are open**: a single-window app never notices,
and a terminal multiplexer with a board of panes drags through treacle.

It was found by reading the call path back from the gesture, not by profiling.
The query is three frames below the event, behind a gate whose own doc says it
exists so that "idle hovers + single-window apps skip the `inner_position()`
queries" — **the author saw the cost and gated the case that is cheap to gate,
leaving the expensive one running once per event.**

The purpose of the query is right and is kept: a cross-window redock has to
hit-test against where windows *actually* are, because a window-manager-placed
window declares no position and sits at a real offset. What was wrong is where
the cost was paid.

## What was ruled out first, and how

The round began as "did recent work cause this?", and the honest answer needed
call paths rather than suspicion. Every recent change to a crate the consumer
depends on was eliminated:

| round | why it cannot be it |
|---|---|
| a screen says how small it can get; reach composes down the clip chain | reachable only from RPC handlers |
| a window says what it gives up to get smaller; a window pans over its layout | the extra scene is RPC-only, and the pan returns immediately unless the binding declares a shrink policy — the consumer declares none |
| one rect intersection, three callers | the same arithmetic, given a name |
| focus settles to a fixed point | two drains and an emptiness check, then `false` |
| a chip row declares how many may be on | **not in the running binary** — it was built before that commit |
| a chart declares what its legend can do | the consumer does not depend on that crate at all |

★ Two of this session's own measurements were wrong before that table was
trustworthy: the first looked only at *this session's* commits, and the second
globbed **one of sixteen** manifests when asking what the consumer depends on.
Both were corrected by re-measuring after the owner pushed back twice.

## What was built

`OriginFreshness` — a generation counter that holds **no coordinates at all**.

The coordinates are the core's (`set_live_window_origins`) and are already there.
What was missing is the answer to *"is what you hold still true?"*, and that is a
question about **events**, not geometry: a window's desktop origin changes only
when the window system moves it, and winit says so. A cache of positions here
would be a second copy of a fact the core owns, and two copies can disagree; a
generation cannot disagree with anything.

Per-move round trips go from one-per-window to **zero**. A window move, a scale
change (the origins are logical pixels), or a change to the set of windows makes
them stale again.

The residue, stated: this is only as correct as the events it is told about. An
origin that changed with no winit event would go unnoticed — which is true of
every `Moved`-driven state in this shell, and is why the invalidation is called
from the coarsest set of events that can possibly move one, not the narrowest.

## ★★ The round's own first cut reintroduced the defect, and nothing caught it

The invalidation was first placed **before** the tracked-window lookup. The
shell-private **drag preview window** is moved by `set_outer_position` on every
pointer event of a drag and is deliberately kept out of the tracked set — so it
invalidated the cache once per event, **during the very gesture the cache exists
for**. The fix would have measured green and done nothing.

A counterfactual that restored that ordering was **caught by nothing**: a unit
test of the pure type cannot see a window that does not exist there.

⇒ **An ordering is not a gate.** The tracked test moved *inside* the pure type
(`note_window_moved(tracked: bool)`), where flipping it breaks a test. This is
R1721's lesson recurring — a defect outside the premise every test shares is one
no test can see — and the repair is the same shape: make the premise a value.
