R1724.decision_summary:
R1724 — a screen is a binding you can arrive at, and the analysis tool stops being three executables at one of its seats.

The behaviour reference this tool is modelled on is ONE application: a shell with an app bar and a navigation rail, and the rail switches between its sections. This tree assembled it as three executables — hello-analyzer-shell 13,854 lines, hello-node-lab 20,655, hello-packet-view 7,035, measured at this round's close with `find examples/<pkg>/src -name '*.rs' | xargs wc -l` and quoted with the command because the three taken mid-round were all wrong by the end of it — and the shell's own rail said so out loud, because three of its seven seats were declared Unavailable::elsewhere, an arm that exists only because a destination here can be finished and still unreachable. R1695 built the model and paint halves of navigating (Destinations / Journey / view_page_region); what neither gave is the half that makes those seats openable: what a destination's page IS when the page is a whole binding with its own externals, its own keymap, its own accessibility tree and its own text caret.

The decision is that the unit of composition is THE BINDING ITSELF, not a new kind of thing an author writes. `pinion_screen::Screen` is the dispatchable surface of a `WidgetView` with the window-level half removed, as `&self` methods so a roster can hold several; `Mount<V>` implements it for any existing binding; `ScreenRoster` pairs the destination roster with the screens behind its keys and is the ONLY way to reach one, so "the screen the journey is not at is not routable, not keyable, not readable and not painted" is a property of the type rather than a rule an author keeps. `hello-node-lab` is mounted at Catalog unedited — its 20,655 lines became a library and a four-line binary, so the demo sweep keeps its per-screen process and the application keeps its sections in one window.

Two mechanical guarantees carry the weight. `Screen` declares every hook and defaults NONE, so a hook added there stops `Mount` compiling until it is forwarded. The other direction — a hook added to WidgetCore / WidgetA11y / WidgetView and never mirrored — is covered by `pinion_screen::coverage`, a census that reads those three traits' own source and fails unless each of their hooks is mirrored, folded into one of Screen's methods, or pinned as the host's WITH THE REASON. There is no fourth answer.

FOUR framework repairs were forced by the first real mount rather than reasoned into existence, and three of them are defects that existed before this round and had no way to be seen. The largest: the mounted screen was DEAD TO THE MOUSE while every gate was green — it painted 139 tagged regions, answered every path on the wire, appeared in the accessibility tree, and `scene/pointer_reach` reported it `routed_by: node_lab`; not one press anywhere inside it reached anything, the screen or the host. Two stacked causes, and removing either one alone left the symptom exactly as it was, which is what made it expensive: `view_page_region` was unconditionally pointer-transparent (a flag that in `Scene::hit_test` skips a child AND ITS WHOLE SUBTREE — right for the overlays it was written for, fatal in front of a page that is a screen), and `resolve_pointer_tag` stopped AT a `Scroll` node, because `Scene::lookup_path_ref` is path-transparent at a scroll only while segments remain and returns the wrapper when handed an empty remainder. The second is harmless while a pan wraps a WINDOW — nothing is below it, and no external carries its tag — and fatal the moment a pan sits between a screen and its own root. A scroll viewport is a clip, not a target, which is the same sentence that fixed its accessibility silence the same evening. `pinion_core::external::with_surface_extent` closes the limit R1700 wrote down and parked for want of a consumer: inside a view, `layout_size` answered the WINDOW, which is right for a screen that fills one and wrong for a screen placed in a region, and R1700's own note guessed the fix would be reading the previous frame's rectangle. It is not — whoever placed the surface knows its extent before the view runs, so the placer states it and nothing is a frame late. And `CoreShell` now reads `V::read_state` inside the binding's root owner scope, the wrap `V::view`, `V::apply_key` and `V::update` have had since R51.146 / R51.152; the inconsistency was visible two lines apart inside `route_intent_through_update` and went unnoticed because a projection read only out of the scene never needs a scope — measured, none of this tree's 236 `read_state` implementations reads a hook. A host whose projection is a fact about WHICH SCREEN it is showing does.
changes_bullets: NEW CRATE `pinion-screen` — mounting a whole binding as one destination of an application.

`Screen`: object-safe, `&self`, NO default methods. Identity (tag / title), the two-phase state protocol (`latch` reads the projection out of the state scene and parks it; every other hook reads it back), the surfaces (`externals`, primary first then extras, in the order the binding declared them), paint (`view`, `view_for_window`, `shrink_policy`), the windows a screen owns, the keyboard (`apply_key` / `_repeat` / `_press` / `forward_key_to_external` / `apply_composition` / `keybinding` as a symbolic NAME, since a typed Event cannot cross a roster of differently-typed screens), the pointer (middle / secondary / wheel / caret / selection drag / dock drop preview / drag image), files, accessibility (`access_node`, `access_node_for_window`, `access_focus_target`, `access_child_invoke`, `focus_ring_style`, `ime_caret_rect`) and `update`.

`Mount<V: WidgetView>`: the adapter. Holds `Cell<Option<V::State>>` plus a revision, because a binding's cached projection is `Copy` and typed PER BINDING and therefore cannot travel in a host's own `State`. An unlatched mount reads its binding's projection out of an EMPTY scene, which is the truthful answer (before you arrive, none of that screen's externals is in the state scene) and is what makes every hook total.

`ScreenRoster`: `Destinations` plus the screens behind the keys that have one. `with_current(journey, body)` is the only way to reach a screen and wraps every call in that screen's extent grant. `page_scene` records the region and applies `pinion_core::shrink::pan`. `latch` is the host's `read_state`. `externals(journey)` is the whole of "a screen you are not at is not routable" — there is no filtering step and no visibility flag. `MountDefect` refuses a mount at a missing key, at a CLOSED destination (a seat saying *not here* while showing the screen), or twice.
`ScreenState { at, revision }`: a host's `Copy` projection — the change detector that repaints a host whose own state is constant while the screen inside it is not.

`coverage`: `WINDOW_LEVEL` (pinned hooks + the reason each is the host's) and `FOLDED` (hooks mirrored under another name + why), with three tests that read WidgetCore / WidgetA11y / WidgetView from their own source and fail on an unanswered hook, a `Screen` method mirroring nothing, or a stale table entry.

`pinion-core` — `with_surface_extent(tag, extent, body)` + `granted_surface_extent(tag)`, consulted first by `layout_size`. Innermost grant wins (a placed screen may place one of its own); the pop is a Drop guard so a view that panics leaves no grant standing; a zero extent is refused where it is made rather than read back as the design size.

`pinion-runtime` — `V::read_state` runs inside `root_owner.run` at all three call sites (boot, `tail`, `route_intent_through_update`), plus a fixture test that counts scope-less reads at each of the three.

`pinion-runtime` — **a scroll viewport is a clip, not a pointer target.** `resolve_pointer_tag` looks through a `Scroll` to what it is a viewport onto (`tag_beneath_a_viewport`). `Scene::lookup_path_ref` is documented path-transparent at a scroll — *"a wrapper, not a path-bearing layer"* — but only while segments remain; handed an empty remainder it returns the wrapper, which is the case every press lands in when nothing deeper is hittable, and that is the normal state of a screen that makes its own paint pointer-transparent and resolves every gesture at its root (R1655; three screens here do it). Looking through cannot take a press away from anything: a `Scroll` tag is a scroll ADDRESS (`scene/scroll {path}`), never an `External`'s, so a press that resolved to one was already forwarded nowhere. Four call sites share the function — hover, the press/release same-control rule, the drop-target fallback and the `scene/pointer_reach` census — so they cannot disagree about what a press addresses. `resolve_pointer_tag` is now `pub`: the test that found the defect had re-implemented it in four lines and therefore did not see the repair, which is the R47 class in its smallest form.

`pinion-widget-paint` — `view_page_region` takes a `PagePointer`. `HostResolves` is the old unconditional behaviour, with R1695's reason kept verbatim; `PageResolves` is an ordinary container, which is safe for the reason transparency was needed in the other arm — `hit_test` descends into children first and returns the container only when no child hits, and a mounted screen's root covers the region. Gated against `hit_test` rather than against the flag, so the two arms are each other's counterfactual.

`pinion-core` — `shrink::pan`'s viewport declares `Silence::layout`. It was a painted, addressable region nobody gave a voice and nobody declared quiet, and nothing had ever met it: every screen declaring `Recourse::Pan` opens at its own comfortable size, so the node does not exist at boot. Placed in a region smaller than its layout minimum it exists from the first frame, and the shell reported `unvoiced: 1`. The declaration belongs in the framework for the reason the whole function does — a viewport the framework mints is not something an application should have to remember to describe.

`hello-node-lab` — becomes a library plus a four-line binary. `src/main.rs` -> `src/lib.rs` (a rename; not one line of the screen changed), `pub fn run`, `pub struct NodeLabView`, `[lib]` in the manifest. The bin name is unchanged, so `RpcSubprocess(example)` and the demo sweep are untouched.

`hello-analyzer-shell` — becomes the analysis tool's ONE application at three of its seven seats. The Catalog seat goes `Seat::Elsewhere("the node graph lab")` -> `Seat::Page`; `screen_roster()` is the one place that says which destinations have a screen; `ShellState.roster: Destinations` becomes `screens: ScreenRoster` with `roster()` reading through it, so there is one roster and not a copy of its destination half beside it. The binding's `State` goes `()` -> `ScreenState`, `create_extra_externals` is the showing screen's surfaces, `external_set_is_dynamic` is true, the page region asks the roster first, and `apply_key`, `access_node`, `access_focus_target`, `position_caret_for_point` and `select_drag_to_point` all delegate to the screen that is showing.

CENSUS SCOPING — four of this shell's own censuses assumed it owns every page. Each now says which destinations it is complete for and asserts that no destination falls out of BOTH censuses: the voices partition, the painted-page distinctness (now pairwise over three pages rather than one comparison over two), the keyboard ring closure, and the locked-region table (16 -> 15, and it left by being derived rather than by being edited).

DOCUMENTATION — fifteen intra-doc links repaired across three crates, every one of them created by this round and none of them visible to a test. Making `resolve_pointer_tag` public turned its existing doc into PUBLIC documentation of a link to a private item (`dispatch_send`); `hello-node-lab` becoming a library did the same to eleven links in its crate doc and its `WidgetView` impl (`spec`, `graph::Role`, `graph::Transport`, `Hit::at`, `SHRINK` x3, `MIN_W`, `MIN_H`, `window_size`, `FLOOR_W`), which had been a binary's private prose the day before; and `pinion-screen`'s own header carried one unresolved link plus two redundant explicit targets. All repaired at the source rather than allowed, since the allow attribute would make the next one silent. The three counts this round wrote in prose were re-measured at its close and all three were wrong -- the mounted lab paints 139 tagged regions and not the 162 taken before the pan landed, and the three screens are 13,854 / 20,655 / 7,035 lines by `find examples/<pkg>/src -name '*.rs' | xargs wc -l`, which is now quoted beside the numbers.

TOOLS — `tools/binding_focus.py` and `tools/assembled_state.py` keyed their population on `examples/*/src/main.rs`. A binding that became a library would have dropped out silently: not reported missing, just no longer counted. Both are keyed on the package now, preferring `lib.rs`.
verification_bullets: THE FLOOR, measured by building a probe against 6.11.1 and running it rather than by reading about it. R1695 measured *arriving*; these are the rows that only appear once a page is a whole screen.

Mounting an existing application window as a page: it stops being a window (`isWindow()` true -> false), its `windowTitle` survives and IS SHOWN NOWHERE, and its status bar becomes invisible — all silently. Its dock still docks.
The page that is not current, sent a press, a key and a wheel: COUNTED ALL THREE.
The page that is not current, in the accessibility tree: reachable as a child, AND ITS LINE EDIT WITH IT, carrying `invisible=1` and nothing more.
A page's own floating tool window when you navigate away: STILL VISIBLE, left on screen over a different section.
State across leaving and returning: RETAINED. The one row it gets right, and the one this round must not regress.

Arriving at a disabled page: arrives anyway. `setCurrentIndex` returns void; an out-of-range ordinal is a silent no-op; the container's accessible value and name are both empty; there is no vocabulary for a page saying why it cannot be entered.
VERIFICATION OF THIS ROUND.

`pinion-core`: the extent grant driven on the axis R1700 left open — un-granted readings unchanged in and out of a view, granted reading answers the region, a grant to a sibling tag says nothing about this one, the floor still applies, innermost wins, the grant does not outlive the scope, a panicking view leaves none standing, a zero extent is refused where it is made.

`pinion-screen`: 13 mount properties + 3 census tests. Only-the-current-screen-has-externals (stated in both directions), the unmounted destination answers `None` everywhere, the latch survives leaving, both halves of the change detector move, a mounted screen lays out in its region AND its owner-scoped key handler reads the same rectangle, a screen's windows leave with it, the title is the current screen's, all three mount defects, the overridden hooks dispatch through the mount (including one whose `None` is a decision and one neither fixture overrides), an unlatched mount reads an empty scene, a screen too big for its region pans inside it, and the grant is scoped to the host's scene.
`pinion-runtime`: a fixture whose `read_state` counts scope-less reads, driven at boot, at the dispatch tail and through the intent route.

`hello-analyzer-shell`: arriving at Catalog paints the node lab (139 tagged regions inside the shell, measured twice at close; the 162 this round quoted mid-flight was taken BEFORE the region grant and the pan landed, when the lab still laid out at the window's 1625 -- a number measured in the middle of a round has to be re-measured at its end, because what the round fixed is what moves it); the surfaces are the showing screen's and nothing at the dashboard; the accessibility tree holds the showing section and only it; the host's state moves when the rail does and not when it stands still.
`hello-node-lab`: its own suite, unchanged by becoming a library.
The demo: `tools/demos/r1724_the_tool_is_one_application.py`.

THE DOC GATE IS WHERE LIBIFICATION SENDS ITS BILL, AND IT WAS NOT RUN UNTIL THE ROUND WAS CLOSED. Two failures, both created by this round and neither visible to any test: making `resolve_pointer_tag` public turned its existing doc into PUBLIC documentation, and that doc links a private item (`dispatch_send`), which `-D rustdoc::private_intra_doc_links` refuses; and `hello-node-lab` becoming a library did the same thing to eleven links across its crate doc and its `WidgetView` impl, which had been a binary's private prose the day before. A binary's documentation is nobody's API and rustdoc treats it that way; a library's is. Both are repaired at the source rather than allowed, because the allow attribute would make the next such link silent. The lesson is the one this project keeps paying for and is now paying on a NEW axis: a gate not run is a gate that passes, and CHANGING WHAT A CRATE IS changes which gates apply to it.

THE CONSUMER'S PIN REPORT, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. A report arrived at this round's close -- pins spreading after maximise/restore and attach/detach -- with the node lab's region grant and region pan as the obvious suspects. Step one of its own diagnostic order is decisive and cheap, so it was run: the node lab standalone and the same lab mounted in the shell, each driven 1440x900 -> 1920x1080 -> 1440x900 through `resize_and_settle`, reading the dial-to-accept distance on all six of its node cards. Both answer 126/122/122/127/126/122 at all three sizes -- not one pixel, and the mounted numbers are the standalone numbers. So the lab's pins are not what moves, and the region grant is not implicated by this measurement. What it does NOT settle: the distance BETWEEN nodes was not read, attach/detach was not driven, and the report's vocabulary ("a widget screen", "attach", "detach") reads like the consumer surface R1723's report came from rather than the analyzer. That question is the consumer's to answer and is recorded as the debt's next step rather than guessed at.

The mounted screen painted 139 tagged regions, answered every path on the wire, appeared in the accessibility tree, reported `unvoiced: 0`, and `scene/pointer_reach` said `routed_by: node_lab` — and not one press inside it reached anything. R1724.publishable_decision_summary:
R1724 — a screen is a binding you can arrive at, and the analysis tool stops being three executables at one of its seats.

The behaviour reference this tool is modelled on is ONE application: a shell with an app bar and a navigation rail, and the rail switches between its sections. This tree assembled it as three executables — hello-analyzer-shell 13,854 lines, hello-node-lab 20,655, hello-packet-view 7,035, measured at this round's close with `find examples/<pkg>/src -name '*.rs' | xargs wc -l` and quoted with the command because the three taken mid-round were all wrong by the end of it — and the shell's own rail said so out loud, because three of its seven seats were declared Unavailable::elsewhere, an arm that exists only because a destination here can be finished and still unreachable. R1695 built the model and paint halves of navigating (Destinations / Journey / view_page_region); what neither gave is the half that makes those seats openable: what a destination's page IS when the page is a whole binding with its own externals, its own keymap, its own accessibility tree and its own text caret.

The decision is that the unit of composition is THE BINDING ITSELF, not a new kind of thing an author writes. `pinion_screen::Screen` is the dispatchable surface of a `WidgetView` with the window-level half removed, as `&self` methods so a roster can hold several; `Mount<V>` implements it for any existing binding; `ScreenRoster` pairs the destination roster with the screens behind its keys and is the ONLY way to reach one, so "the screen the journey is not at is not routable, not keyable, not readable and not painted" is a property of the type rather than a rule an author keeps. `hello-node-lab` is mounted at Catalog unedited — its 20,655 lines became a library and a four-line binary, so the demo sweep keeps its per-screen process and the application keeps its sections in one window.

Two mechanical guarantees carry the weight. `Screen` declares every hook and defaults NONE, so a hook added there stops `Mount` compiling until it is forwarded. The other direction — a hook added to WidgetCore / WidgetA11y / WidgetView and never mirrored — is covered by `pinion_screen::coverage`, a census that reads those three traits' own source and fails unless each of their hooks is mirrored, folded into one of Screen's methods, or pinned as the host's WITH THE REASON. There is no fourth answer.

FOUR framework repairs were forced by the first real mount rather than reasoned into existence, and three of them are defects that existed before this round and had no way to be seen. The largest: the mounted screen was DEAD TO THE MOUSE while every gate was green — it painted 139 tagged regions, answered every path on the wire, appeared in the accessibility tree, and `scene/pointer_reach` reported it `routed_by: node_lab`; not one press anywhere inside it reached anything, the screen or the host. Two stacked causes, and removing either one alone left the symptom exactly as it was, which is what made it expensive: `view_page_region` was unconditionally pointer-transparent (a flag that in `Scene::hit_test` skips a child AND ITS WHOLE SUBTREE — right for the overlays it was written for, fatal in front of a page that is a screen), and `resolve_pointer_tag` stopped AT a `Scroll` node, because `Scene::lookup_path_ref` is path-transparent at a scroll only while segments remain and returns the wrapper when handed an empty remainder. The second is harmless while a pan wraps a WINDOW — nothing is below it, and no external carries its tag — and fatal the moment a pan sits between a screen and its own root. A scroll viewport is a clip, not a target, which is the same sentence that fixed its accessibility silence the same evening. `pinion_core::external::with_surface_extent` closes the limit R1700 wrote down and parked for want of a consumer: inside a view, `layout_size` answered the WINDOW, which is right for a screen that fills one and wrong for a screen placed in a region, and R1700's own note guessed the fix would be reading the previous frame's rectangle. It is not — whoever placed the surface knows its extent before the view runs, so the placer states it and nothing is a frame late. And `CoreShell` now reads `V::read_state` inside the binding's root owner scope, the wrap `V::view`, `V::apply_key` and `V::update` have had since R51.146 / R51.152; the inconsistency was visible two lines apart inside `route_intent_through_update` and went unnoticed because a projection read only out of the scene never needs a scope — measured, none of this tree's 236 `read_state` implementations reads a hook. A host whose projection is a fact about WHICH SCREEN it is showing does.

`Screen`: object-safe, `&self`, NO default methods. Identity (tag / title), the two-phase state protocol (`latch` reads the projection out of the state scene and parks it; every other hook reads it back), the surfaces (`externals`, primary first then extras, in the order the binding declared them), paint (`view`, `view_for_window`, `shrink_policy`), the windows a screen owns, the keyboard (`apply_key` / `_repeat` / `_press` / `forward_key_to_external` / `apply_composition` / `keybinding` as a symbolic NAME, since a typed Event cannot cross a roster of differently-typed screens), the pointer (middle / secondary / wheel / caret / selection drag / dock drop preview / drag image), files, accessibility (`access_node`, `access_node_for_window`, `access_focus_target`, `access_child_invoke`, `focus_ring_style`, `ime_caret_rect`) and `update`.

`Mount<V: WidgetView>`: the adapter. Holds `Cell<Option<V::State>>` plus a revision, because a binding's cached projection is `Copy` and typed PER BINDING and therefore cannot travel in a host's own `State`. An unlatched mount reads its binding's projection out of an EMPTY scene, which is the truthful answer (before you arrive, none of that screen's externals is in the state scene) and is what makes every hook total.

`ScreenRoster`: `Destinations` plus the screens behind the keys that have one. `with_current(journey, body)` is the only way to reach a screen and wraps every call in that screen's extent grant. `page_scene` records the region and applies `pinion_core::shrink::pan`. `latch` is the host's `read_state`. `externals(journey)` is the whole of "a screen you are not at is not routable" — there is no filtering step and no visibility flag. `MountDefect` refuses a mount at a missing key, at a CLOSED destination (a seat saying *not here* while showing the screen), or twice.
`ScreenState { at, revision }`: a host's `Copy` projection — the change detector that repaints a host whose own state is constant while the screen inside it is not.

`coverage`: `WINDOW_LEVEL` (pinned hooks + the reason each is the host's) and `FOLDED` (hooks mirrored under another name + why), with three tests that read WidgetCore / WidgetA11y / WidgetView from their own source and fail on an unanswered hook, a `Screen` method mirroring nothing, or a stale table entry.

`pinion-core` — `with_surface_extent(tag, extent, body)` + `granted_surface_extent(tag)`, consulted first by `layout_size`. Innermost grant wins (a placed screen may place one of its own); the pop is a Drop guard so a view that panics leaves no grant standing; a zero extent is refused where it is made rather than read back as the design size.

`pinion-runtime` — `V::read_state` runs inside `root_owner.run` at all three call sites (boot, `tail`, `route_intent_through_update`), plus a fixture test that counts scope-less reads at each of the three.

`pinion-runtime` — **a scroll viewport is a clip, not a pointer target.** `resolve_pointer_tag` looks through a `Scroll` to what it is a viewport onto (`tag_beneath_a_viewport`). `Scene::lookup_path_ref` is documented path-transparent at a scroll — *"a wrapper, not a path-bearing layer"* — but only while segments remain; handed an empty remainder it returns the wrapper, which is the case every press lands in when nothing deeper is hittable, and that is the normal state of a screen that makes its own paint pointer-transparent and resolves every gesture at its root (R1655; three screens here do it). Looking through cannot take a press away from anything: a `Scroll` tag is a scroll ADDRESS (`scene/scroll {path}`), never an `External`'s, so a press that resolved to one was already forwarded nowhere. `pinion-widget-paint` — `view_page_region` takes a `PagePointer`. `HostResolves` is the old unconditional behaviour, with R1695's reason kept verbatim; `PageResolves` is an ordinary container, which is safe for the reason transparency was needed in the other arm — `hit_test` descends into children first and returns the container only when no child hits, and a mounted screen's root covers the region. Gated against `hit_test` rather than against the flag, so the two arms are each other's counterfactual.

`pinion-core` — `shrink::pan`'s viewport declares `Silence::layout`. It was a painted, addressable region nobody gave a voice and nobody declared quiet, and nothing had ever met it: every screen declaring `Recourse::Pan` opens at its own comfortable size, so the node does not exist at boot. Placed in a region smaller than its layout minimum it exists from the first frame, and the shell reported `unvoiced: 1`. The declaration belongs in the framework for the reason the whole function does — a viewport the framework mints is not something an application should have to remember to describe.

`hello-node-lab` — becomes a library plus a four-line binary. `src/main.rs` -> `src/lib.rs` (a rename; not one line of the screen changed), `pub fn run`, `pub struct NodeLabView`, `[lib]` in the manifest. The bin name is unchanged, so `RpcSubprocess(example)` and the demo sweep are untouched.

`hello-analyzer-shell` — becomes the analysis tool's ONE application at three of its seven seats. CENSUS SCOPING — four of this shell's own censuses assumed it owns every page. Each now says which destinations it is complete for and asserts that no destination falls out of BOTH censuses: the voices partition, the painted-page distinctness (now pairwise over three pages rather than one comparison over two), the keyboard ring closure, and the locked-region table (16 -> 15, and it left by being derived rather than by being edited).

DOCUMENTATION — fifteen intra-doc links repaired across three crates, every one of them created by this round and none of them visible to a test. Making `resolve_pointer_tag` public turned its existing doc into PUBLIC documentation of a link to a private item (`dispatch_send`); `hello-node-lab` becoming a library did the same to eleven links in its crate doc and its `WidgetView` impl (`spec`, `graph::Role`, `graph::Transport`, `Hit::at`, `SHRINK` x3, `MIN_W`, `MIN_H`, `window_size`, `FLOOR_W`), which had been a binary's private prose the day before; and `pinion-screen`'s own header carried one unresolved link plus two redundant explicit targets. R1725.decision_summary:
R1725 — a screen draws its own navigation only where it is the one providing it, and what a place already has is a fact the place states.

R1724 made a screen mountable and the first mount made an existing disagreement visible in one window: at the Catalog destination the shell's navigation rail ran x=0..52 and the mounted screen painted its own at x=52..106 — two rails, side by side, for one application — and the accessibility tree published both of them as `role=navigation`, named *Destinations* and *sections*. Mounting did not create that. It put the two halves of it in the same picture.

Neither screen was wrong, which is why the repair is not in either of them. A screen that has ever run as its own window NEEDS a navigation, and that need stops being true the moment it is placed inside an application that has one — which is a fact about the PLACE, not about the screen, and nothing carried it. `pinion_core::chrome` is that fact, in exactly the shape `with_surface_extent` took a round earlier: the placer states what it provides, for the duration of building the guest's scene, and the guest reads it. Outside any scope the answer is `HostChrome::NONE`, so a binding running standalone behaves as it always did and its own rectangle assertions hold unedited.

THE AUDIT INVERTED THE PREMISE THIS ROUND WAS OPENED WITH, and it cost thirty seconds. The debt this round pays says the guest should omit its rail because it duplicates the host's. Extracted from the behaviour reference's three screens: the reference draws ONE rail of EIGHT seats, identical on every screen, with only the active marker differing — and against that, the shell's rail is 7 seats MISSING `Logs` while the guest's 7 are the reference's list minus `Settings`. The guest's rail was the closer of the two. "It is a duplicate, so delete the guest's" is a shape that can move a reproduction backwards, and the rule this round writes down is to ask which of two overlapping things is the one that matches before deleting either. What made the deletion safe here is a different measurement: every seat of the guest's rail answers `"<name> is not this screen"` and navigates nowhere, so omitting it loses no capability. The missing `Logs` seat is the HOST's gap, registered on its own because closing it needs a vocabulary decision rather than code — `Seat` offers `Page`, `Elsewhere` and `Reserved`, and "in the reference's first phase and not built here" is none of the three.

The declaration is a set (`HostChrome`) over a closed vocabulary (`Part`), not a boolean: a host with a navigation rail and no application bar is an ordinary arrangement, and a guest deciding what to leave out needs the difference. This shell declares `Navigation` and deliberately not `ApplicationBar` — its bar carries the capture source, the capture state and the global search, while a mounted screen's bar carries that screen's subject, and only the first is chrome a page should leave to its host. `Part` rather than `Chrome` because `style::Chrome` already means something else one level down — a band a box keeps of its own edge — and two concepts under one word costs exactly what one concept spelled two ways does, which this tree keeps paying.

The guest derives five things from one predicate — the paint, the accessibility tree, the reserved width, the pane rectangles and what the pointer can reach — because this project's recurring defect is a screen that publishes a rule it does not keep, and that is what two readers of one fact produce.

THE FLOOR, measured by building a probe against 6.11.1 and running it rather than by reading about it. A complete application window — menu bar, tool bar, status bar — placed inside another application's page container: its menu bar keeps drawing (23 px of it), so do its tool bar and its status bar; its accessibility tree carries 2 menu bars, 2 tool bars and 2 status bars, so a reader is told the application has two of each; and there is no property, method or event by which the guest could have asked what its container provides. The nearest available signal is `window()`, which answers the HOST's window — so a guest there can learn THAT it is embedded and nothing whatever about what that place has. Every guest that acts on that boolean must then assume what its host draws, which is why the ordinary outcome is two of every bar.

`Part`: the closed vocabulary of application frame a host can provide — `Navigation` and `ApplicationBar`. Each arm is something a GUEST must be able to decide about itself, so an arm nobody can act on would be a declaration with no consumer. `Part::ALL` and `Part::name()` are one list, so a report cannot name an arm the set cannot hold. Named `Part` and not `Chrome` because `style::Chrome` is a box's own edge band; the collision is recorded on the type.

`HostChrome`: a `Copy`, const-constructible set — `NONE`, `with(Part)`, `provides(Part)`, `is_empty()`, `names()`. A set rather than a boolean because a host with a rail and no application bar is ordinary and a guest needs the difference.

`with_host_chrome(chrome, body)` / `host_chrome()`: a scope, the same shape R1724's `with_surface_extent` took. Innermost wins, so a placed screen that places one of its own answers about ITS guest's surroundings. The pop is a `Drop` guard: a panicking view must not leave a declaration standing, and the direction matters — a stale "the host provides navigation" makes the next screen omit a rail nothing is drawing, and a destination nobody can reach is worse than one drawn twice. R1726.decision_summary:
R1726 — what a surface is holding paints in front of what it is not, and being held is one declaration the paint order, the hit order and the elevation all come out of.

The owner drove the running application and reported three things: a card goes grey when you move it, cards do not overlap, and is not overlapping better UX anyway. Measured, all three are one fact and none of them is what they look like. The card does not go grey — the stationary card's opaque body is drawn OVER it, so only the dim row labels of the held card survive. They do overlap — after a drag the two sit at x=718 and x=720. And overlap was never forbidden here or in the reference, so the question was never whether to allow it. What was missing is that THE THING YOU PICK UP DOES NOT LOOK PICKED UP.

Measured as paint order, which is exactly z-order in this tree: a scene draws depth-first and `Scene::hit_test` walks the same children in REVERSE, so the last child is both drawn last and hit first. On both of this tree's node graphs the dragged item was behind the one it was over — `hello-node-lab` at index 70 against 80, `hello-node-editor` at 12 against 15. Two screens, the same defect, arrived at independently, which is what made this a framework capability rather than one screen's repair.

`ContainerNode::with_held(tag)` / `with_held_group(tags)` is one call that REORDERS, RECORDS and RAISES. The declaration moves the children once; afterwards the order is simply true, `hit_test` already agrees because it reads that order, and `held()` answers WHICH children without re-deriving it from position. THE SECOND CONSUMER CORRECTED THE DESIGN BEFORE IT SHIPPED. THE FLOOR SUPPLIES A MECHANISM AND NO RULE, measured by building a probe against 6.11.1 and running it — two overlapping movable items on a canvas, pressed and dragged. The reference gives every node `box-shadow: 0 4px 14px rgba(0,0,0,.28)` and a z-index; we give a held card an elevation now and a resting card none. `HELD_SHADOW` was deliberately derived from that resting value lifted one step, so adopting the resting shadow is a one-line change per screen and the two will already be in proportion.

4. ★★★★★ THE HARNESS'S DRAG IS NOT THE GESTURE A PERSON MAKES, and this is the round's largest open item. Measured on one screen, one card, two paths: `scene/drag` makes the dragged card follow the cursor; a real pointer leaves it where it is, moves a snap mark, and reflows on release. The dashboard is a tile board and commits on release, so the harness path reproduces a gesture nobody performs — and three of this round's five repairs were hiding behind greens it had given. Registered as `debt-a-harness-drag-is-not-the-gesture-a-person-makes`; the deliverable is a first-class "drive a real pointer and read the scene while the button is down" path, and the throwaway one built here works and belongs in the harness. Until then, a round that touches dragging must drive a real pointer once and LOOK.
STATED LIMITS, NOT DEBTS.

Being held does not reach the accessibility tree. `AccessState` has `focused`, `disabled`, `hovered`, `pressed`, `checked` and `mixed` — there is no `grabbed`, and adding one is an a11y vocabulary decision rather than a consequence of this round. It is the natural next derivation from the same word, and it is left for the round that decides that vocabulary.
The elevation is a shadow on the child. A renderer that composited a held child into its own layer could do better (a real lift blurs what is behind it), and nothing here needs that yet.

`with_held_group` is linear in the children and runs once per frame per surface. Both consumers hold at most a selection, so this is not measured as a cost; a canvas holding thousands would want the partition done against a set rather than a scan of the argument list.

R1727.decision_summary:
A captured pointer arrived as a pair of fractions over a rectangle the router
resolved and then threw away, and that is how a gesture comes to read two facts
at two different times. The fraction is taken over the rect the last PAINT
produced; anything the consumer scales it by is read from the LIVE model; and
when the gesture itself moves that scale, the answer depends on whether a frame
happened between two moves. Measured on the analysis tool's dashboard, one press
from the same pixel to the same pixel, eight interpolated moves:

    a real X11 pointer                 loss@0,4   latency@0,5   topology@0,6
    eight `scene/drag` calls           loss@0,4   latency@0,5   topology@0,6
    ONE `scene/drag` with steps=8      loss@0,10  latency@0,7   topology@0,11

The third is the harness's own march, and it is the delivery every drag
assertion in this tree was made through. A hand supplies the frame, so the wrong
reading hid behind the right answer -- which is exactly the shape the owner
found by hand in R1726 and named an architectural defect: the harness could not
make the gesture a person makes, so it had to ask a person what the screen did.

THE FIX IS THAT THE RECT TRAVELS WITH THE READING. `pinion_core::PointerReading`
carries the fraction and the extent of the rectangle it was taken over, and
`px()` is `cursor - rect.origin` however stale that rect is, because both halves
come from the same rect. `External::pointer_move` takes the reading instead of
two bare `f32`s -- ONE spelling, so all 21 implementors and 195 call sites have
to say which unit they mean, which is what makes the class visible at all.

THE CENSUS FOUND TWO MORE INSTANCES BESIDES THE ONE THAT OPENED IT. The column
resize scaled its fraction by a viewport width read back from a shared
`ScrollState`, and defended itself in its own documentation with an argument
that the two facts could not disagree; the argument was sound and the shape was
not, and the `ScrollState` is now gone from its constructor -- the compiler
reporting an unused import is the proof the second fact is gone. The node editor
multiplied a CANVAS fraction by the WHOLE surface: `capture_normalize` names
`Tag(GRAPH_TAG)` while `on_resize` fills `self.surface` with palette and detail
panel included, so its click-versus-drag dead zone was inflated by
`TOTAL_W / WIN_W` -- two different rectangles in the same function, invisible
because no test stated which one it meant.

THE GATE THE CLASS DEBT NEVER HAD: `assert_gesture_reads_one_fact` drives one
gesture two ways -- as one march and as one call per move -- and requires the
same state. It is the class's own statement, testable without a display.

AND THE HARNESS CAN NOW MAKE A REAL GESTURE. `rpc_verify.RealPointer` moves the
X server's own pointer, calibrates by asking the surface where it thinks the
cursor is (refusing rather than degrading if it does not move with it), and
takes a `hold` callback that runs WITH THE BUTTON STILL DOWN -- so a demo reads
the scene mid-gesture instead of asking a person. That is the capability R1726
registered as missing.

FLOOR, measured by building a probe against 6.11.1 and running it: its move
event carries widget-local PIXELS, so this failure mode does not arise there --
on that axis the floor was ABOVE us and `px()` is the interface it has, which is
worth saying plainly because "be superior to the floor" sometimes means catching
up first. What it does not have is the other half. Across the six classes a
scrolling, tabular, split or sliding surface is built from there -- 441 declared
properties and 274 declared methods -- not one names the extent a paint used,
and none names whether an event was synthesised or came from the window system.
In the same run its live height had reached 512 while its last paint had used
320, and nothing reports the 320.

R1728.decision_summary:
An application's navigation had been a value since R1695 -- ordered, keyed, every
seat carrying a stated reason when it cannot be arrived at -- and nothing in the
framework or in this tree could say whether that value was the RIGHT one. A
roster makes a screen unable to disagree with itself. It does not make a screen
agree with anything else.

MEASURED AT THIS ROUND'S OPEN, by extracting the rail from each of the three
screens the behaviour reference delivers: the reference is one application with
EIGHT sections, drawn in one order, identical on every screen, differing only in
which seat is marked current. The shell reproducing it drew SEVEN, and the
difference was worse than the debt file that sent this round had recorded. That
file said one seat was missing. What was actually true:

  * three of the seven keys were seats the reference does not have -- one of
    them (`catalog`) named after nothing in the reference at all, and two
    (`stream`, `decode`) recorded as "the reference's capture section split in
    two", which is not what they were: the reference's third section is a
    separate thing its behaviour prototype fully implements, with its own rows
    and its own detail pane;
  * two of the reference's sections were ABSENT FROM THE RAIL ENTIRELY;
  * the seat carrying the one section this application had finished was drawn
    with the mark the reference gives its LOG section, and two further marks
    were crossed the same way;
  * and two adjacent seats had no arm in the painter at all, fell through to its
    fallback, and were drawn IDENTICALLY.

Every one of those survived every gate this screen had, and the reason is one
sentence: nothing compared the application with its specification, because there
was nothing to compare it with.

WHY THE TWO ABSENT SECTIONS WERE ABSENT, which is the framework half. A seat that
cannot say why it is inert gets left off the rail, and neither of the two words
available fits a section the reference has working and this build has not
written. `Reserved` claims a later release and takes the section out of the
current scope for anybody planning against the word. `Elsewhere` sends a reader
to go and open a window nobody has built. `Unsupported` says no action changes
it, when building it is precisely what changes it. So the seats were simply
omitted -- and a rail that omits a seat cannot be compared with one that has it,
which is how the divergence stayed invisible for as long as it did.

`UnavailableKind::Unbuilt` is that sentence: in the specification of the release
being built, and not built yet, with `detail` naming what specifies it. It is
general beyond the screen that forced it -- any product assembled against a
written specification passes through a state where a surface is specified,
declared and absent, and a shell that shows such a surface rather than hiding it
is telling the truth about the shape of the finished product. What has had no

R1729.decision_summary:
The analysis tool's rail had one seat left saying `elsewhere` — *built,
shipping, and not here*. That arm exists because this tree assembled a
one-application reference as three executables, so a destination could be
finished and still unreachable, and R1695 spent an arm on saying so rather than
lying about it with *reserved* or *unsupported*.

R1724 mounted the node lab and took the count from three to two. R1728 measured
the rail against the reference and found that two of the remaining three were
not seats the reference has at all — this application had split one section into
two under invented names — leaving exactly one: the capture viewer.

THIS ROUND MOUNTS IT, AND THE WORK WAS NOT IN THE SCREEN. `hello-packet-view`
gained a `[lib]` stanza, its binding gained a `pub`, `fn main` became
`pub fn run`, and a four-line `src/main.rs` runs it in a window of its own. Not
one line of the screen changed. The shell mounts it through
`pinion_screen::Mount<PacketView>` beside the node lab, and the seat opens.

Measured on the running application, which is the only place this claim can be
made: at the dashboard the capture viewer paints **0** regions; at its own seat
it paints **290**, with its root at (52, 52, 1425, 848) — inside the page region,
right of the 52-pixel rail and below the 52-pixel application bar — and the
host's application bar, rail and seat are all still painted. The application's
own conformance reading goes from **5 of 8 to 6 of 8**, and it publishes that
number rather than this entry asserting it.

THE ROUND'S OWN FINDING IS THAT THE COMPILER CLOSED THE ARM. With the capture
viewer mounted, nothing constructed `spec::Seat::Elsewhere`, and an unconstructed
variant is a `dead_code` error under this workspace's lints — so the round did
not have to notice. The arm is deleted rather than kept behind an allow, which
makes the claim the strongest form it can take: **this screen cannot say "built,
shipping, and not here", because it has no way to spell it.** Its return would
be a compile-checked event rather than a comment somebody remembers.

`pinion_core::availability::UnavailableKind::Elsewhere` is untouched and still
has consumers. The vocabulary is the framework's and any product with more than
one surface needs it; what ended is this rail needing it. The seat history, in
full: 3 (R1695) → 2 (R1724) → 1 (R1728) → 0 and the arm gone (R1729).

What remains closed on this rail is closed for reasons no mount can fix: `keys`
and `logs` are sections the reference implements and nobody here has built, and
`topology` and `sessions` are deferred by the reference itself. That is the
honest end state of the integration debt's *first* half — the tool is one
application at every destination it has built — and it leaves the second half,
which is building the two that are missing, stated as a number the application
reports.

ONE FRAMEWORK ASYMMETRY CLOSED, FORCED BY THE SECOND MOUNT.
`ScreenRoster::current_tag` could name the paint root of the screen you are AT
and of no other, while `ScreenRoster::wire` had been publishing all of them since
R1724. A caller asking "is some other screen painted right now" — which is how
you check that leaving a page takes it away — therefore had to navigate there to
learn what to look for, and navigating is the thing under test. `tag_of(key)` is
that, and `current_tag` now delegates to it.

AND THE GATE IS DERIVED RATHER THAN NAMED. R1724 wrote its mount check for the
node lab by name; the capture viewer is the second consumer, and a second
hand-written copy is what this project lifts on sight.
`r1729_every_mounted_screen_paints_itself_where_it_belongs` takes its population
from `ScreenRoster::mounted_keys`, so a screen mounted by a later round is
covered the day it is mounted rather than the day somebody remembers. It asserts
three things per mounted screen, and the third is the one a picture cannot show:
arriving paints regions under that screen's own root; the host's chrome survives
(measured at 6.11.1, a placed application window keeps its own menu bar, tool bar
and status bar on top of its host's, and the tree publishes two of each); and
every OTHER mounted screen is away, which is what makes "the page you left is
gone" a property rather than a hope.

R1730.decision_summary:
R1730 — a section's SURFACES can be checked against surfaces somebody wrote
down, and the analysis tool's third rail seat is BUILT rather than mounted.

R1728 wrote the tool's navigation down as a reviewed artifact and made something
fail when the application stopped matching it; the mechanism found three defects
in its first three runs. It could reach exactly one thing. A table's columns, a
detail pane's sections and a header's parts are an ordered roster of keyed,
titled parts and NONE of them is a destination — they have no standing, nobody
arrives at them — so none could be checked at all, while the reason the rail had
been wrong for several hundred rounds (nothing compared it with anything)
applied to every one of them unchanged.

`pinion_core::conformance` is the half of R1728 that was never about navigating:
`Part` / `SurfaceSpec` / `PartDivergence` / `Divergent` / `Owed` / `Ledger` /
`Unreconciled`. The difference runs in BOTH directions — an absent part and an
INVENTED part are both failures, as are order and title — and the ledger of
accepted differences is judged as an EQUALITY, so three things fail rather than
one: a divergence nobody declared, a divergence PAID OFF and not recorded, and a
divergence whose wording changed. The `Ledger` is a lift rather than an
invention: the shell's own R1728 test carried the struct, the loader and the
three per-entry conditions inline, and the new section needed the same mechanism
for three surfaces of its own, which is the third consumer. The conditions now
refuse a malformed pin at load rather than being remembered per consumer.

`hello-key-patterns` is the reference's third section, built: a 46-high header
carrying the section's name, a DERIVED summary and a live filter over named
columns; a seven-column declaration list; and a 320-wide record pane of eleven
parts whose last is the reference's own action out of the section, drawn and
REFUSED with the reason `docs/analyzer-rail-spec.json` gives the seat it leads
to. Drawing it is required (leaving it off is a divergence) and making it
navigate would be a promise the specification does not keep.

The chain is specification -> tables -> paint and every link is checked.
`docs/analyzer-keys-spec.json` is a separate reviewed artifact; `crate::spec`'s
tables are what the running screen holds; and the integration test reads the
three surfaces BACK OUT OF THE PAINTED SCENE. Both of its rules are derived
rather than listed: which tags belong to a surface is "no further dot after the
stem", so a part's own decoration is excluded by the shape of its name; and the
order is a LINE rule (parts whose painted rectangles overlap vertically are one
line, sorted across it), because the naive (y, x) sort was wrong on its first
run — the header's three parts are centred against different heights, so the
filter box's top edge sits seven pixels above the title's and it sorted first.
Aligning the boxes to make the sort work would have been fixing the screen to
suit the check.

The rail's declared remainder loses `keys`: the entry is DELETED rather than
marked done, because the gate asserts the live difference EQUALS the list.
Reproduction 6 of 8 -> 7 of 8, published by the application itself.

not. It is the same shape as the section this round built and the specification
says so.

the loader lift: an expectation written out in a demo goes stale exactly like

R1732.decision_summary:
An enumeration row in the analysis tool's node inspector COLLAPSES into a roster
you open, the way the behaviour reference draws it, and the inspector is now
checked against a specification somebody wrote down.

## What was wrong, as a number

`pinion_widget_paint::config_form` drew a `FieldType::Choice` row as one chip per
option, laid from the control's left edge, with no wrap, no clip and no scroll.
Measured with the inspector's own `FormStyle::default()` (a 284 px pane):

* three words — the analysis tool's own `mode` row — spend 229 px saying one word;
* six words overrun the control by **50 px**;
* seven words by **113 px**.

The behaviour reference collapses the same field. Its inspector derivation gives
a field five mutually exclusive control kinds and draws the enumeration one as a
CLOSED control carrying the word it holds and an arrow, styled identically to
the text field beside it. So the expanded row was not merely wide: it was not
what is being reproduced.

## What was built

**`pinion_core::widgets::picker`** — `Picker` / `Picked` / `PickerDefect`. The
transient state of choosing: the roster, and where in it the reader is. Not the
value — the value stays in the document until a choice is committed. There is no
`open` flag, because a screen holding no picker has no open picker, so "shut and
highlighting the fourth option" has no spelling. Its wire form goes back through
the constructor's rule (`serde(try_from)`), because a snapshot is a door into
the type as much as the constructor is and §2 #3's `dry_run` restores signals
from one.

**The paint** — a choice row wears the box a text row wears, holding the word it
has and a chevron. The roster is published as its own LAYER
(`FormGeometry::popup`, `option_at`, `on_popup`) rather than as more of the open
row's parts, because a hit test walking the rows in order would resolve a press
on the roster to whichever row it covers. Its direction is DERIVED from a
rectangle the caller passes (`OpenPicker::room`): the pane is the only thing that
knows where the fold is, and flipping against the form's own extent would open
downward off the bottom of a scrolled viewport. The control's ARIA role moves
from radiogroup to combobox with `expanded` derived from the geometry, and the
arrow declares itself folded into the control rather than being announced twice.
The type badge now carries how many words are on offer — the reference's own,
and exactly what a collapsed control makes necessary.

**The gate** — `docs/analyzer-inspector-spec.json`, a separate tracked artifact
holding three surfaces, read back OUT OF THE PAINTED SCENE by the screen's own
integration test. Its ledger runs in both directions: the two second-pass
controls this build has and the reference does not (a clamping stepper for a
bounded integer, per-element rows for an array) are RECORDED rather than
deleted, which is the standing order rule made enforceable.

## The floor, probed by building against 6.11.1 and running it

With real key events under the offscreen platform. Every member of the new type
comes from a row of this table.

| question | there | here |
|---|---|---|
| ask what committing right now would choose | **nothing answers** — of 123 members exactly two name the highlight and BOTH ARE SIGNALS | `Picker::highlighted` |
| a check written the natural way, while the reader has moved | **passes** — asserted the committed index while the open roster showed the fifth row | `Picker::at` is the fact the paint reads |
| a roster with nothing in it | accepted: count 0, index −1, empty text, no complaint | `PickerDefect::NoOptions` |
| a word the roster does not offer | silently ignored — void return, no signal | `Picker::holding` names it |
| an index past the end | accepted, and clears the control to nothing | `point_at` refuses it |
| a letter on the closed control | **commits** — the value moved first→fifth with the roster never shown | a letter opens |
| the same letter again over three words starting with it | never leaves the second match | `typed` advances and wraps |
| arrows on the closed control | commit, one document write per press, and do not wrap | arrows open; movement is not a write |

## Why the split is by SHAPE and not a knob

`Choice` collapses and `Flags` does not, derived from what the value IS rather
than from a setting nobody decided: exactly one of a set is a picker, any subset
of a set is a row of independent toggles. That is the reference's own split (its
enumeration is a closed control and its permission pair is two chips) and the
mature toolkit's (a combo box against a group of check boxes).
changes_bullets: ## Framework
* `crates/pinion-core/src/widgets/picker.rs` (new) — `Picker`, `Picked`,
`PickerDefect`. `over` refuses an empty roster and NAMES a word the roster does
not offer instead of substituting; `highlighted` answers what committing would
choose; `key` is the W3C single-select listbox model (arrows wrap, `Home`/`End`
jump, `Enter`/`Space` choose, `Escape` dismisses, a printable character
searches); `typed` advances through every word starting with the letter and
wraps; `opens` says which keys open a shut control, so nothing is learned
twice. `serde(try_from)` puts the wire form back through the constructor's
rule.
* `crates/pinion-widget-paint/src/config_form.rs` — `OpenPicker`, `PickerPopup`,
`FormGeometry::popup` / `option_at` / `on_popup`, `form_geometry_showing`,

R1732.publishable_decision_summary:
An enumeration row in the analysis tool's node inspector COLLAPSES into a roster
you open, the way the behaviour reference draws it, and the inspector is now
checked against a specification somebody wrote down.

## What was wrong, as a number

`pinion_widget_paint::config_form` drew a `FieldType::Choice` row as one chip per
option, laid from the control's left edge, with no wrap, no clip and no scroll.
Measured with the inspector's own `FormStyle::default()` (a 284 px pane):

* three words — the analysis tool's own `mode` row — spend 229 px saying one word;
* six words overrun the control by **50 px**;
* seven words by **113 px**.

The behaviour reference collapses the same field. Its inspector derivation gives
a field five mutually exclusive control kinds and draws the enumeration one as a
CLOSED control carrying the word it holds and an arrow, styled identically to
the text field beside it. So the expanded row was not merely wide: it was not
what is being reproduced.

## What was built

**`pinion_core::widgets::picker`** — `Picker` / `Picked` / `PickerDefect`. The
transient state of choosing: the roster, and where in it the reader is. Not the
value — the value stays in the document until a choice is committed. There is no
`open` flag, because a screen holding no picker has no open picker, so "shut and
highlighting the fourth option" has no spelling. Its wire form goes back through
the constructor's rule (`serde(try_from)`), because a snapshot is a door into
the type as much as the constructor is and §2 #3's `dry_run` restores signals
from one.

**The paint** — a choice row wears the box a text row wears, holding the word it
has and a chevron. The roster is published as its own LAYER
(`FormGeometry::popup`, `option_at`, `on_popup`) rather than as more of the open
row's parts, because a hit test walking the rows in order would resolve a press
on the roster to whichever row it covers. Its direction is DERIVED from a
rectangle the caller passes (`OpenPicker::room`): the pane is the only thing that
knows where the fold is, and flipping against the form's own extent would open
downward off the bottom of a scrolled viewport. The control's ARIA role moves
from radiogroup to combobox with `expanded` derived from the geometry, and the
arrow declares itself folded into the control rather than being announced twice.
The type badge now carries how many words are on offer — the reference's own,
and exactly what a collapsed control makes necessary.

**The gate** — `docs/analyzer-inspector-spec.json`, a separate tracked artifact
holding three surfaces, read back OUT OF THE PAINTED SCENE by the screen's own
integration test. Its ledger runs in both directions: the two second-pass
controls this build has and the reference does not (a clamping stepper for a
bounded integer, per-element rows for an array) are RECORDED rather than
deleted, which is the standing order rule made enforceable.

## The floor, probed by building against 6.11.1 and running it

With real key events under the offscreen platform. Every member of the new type
comes from a row of this table.

| question | there | here |
|---|---|---|
| ask what committing right now would choose | **nothing answers** — of 123 members exactly two name the highlight and BOTH ARE SIGNALS | `Picker::highlighted` |
| a check written the natural way, while the reader has moved | **passes** — asserted the committed index while the open roster showed the fifth row | `Picker::at` is the fact the paint reads |
| a roster with nothing in it | accepted: count 0, index −1, empty text, no complaint | `PickerDefect::NoOptions` |
| a word the roster does not offer | silently ignored — void return, no signal | `Picker::holding` names it |
| an index past the end | accepted, and clears the control to nothing | `point_at` refuses it |
| a letter on the closed control | **commits** — the value moved first→fifth with the roster never shown | a letter opens |
| the same letter again over three words starting with it | never leaves the second match | `typed` advances and wraps |
| arrows on the closed control | commit, one document write per press, and do not wrap | arrows open; movement is not a write |

## Why the split is by SHAPE and not a knob

`Choice` collapses and `Flags` does not, derived from what the value IS rather
than from a setting nobody decided: exactly one of a set is a picker, any subset
of a set is a row of independent toggles. That is the reference's own split (its
enumeration is a closed control and its permission pair is two chips) and the
mature toolkit's (a combo box against a group of check boxes).

R1732.1.decision_summary:
R1732's own verification prose said the demo sweep found one defect. It found
**two**, and the second is the more interesting one.

## What the filed entry got wrong

R1732's `verification` reads: "`r1651` failed first — its backward check
reported fourteen painted tags the specification does not declare … Repaired by
declaring the five new families there; **the rest of the sweep is green**."

The sweep was 7 of 36 in when that sentence was written. It is not what the
sweep found. `r1692_a_voice_is_judged_not_only_counted` failed too, at demo 15,
and it failed on a **different** defect that the earlier repair does not touch.

## The second defect, which is worth its own paragraph

The type badge declares its silence as *"my text is the name of the row's
description region"*. R1732 gave that badge the option count — `mode · 3` — and
left the description region saying `mode, restart; worked out from the role`.
The redirect then pointed at a node that speaks and says **something else**: a
reader following the label aloud arrives somewhere that does not contain it.

Nothing in the crate could see it. The badge's box was right, the region's
sentence was right, and only the RELATION between them was false — the same
shape as R1656's seven-pixel overflow, one axis over. What saw it was a sibling
application's demo, holding every declared silence to the node it names.

The repair is the derivation, not the sentence: the description region is built
from `type_word(field)` as well, so the badge's words are inside it by
construction and a future round that changes one changes both.

## Why this is a sub-round and not an amendment

The ledger is frozen; an entry cannot be edited once filed. A correction is
therefore its own entry, which is the right shape anyway — "the round said X
and X was false" is a fact about the round that a reader of the ledger should
meet, not a difference they have to notice between two versions of one entry.

## The lesson, stated so the next round can act on it

**Verification prose written while the verification is still running is a
prediction.** R1732 wrote its sweep result at 7 of 36 because the file was ready
and the sweep was not; the sentence was true of what had run and false of the
run. The rule this repository already has — *a number measured in the middle of
a round is re-measured at the end* — reaches prose about outcomes too, and this
is the instance that says so.
changes_bullets: No code change. This entry corrects R1732's own verification record.
The repair the correction is about — `row_access_nodes` building the row's
description region from `type_word(field)` rather than `field.ty()`, so the type
badge's declared silence names a region that really contains its words — is in
R1732's commit, made when the demo reported it. What was not in R1732 is the
statement that it happened.
The demo sweep's true result: **36 node-lab demos, 34 green on the first pass,
two red** — `r1651` (a backward check over painted tags the specification does
not declare, fourteen of them, the round's new `key` and `type` names) and
`r1692` (a declared silence whose redirect no longer arrived at its own words).
Both repaired; ten demos re-run afterwards, all green.

* `docs/.atomic/workspace.atomic.json`, entry `R1732`, `verification` — carries

R1733.decision_summary:
A palette hands the board a footprint, and the board says where it would land.

The behaviour reference populates its dashboard by DRAGGING a row out of the
widget palette onto the canvas. This build could only ever ADD from a palette
row — a click that appended at the bottom — and that was the last first-pass
reproduction gap the reference's GUI element census had open.

WHAT WAS MEASURED FIRST, and it corrected the census. The reference's palette
row is `draggable` AND its click adds; the canvas takes drag-over, drag-leave
and drop; while a footprint is over it the canvas raises a per-cell overlay,
pushes a snap rectangle into the grid at the destination cell, grows the
overlay by THREE rows rather than one so there is somewhere to drop below what
is placed, and covers itself with a dashed frame saying in words what letting
go does. The census had recorded the drag; it had not recorded that the row
carries both, and that is the fact the round turned on.

THE FRAMEWORK HALF IS A TYPE, not a screen. `pinion_core::widgets::tile_grid`
gains `TileDrag`: a board drag carrying EITHER a tile the board already holds
OR a footprint that is not on it yet, exclusive by construction. The reference
spells the same pair as two nullable fields, so every handler must remember to
check the other before acting; three of its handlers do, and the fourth anyone
adds is a defect nothing can catch. Here it is a `match` and the compiler
performs the check.

The drag stores ONE landing, and both `preview` and `drop_on` read it, so the
mark a person is looking at and the cell a release commits to cannot disagree.
R1668 measured that exact failure on the OTHER drag — a six-column card
previewed at column seven and committed at six, because a shell wrote the clamp
and the grid wrote it too — repaired it for tiles already on the board, and
left the same shape wide open for anything arriving from a palette, because
`landing` needed a tile the grid already held. `TileGrid::landing_for` is now
that one clamp and `landing` and `place` are both written in terms of it; it
had been spelled out three times.

`Dropped` has three arms because a release has three outcomes and only one of
them is a change: it landed, it carried the tile nowhere, or it was let go off
the board. R1701 measured what the middle case costs when it is left to a
remembered comparison — a click that carried nothing reflowed the board and
announced a move that had not happened.

THE FLOOR, measured by building two probes against 6.11.1 and running them
rather than reading about it. Across its grid container, its layout base, its
widget class and its item view, NO member answers "where would a w-wide item
land at this cell" — the one name that matches at all is a bool saying whether
to draw an indicator. Two items asked for the same cell both get geometry and
OVERLAP; the add call returns void, so there is nothing to refuse with, and the
position query answers only the first. A drag-move event carries a pixel, and
nothing on the event, the widget or the layout turns it into the cell a release
would use.

AND THE HONEST COUNTER-MEASUREMENT, from the same probes: on the neighbouring
axis the floor is ABOVE us. A target there accepts a payload from a source it
has never heard of, negotiated by format, while pinion's drag session
dispatches only to the source. What the floor cannot do is answer WHICH kinds,
per part, without running a drag — its acceptance is one bool on the widget,
one bool on a row, a kind list declared once per model outside the
meta-object, and a refusal that is a bare bool with no reason. That gap is
registered rather than quietly skipped, with the numbers, and it was not taken
this round because its blast radius is the input contract: R1727 touched that
layer and its population was every demo that drives a drag.

THE GESTURE IS ADDED, NEVER SUBSTITUTED. A press on a palette row arms a
carry, and an abandoned carry falls through to the latched control, so a press
and release on the same row still adds at the bottom exactly as before. The
reference has ZERO keyboard bindings; moving its pointer-only gesture over
instead of the action would take the palette away from a reader who cannot
drag, which is the one way a reproduction becomes a regression.

AND AN AGENT REACHES THE SAME CELL. `add` now takes an optional column and row,
refuses half of one by name, and clamps what it is given by the board's own
rule — because a gesture only a hand can perform is a capability §2 #2 says
must not exist. `carrying` is a new read slot saying WHAT is in hand and
whether it is on the board yet; before it, a palette footprint in flight was
not a tile, not a card and not in the layout, so every question about it had
the same answer as "nothing is happening".

GATE

them swept across every state and every size, all driven through the real

* `tools/demos/r1733_a_palette_hands_the_board_a_footprint.py` — 32 named

verification_bullets: COUNTERFACTUALS — 14 written, 14 CAUGHT.
Six break the framework type (the landing clamp; `place` written in terms of it;
a fresh carry's landing; the preview reading the stored landing; the duplicate

that picks up; the leave that clears the landing; the abandon that falls
through to the latch; the invitation's fresh-only condition; the three extra

* `cargo test -p hello-analyzer-shell` — 96 passed, 0 failed.
* `cargo test -p hello-tile-dashboard` — 28 passed (the tile grid's other

* `cargo clippy -p pinion-core -p hello-analyzer-shell --all-targets

THE DEMO — 32 named checks plus the `assert_eq` comparisons, and **one
real-pointer session**: section F presses a palette row with the machine's own
X11 pointer, carries it onto the board, and asserts the card lands at the cell
the preview named. A harness-driven green and a hand-driven green are not the
same claim, and this round has both.
THE BLAST RADIUS — 29 demos, every one that drives the analysis shell or the
tile dashboard. **29/29 green.** Three reds on the first pass, all real and all
caused by this round's new part tags:
* 16 painted, addressable regions with nobody having decided whether they owe a
reader anything (`unvoiced`) — each part now DECLARES its quiet, and
`spec::SILENCES` states the claim over a `Population::Placeable` derived from
the tier;
* a decoration tag inside a control failing "must be pressable there" — the
demo's population had grown three hand-written exclusions, so rather than
adding a fourth it now DERIVES the exclusion from `scene/voice`: a region the
screen declares quiet is not a control. Sixteen tags excluded, none named.
FOUR MORE FINDINGS the gates produced during the build rather than reading did:
36 inert regions stating a reason no reader is told (the same part tags on a
RESERVED row, which declares itself unavailable and cascades); a two-pixel
overhang on the new grid wrapper (a mark is centred on its intersection, so the
last one reaches half its size past the last line); two backward censuses broken
by the new tags, repaired by counting a ROW by the SHAPE of its name rather than
by a list of exclusions; and five clippy findings.
ONE FLAKE, ROOT-CAUSED RATHER THAN RERUN. The second sweep went 28/29 with
`r1710` red; it passed standing alone and had been green in the first sweep, and
this round touches neither that screen nor the resize path. Two hypotheses were
killed by measurement before the real one was found: CPU load (5 quiet runs and
5 under eight hogs, 10/10 green) and "the re-read is a frame later" (12 rounds,
the re-read identical every time, 127 tags).
The cause is a rule older than the feature it judges. `declared -
declared_and_painted(...)` was written when a window could not pan and its panes
could not scroll. Measured from a fresh boot, 10 rounds of 10: at its own
declared floor the capture viewer paints 127 of the 290 regions its
specification names, and `scene/scroll_reach` answers `lost: 0` and names all
163 of the rest `scrollable`, with the scroll that brings each back. Nothing was
missing; the rule could not say so, and whether anything was out of sight
depended on the state the section ran in — which is what made it intermittent.
R1714 gave the PANE assertion beside it exactly this clause and left this one
behind. Repaired as one harness primitive
(`rpc_verify.declared_but_unreachable`) used by the two demos that had the old
shape, each also asserting `lost == 0` so the screen-wide half is not lost.
Verified: both demos five times each, 10/10, plus the harness's own suite (39
cases, 107 assertions).
THE FLOOR — two probes built against 6.11.1 and run offscreen, not read about:
`probe_drop` enumerates the grid container, the layout base, the widget class
and the item view through the runtime meta-object, puts two items in one cell,
and drives a real drag onto a real target; `probe_accept` asks what a surface
accepts before a drag runs. Their numbers are in the decision and the carry.
THE ROUND'S OWN ERROR, recorded because it cost twenty minutes and would cost
them again. The first counterfactual run was killed by a ten-minute tool
timeout, and it left CF-13's mutation in the tree. The restoration check was a
hand-picked set of greps, and it did not include that case — so the next test
run came back with four reds and they were misdiagnosed as a regression from the
clippy refactor made in between. The check is now mechanical over every case in
the plan (`find` present, `replace` absent, 14/14), and the driver is run in the
background where the tool timeout cannot reach it.
carry_forward_bullets: ONE DEBT OPENED, WITH ITS NUMBERS — a drop target never sees the drag.
`pinion_runtime`'s drag session remembers the External that answered
`begin_drag` and sends `drag_to` / `drag_release` / `drag_cancel` to THAT one.
Nothing reaches the target. So a drop between two different Externals cannot be
spelled: the target cannot declare what it accepts, cannot paint its own
highlight, and cannot receive the drop. This round's palette and board satisfy
the condition by accident — both live inside one composite External.
Measured on the floor at 6.11.1 by driving a real drag onto a real target: it
receives enter / move / leave / drop, each carrying the payload's formats, the
proposed action and the possible actions, and it accepted a payload of a kind
the target had never heard of. That is an axis where the floor is ABOVE us, and
the standing rule says a capability the floor has is one to build even with no
consumer waiting.
NOT TAKEN THIS ROUND, and the reason is scope rather than doubt: the repair is
in the input contract, and R1727 measured what that population is — every demo
that drives a drag. Doing it in the same round as the reproduction would have
made both shallow. Registered as `debt-a-drop-target-never-sees-the-drag` with
the probe numbers and the three things to re-measure before starting.
The same probes measured where pinion's answer should be BETTER rather than
equal, and that is written down with it: the floor cannot say what a surface
accepts before a drag runs. Its widget acceptance is one bool, a row's is one
bool, the kind list is declared once per model outside the meta-object, and the
refusal is a bare bool with no reason. A declared, per-part, reasoned accept set
is what §2 #7 asks for and what a target-side protocol here should carry.
STATED LIMITS, not carry:
* The three extra rows the overlay grows by while carrying are DRAWN below the
last placed card, and whether a person can scroll to all of them on a board
taller than the viewport is the scroll pane's range question, not this
gesture's. The reachability of those cells is asserted directly, and the case
where a board is too tall for the window to reach them proves its own reason
rather than being skipped.
* A reserved palette row has no part tags, so the `palette_row` surface is read
off the rows the specification is about. Both halves of that are stated on
`part_tag_of`: the reference has no reserved rows at all, and a reserved row
declares itself unavailable, so tagging four parts inside one turns one
announced inert region into five — which the harness's own gate caught.
