RESERVED row, which declares itself unavailable and cascades); a two-pixel
overhang on the new grid wrapper (a mark is centred on its intersection, so the
last one reaches half its size past the last line); two backward censuses broken
by the new tags, repaired by counting a ROW by the SHAPE of its name rather than
by a list of exclusions; and five clippy findings.
ONE FLAKE, ROOT-CAUSED RATHER THAN RERUN. The second sweep went 28/29 with
`r1710` red; it passed standing alone and had been green in the first sweep, and
this round touches neither that screen nor the resize path. Two hypotheses were
killed by measurement before the real one was found: CPU load (5 quiet runs and
5 under eight hogs, 10/10 green) and "the re-read is a frame later" (12 rounds,
the re-read identical every time, 127 tags).
The cause is a rule older than the feature it judges. `declared -
declared_and_painted(...)` was written when a window could not pan and its panes
could not scroll. Measured from a fresh boot, 10 rounds of 10: at its own
declared floor the capture viewer paints 127 of the 290 regions its
specification names, and `scene/scroll_reach` answers `lost: 0` and names all
163 of the rest `scrollable`, with the scroll that brings each back. Nothing was
missing; the rule could not say so, and whether anything was out of sight
depended on the state the section ran in — which is what made it intermittent.
R1714 gave the PANE assertion beside it exactly this clause and left this one
behind. Repaired as one harness primitive
(`rpc_verify.declared_but_unreachable`) used by the two demos that had the old
shape, each also asserting `lost == 0` so the screen-wide half is not lost.
Verified: both demos five times each, 10/10, plus the harness's own suite (39
cases, 107 assertions).
THE FLOOR — two probes built against 6.11.1 and run offscreen, not read about:
`probe_drop` enumerates the grid container, the layout base, the widget class
and the item view through the runtime meta-object, puts two items in one cell,
and drives a real drag onto a real target; `probe_accept` asks what a surface
accepts before a drag runs. Their numbers are in the decision and the carry.
THE ROUND'S OWN ERROR, recorded because it cost twenty minutes and would cost
them again. The first counterfactual run was killed by a ten-minute tool
timeout, and it left CF-13's mutation in the tree. The restoration check was a
hand-picked set of greps, and it did not include that case — so the next test
run came back with four reds and they were misdiagnosed as a regression from the
clippy refactor made in between. The check is now mechanical over every case in
the plan (`find` present, `replace` absent, 14/14), and the driver is run in the
background where the tool timeout cannot reach it.
publishable_carry_forward_bullets: ONE DEBT OPENED, WITH ITS NUMBERS — a drop target never sees the drag.
`pinion_runtime`'s drag session remembers the External that answered
`begin_drag` and sends `drag_to` / `drag_release` / `drag_cancel` to THAT one.
Nothing reaches the target. So a drop between two different Externals cannot be
spelled: the target cannot declare what it accepts, cannot paint its own
highlight, and cannot receive the drop. This round's palette and board satisfy
the condition by accident — both live inside one composite External.
Measured on the floor at 6.11.1 by driving a real drag onto a real target: it
receives enter / move / leave / drop, each carrying the payload's formats, the
proposed action and the possible actions, and it accepted a payload of a kind
the target had never heard of. That is an axis where the floor is ABOVE us, and
the standing rule says a capability the floor has is one to build even with no
consumer waiting.
NOT TAKEN THIS ROUND, and the reason is scope rather than doubt: the repair is
in the input contract, and R1727 measured what that population is — every demo
that drives a drag. Doing it in the same round as the reproduction would have
made both shallow. Registered as `debt-a-drop-target-never-sees-the-drag` with
the probe numbers and the three things to re-measure before starting.
The same probes measured where pinion's answer should be BETTER rather than
equal, and that is written down with it: the floor cannot say what a surface
accepts before a drag runs. Its widget acceptance is one bool, a row's is one
bool, the kind list is declared once per model outside the meta-object, and the
refusal is a bare bool with no reason. A declared, per-part, reasoned accept set
is what §2 #7 asks for and what a target-side protocol here should carry.
STATED LIMITS, not carry:
* The three extra rows the overlay grows by while carrying are DRAWN below the
last placed card, and whether a person can scroll to all of them on a board
taller than the viewport is the scroll pane's range question, not this
gesture's. The reachability of those cells is asserted directly, and the case
where a board is too tall for the window to reach them proves its own reason
rather than being skipped.
* A reserved palette row has no part tags, so the `palette_row` surface is read
off the rows the specification is about. Both halves of that are stated on
`part_tag_of`: the reference has no reserved rows at all, and a reserved row
declares itself unavailable, so tagging four parts inside one turns one
announced inert region into five — which the harness's own gate caught.

R1733.1.decision_summary:
The close audit measured a count R1733 had written from memory, and the truth
was both different and stronger.

R1733 justified `Carried`'s two arms against the behaviour reference's two
nullable fields, and said of that prototype: *three of its handlers each have to
remember to check the other, and the fourth anyone adds is a defect nothing can
catch.* Three files carried that sentence — the framework type's own
documentation, the screen's comment where its hand-rolled struct had been, and
the demo's docstring.

Measured, in the prototype's script: the held-card field occurs **three times in
total**, of which **two are guards reading it**, and **nothing anywhere assigns
it a non-null value**. The reorder gesture it was written for moved onto another
field, and the guards it left behind were never removed.

So the count was wrong, and the argument it was making was weaker than what is
actually there. The claim is not "a pair of nullable fields invites a forgotten
check"; it is that this pair had **already** decayed into two live guards on a
value that is always null. A type with two arms cannot reach that state: a guard
on a case that cannot arise is an arm, and an arm nothing constructs is dead
code the compiler names — which is the event R1729 and R1731 both recorded when
it happened to them.

WHY THIS IS ITS OWN ENTRY. The ledger is frozen, so R1733's decision cannot be
amended, and a corrected number that only exists in the source would leave the
store saying something this tree knows to be false.

THE LESSON, which is the reason to file it rather than quietly fix it: this
project measures its own numbers and re-measures them at the close, and R1733
did that faithfully for everything it built. The number it got wrong was about
somebody ELSE's code, where "I read that earlier" felt like measurement and was
not. Re-running the count cost thirty seconds. A count about a reference is a
count, and it is owed the same discipline as a count about this tree — the same
rule R1732 wrote for a debt file's premise, one source over.
changes_bullets: * `pinion_core::widgets::tile_grid::Carried` — its documentation now states the
measurement rather than a remembered count, and states the sharper fact: the
reference's held-card field is read by two guards and assigned a non-null
value nowhere at all.
* The same correction in the test that asserts the property
(`r1733_a_board_carries_one_thing_and_it_names_itself`), in
`hello-analyzer-shell`'s comment where its hand-rolled `Drag` struct had been,
and in the R1733 demo's docstring.
* `tools/demos/r1649_...py` — the trade the R1733 derivation makes is written
down beside it: a real control WRONGLY declared silent now leaves that
population instead of failing there. It is not unwatched — the voice census's
`ghost` / `dangling` / `mumbled` arms judge a mis-declaration and
`r1694_a_locked_seat_is_heard` asserts all three are zero — but a check that
narrows its own population owes the reader that sentence.
verification_bullets: The count was re-derived from the extracted prototype script twice, by two
different queries: every occurrence of the held-card identifier with its
surrounding text (3 occurrences: one guard in the drag-over handler, one guard
and one clear in the drop handler), and every assignment to it (1, the clear).
Against the palette-kind field for contrast: 8 occurrences, with a declaration,
an assignment in the drag-start handler, four reads across the two canvas
handlers and a clear after the widget is added.
Documentation only — no behaviour changed, so the round's own gates stand.
Re-run after the edits: `cargo test -p pinion-core` (3803 lib, 0 failed),
`cargo doc -p pinion-core --no-deps --document-private-items` (clean), and
`cargo fmt --all --check`.
carry_forward_bullets: None. The correction is complete across every file that carried the sentence,
and the audit that found it is the standing close-audit obligation rather than
anything new.
The one thing it leaves for the next round is a habit, not a task: a count about
a REFERENCE is a count. This tree re-measures its own numbers at every close and
had no rule pointing the same discipline outward, because the numbers that go
stale are usually its own. This one did not go stale — it was never measured.

R1734.decision_summary:
A drag in this framework spoke to exactly one party. `External::begin_drag`
opened a session and every later event — `drag_to`, `drag_release`,
`drag_cancel` — went back to the surface that started it, which then had to
decide, on the destination's behalf, what a release would mean. That works when
one coordinator owns both ends, which every in-tree consumer happened to be
(a reorder list, a tab strip, a dock, a tree reparent), and it cannot express a
drop BETWEEN two surfaces at all: the destination is never asked anything.
R1733's palette-to-board satisfied the condition by accident — both halves live
inside one composite External — and that accident is what this round removes.

THE FLOOR IS ABOVE US HERE, AND THAT IS WHY THE ROUND EXISTS. Measured by
building two probes against the reference toolkit at 6.11.1 and running them
offscreen, re-run at the start of this round rather than remembered: a target
there receives the drag — enter 1, move 3, drop 1 — each event carrying the
payload's format list, the proposed action and the set of possible actions, and
it accepted a payload in a format it had never heard of from a source that had
never heard of it. Table stakes, and this tree owed them. The standing
instruction is that a capability the floor has is a capability with a consumer.

AND THEN THE FLOOR STOPS, in three places this round is built around, each one
measured by the same probes. You cannot ask before the drag: acceptance is one
boolean per widget and the decision that matters lives inside an event handler
that has to run; per-part acceptance is a second boolean — three rows answered
yes/no and not one could say WHAT it would take — and the members that do name
kinds are plain virtuals absent from the runtime metaobject a generic reader
walks. A refusal carries no reason: the accept predicate answers a bare bool.
And the preview and the commit are two computations: a move event carries a
pixel, and nothing on the event, the widget or the layout turns that pixel into
the cell a release would use.

WHAT WAS BUILT, `pinion_core::drop_target`. A surface DECLARES what it takes as
data — `DropContract` / `DropClause` / `DropRegion` / `DropActions` — static and
`Copy` for the same reason `IntrospectSchema` is, and published at the reserved
`$drop` path beside `$schema`. The declaration is a PRECONDITION OF DISPATCH:
the router derives the three structural refusals from it (wrong kind, wrong
part, no action in common) and never asks a surface about a drag its own
declaration excludes, so the list that says yes is the list that says no. This
is the rule R1637–R1640 established for actions, applied to the drop. A refusal
STATES WHAT WOULD HAVE WORKED — `DropRefusal` carries a matchable tag AND a
person's sentence, the `ReadRefusal` shape. An acceptance CARRIES ITS LANDING —
`DropAccept { action, landing }`, and `External::drop_commit` takes that
acceptance as its witness rather than recomputing, so a target cannot commit
somewhere it did not just preview. That is R1733's one-landing shape lifted from
one grid widget to the input contract.

`DropActions` IS NON-EMPTY BY CONSTRUCTION and `intersect` answers `Option`
rather than a possibly-empty set, so "accepts the kind, can do nothing with it"
is not a value anybody can build — it is a refusal, and it is the one that names
both sides.

`DragPayload` GAINED ITS ACTIONS AND BECAME `#[non_exhaustive]`. A source states
its kind, its datum and what it can honour in ONE return, because a second
question about one fact is a second answer that can drift from the first — the
class this workspace has recorded repeatedly. It cost twenty-odd struct literals
and it is the last time that will be true here, which is exactly the argument
`SchemaField`'s own docstring makes for constructors over literals.

THE ROUTER now maintains the target half beside the source half: leave-then-
enter pairing on the cursor's own discipline, a re-offer at the release point
whose acceptance IS the commit's witness, and a cancel that revokes the target's
preview as well as the source's — the R937.1 ghost, one surface over. Every
pre-R1734 `External` is bit-identical under it, because dispatch is gated on a
declaration whose default is empty.

WHAT NO FLOOR CAN OFFER, and the reason the round is worth more than parity:
`scene/drop_targets` answers WHERE COULD I DROP THIS, AND WHY NOT THERE, with
nothing in flight. Every judgement it publishes runs the same
`DropContract::admits` the router gates dispatch on, and the point it judges at
is resolved by `drop_point_at` — the function `InputRouter::resolve_drop_point`
itself delegates to. One fact, read two ways, which is the property R1703 made
load-bearing for the wheel. A published answer that is COMPUTED the same way
cannot drift from the behaviour; one merely DOCUMENTED the same way has drifted
every time this workspace has measured it.

THE ANALYSIS SCREEN IS WHERE IT LANDS. `hello-analyzer-shell` publishes its
board's accept set, and its own palette path passes through the same `admits`
call, so the list an agent reads is the list the screen enforces.
`docs/analyzer-board-spec.json` gains a fourth surface pinning that declaration,
and the shell's swept integration test reads it back through the very
`ExternalIntrospect` method the wire answers with — not from the constant behind
it — with a title DERIVED from the clause, so a clause that gained an action
would arrive with a different sentence and the pin would refuse it.

STATED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: the analysis shell is ONE External that hit-tests
itself and paints one scene tag, so its palette-to-board release still resolves
source-side and its declaration is `DropRegion::Surface` rather than a part
list — declaring parts the wire cannot resolve would publish a promise the
router could not keep. The router's cross-surface path is proven in
`pinion-runtime` against two genuinely separate Externals, which is where the
claim belongs. Moving that screen onto the router's session is a different axis
(it also takes pointer capture, so a live session changes how every one of its
gestures is routed) and is registered as its own debt with that measurement.
changes_bullets: FRAMEWORK — `pinion_core::drop_target` (new module).
`DropAction` (Copy / Move / Link) with a wire spelling and its inverse, round-trip tested.
`DropActions`: a NON-EMPTY set by construction. `intersect` answers `Option`, so an
empty common set is a refusal rather than a value. `first` is an exhaustive ladder
rather than `iter().next().unwrap()`, so totality is visible in the code.
`DropContract` / `DropClause` / `DropRegion`: a static, `Copy`, `'static` declaration
shaped exactly like `IntrospectSchema`, because the router asks for it on every cursor
sample of a live drag. `DropRegion::Parts` names composite sub-parts; a whole-surface
clause names none, and the two are distinguishable.
`DropContract::admits(kind, offered, part) -> Result<DropActions, DropRefusal>` — the
framework's DERIVED admissibility, a pure function of the published declaration.
`DropRefusal`: three arms derived from the declaration (`KindNotAccepted`,
`PartNotAccepted`, `NoCommonAction`) plus `Declined(RefusalReason)` for live state.
Each carries a matchable `as_wire_name` AND a person's `sentence` naming the remedy.
`DropOffer` / `DropAccept` / `DropVerdict`. `DropAccept` carries the LANDING as an
`IntrospectValue`, so the preview, the commit and the wire read one value.
`DROP_PATH` (`$drop`), `contract_value`, `refusal_value`, `BOARD_WIDGET_DRAG_KIND`.
FRAMEWORK — `pinion_core::external`.
`ExternalIntrospect::drop_contract()`, default `DropContract::EMPTY`. The declaration
lives on the introspect surface so "accepts a drop" and "can say so" are one act.
`External::drop_offered` / `drop_left` / `drop_commit`. `drop_offered`'s default
REFUSES with a sentence, so a surface that declares and forgets to implement says so
rather than silently accepting.
`DragPayload` gained `actions`, became `#[non_exhaustive]`, and grew
`new` / `with_actions`. Twenty-odd struct literals across seven crates and four
examples converted. The palette drags in `hello-node-editor` now declare `Copy`.
FRAMEWORK — `pinion_runtime::input`.
`DragSession` carries a `DropTargetState { tag, actions, verdict }` — one field, because
"who is being offered this and what did they say" is one fact.
`offer_drag_to_target` (leave-then-enter, gated on `admits`), `release_drop_target`
(re-offer at the release point, then commit with THAT acceptance as the witness, then
leave unconditionally), `cancel_drop_target`.
`drop_point_at` is now a public free function and `InputRouter::resolve_drop_point`
delegates to it, so the wire's answer and the router's routing are one computation.
`declared_drop_contract` is public for the same reason.
WIRE.
`$drop` intercepted beside `$schema` in `scene/query`. A surface that declares nothing
answers an empty array, which is an answer.
`scene/drop_targets` (Read / Scope): a census of every painted `External` and what it
declares; with `kind` (and optionally `action`) every row is JUDGED and every refusal
carries its tag and its sentence; with `at` / `path` one point is answered, naming the
part a release there would resolve to. An action word outside the vocabulary is refused
rather than widened.
The R1585.1 param census gained `action`, which is how it found the new method at all.
THE ANALYSIS SCREEN.
`ShellOracle::declared_drop_contract()` — one clause, `board-widget`, copy and move,
whole-surface (measured reason: the screen hit-tests itself and paints one scene tag).
`ExternalIntrospect::drop_contract` publishes it; `ShellOracle::offered` — the path every
palette press, palette click and wire `add` runs through — ASKS IT FIRST and refuses
with the framework's own sentence.
`docs/analyzer-board-spec.json` gains a fourth surface, `drop_contract`, pinning the
declaration. The shell's swept integration test reads it back through the
`ExternalIntrospect` method the wire answers with, with a title DERIVED from the clause.
`tools/demos/r1734_a_drop_target_is_asked_before_the_drag.py` — 22 named checks plus its
`assert_eq` comparisons, every one asked with nothing in flight.
The R1733 demo's hand-written surface count is derived from the document now; it had
gone stale the round after somebody added a surface, which is its own lesson's evidence.
verification_bullets: COUNTERFACTUALS — 14 of 14 CAUGHT, and one of them was BROKEN first.
Framework plan, gate `cargo test -p pinion-core -p pinion-runtime -p pinion-rpc --lib`:
* CF-1 the contract's kind check is what selects the clauses — CAUGHT
* CF-2 a part clause admits the parts it NAMES — CAUGHT
* CF-3 the offered and accepted action sets are INTERSECTED — CAUGHT
* CF-4 the default action is the first the two sides share — CAUGHT
* CF-5 the wire spelling of an action is the action's own — CAUGHT
* CF-6 a refusal's sentence lists what would have worked, in order — CAUGHT
* CF-7 the wire carries the SENTENCE beside the tag — CAUGHT
* CF-8 the router reads the declaration of the surface UNDER THE CURSOR — CAUGHT
(on the second attempt; see below)
* CF-9 leaving is paired with entering, and on the CHANGE — CAUGHT
* CF-10 the drop point resolver is the one the router routes by — CAUGHT
* CF-11 the reserved drop path answers the surface's declaration — CAUGHT
Screen plan, gate `cargo test --manifest-path examples/hello-analyzer-shell/Cargo.toml`:
* CF-12 the screen's own carry path passes through the declaration — CAUGHT
* CF-13 the declared clause is the one the specification pins — CAUGHT
* CF-14 the pinned title is DERIVED from the clause's region — CAUGHT
★ CF-8 came back **BROKEN** on its first run — it did not compile, so it tested
nothing. The cause is the documented class, hit for the sixth time and by a new
route: the replacement made the `ExternalIntrospect` import the LAST READER of
the line it replaced. Rewritten as a wrong LOOKUP (a truncated tag) rather than
an absent one, it is caught by three `scene/drop_targets` tests.
★★ And the first framework run never started: the driver REFUSED it because the
baseline was already red. That is R1619's own defence working, and what it
caught is a real defect of this round — see below.
TESTS (the crates whose behaviour this round changed, plus their consumers).
* `pinion-core` 3,816 — includes 13 `drop_target` tests and the default-refusal
test for a surface that declares and does not judge.
* `pinion-rpc` 1,285 — includes 6 `scene/drop_targets` tests and the `$drop`
transport test.
* `pinion-runtime` 579 — includes 8 R1734 router tests driven through the
PUBLIC entry points (a real press, real moves, a real release) against four
genuinely separate `External`s: the case that could not be spelled before.
* `hello-analyzer-shell` 96, with the swept conformance test now reconciling a
fourth surface across every state and size it sweeps.
* `pinion-widget-paint` 900, `pinion-shell` 256, `hello-node-editor` 257,
`hello-data-grid` 146, `hello-dnd` 10, `hello-tree-reparent` 11 — the
consumers of the `DragPayload` shape change.
GATES.
* `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features pinion-runtime/vello` — green.
It found four things: a `len` with no `is_empty` on a type that is never empty
(renamed to `count`, because an `is_empty` there would be a method that always
answers `false`), a redundant closure, a `# Panics` section owed by an
`expect` in a rendering path (removed by assembling the map instead of
re-opening a `json!` literal — a panic branch that cannot happen is one nobody
can test), and two imports the payload rewrite had stranded.
* `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --document-private-items` — green, after
three links that a new public function had pointed at private items.
* `cargo fmt --all` — applied.
DEMOS.
* NEW `tools/demos/r1734_a_drop_target_is_asked_before_the_drag.py` — 22 named
checks plus its `assert_eq` comparisons, six sections, PASS. Every question it
asks is asked with NOTHING IN FLIGHT, which is the claim.
* `r1733_a_palette_hands_the_board_a_footprint.py` re-run PASS with a real X11
pointer session contributing (33 named checks). Its hand-written "three
surfaces" had gone stale the round a fourth was added; it reads the count from
the document now.
* Blast-radius sweep: the population is the standing one for an INPUT CONTRACT
change (R1727's rule — "which capability changed", not "which file was
edited") = every demo that drives a drag, plus the two per-surface censuses
whose helper was lifted. **80 demos: 79 green, 1 `exit 2`.**
The one is `r1733`, and `exit 2` there is the RECORDED harness class, not a
code failure: it timed out waiting for `scene/pointer_leave` under sweep
contention, which is
`debt-a-deterministic-demo-has-a-wall-clock-bound` — an open debt whose own
text says a full sweep on this host measured 379 of 589 failing that way and
therefore cannot be used as a verdict instrument. Run on its own it PASSES,
measured three times this round (3.71s, 3.43s, and once before the sweep),
each with a real X11 pointer session contributing. Recorded rather than
re-run-and-forgotten: the zero-flake rule is what makes attributing it
mandatory, and the attribution is a pre-existing bound on the harness's
request timeout, not a new one this round introduced.

R1734.publishable_decision_summary:
A drag in this framework spoke to exactly one party. `External::begin_drag`
opened a session and every later event — `drag_to`, `drag_release`,
`drag_cancel` — went back to the surface that started it, which then had to
decide, on the destination's behalf, what a release would mean. That works when
one coordinator owns both ends, which every in-tree consumer happened to be
(a reorder list, a tab strip, a dock, a tree reparent), and it cannot express a
drop BETWEEN two surfaces at all: the destination is never asked anything.
R1733's palette-to-board satisfied the condition by accident — both halves live
inside one composite External — and that accident is what this round removes.

THE FLOOR IS ABOVE US HERE, AND THAT IS WHY THE ROUND EXISTS. Measured by
building two probes against the reference toolkit at 6.11.1 and running them
offscreen, re-run at the start of this round rather than remembered: a target
there receives the drag — enter 1, move 3, drop 1 — each event carrying the
payload's format list, the proposed action and the set of possible actions, and
it accepted a payload in a format it had never heard of from a source that had
never heard of it. Table stakes, and this tree owed them. The standing
instruction is that a capability the floor has is a capability with a consumer.

AND THEN THE FLOOR STOPS, in three places this round is built around, each one
measured by the same probes. You cannot ask before the drag: acceptance is one
boolean per widget and the decision that matters lives inside an event handler
that has to run; per-part acceptance is a second boolean — three rows answered
yes/no and not one could say WHAT it would take — and the members that do name
kinds are plain virtuals absent from the runtime metaobject a generic reader
walks. A refusal carries no reason: the accept predicate answers a bare bool.
And the preview and the commit are two computations: a move event carries a
pixel, and nothing on the event, the widget or the layout turns that pixel into
the cell a release would use.

WHAT WAS BUILT, `pinion_core::drop_target`. A surface DECLARES what it takes as
data — `DropContract` / `DropClause` / `DropRegion` / `DropActions` — static and
`Copy` for the same reason `IntrospectSchema` is, and published at the reserved
`$drop` path beside `$schema`. The declaration is a PRECONDITION OF DISPATCH:
the router derives the three structural refusals from it (wrong kind, wrong
part, no action in common) and never asks a surface about a drag its own
declaration excludes, so the list that says yes is the list that says no. This
is the rule R1637–R1640 established for actions, applied to the drop. A refusal
STATES WHAT WOULD HAVE WORKED — `DropRefusal` carries a matchable tag AND a
person's sentence, the `ReadRefusal` shape. An acceptance CARRIES ITS LANDING —
`DropAccept { action, landing }`, and `External::drop_commit` takes that
acceptance as its witness rather than recomputing, so a target cannot commit
somewhere it did not just preview. That is R1733's one-landing shape lifted from
one grid widget to the input contract.

`DropActions` IS NON-EMPTY BY CONSTRUCTION and `intersect` answers `Option`
rather than a possibly-empty set, so "accepts the kind, can do nothing with it"
is not a value anybody can build — it is a refusal, and it is the one that names
both sides.

`DragPayload` GAINED ITS ACTIONS AND BECAME `#[non_exhaustive]`. A source states
its kind, its datum and what it can honour in ONE return, because a second
question about one fact is a second answer that can drift from the first — the
class this workspace has recorded repeatedly. It cost twenty-odd struct literals
and it is the last time that will be true here, which is exactly the argument
`SchemaField`'s own docstring makes for constructors over literals.

THE ROUTER now maintains the target half beside the source half: leave-then-
enter pairing on the cursor's own discipline, a re-offer at the release point
whose acceptance IS the commit's witness, and a cancel that revokes the target's
preview as well as the source's — the R937.1 ghost, one surface over. Every
pre-R1734 `External` is bit-identical under it, because dispatch is gated on a
declaration whose default is empty.

WHAT NO FLOOR CAN OFFER, and the reason the round is worth more than parity:
`scene/drop_targets` answers WHERE COULD I DROP THIS, AND WHY NOT THERE, with
nothing in flight. Every judgement it publishes runs the same
`DropContract::admits` the router gates dispatch on, and the point it judges at
is resolved by `drop_point_at` — the function `InputRouter::resolve_drop_point`
itself delegates to. One fact, read two ways, which is the property R1703 made
load-bearing for the wheel. A published answer that is COMPUTED the same way
cannot drift from the behaviour; one merely DOCUMENTED the same way has drifted
every time this workspace has measured it.

board's accept set, and its own palette path passes through the same `admits`
call, so the list an agent reads is the list the screen enforces.
`docs/analyzer-board-spec.json` gains a fourth surface pinning that declaration,
and the shell's swept integration test reads it back through the very
`ExternalIntrospect` method the wire answers with — not from the constant behind
it — with a title DERIVED from the clause, so a clause that gained an action
would arrive with a different sentence and the pin would refuse it.

itself and paints one scene tag, so its palette-to-board release still resolves

list — declaring parts the wire cannot resolve would publish a promise the
router could not keep. The router's cross-surface path is proven in

claim belongs. Moving that screen onto the router's session is a different axis
(it also takes pointer capture, so a live session changes how every one of its
gestures is routed) and is registered as its own debt with that measurement.

R1734.1.decision_summary:
The closing audit found two things R1734 itself did not, and neither is a wrong
number in the entry above — both are about the round's own conduct.

1. THE GATE-REPAIR PHASE IS CODE EDITING, AND IT HAPPENS AFTER THE TEST PHASE.

R1734 ran its full changed-crate suite, and THEN fixed four clippy findings and
three doc-link findings. One of those repairs renamed a public method
(`DropActions::len` → `count`, which edits a test assertion) and another rewrote
a rendering function whole (`refusal_value`, to remove an `expect` a `# Panics`
section would otherwise have owed). The round committed and pushed in that
state.

The commit hook runs `validate-workspace`, clippy and `cargo doc`. IT DOES NOT
RUN THE TESTS. Neither does the push hook — this workspace's own 2026-07-21
directive puts the suite in CI, and the local gate is the round's own
discipline. So nothing between the last test run and the published commit was
checking the repairs.

Re-measured after the fact at the pushed commit: `pinion-core` 3,816,
`pinion-rpc` 1,285, `pinion-runtime` 579, `hello-analyzer-shell` 96,
`hello-node-editor` 257 — all green, so the numbers the entry above publishes
are TRUE of the commit they describe. That is luck rather than procedure, and
recording it as luck is the point.

★ The standing lesson "a number measured mid-round is re-measured at the end"
already existed (R1724, R1727, R1728) and had only ever been applied to COUNTS.
This is the same lesson reaching the SEQUENCE: a repair is an edit, so the
gates that repaired something are not the gates that verified it.

2. THE ROUND ADDED A PER-MOVE COST AND NOTHING MEASURED IT.

Before R1734 a drag move performed ONE scene lookup — the source's. It now
performs TWO: `offer_drag_to_target` resolves the surface under the cursor
through `declared_drop_contract`, and only then does the source's own update
run. The release path is the same shape.

The second lookup happens whether or not the surface declares anything: an
empty contract is the RESULT of the lookup, not a condition for skipping it. In
this tree exactly one surface declares a contract, so every pre-existing drag
now pays the cost and receives none of the benefit.

`find_external_with_tag` is a depth-first walk of the state scene, and a drag
runs it per cursor sample. Registered as
`debt-a-drag-move-now-walks-the-scene-twice-and-nobody-measured-it` rather than
fixed here, and registered rather than left silent because a drag-performance
question is ALREADY open — R1723's carry asks the owner whether dragging is
still slow, and R1734 added work to that exact path before that question was
answered.

Deliberately NOT called a regression: nobody has measured it as slow. It is an
unmeasured cost, the debt says how to measure it (`perf record` during a drag,
not reasoning), and it says what the repair would be if the measurement earns
one — collapse the two lookups where the tags coincide, which for a
self-hit-testing screen is always.

`memory/debt-a-drag-move-now-walks-the-scene-twice-and-nobody-measured-it.md`
— NEW. The per-move lookup R1734 added, what it costs in principle, why it is
registered rather than fixed, and how to measure it before repairing it.
`memory/r1734-a-drop-target-is-asked-before-the-drag.md` — gains the audit's
two findings under their own heading.
`memory/MEMORY.md` — the repeated-lesson line now says the re-measure rule
reaches the gate-repair phase, not only counts.
verification_bullets: Re-run at the pushed commit `86eb6790`, AFTER the clippy and doc repairs that
the round's own test phase had not covered:
* `pinion-core` 3,816 passed / 0 failed
* `pinion-rpc` 1,285 passed / 0 failed
* `pinion-runtime` 579 passed / 0 failed
* `hello-analyzer-shell` 96 passed / 0 failed
* `hello-node-editor` 257 passed / 0 failed
So the entry above publishes true numbers. The finding is that nothing had
established that before the push.
The second finding is a reading of the code rather than a measurement, and the

R1735.decision_summary:
R1734 built the destination half of a drag and all of it speaks INWARD. A
surface declares what it takes, the router derives the structural refusals from
that declaration, a target previews and the commit takes that preview as its
witness — and every one of those sentences is addressed to the target. The
SOURCE, meanwhile, learns nothing: it opens a session and is told where the
cursor is, and whether the thing in its hand can land there is a question it
cannot ask. This round turns the contract around.

THE FLOOR, BUILT AND DRIVEN RATHER THAN REMEMBERED. Three probes against the
6.11.1 release. The first is a runtime census of the drag object's own declared
members: two notifications — one naming an object, one naming an action — and
ZERO members carrying a point. The second and third are live drags, and getting
them to run is itself a finding: the offscreen platform does not run a drag at
all (the cursor position resolves to no window, so the can-drop flag is false
and the nested loop exits immediately), and this build ships no X11 platform
plugin, so the probes run on the framebuffer platform driven by a small RFB
PointerEvent client written for the purpose. That is the only path on this host
by which a real drag reproduces, and "the probe answered zero" and "the
capability is absent" are different sentences.

WHAT THOSE PROBES MEASURED. Crossing an accepting region, bare background and a
refusing region — eleven pointer samples — the source received FOUR
notifications in total: an object and an action on the way in, a null and an
ignore on the way out. The refusing region contributed NOTHING, so a target
that said no is indistinguishable there from no target at all. The source's own
pointer handler ran ZERO times for the whole gesture, and it received ZERO
mouse releases for it either. The call that runs the drag returns an action and
nothing else. So the floor tells a source WHICH OBJECT and WHICH ACTION; it
cannot tell it WHERE, cannot tell it WHY NOT, and cannot separate a refusal
from an absence.

WHAT WAS BUILT. `pinion_core::drop_target::DropStanding` — what letting go
right now would do, told to the source on every move. Three arms and EXHAUSTIVE,
like `DropVerdict` and unlike `DropRefusal`: `Nowhere` (nothing under the cursor
publishes a contract), `Refused` (a declaring surface is here and will not take
this, carrying the matchable tag and the sentence a person reads) and `Accepted`
(carrying the target's own `DropAccept` — the SAME value `drop_commit` receives,
so a source painting from it draws the landing the release will apply rather
than a second computation over the same pixel). The first two arms are separate
for exactly the third measured hole. An exhaustive enum rather than a
non-exhaustive one because a source has to handle all three to paint anything
correct, and a `_ =>` catch-all is precisely the arm that would quietly do the
wrong thing if a fourth case appeared.

IT IS FILLED BY THE CALL THAT GATES THE COMMIT. `offer_drag_to_target` now
ANSWERS the standing instead of returning nothing, so the judgement the router
dispatches on and the judgement the source is told are one value. A second
derivation for the source's benefit would have been the two-computations class
the target half was built to close, one party over. The release path answers the
same way, so "what would happen" and "what happened" are one vocabulary.

TWO LIFTS RATHER THAN TWO SPELLINGS. `IntrospectValue::to_json` moved from the
transport (its only implementation) into `pinion-core`, because a core renderer
needed it too and a second conversion written there would have been two
projections of one enum; the transport delegates. `published_contract` splits
out "what does this resolved node declare" at its second caller.

THE ANALYSIS SHELL JOINED THE ROUTER'S SESSION, and what had blocked it was NOT
what the debt file recorded. That file named the pointer-capture flag and the
single scene tag. Measured: the cause is that the screen's root never opted in
as a drop region. `drop_point_at` prefers the nearest opted-in ancestor and
otherwise falls back to the deepest painted tag — which is `shell.canvas` or a
palette row, neither of which has an External behind it — so nothing dispatched
at all. One line fixes it, and it is also why the declaration can only be a
whole-surface clause: the point that arrives is normalised over that rectangle.
The rest followed the file's own plan: `begin_drag` answers only for a palette
latch, `drag_to_at` revives the cursor the session had frozen (the flag WAS
real, it just was not what blocked dispatch), `drop_offered` and `drop_commit`
own the preview and the placement, and `drag_release_at` clears the latch.
`preview_carry` is the one body the router's path and the screen's own cursor
path both run.

A BEHAVIOUR CHANGED, AND IT IS A CORRECTION. A carry taken off the board and
released back on the row it came from no longer adds a card. R1733 wrote that as
"an abandoned carry falls through to the latch", and it was this screen
re-deriving click-vs-drag and deciding the opposite of the framework's own rule,
under which a press that became a real drag suppresses the trailing click. The
floor sides with the framework: a source that ran a drag receives zero releases
for that gesture. The click path is untouched — a press and release that never
moved still adds, because the router synthesises the release only when the press
did not become a drag — and that is what keeps a pointer-only reference from
costing a reader the only path they have.

AND THE REFUSAL REACHES THE PERSON. `drag_release_at` speaks the standing's own
sentence, so the wire, the toast and the screen reader read one clause. Before
this round the gesture announced whatever the latch did, which is a message
about a different act.

TWO GATES CAUGHT REDS THE PREVIOUS ROUND HAD LEFT, and both are integration
tests that a `--lib` run cannot see: the drop refusal type had four sentences
and no speech drive, and the five `scene/drop_targets` response shapes were
absent from the wire census, so the method was published and its answer was not
discoverable. Repaid here.

AND THE COST THAT ROUND LEFT UNMEASURED IS MEASURED. One state-scene walk — and
it walks the STATE scene, the container of externals, not the paint tree — is
6.0 ns at one external, 76 ns at eight, 913 ns at 256, worst-case tag, release
build, 200,000 repetitions. At 120 Hz that is 0.0001 to 0.011 percent of one
core, so the extra lookup cannot be why a drag feels slow. The two walks per
admitted move became one anyway.

TESTS, all re-run after the last edit rather than quoted from mid-round.

router's drag session, and the previous round's unmeasured extra scene walk),
two of that round's gate reds repaid, and no new debt registered.
Three statements rather than carries, each a capability with no consumer YET
rather than a gap:
* Nothing reads `DropOffer::modifiers`. The floor lets a person choose between
a copy and a move with a held modifier; the plumbing is here and no target
narrows its action from it.

negotiation. Every in-tree drag has exactly one representation, and building
the negotiation now would be the dead-capability shape this workspace has
paid for before.
* Nothing PAINTS a `DropStanding`. The analysis screen uses it on the wire and
in speech; drawing the refusal's reason under the cursor while the drag is
still in flight is the obvious next consumer and is a pixel round.

is the drag still slow? This round answered the narrower question — whether the
scene lookup the previous round added is the cause — with a measurement, and the
answer is no. If it is still slow the cause is elsewhere, and the next step is
`perf record` during a drag rather than a guess.

many pushes (the tally exits 1 and the hook discards its status), and the plain
`cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` ICE on rustc 1.88.0 that the gate steps
around.

nothing in hand is a word and not a silence; over the board it names the action
and the cell; off the board `refused` is a DIFFERENT answer from `nowhere` and
carries a sentence; the release commits the cell the standing named; a refused
release places nothing and the screen SAYS why, in the same clause the wire
published; and the palette's click still adds.
THE BLAST RADIUS. Every demo that drives this screen — 28 of them, including the
new one and the two whose assertions this round corrected — run locally against
the release binary: 28 green, 0 failures.
GATES. `cargo fmt --all`, clippy with pedantic denied over all five changed
crates and all targets, the rustdoc gate, the phase-B tally selftest, and the
reference-name ratchet.
publishable_carry_forward_bullets: No carry. Two debts closed (the self-hit-testing screen's inability to join the
router's drag session, and the previous round's unmeasured extra scene walk),
two of that round's gate reds repaid, and no new debt registered.
Three statements rather than carries, each a capability with no consumer YET
rather than a gap:
* Nothing reads `DropOffer::modifiers`. The floor lets a person choose between
a copy and a move with a held modifier; the plumbing is here and no target
narrows its action from it.
* `DragPayload` carries one kind, so there is no multi-representation format
negotiation. Every in-tree drag has exactly one representation, and building
the negotiation now would be the dead-capability shape this workspace has
paid for before.
* Nothing PAINTS a `DropStanding`. The analysis screen uses it on the wire and
in speech; drawing the refusal's reason under the cursor while the drag is
still in flight is the obvious next consumer and is a pixel round.
One question for the owner, carried forward from R1723 rather than opened here:
is the drag still slow? This round answered the narrower question — whether the
scene lookup the previous round added is the cause — with a measurement, and the
answer is no. If it is still slow the cause is elsewhere, and the next step is
`perf record` during a drag rather than a guess.
External and unchanged: the two Phase B axis judgments that have been STALE for
many pushes (the tally exits 1 and the hook discards its status), and the plain
`cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` ICE on rustc 1.88.0 that the gate steps
around.

R1736.decision_summary:
A press lands where it was aimed, and the gate that watches it can see a
rectangle instead of a point.

A person reported, on their own desktop, that a node created from the palette
could not be selected — and then the sentence that decided the round:
*"sometimes the node is selected and sometimes the background behind it is, so
dragging pans."* Every gate in this tree was green.

**The previous round's recorded reproduction was not a reproduction.** Its probe
pressed nine points inside a card with press → move → move → release, which is a
DRAG: each successful press carried the card away by the delta, so the later
points landed where the card no longer was. Re-measured, the card's painted
rectangle walks 428,143 → 431,145 → 434,147 across the probe, and feeding that
drift back reproduces every row of the recorded table exactly. My own first
re-run made the same 26-of-63 for the same reason. Drag-free, with a real X
pointer and the rectangle re-read immediately before each aim: 63 of 63 at nine
points per card, 56 of 56 at the exact edge and corner pixels, and the
framework's own census reports `astray` 0. **A probe that disturbs what it
measures measures the disturbance.**

**The real defect is one pixel.** The router hands a screen a FRACTION of its
surface and the screen multiplies it back; the fraction was made by an `f32`
division, so the product lands a hair either side of the pixel it came from and
a truncating cast turns "a hair below" into the pixel before. Measured by
walking a real pointer over 600 columns and 600 rows of the running screen and
asking it where it thought the pointer was: **35 of 600 columns and 20 of 600
rows arrived one pixel left or up**, x = 434 among them while 491 and 547 in the
same sweep were exact. Counterfactual, cast reverted and rebuilt: the same 35
and 20. With the repair: **0 and 0**. On a nine-pixel pin that is an eighth of
the target, which is exactly the shape of "it works and then it doesn't".

**The gate could not convict.** `scene/pointer_target`'s eight non-centre probes
only ever RESCUED a rectangle — they ran when the centre disagreed and could
turn `Unreachable` into `Handle`. In the direction that convicts it sampled one
point, and that point was the middle: the last point a transform error moves,
and the one every automatic observer in this tree aims at. All nine are asked
now, always, and each answer is judged against the paint.

**And the framework now keeps what it drew.** `pinion_core::painted` holds every
tagged rectangle of a surface's last frame, in paint order, in that surface's own
coordinates, so a screen that hit-tests itself can resolve a press against what
it painted instead of deriving the geometry a second time. That is the structural
half: the four repairs this repository has made to this class (R1648, R1651.1,
R1662, R1700) each fixed one screen and left the structure that produced it
standing.
changes_bullets: **`pinion_core::external::pixel_of`** — the pixel a fraction of an extent names,
its own function because `layout_point` is not the only caller that will want
it and a rounding rule stated twice is a rounding rule that can differ. The
product is nudged by the largest error the `f32` can carry and then floored;
the nudge is DERIVED from the format (`f32::EPSILON` times the extent), not
chosen, so a genuinely fractional cursor still names the pixel it is inside — a
plain round-to-nearest would move a cursor at 433.6 onto pixel 434, which is the
same defect in the other direction. Asserted over the WHOLE range of five
extents rather than at a sample, because which pixels fail depends on the extent
and any list somebody picks can miss them all.
**`pinion_core::painted`** — `PaintedRegions`, `painted_regions`,
`record_painted_regions`, `forget_painted_regions`, `probe_points`. What a
surface's last frame drew: every tagged rectangle, in paint order, in the
surface's own coordinates, clipped as the renderer clipped it. `stack_at` walks
it topmost-first so a caller taking the first answer it recognises is agreeing
with what the reader sees rather than keeping a z-order of its own. An unpainted
surface answers `None` and not an empty set — the distinction `surface_size`
already draws.
**`pinion_runtime::announce_external_sizes`** records the regions on the same
pass and from the same rectangles as the sizes, so the two halves of one fact
cannot come to describe different frames; a mark belongs to the SMALLEST surface
whose rectangle contains its centre, the same attribution the pointer census
makes, so a screen nested in another does not find its host's controls in its
own stack. `record_painted_surface` is the door for the in-process sweeps, which
have no state scene to walk — without it a fixture would drive a hit test the
running window does not have.
**`scene/pointer_target`** probes all nine points always and judges each answer
against the paint: an answer naming something else is sound exactly when the
paint puts that something else AT THAT POINT. Sixth verdict `Astray`, which is a
defect and which OUTRANKS a centre that agrees — that order is the whole point.
`astray_to` publishes what the offending point resolved to, so the report names
a fact rather than a number. `defects` is now derived from `TargetVerdict::
is_defect` rather than re-listed.
**The node lab's canvas resolves from the paint.** `Hit::on_diagram_from_paint`
walks `stack_at` for the card, pin and picked-link-chrome families and maps each
tag through the same `Hit::of_tag` the census reads by name — so the drawn
rectangle and the pressed rectangle are ONE rectangle, and the overlap priority
is the paint's: the hand-written "chrome, then pins, then cards back to front"
is gone, and the accept-pin's role check went with it because the painter
already declines to draw a pin a role does not accept. Stated in the spec file's
owed ledger rather than hidden: a wire carries no tag so a press on one is still
parsed from the model, and a host frame's grip is its strip, which the paint does
not name apart from the box.
**A selection says what it is on the pointer path.** The sentence sat in the
wire's `invoke("select")` arm rather than at the act, so the reader who uses the
pointer heard nothing and the agent who uses the wire heard everything. It moved
into `apply_selection`, the one place a selection changes — which also makes "a
press that changes nothing says nothing" fall out of the early return it already
had, rather than being a second rule.
**Three lifts, from the third-consumer grep.** `Rect::holds` for the
integer-pixel predicate (this module, a screen's sweep and the region store each
had a private copy, and a hit test is where two copies disagreeing puts a press
somewhere nobody aimed); `painted::probe_points` for the nine, because the
framework's census and the screen's own sweep must not hold two definitions of
"the whole rectangle"; and `record_painted_surface` as above.
**`docs/analyzer-press-spec.json`** — four surfaces (`round_trip`,
`whole_rectangle`, `one_derivation`, `it_says_so`), a separate tracked artifact
so the specification is not written by the hand that has to satisfy it, with
`owed` entries for the three things still short.
**`tools/demos/r1736_a_press_lands_where_it_was_aimed.py`** reads every clause
back with 13 named checks, all driven by the machine's own pointer.
verification_bullets: **The counterfactual is the measurement.** The truncating cast was restored, the
binary rebuilt, and the same sweep re-run with the machine's own pointer:
| | columns arriving wrong | rows arriving wrong |
x = 434 is in the failing set and 491 and 547 are not, which is the "sometimes"
the report described, reproduced and then removed.
**Tests.** 6,006 across `pinion-core`, `pinion-rpc`, `pinion-runtime` and
`hello-node-lab`, 0 failed. Clippy clean on the four with
`--all-targets --features pinion-runtime/vello`.
**The new demo** — `r1736_a_press_lands_where_it_was_aimed.py`, 13 named checks,
every one driven by a real X pointer: 600 columns and 600 rows round-tripping
exactly; the framework's total census reporting `astray` 0 and `unreachable` 0
over 177 painted rectangles of which 62 are addressable; 63 real presses at nine
points inside seven cards, each aimed at a rectangle re-read one call earlier and
released without moving; and the selection speaking on the pointer path in the
sentence the wire uses, and staying silent when nothing changed.
**Blast radius.** The round changed the input contract, so the population is
"every demo that drives a pointer", and the wire census named the three most
affected. Run locally, all green: `r1651_the_node_lab_matches_the_reference`,
`r1700_what_is_drawn_is_what_is_pressed` (all three analysis screens, and the
gate this round rewrote), `r1714_a_window_pans_over_its_own_layout`,
`r1727_a_gesture_reads_one_fact`, `r1733_a_palette_hands_the_board_a_footprint`,
`r1735_a_drag_says_what_letting_go_would_do`. The rest is CI's.
**Gates that fired during the round rather than after it.** The wire census
refused twice — first for a verdict list in the wrong order, then for a field in
the wrong position — which is the R1735 lesson applied one round later, and both
are integration tests `--lib` cannot see. Clippy refused the first draft of the
rewritten census for a 154-line function and an item declared after statements,
which is what produced the two-pass split into `candidates_of` and `judge`.
**The three model tests that broke are the finding, not the collateral.** They
asked what a press reached on a screen that had never painted, and passed while
that question was answerable from the model alone. They now drive the state the
view reads and paint before they aim — which is what a press being a question
about what is ON SCREEN actually costs.
**Floor, built and run at 6.11.1** rather than read: a canvas item that paints
exactly the region it declares is pickable at 100% of the pixels it was drawn in
under four camera transforms including fractional zooms — 13,500 / 9,450 /
11,718 / 9,919 points, no misses. An item whose paint reaches six pixels past its
pick shape leaves 15.4% of its painted pixels resolving to nothing at zoom 100
and 84, and 30.1% at 135, while the framework holds both rectangles, hands out
the larger as the item's bounds and never compares them. A self-painting widget's
eight painted marks are named 0 times.
carry_forward_bullets: **Owner re-test — the one carry, and it is an external dependency.** The sweeps
above were taken on this host's `Xvfb` at 1440x900. The person who reported the
defect was on their own desktop, and **which pixels a truncating cast loses is a
function of the extent** — so "0 of 600 here" does not settle "0 at their window
size". The question to put to them: after this round, does "the node selection
sometimes does not take" still happen? If it does, the instrument is section A
of `tools/demos/r1736_a_press_lands_where_it_was_aimed.py`, run at that window
size. `debt-a-node-made-from-the-palette-is-reported-unselectable` stays OPEN
carrying exactly that, with its recorded diagnosis corrected.
**Two places on the node lab still derive geometry twice**, both written into
`docs/analyzer-press-spec.json`'s `one_derivation.owed` rather than left
unsaid:
* a **wire** is drawn as a stroke between two pins and the paint records no
named rectangle for it, so a press on one is still parsed from the model.
Closing it means giving a wire a painted identity, not teaching the hit test
a second geometry.
* a **host frame's grip** is the strip along its top, and the paint names the
whole box and not the strip — resolving the frame from its paint would make
every card inside it undraggable. Closing it is a change to what the screen
DRAWS, which is why it is not folded into this round.
**Nine points is still a sample of a region**, recorded as
`whole_rectangle.owed`. Every pixel is the honest question and is affordable for
one control at a time — section A does it for the coordinate round trip, where
the failures are dense — but not for every painted rectangle of every screen on
every frame. The nine are chosen to be the ones a transform error moves first.
**Two screens were not re-probed.** `hello-node-editor` has the same
self-hit-testing canvas shape and this round measured only the node lab; and
"does a pointer selection speak" was fixed on one screen, not censused across
the tree. Both are named in the two debt files this round closed.
**Not measured: whether a selection is VISIBLE.** The ring and the inspector
updating on a pointer selection is a pixel-layer question this round did not
ask, and the debt file that raised it says so.

R1737.decision_summary:
A pointer arrives where the pointer is: the framework records the arrival,
compares its own two accounts of it, and publishes the verdict.

R1736 repaired a one-pixel round trip — the router hands a self-hit-testing
screen a FRACTION of its painted rectangle, the screen multiplies it back, and a
truncating cast landed on the pixel *before* the one the pointer was over, at
some coordinates and not others. A press carries no position of its own; it acts
on the cursor the last move recorded, so the whole screen was aimed one pixel
away and a person reported it as *"sometimes the node is selected and sometimes
the background behind it is"*.

**That repair was measured on a screen that happened to publish a cursor field.**
Measured at the start of this round across the five screens here that implement a
hit test of their own: THREE publish one, in TWO incompatible spellings (an
`"x,y"` string and an `{x, y}` object), and TWO publish nothing at all. So the
check that found the defect was not runnable on two of the five, and on the other
three it went through each screen's own vocabulary. The fact was never the
screen's to volunteer.

**The router holds both accounts and was dropping one.** `capture_rel_coords`
resolves the cursor against the rectangle the paint laid out and then discarded
the ORIGIN — exactly as R1727 found it discarding the EXTENT. With both kept, the
pixel the pointer is over is `floor(cursor) − rect.origin`, arithmetic with no
fraction in it, while the pixel the surface will resolve is
`pixel_of(fraction, extent)`. Two derivations of one fact, and
`pinion_core::arrival::Landing` is the framework comparing them. So a round-trip
defect stops being something a sweep has to go looking for and becomes a verdict
published at every pointer event, for every surface, whether or not that surface
says anything about cursors.

**The gate this round wrote was defective in the way R1736 named, and its own
re-measurement is what caught it.** The first draft kept only the last arrival, so
the harness teardown claimed to check every arrival a session caused while
actually checking ONE — the same shape as `scene/pointer_target` probing nine
points where only the middle could convict. The framework counts now, and the
evidence kept is the FIRST drift rather than the last.

**And the cost of measuring killed what it measured.** Querying after every move
is a round trip plus a process per pixel, which loaded this host enough to time

R1738.decision_summary:
An application counts the sections it was judged on, and the count is part of
the verdict.

The analysis tool is one application assembled from sections. R1728 wrote its
*navigation* down as a reviewed artifact and made something fail when the build
stopped matching it; R1730 and R1731 did the same one level down, for a
*section's* surfaces. Nothing added them up.

**Measured over the running application's own wire at the start of this round**,
standing in each of its six open sections in turn: the application's own
`conformance` slot answered `specified 8, reproduced 8` from every one of them,
two sections (`keys`, `logs`) published a verdict about their own surfaces if
you already knew their tag, and four published nothing at all.

The headline is **true about the rail** — eight navigation seats, eight
reproduced. Read as a statement about the tool, which is how it reads, it was
wrong: two of six sections had been compared with anything, and the other four
were not failing a check, they were **absent from the population**. No slot,
test or report anywhere named them.

That is R1737's lesson one level up — *a gate existing and a gate's coverage
being deliberate are different claims* — and the repair is the same one: make
the framework count, and make the population derived.

**`ScreenRoster::conformance` walks the roster**, so there is one row per
destination and a section can be missing from the report only by not being in
the application. Four arms and no catch-all, because four different things are
true of a destination and each needs different work to change: a screen that
answers a written specification; a screen that answers none; a page the host
paints itself, so this roster has no screen to ask; and a destination you cannot
arrive at, carrying the destination's own reason rather than a second wording of
it.

**And `conforms()` is false while any open section is unjudged.** That is the
rule the type exists for. An application assembled from sections must not be
able to report conformance on the strength of the ones somebody happened to
write a specification for — which is precisely the reading the measurement
found, and a report that permitted it would be the same defect with a type
around it.

**Two things the demo found rather than reading.** A section's own wire is
reachable only while the journey is standing in it — this crate's central rule
working — so a client *cannot* assemble this verdict by asking the sections; it
would have to navigate the tool to find out what the tool is, changing what the
reader is looking at in order to measure it. And every part of both judged
sections' specifications is painted **inside the host** as well as in the
section's own window, with the host's own chrome surviving: 36 specified parts
compared against the paint, population taken from the report so the check
cannot look at fewer sections than the application has.

**The floor, built and run at 6.11.1 rather than read.** A paged application of
three pages, one page a part short of what it declares and one with the
specified parts in the wrong order: across the page-stack container, the tabbed
container and a plain page, **312 members were scanned and 0** name a
specification, an expectation or a divergence — there is nothing to write the
statement in. The only channel a page has for declaring what it should contain
is a compile-time per-class annotation, so three pages that built *different*
things report the *same* specification. And the row that decides it: with the
short page and the reordered page in it, the container still answers
`count() = 3`, has no member returning a verdict, a divergence or a count of
pages judged, and nothing failed and nothing was reported.
changes_bullets: **`pinion_core::conformance` gains a typed report** — `SurfaceStanding` (one named surface: what was specified, what the build reproduces, the divergences, the unreconciled and the ledger's own entries) and `DocumentReport` (all of a document's surfaces, with `specified`, `reproduced` and `reconciles` summing across them), built by the new `SpecDocument::report`. The wire form was the ONLY form, and a wire form is where a count goes to stop being a count: an application assembled from several specified sections could serialise each one and could not add two of them together.

**`SpecDocument::wire` now derives from `report`** rather than being a second walk of the same document, and `r1738_the_wire_form_is_the_report_serialised` asserts the two are equal — because the count an application publishes and the count it computes must not be able to disagree about one build.

**`WidgetView::conformance` (default `None`) and `Screen::conformance` (no default).** The asymmetry is the decision: a hook required of every one of this tree's bindings would be edits that say nothing, while a screen written directly against `Screen` is a host's own inline page — the one place where "is this section judged" is a live question somebody should have to answer out loud. `Mount<V>` forwards `V::conformance()`, so a section publishes the SAME verdict whether it runs in its own window or as a page; a section that conforms standalone and is never asked as a page would be two builds wearing one name.

**`ScreenRoster::conformance` → `pinion_screen::ApplicationConformance`.** One row per destination, walked from the roster rather than from a list a caller passes in — which is the whole point, since a section can then be missing from the report only by not being in the application. Four arms, no catch-all: `Judged`, `Unspecified`, `Inline` (the host paints this page itself, so this roster has no screen to ask) and `Closed` carrying the destination's own `Unavailable`. `Unspecified` and `Inline` are kept apart because the work that closes them differs — write the specification, versus give the host's page a `Screen`.

**Not keyed by a `Journey`, and that is stated where the rule lives.** Every accessor that hands out a *screen* is journey-keyed, because reaching a screen's behaviour is what the rule is about. A verdict on what a section is specified to contain is not behaviour, and an application that could only report on the section somebody happens to be standing in would be the defect this repairs.

**`ApplicationConformance::conforms` is false while any open section is unjudged**, so the count of judged sections is part of the verdict rather than a footnote under it. The published value carries `sections`, `judged`, `unjudged`, `closed`, `specified`, `reproduced` and `conforms` beside the rows, because a client recomputing them is a client that can disagree with the application about how much of it was judged.

**A row carries the tag its section is addressed by**, present exactly when a screen is mounted there. Without it, reaching a mounted section's own verdict means already knowing its tag — a client working from a mapping nobody published, which is the failure the report exists to end.

**The two sections that already computed a verdict now answer the hook**, and their own `conformance` slot is derived from it rather than computing it a second time. Measured consequence, worth recording: `built` in each of them now has exactly ONE caller, which is why two counterfactuals written against it came back BROKEN rather than caught (the documented "deleting a helper's only call site" class) and were rewritten against the pin and the wire.
**The shell publishes `/external/sections`.** Its existing `conformance` slot is unchanged and still answers for the rail — this is a second sentence, not a correction of the first.

**`docs/analyzer-sections-spec.json`** is a separate tracked artifact, and unlike its siblings it is a claim about THIS BUILD rather than about the behaviour reference. It therefore does not repeat the seat list — the population is the rail pin's canon, read from there — and holds only the remainder: the four sections nothing judges, each with the reason accepted, plus this round's own two. The gate asserts it EQUAL to the application's unjudged rows, so an entry must be deleted when it is paid.
verification_bullets: **10 counterfactuals, 10 caught.** Six against the framework gate (`cargo test -p pinion-screen`): walking only the open destinations, folding an inline page out of the unjudged count, conflating "no screen here" with "a screen that answers nothing", publishing a title where the section's address belongs, a mount that stops forwarding its binding's verdict, and a report that answers `specified` where `reproduced` was asked. Four against the demo itself (gate = the integration test, which rebuilds): a published verdict that ignores coverage, a paid entry left behind in the reviewed remainder, a section going unjudged with nobody writing it down, and a published population that is not the roster's.

★ Two counterfactuals came back BROKEN rather than caught and were rewritten — the documented "deleting a helper's only call site" class. What they measured on the way is worth keeping: after this round's derivation each judged section's part builder has **exactly one caller**, which is the hook, so nulling the hook makes the builder dead code rather than making the section wrong.

pinion-core **3,839** library tests, pinion-screen (**22** in its mounted-screens integration target, six of them new) and pinion-shell green — 29 test targets, 0 failed, re-run AFTER the two repairs above; `cargo fmt --all`; workspace clippy; `mnemosyne-cli validate-workspace`; `tools/test_hooks.sh`; `reference names` **0 mentions in 0 tracked files**.

**The integration test.** `tools/demos/r1738_an_application_counts_what_it_was_judged_on.py` — **23 named checks** plus the `assert_eq` comparisons, driven against the assembled application. Its D section walks each judged section IN THE SHELL and reads **36 specified parts** back out of the paint, with the population taken from the report rather than written here; the coverage line prints that number, so a run that compared nothing says so instead of passing quietly.

**Re-measured at the END of the round, which is this project's standing rule.** The report answers `sections 8, judged 2, unjudged 4, closed 2, conforms false, specified 36, reproduced 36` — and the 36 is the same 36 the demo compared against the paint, which is the two halves agreeing rather than one number quoted twice. The per-section counts quoted in the module documentation were re-read from the running application at the close: `columns 7/7, detail 11/11, header 3/3` and `columns 5/5, detail 6/6, header 4/4`.

★★★★★ **The closing audit's second question found a defect in this round's own test.** The first draft asserted `doc.wire(&built) == doc.report(&built).to_json()` — which **cannot fail**, because `wire` *is* that expression since this round made it one. A test whose two sides are the same expression would pass while the shape it is about changed underneath it, which is the class this workspace keeps finding, and it was written here **in the round that introduced the derivation**. It is rewritten to check the published form against values written out by hand, with the typed accessors checked beside them.

the verdict.

stopped matching it; R1730 and R1731 did the same one level down, for a
*section's* surfaces. Nothing added them up.

**Measured over the running application's own wire at the start of this round**,
standing in each of its six open sections in turn: the application's own
`conformance` slot answered `specified 8, reproduced 8` from every one of them,
two sections (`keys`, `logs`) published a verdict about their own surfaces if
you already knew their tag, and four published nothing at all.

The headline is **true about the rail** — eight navigation seats, eight
reproduced. Read as a statement about the tool, which is how it reads, it was
wrong: two of six sections had been compared with anything, and the other four
were not failing a check, they were **absent from the population**. No slot,
test or report anywhere named them.

That is R1737's lesson one level up — *a gate existing and a gate's coverage
being deliberate are different claims* — and the repair is the same one: make
the framework count, and make the population derived.

destination and a section can be missing from the report only by not being in
the application. Four arms and no catch-all, because four different things are
true of a destination and each needs different work to change: a screen that
answers a written specification; a screen that answers none; a page the host
paints itself, so this roster has no screen to ask; and a destination you cannot
arrive at, carrying the destination's own reason rather than a second wording of
it.

rule the type exists for. An application assembled from sections must not be
able to report conformance on the strength of the ones somebody happened to
write a specification for — which is precisely the reading the measurement
found, and a report that permitted it would be the same defect with a type
around it.

reachable only while the journey is standing in it — this crate's central rule
working — so a client *cannot* assemble this verdict by asking the sections; it
would have to navigate the tool to find out what the tool is, changing what the
reader is looking at in order to measure it. And every part of both judged

R1739.decision_summary:
A statechart says whether the event went anywhere, and the engine pin is bumped
to the revision that can answer.

The vendored engine moves 44 commits, from `a80b06d` to `7db6aeb`. Among what
those commits add is the one this round consumes: the generated engines now
count the external events they discarded because no transition in any active
state matched, and name the last one. The interpreter had answered that all
along; the generated backends had not, so a document moving to ahead-of-time
compilation lost it.

**What that closes here.** Every Tier-1 widget in this tree is a generated
statechart driven through one facade, and that facade's `send` returned `()`.
The clause requires an unmatched event to be *discarded* and says nothing about
telling anybody, so "the machine answered me" and "the machine threw it away"
were the same value — and they are not recoverable by looking, because a self
transition, a targetless internal transition and a discard all leave the
configuration alone.

The button proves it in one pair: from `idle`, a keyboard activation takes a
**targetless** transition and a pointer-up matches nothing at all. Both leave
the state reading `Idle`. `Sent::Answered` and `Sent::WentNowhere` are the first
values in this framework that separate them.

**Deliberately not `#[must_use]`.** 507 sites in this workspace drive a
statechart and nearly all are a widget acting on its own gesture, where the
answer is already known from the gesture that produced it. The value is for the
callers relaying *somebody else's* event — the wire above all — and forcing five
hundred `let _ =` would teach a reader to ignore the one thing worth reading.

**The wire is the remainder, and it is measured rather than estimated.** An
agent invoking a widget's `send` path gets the resulting state name back, which
for a discarded event is the same name it would have got for a self transition,
so the wire still cannot tell an agent that its event went nowhere. Making that
path refuse is a behaviour change across **21 demos** that drive `send`
symbolically, which is a round with its own population, not a line in this one.
changes_bullets: **The pin moves as a triple**, which is the discipline this repository already had and the tool that enforces it: the `vendor/sce` gitlink, both `rev =` entries in the workspace manifest, and `Cargo.lock`. `tools/pin_sync.py --check-dual-pin` reported the drift while only two of the three had moved — *"vendor/sce gitlink is a80b06d but Cargo.toml pins 7db6aeb"* — and reports `dual pin: SCE@7db6aeb (manifest = lock = vendor/sce)` now.

**`pinion_core::widgets::Sent`** — two arms, `Answered` and `WentNowhere`, derived from the engine's discard counter across one drive rather than from a second account of the same fact. `Sent::answered()` is the predicate; the enum is not `#[must_use]` and the reason is written on the type.
**`Widget::send` answers it**, which is the shared facade every Tier-1 widget's statechart is driven through, so every widget in the tree gains the fact at once rather than one binding at a time.

**`App::send` answers it too** — the same repair one level up, for the application machine that routes window topology. A window event the root configuration does not answer was discarded silently there as well.
**No call site had to change.** `send` returned `()` and now returns a value nobody is forced to read, so the 507 existing drives compile untouched; what changed is that a caller *can* ask.
verification_bullets: **The pin, checked by the tool rather than by eye**: `tools/pin_sync.py --check-dual-pin` → `dual pin: SCE@7db6aeb (manifest = lock = vendor/sce)`.
**The new revision compiles the whole tree**: `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` clean, then workspace clippy (`-D pedantic`) and `cargo fmt --all`.

**Tests against the bumped engine**: pinion-core **3,841** (the two new ones included), pinion-rpc **1,289**, pinion-widget-paint **900**, pinion-runtime **734**, pinion-shell — 29 test targets, 0 failed.

★ **The discriminating test, which is the whole argument for the consumption.** `r1739_a_targetless_answer_and_a_discard_leave_the_same_state` drives two fresh buttons from `idle`: one takes the targetless keyboard-activation transition, the other is sent a pointer-up no transition out of `idle` matches. It asserts the two states are **equal** first — so the test says out loud that looking cannot separate them — and only then that the verdicts differ. A fixture that could tell them apart by state would not be testing this.

**The demo proof the pin-bump rule asks for**: every demo in the tree that drives a statechart symbolically over the wire, plus this session's analyzer set — **42 demos, all green**, run against release binaries built on the new revision.
carry_forward_bullets: **The wire still cannot say it.** A widget's `send` invoke path answers with the resulting state name, which for a discarded event is the same name a self transition would produce, so an agent driving a widget symbolically gets a success that means nothing happened. Measured rather than estimated: **21 demos** drive that path, so making it refuse — or making it report the outcome beside the state — is a behaviour change with its own population and its own round.

**The bump brings capabilities this round did not consume**, listed so the next reader does not have to re-derive them from 44 commit subjects: a host can run its own `<invoke>` type and serve its own `<send>` Event I/O Processor type, a build reports the processor types it has no path for, a machine names the language its expressions evaluate in, an engine reports a macrostep it refused to finish and an `error.*` event nothing answered, and the macrostep now follows past a transition that moves nothing. Each is a consumer-forced seam when something here needs it.

`App::send`'s answer has **no consumer yet** — the window-topology machine is driven from one place and that place does not read the verdict. Recorded as an absence rather than left to look like coverage.
