R1752.decision_summary:
A frame record says WHICH FUNCTION its render number measured, and a window
says how many of each kind it averaged over.

WHAT FORCED IT. The grid debt's third item asks for a font-table handle cache
on a consumer's profile: 44.4% in `read_fonts` / `cff::dict::parse_token` /
`TableRecord::binary_search_by` / `FontRef::table_data`. That file also says,
in its own words, to do items 1 and 2 first and then MEASURE AGAIN. R1748 and
R1749 did them, so this round measured.

THE ANSWER IS THAT THE ITEM'S PREMISE IS FALSE ON THIS TREE, so it is corrected
rather than implemented. One app, 80x24, sixty frames each way: driven by ticks
the window's mean render was 8,452µs against encode 102 and build 50; driven by
screenshots, 10,344µs against encode 104 and build 54. Shaping plus vello
encode -- which is where a font-table lookup lives -- is 152µs, 1.8% of the
frame, in BOTH regimes, and `render_us` is 97.8% with `acquire_us` at 5µs so it
is not a vsync wait either. A font-table cache would be cutting inside that
1.8%. The consumer's 44.4% was true of THEIR app, at ten times the cells on a
different font stack; it is not true here, and this file now says so with the
numbers rather than carrying a figure nobody re-took.

★★★★★ THE ANSWER CAME FROM THE APP'S OWN FRAME ACCOUNTING, NOT FROM A PROFILE,
and three profiles were taken first. Each was invalid, and each for a different
reason: the first sampled the app IDLE (82.58% in one kernel address -- a
blinking cursor repaints once or twice a second); the second forced 128 frames
over `scene/screenshot` and sampled ITS OWN PROBE (`_copy_from_iter` 64.5% plus
serde 21%, with the actual render at 0.81%, because that RPC ships the pixels
as JSON); the third profiled the pixel tests, which have no RPC channel at all,
and sampled wgpu's SHADER COMPILATION (`CharSearcher::next_match`, `memchr`,
`naga::NonMaxU32::new`) because twelve short tests have no steady state. ⇒ "a
profile came out" and "that profile is about this question" are different
claims, and the second has to be argued every time.

WHAT READING `render_us` THROUGH THOSE THREE ATTEMPTS EXPOSED. The submit is an
EITHER/OR: a frame runs `capture_rgba8` or `render`, never both, and
`render_us` brackets whichever ran. So one field had been reporting two
different functions under one name, measured 22% apart, and nothing anywhere
said which. ⚠ The reading most likely to be taken was the one least
interpretable: an agent asks for screenshots, so an agent's frame timings were
capture frames.

AND THE DEMO FOUND A SECOND LAYER OF THE SAME DEFECT. Asserting on `last` FAILED:
`last` is the most recent frame RECORDED, and an idle paint lands between a
request and the read, so a client cannot use it to prove anything about its own
request. The window needed the count as well -- which is also what makes
`mean_render_us` readable at all, since a mean over a window holding both kinds
is a mean over two functions.
changes_bullets: `FrameTiming::captured` + `with_capture`, `FrameClose::captured`, the wire's
`FrameTimingsLast::captured`, and the census entry -- the discriminator reaches
the consumer, because a fact the runtime knows and the wire drops is a fact
nobody has.
`FrameTimingsSnapshot::captured_frames` and its wire and census siblings, plus
a warning on `mean_render_us` to read them together.
The module's own doc now NAMES the convention this is the fourth instance of:
a number here carries a qualifier saying what it is of (`settle_passes` with
`settled`, `gpu_us` with `gpu_timing_supported`, and now these two).
verification_bullets: `cargo test -p pinion-runtime -p pinion-shell -p pinion-rpc` green, clippy over
the three clean, fmt clean -- each judged by an rc written to a file.
Blast radius taken as WHO READS A FRAME TIMING rather than what was edited,
because the wire shape moved: all 18 demos that read `scene/frame_timings`,
zero failures.
A new demo drives both regimes on one window and reads the flag back over RPC:
`ticked mean_render=7453us captured_frames=0 | shot mean_render=9490us
captured_frames=11`.
Counterfactuals 3/3 CAUGHT -- after a first run scored 2/3, and the PASSED one
was the finding: NOTHING IN `cargo test` ASSERTED `captured_frames`. Only the
demo watched it, and a demo is not in the gate a counterfactual runs, so an
inverted count would have shipped. Two tests now pin it, with the capturing
frame deliberately in the MIDDLE of the window -- a fold taking either end
would still be right about a one-element window and wrong there, and an
inverted fold answers 2.
The wire test gives its two frames the SAME duration on purpose: a fixture
where the capturing frame were also the slower one would pass while testing
nothing, because a reader could have told them apart by the number.
carry_forward_bullets: `render_us` still holds a readback whole rather than splitting it. Splitting
needs the backend to time its own internals, which is exactly what `acquire_us`
needed and got in R1361.1; this round adds the DISCRIMINATOR, not the
subtraction, and says so at the field. The same measurement shows why that is
enough for now: the ordinary render is 97.8% of a frame with no capture at all,
so the flag corrects a reading rather than explaining the cost away.
WHAT THE 97.8% IS remains unexplained and is now the grid debt's live question,
in place of the font-table item this round retired. It is CPU time recording
and submitting, with the vsync block already split out at 5µs and the GPU's own
clock at 543µs -- so it is neither waiting nor the GPU.
This tree has no uncontaminated steady-state paint workload: the demo idles,
the screenshot RPC ships pixels as JSON, and the pixel tests are boot-dominated.
Three profiles, three different structural blockers. Recorded here rather than
as a new debt file because the frame accounting answers the question the
profile was for -- but a round that needs a PROFILE rather than a count will
meet all three again.

R1753.decision_summary:
A list drags. `ScrollNode::with_content_drag(ContentDrag::Grab)` makes a
primary-button press that strays past the framework's click-vs-drag threshold
pan the region it started in, and the row it landed on keeps the tap.

WHAT FORCED IT. A consumer's window is 430x932 — phone-shaped. Eighteen rows,
nine on screen, and every row is also a tap target. Measured there: a
press-and-drag moved the offset by 0 px and opened the pressed row instead.
The owner's words, verbatim: "if it is a list, shouldn't it drag?"

★★★★★ THE REPORT'S DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG IN THE DIRECTION THAT MATTERS, and
correcting it is most of this round's value. It grepped
`crates/pinion-core/src/widgets/scroll.rs`, found no function named `pan` /
`drag` / `pointer` / `fling`, and concluded the machinery was absent. The
machinery is in `crates/pinion-runtime/src/input.rs`, and it already included a
LEFT-BUTTON pan: `left_pan_down` / `left_pan_up` / `left_pan_in_flight` (R882),
with press-time pinned targets, the `DragLatch` dead zone, the sub-pixel
remainder carry, and the swallowed-press pairing. The real gap was one line in
`core_shell.rs` — `if self.held_keys.space()` — so the primary pan was armed
ONLY by a keyboard chord, which is the design tool's hand-tool dialect and not
the dialect a finger speaks. ⇒ AN ABSENCE MEASURED IN ONE FILE IS NOT AN
ABSENCE. That is R1751's own lesson, arriving from a consumer this time
instead of from a vendor bump.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY NEW IS AN ESCALATION, NOT A GESTURE. The chord dialect
SWALLOWS the press — no `PointerDown`, no focus — because it is armed before
the press, so nothing else can have a claim on it. A list needs the opposite,
and the order is the whole design: the press reaches the row, so a tap still
opens a card; only on the threshold crossing does the region take the pointer
over, cancel the widget's press so it is not left latched under a gesture no
longer aimed at it, and DROP the press record, so the release resolves in the
pan channel and `pointer_up` never runs at all. That is strictly stronger than
the R794 trailing-click suppression it replaces here — no activation, no caret,
no auto-repeat tick can survive the pan. And `pan_down`'s own exclusivity guard
REFUSED to open a pan while `press_gestures` held the pointer, which is
precisely what had made the handover impossible.

A PRESS ON BARE CONTENT ARMS AT PRESS TIME instead, because there is no widget
to be ambiguous with. The gap doc asked for "a press that started inside the
scroll container", and a press on the padding between rows dispatches no
`PointerDown` at all, opens no capture and arms no drag source — so the
container may have it at once, which is exactly `pan_down`'s reasoning for the
middle button. It opens in the DEAD ZONE, so a press-release in place on empty
background is still a click that moved nothing.

THE WALK CLIMBS. `Scene::content_drag_target_at` is NOT `scroll_target_at` plus
a filter on the answer: a region that declines content drags is TRANSPARENT to
the gesture, so an ancestor that takes them still gets the pan — the W3C scroll
chain — while testing only the deepest node answers `None` for exactly the
nested arrangement that strands a finger on a touch surface. Both walks share
one descent, lifted rather than copied, so the region a pan pins and the region
a wheel resolves cannot come to mean different things.

DEFAULT IS `Off`, opposite to `AutoScroll`, and the asymmetry is the argument
rather than an inconsistency: auto-scroll EXTENDS a gesture the user is already
making, while a content drag CLAIMS one, taking the pointer away from the
widget under it. Defaulting that on would silently convert every rubber band,
cell sweep and marquee in the tree into a pan.

★ THE HANDOVER IS AN EDGE, NOT A LEVEL. `track_press_drag` now reports whether
THIS call latched the press, because gating on the level would re-walk the paint
tree looking for a content-drag region on every move of every drag in the tree
— and the answer is a property of the press POINT, which does not move, so
asking again could not change it. The cancel COUNT is the only observable that
separates the two: a level gate still produces a correct-looking scroll offset,
so a test that checked the offset alone would pass on it.

⚠ TWO OF THE ROUND'S OWN DRIVER BUGS ARE ITS OTHER FINDING, and both are
coordinate-space. A row's snapshot rect is CONTENT-LOCAL, so reading a row
centre and clicking it as if it were a window coordinate aimed two rows away
after a 200 px scroll and opened the wrong row — which is what `scene/click
{path: ...}` (R51.200) exists to prevent. And a `Scene::Scroll` publishes
`viewport`, not `rect`, because it has two rectangles and naming either one
`rect` would make the pair ambiguous. The demo now derives only the row CHOICE
and hands that row to the harness BY PATH, so the conversion has one home, and
asserts that the opened row equals the row it chose — a cross-check between the
two conversions rather than a restatement of one.

NOT DONE, named rather than implied: there is no inertia (a separate axis — it
needs a velocity estimate, a deceleration curve and a frame tick to integrate
on, and it changes where the content comes to rest after the gesture is over),
and focus stays where the press put it, because the shell's press follow-ups
ran before the escalation and are not rewound.
changes_bullets: `pinion_core::widgets::scroll::ContentDrag` (`Off` / `Grab`) plus
`ScrollNode::content_drag` and `with_content_drag` — the declaration a region
makes about whether a press on its content may pan it.
`Scene::content_drag_target_at`, and `scroll_target_at` re-expressed over a
shared predicate walk (`scroll_target_matching`), so the region a pan pins and
the region a wheel resolves are one descent rather than two.
`DragLatch::origin` — published, because a gesture that escalates out of a
press needs the press point rather than the point the escalation was noticed at.
`InputRouter::escalate_press_to_content_pan` plus `content_pan_scroll_at` and
`open_content_pan`: the mid-gesture handover — refuse if anything else owns the
pointer, resolve by the PRESS point, cancel the widget's press, drop the press
record, then apply the delta through `advance_pan` so the first move cannot be
computed differently from every move after it.
`pointer_down` gains the bare-content arm: a press that reaches no tagged
target but lands in a `Grab` region opens the pan channel immediately, in the
dead zone.
`track_press_drag` now returns the RISING EDGE of the latch, so the handover is
attempted once per gesture instead of once per move.
`examples/hello-content-drag` — 430x932, eighteen rows, every row a tap target;
the consumer's shape, with `opened` / `pressed` / `cancels` published so a tap
and a drag are different observations over the wire.
`tools/demos/hello_content_drag.py`, and the example registered in the three
ink censuses and on the `catalog` axis of the Phase B tally.
verification_bullets: `cargo test -p pinion-core -p pinion-runtime -p pinion-shell -p pinion-rpc
-p pinion-tui -p hello-content-drag` green — pinion-core 3859, and the twelve
new R1753 tests among them; workspace clippy with `--all-targets --features
pinion-runtime/vello` clean; `rustfmt --check` clean.
`tools/demos/hello_content_drag.py` PASSes over the wire: a drag starting ON A
ROW pans 0 -> 213 (the clamped maximum) while `opened` stays null and `cancels`
reaches 1; a tap opens the row it aimed at and moves the offset by 0; a drag on
BARE content pans 213 -> 93 with `cancels` unchanged.
The three assertions are a set, not a repetition: a list that always pans
passes the first and fails the second, one that never pans does the reverse,
and WITHOUT `cancels` the first passes on an app whose rows are simply dead.
The pairs in the unit tests are built the same way — the `Grab` and `Off`
fixtures differ in ONE flag and are built from one scene builder, and the
scene-walk tests assert `scroll_target_at` and `content_drag_target_at`
DISAGREE at the same point, which a fixture where they agree could not see.
`python3 tools/phase_b_tally.py --selftest` PASS; the tally reports no
UNCLASSIFIED artifact and demands no re-judgment (catalog example evidence
Ink censuses measured under the pinned font DB via `measure_ink_budgets.py
--add`: containment 0, text-smear 0, scroll-reach 0.
carry_forward_bullets: Inertia (fling) is NOT built and is not a hidden gap: it needs a velocity
estimate, a deceleration curve and a frame tick to integrate on, and it changes
where the content comes to rest after the gesture is over. `ContentDrag` is the
gesture, not the physics; nothing here forecloses inertia beside it.
Focus stays where the press put it. The shell's press follow-ups
(`click_to_focus_for_window`, `position_caret_after_press`) run BEFORE the
threshold decides, and the escalation does not rewind them. Judged acceptable
because the press genuinely happened — but it is a decision, not an oversight,
and a consumer finding it wrong should say so.
The default is `Off` tree-wide, so NO existing surface changed behaviour this
round. Flipping any of them on is a separate judgement with its own blast
radius — every rubber band, cell sweep and marquee sits on this gesture.
`pinion-gap-no-measured-offset-pin.md` — the other open gap on this same
`ScrollState`, untouched here.
The consumer-side half stays the consumer's: a widget that opens on
`PointerDown` will open a card mid-drag whatever the scroll container does with
the motion. The framework does not enforce release-activation, and the example
carries that discipline as a test rather than as advice.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY NEW IS AN ESCALATION, NOT A GESTURE. The chord dialect
SWALLOWS the press — no `PointerDown`, no focus — because it is armed before
the press, so nothing else can have a claim on it. A list needs the opposite,
and the order is the whole design: the press reaches the row, so a tap still
opens a card; only on the threshold crossing does the region take the pointer
over, cancel the widget's press so it is not left latched under a gesture no
longer aimed at it, and DROP the press record, so the release resolves in the
pan channel and `pointer_up` never runs at all. That is strictly stronger than
the R794 trailing-click suppression it replaces here — no activation, no caret,
no auto-repeat tick can survive the pan. And `pan_down`'s own exclusivity guard
REFUSED to open a pan while `press_gestures` held the pointer, which is
precisely what had made the handover impossible.

A PRESS ON BARE CONTENT ARMS AT PRESS TIME instead, because there is no widget
to be ambiguous with. The gap doc asked for "a press that started inside the
scroll container", and a press on the padding between rows dispatches no
`PointerDown` at all, opens no capture and arms no drag source — so the
container may have it at once, which is exactly `pan_down`'s reasoning for the
middle button. It opens in the DEAD ZONE, so a press-release in place on empty
background is still a click that moved nothing.

THE WALK CLIMBS. `Scene::content_drag_target_at` is NOT `scroll_target_at` plus
a filter on the answer: a region that declines content drags is TRANSPARENT to
the gesture, so an ancestor that takes them still gets the pan — the W3C scroll
chain — while testing only the deepest node answers `None` for exactly the
nested arrangement that strands a finger on a touch surface. Both walks share
one descent, lifted rather than copied, so the region a pan pins and the region
a wheel resolves cannot come to mean different things.

DEFAULT IS `Off`, opposite to `AutoScroll`, and the asymmetry is the argument
rather than an inconsistency: auto-scroll EXTENDS a gesture the user is already
making, while a content drag CLAIMS one, taking the pointer away from the
widget under it. Defaulting that on would silently convert every rubber band,
cell sweep and marquee in the tree into a pan.

★ THE HANDOVER IS AN EDGE, NOT A LEVEL. `track_press_drag` now reports whether
THIS call latched the press, because gating on the level would re-walk the paint
tree looking for a content-drag region on every move of every drag in the tree
— and the answer is a property of the press POINT, which does not move, so
asking again could not change it. The cancel COUNT is the only observable that
separates the two: a level gate still produces a correct-looking scroll offset,
so a test that checked the offset alone would pass on it.

⚠ TWO OF THE ROUND'S OWN DRIVER BUGS ARE ITS OTHER FINDING, and both are
coordinate-space. A row's snapshot rect is CONTENT-LOCAL, so reading a row
centre and clicking it as if it were a window coordinate aimed two rows away
after a 200 px scroll and opened the wrong row — which is what `scene/click
{path: ...}` (R51.200) exists to prevent. And a `Scene::Scroll` publishes
`viewport`, not `rect`, because it has two rectangles and naming either one
`rect` would make the pair ambiguous. The demo now derives only the row CHOICE
and hands that row to the harness BY PATH, so the conversion has one home, and
asserts that the opened row equals the row it chose — a cross-check between the
two conversions rather than a restatement of one.

NOT DONE, named rather than implied: there is no inertia (a separate axis — it
needs a velocity estimate, a deceleration curve and a frame tick to integrate
on, and it changes where the content comes to rest after the gesture is over),
and focus stays where the press put it, because the shell's press follow-ups
ran before the escalation and are not rewound.
publishable_changes_bullets: `pinion_core::widgets::scroll::ContentDrag` (`Off` / `Grab`) plus
`ScrollNode::content_drag` and `with_content_drag` — the declaration a region
makes about whether a press on its content may pan it.
`Scene::content_drag_target_at`, and `scroll_target_at` re-expressed over a
shared predicate walk (`scroll_target_matching`), so the region a pan pins and
the region a wheel resolves are one descent rather than two.
`DragLatch::origin` — published, because a gesture that escalates out of a
press needs the press point rather than the point the escalation was noticed at.
`InputRouter::escalate_press_to_content_pan` plus `content_pan_scroll_at` and
`open_content_pan`: the mid-gesture handover — refuse if anything else owns the
pointer, resolve by the PRESS point, cancel the widget's press, drop the press
record, then apply the delta through `advance_pan` so the first move cannot be
computed differently from every move after it.
`pointer_down` gains the bare-content arm: a press that reaches no tagged
target but lands in a `Grab` region opens the pan channel immediately, in the
dead zone.
`track_press_drag` now returns the RISING EDGE of the latch, so the handover is
attempted once per gesture instead of once per move.
`examples/hello-content-drag` — 430x932, eighteen rows, every row a tap target;
the consumer's shape, with `opened` / `pressed` / `cancels` published so a tap
and a drag are different observations over the wire.
`tools/demos/hello_content_drag.py`, and the example registered in the three
ink censuses and on the `catalog` axis of the Phase B tally.
publishable_verification_bullets: `cargo test -p pinion-core -p pinion-runtime -p pinion-shell -p pinion-rpc
-p pinion-tui -p hello-content-drag` green — pinion-core 3859, and the twelve
new R1753 tests among them; workspace clippy with `--all-targets --features
pinion-runtime/vello` clean; `rustfmt --check` clean.
`tools/demos/hello_content_drag.py` PASSes over the wire: a drag starting ON A
ROW pans 0 -> 213 (the clamped maximum) while `opened` stays null and `cancels`
reaches 1; a tap opens the row it aimed at and moves the offset by 0; a drag on
BARE content pans 213 -> 93 with `cancels` unchanged.
The three assertions are a set, not a repetition: a list that always pans
passes the first and fails the second, one that never pans does the reverse,
and WITHOUT `cancels` the first passes on an app whose rows are simply dead.
The pairs in the unit tests are built the same way — the `Grab` and `Off`
fixtures differ in ONE flag and are built from one scene builder, and the
scene-walk tests assert `scroll_target_at` and `content_drag_target_at`
DISAGREE at the same point, which a fixture where they agree could not see.
`python3 tools/phase_b_tally.py --selftest` PASS; the tally reports no
UNCLASSIFIED artifact and demands no re-judgment (catalog example evidence
Ink censuses measured under the pinned font DB via `measure_ink_budgets.py
--add`: containment 0, text-smear 0, scroll-reach 0.
publishable_carry_forward_bullets: Inertia (fling) is NOT built and is not a hidden gap: it needs a velocity
estimate, a deceleration curve and a frame tick to integrate on, and it changes
where the content comes to rest after the gesture is over. `ContentDrag` is the
gesture, not the physics; nothing here forecloses inertia beside it.
Focus stays where the press put it. The shell's press follow-ups
(`click_to_focus_for_window`, `position_caret_after_press`) run BEFORE the
threshold decides, and the escalation does not rewind them. Judged acceptable
because the press genuinely happened — but it is a decision, not an oversight,
and a consumer finding it wrong should say so.
The default is `Off` tree-wide, so NO existing surface changed behaviour this
round. Flipping any of them on is a separate judgement with its own blast
radius — every rubber band, cell sweep and marquee sits on this gesture.
`pinion-gap-no-measured-offset-pin.md` — the other open gap on this same
`ScrollState`, untouched here.
The consumer-side half stays the consumer's: a widget that opens on
`PointerDown` will open a card mid-drag whatever the scroll container does with
the motion. The framework does not enforce release-activation, and the example
carries that discipline as a test rather than as advice.

R1754.decision_summary:
A frame timing says what made it. `scene/frame_timings` now carries `adapter`
— the name, device class and backend of the GPU stack every microsecond in the
record was measured on, plus a derived `hardware` verdict — filled by the
backend after projection like `gpu_timing_supported`, and answered per window
because adapter selection is constrained by the window's surface.

WHAT FORCED IT. R1752 read `render_us`, found it was 97.8% of the frame, and
recorded that in this ledger as a fact about pinion. It was a fact about the
display that round happened to run on. Nothing in the record said so and no
client could have recovered it. ⇒ THAT SENTENCE IN THE R1752 ENTRY IS
CORRECTED HERE: read it as "on the Xvfb display R1752 measured", never as a
property of the framework. The frozen entry cannot be edited; this is where a
reader finds out.

★★★★★ THE ROUND'S OWN PLAN WAS REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT, MID-ROUND, AND THAT IS
THE MOST VALUABLE THING IN IT. The field was built on the assumption that a
virtual framebuffer forces a software rasterizer — which would have made
`device_class: cpu` the explanation for the spread. Asking the two displays
instead of reasoning about them: same machine, same app, same scene (draws
133, 150 ticks), `mean_render_us` was 10,384 us on Xvfb :97 and 997,132 us on
the real Xorg :1 — 96x — with the adapter answering IDENTICALLY both times
(NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 Laptop GPU / vulkan / discrete / hardware true), and
`gpu_us` 491 us against 1,759 us. A visible window on :1 measured the same
997,457 us, so it is not a hidden-window artifact either. The adapter is
NECESSARY — a bug report is not reproducible without it, and `cpu` is a real
state on a host with no GPU — and NOT SUFFICIENT. Every doc this round wrote
about it says so, because a qualifier believed past its evidence is the exact
failure the convention exists to prevent, and this one had already been
believed once.

WHAT THE MEASUREMENT POINTED AT INSTEAD. 133 draws record and submit in
microseconds and the GPU itself spent 1.8 ms, so 997 ms is neither. The only
other statement inside the timed span is `surface_texture.present()` — a block
on whoever consumes the swapchain, billed as work by a field documented as
"record + submit, CPU-side" and "work only, acquire excluded". This is R1361.1's
defect at the other end of the frame: that round split the ACQUIRE block out of
`render_us` and left the PRESENT block in. Registered as its own debt with the
table above, and deliberately not built here — it is a second, larger change
(trait method, forge template, phase partition, wire, census) and folding it in
would make neither reviewable. The demo asserts `present_us` is ABSENT, so the
day it lands this round's stated limit fails loudly instead of going stale.

THE VOCABULARY IS PINION'S, NOT THE BACKEND'S. `GpuDeviceClass` and
`GpuBackend` are closed enums in `pinion-runtime` beside the record, following
`PresentHealth`'s precedent one line away: a wire that echoed wgpu's enums would
change under AI clients that cannot be recompiled whenever a dependency added a
variant. Each token and each verdict is spelled by the type that owns it
(`as_str` / `is_hardware` / `draws`) rather than in the projector — this tree's
idiom at 23 sites, including the `Missed` / `Rung` pair the sibling
`present_health_of` already reads. The self-grep found that; the first draft had
spelled them in `pinion-rpc`.

THE FACT EXISTED AND NOTHING COULD READ IT. `GpuContext` held the adapter in a
private field consumed only by its own `Debug` impl — reachable by a log line
and by nothing else, while every duration pinion publishes is a measurement of
it. `adapter_info()` makes it a value, and `Debug` now derives from that
accessor so a log line and the published fact cannot disagree.

`FrameTimingsSnapshot` STOPPED BEING `Copy`, which cost seven mechanical sites
across five files. The projection takes it by reference now, which is strictly
better than what it replaces: R1537's comment already argued that a `Copy` type
memcpying ~300 bytes per read was worth a reference, and the borrow now runs the
whole way instead of stopping one hop short.
changes_bullets: `pinion-runtime`: `AdapterFacts` { name, device_class, backend } + the closed
`GpuDeviceClass` / `GpuBackend` vocabularies, each with `as_str` and its own
verdict (`is_hardware` / `draws`); `FrameTimingsSnapshot::adapter`, `None` from
the pure fold; the type is no longer `Copy`; the module doc's convention list
gains its fifth case and states that naming the convention did not make finding
this one cheap.
`pinion-gpu`: `GpuContext::adapter_info()` — the adapter was a private field
read only by `Debug`, which now derives from the accessor.
`pinion-forge`: the emitted renderer publishes `adapter_info()`, asserted by the
codegen test beside `surface_health`.
`pinion-shell`: `VelloRenderer::adapter_info() -> Option<AdapterInfo>` (on that
trait, no default, per its stated rule); `adapter_facts_of` beside
`present_health_of`; `ShellCore::set_adapter_facts` + a per-window slot, written
once at renderer creation so the paint path never clones a name; attached at the
read like `produce` / `focus` / `mirror` / `resize` / `gpu_timing_supported`.
`pinion-rpc`: `FrameTimingsAdapter` on the wire (name / device_class / backend /
hardware) + `FrameTimingsOutcome::adapter`, optional so an absent adapter is
absent rather than null-filled; `WIRE_TYPES` entry; `frame_timings` takes the
snapshot by reference; the dispatch slot is `take`n like its three owned
siblings.
Examples: `hello-timeline` and `hello-frame-profiler` read the snapshot by
reference.
verification_bullets: `cargo test -p pinion-runtime -p pinion-rpc -p pinion-shell -p pinion-gpu
-p pinion-forge` PASS; workspace clippy (pedantic, `--all-targets`, vello) and
`cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --document-private-items` PASS.
Counterfactuals 7/7 CAUGHT against the three crates' whole suites: `hardware`
reduced to either operand alone (two cases, each caught by the row the other
cannot explain); `is_hardware` inverted; the read keyed to a fixed window
instead of the asked one; `DeviceType::Cpu` collapsed onto `Other`; the `cpu`
token collapsed onto `other`; the projection dropping the adapter for hardware
devices.
Test fixtures are built so no single-operand implementation passes: the wire
test's seven rows include Cpu-on-Vulkan and Discrete-on-Noop, which disagree
about WHICH term made `hardware` false; the shell test gives three windows
IDENTICAL samples so only the qualifier can distinguish them, and a third
window with no adapter that must not inherit a neighbour's; the app-side
mapping tests assert the five classes and six backends are five and six
DISTINGUISHABLE values, so a constant answer fails rather than passes every row.
The wgpu -> pinion mapping is unit-tested rather than demo-only, on R1752's
lesson that demos are not in the counterfactual gate.
Blast radius: all 19 demos reading `scene/frame_timings` PASS on Xvfb :97,
including `r1539_wire_states_its_shape` (the census) and
`r1752_a_frame_says_which_function_it_timed`.
`tools/demos/r1754_a_frame_timing_says_what_made_it.py` PASS — reports
NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 Laptop GPU / discrete / vulkan / hardware true, checks
both tokens against pinion's closed vocabularies, re-derives `hardware` from its
two terms, and asserts the qualifier is stable across two reads while the
durations move.
Measurement behind the entry, reproducible: `RpcSubprocess("hello-textgrid")`,
150 x `scene/tick {"dt":0.05}`, read `window.mean_render_us`, switching DISPLAY
between :97 and :1. Raw: :97 render 10,384 / gpu 491 / encode 126 / acquire 6;
133 in all three.
NOT verified: what the 997 ms actually is. The attribution to `present()` is by
elimination, not by isolation — the debt note says so and makes measuring it the
first step of paying it.
Pre-existing and not this round's: `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` WITHOUT
`--document-private-items` ICEs on `hello-node-lab`. Reproduced in isolation
with `-p hello-node-lab` on cached deps; already registered, and the gate's own
flags pass.
carry_forward_bullets: `render_us` bills a blocking `present()` as work — the open residue, and the
thing that actually explains the 96x. Registered as a debt file rather than
left in this prose, because a carry paragraph is not a census (R1742's lesson).
Its first step is to MEASURE `present_us`, not to assume it: this round's
attribution is by elimination.
The 997 ms on :1 is suspiciously close to exactly one second, which smells like
a driver timeout rather than a consumer block. If it is, the debt note's
diagnosis is wrong and paying it starts by fixing the note.
The adapter is written ONCE at renderer creation. That is correct today because
the recovery ladder rebuilds the surface from the same instance and device
(`GpuContext::recover` -> `surface.rebuild(&self.instance, &self.device)`), so a
live window's adapter cannot change under it — verified this round. A future
path that re-selected an adapter would invalidate the slot silently.
The `AppShell` -> `ShellCore` plumbing line is demo-covered only; no unit test
can reach it without a real window. That is the same coverage shape
`set_gpu_timing_state` (R1537) and `present_health_of` (R1709) have. The
translation either side of it is unit-tested, which is the part with logic.
The measurements are this machine's two displays. Whether the ratio survives
another GPU or driver is unmeasured.
`FrameTimingsSnapshot` losing `Copy` is a public API break for any embedder
outside this workspace. Nothing outside it exists yet.

R1755.decision_summary:
The engine pin moves to `0ac56f1a45`, eleven commits on from `a8026fd62b`, and
NOTHING NEW IS CONSUMED — which is the finding rather than an omission.

WHAT THE ELEVEN CONTAIN, read before adopting rather than after. Two touch the
macrostep bound this tree started consuming at R1751:
`bbde787f93` lets a consumer compile out the macrostep REPORT, and
`6279c6b80c` puts the truncation log inside that same gate, which its doc had
already claimed. Neither touches the BOUND. The feature is opt-OUT, and
upstream states the reason in the manifest: a consumer who does nothing must
keep the report, because losing it silently is exactly the failure the report
exists to prevent. pinion does nothing, so pinion keeps it — and the three
R1751 assertions are the proof, not the argument: they call
`truncated_macrosteps()` and they pass under the new revision, so the accessors

R1756.decision_summary:
Pro-tool performance is re-judged 90 -> 88, and it is the project's THIRD
DOWNWARD MOVE (after R1577 and R1604) for their reason: a measurement finally
replaced an assumption, so what is new is the meter, not a worse tree.

DEMANDED BY THE TOOL, not chosen: `round-axis` evidence went 14 -> 18 (+29%,
past the band) because R1748, R1749, R1752 and R1754 each declared this axis
and none re-judged. R1744 is the precedent for the shape of this round and
also for its outcome being open — that look HELD at 90, and holding is a
legitimate result. This one does not hold.

THE MEASUREMENT: THIS AXIS'S HEADLINE INSTRUMENT MEASURES THE WRONG THING.
`FrameTiming::render_us` is documented "GPU command-buffer record + submit,
CPU-side", and the shell subtracts the acquire so that it can be called "work
only, acquire excluded". R1754 measured one app, one scene, 133 draws, on two
displays of ONE machine: `mean_render_us` 10,384 us against 997,132 us —
ninety-six-fold — while `gpu_us` was 491 us and 1,759 us and `encode_us` 126 us
and 141 us. One hundred and thirty-three draws record and submit in
microseconds, so on the second display 99.8% of that field is neither recording
nor submitting. The only other statement inside the timed span is
`surface_texture.present()`, which BLOCKS ON WHOEVER CONSUMES the swapchain.

That is R1361.1's defect at the other end of the frame. That round split the
ACQUIRE block out of `render_us` and wrote why: "a window doing 0.7ms of work
reported ~16ms of render and read exactly like a GPU-bound one". It left the
PRESENT block in. A professional profiler's first job is separating "I am slow"
from "I am waiting", and this axis has been judged for 393 rounds on an
instrument that merges them.

WHY WHAT LANDED DOES NOT OFFSET IT. Two qualifiers did land and both reached
the wire: R1752's `captured` / `captured_frames` (whether `render_us` timed a
render or a readback — an either/or, measured 22% apart) and R1754's `adapter`
(which GPU stack produced every microsecond). Both are real capability on the
axis's profiling half. But A FIELD THAT CANNOT SAY WHAT IT MEASURED IS A
SMALLER DEFECT THAN A FIELD THAT MEASURES THE WRONG THING — and the second was
found only because the first two forced someone to look at `render_us` closely
enough to ask what was inside it.

R1748 AND R1749 ARE NOT CREDITED, on R1744's own rule applied a second time.
They removed two per-cell payments from the TextGrid — a rectangle and a glyph
call for every cell — after a CONSUMER reported 4 fps at 13,779 draws. That is
the fourth and fifth instance of the shape R1744 named: a cost that no check in
this repository names, found by a person using the tool rather than by the
tree. Repayment restores credit rather than adding it (R1628), so those two
rounds hold the number up rather than push it further down. Without them the
move would have been larger.

THE REMAINDER GAINS A SEVENTH ITEM AND IT IS NOW THE LARGEST. The six from
R1558 and R1744 are all exactly where they were — present latency external,
footprint what the allocator was asked for, per-node replay absent by
construction, the profile row's address without a general reader, R1550's two
arenas unpinned, and R1744's repeated-work cost model unaudited. The seventh is
the present split, registered as its own debt rather than carried in prose.

R1757.decision_summary:
An agent can now drive a keystroke GESTURE over the wire, not just a keystroke:
`scene/key` takes a burst, and the delivery it lands in is published.

THE HANDOFF WAS ALREADY ANSWERED. sprag's PINION-PR84 asked for an arrival
timestamp on `pinion_core::event::KeyEvent`, and R1658 had delivered the
capability (`KeyArrival` = instant + batch, `KeyPress`,
`WidgetCore::apply_key_press`) three months of rounds earlier. Two of the
report's four "gap proof" items are still true and two are now false, so a
round that read only the true ones would have rebuilt what exists. R1658's own
finding also re-measured as still true: that type has exactly one construction
site in the tree, its own test, so building what was asked would have delivered
nothing to anybody.

The work was therefore R1658's residue — three open debts — and ALL THREE WERE
LARGER THAN THEIR FILES SAID.

(1) "AN AGENT CANNOT SEND A BURST" WAS HALF TRUE. The file said `scene/key`
carries one key, which it did. But `scene/type` already fans a string into one
drain, so CHARACTER bursts had a door; what had none were the NAMED keys — the
arrows a repeat window is actually spent on, and exactly what the reported
defect (a `-r` binding dragging a boundary ten cells) is made of. `scene/key`
now takes `keys: [...]`, alternative to `key` and rejected if both are given,
whose entries are a bare name (an atomic press) or `{key, state}`. The
per-entry edge is not decoration: a pan chord is `Space` down, the arrows,
`Space` up, and the whole claim of that gesture is that the three arrived
together. Parsing completes before anything is enqueued, so a malformed entry
at index five leaves the inbox untouched — a partial burst would be worse than
a rejected one, because the drain would deliver the surviving prefix as a
complete delivery.

(2) PUBLISHING THE READ AXIS EXPOSED AN INSTRUMENT THAT CONSUMED WHAT IT
MEASURED. `scene/input_state` gains a seventh axis, `key_delivery.opened`. The
question an agent has is a DISTANCE — did one request open one delivery, or
three? — because both outcomes leave a different batch open than before, so
equality separates nothing. That is why `KeyBatch::ordinal` is published
despite that type's own rule against arithmetic, and the rule still stands for
Rust consumers, who ask `arrived_with`. Then the measurement: EVERY RPC REQUEST
RAN THE DRAIN AND THE DRAIN OPENED A DELIVERY UNCONDITIONALLY, so the two
`scene/input_state` reads bracketing a burst each opened one and the difference
read three. R1658 wrote the rule as "one drain is one delivery" and the drain
implemented it literally; while the arrival was a Rust-only fact that was
invisible, and it became a defect the moment the field was published. The rule
is now "one drain THAT DISPATCHES A KEYSTROKE is one delivery", which is what
it always meant. The standing lesson: an implementation that was harmless while
unobservable must be re-read by the round that makes it observable.

(3) THE TERMINAL'S RPC DRAIN HAD NO DELIVERY BOUNDARY AT ALL, and no debt file
knew. R1658 gave the terminal LOOP its boundary and left the drain without one,
so a key injected over RPC into a TUI app inherited whichever delivery the last
TYPED key had opened — it claimed to have arrived alongside a keystroke it had
nothing to do with, and a binding asking `arrived_with` would have honoured the
pair. §2 #6 asks the two backends not to disagree about the user's input, and on
this axis they did.

(4) The fourth debt is closed as prescribed: `await_delivery` takes its `poll`
as an argument, which was the whole of what stood in the way, and all three of
its answers are asserted — including that the availability question is asked
FIRST, since it is about the moment the previous dispatch returned.

`pinion_core::event` now says out loud that nothing in it is delivered to a
binding, that a keystroke's facts belong on `KeyPress`, and that the gap cost a
consumer a wrong PR. §5.13 was read from the store and ratified this enum in
Round 5, so deleting it is a spec round and not this module's decision; the
marking is the immediate part of that debt, which stays open.
changes_bullets: `pinion-core`: `KeyBatch::ordinal()` — published for exactly one caller, the
wire, because its question is a distance and not an equality; the type's
no-arithmetic rule still holds for Rust consumers and says so. `KeyBatch`
derives `Default` (== `initial`, pinned by a test, because every fixture in
the tree builds a snapshot with `..Default::default()`).
`pinion-core`: `InputStateSnapshot::key_delivery` — the seventh axis. No
"unavailable" arm: every backend that dispatches a key opens a delivery to
dispatch it under, so a null spelling would be unreachable.
`pinion-core`: `event.rs` states that nothing in the module is delivered to a
binding, that a keystroke's facts belong on `KeyPress`, and that this cost a
consumer a wrong PR. Marking only — §5.13 ratified the enum in Round 5.
`pinion-rpc`: `scene/key` takes `keys: [...]`, alternative to `key`, entries a
bare name or `{key, state}`; parsed whole before anything is enqueued.
`parse_key_state` / `parse_key_stroke_object` / `parse_key_burst` /
`push_key_stroke`, with the single form reading through the SAME object parser
as each burst entry so the two cannot drift on what a keystroke is.
`pinion-rpc`: `DeferredInput::dispatches_key()` — the gate both drains ask.
The match is EXHAUSTIVE over all 27 variants: `#[non_exhaustive]` blocks only
an out-of-crate match, and this is the defining crate, so the compiler is the
gate rather than a grep.
`pinion-rpc`: `scene/input_state` emits `key_delivery.opened`;
`INPUT_STATE_AXES` 6 -> 7.
`pinion-shell` / `pinion-tui`: each drain opens a delivery only when the drain
dispatches a keystroke. The terminal drain had opened NONE before, so an
injected key inherited the last typed key's delivery.
`pinion-tui`: `await_delivery(poll, timeout)` takes its poll as an argument;
`poll_timeout` takes `wants_next_frame`'s answer rather than the core, so the
ACTIVE arm is assertable without staging a live animation.
`tools/rpc_verify.py`: `tf.keys([...])` and `tf.key_delivery_opened()`. The
docstring states that `tf.text()` cannot be a burst because it loops.
verification_bullets: `cargo test -p pinion-core -p pinion-runtime -p pinion-rpc -p pinion-shell
-p pinion-tui` PASS; workspace clippy (pedantic, `--all-targets`, vello) PASS;
`cargo doc --no-deps` PASS on those five crates; `tools/test_rpc_verify.py`
41 cases / 118 assertions PASS.
Counterfactuals 7/7 CAUGHT against those crates' whole suites: the burst
enqueuing only its first stroke; each drain's delivery gate inverted (GUI and
TUI separately, because they are separate call sites with separate copies of
the rule); the ordinal off by one (which keeps every DIFFERENCE right, so only
a test asserting the value catches it); `dispatches_key` inverted; the terminal
boundary answering `Some(carried_over)`; the emitted axis renamed.
CF-2 also reddened R1658's OWN tests, which is the evidence that this round's
gate does not contradict R1658's contract.
The end-to-end test drives a real `scene/key` request through the real
dispatcher and the real drain, then reads the axis over the wire — R1658's
counterfactual had found that every test it wrote bypassed the path the defect
was on, so both halves are asserted at once: the binding sees one gesture, and
the wire says so.
The pair of readings is built so it DISTINGUISHES: one burst advances the
delivery by exactly one, three separate requests by three, and a request that
dispatches no keystroke moves it not at all.
TWO EXISTING GATES CAUGHT THIS ROUND BEFORE ANY OF ITS OWN CHECKS DID —
R1585.1 (the window-column probe must supply every param the surface reads,
so `keys` had to be added to it) and R1627 (the emitted axes are the declared

An agent can now drive a keystroke GESTURE over the wire, not just a keystroke:
`scene/key` takes a burst, and the delivery it lands in is published.

THE HANDOFF WAS ALREADY ANSWERED. sprag's PINION-PR84 asked for an arrival
timestamp on `pinion_core::event::KeyEvent`, and R1658 had delivered the
capability (`KeyArrival` = instant + batch, `KeyPress`,
`WidgetCore::apply_key_press`) three months of rounds earlier. Two of the
report's four "gap proof" items are still true and two are now false, so a
round that read only the true ones would have rebuilt what exists. R1658's own
finding also re-measured as still true: that type has exactly one construction
site in the tree, its own test, so building what was asked would have delivered
nothing to anybody.

The work was therefore R1658's residue — three open debts — and ALL THREE WERE
LARGER THAN THEIR FILES SAID.

(1) "AN AGENT CANNOT SEND A BURST" WAS HALF TRUE. The file said `scene/key`
carries one key, which it did. But `scene/type` already fans a string into one
drain, so CHARACTER bursts had a door; what had none were the NAMED keys — the
arrows a repeat window is actually spent on, and exactly what the reported
defect (a `-r` binding dragging a boundary ten cells) is made of. `scene/key`
now takes `keys: [...]`, alternative to `key` and rejected if both are given,
whose entries are a bare name (an atomic press) or `{key, state}`. The
per-entry edge is not decoration: a pan chord is `Space` down, the arrows,
`Space` up, and the whole claim of that gesture is that the three arrived
together. Parsing completes before anything is enqueued, so a malformed entry
at index five leaves the inbox untouched — a partial burst would be worse than
a rejected one, because the drain would deliver the surviving prefix as a
complete delivery.

(2) PUBLISHING THE READ AXIS EXPOSED AN INSTRUMENT THAT CONSUMED WHAT IT
MEASURED. `scene/input_state` gains a seventh axis, `key_delivery.opened`. The
question an agent has is a DISTANCE — did one request open one delivery, or
three? — because both outcomes leave a different batch open than before, so
equality separates nothing. That is why `KeyBatch::ordinal` is published
despite that type's own rule against arithmetic, and the rule still stands for
Rust consumers, who ask `arrived_with`. Then the measurement: EVERY RPC REQUEST
RAN THE DRAIN AND THE DRAIN OPENED A DELIVERY UNCONDITIONALLY, so the two
`scene/input_state` reads bracketing a burst each opened one and the difference
read three. R1658 wrote the rule as "one drain is one delivery" and the drain
implemented it literally; while the arrival was a Rust-only fact that was
invisible, and it became a defect the moment the field was published. The rule
is now "one drain THAT DISPATCHES A KEYSTROKE is one delivery", which is what
it always meant. The standing lesson: an implementation that was harmless while
unobservable must be re-read by the round that makes it observable.

(3) THE TERMINAL'S RPC DRAIN HAD NO DELIVERY BOUNDARY AT ALL, and no debt file
knew. R1658 gave the terminal LOOP its boundary and left the drain without one,
so a key injected over RPC into a TUI app inherited whichever delivery the last
TYPED key had opened — it claimed to have arrived alongside a keystroke it had
nothing to do with, and a binding asking `arrived_with` would have honoured the
pair. §2 #6 asks the two backends not to disagree about the user's input, and on
this axis they did.

(4) The fourth debt is closed as prescribed: `await_delivery` takes its `poll`
as an argument, which was the whole of what stood in the way, and all three of
its answers are asserted — including that the availability question is asked
FIRST, since it is about the moment the previous dispatch returned.

`pinion_core::event` now says out loud that nothing in it is delivered to a
binding, that a keystroke's facts belong on `KeyPress`, and that the gap cost a
consumer a wrong PR. §5.13 was read from the store and ratified this enum in
Round 5, so deleting it is a spec round and not this module's decision; the
marking is the immediate part of that debt, which stays open.

R1758.decision_summary:
R1758 — a verdict says WHAT IT WAS READ FROM, and a screen that has not painted
cannot say it reproduced anything.

WHAT FORCED IT, measured before any of this round's code existed and re-measured
at R1747's closing sweep before that. Standing on the dashboard of the assembled
analysis tool, so that no other section had painted a frame in the session, the
application's own report said:

    packets  showing=false  reproduced=  0 of 26  away=[all six surfaces]
    lab      showing=false  reproduced=  0 of 15  away=[all three surfaces]
    keys     showing=false  reproduced= 21 of 21  away=none      <-- here
    logs     showing=false  reproduced= 15 of 15  away=none      <-- and here

Nothing was failing. Two sections answered from a frame and two from copies of
their own specification, and the report HAD NO ROOM TO SAY WHICH — so a reader
adding them up got a number that was partly about pixels. A painter drawing
nothing at all would have produced the same 21. R1742 had settled the rule
(judge from the paint; a verdict read from a screen's own tables is structurally
consistent with those tables and cannot fail for the reason judging exists) and
left it as prose in one screen's header; the two screens that predated it were
never revisited.

THE DECISION IS A QUALIFIER, which is the sixth case of the convention R1752
named — a number carries its own qualifier (`render_us`+`captured`,
`gpu_us`+`gpu_timing_supported`, `mean_render_us`+`captured_frames`, a frame
timing + its adapter). `conformance::Evidence{Paint,Declaration}` is stamped by
WHICH ENTRY POINT was taken and not by anything a screen asserts:
`SpecDocument::report` hands the screen nothing and stamps `declaration`;
`report_from_paint` fetches the surface's marks from the framework's store and
stamps `paint`.

WHY THAT IS NOT MERELY A LABEL. It is not gameable in the direction that
matters, because `report_from_paint` substitutes `Built::Away` for every surface
when the store holds no frame: a report carrying `paint` CANNOT claim
reproduction with no frame behind it. An assembled application therefore refuses
to call a `declaration` verdict conformance at all
(`ApplicationConformance::declared()`, and `conforms()` false while it is not
zero) — R1738's coverage rule one level down.

TWO SHAPES BECAME ONE, and a rule was DELETED rather than repaired. A section's
own published verdict was a bare map of surfaces: no total, no qualifier, and no
statement of WHICH parts were specified. `SurfaceStanding` now carries the canon
and `DocumentReport::to_json` publishes the whole verdict, which the host's row
nests under one key instead of spreading three of its facts flat. That deleted
R1738's `parts_of` helper outright: it existed only because a verdict said how
many parts were specified and never which, so the canon had to be fetched from
whatever the section published beside the verdict and identified by "the
sub-document holding every surface" — itself a repair, made at R1747 after a
screen's own `context` table collided with its pin's `context` surface.

RUNNING IT FOUND THE LARGEST ITEM, and it was the framework's rather than a
screen's. Paint marks were attributed to THE SMALLEST SURFACE whose rectangle
contained them, justified as matching `scene/pointer_target`. Those are two
questions that happened to share an answer: which surface a POINT is over is
about rectangles, and which surface drew a MARK is about who drew it. They come
apart exactly at a host's own box HOLDING a nested surface of the same size, so
geometry hands the host's box to the child — the key-pattern header specifies
three parts and reported the third, a box holding a text field, ABSENT while the
frame plainly drew it. Attribution is ancestry now, and it DELETED an existing
workaround: R1747 had prepended the capture viewer's query box by hand, with a
documented limitation that the bar could not then say where in itself the box
sat. Both directions geometry gets wrong are now right — an overlay a host
paints ACROSS a nested surface stays the host's, and a mark a nested surface
paints outside its own rectangle stays the child's.
changes_bullets: FRAMEWORK
`pinion_core::conformance::Evidence{Paint,Declaration}` with `wire()` /
`is_paint()`, carried by `DocumentReport` and published as the FIRST key of
its wire form. `SpecDocument::report` -> `Declaration`,
`report_from_paint` -> `Paint`; the stamp is chosen by a private
`report_with`, so it is not a parameter a caller can assert.
`SurfaceStanding` holds `canon: Vec<Part>` where it held `specified: usize`
(`specified()` is now `canon.len()`, so the count and the list cannot
disagree), and publishes `canon` per surface.
`DocumentReport::to_json` publishes the whole verdict —
`{evidence, specified, reproduced, standing, away, reconciles, surfaces}` —
where it published the surface map alone. `surfaces_json()` is the map for a
caller that wants only it.
`conformance::parts_titled` / `parts_as_read` / `titles_from` lifted: the four
lines every screen judging its own paint writes. Counted at the previous
commit, three files held them (this crate's scene-side fixture, the node lab's
judge, the capture viewer's judge with one per titling rule) and this round
would have added two more screens. `test_fixtures::surface::painted_surface`
now delegates, so a screen's own sweep and the verdict it publishes are one
rule with two entry points.
`pinion_runtime` attribution: a painted mark belongs to the NEAREST ANCESTOR
that is a registered surface, where it belonged to the smallest surface whose
rectangle contained it. Two new framework tests pin both halves (a host's box
holding a nested surface is the host's mark; what the nested surface drew
inside itself is the child's).
`pinion_screen::ApplicationConformance::declared()`, published beside
`judged`; `conforms()` false while it is not zero; each row's verdict nested
under `conformance` instead of three flat keys.
SECTIONS
`examples/hello-key-patterns/src/judge.rs` and
`examples/hello-log-view/src/judge.rs` are NEW and are NOT `#[cfg(test)]`:
each reads its three surfaces out of the last painted frame and hands the
result to `report_from_paint`. Their `built` is gone from `lib.rs`.
The column headers are titled by WHAT THEY DREW (`parts_as_read`), which the
running application could not check before — R1730 asserted it only inside a
unit test of the standalone binary.
Both `painted.rs` sweeps record the frame the way a window does
(`record_painted_surfaces` over the host AND the field, which is its own
surface) and then ask `judge::conformance()`, so the standalone window, the
page mounted in the tool and the unit test are one rule with three entries.
New unit gate in each: with the paint store emptied, the wire reports
`evidence: paint`, 0 reproduced, every surface away with a reason, and does
not reconcile. Its peer in `painted.rs` asserts every surface STANDING once a
frame is recorded — both are needed, because a verdict that is always away is
as uninformative as one that is never away.
`examples/hello-packet-view/src/judge.rs`: the hand-prepended query part is
deleted, and `read`/`named` delegate to the framework's readings. Its R1747
test is restated to the corrected rule — that gate is what caught the
attribution change, which is what it said it was for.
DEMOS
New `tools/demos/r1758_a_verdict_says_what_it_was_read_from.py`, five
sections, driving the assembled tool.
`r1738` loses `parts_of` (39 lines) and reads each section's canon out of the
verdict; its standalone comparison now stands IN the section first, because a
row read from another page is about a frame that is not in the application.
`r1730`, `r1731`, `r1742`, `r1747` read the new shape and assert the
qualifier; `r1747` additionally holds the published canon against the pin it
reads off disk, key for key and in order.
verification_bullets: MEASURED, not argued. Every number below was re-taken at close, because a gate
repair is an edit and a number taken mid-round has aged.
`cargo test --workspace`: 348 targets, 13,245 tests, 0 failures.
The eight crates this round changed or consumes: 23 targets / 5,003 tests.
`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features pinion-runtime/vello`
followed by `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --features pinion-runtime/vello
--document-private-items`: clean. The doc half caught two of this round's own
links (a public doc pointing at the private `judge` module, twice, and two
redundant explicit targets).
COUNTERFACTUALS 13 of 13 CAUGHT, across five gate suites, re-run at close:
* core (4) — `report_from_paint` stamping the other qualifier; `report`
stamping this one; the canon published by title instead of by key; the
away-substitution removed so an unpainted screen is asked to build anyway.
* screen (2) — `conforms()` ignoring how a verdict was reached; `declared()`
counting the wrong half.
* runtime (2) — attribution taking the outermost surface instead of the
nearest; a surface's own node dropped from the host that drew it (the
pre-R1758 behaviour).
* key-patterns (3) — the painter drawing one column fewer than the
specification fixes; the header's parts titled from another surface's
table; the two lower surfaces reading each other's stems.
* log-view (2) — the same painter break on the second section; the section
judging a surface nothing paints.
★ Two cases came back BROKEN first and both causes are already in the
driver's own docstring — the replaced text was the last user of a constant,
and of an import. Repaired by SWAPPING rather than replacing, so every name
stays used and each case is still exactly one lie.
BLAST RADIUS: the 61 demos that touch the analyzer sections, the conformance
wire, or the paint store whose attribution changed. 61 of 61 pass. One
(`r1684`) failed once under concurrent load with `wgpu device request failed:
Parent device is lost` and passed on its own — an infrastructure loss, named
rather than folded into the count.
The new demo drives the assembled tool through five sections and is the
round's claim end to end.
`python3 tools/phase_b_tally.py --selftest` PASS;
`python3 tools/changelog_rounds.py --check` clean.
FLOOR, measured by building a probe against the reference toolkit 6.11.1 and
running it (the probe is not tracked):
768 members scanned across the page stack, the tabbed container, the table
view, a plain page and two leaf widgets. 0 name a verdict, a specification,
evidence, a divergence or a canon.
The structural answer — which parts does this page have — is IDENTICAL for a
page on screen and a page never shown, so a conformance check written there
passes unchanged for a page nobody opened.
0 members mentioning paint return anything at all; `grab()` hands back pixels
with no structure and renders a never-shown page ON DEMAND, so not even the
pixels distinguish it.
⚠ The honest half is the sharper one: the toolkit CAN tell that a page is not
visible. What it cannot do is connect that to a judgment — and that is
precisely the shape the defect had here. This application already published
`showing` per row, and the two table-answering sections published `21 of 21`
beside `showing: false` without contradiction.
carry_forward_bullets: OPEN, and each is a `debt-*` file rather than a sentence here — R1742's rule
that a carry clause is not a census.
`debt-a-verdict-qualifier-says-what-was-handed-not-what-was-read` (NEW). What
`Evidence` claims is what the FRAMEWORK HANDED the screen, not what the screen
read. A screen may call `report_from_paint` and ignore the regions it is
given, and the stamp would still say `paint`. One direction is closed by
construction — a `paint` verdict cannot claim reproduction with no frame,

thing a round runs by hand and not a standing gate. That is stated in

`debt-two-judged-sections-answer-from-the-model-not-the-paint` is CLOSED, and
its closure records what it could not see: the prescription it carried was
right and INCOMPLETE, because a layer below it — the framework's mark
attribution — was the reason the prescription's first step failed. A debt
file's "how to start" section describes what that debt could see.
The `nested_under` unification that debt asked for is no longer needed and is
recorded as such rather than silently dropped: R1738's gate reads the canon
out of the verdict now, so the shape a section publishes its specification in

nothing depends on it.
`docs/analyzer-sections-spec.json` still owes two, unchanged by this round:

The round number: another session held R1757 in a worktree, uncommitted, with

round moved 85 occurrences from R1757 to R1758 mid-flight. A round number is

The worktree tool grows the half it was missing: a way BACK, and a round
number that is claimed rather than derived.

WHAT WAS WRONG. `tools/worktree.sh` had `add` / `list` / `remove`, which is to
say the front half of a round had a tool and THE HANDOFF BETWEEN THE HALVES HAD
NONE. R1757 landed by hand and every step of it is the argument for this round:
the patch was exported, `git apply` was tried, then a `cp` loop, and the three
questions that make any of that legitimate — do the two trees agree on HEAD,
does my file set collide with what the main tree already holds uncommitted, did
the worktree touch a main-tree-only path — were answered by hand, with
`comm -12` and eyes. Two of those three protect work that is NOT MINE. A check
made by hand is a check that will one day not be made, and the day it is not
made the loss is silent: a `cp` over another session's uncommitted file leaves
no diff to review and nothing to recover from.

`land` asks all three and REFUSES. It never merges, never commits, never
stages; it copies, verifies the bytes arrived with `cmp`, and prints the exact
`git add` line for what it moved. The round still closes in the main tree,
because that is where the ledger lives and the ledger is why closure is serial
in the first place.

IT REFUSES WHAT IT CANNOT EXPRESS, by name. A delete, a rename, a submodule pin
move, and the two ledger paths each get their own verdict rather than a guess.
A delete could have been replayed with `rm` and a rename with two more copies —
both are destructive actions derived from a two-character status parse, and
this file's own history says what that is worth: the first
`classify_submodule_status` guessed and printed "verified" on a fatal git error.

ROUND NUMBERS ARE NOW CLAIMED. `git log` cannot see a round that has not
committed, so two sessions starting the same afternoon derive the same next
number. Measured 2026-08-21: R1757 and R1758 were both begun as "R1757", and
the collision surfaced only because one session happened to read the other's
memory file — after which 85 sites were renumbered. `add` claims the next
number past both git's newest AND every live claim, into the state directory it
already keeps; `list` shows every claim. Two `add`s in a row now yield R1759 and
R1760, which is the property the collision lacked.

THE REMOTE BUILD LANE IS UNREACHABLE FROM A WORKTREE, and that is NOT fixed
here. `bx` resolves its repo root from the current directory and has no
override, so with the shell pinned to the main tree it rsyncs the MAIN tree to a
build host and then runs the worktree's `--manifest-path` against a directory
that is not there (measured: exit 101 in 17s, and the "trees agree" line is true
about the wrong tree). R1757 therefore ran all eighteen of its builds with
`--local` while pc2 held 21 free cores of 32 and this host was 21GB into swap.
The fix belongs in `~/.claude/remote-build`, which is its own repository and
machine-wide across 51 projects, so from here it is a handoff
(`docs/handoff-bx-root-flag.md`) plus the pinion-side half: `add` now prints a
paste-ready `wtb` function, and says in the same breath that it forces local
execution and is a stopgap.

WRITING THAT HANDOFF BROKE THE TARGET REPOSITORY FOR A MINUTE, which is the
round's sharpest lesson and is recorded rather than tidied away. The first draft
was written INTO `~/.claude/remote-build`, on the sprag precedent that a handoff

sides disagree forever and every gate that sends that repository refuses. It had
already cost four days of red tests on a `bin/bx.bak-*`. The file was removed and
the repository restored; the handoff lives in pinion, where the requirement
originates.

R1760.decision_summary:
R1757's published counter free-ran on the clock, CI caught it, and the repair
is that a delivery's NUMBER is claimed by a keystroke rather than handed out at
the door.

WHAT WAS BROKEN. R1757 published `key_delivery.opened` on
`scene/input_state` and told agents to read it either side of a burst, the
difference being how many deliveries the request opened. That reading was FALSE
in a live windowed app. `AppShell::new_events` opens a delivery on EVERY winit
iteration, so the counter advanced on nothing but time: the difference an agent
measured was "my burst, plus however many idle iterations happened while I
waited". Two demos that assert `scene/input_state` is side-effect-free — it is

R1761.decision_summary:
R1761 — a page the host paints itself answers for itself, and the route that had
been written down for twenty-three rounds would not have worked.

WHAT FORCED IT. R1738 counted the sections of the assembled analysis tool that
had been judged against a written specification, found four of six unjudged, and
recorded the closing move for the two `inline` ones in the framework's own type:
"the host paints this page itself, so there is no screen to ask; closing it means
giving that page a `Screen` of its own, which is what the trait being public is
for". `docs/analyzer-sections-spec.json` repeated it. R1742 and R1747 closed the
two `unspecified` entries. The two `inline` entries did not move for twenty-three
rounds, and the reason recorded beside them was cost: "a refactor of a 16.9k-line
binding".

THE INSTRUCTION WAS WRONG, AND MEASURING IT IS THE ROUND. Asked over the wire,
standing on the dashboard, where this section's surfaces actually are:

    shell.canvas    1096x802 at (52, 98)     <- the page region a screen is given
    shell.subbar    1096x46  at (52, 52)     <- that section's layout bar, ABOVE
    shell.palette    292x848 at (1148, 52)   <- that section's palette, BESIDE

A host paints a section's chrome outside the page region because that is what
chrome is, and a screen judges what it paints. So the recorded route would have
produced a verdict blind to 298,032 px2 of its own section — including the
palette, which is where the reference makes its whole argument about what the
first release contains. The expensive route was also the wrong one, and nobody
had checked because the instruction was written from the type rather than from a
frame.

THE DECISION: A SCREEN AND A VERDICT ARE TWO AXES. `pinion_screen::SectionJudge`
answers one question — how much of a written specification is on the frame — and
grants nothing else: no paint, no hit test, no keys, no accessibility tree. It is
registered per destination through `ScreenRoster::judging`, which refuses a key
the roster does not hold, a key it declares closed, a second judge at one key,
and a key that already has a screen. That last refusal is the one worth having:
two things claiming to answer for one section would make a verdict depend on
which registration a lookup reached first.

The report is not `Option`, unlike `Screen::conformance`. A binding is mounted
for a hundred reasons and judging is not one of them, so a screen may honestly
answer nothing; a judge exists for no other purpose, so registering one IS the
claim that this section is compared with something. A host with nothing to
compare registers nothing and the row still reads `Inline`.

WHAT A JUDGE CANNOT WORK OUT FOR ITSELF, and why the framework tells it. A
mounted screen that is not showing has no recorded frame, so `report_from_paint`
answers away for all of it structurally. A host's inline page has no surface of
its own: its marks are the host's, and the host's store is full of whatever page
it is painting INSTEAD. A judge could notice that by finding none of its own
parts, and that is exactly the escape hatch R1742 refused one level down — "away
because I found nothing" makes every absence an excuse. So `Showing` is handed in
by the roster, taken from the `Journey` once, and it is the same value the row
beside the verdict publishes: the verdict and the label on it cannot disagree.

WHAT THE SECTION IS JUDGED AGAINST. `docs/analyzer-dashboard-spec.json` is new
and is a claim about the behaviour reference in neutral vocabulary: the layout
bar's four parts, the palette panel's heading, its three group headings, its
thirteen entries and two counts, and the four cards the board opens with. It is a
SECOND document for one screen, which is normally this project's defect, and the
seam is evidence rather than screen: `analyzer-board-spec.json` beside it holds
five surfaces two of which are not paint at all (a drop contract is a
declaration; a drop standing is what a router hands a source mid-gesture) and
three of which exist only while a placement is in flight. Those are judged by a
driven sweep that can perform a gesture; this one is judged from the frame, at
any moment, by a running application answering a host. A paint-stamped report
that quietly answered two of its surfaces from a declaration would be the defect
R1758 repaired one level up. The two documents name disjoint surfaces and a test
asserts it.

WRITING THE SPECIFICATION DOWN FOUND THREE THINGS A READER SEES AND NOTHING
COULD NAME. The layout bar draws four things and three were tagged: the placed
count was loose ink, so the only part of that bar which is not a control was the
one no specification could reach. The palette panel's own title and its one-line
hint were loose ink for the same reason. All three are addressed now, which is
what makes two of the five surfaces checkable at all — and the fourth thing was
a reproduction gap: the reference writes which release fills each palette group
into the group's own heading, and this build painted the group and dropped the
release. It is derived from the section's tier now rather than typed beside it,
so a section retiered cannot keep a heading that says otherwise.

THE TWO DIFFERENCES THIS BUILD HAS ARE DECLARED, not deleted. Its palette hint
offers a second way to place a widget (the reference offers one), and its third
group is named for a wider set than the reference's third because it holds two
widgets that act on the system under study rather than report on it. Both are
ledger entries with their reasons, which is the direction this project's rule
about the reference runs: what the reference has and this build lacks is built,
and what this build has beyond it is kept and recorded.
changes_bullets: FRAMEWORK
`pinion_screen::SectionJudge` — one method, `conformance(&self, Showing) ->
DocumentReport`, for a page a host paints itself. Not `Option`, unlike
`Screen::conformance`: registering a judge IS the claim that this section is
compared with something.
`ScreenRoster::judging(key, judge)` with four refusals — no such destination, a
closed destination, a duplicate judge, and a key that already has a screen. The
last is new in kind: two things answering for one section would make the verdict
depend on registration order.
`conformance::Showing{OnScreen,Elsewhere}`, taken from the `Journey` once and
handed to the judge, so the verdict and the `showing` label beside it are the
same value. A judge deriving it from its own missing marks would be the "away
because I found nothing" escape hatch R1742 refused.
`MountDefect` renamed `RosterDefect`: every arm was about a screen and a
destination's answer can now be a screen or a judge.
`SectionStanding::Inline` now means "the host paints this page and NOTHING
answers for it"; its `why()` sentence says so, and the arm's own closing
instructions were rewritten from the measurement rather than from the type.
SHELL
`examples/hello-analyzer-shell/src/judge.rs` is NEW and is NOT `#[cfg(test)]`:
the dashboard's verdict, read from the paint, published to the roster.
`docs/analyzer-dashboard-spec.json` is NEW — five surfaces of the dashboard
section, from the behaviour reference in neutral vocabulary, with two declared

Three parts a reader sees became addressable: `shell.subbar.count`,

`spec::section_heading` — the palette group heading now says which release fills

from the section's tier, so a retiered section cannot keep the old marker.
`spec::LAYOUT_BAR` and `spec::PALETTE_FOOT` — this screen's own names for the
parts that are values rather than labels.
PIN
`docs/analyzer-sections-spec.json` loses its `dashboard` entry (the gate asserts

fails as loudly as a section that went silent) and its header records why the

4 judged, 2 inline (`dashboard`, `settings`), 2 closed, `reproduced 0 of 77`
standing on the dashboard. Then the rectangles that refuted the recorded route:

MEASURED AFTER: `dashboard` judged, evidence `paint`, 26 of 28 parts across five

passed, 0 failed. New: two roster tests, the disjointness test, and

Counterfactuals 11/11 CAUGHT across two gates (`cargo test -p pinion-screen`,
`cargo test -p hello-analyzer-shell`): the four-way refusal, the `Showing` the
roster hands the judge, the judge lookup, the row's own `showing`, the away
condition, the release marker derived from the tier, a card titled by its
address rather than its kind, a renamed paint tag, a surface read off a
neighbour's stem, a ledger sentence that stopped describing its difference, and
the sweep's own paint recording.
BLAST: every demo that drives this shell — 34 — plus this round's own. Three old
gates refused the round's first draft and each was a finding: the backward
census refused an undeclared tag (`shell.palette.head.hint`), the voice census
refused three undecided regions, and `r1738`'s row invariant (`a tag exactly
when judged`) was a true statement about a world where only screens could be
judged.
🟥 ZERO-FLAKE: `r1742` and `r1747` each failed ONCE in a 34-demo sweep and passed
20 of 20 isolated re-runs afterwards — a read racing the render, which
`wait_until`'s own header names as the reason it exists. Root cause: a verdict
read from the paint is a fact about the last frame, `tick(dt)` moves the clock

every site in the five demos that navigate and then read a paint-derived

other three read at boot, where `boot_grace` already covers it.

reason is replaced rather than carried: the mechanism exists now, what is

address, and it has neither the page heading the reference opens with nor the

already draws would be R1747's defect on purpose — a document that cannot fail —

🟥 `debt-nothing-forgets-a-surface-that-stopped-painting` gained this round's

and the seam is EVIDENCE — a declaration and a driven gesture on one side, a
frame on the other. Nothing yet prevents a third document about the same screen
from being added under a third seam.
