R1772.decision_summary:
R1772 — THE CAPTURE VIEWER SAYS WHAT IT CAN DO, AND BY WHICH CAUSE.

The round took `debt-the-capture-viewer-has-no-operation-table` and re-measured
it first. The debt's EVIDENCE had gone stale while its headline claim stayed
true — the same shape R1747 recorded about a remainder's `why`, and the second
time this session that a debt's numbers were wrong in a way that did not change
what needed doing.

WHAT THE RE-MEASUREMENT FOUND. R1707 recorded what the missing table cost: the
filter bar drew a three-clause query, three saved chips and a `kept / total`
readout while nothing typed moved the list, there was no `filter` verb, and
there was no text input on the screen at all — with every check on that example
green. Measured at the head of this round, the `filter` verb routes and the
query is real; a later round fixed them. What is still true is the headline:
of the analysis tool's three screens, two carry an operation table and this one
does not. A screen census counts what IS drawn, so an operation a screen cannot
perform paints nothing and is invisible by construction. The table is the list
that can hold an absence, and R1677 is the measurement that says so — the first
run of the sibling screen's table found SIXTEEN of thirty operations absent
while every check on that example was green.

WHERE THE POPULATION COMES FROM. The behaviour reference, extracted rather than
invented: its capture section binds ONE named handler (the filter box) and two
per-row click closures (a message row, a decode-tree row), over three
scrollable regions. Seven operations, not thirty. That is the reference's shape
— its capture view is much smaller than its node canvas — and recording it as
seven rather than padding it is the honest reading.

★★★★★ WHAT WRITING THE TABLE FOUND, AND NOTHING ELSE WOULD HAVE.
`Operation::witness` is mandatory: a row cannot be written for an operation
whose effect nothing publishes. Three rows had no slot to name.

* THE REFERENCE OFFERS THREE SCROLLABLE REGIONS AND THIS BUILD PUBLISHED NONE
  OF THEIR OFFSETS. It held all three, hit-tested with them, and told a client
  nothing — so an agent could neither cause a scroll nor ask whether one had
  happened. `scroll` is published now, which makes those rows OBSERVABLE. That
  is a different thing from causable, and the table is what says which.
* `row_count` IS A CONSTANT. The first draft witnessed the two filter rows on
  it — an entry that could never fail. What moves is `kept_rows`. R1707
  measured a build where that number stood still whatever was typed; the number
  is right and the filter is real, and writing the witness column is what forced
  the check of which slot actually moves.

THE ASYMMETRY THE TABLE EXISTS TO EXPOSE. Every one of the seven is reachable
here by SOME cause — a measurement, not a foregone conclusion, given what the
sibling's first run found. And three of the seven are reachable ONLY BY A
PERSON: the three scrollable regions have no action on this screen. A count of
features cannot say that, and the `verb`/`gesture` pair is the whole reason it
can be said now.
changes_bullets: SCREEN — `examples/hello-packet-view`.
* `spec::OPERATIONS`, seven rows in the behaviour reference's own order —
filter the capture, clear the filter, select a message, scroll the message
list, select a decoded field, scroll the decode tree, scroll the byte pane.
`spec::OperationSpec` re-exports `pinion_core::operation::Operation`, the same
type both siblings use, so this screen needed rows rather than a lift.
* `scroll` on the wire: where each of the three panes has been scrolled to, all
three in one read because the question is *where is this screen scrolled to*
and three reads taken a frame apart answer it worse. Published because
`Operation::witness` is mandatory and those three rows had no slot to name.
* `operations` published in `spec_json`, with `absent` DERIVED rather than
stored so an operation cannot be declared missing and reachable at once —
the same shape both siblings publish, so a client walking three sections
reads one answer.
GATE — `r1772_every_declared_way_of_causing_an_operation_causes_it`.
Drives both causes of every row from a reset screen and fails on a cause that
causes nothing. Its supporting pieces are where this round's findings live:
* `invoke_for_test` reads the argument's type off the PUBLISHED SCHEMA
(`field_for(verb).ty`) instead of assuming text.
* `fresh_state_reaching` resets rather than constructs — `use_view_state` is a
hook — and reaches a row's `needs` through that operation's OWN declared
cause, so a precondition is met the way a person meets it.
* `witness_of` reads through the screen's introspection rather than off the
state, so a slot that moved internally and is not published reads as *did not
move*. That is the honest answer to *can an agent see this happen*, and it is
why the three scroll rows needed `scroll` published before they could exist.
* `scroll_somewhere_it_overflows` sweeps the sizes the screen declares it
supports, because whether a pane overflows depends on the window and this
build's capture is sixteen messages.
* Two ratchets as equalities: nothing absent, and exactly three reachable only
by a person.
DEMO — `tools/demos/r1772_the_capture_viewer_says_what_it_can_do.py`, six
sections over the wire: the table is published and `absent` is derived; nothing
the reference offers is beyond this build by both causes; ★ three of the seven
only a person can cause; each verb moves the slot its row names; the three
scroll rows are observable; and a precondition is refused with a reason rather
than silently ignored.
verification_bullets: RE-MEASURED FIRST, BEFORE ANY CODE.
* `hello-packet-view` has no `OPERATIONS`, while both siblings do — the debt's
headline claim, confirmed by reading the three `spec.rs` files.
* Its `filter` verb IS routed and `run_filter` is real — the debt's own cost
evidence, refuted. The entry point for this round was the re-measurement, not
the file's numbers.
* `pinion_core::operation::Operation` is already the framework's type and both
siblings re-export it, so this screen needed no lift — it needed rows.
* Population extracted from the behaviour reference's capture section: one named
handler, two per-row click closures, three scrollable regions.
THE GATE, AND THE FIVE THINGS IT CAUGHT WHILE BEING WRITTEN.
`r1772_every_declared_way_of_causing_an_operation_causes_it` drives BOTH causes
of every row from a reset screen, asserts the specification and the gesture
drivers name the same operations in both directions, checks a `needs` names a
real row, and holds two counts as ratchets. Every failure below was a real
disagreement rather than a typo, and each is written into the code where it was
found:
1. `select_message` declares `int` and the driver sent text — `expected a row
index`. Repaired by DERIVING the argument's type from the published schema
(`IntrospectSchema::field_for(verb).ty`), so a row cannot be written whose
argument the screen would refuse and the driver survives an action changing
type.
2. `hdr.kind` is not a field this decode holds — an invented path, refused by
the map. Replaced with `l0.link`, which the specification declares.
3. `use_view_state()` is a HOOK — one state per owner scope — so the "fresh"
state was the same one, and the field reset used `select_field(state, "")`,
which returns early for a path the map does not hold. So the field kept the
previous row's value and the gate reported a working gesture as broken. A
reset that can silently not reset is worse than none.
4. `ScrollState::scroll_by` clamps to a maximum the LAYOUT measures, so a scroll
on a screen that has never been laid out moves nothing. The drivers paint
first — which is also what a pointer scroll requires.
5. This build's capture holds SIXTEEN messages where the reference's holds
184,392, so at the size this screen opens in the panes genuinely do not
overflow. The driver now sweeps the sizes the screen already declares it
supports, making the claim *a person can scroll this pane at some size this
screen is laid out for*. If none overflowed it would fail — which is the
answer that would mean the row must not claim the gesture.
FINAL STATE.
* `cargo test -p hello-packet-view --lib`: 52 passed, 0 failed.
* Two ratchets, both equalities: `absent == 0` (every operation the reference
offers is reachable by some cause) and `agentless == 3` (the three scrollable
regions have no action, so an agent cannot cause them).
carry_forward_bullets: CARRY — one, and it is a measurement this round made rather than a task it left.
THE THREE SCROLLABLE REGIONS HAVE NO ACTION. A person scrolls them and an agent
cannot. That is now declared, counted and ratcheted (`agentless == 3`) rather
than unknown, which is the whole of what this round was for — but it is not
repaired, and repairing it is a decision about the framework rather than about
this screen: the wire has a scroll path of its own (`scene/scroll` against a
tagged pane), so the question is whether a scrollable pane should also publish a
screen-level action, or whether the framework's path is the answer and the
table's `verb` column should be able to name it. Both siblings would be affected
by that answer, so it is not something to settle inside one screen's round.
Registered rather than done.
NOT CARRY, stated so it is not mistaken for one:
* Seven rows and not thirty is the REFERENCE's shape — its capture section binds
one named handler and two per-row closures — not a shortfall in this table.
* This build's capture holds sixteen messages against the reference's 184,392.
That is a fixture size, deliberately, and the round's only dependence on it is
that the scroll drivers must sweep for a size where a pane overflows. It is
written into the driver where the next reader will meet it.
* `row_count` being a constant is correct: it answers how many messages the
capture holds. `kept_rows` is what a filter moves. The round's contribution
is that the table now names the right one.

R1773.decision_summary:
R1773 — THE RAIL THIS SCREEN DRAWS IS THE ONE THE REFERENCE STATES.

The round took `debt-the-analyzer-is-three-applications-with-three-rosters` and

R1774.decision_summary:
R1774 — EVERY SCREEN ASKS WHETHER ITS SWEEP REACHES BOTH SIDES OF EVERY CLAMP.

The round took `debt-the-clamp-gate-covers-one-screen-of-three` and began, as the
rule demands, by re-measuring it. The debt held up: `r1669_the_sweep_reaches_both_
sides_of_every_clamp` still lived in screen C's painted module alone, and the two
sibling screens carry guards of the same shape that nothing interrogates.

THE DECISION: the debt named two ways to close it and said which was premature.
Option 1 is three screens each holding the same test; option 2 lifts the record
and the assertions and leaves each screen supplying only its own observations.
R1669 chose neither because there was ONE consumer and a lift with one consumer
is a guess. There are three now, which is exactly the shape
`three-site-internal-duplication-substrate-lift` asks for, so option 2 is taken:
`pinion_core::test_fixtures::clamp::{Sides, ClampCensus}` owns the rule — the
population is not empty, every observable was reached on its clamped side, every
one was seen unclamped — and each screen owns WHICH observables it has and how to
read one off a painted frame. Screen C returned its private copy; A and B are the
second and third consumers.

★★★★★ WHAT THE ROUND ACTUALLY FOUND, and it is not the lift. The new gate went
RED SIX TIMES across the two new screens and the screen was at fault ZERO times.
Every failure was the observable I had written, and each was a distinct way for a
check to be unable to pass:

1. IT READ THE GUARD'S INPUT INSTEAD OF ITS EFFECT (screen A, `card: digest rows`).
   `form.fields().len() > 3` is the condition `take(3)` tests;
   `card_rows(..).len() < form.fields().len()` is what the guard DID. They agree
   today — and an observable that restates the condition would go on agreeing
   after the guard was deleted, which is the one thing this census exists to
   notice. The dual of an assertion that can never fail.

2. IT SWALLOWED A REFUSAL (screen A). The state that shortens a card's form runs
   after the state that fills every field with an invalid value on purpose, and
   `remove_row` commits the edit in flight before it removes anything. Every
   removal was refused and `let _ =` discarded the refusal, so a state that did
   not happen looked like one that did. Made loud, it named its own cause in one
   line — `host is worked out from the frame, not written here` — which is the
   screen correctly refusing to remove a DERIVED row. The state now removes only
   authored rows, and only until the digest fits.

3. IT NAMED A TAG NO PAINTER EMITS (screen B, the byte grid). The census reported
   the family clamped on every frame, 0 of N built, always. The function that
   produces that tag says in its own doc comment that nothing paints it: a byte
   row is an ANNOUNCEMENT composed of the eight cells and the offset beside them.
   A permanent 0-of-N is indistinguishable from a screen that truly always
   truncates. ★ The lifted vocabulary is what caught it: `never_full` is exactly
   the signature of a phantom tag, and the floor clause is what refuses an empty
   derivation — between them the three clauses catch both an observable that can
   never fail and one that can never pass.

4. IT CALLED FOUR THINGS CLAMPS THAT HAVE NO DROP-BRANCH AT ALL (screen B).
   Derived rather than excluded by name, which is screen C's own precedent: a
   family the STATE sizes can come out shorter than it asked for and is a clamp;
   a family the SPECIFICATION sizes is a fixed strip that nothing tests for fit.
   The four spec-sized families are not dropped from the gate — they get the
   assertion that IS true of them and would be false the moment such a branch
   appeared: every member built at every swept state and size, the declared floor
   included. Containment keeps them inside their strip; this keeps them from
   vanishing silently.

★★★★★ AND THEN THE NEW STATE BROKE A TEST, AND THE CAUSE WAS THE STATE'S
POSITION. Adding the state that shortens a card's form made
`r1655_a_press_anywhere_on_a_card_reaches_that_card` fail: six points of one card
reached a different card. `free_spot` searches for a clear position for a new
card and did the whole search against ONE CONSTANT, `(146, 96)` — it used that
figure both for each card already on the canvas and for the card being placed. A
card's height is a function of how many digest rows it shows, which is the very
quantity this round's census reads, so the new state changed a card's height and
the assumption broke.

★★★★★ AND I REPAIRED THE WRONG THING THREE TIMES, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH
RECORDING. Every attempt was aimed at the placement search. Attempt one measured
the cards being AVOIDED: the count did not move (6). Attempt two also measured
the card being PLACED: the count got WORSE (18). Attempt three moved the search
into drawn canvas units on a coordinate-frame hypothesis: NO CHANGE AT ALL (18),
which was itself the evidence that the hypothesis was empty — for a free-floating
card the drawn box reduces to the stored position, so attempt three was attempt
two rewritten.

THE ACTUAL CAUSE WAS THE NEW STATE'S POSITION IN THE ARRAY. `STATES` accumulates
— state n is every edit up to n — and the new state was inserted in the MIDDLE of
it. It added a second free card, and the later `with a card the palette added,
then dragged` state then dragged its card onto that one. So the mover was a DRAG,
and a card dragged onto another card is a person's prerogative, not a defect. The
repair is one line of ordering: new states go at the end, with the reason written
at the site. Nothing was wrong with the placement code at all.

★★ WHY IT TOOK FOUR STEPS: the gate reported `ANOTHER card (RSP-10), 6` and never
said WHERE. Every repair was a guess against a count. Printing the two rectangles
gave the geometry; printing every box AND THE STATE'S NAME gave the cause, in the
first line of the first run — `with a card the palette added, then dragged`. The
instrument fixes were worth more than all three repairs they adjudicated, and the
lesson is not about clamps: A GATE THAT REPORTS AN OVERLAP OWES THE READER THE
OVERLAP.

★ WHAT WAS KEPT AND WHAT WAS NOT CLAIMED. The placement search keeps its
measured form — `card_extent`/`drawn_box_of` instead of a `(146, 96)` constant —
because measuring is right even though assuming was not the bug, and
`drawn_box_of` is lifted so the search and the fit read one derivation. IT IS NOT
CLAIMED TO HAVE FIXED ANYTHING: no defect in it was ever demonstrated. And the
invariant this exposed is asserted at its true width — `free_spot` promises only
that a card IT places lands clear, so the gate adds cards and checks that, rather
than forbidding two cards to overlap, which would have made the screen refuse a
legal act to keep a test quiet.

R1775.decision_summary:
R1775 — DOES THE HOST PAINT ON TOP OF THE SCREEN IT IS SHOWING?

Nobody could ask. That is the round.

WHERE THIS CAME FROM. The assembled tool was run on a real desktop and its
reader reported four things by looking at it. One was `the node lab section is
covering another rectangle`. It was this shell's status toast, sitting on the
mounted screen's own palette — and every gate in this tree was green, because
none of them asks a question that spans the host/guest seam. Containment gates
ask whether a mark lies inside the box that OWNS it, and a floating overlay is
its own top-level box. Overlap gates compare marks of ONE screen. A host mark
over a guest mark falls between them, and could not be seen from inside either.

WHAT WAS BUILT. `pinion_screen::layering` — `host_marks_over_guest`,
`region_of`, `assert_host_clears_guest`. Two decisions in it are load-bearing:

* THE HOST IS DERIVED FROM THE SCENE, NOT FROM A NAME. A mark belongs to the
guest when the guest's node is one of its ancestors. A tag-prefix convention
would have made spelling load-bearing in a second place, which this tree has
paid for before.
* AN ANCESTOR OF THE GUEST IS NOT OVER IT. Without that clause the window root
covers every guest and the check reports nothing usable.

★★★★★ AND THE FIRST RUN REFUSED MY OWN VERSION OF THE SECOND CLAUSE, for the
reason the module exists. I identified a container by asking whether it
GEOMETRICALLY CONTAINED the page. Measured on the first run: the region a
mounted screen receives is `(52, 52, 1425, 848)` in a 1440-wide window, so
52 + 1425 = 1477 and the page hangs OUTSIDE its own root — no ancestor contains
it, and the root was reported as covering the guest. Geometry cannot answer a
question about structure, least of all here, where a region overflowing its
window is one of the defects this module helps find. Ancestry is read from the
ancestor chain the walk already carries, and the measured numbers are pinned in
a unit test named for what they show: a holder can be smaller than what it holds.
That overflow is also independent evidence for the sibling debt a reader opened
the same day — the tool ships at 1440x900 against a mounted screen's derived
minimum of 1625.

THE MEASUREMENT. Across all four mounted destinations, exactly ONE host mark
reaches a guest mark: `shell.toast`. No other painter of this host draws into
the region it gave away.

★★★★★ AND THEN THE REFERENCE OVERTURNED THE RULE I WAS ABOUT TO WRITE. The
obvious gate is *a host paints nothing inside the region it handed over*. The
reference's own toast is `position: fixed; bottom: 22px; left: 50%;
transform: translateX(-50%)` — it floats over whatever content is beneath it.
What makes that acceptable there is that it LEAVES:
`setTimeout(() => this.setState({toast: null}), 2600)`. Ours does not, which is
why the reader saw two of them stacked. So the honest rule is not *nothing
overlaps* but *what overlaps is transient*, and that CANNOT BE ASSERTED FROM ONE
FRAME. Had the reference not been opened, this round would have shipped a gate
forbidding what the thing it reproduces does.

WHY THE FIX IS NOT IN THIS ROUND, and it is an invariant rather than a
preference. A lifetime cannot accumulate inside `view`: §6.3 makes the view
function SYNC AND PURE so that `dry_run` holds, and a round that quietly
accumulated time there would be trading a binding invariant for a repair.
`Frame` carries `dt`, so the value is expressible; WHERE it accumulates is a
seam decision (`Screen::reconcile_frame` is the candidate) and belongs to the
round that makes it.

SO THE GATE IS A RATCHET: the set of host marks reaching a mounted screen is
exactly `{shell.toast}`. It fails when the set GROWS, which is new chrome drawn
into a region the host gave away, and it fails when the set shrinks without
being updated, which is the round that repairs the toast. The population is
derived from `mounted_keys()` and `tag_of()` rather than written down, because a
hand-written list goes stale on the round a screen is mounted — the round this
check most needs to run.
changes_bullets: FRAMEWORK — `pinion_screen::layering`, a new module: the question of whether a
host paints inside the region it handed to a guest.
* `host_marks_over_guest` — every host mark lying over a guest mark, each with
BOTH tags and BOTH rectangles, because a report of an overlap owes the reader
the overlap.
* `region_of` — where the guest's own node is, when it is on the frame.
* `assert_host_clears_guest` — the strict form, with population clauses first: a
frame with no guest, or a guest that drew nothing, satisfies the overlap clause
vacuously.
* Host and guest are split by the SCENE TREE, and ancestors of the guest are
excluded structurally rather than geometrically. Four unit tests, one of which
pins the measured numbers that refused the geometric form.
SHELL — `examples/hello-analyzer-shell`.
* `r1775_the_host_does_not_paint_on_the_screen_it_is_showing`, over every
mounted destination, with the population derived from `mounted_keys()` and
`tag_of()` rather than written down.
* A RATCHET on the set of host marks that reach a guest — exactly
`{shell.toast}` — with the reference's own floating toast quoted at the site as
the reason the stricter rule would be wrong.
verification_bullets: RE-MEASURED FIRST. The debt was opened hours earlier in the same session and its
own prescription was checked rather than followed — which was the right call,
because it was wrong: it said to gate on `host marks and guest marks do not
overlap`, and the reference's toast overlaps by design.
LOCAL GATES, both crates whose behaviour changed, full suites: `pinion-screen`
8 + 14 + 27 + 2 passed 0 failed; `hello-analyzer-shell` 102 passed 0 failed.
`cargo fmt --all` clean; `cargo clippy -p hello-node-lab --all-targets` clean.
WHAT THE NEW GATE CAUGHT, in order, all on its own runs:
* the geometric ancestry test, refused by the first run with the numbers that
show why (a page reaching x=1477 in a 1440-wide window);
* `--lib` against a package that has no library target, which is a fact about
this example rather than about the code;
* `pinion_core::Rect` is ambiguous between `region::Region::Rect` and
`scene::Rect` — found by the PUSH gate, which compiles the working tree.
MEASURED POPULATION: four mounted destinations, one host mark over a guest
across all of them.
carry_forward_bullets: OPEN, and named in `debt-the-host-paints-a-toast-onto-the-guests-content`:
* THE LIFETIME. The reference clears its toast after 2600ms and ours never
clears. This is the same item as `debt-three-screens-each-paint-their-own-status-
message`'s note that none of the three disappears, and it is what the reader
actually saw. Blocked on a seam decision, not on effort: §6.3 makes `view` pure
so `dry_run` holds, so time cannot accumulate there. `Screen::reconcile_frame`
is the candidate.
* THE PLACEMENT. The reference's toast is window-fixed at `bottom: 22px`,
horizontally centred. Ours is at `canvas.x + 24, win_h() - 58` with a hard-coded
width of 560 — three differences, and the x is measured against `canvas_rect()`,
which stopped being the region a destination receives when screens were mounted.
`page_rect` is the function that knows the difference and the toast does not use
it.
★ A PERSON CLOSES WHAT A PERSON REPORTED (R1736): the reader saw this on a real
desktop, and the ratchet going to zero is not the same as the boxes no longer
piling up in front of them.

R1776.decision_summary:
R1776 — WHAT THE HOST PAINTS OVER A GUEST LEAVES.

R1775 built the vocabulary for asking whether a host paints inside the region it
hands to a screen, measured that exactly one mark does — this shell's status
toast — and stopped there, because the rule it wanted to write was wrong and the
repair it wanted to make was blocked. This round writes the right rule and makes
the repair.

WHAT THE READER ACTUALLY SAW. Two status boxes stacked at the foot of a mounted
screen, over its palette and over its own hint strip: this shell's `Node Lab
section` and the guest's `selected R-01`, both permanent. The overlap was the
symptom. THE DEFECT WAS THAT NEITHER ONE EVER LEFT.

THE REFERENCE IS WHERE THE RULE COMES FROM, and it refuses the obvious one. Its
toast is `position: fixed; bottom: 22px; left: 50%; transform: translateX(-50%)`
— it floats over content by design. What makes that acceptable there is
`setTimeout(() => this.setState({toast: null}), 2600)`. So `a host paints nothing
inside the region it handed over` would forbid what the thing being reproduced
does, and the honest rule is `what overlaps is transient`.

THREE DIFFERENCES FROM THE REFERENCE, MEASURED, AND TWO ARE CLOSED HERE.
* LIFETIME: ours had none. `TOAST_SECONDS = 2.6`, the reference's own number.
* VERTICAL: ours was `win_h() - 58`; the reference is 22px from the window's
foot.
* HORIZONTAL: ours was `canvas.x + 24`; the reference is centred. The x is the
one that caused the report — `canvas_rect()` is the rectangle the DASHBOARD uses
for its canvas, and once screens were mounted that stopped being the region a
destination receives. `page_rect` is the function R1695 built to know the
difference, and the toast never used it.
* WIDTH stays a constant against a reference that sizes to content, and is left
open on purpose: this shell has no text measurement of its own, and inventing a
third approximation of one would add the duplication a later round has to
remove. Named in the carry rather than quietly shipped.

★★★★★ THE INVARIANT DECIDED THE DESIGN. A lifetime cannot accumulate in `view`:
§6.3 makes the view function sync and pure so `dry_run` holds, and a toast that
aged itself while being drawn would trade a binding invariant for a repair. The
seam already existed — `Owner::register_animation` / `tick_animations`, which
backends call once per paint with the frame's `dt` (`pinion-runtime`'s core
shell). What was missing was anything using it for a LIFETIME rather than for a
spring. So the toast's clock is a `Tickable`, registered once through
`register_animation_once` because this hook re-runs on every view pass and a
second registration would count the life down twice per frame.

AND AN EXPIRED TOAST IS ABSENT FROM THE SCENE, not painted transparently. A mark
that is drawn invisibly is still in the tree, still in the accessibility
tree, and still over the guest as far as `pinion_screen::layering` is concerned —
which is to say it would still be the thing the reader complained about.

THE GATE IS THE ONE R1775 COULD NOT WRITE. It says the toast is over the guest,
then runs the framework's own clock 200 times at 1/60s, then says nothing of the
host's reaches the guest. Both clauses are load-bearing: without the first, a
shell that painted no toast at all would pass while reproducing nothing. And the
clock is advanced in the steps a paint loop actually takes rather than in one
jump, because a lifetime that only expires when handed its whole duration at
once is not one a running application would ever reach.
changes_bullets: SHELL — `examples/hello-analyzer-shell`.
* `TOAST_SECONDS = 2.6` — the reference's own number, and `toast_life`, a signal
holding what is left of it.
* `ToastLife`, a `Tickable` registered once via `register_animation_once`, so the
paint loop counts the life down and `view` stays pure per §6.3.
* `say` restarts the life, which is what makes a second message replace a first
rather than queue behind it.
* `toast_scene` is placed against the WINDOW — centred, 22px from its foot —
instead of against `canvas_rect()`, which stopped being the region a destination
receives when screens were mounted.
* An expired toast is omitted from the scene rather than drawn invisibly.
* `r1776_the_hosts_toast_leaves_the_screen_it_is_showing` — over the guest, then
the framework's clock at 1/60s x 200, then clear.
* R1775's ratchet keeps its value and its comment now points at the transience
gate for what the repair looks like, since the toast is still over the guest on
the frame where it is alive.
verification_bullets: LOCAL GATE, the one crate whose behaviour changed, full suite and not
target-limited: `hello-analyzer-shell` 103 passed 0 failed. `cargo fmt --all`
clean.
THE NEW GATE IS NOT VACUOUS: it asserts the toast IS over the guest before the
clock runs, so a shell that stopped painting one would fail rather than pass.
TWO COMPILE REFUSALS, both mine, both fixed at the site: `pinion_core::speech`
is not where `Utterance` lives from this crate, and
`Owner::register_animation_once` is `#[must_use]`. The second is dropped
deliberately and says why at the site — the owner holds the ticker and this
shell reads the toast through `toast_life`, so a second handle would be a second
way to reach one fact. That reason is written down because this same session
lost a round to a `let _` that swallowed a refusal.
carry_forward_bullets: OPEN.

content. Blocked on this shell having no text measurement of its own; the
capture viewer's `run_width` is that screen's, and a third approximation would be
duplication rather than a repair.
* THE GUEST'S OWN STATUS MESSAGE is untouched. This round fixed the HOST's toast;

demonstrated and the other two can copy it — the seam is

* A PERSON CLOSES WHAT A PERSON REPORTED (R1736). The reader saw two boxes

★ STALE PROSE FOUND WHILE READING: `crates/pinion-core/src/animation.rs` carries

Measured: `pinion-runtime`'s core shell documents backends calling it once per

R1777.decision_summary:
R1777 — THE ENGINE PIN MOVES TEN COMMITS, AND THE EMIT DOES NOT MOVE AT ALL.

Asked for directly. What makes it worth an entry is not the bump — it is that
this tree can now ANSWER the question a bump raises, and could not two rounds
ago.

WHAT MOVED. `vendor/sce` from `ebee8c932a` to `c00722f06f`, ten commits.

WHAT THE PIN BUMP IS, and the gate said each leg out loud. This repository's
pin is a TRIPLE — the submodule gitlink, two `rev =` sites in `Cargo.toml`, and
the lock — and `pin_sync.py --check-dual-pin` refused twice before it agreed,
each time naming a different leg: first that the gitlink and the manifest
disagreed, then that the submodule was CHECKED OUT at the new rev while the
INDEX still recorded the old one. That last one is the leg a person forgets,
because the working tree looks right. Settled at `dual pin: SCE@c00722f
(manifest = lock = vendor/sce)`.

★★★★★ THE ROUND'S REAL CONTENT: THE EMIT WAS ASKED, NOT ASSUMED. Since R1766
the statechart emit is a TRACKED artifact rather than an `OUT_DIR` product, and
`committed_statechart_emit_equals_what_the_pinned_generator_produces` compares
the committed bytes against a fresh run of the newly pinned generator. It
passes: the emit is byte-identical under the new pin.

The order that made that an answer rather than a ritual: the gate was run BEFORE
any regeneration. Regenerating first would have produced a green tree and
destroyed the question — the diff would have been applied and nobody would ever
know whether there was one. R1765 could only answer this by building the crate
twice against two pins and diffing two `OUT_DIR`s by hand; R1766 made the emit
tracked precisely so a later round could ask it in one command. This is that
later round.

READING PREDICTED IT AND THE GATE PROVED IT, which is the correct division.
Measured before touching anything: `sce-build/src` — the generator — does not
appear in the ten commits at all; only `sce-build/tests/`. The Rust runtime this
framework links does appear, and its whole diff is FIVE LINES, every one of them
a `///` doc comment shortening an intra-doc link. The rest is upstream's own CI,
gate registry, mutation harness and C++/Go tests, which pinion does not consume.
So this bump is behaviourally a no-op for this tree, and the emit result is what
that predicts — but the prediction is not what makes it true.

★★ AND A DEBT THAT WAS NOT MOVED, CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. `SCE-006` — the
one R1768 opened, where an engine with atomic `<parallel>` regions publishes a
`(chain, current)` pair its own validator refuses — names two files as its
source: `helpers/configuration.rs`'s `validate` and `engine.rs`'s
`get_current_state`. THOSE ARE EXACTLY THE TWO FILES THIS BUMP TOUCHES. The
temptation to read that as "upstream fixed it" is the reason it was checked: all
five changed lines are comments, `CurrentNotAtomic` is untouched, and the debt
stands. A file moving and a rule moving are different facts.
changes_bullets: PIN — `vendor/sce` `ebee8c932a` -> `c00722f06f`, all three legs in one commit:
the submodule gitlink, both `rev =` sites in `Cargo.toml` (`sce-rust-runtime`
and `sce-build`), and `Cargo.lock`.
NOTHING ELSE CHANGED. The committed statechart emit under
`crates/pinion-core/generated/` is byte-identical under the new pin, so there is
no regeneration in this commit and no source edit anywhere in the tree.
verification_bullets: RE-MEASURED BEFORE TOUCHING ANYTHING, and every claim below is a gate's answer
rather than a reading:
* `pin_sync.py --check-dual-pin` — refused twice, each time naming a different
leg, then `dual pin: SCE@c00722f (manifest = lock = vendor/sce)`.
* THE EMIT GATE, run BEFORE any regeneration so the question could still be
asked: 4 passed 0 failed, including
`committed_statechart_emit_equals_what_the_pinned_generator_produces`. The emit
is byte-identical under the new pin and this commit contains no regeneration.
* `cargo test -p pinion-core -p pinion-runtime` — 3889 + 600 + 3 + 1 + 4 + 4 +
47 passed, 0 failed. These are the crates that consume the engine.
* THE WIRE DEMO, which is the blast-radius proof rather than a compile check:
`r1769_a_client_hands_a_configuration_back.py` PASS in 5.18s. It drives
`hello-toggle` over `scene/query` and `scene/invoke`, and separates DRIVING to a
configuration from RESUMING to it by the mark the activation edge leaves — same
statechart state, different `value`. An engine whose entry semantics moved would
fail there, and it is the reason a bump is proved by a demo and not by a build.
NOT MOVED, AND CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: `SCE-006`. Its two source files are
exactly the two this bump touches, and all five changed lines in them are `///`
doc comments — `CurrentNotAtomic` is untouched and the debt stands.
carry_forward_bullets: * `SCE-006` REMAINS OPEN and was re-checked this round rather than carried
blindly: an engine whose `<parallel>` regions are atomic publishes a
`(chain, current)` pair its own `validate` refuses. Upstream touched both files
it names, in comments only.
* THE TEN COMMITS ARE MOSTLY UPSTREAM'S OWN GATES — a gate registry, a mutation
harness, per-gate timing, a five-minute push ceiling. None of it reaches this
tree, but it is worth knowing the neighbour is working on the same problem this
session spent seven failed pushes on: what a push costs and what it is allowed
to take.
* WHAT THIS ROUND DID NOT DO: the toast lifetime lift
(`debt-three-screens-each-paint-their-own-status-message`) was the planned next
round and is displaced, not dropped. Its shape is measured and written down —
lift the LIFETIME and the HOLDER, leave the placement, three consumers, and the
capture viewer's `RefCell` is the one with no reactivity at all.

R1778.decision_summary:
R1778 — WHAT LIFTED IS THE LIFETIME AND THE HOLDER, NOT THE BOX.

A reader ran this tree's analysis tool and saw two status boxes stacked at the
foot of a mounted screen. R1776 gave the host's one the reference's 2.6 seconds.
This round does the other two, and does it by lifting rather than by repeating.

the three screens paint a status message three different ways — a floating box

R1779.decision_summary:
R1779 — THE HEAVY PAIR MOVES TO CI, AND THE MEASUREMENT THAT JUSTIFIED IT TURNS
OUT TO BE UNABLE TO JUDGE IT.

Asked for directly: move the heavy gates to CI. Done, and verifiable. What the
round is worth recording for is what trying to VERIFY it found.

WHAT MOVED. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features
pinion-runtime/vello` and `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --features
pinion-runtime/vello --document-private-items` no longer run in `pre-commit` or
`pre-push`. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` already ran both with byte-identical
flags, as consecutive steps of one job on one `target/` — which is the
arrangement the hooks' own comment demands, since rustdoc is cheap only when
clippy warmed the build. CHECKED AS A MOVE BEFORE THE REMOVAL: a gate deleted
here and absent there would have been a gate deleted.

★★★★★ THE FIRST ATTEMPT MADE IT WORSE, AND THAT IS THE ROUND'S FINDING. A fully
warmed push hook measured 237s before; after removing the pair it measured
830s. The heavy pair was not the cost — IT WAS THE THING PAYING FOR EVERYTHING
ELSE. clippy warmed one `target/` and the statechart-emit ratchet rode it for
free; its own comment said so in as many words ("near-free once clippy has
warmed the build"), and that sentence was a DEPENDENCY, not a description. With
clippy gone the ratchet compiled the whole SCE chain — `libxml`, bindgen,
`sce-build`, `pinion-forge` — by itself.

THE REPAIR IS PATH-GATING, and it is this repository's own idiom: `pre-commit`'s
clippy had always been gated on "staged files include `*.rs`". The emit can only
go stale if a chart, the committed emit, the generator's `build.rs`, the
`vendor/sce` gitlink or a manifest moved, so it runs only when the pushed range
carries one of those — derived from the same range the commit-message lint
already walks, so two gates cannot disagree about what is being published. An
ordinary push now compiles NOTHING.

★★★★★ AND THEN THE MEASUREMENT DISSOLVED. Three warm runs of the same tree in
the same state: 366s, 368s, 251s. The spread is 115s — LARGER THAN THE BIGGEST
STEP ANYONE HAS ATTRIBUTED. So the wall clock on this machine cannot hold the
effect of a single change, and the round's own earlier reading ("237 to 368, a
regression") was noise. Checked load-independently: BOTH the before and after
runs compiled nothing at all, which is the fact that actually distinguishes them
and it is not a time.

WHAT THE PROFILING FOUND ANYWAY, and none of it had ever been measured:
`tools/test_hooks.sh` is **65.83s**, the single largest step, against
documentation that called it "plain bash, runs in milliseconds" — inferred from
"plain bash", never timed. `cargo fmt --all --check` is 26.82s. The two
mnemosyne gates are 19.09s together. `du -sbL target/` is 0.52s against a
documented ~0.12s, which is fine. And `wire_only_deps.py --check` is **0.27s
warm against 119s cold — 440x** — which is why "moving this gate saves N
seconds" is not a calculation that can be made here at all.

★★ THE INSTRUMENT FAILED THREE TIMES and the failures are recorded because the
next person will reach for the same one: piping the run into a filter produced
an empty log (killed); `2>&1 | awk '{print systime(), $0}'` gave 213 lines with
ONE timestamp, because awk flushed at exit; and `stdbuf -oL` with `fflush()`
still gave a span of zero, because the buffering is in the HOOK's own output,
not in awk. A pipe cannot timestamp this. The only instrument that can is the
hook stamping its own steps, which is a change of its own and is registered
rather than smuggled in here.

WHAT THE TRADE COSTS, stated in both hooks and in `CLAUDE.md`: a clippy or
rustdoc violation now surfaces AFTER publishing. The stop-the-line gate bounds
that — it refuses to push onto a base whose last completed CI run failed — and
`cargo fmt` stays local because formatting drift is what makes a diff unreadable.
changes_bullets: HOOKS — `.githooks/pre-commit` and `.githooks/pre-push`.
* `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features pinion-runtime/vello` and
`cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --features pinion-runtime/vello
--document-private-items` no longer run in either. Both already ran in
`.github/workflows/ci.yml` with byte-identical flags, as consecutive steps of
one job on one `target/`.
* `cargo fmt --all --check` STAYS in both — cheap, and formatting drift is what
makes a diff unreadable.
* The long rationale above each was RETARGETED rather than deleted. R1214's
measurement (nothing ran rustdoc until then, which is how ~1000 broken links
accreted from ~R683 unseen) and R1695's (clippy and rustdoc are one unit,
because rustdoc is cheap only when clippy warmed the build) are both still true
and still needed — the second is a constraint CI has to keep, and the comment
now says so.
DOCS — `CLAUDE.md`'s hook section listed a `pre-commit` that no longer exists.
It now lists what each hook actually runs, carries the measurement that decided
the move, and states what the trade costs.
verification_bullets: CHECKED AS A MOVE FIRST: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs both commands with
byte-identical flags before either was removed from a hook.
GATE LIBRARIES: `tools/test_hooks.sh` rc=0 — which is what verifies the new
`tmp_paths` derivation did not break them.
THE GATED RATCHET WAS SEEN SKIPPING FOR THE RIGHT REASON: `pre-push: statechart
emit — no chart, emit, generator or pin in this push`, on a range that carries
none of them.
BOTH HOOKS PARSE (`bash -n`), and no executable `cargo clippy` / `cargo doc`
remains in either — every surviving mention is a comment.
TIMINGS, all warm unless stated: hook total 366s / 368s / 251s (spread 115s);
`test_hooks.sh` 65.83s; `cargo fmt --all --check` 26.82s; `validate-code-refs`
9.97s; `validate-workspace` 9.12s; `test_rpc_verify.py` 11.20s;
`analyzer_census --check-proofs` 3.86s; `gh run list` 1.11s; `cargo metadata`
0.52s; `du -sbL target/` 0.52s; `wire_only_deps --check` 0.27s warm and 119s
cold. Identified ~128s of a 251-368s total.
★ WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: that the hook got faster. Three warm runs disagree by
more than the largest step, so the wall clock cannot judge this change. What can
be judged is that the removed commands are gone from the hooks and present in
CI, and that an ordinary push now compiles nothing — both runs of the before/
after pair emitted zero `Compiling` lines, which is the load-independent fact.
carry_forward_bullets: OPEN — `debt-the-push-hook-has-never-been-profiled`, registered this round with
every number above. Its three demands: put a step timer IN the hook (a pipe
cannot do it, measured three ways); take several samples, because the spread is
115s and this round drew a conclusion from one; and start at `test_hooks.sh`,
which is the largest attributed step and was documented as "milliseconds".
★ AND ONE RULE THAT CAME OUT OF IT: do not compute "moving this gate saves N
seconds". The gates warm each other's builds, so removing one hands its share to
the next — `wire_only_deps` is 440x cheaper warm than cold, and which it is
depends on what ran before it.
DOCS — `CLAUDE.md`'s hook section had named eight of thirteen steps and had one
wrong cost. It now derives the list from what the hook prints, with the command
to re-derive it, rather than carrying a hand-written copy.

R1780.decision_summary:
R1780 — THE WIRE SAID WHAT WAS ASKED FOR AND NEVER WHAT HAPPENED.

A debt stood for 84 rounds: `TextAlign::Center` "does nothing on an absolutely
placed run", measured three times off rendered pixels, with the property alive
the whole way down — published, round-tripping through `scene/snapshot`, part of
the text cache's key, mapped to parley, and refused by the self-hosted fast path
when it is not `Start`. The debt could only record that SOMETHING made it inert
and that "which node shape honours it" was unknown. Both of its claims were
tested this round. ONE WAS WRONG AND ONE WAS RIGHT, and the round's own reading
got the second one backwards for twenty minutes.

★★★★★ CLAIM ONE WAS WRONG: THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE BOX, NOT THE PLACEMENT.
Alignment is applied by `layout.align(..)` AFTER `break_all_lines(break_at)`,
and `break_at` is the `max_width` the cache is handed — which the paint adapter
takes from the node's own rectangle (`if t.rect.w > 0`). So an alignment moves a
run WITHIN THE WIDTH IT WAS GIVEN, and a box the size of its own text is a box
with nowhere to move. That is the property behaving exactly as specified. The
labels the debt measured were built with `run_box(text)` — a box the size of the
text. The pixel rig it cites as "works" builds its node with a header's box
width. The repair that fixed the screens put the label in a flex row wider than
it. Every one of those is the same fact.

Pinned by `pinion_text::cache::tests::r1780_an_alignment_moves_a_run_within_the_width_it_was_given`:
a text-width box is an identity, a box three times as wide moves the run BY HALF
THE SLACK, and no width at all is an identity too. The second clause is what
makes it a measurement — "it moved" passes for any movement, and only "by half
the slack" says an alignment is an alignment.

★★★★★ CLAIM TWO WAS RIGHT, AND THIS ROUND FIRST WROTE THE OPPOSITE. Reading the
wire types, it looked answered: `scene/text_blocks` reports the block's `width`
and each line's `x`, whose own field documentation calls it the place "where
BOTH the text indent and the alignment land", with `advance` and
`trailing_whitespace` beside it. That was written into the debt as a refutation.
Then the test ran and came back with an empty list, because of this:

    fn is_block(t: &TextNode) -> bool {
        t.block.is_some() || !t.style.text_indent.is_none()
    }

A NODE THAT DECLARES ONLY AN ALIGNMENT IS NOT A BLOCK, so the one surface
carrying the alignment's EFFECT excluded exactly the nodes whose only
declaration was an alignment. The fields existed; the node was not in the
report. Reading found the fields and running found the absence.

SO THE DEFECT IS SHARPER THAN EITHER VERSION: `scene/snapshot` reports the
`text_align` that was REQUESTED, for any text node; `scene/text_blocks` reports
where the line LANDED, for a set that leaves those nodes out. The wire said what
was asked for and never what happened — the class this tree has paid for
repeatedly, one level up from a property that is merely wrong.

THE REPAIR IS ONE LINE: a declared, non-default alignment makes a paragraph.
`Start` stays out, because a default nobody asked for is not a declaration and
reporting every unstyled label would drown the paragraphs this surface exists
for. `only_declared_paragraphs_are_reported` stays green beside it, which is
what says a plain label is still not a block.

★★ AND THE PROOF'S FIRST DRAFT DIED ON ITS OWN PREMISE, usefully: it took its
flush baseline from `TextAlign::Start` — the value the repair had just correctly
excluded — so the baseline call came back empty. Comparing ONE declaration
across TWO widths needs no baseline and is the sentence the test's name already
made: with room, `x` is half the slack; with none, `x` is zero and the wire says
so.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: that the screens are now centred. A chip that gives its
label a text-sized box is making a layout choice, and the reader who reported
`tcp` / `tls` sitting off-centre was seeing that choice, not this defect. That
half moved to `debt-text-is-not-centred-in-the-box-that-holds-it` with the
mechanism attached, so the next round starts from what the box is rather than
from what the property does.
changes_bullets: WIRE — `pinion-rpc`'s `scene/text_blocks`.
* `is_block` now counts a declared, non-default `text_align` as a paragraph, so
the one surface that reports where a line LANDED no longer excludes the nodes
whose only declaration is an alignment. `Start` stays out: a default nobody
asked for is not a declaration.
* `r1780_the_wire_shows_whether_an_alignment_had_room` — one declaration across
two widths. With slack the reported line `x` is half of it; with none it is
zero, which is the wire saying the declaration had nowhere to go.
FRAMEWORK — `pinion-text`.
* `r1780_an_alignment_moves_a_run_within_the_width_it_was_given` pins the rule
an 84-round debt could not name: identity at text width, half the slack at three
times it, identity with no width. Sits in the cache's own test module.
DEBTS.
* `debt-a-declared-text-alignment-does-nothing-on-an-absolutely-placed-run` —
CLOSED, with both of its claims judged and the round's own wrong turn recorded.
* `debt-text-is-not-centred-in-the-box-that-holds-it` — re-aimed: the screens'
labels are not off-centre because a property fails, but because a chip gives its
label a box the size of the text. The question is what box, not what property.
verification_bullets: LOCAL GATES, both crates whose behaviour changed, full suites: `pinion-rpc` 1301
passed 0 failed; `pinion-text` 106 passed 0 failed; every other target in those
two packages green, 0 FAILED lines in the run. `cargo fmt --all` clean.
THE NEIGHBOUR THAT GUARDS THE CHANGE: `only_declared_paragraphs_are_reported`
stays green, which is what says a plain label is still not a block — the risk of
widening `is_block` is exactly that it swallows every label, and that test is
where it would show.
WHAT RUNNING CORRECTED, twice, and both were readings:
* "the discriminator is absolute placement" — refuted by the cache measurement;
it is the box width.
* "the consumer can already see it" — WRITTEN INTO THE DEBT as a refutation of
its second claim, then refuted itself when the test came back with an empty
list. The fields were there; the node was not in the report.
THE PROOF'S OWN FIRST DRAFT FAILED ON ITS PREMISE, taking a baseline from the
one value the repair excludes. That is recorded rather than quietly fixed,
because the repair it tests is what made the baseline invalid.
carry_forward_bullets: * `debt-text-is-not-centred-in-the-box-that-holds-it` stays open and now carries
the mechanism: a label given a box its own size cannot be centred in it. The
next round on it starts from the reference — how the canon places a chip's label
— and the idiom is already in the tree (`view_button`'s flex row with
`JustifyContent::Center`, which is what R1695 used to fix the shell).
* ⚠ THE PAINT GATES STILL DO NOT ASK ABOUT PLACE. That was true before this
round and is true after it; what changed is that a declaration's effect is now
visible on the wire, so a gate that wanted to ask has something to read. If one
is built it must carry the distinction this round found: "the declaration was
ignored" and "the declaration had no room" are different findings.
★ A PERSON CLOSES WHAT A PERSON REPORTED (R1736). The reader saw `tcp` / `tls`
sitting off-centre in a window. Nothing on their screen has moved yet.

R1781.decision_summary:
R1781 — THE ROUND KEPT TRYING TO BUILD SOMETHING THAT ALREADY EXISTED, AND THE
THING THAT DID NOT EXIST FOUND A SECOND DEFECT ON ITS FIRST RUN.

A reader ran the assembled tool and found the node lab's inspector cut off. A
debt was opened for it the same day, saying the shipping window is below what a
mounted screen declares it needs, and that the shipping size sat "outside the
judged population". This round took that debt and re-measured it, as the rule
demands. THREE OF ITS PREMISES FELL, one after another, and every one of them
would have produced a duplicate of something already in the tree.

★ ONE — "the shipping size is outside the judged population". No: R1767 measured
this exact size and recorded `118 of 133`, and `r1770_a_verdict_says_what_size_
it_was_read_at` carries both readings in its own header.

★ TWO — "no gate asserts anything there". No: that demo's SECTION D drives the
real binary at `SMALL = (1440, 900)` and asserts the whole story — that the tool
does not claim to conform at the window it opens in, that the lab's three
surfaces DECLINE to be judged rather than failing, that the reason names BOTH
the width the screen declares it lays out at and the width it was actually
given, and that the second is smaller than the first, which is what makes an
"away" honest rather than a judge that would have failed. Nothing about the
state the reader met is unmeasured or unexplained.

★ THREE — "so re-ask it in process". Not possible, and the failure said why
twice. A first draft painted once at the opening destination and got
`reproduced = 26` against the demo's 118; walking every destination first
changed nothing. The cause is not a regression: this harness records ONE surface
(`record_painted_surfaces(.., &[VIEW_TAG])`) where the running binary records
every mounted screen's, so a walk-level verdict cannot be assembled here at all.
That is `debt-the-in-process-sweep-cannot-mount-a-screens-extra-externals`, met
from the inside — and R1767's own finding from the other side, since asking a
walk-level question of a single frame is the same error inverted.

★★★★★ WHAT WAS ACTUALLY MISSING IS ONE LAYER DOWN. The demo says the tool
declines at this size. NOTHING SAYS WHY IT HAD TO: that `WIN_W` and a mounted
screen's declared comfortable width were chosen in different rounds and cannot
both be satisfied. That is not a fact about a frame — it is two declarations
sitting side by side, and comparing them needs no surface, no walk and no
window. `r1781_the_shipping_window_cannot_give_every_screen_what_it_declares`
does exactly that, and `ScreenRoster::shrink_policy_of` is what lets it: the
same asymmetry `tag_of` closed at R1729, one property over — a screen's size
policy reached `page_scene` and nothing else, so a host could not ask what its
guests need without navigating to each of them.

★★★★★ AND IT ANSWERED **TWO**, WHICH IS THE ROUND'S FINDING. The expected answer
was `["lab"]` — that is what the reader saw and what the demo's prose describes.
Measured:

    lab      declares 1625, given 1388 — short by 237
    packets  declares 1425, given 1388 — SHORT BY 37

The capture viewer does not fit either, and nobody has ever said so — not a
demo, not a debt, not the reader. Thirty-seven pixels of a three-pane screen do
not announce themselves the way a missing inspector does. It was found by
comparing two constants rather than by looking at a window, on the check's first
run, and it is the reason this gate is not a duplicate of the one that already
existed: THAT one reads a frame, THIS one reads a declaration, and they cannot
substitute for each other.

WHAT IS NOT FIXED, deliberately: the ratchet pins the SET of screens that cannot
fit, not a demand that it be empty. Closing it means choosing between a window
bigger than most laptops, a toolbar overflow affordance that does not exist, and
a screen decision three rounds paid for. What may not happen is the set changing
while nobody notices — which is exactly how the second entry got there.
changes_bullets: FRAMEWORK — `ScreenRoster::shrink_policy_of(key)`: what the screen mounted at a
destination declares it needs to lay out in. The same asymmetry `tag_of` closed
at R1729, one property over — the policy reached `page_scene`, which applies its
recourse, and nothing else, so a host could not ask what its guests need without
navigating to each one. `None` both for a destination with no screen and for a
screen that declares no policy: one that concedes nothing did not ask and get
refused.
SHELL — `r1781_the_shipping_window_cannot_give_every_screen_what_it_declares`.
Derives what a mounted screen receives (the window less the host's rail) and
compares it with each screen's declared comfortable width. A ratchet on the SET
that falls short, with the measured widths in the failure message, and a floor
on the population so an empty roster cannot pass it vacuously.
verification_bullets: RE-MEASURED FIRST, and it is most of the round: three premises of the debt fell
before any code was written, each one pointing at something the tree already
had. The evidence for each is named in the decision above.
LOCAL GATES, both crates whose behaviour changed, full suites:
`hello-analyzer-shell` 104 passed 0 failed; `pinion-screen` 8 + 14 + 27 + 2
passed 0 failed. `cargo fmt --all` clean.
THE RATCHET WAS SET FROM THE RUN, NOT FROM EXPECTATION. It was first written
`["lab"]` — the reader's report and the demo's prose — and the first run
answered `[("packets", 1425, 1388), ("lab", 1625, 1388)]`. The expected value
was corrected to what was measured, and the second entry is a defect nothing in
this tree had recorded.
★ WHAT THE FAILED ATTEMPTS PROVED, which is worth as much as the gate: a
walk-level conformance verdict cannot be assembled in this harness. Two runs
said so — `reproduced = 26` before walking the destinations and `26` after —
against a demo that measures 118 at the same size, because the harness records
one surface and the binary records every mounted screen's.
carry_forward_bullets: * `debt-the-shipped-window-is-below-a-mounted-screens-minimum` stays OPEN and
its axis statement is corrected: the state is measured, gated and explained
already; what this round added is why it is forced. The three repairs remain a
design choice nobody has made.
* ★ NEW, AND UNREPORTED UNTIL NOW: the capture viewer is short by 37px at the
shipping size. It is in the ratchet rather than in a new debt because it is the
same conflict with a different pair of numbers, and splitting it would make two
files that must be closed together.
* ⚠ THE IN-PROCESS HARNESS CANNOT ANSWER WALK-LEVEL CONFORMANCE — recorded here
because this round spent two runs discovering it and the next round to reach for
that number will otherwise spend two more. The demo is the instrument for it.
★ A PERSON CLOSES WHAT A PERSON REPORTED (R1736). The reader's inspector is
still cut off; this round made the reason gated, not gone.

NEVER SPLIT IT.

violations in a test R1780 itself wrote, and stop-the-line then refused to
publish R1781 on top of it. A red is paid off as its own round; this is that
round, and the thing it found is one level above the red.

★ THE VIOLATIONS WERE FOUR, NOT TWO, AND ONE CRATE CANNOT SEE THEM. CI and the
handover both named two, in `pinion-rpc`. A workspace clippy found two more in
`pinion-text` — R1780 touched two crates and cargo stops at the first that

population: a workspace gate needs a workspace run, not the touched crate's.

that suppresses nothing and that nobody can see. `#[expect]` turns exactly that
into a compile error, and the tree stands at 349 `allow` against 16 `expect`;
the premise that a `clippy::` expectation is NOT unfulfilled under a rustc-only
build was checked by running one (`cargo check -p pinion-chart --all-targets`,
exit 0) rather than recalled.

★★★★★ WHY IT REACHED main AT ALL: R1779, one round earlier, moved clippy AND
rustdoc out of both hooks into CI, as ONE item, justified by ONE number — a
fully warmed `pre-push` took 237.33s. THAT NUMBER WAS NEVER SPLIT BETWEEN THEM.
Split here, one variable at a time on this tree: clippy with nothing changed
4.6s; clippy after an edit that invalidates the graph 119.6s; rustdoc, same
tree, started immediately after that clippy, 394.6s. EIGHTY-SIX TIMES APART.

carried the tell — removing clippy made the hook SLOWER, because the
statechart-emit ratchet had been riding its warm build. The round wrote that
sentence down and still treated the two as one item.

★★★★★ AND THE PAIR IS NOT A PAIR. R1779's comment asserted rustdoc is cheap

times and publishes once, and what this protects is what gets published. Rustdoc
stays in CI: its cost is real and a broken intra-doc link does not compile-break
a consumer.

principle — a gate removed here and absent there would have been a gate
removed — was performed once, by hand, and nothing re-performed it. The two lint
gates now live in DIFFERENT files, which is precisely the arrangement a reader
cannot verify by looking at one. `tools/test_hooks.sh` asserts that the push
hook and CI run the same clippy flag for flag, that each runs it AT ALL (the
presence assertions come first, because a bare equality passes vacuously when
both are missing), and that rustdoc is still in CI, its only home.

read as a number rather than matched as an option name — a grep for the name
would have called the default armed.

R1783.decision_summary:
R1783 — A DEMO CLOCK THAT EVERY AUTHOR READ AS MILLISECONDS, AND THE ROUND
THAT MADE A LIFETIME TELL THE TRUTH IS WHAT REVEALED IT.

R1782 paid a clippy red and, while reading CI to check it, found a second one
nobody could see: eight analyzer-shell demos failing in the sweep, hidden for
two rounds because the sweep job is `needs:`-gated on the clippy job that was
failing. This round pays that red.

★★★★★ FOUR HYPOTHESES WERE FORMED BY READING AND ALL FOUR WERE WRONG.
① "the opening sentence expired" — no: section A presses BEFORE it reads.
② "the toast covers the palette" — no: the toast spans x 440..1000 and the
palette 1148..1440. ③ "the `said` path is unsupported" — no: the probe's own
`EXT` was wrong. ④ "the harness passes a measured dt, so a lifetime burns
fast" — no: a headless run INJECTS dt (`DeferredInput::Tick { dt }`, and
`dt == 0.0` is a frozen clock). What answered was a run with one variable
changed and nothing else.

★★★★★ WHAT THE MEASUREMENT SAYS. The press DOES speak — `said` answers
`Decode Inspector added` immediately after it, and `cards` gains the widget.
What empties it is ONE `tf.tick(16)`. Isolated across five values on the same
press: `tick(0.016)`, `tick(0.5)` and `tick(2.5)` all leave the sentence
standing; `tick(2.7)` and `tick(16)` return `None`. The boundary is the
toast's own 2.6-second life, exactly. `tick(dt)` TAKES SECONDS, and
`tick(16)` advances sixteen of them.

★★★★★ WHY IT WAS GREEN UNTIL R1777, WHICH IS THE FINDING RATHER THAN THE
BUG. R1776 gave the shell's toast its lifetime and gated the SCENE on
`toast_life > 0.0`, so the toast left the screen on expiry — but the `said`
and `toast` WIRE slots read a sentence signal that expiry never cleared, so
the wire went on reporting something the screen had stopped showing. R1778
lifted the holder into `pinion_core::utterance::Saying`, whose `tick` writes

R1784.decision_summary:
R1784 — THE SIZE QUESTION REACHES EVERY SECTION A READER CAN OPEN, AND THE
DEBT'S OWN PRESCRIPTION WAS THE THIRD ONE THIS SESSION TO FALL ON CONTACT.

The integration debt says the structural remainder is that `dashboard` and
`settings` are still the host's inline pages, so the roster has no `Screen` to
ask, and names making them screens as the close. Re-measured at entry, as the
rule demands: R1761 had already refused that shape ON A MEASUREMENT, and left
the measurement in a comment beside the code. The page region a screen would
be granted is 1096x802 at (52, 98) while the section's layout bar is 1096x46 at
(52, 52) and its palette 292x848 at (1148, 52) — both OUTSIDE the page, because
a host that paints a page's chrome paints it beside the region rather than in
it. A screen there would state and judge for a rectangle that is not the
section. So the prescription would have produced something quieter than the
silence it replaced.

★★★★★ THE REAL REMAINDER WAS THE GATE'S POPULATION. R1781 gave a host
`shrink_policy_of` and wrote the ratchet that uses it as a walk over
`mounted_keys` ending in `assert!(asked >= 4)`. This application opens SIX
sections. Four are mounted screens; the two the host paints itself were not
failing the check — THEY WERE NEVER IN IT — and the assertion read as though it
covered the tool. That is R1738's finding one property over: there a section
that published no verdict was absent rather than short, and the remedy was to
build the population from the roster. Here it is layout, and the remedy is the
same shape.

WHAT THE FRAMEWORK GAINED, in `pinion-screen`: `ScreenRoster::laying_out(key,
policy)` — a destination the host paints itself declares what it lays out in —
and `unsized_keys()`, which names the open destinations that cannot answer.
The second is the one a gate should assert on: "four screens declared a size"
is true of an application with four sections and of one with forty, and only
the unanswered set says which sections the question never reached. `laying_out`
refuses a key that has a screen, for the reason `judging` refuses one — a
screen states its own policy, and a second source would make what a section
lays out in depend on which registration a lookup reached first. So an empty
set is a claim about the screens too, not only about the host's diligence.

WHAT THE CONSUMER GAINED: both pages declare, and both numbers are DERIVED.
The dashboard's floor comes from its own board — a card spanning `n` columns is
`n * pitch - GAP` and the pitch is `(canvas - GAP) / GRID_COLS`, so the canvas
follows from how narrow a card may be, and that number is `FLOAT_MIN_W`, what a
card clamps to once torn off, extracted from the reference's source at R1697. A
card legible detached and illegible in place would be this shell disagreeing
with itself about one thing. The narrowest span is read from `spec::BOARD`
rather than written down, so a placement moving from five columns to four moves
the floor with it. The settings page's comfortable width is the one it already
refuses to exceed (`SET_MAX_W` plus its inset) and its floor is where a title
and the widest control seat stop fitting on one line.

★★★★★ THE FIRST RUN CAUGHT A DEFECT IN THIS ROUND'S OWN WORK, which is the
second time a widened population has done that here. It reported
`("dashboard", 1176, 1096)` — and 1176 - 1096 is `RAIL_W + PALETTE_W` less the
rounding. The declaration had been written as the SECTION's width, on R1761's
measurement that a section is wider than its region, and compared against the
REGION, because that is what a `ShrinkPolicy` is: the thing `page_scene`
applies. The measurement is true and it is not what the type expresses. It now
lives where it belongs — an assertion that the dashboard's region is narrower
than a mounted screen's, so the two readings cannot silently converge — and the
constant is the region's own floor.

AND A SECOND SELF-CORRECTION, from the standing lesson rather than from a run:
the new derivation test was first inserted between the ratchet's doc comment
and its function, which is the exact hazard this session had already recorded
once. Moved below it.

NOT CLOSED: the shortfall set is still `["packets", "lab"]`. R1781's reasoning
holds — closing it means choosing between a window bigger than most laptops, a
toolbar overflow affordance that does not exist, and a screen decision three
rounds paid for. What this round changes is that the question was asked of
every section rather than of two thirds of them.
changes_bullets: `crates/pinion-screen/src/roster.rs`: `laying_out(key, ShrinkPolicy)` — a
destination the host paints itself declares what it lays out in — and
`unsized_keys()`, the open destinations that cannot answer, in roster order.
A third map beside `judges` for the reason that one is beside `screens`: a size
is not a screen with most of it missing, and the alternative is the screen
R1761 measured and refused. `shrink_policy_of` now falls back to it; the two
sources cannot hold one key, so the lookup has no precedence to get wrong.
`RosterDefect` gains `SectionAlreadySized` and `DuplicateSize` — every refusal
a judge gets, a size gets, plus the one that is only a size's.
`examples/hello-analyzer-shell/src/main.rs`: `narrowest_span()` reads the
narrowest card from `spec::BOARD`; `board_canvas_floor()` derives the canvas
that keeps that card no smaller than the same card torn off (`FLOAT_MIN_W`);
`DASHBOARD_MIN_W` / `DASHBOARD_MIN_H` and `SETTINGS_MAX_W` / `SETTINGS_MIN_W` /
`SETTINGS_MIN_H` follow from the page metrics already there. Both pages are
registered with `laying_out`, `panning` rather than `rigid` because both keep
laying out below their comfortable width — the board scrolls, the settings
column narrows to its cap.
`examples/hello-analyzer-shell/src/painted.rs`: the R1781 ratchet's population
is every OPEN destination, it asserts `unsized_keys()` is empty before counting
anything, and it compares each declaration against `page_rect(key).w` — the one
place the per-destination grant is already expressed — rather than against one
window-less-rail figure that is right for four of six. Two assertions state the
readings that must not converge: that every open destination answered, and that
the dashboard's region is narrower than a mounted screen's.
`r1784_the_boards_floor_is_derived_from_the_layout_it_opens_with` is what makes
the derivation's DIRECTION checkable: recomputing the narrowest span over
`spec::BOARD` at runtime, and asserting the derived floor actually keeps a card
at `FLOAT_MIN_W`. Without it the `const fn` could read the widest span and no
size gate would move, because a smaller floor is one the window still satisfies.

and `hello-analyzer-shell`. `cargo fmt --all` clean, and `cargo clippy
--workspace --all-targets --features pinion-runtime/vello` run as the push gate
runs it — which caught one violation of this round's own
(`explicit_auto_deref` in the new `unsized_keys`) before it could reach CI, the
discipline R1782 restored the gate for.
★ THE FIRST RUN OF THE WIDENED RATCHET FAILED, AND ITS FAILURE WAS THIS ROUND'S
OWN: `("dashboard", 1176, 1096)`, a difference of exactly `RAIL_W +
PALETTE_W` less rounding, because the declaration had been written as the
section's width and compared against the page region. Recorded rather than
quietly fixed: a widened population catching the round that widened it is the
second time that has happened here, and it is the argument for widening.
★ AND A SECOND SELF-CORRECTION WITHOUT A RUN: the new derivation test was
first placed between the ratchet's doc comment and its function — the exact
hazard this session had already recorded once — and moved below it.
FIVE COUNTERFACTUALS, run through `tools/counterfactual.py` with the gate as
both crates' suites: the unanswered set inverted so it names the ANSWERED
sections; the refusal that stops a host declaring over a mounted screen
disabled; the lookup's fallback to a host declaration removed; the board floor's
derivation reading the WIDEST span instead of the narrowest; and the gate
reading one grant for every destination instead of the per-destination one.
Each is a wrong answer rather than an absent one, so no case is a compile
error and no import is left without a user.

SHARPEST RESULT: nothing caught the gate reading a single grant for all six
destinations, because both host-painted pages fit under either reading — the
dashboard wants 832 and is handed 1096 by its region or 1388 by the old
figure. The correction was right and NOTHING WAS HOLDING IT. The repair is the

cannot satisfy. Re-run as CF-5b: CAUGHT. So the round's counterfactuals are

NOT RUN HERE: the demo sweep, which is CI's job. This round changes no paint

that reads them runs in the crate's own suite.

R1785.decision_summary:
R1785 — THE ENGINE LEARNED TO SAY A MACHINE HAD STOPPED, AND NOT ONE OF THIS
FRAMEWORK'S FIFTEEN CHARTS CAN EVER BE IN THAT STATE.

The pin moves `c00722f` -> `87f4b1d`, six commits, in the four legs this
repository requires: the `vendor/sce` gitlink, both `rev =` sites in
`Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, and — since R1766 — the committed statechart emit.

★★★★★ WHAT THE EMIT SAID, IN ONE `git diff`. Fifteen files changed by exactly
one line each, and the line is `template-hash`. The generated code this
framework runs is BYTE-IDENTICAL across the bump; what moved is the
generator's template identity, which upstream's own commit says it re-pinned.
R1765 had to build the crate twice against two pins and compare two `OUT_DIR`s
by hand to answer that question. R1766 made the emit a tracked artifact
precisely so it could be read, and this is the first bump where the reading was
one command.

WHAT WAS CONSUMED. Upstream added `unseen_external_events()` and
`last_unseen_event()`: a count of external events a machine never dequeued
because it had already stopped. Its documentation gives the reason as a table —
a host that sent an event and saw nothing move has three candidates, and only
two of them were previously distinguishable. `pinion_core::widgets::Sent` is
this framework's own vocabulary for exactly that question and had exactly those
two arms, so the consumption is a third: `Sent::NeverSeen`, with `was_seen()`
beside `answered()`.

★ THE ORDER THE COUNTERS ARE READ IN IS THE PART THAT COULD BE WRONG WITHOUT
LOOKING WRONG, so it is asserted rather than commented. A machine that has
stopped never reaches the point where an event could be discarded, so reading
the discard counter first would answer `Answered` — *the machine did something
with it* — for an event nobody looked at, which is the confusion the arm exists
to end.

★★★★★ AND THE ARM IS UNREACHABLE HERE, WHICH IS THE FINDING. W3C SCXML 3.13
ends the main event loop at a top-level final state, and NOT ONE of this
crate's fifteen statecharts declares a `<final>` at all — because a widget is a
thing that keeps running, and a button that reached a final state would be a
button nobody can press again. So the framework can now say something no
document it owns can cause.

That is stated as a test rather than left as a gap: the walk finds every chart
under the crate and asserts none can stop, so the day one gains a final state
the assertion fails and asks for a driven proof instead of coverage. An
assertion that cannot stand moves to where it can be seen rather than being
dropped, which is this project's own rule about exactly this shape.

`Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock` (via `cargo fetch`), and the committed emit
regenerated with `PINION_REGEN_STATECHARTS=1`. `tools/pin_sync.py
--check-dual-pin` reports `SCE@87f4b1d (manifest = lock = vendor/sce)`.
`crates/pinion-core/generated/`: fifteen files, one line each, all of it
`template-hash`. No generated code changed.
`pinion_core::widgets::Sent` gains `NeverSeen`, and `Sent::answered()` gains
`was_seen()` beside it — the question a caller asks before rewriting a guard.
`Widget::send` now derives the verdict from BOTH counters through
`Sent::from_counts`, unseen first; `Widget::unseen()` is the monotone reading
for a caller that cannot reach `send`'s return value, matching `discarded()`.
TWO TESTS, and the second is the round's finding: `r1785_the_third_answer_is_
read_before_the_second` pins all three arms and the ordering clause, and
`r1785_no_chart_here_can_stop_so_nothing_can_be_unseen_yet` walks every

R1786.decision_summary:
R1786 — THE SECOND ENGINE DIAGNOSTIC IN A ROW THAT NOTHING HERE CAN CAUSE, AND
THE TWO SHARE A REASON.

R1785 bumped the SCE pin and consumed one of the six commits it brought. This
round consumes the second: `undecodable_payloads()`, a count of events that
arrived carrying a payload announcing itself as structure which the datamodel
could not read as one.

WHAT THE CLAUSE LEAVES OUT. W3C SCXML B.2.8.1 requires the fallback — content
the processor cannot interpret becomes a space-normalized string — and
requires nothing about telling anybody. So a document reads
`_event.data.field`, gets nothing, assigns nothing, and the run continues.
Upstream measured that on three independent Lua implementations: a payload in
Lua's own table syntax silently emptied every variable the receiving
transition assigned, including the one that primes the next session. The count
deliberately excludes prose delivered as text, which is the ladder working
(W3C test 562) — a diagnostic that fires when nothing is wrong is one nobody
reads.

★★★★★ AND IT CANNOT MOVE HERE. Measured on the committed emit: all fifteen
charts declare `type Payload = ()`. This framework's widget charts carry no
`_event.data` at all, so the counter is nailed at zero by construction —
exactly as `Sent::NeverSeen` was nailed by no chart declaring a `<final>`.

TWO IN A ROW IS A PATTERN, NOT TWO COINCIDENCES. pinion's widget charts are
minimal: no final states, no event data. An engine diagnostic about either is
therefore a surface this framework OWES ITS CONSUMERS and cannot exercise
itself. That is the reason to build it rather than a reason to skip it: a
consumer's own document may carry payloads, and a framework that hides a
diagnostic its engine publishes has decided for them.

★ THE UNREACHABILITY IS READ OFF THE EMIT, NOT OFF THE SOURCES, and the
difference is the point. The payload type is the generator's conclusion —
emitted when a transition guard reads a typed field — so a `.scxml` says what
was written and the emit says what was concluded, and only the second
determines whether the counter can move. R1766 made the emit a tracked
artifact; this is the second round in two to spend that.

Both unreachability claims are assertions rather than gaps: each fails on the
day the condition changes, and what it asks for then is a driven proof rather
than coverage.

★★★★★ AND THEN THE COUNTERFACTUALS MOVED THIS ROUND'S PRODUCT OUT OF THE PLAN.
Three cases, one CAUGHT and TWO PASSED — and the two were the same hole in two
tests written a round apart. **A demand-assertion is its own only guard.**
Break its predicate and it reports "all clear" from that moment for ever:
disarming the payload walk's report went unnoticed, and so did changing the
final-state walk to look for a spelling no chart uses. Recognising a shape
rather than a bug is what two independent instances buy.

The remedy is this project's own rule applied one level up — a fixture asserts
it can DISTINGUISH before its verdict of "no difference" means anything. Both
walks now read a named predicate and a control asserts each recognises a
positive case, refuses a negative one, and refuses the near-miss a loose
predicate would swallow.

★★★★★ THE CONTROL FAILED ON ITS FIRST RUN, WHICH IS SHARPER THAN THE HOLE IT
WAS WRITTEN FOR. `<final` is a prefix of `<finalize` — an `<invoke>` child, not
a state anything ends at — so the predicate R1785 shipped would have fired on a
chart that cannot stop. The near-miss case existed because a loose substring is
a class this project has a standing rule about, and it caught a live instance
of that class immediately. The predicate now requires an element boundary.

`r1786_no_chart_here_carries_a_payload_so_none_can_be_undecodable` walks the

rather than the `.scxml` sources because the payload type is the generator's

★★★★★ `r1786_both_walks_can_see_the_thing_they_look_for` IS THE ROUND'S REAL

the processor cannot interpret becomes a space-normalized string — and
requires nothing about telling anybody. So a document reads

transition assigned, including the one that primes the next session. The count
deliberately excludes prose delivered as text, which is the ladder working

reads.

charts declare `type Payload = ()`. This framework's widget charts carry no
