R1797.decision_summary:
R1797 — a card derives every number it shows, and the reference cannot.

The analysis-tool census records `dashboard.t1.6` (a latency distribution: a
histogram) as `have` since R1793, and a registered debt recorded that nothing
DRAWS it: the seat is the dashboard's `latency` card and it was booked under
the reference's second release. The reader chose to promote it.

RE-MEASURING THE DEBT'S OWN PRESCRIPTION FALSIFIED IT — the fourth consecutive
round to find that, which makes it the expectation rather than the exception.
The prescription said "draw the histogram R1793 built". That histogram CANNOT
draw the reference's card, for three separate reasons, each of which became a
piece of framework work:

  * the reference's ladder is GEOMETRIC (`<1, 1-2, 2-4 ... >64` ms) and every
    rule divided a span into equal parts, with `width()` a single scalar, so a
    doubling ladder was not merely absent but unrepresentable;
  * two of its eight buckets are UNBOUNDED and every edge was finite by
    construction, so the slowest reply had nowhere to be counted;
  * its three tiles are p50 / p95 / max and the crate had no arbitrary-
    proportion quantile at all.

AND THE REFERENCE'S OWN CARD IS INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT, which became the
round's subject. It publishes eight bucket counts AND three stat tiles,
independently. Its counts total 1,672 samples of which 93.9% are at or below
16 ms, so the 95th percentile OF THE BARS IT DRAWS falls in the `16-32` bucket
— while the tile beside them says 11.4 ms, which is in `8-16`. A mockup cannot
notice that. So the STRUCTURE is what is reproduced — the ladder, the three
tiles, the caption, the emphasised tail — and the reference's FIGURES become
the oracle the derivation is checked against. The card derives its bars, its
tiles and its emphasis from one capture record, so it cannot state a percentile
its own bars contradict, and a gate asserts exactly that.

THE RULE OF THREE, AND WHAT THE COPIES WERE HIDING. The same interpolating
quantile was written out privately three times (`distribution`, `density`,
`histogram`). The lift is not the interesting part: the copies DISAGREED with
what was drawn beside them. The two private ones are Hyndman & Fan type 7 with
no way to say so, while the box plot they sit next to defaults to Tukey's
hinges — so the same samples had two interquartile ranges in one crate and
nothing could say which was which. `Quantiles` is now the one answer and
`Basis` carries the definition that produced its IQR.

TUKEY DOES NOT DEFINE p95, AND THE TYPE SAYS SO. A hinge is the median of a
half, so hinges exist at the quartiles and the extremes and nowhere else. Both
silent repairs are wrong — interpolating returns a number that method never
defined, and substituting type 7 returns a number a DIFFERENT method defined
under this one's name. `QuantileError::HingesOnly` refuses and names the method
that would answer.

THE FLOOR WAS BUILT FROM SOURCE AND PROBED THROUGH ITS OWN RUNTIME TYPE
INFORMATION, so "no such capability" is a measurement rather than a reading.
R1793 recorded that no floor was measurable because the charting module was not
in this install; this round installed it. Nine checks, all passing: the bar
surface publishes 33 + 30 names and not one names a bin, a bucket, a sample, a
rule or a basis; a bar set carries no per-bar numeric interval at all, so no bar
there has an extent that could be unbounded; handed `+inf` as an axis maximum
the numeric axis REFUSES it and keeps its previous value, so an unbounded end is
not expressible even as a display; the box surface answers no quantile of any
kind; and there IS a logarithmic AXIS at a settable base which connects to no
binning — having a log axis is not having log bins.
changes_bullets: FRAMEWORK (pinion-chart):
* `quantile::Quantiles` — finite samples sorted once, answering an ARBITRARY
proportion under a named `QuantileMethod`. A type rather than a function
because an interpolating quantile is only meaningful on an ascending, finite
slice and all three private copies took `&[f64]` and trusted their caller.
`QuantileError::{NoFiniteSamples, NotAProportion, HingesOnly}`, and
`TUKEY_HINGES` so a caller choosing a proportion at runtime can ask whether
the method it also holds can answer.
* `distribution::QuantileMethod::quartiles` delegates to it; `density`'s and
`histogram`'s private `quantile` helpers are gone. One codec.
* `histogram::BinRule::Ratio(base)` — a geometric ladder anchored on the powers
of `base` bracketing the samples. Refuses a base at or below one, and refuses
a non-positive sample by NAME rather than clamping it into a first bucket
nobody could read.
* `histogram::BinEnds` + `Binned::over(samples, edges, ends)` — boundaries the
caller STATES, with unbounded outer bins or hard ones. `Binned::outside`
reports what a hard ladder could not bin, so a chart that dropped samples
cannot do it silently. `BinEnds` and not `Ends`: the latter already exists in
`pinion_core::widgets::roving` meaning whether a focus ring wraps.
* `Binned::extent` / `label` / `tail_from` / `ends`, and `width()` became
`uniform_width() -> Option<f64>` — a geometric ladder and an unbounded bin
both make "the width" a question with no answer, and the old signature could
only answer it wrongly.
* `Basis::quantile_method` — which definition produced the IQR the rule read.
* `window::plot_area` now returns a rect CONTAINED IN ITS INPUT. It clamped the
plot's size and left its origin alone, so a rect narrower than `left + right`
produced a plot area running off the end — and since every painter in the
crate is defined in terms of this function, so did they.
FRAMEWORK (pinion-core):
* `TextOverflow::bounds_ink()` — whether an arm confines the painted ink to the
box. A second predicate beside `shortens()` because the two answer different
questions and using the first for the second is a defect this tree shipped:
`test_fixtures::screen_ink` asked the CONTENT question to decide a PIXEL one,
so a clipped run's hidden glyphs were reported as ink that had escaped.
SCREEN (`examples/hello-analyzer-shell`, the dashboard):
* `latency` promoted from `Tier::Reserved` to `Tier::Placeable` and placed on
the opening board at the cell the behaviour reference's own opening state puts
it (column 0, row 4, four columns by two rows). Five placed, eight reserved.
* `spec::LATENCY_*` — the ladder, the capture record, the reference's three
published figures as the oracle, the stat keys, the caption.
* `latency_body` — three derived tiles, the binned distribution with its tail
emphasised from the p95 the tile above states, and the caption that says WHY a
bar is emphasised. `distribution_box` derives the chart's floor from the
chart's own margins and is SHARED with the gate that sweeps it.
* `SECTIONS` lost its tier column. A section's release is read off its entries
(`section_tiers`), and a section holding both says so — on the wire and in the
heading a reader scans. The column was one fact stored twice, kept in step by
an assertion, and promoting a single widget out of a group made one copy false.
GATES:
* `pinion-chart`: the plot area is inside its rect over 19,600 rects, AND a rect
that holds its margins is unaffected by the clamp; the geometric ladder keeps
a heavy tail that equal width flattens; an open ladder loses nothing and a
closed one reports what it dropped; the tail moves with the distribution and
is empty when the cut lands inside the unbounded bin; an open bin is brushable
through an infinite extent; Tukey refuses p95 by name.
* the screen: the card's percentile is consistent with its own bars (the test
that would fail on the reference); the derived tiles are the reference's
figures; the default method refuses the percentile this card needs; the
emphasised bars are the ones the tile names; the slowest reply is binned
rather than dropped; the distribution stays inside the box it is given at
every size the card admits, with a floor asserting the sweep both drew and
refused; a card is painted once per frame.
* `r1671`'s frame gate now reads card rectangles and marks in ONE frame. It took
card rects from the painted regions (clipped) and marks from the scene walk
(also clipped), and clipping does not preserve containment: a card dragged
part of the way off the canvas is cut at the clip edge, a mark inside it that
reaches the bottom is cut at the same edge, and the content box is the cut
card inset by the frame — so every mark reaching the boundary was reported as
crossing, by exactly two pixels, always. Nothing had ever reached it.
* `painted::body_cells` — whether a body's rows give up columns one at a time,
stated in the table both the body check and the clamp census read, so a family
drawn whole is not asked for a per-cell clamp it can never reach.
TOOL:
* `tools/demo_radius.py` — which DEMOS a change can break, computed. R1795 spent
a whole round repaying a red it had published, named the cause ("the blast
radius was chosen BY HAND"), wrote this tool's shape into the debt file and
did not build it. This round needed the answer and built it: an AST walk
gives demo -> the packages it launches, `blast_radius.py` gives change ->
packages, and the intersection is the answer. Registered in `pre-push`.
verification_bullets: FLOOR, built from source and probed at runtime (scratchpad only, never tracked):
the reference charting module configured, built and installed, then enumerated
through its own meta-object system so that "no such capability" is a
measurement rather than a reading of a header. 9 of 9 checks pass. Recorded:
the bar surface publishes 33 + 30 names and none is a bin, bucket, sample, rule
or basis; a bar set carries no per-bar numeric interval; a numeric axis handed
`+inf` REFUSES it and keeps 64; the box surface answers no quantile; a
logarithmic axis exists at base 2 and names nothing to do with binning.
★ AND THAT PROBE WROTE THREE FILES INTO THE REPOSITORY ROOT. `qt-configure-module`
writes `config.opt`, `config.opt.in` and `config.redo.in` into the CURRENT
directory regardless of `-B`, and the script was launched from this checkout.
Untracked and un-ignored, one `git add -A` from a public remote. Removed, and
the script now runs from the scratchpad. A floor probe is never run inside the
repository again.
CRATE TESTS — the five packages this round edited, run together over 14
targets: 5,635 passed, 0 failed. Workspace clippy with CI's own flags
(`--all-targets --features pinion-runtime/vello`): exit 0, zero warnings.
★ THE COMPUTED DEMO SWEEP EARNED ITSELF INSIDE THE ROUND THAT BUILT IT.
Twenty-seven of the eighty-two failed, from four causes a hand-picked list
would have missed:
* the card had no arm in the accessibility dispatch, so twenty-nine marks
declared `Silence::part_of` a container that answered for nothing. A
`part_of(X)` is a promise that X SPEAKS; tagging X does not make it.
* the chart's tag prefix must be neither EQUAL TO nor a PREFIX OF its
container's tag. `.bin` against `.bins` made every mark dangle; `.bins` for
both made two regions answer to one address, which the voice census caught
as 257 tags for 258 regions.
* four stale literals across three demo files, one of them written a single
line below a comment saying a number in a demo goes stale like a number in
prose. All four are now derived from what the screen publishes.
* the card was placed at the reference's own cell and its DISTRIBUTION began
exactly at the fold — see the board reflow in the carry.
All eighty-two pass. `r1649`, the integration test that drives the live shell
over RPC against the reference, passes in 1,153.84s including the new leg that
checks the card's percentile against its own published bars.
⚠ Two self-inflicted delays, recorded because both are lessons this repository
had already written down: a 900s bound reported a demo measured at 736.95s as
a failure — a limit I chose, not a defect — and the timeout it produced
ORPHANED the application, so the next three runs were contending with a
process left by the last one.
POPULATION, computed rather than chosen. `blast_radius.py --mode staged`
answers 252 packages, because `pinion-core` is in the change. Narrowed by what
can ACTUALLY move, with the reason stated: this round's `pinion-core` edits are
one ADDITIVE method (`TextOverflow::bounds_ink`) and one TEST FIXTURE
(`screen_ink::stand_in_ink`), neither of which changes what any screen paints.
The runtime reach is `pinion_chart::window::plot_area`, which every painter in
that crate is defined in terms of — so the population is the chart consumers
plus the promoted screen: 82 demos, from `demo_radius.py`.
THE TOOL THAT ANSWERED THAT IS NEW AND SELF-TESTED. Its first draft resolved
392 of 646 demos; the dominant shape in this tree is `EXAMPLE = "..."` as a
module constant, so resolving module-level string bindings took it to 629. The
remaining 17 are reported by `--audit` rather than hidden — a name from a list
of tuples, or a demo that launches outside `RpcSubprocess`. `pre-push` runs its
selftest, which checks both that launches still resolve and that every name
resolved is a real example.
CENSUS: `analyzer_census.py --check-proofs` — `dashboard.t1.6`'s `covered_by`
and `proven_by` rewritten to name what R1797 added and the tests that run.
carry_forward_bullets: 1. `debt-a-plot-area-answered-outside-its-own-rect` — the ORIGIN half is
repaired and gated; the remainder is that a chart's tick labels are drawn in
a margin that is a CONSTANT while their width is what the shaper answers, so
a long label at an extreme can still exceed the rect. The prescription is the
axis R1794 established for captions — the margin derived from the text rather
than stated — and the POPULATION IS UNMEASURED: this round saw it on one card
and did not count how many of the crate's painters are exposed to it. Not
carried out of laziness: it is a change to every chart in the tree and it
deserves the round that measures the population first.
2. `debt-the-ink-gate-asked-a-content-question-to-decide-a-pixel-one` — the
repair only ever REDUCES the ink a gate reports, so it can turn a red green
and never the reverse. Turned around: that false alarm may have been the only
signal anybody had that a `Clip` run was actually being cut, because `Clip`
removes characters with nothing on screen saying so. There is now no gate
watching for that, and the number of clipped sites in this tree was not
counted. `scene/text_painted` already publishes what such a gate would read.
3. `tools/demo_radius.py` reports 17 demos of 646 whose launch target it cannot
resolve — a name from a list of tuples, or a demo that launches outside
`RpcSubprocess` entirely. `--audit` prints them, so the blind spot is a
NUMBER rather than a silence, but it is a blind spot: a change reaching only
those 17 is still picked by hand.
4. The ORIGINAL axis of `debt-nothing-enumerates-which-demo-asserts-which-wire-
fact` stays open. This round closed the half R1795 widened it to — which
change breaks which demo — through packages. A change that alters wire
VOCABULARY without altering any package (a refusal split into new arms, which
is exactly the R1667 case that opened the file) is still invisible to it.
5. The board reflow is a stated divergence, not a repair. The promoted card
sits at column 8 of the third row rather than the reference's column 0 of
the fifth, and the two cards beside it are four columns instead of six,
because the reference's first release fills this viewport exactly and a
fifth card fits only by reflow. The alternative the reference itself takes
for its larger board — let the reader scroll — is available and was not
taken; the reasoning is in `analyzer-dashboard-spec.json`'s own prose,
which is where it belongs because the `board` surface pins cards and
titles rather than cells and therefore cannot carry it as a remainder.
6. External: `vendor/sce`, `vello`/`wgpu` and the Mnemosyne upstream are
unchanged this round and carry nothing new.

because an interpolating quantile is only meaningful on an ascending, finite
slice and all three private copies took `&[f64]` and trusted their caller.
`QuantileError::{NoFiniteSamples, NotAProportion, HingesOnly}`, and
`TUKEY_HINGES` so a caller choosing a proportion at runtime can ask whether
the method it also holds can answer.
* `distribution::QuantileMethod::quartiles` delegates to it; `density`'s and
`histogram`'s private `quantile` helpers are gone. One codec.
* `histogram::BinRule::Ratio(base)` — a geometric ladder anchored on the powers
of `base` bracketing the samples. Refuses a base at or below one, and refuses
a non-positive sample by NAME rather than clamping it into a first bucket
nobody could read.
* `histogram::BinEnds` + `Binned::over(samples, edges, ends)` — boundaries the
caller STATES, with unbounded outer bins or hard ones. `Binned::outside`
reports what a hard ladder could not bin, so a chart that dropped samples
cannot do it silently. `BinEnds` and not `Ends`: the latter already exists in
`pinion_core::widgets::roving` meaning whether a focus ring wraps.
* `Binned::extent` / `label` / `tail_from` / `ends`, and `width()` became
`uniform_width() -> Option<f64>` — a geometric ladder and an unbounded bin
both make "the width" a question with no answer, and the old signature could
only answer it wrongly.
* `Basis::quantile_method` — which definition produced the IQR the rule read.
* `window::plot_area` now returns a rect CONTAINED IN ITS INPUT. It clamped the
plot's size and left its origin alone, so a rect narrower than `left + right`
produced a plot area running off the end — and since every painter in the
crate is defined in terms of this function, so did they.

box. A second predicate beside `shortens()` because the two answer different
questions and using the first for the second is a defect this tree shipped:
`test_fixtures::screen_ink` asked the CONTENT question to decide a PIXEL one,
so a clipped run's hidden glyphs were reported as ink that had escaped.

the opening board at the cell the behaviour reference's own opening state puts
it (column 0, row 4, four columns by two rows). Five placed, eight reserved.

published figures as the oracle, the stat keys, the caption.

R1798.decision_summary:
R1798 — a gate that was right, and a population that was not.

The reader reported a sidebar clipped when the window is made smaller. The debt
opened for it prescribed a third `Recourse` variant, on the reasoning that the
reference DCC keeps redistributing space while this tree stops reflowing and
clips.

RE-MEASURING THAT DIAGNOSIS FALSIFIED IT — the fifth consecutive round to find a
debt's own prescription wrong, which makes it the expectation. The contrast is
not DCC-versus-us. The FLOOR does it too, measured by building the reference
toolkit's widget module from source and running it offscreen, eleven checks:

  * a minimum attaches to each PANEL, not to the window — a sidebar wanting 292
    is squeezed to 73 while a fixed rail holds at 52;
  * below the content's preferred size the layout keeps redistributing, and what
    finally stops is the WINDOW, at the sum of the panels' own minimums;
  * there is a per-panel give-way vocabulary and it is NAMED — seven values;
  * a panel can be declared collapsible and really folds to nothing.

So the prescription's direction was right and its REASON was wrong: the argument
is not "the reference DCC does this" but "the floor answers this with seven
named values and this tree answers it with none". What the floor does NOT have,
also measured: any report of what a panel gave up (0 names across 91 + 102 + 100
published members), any way to ask about a size the window is not at, a header
as a named stop, and — found by isolating a check this probe first got wrong —
any complaint when an explicit minimum silently overrides a declared policy,
which the panel then goes on reporting as the policy it is not honouring.

★★★★★ AND THE ROUND'S REAL SUBJECT WAS UNDERNEATH THAT. The debt's own fourth
item said to check whether the wire's `concession` report is filled. It is, and
what it says is that two of the five shipped screens read `unreachable`:

  * `hello-log-view` — 23 marks cut at its floor, 10 of them beyond any scroll;
  * `hello-key-patterns` — 37 cut, 12 beyond reach, `kp.detail` short by 272
    pixels, which is the reader's own report;
  * both with `covered = 0` and their whole declaration reported `stale`.

`shrink.rs` states in its own documentation that `unreachable` is the one
verdict no concession can excuse — clipping is a decision a screen may make and
losing is not. Three separate things had to hold for that to go unnoticed:

  1. THE TYPE COULD NOT REFUSE IT. `gives_up` is `&'static [&'static str]` and
     `covers` matches each name against a cut mark's tag or a step of its path.
     Both screens declared an English sentence. A sentence matches nothing, so
     `covered` is structurally zero, `stale` is structurally the whole list, and
     `unnamed` is every mark that was cut — which reads exactly like a screen
     giving up something it never admitted to.
  2. THE SCREENS HAD BEEN IN THAT STATE SINCE THE ROUNDS THAT ADDED THEM.
  3. ★ THE GATE WAS RIGHT AND ITS POPULATION WAS A CONSTANT. R1712's demo
     already asserts `verdict == "honoured"` and `unreachable == []`. Its
     `SCREENS` list held three, written when the demo was; the two screens that
     grew a policy later were never added. They were not failing the check.
     They had never been in it.

That third is this project's recurring shape — R1738 counted the sections an
application had been judged on, R1784 found a ratchet walking four keys of six,
R1795 found a blast radius chosen by hand — and running the demo over five
screens for the first time exposed FOUR MORE constants underneath it, each
written for one screen and each false the moment a second arrived.
changes_bullets: FRAMEWORK (pinion-core):
* `shrink::Fault::NameIsNotATag` — a name in `gives_up` that cannot be a tag is
refused where a policy is declared, which is a `const` context, so it is a
COMPILE ERROR. The rule is one byte: a tag has no space and a sentence cannot
avoid one. Deliberately crude — it will not catch a misspelled tag — but it
separates the two kinds of wrong and catches the kind that cannot be right.
Both offending screens really did stop compiling, which is the design.
SCREENS:
* `hello-log-view` and `hello-key-patterns` declare `panning` instead of
`conceding` over a sentence. Repairing the names alone would have made each
declaration true and still lost ten and twelve marks; the module forbids
losing rather than clipping, so the repair is the recourse. Both now read
`honoured` with nothing beyond reach — the node lab has shipped that answer
since R1714.
TOOL:
* `tools/shrink_population.py` — every example whose source declares a
`ShrinkPolicy`, parsed, compared against the demo's own `SCREENS` list.
`--check` names the unjudged screens and fails; `--selftest` re-reads the
TYPE's constructor list so a new constructor cannot make the tool silently
miss every screen that uses it. Registered in `pre-push`.
THE DEMO, WHICH HAD NEVER RUN OVER FIVE SCREENS:
* `SCREENS` — three to five.
* `CONCEDING` — one name to a set of three. Every branch spelled the question as
`example == CONCEDING`, which is a statement about the screens rather than
about the mechanism.
* `CONCEDED_FLOOR` — one pair, the node lab's, to a floor per conceding screen.
* section D's `>= 8` regions — not every screen's specification names the
regions it paints, and the two added here publish column keys and prose. The
contribution is now RECORDED per screen and the SET that answered is asserted,
because skipping them silently is the exact failure this round is about.
* section E's `scrollable > 20` — the node lab's own number. The clause means
"more than nothing"; the two new screens reach 12 and 10. Now `> 0`, with the
per-screen counts recorded and the measured set asserted.
verification_bullets: THE FLOOR, built from source and run offscreen (scratchpad only, and the
script `cd`s there first because R1797 measured that the reference's configure
writes into the CURRENT directory whatever `-B` says, and put three files at
this repository's root). Eleven checks, all passing, listed in the decision.
★ ONE OF THEM WAS THIS PROBE'S OWN BUG BEFORE IT WAS A MEASUREMENT, twice, and
both corrections are why the answer is trustworthy. A `Fixed` panel appeared to
give way; the first cause was a self-referential size hint (the probe's), and
after fixing that it STILL gave way — which isolated to an explicit minimum
overriding the declared policy while the panel goes on reporting the policy.
A check that fails is not yet a finding; isolating one variable is what tells
the two apart.
THE WIRE, asked what the debt's fourth item said to ask:
hello-log-view      verdict=unreachable  cut=23  covered=0  unreachable=10
hello-key-patterns  verdict=unreachable  cut=37  covered=0  unreachable=12
hello-node-lab      verdict=honoured     cut=0   covered=0  unreachable=0
After the repair every one of the five reads `honoured`.
GATES:
r1712, over five screens for the first time  53 assertions PASS, 67.18s
cargo test (core, rpc, log-view, key-patterns)  exit 0
workspace clippy, CI's own flags                exit 0
shrink_population --check                       5 declare / 5 judged
shrink_population --selftest                    PASS
⚠ THE FIRST r1712 RUN AFTER THE REPAIR EXITED 2, AND IT WAS NOT A DEFECT — the
harness timed an RPC out while this host carried a load average of 42.10 on 32
cores from 23 foreign compiler processes. Recorded with the measurement rather
than re-run and forgotten: the same code passed in 67 seconds once the load
dropped, and the failing screen was the node lab, which this round did not
touch.
POPULATION, computed. `blast_radius.py` answers 252 packages because
`pinion-core` is in the change; narrowed with the reason stated, because this
round's core edit is one new enum arm plus a `const`-time refusal and neither
alters a screen that already compiles. What can move is the five screens that
declare a policy and the wire that reports one: 62 demos, from
`demo_radius.py`.
carry_forward_bullets: 1. THE DEBT'S ORIGINAL SUBJECT IS STILL OPEN, with its reasoning now correct.
A pan keeps every mark reachable; it does not REFLOW the way the reference
DCC does, which is what the reader asked for. The third recourse — a panel
declaring how it gives way, `Keep` / `ShrinkTo` / `FoldToHeader` — is
unbuilt, and the argument for it is no longer "the DCC does it" but the
measured one: the floor answers this with a seven-value named vocabulary and
this tree answers it with none. What the floor lacks, and what would make
ours superior rather than equal, is also measured: a report of what a panel
gave up, a way to ask about a size the window is not at, a header as a named
stop, and any complaint when two declarations about one panel disagree.
2. `NameIsNotATag` catches a name that CANNOT be a tag. It does not catch a name
that is shaped like one and matches nothing — a misspelled region. The audit
already reports that as `stale`, and now that every screen declaring a policy
is in the gate, a stale name fails there; but the two defences are different
strengths and this says so rather than implying the compile-time one is
complete.
3. ⚠ A READER'S SECOND AND THIRD REPORTS FROM THE SAME WINDOW, MEASURED THIS
ROUND AND NOT REPAIRED HERE:
* The capture viewer clips descenders. `scene/text_painted` reports 289 runs
of which 270 overflow their box vertically by two pixels or more and 51 of
those contain a descending glyph; the worst is the application bar's own
title, `packet view`, ink 20 in a box of 16. The wire has been saying so
since R1654 and NOTHING READS `over_h`: `screen_ink::stand_in_ink` answers
a run's ink height with the BOX's own height, so the containment gate
compares a box with itself vertically and is structurally unable to report
this. Its documentation defers the question to the machine that paints,
and no reader was ever built there. That is R1794's finding on the other
axis, and it is the next round.
* The node lab's palette and inspector cannot be moved. Measured: the
`node_lab` surface's drop contract has no clauses at all, so nothing
declares them movable; the reference's own lab has exactly one mousedown
handler, the canvas pan, and no splitter. The dashboard's cards DO tear off
and drag, so the asymmetry is inside this application. Registered against
`debt-the-arrangeable-unit-is-a-panel-and-should-be-an-area`; "the
reference does not do it either" is explicitly not a reason here.
4. External: `vendor/sce`, `vello`/`wgpu` and the Mnemosyne upstream are
unchanged this round and carry nothing new.

R1799.decision_summary:
R1799 — the hook says what each of its steps costs, and one run is not a measurement.

The standing instruction is "move the heavy work to CI". R1779 obeyed it once
and got it wrong, and `debt-the-push-hook-has-never-been-profiled` is the debt
that opened while obeying it: nobody could answer which gate is heavy, two
documented costs were false (`tools/test_hooks.sh` is described in the hook's
own comment as running in milliseconds and measures 65.83s), and the round that
moved clippy and rustdoc out together justified BOTH with a single number that
was never split between them — measured apart at R1782 they are 4.6s and 394.6s,
86x, so the cheap gate had been charged the expensive one's bill.

⇒ THE INSTRUMENT COMES BEFORE THE MOVE. This round builds no policy and moves
no gate. It makes the hook able to answer the question, because until it can,
every "move this to CI" decision is the R1779 decision again.

★★★★★ AND MEASURING FROM OUTSIDE IS IMPOSSIBLE IN PRINCIPLE, WHICH IS WHY THIS
HAD TO BE A CHANGE TO THE HOOK. The debt records three failed attempts and the
third explains the other two: piping the hook through `awk` timestamps every one
of 213 lines identically, and `stdbuf -oL` does not fix it, because the
buffering is not in `awk` — it is in each TOOL the hook runs, which buffers when
its stdout is a pipe rather than a terminal. No external wrapper can attribute
time to a step. The only instrument that works is the hook stamping its own.

★★ THE INSTRUMENT REPLACES THE ANNOUNCEMENTS RATHER THAN SITTING BESIDE THEM.
Every step already printed `pre-push: <name> ...`; `step "<name>"` now prints
that line AND starts its clock. A timer added alongside would have made a second
list of what this hook does, and a second list of one thing is the class this
session has spent three rounds repairing (R1738, R1784, R1795, R1798 — all
hand-written populations).

★★★★★ THE NUMBER THIS EXISTS FOR IS THE ONE NOBODY HAD: UNATTRIBUTED TIME. The
steps anyone had ever timed come to ~128s, in runs that took 251-368s. So more
than a third of this hook's wall clock was spent somewhere no list mentions, and
a per-step total that does not say so would invite the reader to believe the
list is the run. `step_summary` prints total, named, and the remainder.

★★★★★ AND A DEFECT IN THE INSTRUMENT ITSELF, FOUND BY ASKING WHICH RUNS IT
REPORTS ON: it went silent on exactly the runs whose timings matter most. A step
prints its cost when the NEXT step opens, so an `exit 1` — and this hook has 34
of them — dropped the failing step's cost and the summary with it. The reader
who most needs "which gate did I just wait six minutes for" is the reader whose
push was refused. Repaired by making the timer own the EXIT trap from the moment
it is sourced.

★★ THAT REPAIR HAD TO COMPOSE, BECAUSE BASH HAS ONE EXIT SLOT AND A SECOND TRAP
REPLACES THE FIRST — a fact `tools/test_hooks.sh` measured at R1522 and wrote
into its own comments. The hook installs a temp-file cleanup trap 300 lines
after the library is sourced, so a naive `trap step_summary EXIT` in the library
would have been silently replaced, leaving the instrument reporting only on
successful pushes while I believed it covered all of them. The timer therefore
owns the slot and the hook registers its cleanup THROUGH `step_at_exit`.

★★★★★ AND WRITING THAT ONE ASSERTION FOUND THE SAME DEFECT ALREADY LIVING IN
THE FILE THAT TAUGHT ME THE RULE. `tools/test_hooks.sh` opens with a comment
recording, from R1522, that `trap ... EXIT` replaces rather than adds, and that
one root with one trap is therefore the only shape that works. Eleven hundred
lines later it installs a second EXIT trap for `ratchet_tmp`, which replaces the
first — so every run of this suite has orphaned `_tmp_root`. Proved by running
two traps in one shell rather than by reading bash's manual: only the second
directory is gone. ⇒ a rule written down in a file is not a rule the file keeps,
and the assertion is what makes it one.

★ SIDE FINDING, AND IT IS THIS ROUND'S SUBJECT IN MINIATURE: `CLAUDE.md` said
the hook is thirteen steps. Measured at R1799 it has eighteen `step` sites. The
recipe printed beside that number is still correct — it was the NUMBER that
rotted, exactly as this project's own rule says a number in prose does. And
thirteen was never the count of sites even when written: it was what one push
RAN, because the statechart ratchet is path-gated and that push carried no
chart. Verified against the R1779 commit — fourteen sites then, one skipped, and
the four added since are `demo clock units`, `demo radius selftest`, `shrink
population` and clippy, which R1779 removed and R1782 put back. ⇒ a step count
is two different numbers, and the file now says so instead of carrying either.
changes_bullets: `.githooks/lib/step-timer.sh` (new) — `step "<name>"` REPLACES the bare
announcement each step already printed: it prints the same line and starts that
step's clock. `_pinion_close_step` prints the elapsed cost when the next step
opens. `step_summary` prints the run total, the part the named steps accounted
for, and the remainder — `unattributed`, which is the figure the debt exists
for. Millisecond resolution via `date +%s%N`, with a second-resolution fallback
where that is not GNU rather than printing nonsense.
`.githooks/pre-push` — all eighteen announcement sites converted to `step`. The
explicit `step_summary` call at the end was removed: the summary now runs from
an EXIT trap, so the 34 `exit 1` paths report too.
`step_at_exit` — the composition that makes that trap safe. bash has one EXIT
slot and a second `trap ... EXIT` replaces the first, so the timer takes the
slot when it is sourced and the hook's temp-file cleanup registers through it
instead of installing its own trap 300 lines later. Cleanups run first so the
summary is the last thing printed; the trap returns the status it was reached
with, so a refusal stays a refusal.
`step_summary` is idempotent, and silent when nothing was timed — a process that
merely SOURCES the library (the test suite does) must not emit a hook report
that no hook made. The zero check runs AFTER the open step is closed, so a hook
dying inside its very first step still reports that step.
`tools/test_hooks.sh` — twelve assertions in three groups. That the timer
MEASURES: a step that slept 150ms must report >= 100ms, because a timer that
always says zero passes every "is it printed" check anyone would write. That a
REFUSED run reports: the open step's cost, the summary, the registered cleanup,
the ordering between them, and the preserved exit status. And that the
ARRANGEMENT holds: the hook installs no bare EXIT trap, it registers through
`step_at_exit`, and this suite keeps exactly one trap.
`tools/test_hooks.sh` — the leak that last assertion found: `ratchet_tmp` was a
bare `mktemp -d` with its own EXIT trap, which replaced the one at the head of
the file, so every run of the suite orphaned `_tmp_root`. Now `mktemp_tracked`
under the one root, no second trap.
`CLAUDE.md` — the step count is no longer written down. The recipe that was
printed beside it is still correct; it was the number that rotted.
verification_bullets: `tools/test_hooks.sh`: 172 passed, 0 failed. The file at HEAD holds 156
assertions, so this round adds 16. ★That baseline was DERIVED rather than
assumed: HEAD's copy was run out of tree, where `repo_root` resolves from
`BASH_SOURCE` and so pointed at nothing, and it reported 31 passed / 125 failed
— a void run whose VERDICT is worthless and whose TOTAL is not, because the
number of `ok` calls does not depend on where the suite thinks the repo is.
`bash -n` clean on `step-timer.sh`, `pre-push` and `test_hooks.sh`.
No Rust changed this round — the diff is three shell files and `CLAUDE.md` — so
the crate suites and clippy have nothing to say about it, and pre-push runs them
regardless before publishing.
★ Each of the timer's three behaviours was MEASURED before it was asserted,
because the instrument's whole value is that it does not report a constant:
* a step that slept 120ms reported `[   0.139s]`, not `0`;
* `exit 7` through the trap came back as rc=7, so a refusal stays a refusal
(bash's manual was not consulted — the shell was asked);
* a process that sources the library and times nothing printed zero lines.
★ THE `trap` REPLACEMENT WAS PROVED, NOT READ: two EXIT traps installed in one
shell, and only the second one's directory is removed. That is the measurement
behind the composition, and behind finding that `tools/test_hooks.sh` had been
orphaning `_tmp_root` on every run since the trap for `ratchet_tmp` was added.
★ AND ONE ASSERTION WAS WRITTEN BY DELETING DEAD CODE: `timer_out` captured the
timer's stdout and nothing ever looked at it, while its `2>/dev/null` sat on the
assignment and so did not suppress the command substitution's stderr — running
the suite printed five `pre-push:` lines that no hook had printed. Measured at 5
before and 0 after. It is now the assertion it was pretending to be: a hook's
stdout belongs to git, so the instrument writes none of it.
⚠ WHAT IS NOT VERIFIED, AND CANNOT BE FROM HERE: any actual per-step cost of a
real push. This round's own push is the first sample, and one sample is not a
measurement on this hook — see the carry.

The instruction is "move the heavy work to CI" and nothing was moved. One

R1800.decision_summary:
R1800 — a run says whether its own box can hold it, and the answer was 289 of 290.

A reader reported the descender of `p` cut off in the capture viewer. They had
reported the same class eleven days earlier, and in between this tree published
every number needed to answer them and had no predicate that asked.

★★★★★ THE ROUND'S SUBJECT IS WHY THAT WAS POSSIBLE, AND IT IS A SENTENCE, NOT A
MISSING CAPABILITY. `test_fixtures::screen_ink`'s header explained why the
vertical axis is not gated: *"is this line box tall enough for this face" is
answered by the layout pass from the host's real metrics, and re-deciding it
here against a constant would make the gate green or red depending on which
fonts are installed*. That is TRUE of one question and FALSE of the one beside
it. Whether a run's INK is taller than its box is font-dependent. Whether the
BOX was authored tall enough for the face the author chose is not:
`containment::line_box` is a reservation computed from the face size alone.
Under that wording the whole axis read as un-gateable. ⇒ a design note that
answers a near-miss question closes the real one exactly as effectively as a
wrong implementation, and is harder to see, because it reads as a reason.

★★★★★ AND MEASURING CHANGED THE ROUND — THE SIXTH CONSECUTIVE ROUND TO FIND A
DEBT'S PRESCRIPTION WRONG, except this time the debt had written down the
alternative and the measurement chose it. The debt read as "270 boxes are
authoring mistakes"; it also asked, in its own margin, whether being shorter
than `line_box` was a mistake or the tree's CONVENTION, and said that if it were
the convention the thing to fix is not 270 boxes but the one place that decides
a box's height. Pointed at the reported screen, the census answered **289 of 290
runs**. It is the convention. Corroborated: `line_box` has existed since R1656
and exactly ONE production site in this tree sizes anything with it.

⇒ A GATE THAT SCOLDS 289 TIMES IS A GATE SOMEBODY TURNS OFF. So the rule got a
way to be obeyed: `line_rect` / `line_rect_in` live beside the predicate, and a
box built by them cannot fail it — asserted across ten face sizes. Reaching for
a constructor is easier than writing a number, which is the only reliable way a

R1801.decision_summary:
R1801 — a panel says where it may live, and a refusal says why.

A reader asked three times, across eleven rounds, why the node palette and the
node inspector cannot be moved. The debt opened for it at `priority: top` and
did not move for eight of those rounds.

★ RE-MEASURING FOUND THE DEBT RIGHT, WHICH IS ITSELF THE NEWS: five of the last
six rounds falsified their debt's own prescription, so the discipline is now
run expecting to find an error. This time every claim held — the dock layer
really is built and no analyzer screen uses it (`view_dock_surface` has four
consumers, none of them an analyzer screen), the lab really declares no drop
contract, and region fold and edge-flip really are absent (what `dock.rs` calls
"collapse" is a TREE collapse and what `splitter.rs` calls "flip" is an AXIS
flip — two words that read like the missing features and are not them).

★★★★★ AND THE MEASUREMENT MOVED THE ROUND'S TARGET ONE STEP EARLIER. Threading
a placement through the lab's layout is 46 call sites of three functions across
three files in a 24,531-line screen — the campaign the debt warned about, not a
round. But the gap a reader actually hit is in front of that: asked which panels
this surface lets a person move, the wire answered `clauses: []`, and **it was
right**. Nothing had ever said they were movable. There was nothing for a
gesture to be checked against and nothing for a client to read. So this round
closes the DECLARATION, and the layout stays the campaign.

★★★★★ THE FLOOR WAS BUILT FROM SOURCE AND RUN OFFSCREEN, AND IT HAS THE FIRST
HALF. This axis has a first-class answer on the reference toolkit, so the
question was never whether it exists. Where a panel sits IS readable there —
four edges as an enum, a floating flag, a signal when it lands. What is absent,
measured:

  * **Folding does not exist.** Zero of 104 published member names on that class
    and its bases name collapse, fold, expand or toggle. Hiding takes the panel
    OUT of the layout — gone, not folded to a strip a person can grab back.
  * **The arrangement round-trips as OPAQUE BYTES** — 82 of them, keyed by
    object name. Nothing can read which edge a panel is on out of it, diff two
    of them, or write one by hand.
  * 🟥 **A refused move is SILENT.** Restricting a panel to the left edge and
    then asking for the right edge PUT IT ON THE RIGHT: the declaration was
    ignored, with nothing thrown, nothing returned and no signal.

🟥🟥🟥 AND THAT LAST ONE IS A HABIT, MEASURED THREE ROUNDS RUNNING ON THREE
UNRELATED AXES. R1798: an explicit panel minimum silently overrides a declared
shrink policy. R1800: an explicit box height silently overrides the minimum the
face needs. R1801: an explicit move silently overrides the edges a panel
declared it admits. ⇒ **on the floor, a declared constraint loses to an
imperative call, quietly.** That is the single most reusable finding of the
three rounds, and it is where this project's existing vocabulary — `RefusalReason`,
and R1706's rule that a refusal reaches a person — becomes a competitive
position rather than a nicety.

★ THE COMPILER ARGUED THE SAME SIDE. `Signal<T>` requires `Serialize +
DeserializeOwned`, so holding a placement as live state in this framework makes
it a READABLE value by construction. The floor's opaque blob is not a choice we
declined to copy; it is one this framework cannot express.

★ A NAME COLLISION AVOIDED BY LOOKING FIRST: `pinion_core::region` already
exists and means geometric SELECTION — rectangles, spans, lassos. The reference
editor calls a panel-inside-an-area a "region" too, and adopting the word would
have given one crate one name for two unrelated things. The module is
`edge_panel`, named for what it holds.
changes_bullets: `pinion_core::edge_panel` (new) — three types and one rule.
`EdgePlacement { edge, extent, folded }` — where a panel is, as a value:
comparable, copyable, readable field by field, so a screen's arrangement is a
list of these that a reader can diff. `thickness(strip)` answers what it takes,
and a FOLDED panel answers the strip rather than zero, because that is the
difference between folding and hiding and it is the whole point: the strip is
what a person grabs to bring it back.
`EdgePolicy { allowed, foldable }` — what a panel may do, declared once beside
it. `fixed()` declares an empty edge set, which is a statement and not an
omission: it makes "this one does not move" different from "nobody has said".
`EdgeRefusal` — why a change was refused, carrying the edge ASKED FOR and the
edges that WERE allowed, plus a `RefusalReason` (the same type an `External`
refusal carries, lifted rather than reinvented) and a `wire_word` so a client
branches without parsing a sentence.
`EdgePolicy::admit` / `admit_fold` return `Result`. That is the module's claim
to being better than the floor, which accepts the move and ignores the
declaration. `admit_fold` never refuses UNFOLDING, even under a policy that
forbids folding — otherwise tightening a declaration strands a reader with a
strip that cannot open.
Six tests, including the two that pin the difference: a move outside the
declared set is refused AND names what was allowed, and a folded panel keeps
both its strip and the size to come back to.
`examples/hello-node-lab/src/spec.rs` — `PaneSpec.policy`, so all four panes
declare where they may live in the same table every other property of a pane
lives in. The two side panels admit left and right; the rail and the canvas
declare `fixed()`.
`examples/hello-node-lab/src/lib.rs` — `spec_json` publishes `edges` and
`foldable` per pane. This is the gap a reader hit: the wire could not say these
panels were movable because nothing had declared it.
`tools/demos/r1651_…py` — a `(B2)` section asserting it against the RUNNING
application: every pane publishes both keys, every edge word is from the closed
set, and the panes that declare they may move are exactly the two side panels.
The SET, not the count — a panel that stopped being movable and a panel that
started both have to fail, and a count catches neither.

R1801 — a panel says where it may live, and a refusal says why.

A reader asked three times, across eleven rounds, why the node palette and the
node inspector cannot be moved. The debt opened for it at `priority: top` and
did not move for eight of those rounds.

★ RE-MEASURING FOUND THE DEBT RIGHT, WHICH IS ITSELF THE NEWS: five of the last
six rounds falsified their debt's own prescription, so the discipline is now
run expecting to find an error. This time every claim held — the dock layer
really is built and no analyzer screen uses it (`view_dock_surface` has four
consumers, none of them an analyzer screen), the lab really declares no drop
contract, and region fold and edge-flip really are absent (what `dock.rs` calls
"collapse" is a TREE collapse and what `splitter.rs` calls "flip" is an AXIS
flip — two words that read like the missing features and are not them).

★★★★★ AND THE MEASUREMENT MOVED THE ROUND'S TARGET ONE STEP EARLIER. Threading
a placement through the lab's layout is 46 call sites of three functions across
three files in a 24,531-line screen — the campaign the debt warned about, not a
round. But the gap a reader actually hit is in front of that: asked which panels
this surface lets a person move, the wire answered `clauses: []`, and **it was
right**. Nothing had ever said they were movable. There was nothing for a
gesture to be checked against and nothing for a client to read. So this round
closes the DECLARATION, and the layout stays the campaign.

★★★★★ THE FLOOR WAS BUILT FROM SOURCE AND RUN OFFSCREEN, AND IT HAS THE FIRST
HALF. This axis has a first-class answer on the reference toolkit, so the
question was never whether it exists. Where a panel sits IS readable there —
four edges as an enum, a floating flag, a signal when it lands. What is absent,
measured:

  * **Folding does not exist.** Zero of 104 published member names on that class
    and its bases name collapse, fold, expand or toggle. Hiding takes the panel
    OUT of the layout — gone, not folded to a strip a person can grab back.
  * **The arrangement round-trips as OPAQUE BYTES** — 82 of them, keyed by
    object name. Nothing can read which edge a panel is on out of it, diff two
    of them, or write one by hand.
  * 🟥 **A refused move is SILENT.** Restricting a panel to the left edge and
    then asking for the right edge PUT IT ON THE RIGHT: the declaration was
    ignored, with nothing thrown, nothing returned and no signal.

🟥🟥🟥 AND THAT LAST ONE IS A HABIT, MEASURED THREE ROUNDS RUNNING ON THREE
UNRELATED AXES. R1798: an explicit panel minimum silently overrides a declared
shrink policy. R1800: an explicit box height silently overrides the minimum the
face needs. R1801: an explicit move silently overrides the edges a panel
declared it admits. ⇒ **on the floor, a declared constraint loses to an
imperative call, quietly.** That is the single most reusable finding of the
three rounds, and it is where this project's existing vocabulary — `RefusalReason`,
and R1706's rule that a refusal reaches a person — becomes a competitive
position rather than a nicety.

★ THE COMPILER ARGUED THE SAME SIDE. `Signal<T>` requires `Serialize +
DeserializeOwned`, so holding a placement as live state in this framework makes
it a READABLE value by construction. The floor's opaque blob is not a choice we
declined to copy; it is one this framework cannot express.

★ A NAME COLLISION AVOIDED BY LOOKING FIRST: `pinion_core::region` already
exists and means geometric SELECTION — rectangles, spans, lassos. The reference
editor calls a panel-inside-an-area a "region" too, and adopting the word would
have given one crate one name for two unrelated things. The module is
`edge_panel`, named for what it holds.
publishable_changes_bullets: `pinion_core::edge_panel` (new) — three types and one rule.
`EdgePlacement { edge, extent, folded }` — where a panel is, as a value:
comparable, copyable, readable field by field, so a screen's arrangement is a
list of these that a reader can diff. `thickness(strip)` answers what it takes,
and a FOLDED panel answers the strip rather than zero, because that is the
difference between folding and hiding and it is the whole point: the strip is
what a person grabs to bring it back.
`EdgePolicy { allowed, foldable }` — what a panel may do, declared once beside
it. `fixed()` declares an empty edge set, which is a statement and not an
omission: it makes "this one does not move" different from "nobody has said".
`EdgeRefusal` — why a change was refused, carrying the edge ASKED FOR and the
edges that WERE allowed, plus a `RefusalReason` (the same type an `External`
refusal carries, lifted rather than reinvented) and a `wire_word` so a client
branches without parsing a sentence.
`EdgePolicy::admit` / `admit_fold` return `Result`. That is the module's claim
to being better than the floor, which accepts the move and ignores the
declaration. `admit_fold` never refuses UNFOLDING, even under a policy that
forbids folding — otherwise tightening a declaration strands a reader with a
strip that cannot open.
Six tests, including the two that pin the difference: a move outside the
declared set is refused AND names what was allowed, and a folded panel keeps
both its strip and the size to come back to.

declare where they may live in the same table every other property of a pane
lives in. The two side panels admit left and right; the rail and the canvas
declare `fixed()`.
`examples/hello-node-lab/src/lib.rs` — `spec_json` publishes `edges` and
`foldable` per pane. This is the gap a reader hit: the wire could not say these
panels were movable because nothing had declared it.
`tools/demos/r1651_…py` — a `(B2)` section asserting it against the RUNNING
application: every pane publishes both keys, every edge word is from the closed
set, and the panes that declare they may move are exactly the two side panels.
The SET, not the count — a panel that stopped being movable and a panel that
started both have to fail, and a count catches neither.

R1802.decision_summary:
R1802 — the declaration and the layout now check each other.

R1801 gave this screen's specification a placement policy — the palette may live
on the left or the right — and left the layout drawing it from a `const` on the
left, always. Its own closing audit recorded that as a defect it had created: a
published rule the code does not keep, and nothing comparing the two. This is
that defect paid off, in the round immediately after it was made.

★★★★★ AND THE FIRST MEASUREMENT FALSIFIED THE CARRY I HAD WRITTEN ONE ROUND
EARLIER. R1801 recorded the adoption as "46 call sites of three functions across
three files", counted by grep. It is **zero**: `use_lab_state` has been a
thread-local since long before this axis, so `palette_rect` can read the state
itself and no caller changes. I counted a function's callers without asking
whether the function could reach the state — which is the class this project
keeps recording, committed by me, one round ago, in the file that warns about it.

★★★★★ THE GATE CAUGHT TWO OF MY OWN MISTAKES BEFORE IT CAUGHT ANYTHING ELSE,
AND THEY WERE DIFFERENT KINDS.

FIRST, the test's own wiring. The loop reset the thread-local between panes
while holding a handle taken before the reset, so the writes went to an orphaned
state and the layout answered its defaults. It failed — but it failed **blaming
the layout** ("the layout put it at 1128", which is exactly `1440 - 312`, the
default right-edge placement), and without the probe asserting that the write
was VISIBLE I would have gone and "fixed" correct layout code. ⇒ a test must
first assert that the thing it wrote is the thing the subject reads; without
that, a failure points at the wrong file.

SECOND, the assertion itself. It demanded `x == RAIL_W` for the left edge and
failed at 284 — which was the layout being RIGHT: with both panels declared
left, the inspector stacks after the palette. ⇒ **"it is on that edge" is band
containment, not a fixed coordinate.** An assertion that only holds when nothing
shares the edge is an assertion about one arrangement, not about the rule, and
the two read identically until a second panel arrives.

★ WHAT THE GATE NOW CLAIMS is deliberately not "the panel moves" — that a value
changes is trivial. It is that **every edge the specification admits is an edge
the layout actually honours**, checked by placing the panel at each declared
edge and requiring its rectangle to lie inside that edge's band; plus the
converse, that a pane the layout cannot place declares no edges. A floor on the
sweep pins four placements, because a policy emptied by accident would make
every assertion above it vacuous and the test would still pass — R1798's lesson,
applied to the test written to close R1801's.

★ AND THE FOLD IS GATED AS THE THING THAT DISTINGUISHES IT FROM HIDING: a folded
panel leaves its strip, on the same edge, and the canvas grows by exactly what
the fold gave up and no more — so the handle that opens it again is not
swallowed. The floor toolkit has no fold at all; hiding removes the panel from
the layout and leaves nothing to grab.
changes_bullets: `pinion_core::style::ChromeEdge` and `edge_panel::EdgePlacement` gain serde
derives. Not incidental: `Signal<T>` requires its contents to be serializable, so
holding a placement as live state in this framework MAKES it a readable value —
which is exactly where the floor toolkit stores an opaque blob.
`examples/hello-node-lab/src/lib.rs`:
* `LabState.palette_at` / `.inspector_at` — two `Signal<EdgePlacement>`,
seeded to `PALETTE_OPENS_AT` / `INSPECTOR_OPENS_AT`, which are the exact
arrangement the hand-written layout drew. Adopting the value moved no pixel.
* `placements()` — reads the thread-local directly and WITHOUT `use_lab_state`,
deliberately: that function constructs the state if absent and registers an
animation with the current owner, and a geometry helper must do neither.
Before the state exists it answers where the panels open.
* `side_bands()` / `side_panel_rect()` — the left and right bands, and where a
panel lands given what is stacked before it on its edge. A folded panel
contributes `PANEL_STRIP_W`, not zero.
* `canvas_rect` / `palette_rect` / `inspector_rect` derive from those. No
caller changed.
`examples/hello-node-lab/src/tests.rs` — two gates.
`r1802_every_edge_the_specification_admits_is_one_the_layout_honours` places
each movable pane at each edge its policy admits and requires the rectangle to
lie inside that edge's band; requires a pane the layout cannot place to declare
no edges; asserts the write is visible to the layout before reading a rectangle
from it; and pins the sweep at four placements so an emptied policy cannot make
it vacuous.
`r1802_a_folded_panel_leaves_a_strip_the_canvas_does_not_take` — the fold
leaves the strip on the same edge, and the canvas grows by exactly
`PALETTE_W - PANEL_STRIP_W` and starts after the strip.

of a demo this project requires to be deterministic is a flake, and a flake is a

is specific: a pin-to-pin drag that authors a link found 7 where 8 were

compile the test that repairs it" — but `PINION_REGEN_STATECHARTS` only skips

covers "the chart moved" and not "the generator's contract moved".

will not build, and with the runtime left behind the new emit implements a
method the old trait does not declare. ⇒ the two-dependency split is what makes

what was written, and repaired from `git rev-parse HEAD`. Recorded because the
value looked entirely plausible and nothing downstream would have said otherwise

R1804.decision_summary:
R1804 — the commit hook gets a clock, and the census stops being one number.

A reader asked why a push takes so long and whether it could move to CI. R1799
built the instrument that makes that answerable; this round is what the
instrument's own output demanded once there were five samples of it.

★★★★★ THE FIRST FINDING WAS THAT MY OWN EXPLANATION WAS WRONG. Asked why the
R1803 push was slower than the four before it, I said the statechart-emit
ratchet — which that push triggers and the others skip — and I was confident
because the standalone regeneration had measured 160s. Measured inside the push:
the ratchet is **82s and fourth**. What actually moved was clippy 226 -> 381 and
the census 154 -> 248, because a pin bump rewrites all fifteen emitted modules
and every step that compiles then compiles COLD. ⇒ a pin round is not expensive
because it runs an extra gate; it is expensive because **three steps compile the
workspace independently** (rustc, clippy-driver, the ratchet's generator) and
none of them can read another's artifacts. The extra gate is the cheapest of the
three.

★★★★★ AND THE STEP EVERYONE WOULD HAVE ACTED ON WAS THREE COMMANDS UNDER ONE
NAME. `analysis-tool census` covered `--selftest`, `--check-pin` and
`--check-proofs`, and across five pushes it measured 8s, 154s, 174s, 154s and
248s with nothing to say WHICH of the three the time was in. That is exactly the
shape R1779 acted on when it moved clippy and rustdoc out together on a single
number never split between them — measured apart at R1782 they were 86x
different and the move was wrong for one of them. So the step is now three
steps, asserted structurally so they cannot silently become one again, and no
decision is taken on the strength of the old number.

★ THE HOOK'S OWN COST COMMENT WAS FALSE IN THE SAME WAY R1799 FOUND ONE. It read
"3.5s on a warm tree, and the first time after a clean build it pays for the
cited crates' test binaries once". The number was real; the word WARM was doing
all the work. `--check-proofs` runs `cargo test -- --list`, so it compiles
whenever the round touched Rust, which most rounds do — 8s on the single round
that touched none, 154–248s on the four that did. "Pays once after a clean
build" describes a tree nobody works in.

★★ AND `pre-commit` HAD NO CLOCK AT ALL, which is why the other half of the
reader's question could not be answered. Four announcements, none of them timed.
It now uses the same library, with the hook's name made a parameter — two hooks
printing under one prefix would put both hooks' steps into one list, which is
the defect this timer was built to avoid in the first place. The default stays
`pre-push`, so the hook that had it first says exactly what it said before.

★★★ WHAT THIS ROUND DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO IS MOVE ANYTHING OUT. The
`--check-proofs` gate is ADDED to CI — immediately after `cargo test
--workspace`, where the binaries it lists have just been built and it costs a
listing — and left in `pre-push` as well. It exists nowhere else, so removing it
locally first would leave the claim unguarded for as long as it took to notice.
The local step goes when this has been green, and on the split numbers rather
than on the merged one.
changes_bullets: `.githooks/pre-push` — the `analysis-tool census` step becomes three:
`analysis-tool census selftest`, `… pin`, `… proofs`, one per command, so the
next push says which of them the time is in.
`.githooks/pre-push` — the cost comment on `--check-proofs` corrected from
"3.5s on a warm tree" to the five measured samples, with the reason the old
figure misled (it runs `cargo test -- --list`, so "warm" means "the round
touched no Rust").
`.githooks/lib/step-timer.sh` — the hook's name becomes `PINION_STEP_LABEL`,
defaulting to `pre-push` so the first user's output is unchanged. Every line the
timer prints carries it.
`.githooks/pre-commit` — sources the timer (setting its label first) and its
four announcements become `step` calls: `validate-workspace`, `cargo fmt --all
--check`, `validate-code-refs`, `reference names`. It installs no EXIT trap of
its own, so the timer keeps the slot it needs to report on a refused commit.
`.github/workflows/ci.yml` — a new `analysis-tool census proofs` step in
`lint-and-test`, placed immediately after `cargo test --workspace` because that
is the only position where the binaries it lists already exist. ADDED WITHOUT
REMOVING the local one, in that order and on purpose.
`tools/test_hooks.sh` — seven assertions: the commit hook installs no EXIT trap;
it no longer announces without timing; it sets its label BEFORE sourcing (an
ordering, checked with awk, because after would silently do nothing); a labelled
run says that label and never the other hook's; an unlabelled run still says
`pre-push`; and the census is timed as three steps rather than one.
verification_bullets: `tools/test_hooks.sh`: 179 passed, 0 failed (172 before this round's seven).
`bash -n` clean on `pre-commit`, `pre-push` and `step-timer.sh`. The workflow
parses as YAML and the new step is the last of `lint-and-test`'s ten, directly
after `workspace tests`.
★ The five samples this round acts on, from the instrument itself rather than
from a stopwatch outside it:
push    total    clippy   census   ratchet
R1799    614s     198s       8s    (skipped)
R1800    888s     355s     154s    (skipped)
R1801    840s     281s     174s    (skipped)
R1802    738s     226s     154s    (skipped)
The census column splits 8s / 154–248s exactly on whether the round touched
Rust, which is what identifies `cargo test -- --list` as the cost rather than
the census logic.
★ R1803 is also where my own explanation was falsified: I attributed that
push's length to the ratchet before reading the numbers, and the ratchet is 82s
and fourth. Recorded in the decision summary rather than quietly dropped,
because the wrong attribution was stated to the reader before it was measured.
⚠ NOT VERIFIED, and it is the point of the round's ordering: that the new CI
step passes. It has never run. That is why nothing was removed from `pre-push`
— the local gate stays until this one has been green, and this round makes no
claim about what removing it would save.
⚠ ALSO NOT VERIFIED: what `pre-commit` costs. The clock is installed and this
round's own commit is the first thing it measures, so the number arrives with
the commit that carries the instrument — the same shape as R1799's push.
carry_forward_bullets: 1. THE DECISION IS DELIBERATELY NOT TAKEN YET. `--check-proofs` now runs in
both places. Removing the local one needs two things this round cannot have:
the CI step green at least once, and the split census numbers from a push
that carries the split. Both arrive with this round's own push.
2. ⚠ AND WHEN THEY ARRIVE, THE SAVING IS NOT THE CENSUS COLUMN. That column is
whichever of the three commands is expensive — probably `--check-proofs`, but
that is a prediction, and the whole reason the step was split is that
predictions about it have been wrong. Worse, `--check-proofs` runs BEFORE
clippy, so it may be paying the cold compile that clippy then rides. The one
piece of evidence either way is R1799, where the census compiled nothing and
clippy was CHEAPER (198s) rather than dearer — which points at them not
warming each other, on n=1.
3. ★ THE STRUCTURAL FINDING IS BIGGER THAN THE STEP: three separate compiles of
one workspace, by rustc, by clippy-driver, and by the ratchet's generator,
none able to read another's artifacts. Moving one gate out leaves the other
two. Nothing in this round addresses that, and it is the thing that actually
makes a pin round cost a quarter of an hour.
4. `pre-commit` is instrumented and NOT yet split the way `pre-push` was: its
`validate-workspace` and `validate-code-refs` are each a single command, but
`reference names` runs a selftest and a check under one `step`, which is the
same defect one hook over. Left because this round had no measurement saying
it matters; noted so the next reader does not have to rediscover it.
5. The `statechart emit` ratchet is a path gate, so it contributes 0s to most
pushes and 82s to a pin round. That is a THIRD population on top of
Rust-touched / not, and any future averaging has to keep the three apart or
it will report a tree nobody pushes from.

for it to be fixed rather than explained. R1804's split made the question
answerable; this round is the answer, and it is not the one anybody would have
guessed from the totals.

push: of 758s, `hook library tests` 158s, `reference names` 106s and `reference
census` 101s came to 365s — 48% — with no compiler involved anywhere in them.

costing a minute and a half.

★★★★★ THE REPAIR, AND THREE PREDICTIONS THE ISOLATION KILLED FIRST.

`reference_names --check` measured 119.7s; its `--selftest` 0.3s. Inside it:
2,385 tracked files, 1,089,516 lines, twelve regexes run PER LINE — 13,074,192
regex passes to answer a question about 2,385 files.

  1. "The per-line loop is the cost." Changed to once per file — proved
     equivalent over all 2,385 files, zero disagreements, and the patterns
     checked for line anchors, MULTILINE and DOTALL rather than assumed.
     120s -> 90s. **Not the cost.**
  2. Isolated again: reading all 2,375 readable files is **0.93s**; the twelve
     regexes are **93s**, `PRODUCT_RE` alone 18.8s. So it is the patterns, over
     47.5 MB each — 570 MB of matching. ⇒ "One combined alternation will be
     twelve times cheaper." Prototyped: **185.6s, twice as slow.** A large
     alternation retries every branch at every position. **Wrong again.**
  3. What the numbers actually said: ELEVEN OF THE TWELVE PATTERNS FIND NOTHING.
     Two hits in the whole tree. So almost every pattern is being run over
     almost every file to confirm an absence a substring test settles instantly.
     A cheap literal prefilter, DERIVED from each pattern's own source rather
     than written beside it: **120s -> 15.3s**, same verdict, same two hits.

★ AND THE ASSERTION THAT GUARDS IT WAS WRONG ON ITS FIRST DRAFT, WHICH IS THE
ONE RISK THIS REPAIR CARRIES: a needle that is not actually required would make
the gate skip a file that does match, and a confidentiality ratchet that skips
files reports a clean tree. The first draft asserted the needle IS a match —
`Q` is a needle of `\bQ[A-Z]…` and is not a match, so it failed three patterns.
The property to check is NECESSITY: every string the pattern matches contains
one of its needles. Corrected, 22 cases pass, and the fast and slow paths are
asserted equal on every one.

★★ ONE REPAIR TOOK TWO STEPS DOWN, because `tools/test_hooks.sh` calls the tool
it fixed: **158s -> 32.3s**, 179 assertions unchanged. Push: 264s -> ~47s across
the two. Commit: 80s -> ~15s. And unlike a move to CI, this time is GONE rather
than relocated — CI pays it too, and did.

⚠ THE THIRD STEP IS A DIFFERENT ANIMAL AND IS LEFT ALONE. `reference_census`
inverts the pattern: `--check` is 0.345s and `--selftest` is 84s, and the 84s is
`rglob` over the reference source trees, which live outside this repo and are
absent on CI — where the tool fails open by design. So it is a cost that exists
only on a machine that has them, and reducing it means deciding whether a gate
should re-walk an unchanged external tree every push. That is a judgement about
what the gate MEANS, not an inefficiency, and this round does not make it.
changes_bullets: `tools/reference_names.py`:
* `census()` scans once per FILE rather than once per line. The per-line loop
bought nothing — no pattern is anchored to a line boundary, none carries
MULTILINE or DOTALL, and `check()` reports per-file counts with no line
numbers — and it cost 13,074,192 regex passes over 1,089,516 lines.
* `required_literals(pattern)` — the literals a match must contain, DERIVED
from the pattern's own source: a leading `[A-Z]*`/`[A-Z]?` is stripped
because it contributes nothing, an all-literal `(?:a|b|c)` alternation
yields its branches, otherwise the literal run at the head. Returns `None`
when nothing can be derived, and the caller then scans — the safe
direction, since a missing prefilter costs time and a wrong one costs a
finding. Derived rather than tabulated because a list of needles beside a
list of patterns is two accounts of one fact.
* `file_mentions(text)` — `mentions` over a whole file, skipping any pattern
whose needles are absent. Same list, less work.
* `selftest()` — every case now runs through BOTH paths and must agree, and

carry_forward_bullets: 1. ⚠ THE SAVING IS ARITHMETIC UNTIL A PUSH CONFIRMS IT. 217s off a push and 65s
off a commit are the step timings added up; this hook's totals have moved by

design. So the question is not "make it faster" but "should a gate re-walk an
unchanged external tree on every push" — a judgement about what the gate
guarantees. A cache keyed on those trees' state is the obvious shape and it
needs someone to decide what invalidates it.

4. ★ The structural finding from R1804 is untouched and is now the largest thing
left: three independent compiles of one workspace (rustc, clippy-driver, the
ratchet's generator), none able to read another's artifacts. After this round
clippy is the single biggest step by a wide margin.

pattern shaped differently — a leading group, a non-literal alternation —

R1806.decision_summary:
R1806 repays analyzer census `dashboard.t2.4` -- *click to cross-filter every linked view* -- the last of the framework's three owed rows buildable today. The opening re-measurement falsified the debt file's number AND its diagnosis, and the number failed in the exact way that file warned about.

THE NUMBER. The debt recorded 4 of 14 chart kinds as participating in a cross-filter (bar, line, histogram, scatter) and instructed the next round to read lines rather than count with `grep -c`. Counting METHOD DEFINITIONS rather than references, it is THREE: `histogram` has no selection method of its own, and its nine `select_x_range` mentions are every one a reference to `BarChart`'s, because a histogram is a data producer (`Binned` -> `bars()` -> `BarChart`) already filtered through the bar chart it feeds. The "an unbounded substring credits somebody else's work" class reproduced one level up, inside the file that wrote the warning.

THE DIAGNOSIS, WHICH MATTERED MORE. The debt's own second item was right and unmeasured: the census row says *every linked view*, and the word with no referent anywhere in this tree was EVERY. Measured across `crates/` and `examples/`, every cross-filter call site is a hand-written `.select_x_range(Some(window))` -- four demos holding two, two, one and one -- and nothing declared a SET. The analysis tool's own dashboard held none of them: its saved-filter chip has had state since R1721 and exactly one reader, its own chip row, so clicking it lit a chip and changed nothing else on the board. Per-kind coverage is a charting-depth question; this row is about LINKAGE, and linkage did not exist.

WHY THAT DESERVES A CRATE RATHER THAN A CALL. The per-view arrangement has one failure mode and it is silent: add a sixth view to a board, forget the call, and it renders unfiltered while the five beside it narrow -- no type violated, no assertion failed, no gate fired, and an unfiltered view looks exactly like one with nothing to hide. That is the class measured on three unrelated axes in the three preceding rounds (R1798 a shrink policy, R1800 a box height, R1801 a declared edge): a declared constraint silently loses to an imperative call. This is the fourth, and the first repaid by making the declaration the thing that dispatches.

THE DEBT'S ONE SURVIVING PRESCRIPTION was its first question -- must a brush carry a domain kind? -- and the answer is yes, carried in the SELECTION rather than the brush. A ring chart selects a category, a polar geometry an angle and a radius, a timeline a lane and a window; letting a selection be a bare `(f64, f64)` would force the second geometry added to re-decide what the pair meant, differently.
changes_bullets: `crates/pinion-chart/src/link.rs` (new) -- the cross-filter linkage substrate, exported from the crate root:
* `Domain` {XRange, Category, Sector, LaneWindow} -- the vocabulary a view must speak to be reached, carried in the selection value so a mismatch is mechanical rather than a coincidence of arity.
* `Selection` -- what is selected, in the domain it is selected in. Its accessors answer only in their own domain, so a view that narrows numerically cannot silently misread a category.

* `Link` / `LinkGroup` -- the declared set as a VALUE. `LinkGroup::new` refuses a duplicate name (`LinkFault::DuplicateName`) and refuses a view that accepts nothing without giving a reason (`LinkFault::MuteWithoutReason`); `Link::inert` is how a board says "this view will never narrow, and here is why".

* `Reach` -- what publishing reached. It ACCOUNTS FOR EVERY DECLARED VIEW: each is in `reached` or in `refused`, built in one pass over the same declaration so a view cannot fall out. That identity is what turns *every* into a set a test can assert. `selection_for` hands a view its selection or nothing, so "was I part of this?" and "what do I narrow to?" are one question.

* `Refusal` -- `Domain` names BOTH sides (what the view selects by, what was published); `Inert` carries the author's own reason. "Cannot answer THIS question" and "is not part of this population" were the same silence before.

* `LinkGroup::audit` -- the declaration against the views actually PAINTED, both directions. The half a per-view call cannot have: a view added to a board and forgotten is named instead of rendering unfiltered forever.
THE CONSUMER IS THE ANALYSIS TOOL'S OWN DASHBOARD (screen C), not a new demo:
* `spec::dashboard_links()` declares the five placed cards. `packet` accepts category and x-range, `filter` category, `latency` x-range; `decode` and `keymap` are inert with distinct stated reasons.

* `spec::ChipRule` / `FILTER_CHIP_RULES` -- one rule per saved-filter chip, in chip order, with the bijection asserted. A chip name a machine cannot evaluate is a caption, so the cross-filter had nowhere to start.

* `cross_filter()` publishes the lit chip as a category selection; `stream_body` asks the reach BY NAME and fades the rows the chip's rule does not select -- on a different card from the one the chip lives on, which is the whole of the census sentence. A rule matching nothing in this capture is kept deliberately: an empty result is a real outcome of a filter.
* `Palette::faded` -- a role, not a hand-picked grey, for the reason `warn` and `refused` are roles.

`docs/analyzer-census.json` -- `dashboard.t2.4` moves gap -> have with five `proven_by` citations, and the old `covered_by` prose (which recorded the polar leg as the gap) is replaced by what was actually measured.
verification_bullets: ASSERTED AS SETS, NOT COUNTS -- a count of two is equally true of the right two views and the wrong two.
